Mercer, North Dakota
1905-2005

Dedication

With gratitude for their perseverance, we dedicate this book of Mercer Memories
to the early settlers of our community. We are thankful for their unwavering
efforts to establish our community in spite of all the trials and tribulations
of those early years on the prairie. May we, who are still here, continue to
follow their dedication.

Acknowledgements

We request that you forgive us if we have erred. We worked with the materials
that you provided for the family histories. We made every effort to be accurate
with the material that came from your memories and family records and such are
seldom infallible. If your family was omitted, it was unintentional.

We are indebted to all of you who shared your scrapbooks, clippings collections,
photo albums, school yearbooks and oral history. We also want to thank the
McLean County Recorder and the Sheridan County Recorder for their patience in
helping us interpret legal records. Special thanks go to Ethel Mart of BHG, Inc.
for her guidance, patience and indulgence in the production of this book. We
studied information at the North Dakota Historical Society Archives in Bismarck,
the Minnesota Historical Society in St. Paul and McLean County Historical
Society in Washburn. In addition, we researched atlas, school, census, church
and cemetery records. We hope we have not omitted any era or phase of
development of our community.

The early history of our community would not have been possible without the
issues of the Mercer Telegram which were published from 1907-1919 and which are
on microfilm at the North Dakota State Historical Society Archives in Bismarck.
We are grateful for their efforts to preserve our early history.

A special thank you for the memorials given by Lloyd Westerlind in memory of his
parents Robert and Caroline Westerlind; Aletha Gessele Vossler in memory of
Arley Vossler; James Gessele and Joyce Gessele Gulseth in memory of their
parents Ted and Alvira Gessele; and Mary Ann Westerlind in memory of Arnold
Westerlind, and in memory of Herbert and Martha Thompson by family and friends.

We hope this book of Memories will help you remember Mercer as it was in the
past, is in the present and will be in the future.

The history book is much larger than our wildest dreams! Thank you to all of you
who have encouraged us, supported us and maybe prayed for us. We spent some time
talking with God ourselves!

Mercer, North Dakota: Before There Was Even A Town By James Gessele

Mercer, N.D., Sept. 15, 1909

We have two general stores right now,
                Who's prices are in reach;
        To the Hardware store we proudly bow
                Because it is a peach.
        A Meat Market, a Hotel fare,
                With everything to eat,
        A rest in our new barber chair
                Just simply is a treat.
        Three lumber yards, with prices right
                Two livery barns as well,
        A Printing office right in sight
                Where all the truth we tell.
        The Implements that are handled here
                Are certainly all right;
        The Feed Mill run by Johnie dear
                Is simply out of sight.
        The First State Bank so nobely stands
                Beside our great Pool Hall,
        But Hedahl's Furniture so grand
                Just simply beats them all.
        Of Real Estate men we have but two
                And that is quite enough,
        The rest we had did not much do
                But left with people's stuff.
        Of Elevators three we score,
                Blacksmith shops just two;
        If we should tell of any more,
                It hardly would be true,
        But in another year from now
                It would be no surprise
        To see our little bumper town
                Just twice its present size.

The above display of boosterism first appeared in the September 24, 1909, issue
of The Mercer Telegram. Apparently penned by owner/editor Nils Olesen, it
followed on the heels of repeated sloganeering in previous issues under the
banner "All Roads Lead to Mercer." Beyond promoting local businesses, the
Telegram displayed a keen sense of local history with its several published
sketches of community pioneers. Perhaps beneath the commercial rhyme there lay a
loftier intent. It may have been recognition by proud merchants in joining the
ranks of a community long before 1909, indeed prehistoric, situated on the
crossroads of people and events that would so profoundly shape the Dakota
experience.

Those people and events left their imprint by virtue of roads and, their
forerunners, trails. They were the paths of the aboriginal inhabitants in search
of food and shelter. They were the settlers' and entrepreneurs' rutted
defacement of the prairie. They became military hallmarks for the punitive and
intimidating measures assuring the white man's presence. They marked a
livelihood for ranchers in search of grazing in the hinterlands of McLean
County's eastern coteau.(1) Later they evolved into the railroad's ribbon scar
on the prairie landscape. They were straightened in well-ordered fashion
according to the white man's dictates into township and county roads, and
eventually, highways.

We review the pre-1905 people and events associated with these trails and roads
to lend context to the town's origins.

Early Inhabitants: Native Americans

Plains Indian village way of life first appeared about 1,000 A.D. and centered
around settlements on the Missouri River and its tributaries. From these evolved
by modern times at least seven Tribal Peoples who lived in North Dakota at
various times.(2) Of interest to us are the earthen lodge dwellers along the
Missouri River (Arikara, Hidatsa and Mandan tribes), the Yankton-Yanktonai or
"Middle Sioux," and the Turtle Mountain Chippewas.

The Mandans are reputed to have lived longest in the state, and the Hidatsas, a
smaller tribe, were allied with them. Later in the 1800s they were joined by the
Arikaras who originated in Nebraska. These peaceful farmer/gardeners along the
Missouri riverbanks lived in relative prosperity in earth lodges amid their
cornfields. They were great warriors and hunters and moved out onto the
adjoining plains in summer to live in temporary tepees while locating and
killing buffalo.(3)

The Upper Yanktons lived in combination riverine/grass plains setting found
between the Missouri River and the James and Sheyenne Rivers in central-eastern
North Dakota. Once inhabitants of Minnesota forests, they were driven out onto
the plains by the Chippewa nation. Here they gained renown as traders, and they
became very powerful.(4)

The Turtle Mountain Chippewas (or Metis as they were known in Canada and
descendants of Plains Chippewa and French fur traders) were buffalo hunters from
the north who roamed the plains as far south as the Yankton Sioux territory.(5)

One only needs to wander through a pasture, stroll Brush Lake's shores, or climb
the slopes of Prophet's Mountain four miles northeast of Mercer to note the
sheer number of Plains Indian artifacts and imprints left behind. Arrow- and
spearheads, weapons, tools and implements abound. Occasionally rocks inscribed
with animal or human pictographs are unearthed. Patterns of stone stud the
hilltops, meaningless to the white man but nevertheless significant. On the
north slope of Prophet's Mountain, nowhere near any cultivated farmland, one
finds a row of small stone piles spaced at regular intervals and running for a
quarter mile.(6) Circles of stone, stones set in parallel, and stone effigies of
animals are still being discovered.

        Photo: Turtle effigy located on Mercer Township ranch.

Medicine Hill Township pioneer Jonas Christensen was among the first to heed a
culture that had preceded him in his neighborhood. He and state historian Dana
Wright roamed the lesser hills and ravines of Dogden Butte(7) and Prophet's
Mountain in the 1950s, noting Indian relics and stone formations and mapping
early trails. They paid particular attention to Medicine Hill, a conspicuous
butte near the center of Section 23, Twp. 148-79, overlooking Postel and Cherry
lakes. Even today a large stone without markings caps the hipptop and stone
rings are found on its southwest side. According to lore it was a burial ground
for medicine men, Indian shamans having supernatural powers to cure diseases and
control spirts.

        Photo: Sweat lodge site on Mercer Township ranch. (Photos by James
        Gessele)

        Photo: Series of hilltop stone rings on Mercer Township ranch.

Undoubtedly, Prophet's Mountain played a major role in regional Indian life and
lore and even had an impact on how white settlers moved through the area. An
aggregate of steep hills and deep ravines and coulees ascending roughly 300 feet
above the surrounding plains to a summit more than 2,100 feet above sea level,
the 'mountain' is a prominent local feature of the grander Coteau du Missouri
(French term meaning "hilly region overlooking the Missouri"). Located within
sight of the town Mercer, it makes up almost one-fourth the landmass of Prophets
Township (Twp. 147-78) in neighboring Sheridan County.

The Wisconsin glacier, the last of perhaps four ice masses during the Ice Age of
a million years ago, moved southward from Hudson Bay. It pushed massive amounts
of boulders, gravel, sand and clay onto the Missouri Plateau. Here it stopped,
and then pleasant weather set in. As the ice melted, it dropped its colossal
burden of earth and rock debris and left a band of rough, hilly country ten to
twenty miles in width paralleling the Missouri on its eastern-northeastern
flanks. Prophet's Mountain, a part of the Dogden Range,(8) is the moraine
deposit of that glacier melt and retreat.(9) The melting ice created huge
streams that flowed south and southwestward to the Missouri River. Even Glacial
Lake Souris, occupying what is today's Souris River Valley and cut off by the
huge ice mass to its north, sought an outlet to the Missouri River through a
channel west of Dog Den Butte. These streams were of short duration in Ice Age
terms and had no time to gouge out deep river beds. Once the glacier had
retreated and the watercourses had subsided, what remained were the
Strawberry/Long/Crooked Lakes chain at the base of Dogden Butte, the Brush Lake
chain below Prophet's Mountain, and placid Turtle Creek, eons ago the torrent
draining both lake complexes to the Missouri.(10)

The Prophet's butte became not only an Indian refuge and hunting ground; it also
became sacred ground. As late as 1913, Indians were returning to the area to
erect monuments and commemorate their dead.(11) Joseph Taylor, a very early
McLean County pioneer, became noted for fraternizing with the indigenous
population. In one interview he captured a Native American tale of how the butte
got its name. The 1877 account, found by Mary Ann Barnes (another noted county
historian) among the "kept papers by a Washburn Leader scribe, Joseph Taylor,"
follows:

How Prophet's Mountain Got its Name(12)

  " 'Preparation Point,' Nov. 3, [18]77, Johnny Smith, Black Horn, White Face
  and two other Gros Ventres(13) camped here last night. At my request, Black
  Horn told the story of the great flood that come down from the North, about
  400 years ago. Black Horn's story was realistic, though Johnny's
  interpretation may have given it much of its coloring. I will make further
  inquiry among the Gros Ventres writing it out.

  "The Gros Ventres are better at describing incidents than computing the
  chronology of time which separate occurrences, but fully 400 years have passed
  since the winter of the big snow came, that melted in the late spring and the
  winter lay upon these plains so deep that the Mouse River ox-bow became a
  great sea that found outlet on the breaks of the Missouri, thence on down to
  the Gulf. Some supposed that convulsions in the Arctic seas may have forced a
  tidal wave down toward Hudson Bay, thence across dividing lands submerging
  everything in its way.

  "At the time of the big deep snow that fed the Arctic sea surge, the Gros
  Ventres lived in five villages, the principle one of which was at the junction
  of the Wintering and Mouse rivers. In this camp was an old medicine man, who
  had prophetic gifts. He dreamed that a great flood of waters would come down
  from the north, and that the only land left dry would be the Dog Den range.
  For the most part, the old fellow's dream of warning was laughed at; but a few
  of the faithful followed him over to the Dog Dens and the butte further south,
  now known as Prophet's Mountain. Those who remained in the Mouse river valley
  were caught up by the flood and drowned. A village on the Heart [R]iver was in
  part saved by the activity of the terrified villagers, by reaching the high
  bluffs south of the Little Heart River. Since that date the Gros Ventres are
  more chary of prophetic warning.

  "So, ever after this butte was known as Prophet's Mountain because the old
  medicine man's prophecy proved true, that it and the Dog Den buttes would not
  be flooded but all other land would be."

Sheridan County historian Walter Essig writes that before the white man, the
region's coteau was a "happy hunting ground" in the truest sense. Vast herds of
bison, deer and antelope ranged the prairie; waterways teemed with countless
waterfowl. But central to the various tribal needs were the bison. The animals
provided food, clothing, shelter and implements. June and November were the
prime dates for the buffalo hunt, and life centered on these events.(14) This
was an ancient ritual predating the plains introduction of the horse by the
Spaniard Coronado in 1541. Before the horse, Indians either drove thundering
herds over cliffs or corralled them.

How did the tribal groups interact given their common interest in the buffalo
hunt and the vast herds found on overlapping hunting grounds? Essig writes: "The
limits of the region hunted were fixed by fear of the hostile Sioux. The
Chippewa (Metis) did not fear the Sioux in battle but, being peaceable, did not
wish to clash with them." The Dogden Buttes, including Prophet's Mountain,
appeared to mark the northern hunting boundary for the Sioux. The Metis
generally confined their hunts to western McHenry County.(15)

An incident where this arrangement went awry is found in Bob Cory's regular
feature article in the September 5, 1970, Minot Daily News. Cory, borrowing
heavily from Canadian historian William Morton's article titled "The Battle of
the Grand Coteau," wove the account of a battle between a Metis hunting camp and
a Sioux war party on July 13-14, 1851, near Dogden Butte.(16) A summary of the
account follows:

  The Metis hunters, underway for four weeks from the east, spotted a Sioux
  encampment near Dogden by spyglass. They immediately formed a defensive camp.
  Typical of the Metis, they traveled with a large number of Red River carts and
  these they placed in a large circle. They had slaughtered and butchered many
  buffalo and had sufficient dried meat to pile up as part of their defense.
  Long poles used as frames for drying meat were laid between the wheel spokes
  and every last item of pack and baggage, hides and dried meat was piled up
  between the carts.

  The Metis camp, part of a larger party of mixed bloods about twenty miles
  distant, was made up of seventy-seven men and boys old enough to shoot rifles
  and included many women and children. Trenches were dug under the carts to
  shelter the latter. The men dug rifle pits outside the cart encirclement and
  from there carried out their defensive sniper fire.

  The Metis were able to hold off the Sioux warriors - said to number about
  2,000 - and their repeated charges and circling on horseback. The Metis were
  good riflemen and had plenty of ammunition. The Sioux also had rifles but
  apparently ran low on ammunition and then relied on their arrows. The Sioux
  eventually withdrew - what role a sudden thunderstorm played on the second day
  is not known - and their losses were placed at eighty men and sixty-five
  horses. The mixed bloods suffered one death (a hostage who was killed while
  trying to make a break for camp) and twelve horses and four oxen. It was said
  that Sioux war parties never again did battle with mixed blood buffalo
  hunters.

Epidemics of smallpox in 1837, cholera in 1851 and smallpox again in 1866
decimated the Native American population in the Upper Missouri region,
especially among the Mandans. Eventually the earthen lodge dwellers relocated
further up the Missouri and resided near Fort Berthold, a trading post
established in 1845. The Mandans, Hidatsas and Arikaras, some 2,000-3,000 strong
living around the fort, became known as the Three Tribes.(17) Here they led
destitute lives. Shifting from confrontation with the Metis, the war-like Sioux
now repeatedly harassed and intimidated the Three Tribes who no longer dared
venture out in search of bison. The Yanktonai camped in the Dogden buttes as far
north as Cottonwood Lake and used the hills as a fortress and lookout as well.
From this vantage, they carried out theft of Mandan horses. Sometimes the
victims gave pursuit as far as the buttes but then lost the chase when the Sioux
were able to take refuge in the rugged terrain.

But the Mandans did occasionally exact revenge(18) A wagon train correspondent
reported in 1866 that previous to the entourage's arrival at Fort Berthold two
Sioux Indians had stolen several Mandan ponies. The Mandan chief and several of
his warriors had given pursuit, succeeded in killing the thieves and returned
with their severed heads. The trophies were hanging from poles when the wagon
party arrived at the fort.

As adept as the Indians were in their buffalo hunting, nothing hastened the
demise of these animals as much as the arrival of the white man. Wholesale
slaughter of the beasts almost brought about their extinction. At the three-
quarter mark of the nineteenth century only small straggler herds remained.
Frontiersman Joseph Taylor recorded the slaughter of the last herd in the area:
"In 1874, a band of sixty buffalo were discovered near Prophet's Mountain, a
butte ten miles [actually twenty-two miles] south of the Dog Den, and a few
miles west of that place [likely in the vicinity of Brush Lake], by a hunting
party of Sissetons [Sioux]. The buffalo were surrounded and slain by the red
hunters. The destruction of this band ended the buffalo among the lakes and
buttes of the Coteau du Prairie, with a very few straggling exceptions."(19) The
only evidence today of their place on our landscape is seen in occasional
buffalo wallows: huge, eroded dish-like depressions on virgin range and
pastureland.

The White Man Cometh
Early Traders

The state's first documented white man was Frenchman/fur trader Pierre La
Verendrye. He may have been the Mercer area's first Caucasian visitor as well.
Aside from promoting trade with Indians, he was always keen on finding an
overland route to the "Western Sea" (Pacific Ocean). On October 18, 1738, he
struck out on a foot expedition from today's Portage la Prairie, Manitoba, to
visit the "Mantannes" (Mandans) near the "River of the West" (Missouri). He
headed southwestward with a party of fifty-two Assiniboin Indians and arrived at
a Mandan earth-lodge village on December 3. It was quite probably today's ruins
village located on Apple Creek at Menoken, thirteen miles east of Bismarck.(20)

Verendrye kept a travel log and recorded compass readings. Although the records
are sketchy, a map recreating the expedition course, with adjustments made for
magnetic declination,(21) reveals that his party may well have skirted the
eastern slopes of the Dogden coteau and Prophet's Mountain the last week of
November 1738.(22) Quite ill throughout much of the expedition, Verendrye
remained in the village for ten days and then returned to Canada on foot
again.(23) We can only wonder how he survived the harsh December winds skimming
the prairies.

Verendrye's observation of the Mandans bartering with the Assiniboins for
muskets, axes, kettles, powder, bullets, knives, awls, and so forth, did not
herald the opening of trade with the Plains Indians. A system of trade between
the Assiniboins and the Mandans had begun as early as 1680.(24) This trade
system began to flourish after the British captured Montreal in 1760. Hudson's
Bay Company and the North West Company built forts, and English merchandise was
sent regularly to Mandan and Hidatsa villages on the Missouri at the mouth of
the Knife River - current day Stanton, North Dakota.

The first of these expeditions was organized in 1794 by René Jusseaume, later to
become an interpreter on the 1804 Lewis and Clark Expedition.(25) Traders moved
on foot or horseback over a 250-mile trail following the Souris River from
Canada, across the Turtle Mountains, heading for the Dogden Buttes region in
northern McLean County, where the hostile Sioux were a constant danger. They
continued southwestward through the Crooked Lake-Strawberry Lake area down to
the Missouri.

David Thompson, astronomer/surveyor/explorer working for the Hudson's Bay
Company, organized his own trade mission in 1797 and hired Jusseaume to
accompany him. They set out from Canada on November 28 and spent Christmas Eve
encamped at Dogden Butte. Eventually they reached Mandan and Hidatsa villages on
the Missouri and spent two weeks bartering with the Indians. It was here that
Thompson worked on the first map ever made in North Dakota. Among the Native
Americans he was known as Koo-Koo-Sint, the Looker at Stars.(26)

The commercial route to the north continued for a time, but as the young United
States grew in size, its sphere of influence expanded, especially after the
Lewis and Clark Expedition. U.S. backed companies began to open trade with
tribes in the region. New traders appeared from the south up the Missouri River,
eventually eclipsed by the arrival of steamboats and more white men. However,
terrible epidemics took a staggering toll on the Indian population and trade
dropped off considerably.

Gold in Montana: An Era of Expeditions

White intrusion upon Indian lands grew with passing of time. It reached
significant levels in 1849 with the organization of the Minnesota Territory and
the thousands of gold seekers storming overland to reach California. Tensions
between settlers and natives mounted in neighboring Minnesota to the point of
the Sioux Uprising of 1862. Soon northern Dakota Territory saw troops under
Generals Sibley and Sully in pursuit of hostile Sioux who had fled Minnesota,
and bloody battles ensued.

Sully returned in 1864 in search of, and bent on punishing, the still defiant
Sioux. His punitive expedition to the upper Missouri resulted in the battle of
Killdeer Mountain in July in which the Indians were completely defeated. It was
a hot, dry summer - water and provisions had been in short supply - as Sully's
exhausted troops headed homeward along the east side of the Missouri to Fort
Rice below Bismarck.

On August 31, they camped at the mouth of Snake Creek where Sully, reacting to
rumors of a large band of Santee Sioux ahead, led by Chief Inkpaduta, decided on
a detour to the Dogden buttes. All during the day of September 1, Sully's troops
encountered huge herds of buffalo, in the thousands, an ironic underscoring to
the starving Three Tribes they had encountered on their August 28-29 stop at
Fort Berthold. They bivouacked that night near a small lake in the vicinity of
current Benedict, North Dakota, with a herd of nearly ten thousand buffalo
blackening the hills nearby.(27)

Next day the expedition headed northeast and then southeast some sixteen miles
when they made camp near a small lake five miles west of Dogden Butte.(28) Still
encountering huge herds, Sully forbade killing of buffalo along the way lest the
shooting tip off the Indians. Sully reached the "big mound on the Sheyan"(29)
but learned he was too late. The Sioux had hastily decamped, and from the summit
the soldiers observed the retreating Indians off in the distance. Robbed of his
element of surprise, Sully gave up the chase and returned to camp west of the
butte before heading home.(30)

But had Inkpaduta really retreated northeastward as it appeared? Early pioneer
and historian Joseph Taylor concludes the wily Sioux simply sought refuge in the
deep and secluded Dogden ravines. Sighting of any retreat was merely part of a
ruse.(31) This view gains some credence from an account by a Sully lieutenant
describing the expedition's departure from Dogden the following day. As the
troops broke camp on September 3, a small contingent remained behind for a
little "sport" running of buffalo and cutting out trophy tongues from their
kill. The hunters suddenly came under attack from about twenty Sioux warriors.
At full gallop across the open plains, they eluded the Indians in a ten-mile
pursuit when they at last reached haven among Sully's rear guard.(32)

That day, the troops marched south-southeast some twenty-three miles, eventually
through western Medicine Hill and Wise Townships, to camp at the foot of "Corn
Stalk Butte"(33) between two lakes, variously described as of good and poor
quality water - quite likely between Blue and Brush Lakes of the Brush Lake
chain.(34)

The military column encountered waves of roaming buffalo through their lines
that day and faced the danger of a stampede. The party remained here through
Sunday, September 4. On that day there was "preaching and gambling only 20 rods
a part."(35) Rain fell and the weather turned so cold the soldiers hardly dared
pull their guns from under blankets to fire at the buffalo in their very
midst.(36)

        Map: General Sully's Northwestern Indian Expedition of 1864. Courtesy of
        the Minnesota Historical Society.

The march continued southward September 5 through western Mercer and Park
Townships, and camp was made at Painted Woods Creek in Heaton Township.(37) The
weather was still cold and rainy and buffalo were plentiful. One of the beasts
entered camp and stampeded the mules.(38) The expedition finally reached Fort
Rice on September 8.

(See McLean Trail, page 12 and Sheridan Trail, page 13)

Almost a year later, Sully was still on the watch for Sioux. On June 6, 1865, he
reported to the North West Company of scouting accounts that placed some 400
Santee lodges near Corn Stalk Butte (Prophet's Mountain) twenty-two miles south
of Dogden Butte.(39) Later records indicate no substance to these reports.

The discovery of gold in Montana in 1862 set the stage for northern Dakota's own
influx of overland wagon trains. At first, relentless prospectors went up the
Missouri River by steamboat to Fort Benton in Montana. However, Minnesota
businessmen sensing a profit to be made, heavily promoted a wagon trail across
northern Dakota Territory on which they could transport supplies to the mines
and sell goods. They did this in spite of warnings about Indian hostilities. As
a result, eight large wagon trains were organized in Minnesota between 1862-
1867.(40) The Civil War served somewhat as a distraction, but by 1866 the Mercer
area was directly in the thick of this activity.

Walter Essig undertook field studies in the 1970s to identify two trails in
particular: the traces left by the Minnesota-based Holmes and Fisk wagon trains
in Sheridan and McLean Counties. He scoured virgin pastures for their remnants
and soon became caught up in the diaries kept by the train leaders.

The first of these trains was organized and led by Thomas Holmes, an adventurer
from the east then living in Minnesota.(41) The expedition departed from
Shakopee, Minnesota, early June 1866.(42) The intent was to reach the Big Bend
on the Missouri River above present day Stanton, North Dakota, and to continue
the journey by following the stream into Montana and on to the gold mines. The
party was made up of about 200 men, ten women and ten children. The wagon train
consisted of seventy-four fully loaded wagons and 400 head of livestock. The
entourage departed from Fort Wadsworth on June 17 and moved northwesterly into
Dakota Territory until it reached the James River. This they followed upstream
to below Jamestown. From that point they followed the Pipestem Creek to the
Sykeston, North Dakota, area and then struck out northwest across Wells County.
On June 29, they entered Sheridan County in northern Fairview Township and
commenced heading southwest. Essig in his manuscript collection suggests the
Holmes train would have been better served at this point if they had taken a
westerly course to the Big Bend.(43) It would have been shorter with better
terrain and sources of water. Essig surmises the scouts were not familiar with
the remaining terrain to the Missouri River.

Following their southwesterly course on June 30, they encountered a herd of 300-
400 buffalo some four miles north of today's Denhoff. After a short hunt and
replenishment of meat supplies they camped near a slough that was not only
alkaline but had been befouled by the buffalo. What follows is Essig's
commentary based on fieldwork and extracts of a travel diary kept by expedition
member William Johnstone:(44)

        Engraving: Thomas Holmes, expedition leader (Engraving from The Southern
        Minnesota, March, 1931)

The Holmes Wagon Train of 1866(45)

  "On the morning of July 1 they started out upon a more southwesterly course.
  By now both people and animals were desperate for water. All of the men that
  could be spared from the wagon train spread out to the left and right of their
  route searching for water. In this manner they passed by about a mile and a
  half to the north of present McClusky. After traveling thus for a distance of
  10 miles they did find a spring oozing out of the side of a scraggy hill.
  There was only enough water for the people. During their noon stop they
  received a rain shower which gave the animals some relief. The location of
  this spring could not be determined. The noon stop would have been just to the
  east of present Pickardville, in the vicinity of the Pickard farm which is
  located in Section 12, Twp. 146, Rge. 78 [Pickard].

  "During the afternoon they traveled southwest, the terrain becoming more
  hilly. In that area are many sloughs and potholes which would have required
  considerable meandering. Consequently they would have traveled fewer miles in
  a direct mile than the 20 miles they recorded for the day. They camped that
  night by a small lake of poor water. Their night camp would have been in the
  vicinity of Section 1, Twp. 145, Rge. 79 [Mercer], just within McLean County,
  and about 6 miles south of present Mercer.

  "After traveling 12 miles [traveling westward they crossed the northern tier
  sections of Park and Koenig Townships] during the forenoon of July 2, they
  came to a large valley where they found some water of poor quality. They were
  now in Turtle Creek, having reached this in Section 12, Twp. 145, Rge. 81.
  After dinner they moved down stream for a distance of 4 miles to where there
  was a spring of good water. There they remained for the rest of that day.
  Johnstone reported that they had found petrified wood scattered on the surface
  at this location, and it is interesting that the early homesteaders had opened
  a small pit into the west bank of the stream to mine lignite coal. This camp
  site would have been located on Turtle Creek, in the west central part of
  Section 29, Twp. 145, Rge. 80 [Koenig], and about 8 miles northeast of present
  Washburn."

From that point the Holmes train traveled generally westward and eventually
reached Fort Berthold on July 7.

A second wagon train crossed Dakota Territory in July 1866. This was led by
James Liberty Fisk who had undertaken three previous expeditions (1862-1864),
the latter having caused him some notoriety. The 1864 expedition through today's
southwestern North Dakota was marked by an Indian attack. Fisk had undertaken
the ill-fated journey in spite of repeated warnings from government agents about
prevailing Indian hostility. General Sully angrily dispatched some of his
cavalry to rescue Fisk, whom he disdained as a swaggering, meddlesome braggart
and an obstacle to "making peace" with the Indians.(46)

        Photo: Colonel James L. Fisk (Photo by John Holyland of Washington, D.C.
        Courtesy of the Minnesota Historical Society)

Of Fisk's fourth expedition, Essig writes that it was organized and assembled in
St. Cloud, Minnesota.(47) The train consisted of 133 wagons and a dozen Red
River carts. The party was made up of more than 300 men, about thirty women and
several children - a larger expedition than the Holmes expedition that had
struck out earlier.(48) As with the Holmes train, the destination was the Big
Bend of the Missouri River.(49) The group left St. Cloud on June 7, reached Fort
Abercrombie on the Red River on June 22 and continued traveling westward to the
James River. Once across the river, it took a northwesterly course to the Coteau
du Missouri.

        Map: Plat map of McLean County North Dakota

        Map: Plat map of Sheridan County North Dakota

On July 10, now in northern Burleigh County, the entourage experienced hot winds
and the temperature stood at 101°. They encountered herds of buffalo and killed
several to replenish food stocks. July 11 they entered Sheridan County at the
southeast corner of Edgemont Township, and traveling west-northwest, they camped
near a spring located in the NE¼ of Section 15. We continue Essig's commentary
based on fieldwork and extracts from the diary of Robert E. Fisk, expedition
member and brother of James L.:

Fisk Wagon Train Route of 1866(50)

  "The spring by which they camped during the night of July 11 they named "Cold
  Spring" because they found chunks of ice in it while digging it out. It was
  strong flowing and provided sufficient water for the people and also the
  animals. This spring was still strong flowing in recent years. It has since,
  however, been dug out as a livestock watering dugout.

  "On the morning of July the 12th they traveled west-northwest for a distance
  of 5 miles, crossing the Sheridan-McLean [C]ounty line. A mile or so beyond
  this they stopped for the noon hour, and were then near the site of the Holmes
  night camp of July 1, 1866. They were now about 6 miles south of present
  Mercer, and a mile or so to the east of Highway 41.

  "Very early that morning Fisk and his half-blood guide had ridden to the
  southwest scouting for the Missouri River. After going a distance of 12 miles
  they did spy the river, and he came to the same false conclusion, as Holmes
  had apparently also done, that the bend of the Missouri River at Washburn was
  the Big Bend of the Missouri River that they had been aiming for. By the time
  Fisk rejoined his wagon train, at about 3 p.m., it had apparently already
  encountered the tracks left by the Holmes expedition. He immediately changed
  his direction of travel from northwest to southwest - actually more to the
  south of west. He apparently believed he would find Fort Berthold in that
  direction. Actually, if he had contin[u]ed upon a course of west-northwest
  from this point, he would have arrived directly upon his destination, the Big
  Bend of the Missouri River.

  "However he chose to follow the tracks left by the Holmes party that afternoon
  [across Park Township's northern tier of sections], and camped near a small
  lake. They were now in Section 12, Twp. 145, Rge. 80 [Koenig], in McLean
  County. They had traveled 5 miles during the forenoon, plus 7 miles for the
  afternoon, for a total of 12 miles this day.

  "On the morning of July 13th, still following the Holmes tracks in a direction
  slightly south of west, they arrived at Turtle Creek. They did not mention
  crossing this creek in their diary but it would have been in the northeast
  corner of Section 12, Twp. 145, Rge. 81, and distant about 5½ miles from the
  last night's camp. It is at this place where the Holmes expedition went 4
  miles downstream to Section 29, Twp. 145, Rge. 80 [Koenig], and stopped
  overnight by a strong spring.

  "Fisk did not do this. He left the Holmes trail, crossed the creek, and after
  traveling another 3 miles stopped for dinner in Section 15, Twp. 145, Rge. 81.
  No water was available at this place, which was located about 7 miles north
  and 3 miles east of present Washburn."

Eventually Fisk reached his destination on the Missouri River, but, like Thomas
Holmes, only after several miscalculations. Although both expeditions took
divergent routes to reach the Big Bend, diary entries reveal what they faced in
common. Both found an abundance of meat and fowl on the open plains. Both
struggled to find adequate water supplies, sometimes settling for water tainted
by alkali. Both resorted to resourcefulness when faced with lack of fuel on the
treeless prairies and gathered buffalo chips (dried manure) instead.

        Photo: Fisk Expedition of 1866 (Photo by Illingworth and Bill taken near
        Fort Ransom. Courtesy of Montana Historical Society.)

The Minnesota sponsored wagon trains brought heavy pressure for a bona fide
overland road from Minnesota to Montana. After the Civil War, the government
responded by assigning General Alfred Terry at Fort Snelling, Minnesota, the
task of establishing an official route and supplying protective measures. He
carried out orders in 1867, establishing a route and selecting sites for three
forts to protect travelers: Fort Ransom on the lower Sheyenne River, Fort Totten
at Devils Lake, and Fort Stevenson on the Missouri's Big Bend. Fort Stevenson
was established to protect not only travelers but also the local Mandans and
Hidatsas from Sioux attacks.(51)

Of local interest is the Fort Totten-Fort Stevenson military trail, drawing a
126-mile arc from the Missouri Big Bend northeastward to Crooked Lake on a
heading south of Dogden Butte in northern McLean County and along the northern
parts of Sheridan and Wells Counties. Its paramount role was its vital link to
Fort Totten that relied on supplies arriving at Fort Stevenson by steamboat up
the Missouri and then being transported eastward on the trail. Travel between
the two posts was always dangerous, especially for the lone traveler or the mail
couriers; fuel and shelter were a scarce commodity over the span. The hostile
Sioux, including the young warrior Sitting Bull, lay in wait to attack,
especially in the Strawberry Lake and Dogden Butte neighborhood. Sitting Bull
was a particular annoyance to General de Trobriand, the Fort Stevenson camp
commander, who could not abide late or non-delivered mail. The trail fell from
use in 1872 when a safer supply route from Fort Seward at Jamestown to Fort
Totten was established.

Apparently not all violence on the route was instigated by the Sioux. Joseph
Taylor writes of the trail and the Dogdens as a place of intrigue and mystery.
He relates the incident of an elderly German vagabond immigrant who made his way
to Fort Stevenson from Fort Peck, Montana, the summer of 1868.(52) Appearing
tattered and poor, he bought provisions and set out for Fort Totten in a
dilapidated wagon drawn by an old Cayuse. Among those who observed his movements
was a Scotch Indian mail courier named MacDonald, the same courier leaving for
Fort Totten the following day on his scheduled round.

When MacDonald went missing after four days, Fort Totten officials sent out a
search party. Near Strawberry Lake the troops encountered dense smoke hanging
over the plains and a wide area scorched by fire. Amid the devastation, they
discovered the old German's scalped corpse, and hands and feet dismembered, and
the wagon hacked to pieces. Next day a mile east of the lake they discovered a
partially burned mail sack and MacDonald's scorched, bullet-ridden buckskin coat
smeared with blood. All this pointed to the courier's demise, but no body could
be found.

Upon formal investigation it was learned the old German had $40,000 in gold dust
when he left the Montana gold mines, his shabby attire meant to keep robbers at
bay. Officials also noted none of the trading posts in the area reported
significant amounts of gold offered by bartering hostile red men. MacDonald came
under immediate suspicion for doing in the old man and making it look like the
work of Indians. The suspicion gained substance two years later when Fort Totten
troops sent to Fort Snelling spotted MacDonald in a St. Paul railway depot
crowd. When they called out his name, he swiftly faded into the throng.

There is another footnote to the mysteries along the Fort Totten-Fort Stevenson
military trail, in the land of strange disappearances, to which historian Dana
Wright makes reference.(53) He speaks of the grisly discovery made in pioneer
days of human skulls - ostensibly white men - and a flintlock gun in woods on
the south shore of Postel Lake immediately south of Medicine Hill. Although more
than ten miles from the established trail, it is not inconceivable that the
victims had veered off course or were compelled to seek refuge there in their
journey between the two forts. Another possibility is that the remains were
those of Hudson's Bay traders earlier in the 1790s who tramped through the
Dogdens on their way to the Mandans and Hidatsas on the Missouri.

Early Settlers "With a Buckboard and an Old Plug Horse"

The trio of Joseph H. Taylor, William H.H. Mercer and Dan Williams goes down in
local history as the region's first white settlers. How the three men became
fast friends is not known, but a chance assignment given to Williams would send
them on a watershed journey. To paraphrase W.T. Wasson's high-flown assertion
in The Mercer Telegram, their trip to Fort Benton, Montana, set the stage for
this region to become civilized and to evolve into America's breadbasket.(54)

In the spring of 1867, according to Wasson's account, Dan Williams had been
appointed administrator of an estate by the territorial court in Yankton. The
assignment was to take him to Fort Benton and he was allowed two assistants. He
chose his two friends as travel companions and they set out on the 500-mile
journey up the Missouri River "in an old time buckboard and one old horse."

Supplies and escorts were promised them, and these they were to secure at
various government fortifications along the way. They accepted supplies; they
would not hear of any troop escorts. Only ten miles out from Fort Pierre on
their way to Fort Sully they were accosted by sixty Sioux braves who immediately
relieved them of their tobacco supplies. In return the Indians offered their
"escort services" through Arikara country. They arrived safely at Fort Lincoln,
and from there they completed the expedition to Montana alone. Their business
completed at Fort Benton, they retraced their steps back to Yankton. They were
so impressed by what they had seen, they vowed to return.

        Engraving: Joseph H. Taylor (Engraving from Pioneer Days of Washburn
        North Dakota and Vicinity: Book One)

The three did return to the Missouri above Bismarck in May 1869. Taylor gave up
his position as publisher of the Dakota Democrat in Yankton and Mercer bid
farewell to a brickyard job in Sioux City, Iowa.(55) By 1871 they had staked
their claims in today's Painted Woods Township, hard by the river, just inside
Burleigh County.

Taylor, born in 1844 and a Union Army veteran of General Sibley's 1863-64
expedition, was a true frontiersman. Wearing a buckskin suit and moccasins and
carrying a knife and pistol, he lived in a log cabin with a dirt floor without
windows that he called Preparation Pont.(56) It was located in Section 3, Twp.
142-81 (Painted Woods). Later in life, he was employed as the Washburn Leader's
local "scribe," completed the publication of three books on frontier life, and
served a four-year stint as County Register of Deeds.

Daniel Rossiter Williams, born May 10, 1846, in Stonington, Connecticut,
established a well-appointed ranch at Painted Woods. Locally, he was among the
first to utilize coteau grazing land. In 1883, he was named warden of the
Territorial prison in Bismarck and served for eight years.(57) Despite his
achievements, he had the misfortune of living in the shadow of his younger
brother, "General" E.A. (Erastus Appleman), a noted Territorial and State
Legislator who was instrumental in drawing up the legislation that created
McLean County in 1883. Dan Williams died January 29, 1917, in Bismarck.

        Photo: Dan R. Williams (Photo by Barry Photographer, Bismarck, D.T.
        Courtesy of the State Historical Society of North Dakota A4285.)

Mercer - his real name was William Henry Harrison Musser - was born in Centre
County, Pennsylvania in 1845. At age sixteen he enlisted in the Union Army and
fought in the Civil War. His liaison with Taylor and Williams led in 1873 to his
Painted Woods Ranch in Sec. 15, Twp. 142-81 (Painted Woods). At some point after
his 1869 arrival, he married a certain Mary Jane (maiden name unknown) from
Illinois. They had three children: William, born September 1871, a second son
named William, born March 1882, and Mary Jane, born October 1883. Mercer's noted
achievement was to have opened the first farm north of Bismarck in 1877 when he
broke 120 acres of prairie and raised a bumper crop of wheat. No threshing
machine was available at the time so the entire harvest was flailed by hand and
yielded 2,000 bushels.(58)

In Mary Ann Barnes Williams' chronicles, Mercer is described as an educated,
sociable fellow with many friends.(59) He was also a civic-minded man.(60) In
January 1873, the territorial legislature in Yankton created Burleigh County,
and by June of that year Dakota Territory Governor Burbank appointed three
county commissioners. Mercer was one of the appointees, and he wasted no time in
convincing his colleagues to elect his old buddies to office. Dan Williams
became Register of Deeds; Joe Taylor was appointed Justice of Peace for Painted
Woods. Mercer County later came to be named after him.

Always the three men were curious about what lay beyond Painted Woods. Taylor,
the adventurer, instigated trips up and down the Missouri and usually ensnared
his two married friends in the action. By Taylor's own admission, he and Mercer
undertook a foolhardy journey in July 1871 down the Missouri in a bullboat to
Yankton through Sioux country.(61)  They returned unscathed, but with a pregnant
wife back home, Mercer must have rued the entire escapade.

Once Indian hostilities had abated after 1876 (Battle of the Little Bighorn),
the trio dared venture more upon the rolling prairie to the east and northeast.
They discovered a vast, undulating plain, lush with grass now that the buffalo
herds had disappeared, cratered with potholes and sloughs. These pioneers
immediately identified an area - today's eastern McLean County, most of Sheridan
County, southwestern Wells County, and northern Kidder and Burleigh Counties -
as prime rangeland, an adjunct to ranching operations at Painted Woods.

        Photo: Wm. Mercer ranch house at Painted Woods. (Courtesy of the State
        Historical Society of North Dakota A2313.)

Soon these gentlemen set out from the river bottom ranches in the springtime,
driving their cattle herds northward (likely up the Turtle Creek valley) and
then northeastward. Speculation is that Williams moved his herd to the Brush
Lake area; Mercer pushed ahead to the foothills of Prophet's Mountain, two and
one-half miles southeast of his namesake town in Section 7, Twp. 146-78
(Pickard). Even Joe Taylor became a cowpuncher when in 1884 he was left in
charge of a herd immediately north of Dogden Butte and wintered there while his
boss returned to ranch operations on the Missouri.(62) Cow camps were
established and any structures on site were likely transitory in style and
construction. The basic need was to provide shelter against the elements on the
open prairie.

In the case of Mercer, the camp was located on railroad land. McLean and
Sheridan Counties had been surveyed in the 1870s and sections dedicated to the
Northern Pacific Railway were identified. Mercer either leased his cow camp site
from the railway or simply played the role of squatter. Settlers had not yet
arrived, so vast unclaimed acres were used for open grazing. In autumn the herds
were usually driven southward again, back to their home river bottom ranches.

Cattle Trails & a Road to Washburn

The inexorable march onto the coteau continued. Other ranch settlers followed
Williams' and Mercer's footsteps, and more cow camps and settlements appeared.
The New Home Township area provided excellent rangeland, and, in the late 1870s,
a small Brush Lake community in Wise Township had taken root. The settlers were
still terrified by Sitting Bull's earlier rampage. Although now one usually
encountered peaceful but hungry tribesmen. Young Ivy Lambert, living with her
parents on Brush Lake's eastern shore, related later in life - as one of McLean
County's pioneer country school teachers - how the settlers' real peril lay in
another dreaded menace on the plains, the prairie fire. A fire indeed devastated
the area, destroying property and vast reaches of grassland, and a bucket
brigade provided no defense.(63)

Prairie fires loomed large again the summer of 1886 when the plains were
scorched by an unrelenting drouth and fires were easily kindled. But the
region's pioneers were spared. With little or no hay supply in the fall of 1886,
the settlers hunkered down for the winter. It came early, on November 5, when
the first of many blizzards swept across the plains. Snow depths on the level
reached as much as four to five feet. Some people perished that winter; loss of
open range cattle was staggering.(64)  The settlers survived, stayed put, and
their numbers increased by the end of the decade. Prominent among them in the
Brush Lake community were the Merry brothers, William and John, sons of Lorenzo
Merry who had arrived at Painted Woods in 1873 by team from Ottertail County,
Minnesota.

The settlers' and ranchers' movements generated traffic, and from it evolved a
trail, known variably as the Brush Lake-Martin Road or the Rancher's Washburn
Trail.(65) It arose in Rosenfield Township (150-76) in north Sheridan County on
the Fort Totten-Fort Stevenson Military Trail and coursed south-southwest
through Granville (149-76), Harris (148-77) and Mountain City (147-77)
Townships. It took a southwesterly direction as it skirted the east side of
Prophet's Mountain and ran through northwestern Pickard Township (146-78), in
the immediate vicinity of William Mercer's Coteax Ranch.(66) It continued
southwestward into McLean County through Mercer Township (likely Sections 13,
14, 22, 28, 32, and 33, Twp.146-79), through northwestern Park Township
(Sections 5-7, Twp. 145-79), and traversed neighboring Koenig Township (Twp.
145-80) southwesterly. Here it eventually merged with the Holmes expedition
trial of 1866 and on towards the Washburn vicinity.

The trail garnered a reputation for rancher hospitality. Settlements along the
way, such as Baardson's Ranch (Sec. 2, Koenig Twp.), Howell's Ranch (Sec. 30,
Prophets Twp.), Mercer's Ranch (Sec. 7, Pickard Twp.), Beck's Horse Ranch (Sec.
22, Georgetown Twp.), and the George Curtis Ranch, became customary stopovers
for travelers. Ranchers were always willing to provide shelter. Even later as
the homesteaders arrived, a helping hand was extended to the sodbuster
newcomers.

A 1908 Mercer Telegram(67) article cites Major J.R. Howell particularly as one
providing a favorite stopping place for travelers. Howell, born in Indiana in
1840, enlisted in the Union Army in 1856 and was mustered into service in 1861
as a drummer-boy. By the end of the Civil War he had undergone several
promotions. He was caught up in the post-war western migration fever and helped
construct one of the first telegraph lines to the Rockies. He came to Dakota
Territory in 1883 and took up farming until 1897. He served in various offices
of state government in South Dakota. In 1900, he purchased his ranch in
Prophet's Township.

Another prominent rancher was John Beck, born in Germany and arriving in
Minnesota at age three. He operated a general store in Wendell, Minnesota, moved
to then eastern McLean County in 1900, and homesteaded a ranch, still in the
family, northwest of McClusky. He was elected sheriff of McLean County in 1906
and lived in Washburn until the 1909 division of Sheridan County. He maintained
his ranch throughout this time and became the prime horse trader to the throngs
of immigrants arriving on the scene.(68)

In spite of the ranchers' good will and neighborliness there lurked an unsavory
element. By 1884 horse thievery had reached epidemic proportions in the region.
McLean County had been organized in 1883 and its new sheriff, John Satterlund,
faced the immediate task of hunting down the criminals.(69) The new county lay
next to a huge unorganized district that stretched to Montana and it was a haven
for the lawless. Their activities soon spilled over into McLean County.
Vigilante groups from as far away as Montana often joined the hunt. Any culprits
caught were summarily dispatched by hanging. Such was the fate of one gang
caught near Crooked Lake, where years later Satterlund discovered their
skeletons.(70)

Criminal activity was not restricted to stealing. Gangs exploited the area as a
sanctuary before surreptitiously moving their booty across local ranchers'
trails into Canada. A local legend holds that rustlers moved their stolen
animals by night up and down Turtle Creek to Section 18 of Koenig Township (Twp.
145-80) - a site later to become known as the Peterson Ranch - where a glowing
lantern was hoisted high on a post overlooking the creek. The lantern became a
rendezvous, where in the dark the horses were herded eastward twelve miles
through northern Koenig and Park Townships along the old Holmes expedition trail
of 1866, thence northeastward into Sheridan County along the same trail, on to
the Turtle Mountains, and eventually into Canada.(71)

River bottom ranchers were not the only ones to encroach upon the coteau. 1883
saw the organization of a fledgling McLean County. It also witnessed the
founding of the town Sykeston in eastern Wells County. Built on a twelve-mile
branch railway from Carrington, it attracted an influx of ranchers and
homesteaders. The newcomers soon moved to western Wells County, and ranchers
viewed neighboring Sheridan County's rolling terrain as free range for their
grazing purposes. In 1890, McLean County boundaries were expanded and all of
Sheridan County was annexed. Overnight, a larger segment of population needed to
conduct business at its county seat in Washburn, and the Rancher's Washburn
Trail fell into heavy use.

In 1893, the town of Harvey in northwestern Wells County was founded on the
newly constructed Soo Line Railway. Settlers arriving by rail in huge numbers
soon streamed into now northeastern Sheridan County and a new trail evolved.
This one traversed the area in a direct line from Harvey to McClusky where it
merged with the Holmes trail of 1866 and wended its way to Washburn: the
Harvey-Washburn Trail.

Early settlers yearned for communication with the outside world, and the
government was quick to provide mail service where feasible. Washburn was the
terminus for several mail routes in the 1880s. Stages in that day were buckboard
wagons for summer travel and small covered sleds for the winter, either mule- or
horse-drawn. Stations located at fifteen to twenty-mile intervals at ranches or
settlements provided shelter, fresh horses, provisions and for mail
exchange.(72) Some time between 1886 and 1890 a route to Turtle Lake - not the
town - was established.(73) Eventually the Brush Lake settlement grew to where
it merited Star Route status, i.e. stage line service and mail delivery. In
1895, Dan Williams had established a permanent ranch on the shores of Brush Lake
(NW¼, Sec. 27, Twp. 147-79, Wise) and in 1898, the Ingersoll-Turtle Lake route
had been extended to his spread. A rural post office was established in his home
and Williams was its postmaster. It was named Ethel, after nearby Lake Ethel, in
turn named for the daughter of rancher John Merry.(74) The facility was closed
October 15, 1900.

End of an Era

The century was drawing to a close, and on the horizon lay the pent intentions
of homesteaders to take their place next to the pioneer coteau ranchers. A new
era was dawning, and, as if by fate, the life of this area's namesake, William
Henry Harrison Mercer, also came to an end. He died August 12, 1901. The
following - composed in all likelihood by compatriot Joe Taylor - is an obituary
that appeared in the August 17, 1901, edition of The Washburn Leader:

  "A shock to his friends and a surprise to all was the word brought into
  Washburn Tuesday afternoon that W.H.H. Mercer, of the Coteax ranch was being
  brought into Washburn by his son[,] a corpse. He had been ailing for some
  time[,] now better - now worse, but seemed in usual health after dinner,
  Monday when mounting a pony he went out on the prairie to round up his cattle,
  while his boy took the work team to cut hay in the slough hard by. These were
  the only two persons about the place, Mrs. Mercer having left for the Painted
  Woods the day previous. The first intimation the boy had of misfortune was the
  arrival of his father's pony saddled and bridled, but without its rider.
  Suspecting something went wrong, he rode over to the Brush Lake settlement for
  assistance. Dan Williams and others responded, and on Tuesday morning Mr.
  Mercer's lifeless body was found about two miles from his ranch. All
  appearances indicated that he had been dead several hours. His face was
  blackened by heat and dust, and marks on the grass show that the pony must
  have been held by him while on the ground, several hours before the bridle
  reins were relaxed in his hands by death.

  "After Mr. Mercer's remains were brought over to Washburn the local G.A.R.(75)
  post took charge, and Dr. Forbes was called on to make an examination, which
  he proceeded to do, satisfying himself that death came to Mr. Mercer from
  natural causes, probably heart disease. On account of heat and the fact that
  decomposition had already set in the body was taken out for burial about 9
  o'clock Wednesday morning and deposited in the Washburn cemetery, surrounded
  by many of his old comrades - army and others. Chaplain Ranard of the G.A.R.
  post made a few remarks reciting Comrade Mercer's war record as that of a true
  and brave soldier.

  "William Henry Harrison Musser was born in Center Co. Penna 57 years ago. At
  16 he enlisted in the 49th Pa. Vol. which was a part of Hancock's fighting
  brigade, and took part in all bloody battles from Williamsburg on the
  Penensula [sic] with McClellan's Potomac army to the "bloody angel" under
  Grant at Spottsylvania. His time [of] service was three years and two months.
  He never applied for a pension until two years ago, but no pension came for
  him. He had no "hospital record" - nothing but an active service and everday
  fighting one while with his regiment."

Homesteaders, Ho!

At the close of the nineteenth century several factors loomed that would foster
the largest influx of settlers the Mercer community would ever witness. Foremost
was the lure of free land or, at worst, cheap land. A settler who arrived in
North Dakota could buy land from the government (Pre-emption Law), secure it
free of charge by making certain improvements (Homestead or Timber Culture
Acts), or buy it from the Northern Pacific Railroad. Under pre-emption the
government sold quarter sections of land (160 acres) at $1.25 an acre. It also
gave away quarter sections under homestead to anyone who lived on the land and
cultivated a portion thereof for five years. Under timber culture provisions (a
tree claim) the quarter section was given away at the end of eight years if
forty acres of trees had been planted and 675 were still living. If a settler
wished immediate title to his free homestead acres he could pay cash at the same
rate as under pre-emption.

The Northern Pacific Railroad also had land to sell - lots of it and at good
terms. Chartered by Congress in 1864, the NP had received a huge land grant from
the government of forty sections per track mile in Dakota Territory. Sale of
these sections was meant to finance railway construction. Nearly one-fourth of
North Dakota had been granted to the NP.(76) To entice the immigrants, railway
companies undertook massive promotions and advertising, both domestic and
foreign. Rail connections, although lying only on this area's periphery, were
still close enough to make two-day wagon jaunts feasible. In many cases the
jaunts turned into weeklong overland treks from the Eureka, South Dakota area.

Norwegians arrived first in the state and settled mostly in the eastern counties
and along the Great Northern Railway corridor in the northern part as it wended
westward. They tended to be second generation immigrants from states such as
Wisconsin, Minnesota and Iowa. The German-Russians came later and their
settlements clustered in a triangle from Dickey County to Hettinger County at
its base and to McHenry County at its apex. Almost all of their numbers were
either fresh off the steamboat or from a winter's stay in South Dakota. These
two ethnic groups made up the bulk of newcomers, although there were English,
Scots, Swedes, Danes and Ukrainians as well. Locally, the area south of Mercer
was almost exclusively German-Russian. North of town there was a mixture of
Scandinavians and German-Russians although the latter was in the majority. The
Mercer corridor was sandwiched by Ukrainian settlements in the Wilton and Butte
communities. Once the town of Mercer arose, its population was a mix of
Anglo-Saxon, Scandinavian and German-Russian.

The homesteader numbers were so great a mere cross-section is used to recount
their arrival. Against the backdrop of free or cheap land, the mode of travel of
that time, and the nationalities involved, consider...

  ...Haldor B. Thompson, born at Utne, Hardanger, Norway. He immigrated to
  America and settled in Wisconsin. Traveling by team and wagon, he and his
  family arrived in McLean County in 1885. He homesteaded two miles north of
  Washburn and filed a tree claim nine miles northeast of Washburn. In 1905 his
  son Helmer Bue purchased railroad land five and one-half miles southwest of
  Mercer and Haldor moved in with his sons.(77)

  ...the Immanuel Hofer, Christoph Singer and Balthasar Kleingaertner families.
  They hailed from Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, a German colony in South Russia,
  sailed on the same steamer to Halifax, Nova Scotia, in 1903, and traveled by
  rail to Winnipeg and on to Harvey. There they were greeted by fellow
  Hoffnungstal colonist Wilhelm Goll and escorted by wagon down the Rancher's
  Washburn Trail to the very doorsteps of their homestead claims in Mercer and
  Park Townships. Old Hoffnungstal neighbors, Friedrich Laib, Andreas Bossert
  and Friedrich Schlepp, who had arrived in 1902, toasted their arrival.(78)

  ...the Danish connection in Medicine Hill Township. Brothers Martin and
  Christ Peter (C.P.) Christensen and their cousin Jonas arrived in 1902 from
  Hutchinson, Minnesota. They had journeyed on the Soo Line Railroad to Balfour,
  North Dakota, at the behest of land promoter and distant cousin Jergen Billie.
  They then traveled by wagon to scout for suitable land. Their brother Fred
  Christensen followed suit in 1906. In 1903 Martin and C.P.'s cousins Jonas,
  Anton and Christ Christensen, all brothers and also from Hutchinson, returned
  to Medicine Hill and filed claims seven miles north of Mercer. In 1905 Jonas,
  Anton and Christ were joined by their two brothers Nels and Jergen and by 60-
  year-old native Dane and patriarch of the clan, Peter. All filed for
  homestead.(79)

  ...Jacob Just. Born in Kassel, Odessa, South Russia, he arrived in McIntosh
  County, North Dakota, in 1894 at age 14. At age 22, and not finding suitable
  homestead land available in McIntosh County, he and his brother Frederick
  traveled one hundred miles north to Park Township on bicycles. Jacob, not
  aware that hostilities had long since ceased, carried a pistol in the event of
  an Indian attack. He filed his claim (Section 10, Park Township) and arranged
  for his intended bride, Katharina Vossler, to file her claim on the adjacent
  quarter section. They exchanged vows, returned to their claims, and proceeded
  to construct a single tarpaper shanty directly over the quarter section line.
  Homestead requirements for making improvements on both quarters were met. It
  was within the law.(80)

The new settlers were brave and resourceful who nonetheless felt lonely and
isolated on the barren prairie - even the German Russians who were attuned to
the vast, treeless and rolling steppe of South Russia. Comforts, let alone basic
needs, were hard to come by. Occasionally one found small stores selling
provisions. These were usually associated with rural post offices where
connecting stage lines made necessary deliveries: i.e., the Kinney and Hetzler
stores in Sections 29 and 8, respectively, in Medicine Hill Township, the
Eastman post office on the Frank Pace homestead in Section 24 of Park Township,
the Krush store (remnants of stone foundation still visible) in Section 32 of
Park Township, or the Ethel post office on the Dan Williams ranch at Brush Lake.
Other than that, the nearest "big city" shopping was located in Washburn or
Harvey. Obviously a community was in place that needed a trade center.

The Railroad
Sykeston Branch

The Jamestown Northern Railroad Company was incorporated in 1881 with the intent
of operating a line between Jamestown and the Canadian border. Unable to raise
capital, it sold mortgage bonds to the Northern Pacific Railway, and by 1883 a
rail had been constructed to Minnewauken via Carrington. As bondholder, Northern
Pacific called all the shots, and in 1898 its total control of the Jamestown
Northern became official when that company folded.(81)  The new line included a
twelve-mile extension in that year westward from Carrington to the railhead of
Sykeston, named after wealthy English land tycoon, Richard Sykes. The extension
was built in return for the Englishman purchasing large NP land tracts in Wells
County.(82)

As Sykes claimed later, NP also promised further westward extensions to foster
settlement and land sales. NP officials, including President C.S. Mellen, were
reneging. After all, Northern Pacific was still recovering from its second
bankruptcy (1893). So in 1896 Sykes undertook badgering the company with a
blizzard of correspondence. He used various arguments about economic feasibility
in support of a sixteen-mile extension to later-named Bowdon. He often cited how
potential settlers were waiting on Northern Pacific for some action. After a
visit to Eureka, South Dakota, in July 1898, he wrote to Mellen:

  "Their [people of Eureka] attention is just now turned to the district in the
  western part of Wells Co. and eastern part of McLean Co., ND and I am informed
  that if your road should be extended it would be given specially to the
  station at the end of the extension. The reason for this is that the [German]
  Russian families who have gone into Wells Co. have reported so favorably that
  there will be a great exodus shortly from that part of SD to Wells Co. and
  McLean Co."(83)

Northern Pacific personnel heard Mr. Sykes. They pondered how to protect NP's
territory from inroads made by the Soo Line northwest from Carrington, and eyed
a potential coal cargo market eighty-five miles to the west in the lignite
fields near the Missouri River.(84) In March 1899, C.S. Mellen ordered
construction of the line. In April a contract was awarded, and the line was
completed to Bowdon that same year. The stage was set for further expansion onto
the coteau.

Convinced of their wisdom in establishing the Bowdon railhead, NP officials
began looking westward. Ever the expansionist, C.S. Mellen was still bent on
improving a railway he once had dubbed as "two streaks of rust across the
prairies."(85) By virtue of establishing the Bowdon site, the company's land
commissioner inflated the value of remaining NP lands to the west by 50 percent
and easily found a theoretical source of revenue to cover the higher future
construction costs over the hilly coteau area.(86) The cost per mile could
easily reach $12,000 across the Dogden range. Armed with these projections and
still wary of any Soo Line intrusion on its territory, Northern Pacific
undertook surveys in 1900 and completed a twenty-six-mile rail extension to
Denhoff in 1902.

1902 to 1904 were years of indecision for the NP. Keen on competing with the Soo
Line, company President Mellen proposed a northwesterly extension from Denhoff
across the Dogdens to the Missouri, engineering reports to its infeasibility
notwithstanding.(87)  A December 1902 reconnaissance report, citing grade
problems and rocky soils unable to sustain grain farming, finally convinced the
president of the route's folly. He settled for the suggested scaled-back,
grading-only southern route to Turtle Lake with an option to extend to the
Missouri and laying track after 1903.(88) However, he continued his assertions
that the board had given him free rein to proceed with a project. He made good
on that authority in February 1903 upon rumors that Soo Line would purchase the
Bismarck, Washburn & Great Falls Railroad (Bismarck/Wilton/Washburn). A worried
president immediately ordered bids for a Denhoff extension to the Missouri.(89)
Unfortunately, bids at the April opening were so high that Chief Engineer W.L.
Darling convinced NP brass to reject them.(90)

Matters stood here for the remainder of the summer. Decisions were not
forthcoming; the St. Paul office was deluged with pleas from developers and
favor seekers and cries for movement on extension. The NP staff had tough
questions to answer about the economics of a rail extension, questions raised in
large part by the company's nemesis, James J. Hill.(91) The NP's 1893 bankruptcy
resulted in competitor Hill of the Great Northern Railway and his friends
acquiring majority stock holdings in the troubled company. In reality, Hill ran
the NP and cast a wary eye over any Northern Pacific expansion plans. This
explains in part Charles Sanger Mellen's departure from Northern Pacific by
summer's end in 1903 for reasons of being "called back to the New Haven road
(New York, New Haven & Hartford Railroad)... to solve [its] difficult
transportation problems."(92)  On October 21, 1903, Howard Elliott, an up and
coming forty-three-year old railroad executive, was elected president and
director of the NP.

        Engraving: Howard Elliott President of the Northern Pacific Railway
        Company.

Elliott's initial handling of a Denhoff extension was austere. In reply to a
Turtle Lake developer's request for a construction timetable, he brusquely
replied he had no plans for expansion and that 1904 was not a good year to
expend any large sums of money.(93) But the Soo Line proceeded with acquiring
the Bismarck, Washburn & Great Falls Railroad that year, and Elliott took an
immediate interest in the local scene. He arranged a tour of the twelve-mile
wide, north-south valley running through central Sheridan County between Denhoff
and the coteau. He was curious about its farming and grain hauling potential. He
came away impressed and also very nervous. There were rumors that Soo Line was
contemplating an extension from Anamoose southward through the Sheridan valley,
through northern Burleigh County and then to Roosevelt (a.k.a. Marie Siding) on
the Soo Line midway between Wilton and Washburn.(94) Elliott called yet again
for a field study of a northwestern route through the hill region to the
Missouri. The engineering staff complied, and its August 6 report was again very
negative. A month later the chief engineer reported that estimated per mile
construction costs to the Missouri had risen to almost $16,000.(95)

Once more the matter rested - for six months. Elliott took no action until March
1905 when he authorized bids for a fifteen-mile extension to Station 1
(McClusky). Before low bidder D. Grant and Company of Faribault, Minnesota,
could begin work in May, Elliott had already authorized construction of
additional track miles to Station 3 (Turtle Lake). The matter was settled:
Northern Pacific had chosen a southern route to Turtle Lake that would skirt the
south slopes of Prophet's Mountain within one-half mile of William Mercer's
ranch site. On June 9 Elliott was on a roll. The NP board of directors had
authorized him to proceed at his discretion, and he then approved expenditures
for an extension from Turtle Lake to the Missouri River.(96) In the last
analysis, Northern Pacific management's action to build the Denhoff extension at
all was based not only on rival jealousy of Soo Line but also on the drawn out
realization that it was laying tracks into a region already teeming with new
settlers, a market waiting to be tapped.

        Map: 1904 Northern Pacific Ry. Construction Map

Station #2: "A Rose by Any Other Name..."

In early spring 1905 NP had finalized three new station locations on the
extension. Spacing between sites adhered to company policy at never more than
fifteen miles. Past marketing analysis had determined that farmers would
tolerate no more than seven-mile wagon hauling of grain to market. The NP's
choices for stations #1 (McClusky) and #3 (Turtle Lake) were at odds with
existing town sites. The company was unrelenting in choosing its own sites
because of a hard lesson learned at Denhoff. NP had allowed the Denhoff site as
a favor to a developer, a location whose hilly terrain had farmers fuming. This
time NP insisted the two towns had to move.(97)

The railway's solution to final townsite location and platting was to leave it
to an independent company. Officials chose businessmen Charles W. Wing of
Carrington and J. Austin Regan of Fessenden and their McLean County Townsite
Company to carry out the task.(98) Wing, especially, would move resolutely on
the issue. He himself had once faced business relocation when Northern Pacific
bypassed Newport, North Dakota, and he had to move his store to Melville and
eventually on to Carrington, moves he never regretted. NP's land commissioner
Thomas Cooper weighed in with suggestions for town names. Although the company
had no definite names in mind, provisionally it favored  "McClusky," provided
the existing plat of McClusky could be vacated. "Turtle Lake" was recommended
for station #3 because it was appropriate and well known, even though there
might be strong objections to vacating the current townsite. For station #2 he
had the name "Coteau" in mind because it was geographically appropriate.(99)

The McLean County Townsite Company hired surveyors to lay out the townsites and
draw plats. The name "Coteau" never stuck. On July 24, 1905, Wing and Regan
filed the plat of Mercer, located in the SW¼ of Sec. 2, Twp. 146-79, two miles
northwest of the Mercer Ranch site. Four days later they filed plats for
McClusky and Turtle Lake.(100)

Get Busy and Wake Up...

Construction was underway in May and Chief Engineer E.J. Pearson was confident
the project was off to a good start. An average force of teams (horses),
laborers and teamsters was being maintained. It appeared more teams would be
hired and that May construction progress reports for the first fifteen miles
would reflect 30 percent completion of grading.(101) This was welcome news in
light of an anticipated tight labor market in construction projects for 1905.
Contractors in North Dakota commonly assumed that a labor shortage could arise
by August with arrival of the harvest season in the Red River Valley.

At the beginning of July, progress had slowed and Pearson made the dour
prediction that grading work would run to mid October. The contractor, D. Grant
and Company, had pulled several teams off the Denhoff extension to work on
another project of theirs for Soo Line in Minnesota. Anticipating conflicts with
the coming harvest, Pearson urgently requested more hiring. Matters worsened on
July 26 when ten teams simply disappeared from the D. Grant camp and returned to
Fargo for harvest work. That same morning all the Austrian shovelers (steam
shovel operators) went on strike for a 25-cent wage hike to $2.00 per day, the
same as wages at Soo Line.(102) Their demands were met and work proceeded, but
without team replacements.

Pressure was mounting on Division Engineer W.C. Smith. Laborers were walking off
the job and the contractor was doing little to attract replacements. Track
laying operations began August 22, two full weeks behind schedule. Earlier he
had sacked his field engineer for drunkenness on the job, and the replacement,
J.R. Preble, was slow in responding to headquarter's requests. An exasperated
Smith fired off a broadside: "I want you to get busy and wake up and get some
life into your reports."(103)

By autumn, it was clear to everyone that Northern Pacific would be lucky to have
an operational line to Turtle Lake that year - never mind an extension to the
Missouri. In October, Smith lashed out at the contractor's field representative,
Samuel Grant, and threatened retainage on payments for non-performance. Smith
alleged that even though new labor recruits were being sent to Denhoff, no
hiring personnel were there to greet them. He accused Grant of sleeping until
noon and spending too much time hunting ducks.(104)

        Photo: The "Limited" heading east out of Mercer Station. Note ice house
        left foreground and tool house. (Courtesy Roy Nielsen, Jr.)

Rail bed grading in and near the townsite began in mid August and was 50 percent
complete a month later. As the crews moved westward and neared the Jacob Braun
farm in Section 6, Twp. 146-79 (Mercer), NP officials learned of an oversight to
negotiate a one-and-one-half acre right-of-way easement. Braun promised not to
hold up progress but did demand a $21 per acre settlement.

As grading proceeded through town, mild controversy arose concerning a longer
track siding west of Main Street to accommodate a third grain elevator. Did the
station really merit a third one considering the time and extra cost for earth
embankment requirements? It was completed nevertheless, and soon the Jamestown
branch office made recommendations for trackside facilities: a section house
(with privy, well and pump), an icehouse (twenty-ton capacity), tool house,
grain platform and a two-car stockyard. Within a month, preliminary site
recommendations were made for the grain elevator companies: Great Western
Company, Andrews and Gage, and Regan and Lyness.(105) Conspicuously absent was
recommendation for a depot.

Switches and Frogs in Place

Local grading was complete in the first week of November, and laying of rail in
Mercer commenced Monday, November 6.(106) That day, sixty laborers and one
foreman laid the entire rail span through town and one hundred feet of siding.
The following day, November 7, 1905, the remaining twelve hundred feet of siding
were installed as well as both east and west switches and frogs.(107) In the
afternoon, a temporary spur was installed and boarding cars(108) were brought
