forward: Mercer's first rail traffic. At last, an official station, and the way
was paved for a town to arise on the prairie. No one contemplated another kind
of road in the future that could threaten Northern Pacific, or the town's
livelihood for that matter.

Railroad Postscripts

1905-1906: The late season for track laying in 1905 was underscored by a heavy
snowfall to hit the area on November 27. On December 4, crews were shoveling out
railcars and equipment and clearing the track bed of drifted snow in the last
push to lay rails to Turtle Lake. The final rail was in place by December 30,
but it had been a close call. In a letter to NP's Elliott, the General Manager
placed the Denhoff to Turtle Lake extension into operation as of January 4,
1906. The following spring there was no serious consideration of an extension to
the Missouri. The three major railroads had been locked in such severe
competition that a move for expansion by one was immediately met by threats from
the others, an early twentieth century example of "mutually assured
annihilation" as it were.

        Photo: NP water tower one mile east of Mercer.

1905-1906: Almost in afterthought, NP engineers scrambled in late August 1905
for a reliable, high quality, boiler-compatible water supply for the steam
engine. During construction that year the engine was forced to tow a water
tanker on its runs. The only reliable water on the Denhoff extension appeared to
be in the Mercer vicinity. One source was a pond fed by a spring at the Mercer
Ranch site. Another was the Washburn spring located three-fourths mile east of
town - a long-time source for community water needs and its cupolaed shed still
standing today. In January 1906, Winnor, Torgerson & Shepardson Company (lumber
yard) was hired to dig two wells: one for the section house and another for a
trackside site one mile east of town to tap the Washburn vein, for a total cost
of $86.50. In March a fifty-foot water tower and windmill were constructed near
the well east of town.(109)

1906: A plea went out June 5 from the branch superintendent: "Mercer has
increased very rapidly and I am instructed to have R.F.A. prepared for a station
building."  A week later, St. Paul headquarters dutifully provided an estimate
for a two-story combination depot with living quarters of 24'× 59', including
privy and coal shed, at $2,898.(110) However, the building wasn't constructed
until late 1907 or early 1908.

        Document: Northern Pacific Railway Collection (Courtesy of the Minnesota
        Historical Society.)

1906: Dana Wright served a stint as engineer on the local railroad and
reminisced: "When running an engine for the NP Ry soon after the railroad was
built, a heavy gasoline engine on a flat car was to be spotted at a Mercer
elevator to be unloaded. On the siding east of the elevator was a string of
boarding cars occupied by an extra gang of Italians. The siding sloped rather
steeply to the east. The boarding cars had to be pulled out, the flat car picked
up behind and all shoved back till the flat car was spotted opposite the
elevator. The locomotive was a small one and had difficulty in pushing the
string of cars up the grade, and the "slack" had to be taken up and a stiff
shove given the string. This upset some of the Italian's stoves and other
furniture in their cars and they came boiling out to get revenge. No action was
taken though and we got away without getting a licking."(111)

1908: "The N.P. water tank froze up and burst the night of the 6th inst.
[December] the water ran over and froze on the track, nearly wrecked the
Limited."(112)

        Photo: January 1936. Bucking snow through Mercer Station. Note
        stockyards and Standard Oil bulk plant in background. (Courtesy of
        Richard Ketterling collection)

1913: C.S. Mellen led the New Haven road into such a huge program of expansion
and enormous expenditures that its credit almost collapsed in 1913. He resigned
that year and was succeeded - ironically for a second time - by Howard
Elliott.(113)

1950: The NP's engine and fourteen freight cars were derailed September 21,
1950, between Chaseley and Hurdsfield, North Dakota. Henry Lee, engineer, Albert
Wagner, fireman, and Ray Tschider, brakeman, were all killed in the tragic
accident when the engine's boiler exploded.(114)

1970: The Northern Pacific Railway, the Great Northern Railway, the Chicago,
Burlington and Quincy Railroad, and the Spokane, Portland and Seattle Railway
all merged into one new company: the Burlington Northern Railway.

1970-1980: Having lost the U.S. Postal mail carrier contract, the railroad went
into sharp decline when it was forced to rely on freight shipments for its
profits. Freight was reduced to just elevator grain hauls, at first to weekly
runs, later even more infrequently.

1987: The Red River Valley & Western Railroad Company acquired Burlington
Northern's Carrington branch. By then Mercer was a truck station only and no
grain rail shipments originated here.

1995: The Red River Valley & Western Railroad Company abandoned the Carrington
branch from Bowdon to Turtle Lake.

        Photo: The William Musser headstone as it appears in the Riverview
        Cemetery in Washburn. Mercer was named after him. (Courtesy of Nathan
        Grubb)

In the Beginning... By James Gessele

It was a hot July 24, 1905, when Charles W. Wing and J. Austin Regan entered the
McLean County Courthouse in Washburn to file the Mercer townsite plat.
Encompassing just over twenty-five acres of land, the less than imposing
Original Town plat was nevertheless a player among many in the trade center
fever and town boom gripping North Dakota at the time. No one had witnessed the
creation of so many prairie towns at the same time before, nor would they ever
again.

Earlier that year, Northern Pacific Railway had selected Wing and Regan, both
established businessmen, to carry out the townsite selection for the new Denhoff
rail extension to Turtle Lake about to get underway. The two men formed the
McLean County Townsite Company to purchase sites chosen by the railroad and
hired surveyors to carry out the platting. The Mercer plat they carried that
July day was not much different than the surveyor's many previous town drawings.
The charge of the day was to move expeditiously, and if that meant the railroad
towns all took on a "cookie cutter" appearance, so be it. If anything, the
sameness and lack of innovation might have a reassuring effect on potential
business development.

Following urban design standards of the day, the town layout followed a simple
grid pattern. The uniform town block of 300 feet square was adhered to,
containing lots 140 feet deep, twenty-five feet wide and backed by a twenty-foot
alley. The long narrow lots on Main Street would guarantee that buildings of
uniform shape and size would appear - usually balloon-frame, false-front stores
- the pride of every small merchant nevertheless. In addition, the plat was of
modified "T-Town" design in which the railroad, at the south end of the plat,
formed a T-crossbar to Main Street which ran northwards and perpendicular to the
tracks. This arrangement was meant to place focus on a cluster of businesses
away from the tracks and diminish the need for rail crossings.

On the face of it, Mercer's original "T-Town" layout would appear to favor
direct entrance into the town's commercial area from the north but provide
circuitous access to Main Street from the south. Indeed, an early railroad plat
reveals one principal track crossing at the far west end of town in alignment
with Second Street West. Once the town established itself as a trade center and
farmers from all directions required ready access to the grain elevators and to
Main Street from all directions, the need for a major track crossing became
readily apparent. A Main Street crossing was established early on to the benefit
of everyone, especially farmers to the south, one that remained safe throughout
the railroad's existence.

Although construction of buildings began almost immediately after the railway
went into operation and lumber could be delivered to the site, a genuine
building boom may have been somewhat stifled - ironically by existing state rail
regulations. In 1901 the state enacted legislation requiring railways to
establish and maintain agencies (depots) in towns doing a minimum $25,000 in
freight business annually. The immediate effect was for railways to shut down
many agencies that failed to reach this threshold and to wait out freight
hauling performances in newly founded towns before putting up any depots.
Freight charges in towns without an open agency were pegged at a higher rate,
thus those towns suffered reduced market areas. In 1903, none other than J.
Austin Regan, then a state senator, introduced successful legislation decreasing
the threshold to $15,000. The railroads did not immediately comply and chose to
test the law's provisions. Not until 1907 were all rail lines required to
provide daily passenger or mixed passenger-freight service. These factors taken
together may explain why Mercer depot construction was delayed to as much as
late 1907. A construction photo reveals snow on the ground, workers clad in
heavy coats, and the presence of some Main Street businesses and private
residences in the background.

        Photo: Mercer depot under construction. (Courtesy John Westerlind.)

        Photo: Mercer depot - 1907-1970 (Courtesy of Richard Ketterling
        collection)

        Photo: Section house as it appears today.

Records are unclear as to which town structures were the first to be erected,
although one can assume that the Northern Pacific's section house and a lumber
yard were the first to appear in 1906. Among kept Northern Pacific files there
is one receipt of services dated January 1906 to Winnor Torgerson & Shepardson
Company (lumber company) for the sinking of an eighty-foot well at the section
house site. The house was located north of the tracks immediately east of the
yet to be built depot. This was in contradiction to Jamestown Super-intendent
A.M. Burt's recommendation that it be built at the far west edge of town near
the planned track crossing. In 1928, depot agent F.A. Sommars bought the
structure from NP, purchased the easterly half of Lot 20, Block 7 from Alle
Dokovna, and moved the house directly northward onto this lot. In 1929 he sold
the lot and house to Emanuel Schlaht. It still stands there today at 110 First
Street East. It is also probable that an NP tool house, a grain loading platform
and the stockyards were built soon after the railway became operational, and
surely the three grain elevators were in place by 1907.

In addition to Winnor Torgerson Lumber Company, other very early entrepreneurs
included Christoph Sackmann and John Ketterling. The Sackmann family arrived in
early February 1906  from South Dakota and lived over winter on the brother-in-
law Karl Degg farm north of town. Early spring of 1906 Sackman was building
Mercer's first residence on Second Street West in Block 4 and Degg was erecting
Mercer's first livery stable on Rice Street on Lots 9-11, Block 4. Sackmann
assumed management of the livery. Neither building remains standing.

        Photo: Christoph Sackmann residence. Mercer's first family home.
        (Courtesy of Richard Ketterling collection)

        Photo: John Ketterling house. (Courtesy of Richard Ketterling
        collection)

In April 1906 the John Ketterlings arrived from Bowdle, South Dakota, where he
had been employed in the local flour mill. With some assistance from the Bowdle
people, Ketterling began erecting Mercer's own mill on the east side of Rice
Street in Block 5 and his home in Block 4 on the southwest corner of Wing and
Rice Streets. Neither building remains today.

Perhaps the second oldest residence still standing is the home on the northeast
corner of Rice and Regan Streets in Block 5. The Adolph Singer family moved into
this new home in 1907 when Singer purchased the Degg Livery Stable and Dray
Service immediately across the street. Christoph Sackmann, who had been manager
of the stable, moved on to run a butcher shop on Main Street.

An article in the March 26, 1908, issue of the Mercer Telegram gives us a
perspective of building activity up to the spring of that year and what the
speculative winds held for the immediate future. Under the headline "Watch Our
Town Grow in 1908 - Mercer Has The Trade Territory, and is Nicely Located Only
Twenty-five Minutes From Brush Lake," the editor crowed, just as was printed and
here quoted:

  "Mercer is on the verge of a boom, and will surprise its larger neighbors
  before many moons. The two most important events are the purchase of the
  South-side by James Rice, who expects to make it an attractive suburban
  addition. Not of less importance is the increasing trade territory prospects
  which will be made possible in the recent Doering enterprise [Lot 18, Block 6
  on Main Street]. Michael Doering has secured a partnership of his brothers and
  several brother-in-laws who are bankers in South Dakota and the new firm will
  give Mercer a big department store, backed by an almost unlimited amount of
  money. Sam Doering who was here two weeks ago to look over the situation was
  so well pleased with our little burg that he has sold his interests in Kramer,
  and will assist Michael in the management here. Both Sam and Mike will build
  residences and remodel the store as soon as the frost is out of the ground.
  There is no question but that Mercer will have double the brisk trade it
  enjoyed last year, coming from a much larger territory.

  "A local telephone is to be installed before April 15th. A pool hall and
  restaurant with a hall above will be erected as soon as possible. The promoter
  is A.N. Stewart who will undoubtedly give Mercer and its territory better
  booming than any other town along the extension will receive this summer.

  "The Commercial Club are getting busy, and Charlie Wise has engaged Co.
  Surveyor Breitzmann to plat lots at Brush Lake, which bids fair to become a
  popular summer resorts.

  "Every body boost together for 'All roads lead to Mercer' is the popular
  slogan of 1908."

        Photo: Adolph Singer house.

Like every other townsite agent, the McLean County Townsite Company worked
diligently at promoting lot sales and projecting an image of town growth. Unsold
lots detracted from that image and they also cost the agent in taxes. In many
instances, the agents - Charles Wing and J. Austin Regan in this case - quickly
sold off remaining lots to another developer at a profit the market would bear.
A sale was consummated in June 1908, whereby Nels Olesen purchased some unsold
property in the Original Town plat of Mercer as well as in the remaining twenty-
one unsubdivided blocks and Outlots A and B. The unsubdivided portion came to be
known as Olesen's Addition.

Olesen may have experienced a modicum of profit from his purchase. A real
building boom was apparently underway in 1909, and more realistic accounts -
laced with far less boosterism - are tellingly available from the rural
residents. Farmer Balthasar Kleingaertner reported in the July 29, 1909, edition
of the Dakota Freie Presse that "A lot of building is going on in the country as
well as in town... Georg Stoller [Stohler] is building a new home. Stoller
bought the general store from Michael Doering and is doing good business." Jakob
Schlepp reported in the November 18, 1909, edition of the same newspaper that "A
lot of construction has been going on in our town this year. We had one
lumberyard but now we already have three. Currently a new business place is
going up. In general there is a lot of construction underway. The town has
doubled in size over the past year."

By April 1909, the town's thoroughfares were getting names: Regan and Wing
Streets, named after the men who filed the town plat; Stohler Street, named
after George Stohler, the merchant who succeeded the Doering business venture;
Max Street (unclear as to who was recognized); Rice Street, in honor of James
Rice; North Street, leading to the cemetery; Railway Street, in the east side of
town paralleling the railroad along its north side; Main Street; Second Street
West; First, Second and Third Streets East. Mercer was coming into its own.

Women Homesteaders By Bev Christensen

Thousands of women took homesteads in North Dakota. Most were single women, but
around fifteen percent were widows, according to H. Elaine Lindgren in Land in
Her Own Name. Married woman were considered ineligible to acquire public lands,
unless they were the head of the household. About one percent of the women were
divorced, separated, or deserted. Many children over twenty-one, and parents
often combined homesteading efforts. Most women came with either family or
friends, and tried to stake claims close to each other. The majority of women
claiming land were between the ages of twenty-one and twenty-five. There was an
excitement in the air, as this was one of the last opportunities to be a part of
the development and growth of our country.

Although adventure was an important part of the decision, most women saw it as a
financial investment. Once one acquired the title to 160 acres, the claim became
an asset that could be sold or traded for something else of equal value.

Homesteading allowed young widows a second chance and provided a home for their
children. The older widow often settled near her grown children, as was the case
with Rev. Keller's mother-in-law, Emily Bartz.

If a woman scheduled her marriage after she filed on a claim, she could retain
the right to her homestead property if her husband was not proving up at the
same time. Both could prove up simultaneously after 1914, if they had already
lived on their separate claims for one year.

After making entry, a homesteader had six months to establish actual residence
in a house built on the land. The shack or shanty could be as small as eight by
ten feet. The small house was easier to heat and take care of, and considered
"cozy" by some. Often, fathers, brothers, or other relatives helped construct
the shack for the woman homesteader. Some men made extra money by building
shacks for homesteaders. After the shack was built, a fire break was plowed
around it to prevent burning in case of a prairie fire. A sod house or dugout
with sod walls and a dirt floor was more difficult for a woman to make livable.
It was a temporary home to live in while proving up.

The winter of 1906-07 was the worst known up to that time in the Dakotas. Many
buildings were covered completely by huge snow drifts, and the temperature
dropped to forty below many times.

As settlement progressed, the proportion of women to men increased. Many women
had other occupations that they pursued simultaneously with their homesteading.
There was a demand for schoolteachers, housekeepers, cooks, and other
occupations. Annetta McFadden worked in Mercer as a nurse and also helped in the
store while homesteading. Hattie Ovre baked bread for area bachelors while she
held down their claim by Brush Lake.

Many homesteaders met their future spouses during their homesteading days. The
hardships of homesteading were offset by the good times. There were
get-togethers for parties and dancing, card playing, picnics, baseball, and
visiting. Most women did not purchase a team of horses or oxen, but had a riding
horse or a horse and buggy.

Katherina Vossler filed on 160 acres in Section 10 of Park Township, which
joined her fiance, Jacob Just's homestead. They married on March 22, 1903, and
built their tar-paper shack on the section line where their land joined.

Juliana Hanson, a widow, homesteaded with her twelve-year-old daughter Carlie,
in 1904 in Section 2 of Wise Township. Her father, Soren Petersen, filed on a
homestead nearby at the same time. Julianna married a neighbor homesteader Jonas
Christensen in 1906 at Rev. Keller's home. The next day, the neighbors noticed
them moving her better shack up to his homestead, and learned of their marriage.
Julianna then traded her claim for Nels Olesen's adjoining homestead land to the
north.

        Photo: Carlie and Juliana Hanson. (Courtesy of Christensen collection)

Elizabeth Stein and her mother Margaretha homesteaded in Section 17 and 21 in
Medicine Hill Township in 1905. While living on her claim, Elizabeth and her
sister Margaret helped during threshing by hauling bundles. Their primary means
of transportation was walking. To keep her feet warm in the winter when she
walked to her brother John's or her mother's homestead, Elizabeth would wrap
gunny sacks around them. Then she would wet them with water, which quickly
froze. She said that kept her feet nice and warm. One winter a blizzard almost
covered her shack. She forced the door open a few inches at a time, and by
bringing the snow inside her shack, she was finally able to dig herself out. Her
sister Caroline married K.B. Presser. After Elizabeth spent the required time on
her claim, she hired out doing housework. Christ Stradinger had a homestead
beside hers. They traveled by horse and sleigh to Washburn on January 15, 1909,
where they were married.

        Photo: Elizabeth Stein. (Courtesy of Lila Stradinger)

Emma Christensen was twenty-four years old when she filed on a claim in the
spring of 1906 in Section 35 of Medicine Hill Township. Her brothers C.P.,
Martin and Fred Christensen lived nearby. Her sister Trina, who was married to
Nels Olson, lived nearby also.

        Photo: Emma Christensen. (Courtesy of Duane Christensen)

Golda Howell was 23 years old when she homesteaded on September 6, 1902, on
Section 6 in Prophet's Township, near her father, and her brother Charles. Both
Golda Howell and Emma Christensen died before they were able to prove up their
homesteads. As legal heirs, both fathers, James R. Howell and Hans Peter
Christensen filed the final homestead papers, and proved up their daughter's
homesteads.

In 1883, Olga Olson was the first white child born in what is now McLean County.
She homesteaded on Section 14-146-79 one mile south of Mercer in 1905 at the age
of twenty-two. She married Christ Thompson, a rancher from Mercer on November
27, 1908. They lived on her homestead for the final year of her five year
residency requirement to gain title to her claim.

        Photo: Olga Olson. (Courtesy of Karen Boyko)

Maggie Rensgard took up a 40 acre homestead in 1909 to provide a home for her
children. It was in Section 11 of Wise Township, just south of the Sprout
School. Maggie proved it up in 1914 with patent number 385638. She spoke
Swedish, and was said to be distrustful of men. Story has it that her homestead
shack blew over one stormy night, and that they ran for shelter to their nearby
neighbors, Jens and Sarah Bille. The Bille's lived where Joel Stradinger now
lives. Maggie's daughter Josie Johnson, married Tony Christensen, who
homesteaded the present Dave Presser's farm.

Sarah Christensen filed on a homestead in Section 24 of Wise Township in April
of 1906 at the age of twenty-one. Her parents, Peter and Johanna, homesteaded
nearby. She also had six siblings in the area that were also homesteading. They
were Nels, Jonas, Tony, Christ W., and Jorgen Christensen, and Mary (Julius)
Johnson. Sarah married a nearby homesteader, Jens Bille in 1909.

        Photo: Sarah Christensen. (Courtesy of Duane Christensen)

The women who consolidated their acres with a close relative or spouse made a
significant economic contribution to the farming operation. The increased assets
could be used for mortgages, which allowed further investment and expansion.
Some women sold their homesteads for cash or assets to invest in other ventures.
But those women who kept their land passed down a legacy to their descendants.
Many women as well as men developed a strong bond as well as a certain reverence
for the land. Although the homesteaders may have suffered greatly at times,
their lives were filled with purpose and determination. They will be remembered
as capable, strong, independent, and courageous. And they had a sense of
adventure as they helped build their new community. The homesteaders will
forever be a part of the history of Mercer.

Scandinvanian Settlers and Others By Bev Christensen

Some people say settlers were the real heroes of the west. The Norwegians were
the largest immigrant group of settlers in North Dakota. In Norway, inheritance
customs and overpopulation made the dream of holding land remote. Norway lost a
quarter of its population between 1850 and 1900, when many immigrated to the New
World. In America there were plenty of acres on new frontiers, first in
Wisconsin, and then Minnesota and Iowa. With the expansion of the railroad and
the removal of the Indian menace, Norwegians pushed on into North Dakota. It was
actually the third and fourth stages of immigration by Norwegians moving
westward across America. North Dakota was a place to farm, and they were
attracted by the availability of free or cheap land.

        Photo: Andrew Calheim. (Courtesy of Lila Calheim Stradinger)

The land they found was very different from Norway. Instead of pine trees, they
found prairie. Instead of fjords, there were potholes. Instead of mountains
that sheltered small villages, they found only openness on the prairie, and
relentless winds. Early Norwegian arrivals selected wooded land along rivers,
creeks and lakesides, leaving upland fields to be plowed by late comers.
Norwegians, like other immigrant groups, settled near their fellow country
people when possible. The familiarity of the same language, customs, and faith
gave the settlers comfort and camaraderie.

Historians say Norwegian settlers, perhaps more than other Scandinavians and the
Germans, were individualists. They were also more nationalistic in the last half
of the 19th century than were the Swedes or Danes. They feared losing their
Norwegian culture and were instrumental in organizing and patronizing private
colleges like Luther College in Iowa. The Lutheran church is credited with being
the foremost ethnic organization for Norwegians and it played a large role in
preserving their heritage. Our Savior's Lutheran Church in Mercer held Norwegian
services once or twice a month in the early days.

The Norwegians enjoyed lutefisk and lefsa with their families and friends,
especially at holidays. "Ludefisk" arrived at Mercer by the barrel in the early
days. Norwegians also enjoyed Romegrot, a sweet cream porridge.

Some early Norwegian settlers in this area were Hedahls, Totdahls, Hjelles,
Thompsons, Calheims, Fibelstads, Ovres, Berges, Petersons, Nilsons, Glads, Ole
Lockrem, Knute Lee, John Anderson, John Hogen, and Chris Walle.

Many Norwegian homesteaders filed on their claims as bachelors. They sent back
for their brides and families after they had built their shanties, and turned
the sod. Many Norwegian settlers had begun to learn English and American ways in
Minnesota or the Midwest, and fit into Dakota life with relative ease. They
mingled with their neighbors, built churches and schools to educate their
children, and blended into North Dakota life. They often stressed high school
and college level education. Settling in North Dakota took courage and faith in
the future. Today there are more Norwegians in North Dakota than any other
ethnic group. They and their Scandinavian cousins play an important role in
McLean County and North Dakota.

        Photo: Cover of a ludefisk barrel

The country of Denmark was more industrialized than Norway and most Danes were
business people. Many of them chose to leave Denmark even before the year 1870.
Between 1870 and 1914 some 300,000 Danes immigrated to North America, yet
Denmark was not as affected by this as was Norway and Sweden.

Danes quickly assimilated into American society, learning the new language and
customs. Over ninety per cent of the Danish people were Lutheran, the official
church of Denmark. It is said there were two types of Danes, "Happy" Danes, and
"Holy" Danes. Some Danish food included aebleskiver, a ball shaped pancake with
apples in the center, Danish Krem, and sweet soup, which was made with dried
fruit. Many early Danish homesteaders settled north of Mercer and started St.
Ansgar's Danish Congregation and cemetery.

Some of the Danes included Nels Olesen, Christensens, Anton Nielsen, Skows,
Sorlees, Soren Nielsen, Jake Nelsen, O.P. Nelson, Pete Nelsen, Rev. Fred
Petersen, Soren (Miller) Petersen, Pete Petersen, Sam Petersen, Ole Raasmussen,
Jens Bille, Christ Skow, Peter Nelsen, Julius Johnson, and Peter Matsen.

Between 1867 and 1870 nearly 450,000 people left Sweden because of lack of jobs
and a shortage of food. Most went to the United States and settled in the
Midwest. The Swedish language is a Germanic language that resembles Danish and
Norwegian. People from all three countries could usually understand each other.

Swedish ethnic foods include Swedish rice, herring, sardines, Swedish meatballs
and pancakes, krumkaka, and rosettes.

Some of the Swedes in this area were Robert and Victor Westerlind, Knut Widen,
Joe Peterson, John Swenson, Fred Freeberg, Peder August Fransin, alias Gust
Fransin, (The Terrible Swede), Maggie Rensgaard, Frank Carlberg, and August
Palmer.

Other ethnic groups represented in early Mercer were Jewish (Nieman, Dakovna),
Irish (Shorty Kline, McFaddens, Robert McGrath, and Sprouts), Romanians (Fred
and August Rittenbach, Carl Okert, Daniel Klatt, and Samuel Rust), Austrians
(Pressers, Fiesals, Sczelaps, Konskis, and Kulsqkskis), and others.

These various ethnic settlers had tenacity and left their legacy for future
generations. They played a major role in making Mercer what it is today. Despite
the decline in population, Mercer and the surrounding area, including Brush
Lake, continues to be a great place to live or visit.

Germans from Russia By James Gessele

Germans from Russia are not German nationals. Neither are they Russian by blood.
Theirs is a unique heritage rooted in an odyssey beginning with Catherine the
Great, a German princess who became Russian by virtue of her marriage to Czar
Peter III. After Peter's death in 1762 and her assumption of the mantle Czarina,
Catherine faced serious issues of the day. One of them was the problem of
feeding a starving populace, especially in the cities. Catherine immediately
focused on the vast, arable but largely undeveloped reaches of the Russian
steppe and remembered the frugal and efficient farmers of her home country. She
was convinced her countrymen could provide an answer. In 1763 she issued a
manifesto inviting western Europeans, especially those from the German
provinces, to settle in Russia. Included in the manifesto's promises were those
of free land, freedom from military conscription, and the freedom of one's own
language, churches and schools. The first arrivals settled in colonies on the
lower Volga River and became known as Volga Germans.

In 1804 a second proclamation was issued, this from Catherine's grandson Czar
Alexander I. The same promises were made, but the aim this time was to settle
areas north of the Black Sea - today's Ukraine - and the Crimean Peninsula.
Recruits enlisted immediately, mostly for economic and political reason. They
hailed principally from Baden, Bavaria and Wuerttemberg. The Napoleonic campaigns
of 1805-1807 interrupted immigration, but a second wave was underway after 1817.

Early life for the pioneer colonists of South Russia was rugged. Crop disasters
were the norm and disease ran rampant; nevertheless these people survived and
their colonies flourished. Usually each colony was of one religion - Lutheran,
Catholic, Mennonite, Evangelical, Baptist - and struggled to maintain its
identity. The colonies, isolated even from one another, still maintained a
distinctively common identity and culture. Mostly it was German, yet colored by
Russian influences.

By the end of the 19th century, Czars Alexander II and III had suspended most
manifesto promises, thus threatening a culture as the colonists knew it.
Dismayed and feeling betrayed, many of them emigrated to the New World by the
advent of the twentieth century. The offer of free land beckoned again, and most
headed for the prairie lands of North America. The Volga Germans settled
principally in the Southern Plains states of Kansas, Nebraska and Oklahoma; the
Black Sea Germans headed for the Dakotas and the Canadian provinces.

The first Black Sea German homesteads were established twenty miles northwest of
Yankton, Dakota Territory, in April 1873. Once most homestead land was taken up
by the early 1880s, the immigrants moved northward, still using Yankton as their
touchstone onto the Plains. They preferred South Dakota's northern counties to
its central region because they were better suited to raising wheat.

The northward tide continued and by 1885 German-Russian immigrants had landed in
McIntosh County in what was to become North Dakota. The availability of free
land and the development of railroads to get to it spurred the growth of
communities, predominantly German-Russian, across southern North Dakota. German-
Russian Baptists, who had migrated to Canada via Bessarabia (today Moldava)
across the Dobrudja in Romania, began settling in Wells County in 1884. Closer
to home, a group of immigrants from Johannestal, Odessa, South Russia settled in
the Underwood neighborhood in 1896.

With the dawn of the twentieth century, a second wave of German-Russian
immigrants arrived that would populate central and eastern McLean County and all
of Sheridan County. Hundreds arrived in 1902 from foreign soil. They were joined
by their cousins, now first generation Americans from populated regions of South
Dakota (especially the Eureka area), in search of free land and a second Dakota
home.

Upon their arrival on the plains, the Germans from Russia set out emulating a
life-style as they knew it back in the homeland. They continued their clannish,
isolationist ways and at first resisted Americanization. They clung to their
German language and were still speaking it almost exclusively in public and in
their churches fifty years after they had arrived in this country. Until the
1930s many had not learned the English language until their first school visit,
and, to make matters worse, school attendance was erratic. They disdained
compulsory education because it got in the way of their farming operations.

In their old homeland they were the prosperous farmers, the ones with better
homes, animals and fields, the leaders respected by their Russians neighbors. In
America the table had turned. They stubbornly adhered to farming practices that
worked for them in Russia but didn't necessarily guaranty success in this
country. Now they had an underdog reputation and were looked down upon by other
nationalities. Awareness of this was incentive enough to change, and it came
about gradually with the passing of time, especially in post World War II years.
From that time onward the Germans from Russia had become integrated into
American society equal to any other ethnic group.

        Map: South Russia

Nels Olesen (Our Town Dad)

Nels and Trina (Christensen) Olesen By Beverly Christensen

Nels Olesen came to the Mercer area in 1903 and homesteaded in Medicine Hill
Township. He was an interesting and multi-talented early promoter of Mercer. In
fact, you could call him an entrepreneur. After proving up his homestead, he
became Mercer's first postmaster, built and ran the first hotel at Mercer, and
was the first editor of Mercer's newspaper, The Mercer Telegram.

Nels Olesen was born in Denmark in 1875. His father, Rasmus Olesen was born Nov.
2, 1833. Rasmus married Maren Sorensen in 1858 in Denmark. They were blessed
with thirteen children, nine boys and four girls, but three of Nels' siblings
died in infancy. Nels came to the U.S. in 1883 with his parents and family, and
they settled near Hutchinson, MN in McLeod County. Nels attended two years of
high school and then a year at Trinity Seminary at Blair, Nebraska. He also
attended Ansgar College in Hutchinson, Minnesota.

He served a term as postmaster at Heatwole, south of Hutchinson, followed by
three years of mercantile life.

        Photo: Trina (Anna) Kathrine Christensen

Nels married Trina (Anna) Kathrine Christensen of Hutchinson on October 6, 1899.
Trina was born August 10, 1877, to Hans Peter Christensen and Anna Fredrickson.
Both her parents were born in Denmark. Hans immigrated in 1864, and Anna in
1866. They settled in a Danish community in Chicago, but were forced to move
after the Chicago fire. Her parents then settled at Hutchinson, where they were
married. Trina's twin Metta died at the age of two.

Trina's brothers, Chris P. and Martin Christensen homesteaded at Mercer in 1902.
Nels and "Anna" Olesen also caught the homestead fever, and came to North Dakota
in 1903. Nels homesteaded 7 miles north of Mercer in Sect. 34 in Medicine Hill
Township. He proved up his claim by commutation in 1906. (The 5-year residency
requirement was waived upon payment for the land at the rate of $1.25 to $2.50
an acre after a fourteen-month residency, and cultivation).

Trina's brother Fred Christensen, homesteaded nearby in 1906. Their twenty-four-
year-old sister Emma, also took up a claim just north of C.P.'s homestead that
spring. Unfortunately, Emma got sick and died of pneumonia that fall.

More sadness struck the Olesens around 1906, when two of their sons died. Hans
Christian Olesen, born in 1900, and baby Lawrence Edward Olesen are buried in
the Danish Cemetery 7 miles north of Mercer.

Their other children born at Mercer were Victor Nathaniel, born January 9, 1902,
Raymond Henry, born July 9, 1905, Myrtle E, born May 27, 1909, and twins Alphina
Christine and Omina Hansine, born April 28, 1911. Violet Eleanor was born
February 14, 1914, at Norma, ND, and Virgil Grenora Olesen was born November 6,
1916, at Grenora, ND.

        Photo: Raymond and Victor Olesen

Nels Olesen was appointed Mercer's first Postmaster when the Post Office was
chartered on October 2, 1905. He held that position for one year.

In 1906-07, Nels hired Fred Sorenson to build the first hotel in Mercer. He
named it Hotel Olesen. It was located on lots 3 and 4 of block 5. In March of
1908, he installed a fine cigar stand, and did good business. Nels sold the
hotel to Ole S. Hedahl in Sept.1908. The wood building burned, and was rebuilt
in 1910.

The May 7, 1908, Telegram reported Nels Olesen and family were comfortably
settled in their new home. Nels was elected a Mercer Township supervisor in
1908, and in 1910, was elected Justice of the Peace in Mercer.

Nels was the publisher of the newspaper, The Mercer Telegram. The first issue
was published August 20, 1907, and W.T. Wasson was the proprietor. Jennie Nelson
was the typesticker in 1908.

On June 3, 1908, while returning home from Hutchinson, MN, Nels Olesen purchased
the Mercer town site from Regan and Wing, plus the half section joining the west
side of the town. He advertised a special sale of lots for the next thirty days.
Two weeks later, Nels had sold twenty-five lots. The additional west lots are
called the Olesen addition, and were sold later.

Nels and his wife held meetings of the newly formed Commercial Club at Hotel
Olesen. He spent considerable time and money promoting the growth of Mercer.

Nels donated a block north of the depot telegram office on the east side of Main
Street in June 1908 for the development of a town park. Martin Wassenberg broke
it up, and the Commercial Club planted the trees that are still there today.

Nels purchased The Mercer Telegram in January of 1909. In June, his brothers,
H.P. and Ole Olesen of Hutchinson visited "Editor Olesen at Mercer."

In May 1909, Sorensen and Meadley Well Drillers dug a 125 foot well on Nels farm
south of the tracks. His land joined the town site. In June of 1909, The Mercer
Telegram reported "Editor Olesen is building a four roomed cottage on one of his
numerous lots east of town. When completed, it will be occupied by Mr. and Mrs.
George Heinze." George worked in the Telegraph office. This house is now the
residence of Emma (Emanuel) Hinsz.

That fall, Nels bought three horses from Nels Peterson, and prepared for
farming. Nels Olesen was also the Superintendent of the newly reorganized
Norwegian Lutheran Sunday School the fall of 1909.

Nels Olesen was listed as the cashier of the new bank at Mercer in the Dec. 10,
1909, Telegram. O.S. Hedahl was the vice president. In the February 11, 1910,
Mercer Telegram, Editor Nels wrote, "About a year ago, I purchased The Mercer
Telegram from W.T. Wasson. Ten months from that date, I sold out to George
Heinze, figuring on taking up the banking business. But I soon found that the
banking business is not half as interesting as the newspaper work. Therefore I
resigned from the bank and now have bought half interest in the Telegram."

The following article was found in the March 4, 1910, Mercer Telegram, "A NARROW
FIRE ESCAPE-The furnace in the Telegram building became overheated last Saturday
morning, and caused quite an exciting time to the occupants. Before seating
themselves at the breakfast table last Saturday morning, the family of George
Heinze shut off the registers of the furnace on account of the warm weather. In
about 15 minutes, one of the girls went into the parlor, where she saw smoke and
flames issuing from the wall above and around the register, and called out
"Fire!" The Rev. Mr. Sapp, who had been a guest of the family the evening
before, rushed into the kitchen, grabbed the water pail and into the parlor he
went, while George went to the phone, called up central, who gave the alarm. In
less time than it takes to tell, about 50 men gathered with water pails and
chemical fire extinguishers, while the water tank stood outside the door. After
several boards were ripped off and the base of the fire discovered, it was
gotten under control and easily put out." That fall, a new printing office
measuring 24 × 40 feet was constructed.

In March 1910, Nels Olesen had a well drilling machine, which dug a
seventy-foot well for Sam Okert, with good water. He hired Martin Wassenberg as
foreman of the Olesen Well Digging Company. That month Nels purchased a quarter
section of land.

In the spring of 1910, the Mercer Coopertative Company was organized by local
farmers. The company purchased George Stohler's Store building, lots and stock.
There were about fifty subscribers and Nels Olesen was elected Secretary of the
Board.

The fall of 1910, Nels Olesen and C.G. McLaughlin held a big auction.

Nels' father, Rasmus Olesen, died April 26, 1911, at the home of Nels' sister,
Mrs. S. Simonsen of Daneville, ND. Nels and Anna's twin daughters were born two
days later, so he was unable to attend his father's funeral and burial at
Daneville.

In 1912, Nels apparently also began to practice law. The Mercer Telegram, May
17, 1912, ran this notice, "Nels Olesen vs. Peter Olson and Anton Peterson,
Estate of Carl Peterson, late of Mercer."

The spring of 1912, Nels Olesen ran for the legislature in the 46th district. He
lost in June, and seemed to become discouraged after that effort. In July 1912,
Nels Olesen and J.R. Washburn formed the Mercer Land and Stock Company, with
their office in the Telegram building.

Nels decided to sell the newspaper, and other interests, and started to do
evangelistic preaching. He sold the newspaper March 1, 1913, to Trix Monson of
McClusky, but got it back five months later. A short time later, he finally got
rid of it for good.

Around 1913, Olesens moved to Norma, N.D., near the Danish settlement at
Kenmare, N.D. He ran a small newspaper there for about two years. Next, Nels and
his family moved to Grenora, N.D., where he practiced law briefly. From there
they moved to Minneapolis. In 1927, they moved to California, where Rev. Olesen
pastored Assembly of God Churches. In 1939, they moved to Chico, CA, where they
resided the remainder of their lives.

Nels Olesen died on August 19, 1950, at Chico, California. Trina "Anna" died on
February 11,1959, and they are buried in the Chico Cemetery.

        Photo: Nels and Trina Olesen's wedding picture. (Photo courtesy of Duane
        Christensen.

Mercer's Roads and Highways By James Gessele

The prairie landscape dictated where trails were posted. If the traveler
encountered a body of water or high terrain, he simply made a detour. The trails
immediately took on a meandering characteristic. Once settlers populated their
claims, fences and grain fields identified the holdings, and traffic was
diverted to section or quarter section lines. A roadway system evolved
resembling a grid pattern.

State lawmakers were quick to recognize the grid system and declared that
thirty-three feet on either side of the section line were dedicated for public
roadways. In 1899, state legislators also handed responsibility for these
roadway corridors to county commissioners or township boards. With the state
abrogating its responsibility, it was left to these government entities to
decide on roadway location or even which section lines could be closed where no
need for a road was demonstrated. Therefore, roadway conditions from one locale
to another varied as to the whims of local leaders.

Early issues of The Mercer Telegram made it clear that town fathers actively
supported a better road system. This was mirrored in their commercial slogan
"All Roads Lead to Mercer," a campaign to attract increased commerce through
growth of the town and from farmers seeking a market. A March 26, 1908, Telegram
banner touted: "Mercer Has The Trade Territory and is Nicely Located, Only
Twenty-five Minutes from Brush Lake." Clearly, automobile speeds were not
setting travel time standards. The Mercer Commercial Club actively lobbied the
County Commissioners to build a road north of town and in June 1908 they won a
concession.

The first roadways were but a slight improvement over prairie trails. Miniscule
construction funds precluded doing much excavation. Small amounts of excavation
were taken up from the prairie soils and placed in the roadway's center. To
achieve uniform grade in level areas, in-place materials were "drifted" back and
forth. Occasionally horse-drawn scrapers were utilized, but the blade grader,
powered by horses or a tractor, was the equipment of choice. Shoulders and ditch
sections were unheard of. Ultimately this road design failed miserably for the
faster automobiles coming on the scene, and roadways were not convenient for the
growing through traffic.

Mercer's first auto owner was John Thurlow, local section foreman for the
railroad and apparently the town's first and only auto rental agency. The June
19, 1908, Telegram headlined Thurlow's garage as the "Mercer Auto Livery" and
that customers had already lined up to rent the vehicle. It went on that the
town - in sharp contrast to earlier claims of twenty-five minutes - was now only
one minute from Brush Lake. Little could Thurlow know how Dakotans would take to
the horseless carriage. A January 5, 1917, Telegram article cited telling 1916
statistics from the Washburn Leader. 553 cars were registered in McLean County
in 1915; in 1916 there were 1,148, an average of one car for every thirteenth
county resident.

The administration of roadway construction and maintenance, as left to the
counties and townships, was adequate for the time. A State Highway Commission
was created in 1913, albeit a weak one with no funding and serving only in
advisory capacity. But Mercer's leaders worked diligently for better roads
within a system facing some serious challenges. A Telegram article of June 2,
1916, provides insight into how it all worked:

  "Road work started in earnest in this township Wednesday morning with an
  excellent crew of men and teams under the supervision of Road Overseerer [sic]
  Miller and will continue until the appropriation of $1500 is expended. Several
  of the streets in town will be put in shape and Main Street graveled and after
  that the main traveled roads leading into town will be worked. The [Township]
  Supervisors will work in connection with the plans of the County Commissioners
  in shapeing [sic] the road leading to Wilton so that the county grading outfit
  can get over here when our township has completed the necessary preliminary
  work for the grader. The road will also have to be surveyed. The improvement
  of this road in dollars and cents will be the biggest accomplishment in the
  history of the township. [I]t will stimulate trade to the town that we have
  been unable to get in the past and in grain hauling time enable a large number
  of farmers to haul bigger loads than has been customary in the past."

        Photo: Early road grading led by John Ketterling. (Courtesy of Richard
        Ketterling collection.)

Within a month of this report, President Woodrow Wilson signed the Federal Aid
Road Act, a move that would profoundly alter the state's road system.(1) Now
federal funds for road improvements were available premised on participating
states having a state highway department to supervise construction and
maintenance. Before the state could even take up enabling legislation,
townspeople became engaged in the issue. In the fall of 1916 James Rice ran for
state representative on a platform promising Mercerites a loud voice in
determining a state road system. At year's end the Telegram was trumpeting the
possibility of a main road between Wilton and Butte passing through Mercer.(2)

The Legislature established the State Highway Commission in March 1917 and
meetings were held throughout the summer in mapping a state highway system. In
November it published a tentative system map proposing almost 2,300 miles of
state-wide road, including a road from Turtle Lake eastward through Sheridan
County, the future Highway 7.(3) It did not include a state road from Wilton to
Butte. It was a great plan that soon encountered a major hurdle: U.S.
involvement in World War I. The ensuing equipment, material and manpower
shortages effectively halted construction for the next four years.

Faced with growing motorized traffic and no forthcoming road improvements,
community groups and businessmen had little recourse but to work with existing
primitive conditions. Private groups took renewed interest in limited powers
granted them in the 1913 highway legislation. They were sanctioned to
participate in improvements and marking of roads as long as they worked with
county commissioner approval. So they banded together in trail associations to
promote traveler trade, designating roadways as trails and marking them with
various colors painted on posts and poles along the route. Appropriate
signboards with colored arrows to indicate turns were supplied.(4) Thus arose
the Red National Trail to denote what was to become US Highway 10 (I-94), Blue
Trail for the later Highway 7 (200), and Red Trail (McLean County 25) for what
became and still is a county road from Wilton to Highway 7 near Turtle Lake.(5)

In 1921 Congress approved an increase in federal aid to highways. Participating
states had to identify a system of primary interstate and secondary intercounty
routes, and maintenance of highways was mandatory. The state wasted little time
and, by 1922, the approved state highway system included - now with designation
numbers - Highway 7 across the state and Highway 41 from Wilton to Mercer and
from Turtle Lake to Ruso. Again, no state road was mapped between Mercer and
Butte.(6)

Grading got underway seriously in the 1920s to the extent the decade was marked
as one of the most active in state road construction. More sophisticated design
and equipment came into play. Roadways were surveyed and ditch sections became
standard. A recommended road construction team included two tractors, an
elevating and a blade grader, forty head of horses, six-eight fresnos (scoop
excavators drawn by four horses), and fifteen 1½ cubic yard dump wagons.(7) The
elevating grader or "mucker" proved the most revolutionary for the time, for it
excavated and conveyed ditch cut materials directly onto the roadway or into
dump wagons.

In June 1922, the State Highway system map identified a few miles of Highway 7
west of Turtle Lake as earth graded to new standards. Only twenty miles of
roadway were graveled throughout the state.(8) By contrast, in June 1927 the map
revealed Highway 7 from Turtle Lake to McClusky had been earth graded and
graveled, 1,338 miles of state road were graveled and ten miles had been paved -
the ten-mile stretch of Highway 10 west of Fargo.(9) Highway 7 from Turtle Lake
at that time followed the south lines of Lake Williams and Wise Townships, then
turned southward into Mercer. It coursed along Wing Street and First Street
East, turned eastward and paralleled the north side of the railroad tracks,
staying on the section line out of McLean County and following a meandering
course across the northern tier sections of Pickard Township.

After 1923, roadways no longer had color markings. Highways were now posted with
a new Indian head marker and the highway number in the center. Chief Engineer W.
G. Black selected the Indian motif modeled after the profile of the Hunkpapa
Sioux named Red Tomahawk. As a sergeant in the Indian police he had gained
notoriety for his involvement in the shooting death of Sitting Bull.(10) The
late 1920s saw the first serious attempts at highway snow removal. Early policy
had been to avoid snow removal, leaving it on the roadway and packing it to such
a depth that later snowfalls would not collect on it. If roads were blocked with
drifted snow, they remained that way until local crews cleared the roadways - by
hand. "Maintenance" began with onset of the spring thaw, and snow was placed on
bare spots "to improve and prolong the sledding."(11) In 1928 snow fences were
installed at strategic locations and by the early 1930s the Highway Department
was acquiring snow removal equipment.(12)

In response to joblessness during the Depression, Congress increased federal aid
to the states even more in 1930. Requests for road improvements poured in but
the state had no matching funds. At the end of 1930 the federal government
relented and advanced the state $1.3 million. From 1930 to 1939 the state
expended $51.5 million which the federal government provided as non-matching
emergency aid.(13) It provided thousands of jobs to men, most of them farmers.

Highway 41 was completed during this era. By April 1932, the roadway had been
graded and graveled from Wilton to twelve miles north. 1932 saw grading of the
road to Mercer and the final stretch was graveled in 1933.(14)

North Dakota Highway Commission Official State Maps

Postscripts

1952: Highway 7 was totally reconstructed and given a new alignment. It
      immediately came under attack from the public for being too narrow.
1952: McLean County voters approved a five-mill levy for the construction of
      farm to market roads.
1959: Highway 41 regraded and graveled.
1961: Highway 41 paved
1964: Highway 7 widened and paved
1964: McLean County voters approved a ten-mill levy to provide for bituminous
      surfaced farm to market roads. County Road 33 (Mercer to Butte) was hard
      surfaced under that program.
1970: Highway 7 redesignated as Highway 200
