BANKS

The First State Bank of Mercer

        Photo: The white building on the corner was the First State Bank of
        Mercer.

The First State Bank of Mercer opened on November 19, 1909, with $10,000 capital
stock. Nels Olesen was the first cashier and served in that position for one
year. T.L. Beiseker was president and O.S. Hedahl was vice president. The
building was destroyed (damaged) in the Main Street fire of August 1910. It was
rebuilt, reorganized and managed by O.S. (Ole) Hjelle. William Lierboe and
R.T. Lierboe of Turtle Lake were the bank officers. Mr. Hjelle continued as
cashier until the bank became a casualty of the bank crash in 1929.

        Document: An ad in the Telegram.

The tin-clad building became the home of the Mercer Post Office for many years.
At the present time, it is the shop for the Jans Construction Company.

        Photo: The tin-clad bank building still stands.

        Document: A check written from bank funds April 11,1931.

Mercer State Bank

        Photo: Mercer State Bank, 1913, F.O. Freeberg, cashier. (Photo courtesy
        of Evelyn Freeberg)

The Mercer State Bank was organized in 1910 and opened on February 13, 1910.
T.L. Beiseker was president and O.S. Hedahl was vice president. F.O. Freeberg
was recruited from the First National Bank in Kenmare, North Dakota, to serve as
the cashier. The bank was/is located in the northeast corner of the McFadden
(Freeberg) Store. The bank was managed by Mr. Freeberg and his son Conrad until
August 1944, when it was voluntarily liquidated and a pay station in Mercer was
established by the Farmers Security Bank of Washburn. After the death of F.O.
Freeberg, Conrad continued as cashier until his death in February 1967.

At the request of many of the customers, Harold Hepper and Art Froehlich of the
First National Bank of McClusky established a branch office in Mercer in May
1967. The bank/store combination was remodeled. The branch office is still
operational.

The early banks did complete banking operations and wrote life and fire
insurance and made loans. Also available were steamship tickets for persons who
wanted to travel to the "old country."

        Photo: The present bank is a branch office and still operational.

BARBER SHOPS  (Tonsorial artists)

One of the first barbers in Mercer was Walter Christianson who commuted from
McClusky. His ad appeared in the Mercer Telegram in 1910. Soon after (1915),
Bill Norris began his long career as Mercer's barber. Other remembered barbers
were L.H. Harrum, Clarence Logue, Alvin Just, Joe Berg and Tom Merkel.
Apologies to those omitted.

The services provided shaves, haircuts, shampooing, massages and singeing.
Always available for sale were talcum powder, face cream and hair tonic.

There hasn't been a resident barber in Mercer for many years.

BARS/ SALOONS/ POOL HALLS

There has been "fire water" available since the appearance of the white man in
the Dakota Territory. There were places where alcohol was available in Mercer
since early days. These were often in combination with food or recreation, such
as in the pool halls. There were several "blind pigs" in the community. These
were usually shacks on the edge of town which sold illegal booze - either
purchased or home brewed. In the December 1910 edition of the Telegram, there
was an item about the raiding of one of the "blind pigs."  During the
prohibition days, there was a lot of boot-legging, with stills located in the
various areas, especially in the hills of the Prophets. A 1916 item told about
the conviction of one of the boot leggers.

In Mercer one of the remembered places was on the east side of Main Street in
the building which at one time was Logue's Variety Store and Barber Shop and
later Herb Gaub's Hardware and Plumbing. The location is the present residence
of Stan and Angie Misek. Another was on the west side of Main Street and was
located in the building of the early meat market and locker plant. This
building was replaced by Jim Murray Construction. The names of the
establishments varied with the owners.

The building that has been utilized for many years as a bar is the present
Chester's Lounge on Main Street. It is the original little white school house
which was moved from the school grounds in the 1920s. Originally it was a two-
room building. In the 1970s Arnold Schlafman built an addition. At the present
time, it is the only bar in Mercer, and the owners of Chester's Lounge are Al
Toman and Les Petryzen.

There are no complete records of saloon/bar operators. The following are
recollections by persons in the community. The list is not complete and
apologies to the ones omitted. The recalled names are Harry Kline, Gary and
Betty Flemmer, Walter Hoff, Alvin Bracket, Arnold Schlafman, Ed Pederson, Dan
Ketterling, Mike Bauer, Otto Hulsebus, Carl Littke, Howard Brewster, Dusty
Fandrich, Jack Hansen, Dean Diede, John Lippert, Fred Eckman and Gordon Schell.

The early pool halls were part of eating places and were located on the west
side of Main Street. Some early ones who advertised in the Telegram were
McComb's Pool Hall and the City Billiard Parlor. The first pool hall was
operated by Melvin McComb, Charles McLaughlin and Nels Peterson in 1908.

In August 1910, fire destroyed the pool hall, town hall and the First State
Bank. The pool hall was rebuilt and opened in September 1910 with a dance and
music by the Mercer Orchestra. According to the ad in the Telegram, this
building had a soda fountain, ice cream parlor and a ladies' room in the front
end. In December 1916, it had a bowling alley.

Bill Norris and Chris Nelson were managers in 1916. Others known to have
operated a pool hall are Chris Skow, Ed Peterson, Martin Peterson, Shorty Kline
and Ted Neumiller. Apologies to those omitted.

Many of the later cafes had a pool table in addition to tables for cards and
other games. At the present time, there is a pool table in Chester's Lounge.

        Photo: One of the early pool halls. Some of the people identified are
        (from left) Christ Stradinger (partially hidden), Tom Gardiner, Bill
        Ladwick, Martin Wassenberg and Mike Swartoine. (Courtesy of Edna
        Stradinger Glad)

MERCER BLACKSMITHS

The front page poem about Mercer that appeared in the Mercer Telegram on
September 24, 1909,   has a line that says, "Blacksmiths shops just two."
Further research in the Telegram notes that in April 1908, Samuel Okert was a
blacksmith in the King building on Main Street. At the same time, Daniel
Fandrich was a blacksmith who had a business called the Pioneer Shop which was
located south of the livery barn. Fandrich's shop was sold to Samuel Okert in
February 1909.

        Photo: John Gardiner. (Courtesy of Willa Gardiner Murray)

The Telegram further notes that two blacksmiths left in June 1909. They were
named Lacey and Demming. John and Tom Gardiner bought out Lacey. So the two
blacksmiths referred to in the poem were Samuel Okert and Tom Gardiner.

Karl Rennich bought out Gardiner in March 1911 and operated the shop until he
suddenly died of pneumonia in October 1933. The newer Rennich shop was located
on the west side of north Main Street. After his death, it remained unoccupied
until it burned down in the 1950s. The location is now occupied by the home of
Gerald Schlafman.

In addition to his blacksmith and repair skills, Karl Rennich was a blacksmith
artisan who forged crosses, fences and gates for cemetery lots. No doubt it
was a skill he learned in South Russia where the iron works were used to
decorate the graves.

The illustrated cemetery gate was hand crafted by Rennich circa 1928 and was
part of a fence around the Rennich plot in the Mercer Hillside Cemetery. In the
early 1960s, the gate and fence were removed because of crumbling concrete in
which they were set and an overgrowth of lilac bushes. In March 2001, the gate
was donated by the Rennich family to the Germans from Russia Heritage Society in
Bismarck. It has been placed on display at the entrance of the Society's
headquarters in Bismarck. In the Zion Lutheran Cemetery south of Mercer, stand
seven wrought iron crosses (schmiedeiserne Grabkreuze) made by Karl Rennich
between 1911 and 1920. They were made to mark the graves of the children of the
Friedrich and Rosina Just family. In August 2002, a replica of Rennich's iron
crosses was made on the anvil and forge by Karl's grandson, Mervin Rennich. It
was placed over the Rennich graves in the Mercer Hillside cemetery.

        Photo: (Photo courtesy of Merv Rennich)

Rust's Machine and Mfg. Co.

        Photo: Andrew Rust with one of the popular Rust Bale Bunchers
        manufactured at the Rust Machine & Mfg. Co. plant at Mercer.

Andrew and Ida Rust bought the Gardiner blacksmith shop in 1945. It was renamed
Rust Machine Shop. In 1954 it was rebuilt to include a machine manufacturing
firm. The new building is located along North Dakota Highway #200 and is
presently Ray Murray's shop. The office was located in the front part of the
new 40 by 100-foot steel building where Ida did the bookkeeping for their
manufacturing business. The popular Rust Bale Buncher was one of the ideas that
Andrew had in mind for some time before making it. After Andrew's death in
1973, Ida sold the business to Paul Robey of Minneapolis and Dwight Enockson of
Washburn.

The present Mercer Machine Shop is owned and operated by Ron Schatz. After
working for the Rust Manufacturing Shop for seventeen years, he opened his
business in 1985. The building was originally the Jake Braun and then Christ
Heim garage on Main Street.

Ron grew up on a farm near Regan and his interest in welding began as a young
boy. He took an auto body repair course at Bismarck Junior College but found
out that he didn't like that kind of work. Ron is a "90s" blacksmith. He
doesn't have to heat his metal and hammer it to form or shape it. Instead he
puts it in a lathe or metal press, flips a switch and the job is done.

        Photo: Ron Schatz at work. (Photo by Bev Christensen)

CAFES/RESTAURANTS

In the early days, cafés/restaurants/coffee shops and lunch counters were in
combination with the hotel, saloons/bars and pool halls. The 1908 issues of the
Telegram had ads for the McComb's Pool Hall and Restaurant and the City Billiard
Parlor operated by McLaughlin and Peterson which had a pool room and amusement
hall with a lunch counter.

        Photo: The Eckman Cafe: seated in back, Jake Singer. The other two are
        unidentified. Helen and Fred Eckman are behind the counter. (Photo
        courtesy of Dennis Eckman)

A pool hall/restaurant managed by McComb and Knecht burned in the August 1910
Main Street fire. It was rebuilt and opened within a month. According to the
ad, it had a soda fountain, ice cream parlor and featured a ladies' room in the
front end.

The longest surviving and best remembered restaurant/recreation establishment
was Sam's Café first owned by Doxie and Sam Norris. It was in the building known
as the little white school house built in 1907 and moved from the school yard to
Main Street. The building, with an addition, is still in use as Chester's
Lounge. After Sam died, Doxie married Merle Berge and they continued to operate
the café until 1957 when it was sold to Herbert and Melvie Wanner. The Wanners
and the John Daffe family operated the restaurant. It was during this time that
Highway #41 was improved and paved and Sam's Café was open 24 hours a day. Meals
were served family style to accommodate the shift workers as construction was
underway day and night. Other remembered managers of Sam's Café were the John
Makeeffs, Albert Klines and Howard and Vivian Brewster. Apologies to omitted
ones.

        Photo: Rolly Seibold in the doorway of Sam's Cafe.

        Photo: Arlo Eckman's fifth birthday party with his friends. (Courtesy of
        Dennis Eckman)

In the early 1940s, Eckman's Palace (the Cozy Inn) was operated by Fred and
Helen Eckman. It was located in a building south of the Freeberg Store. It had a
café and sold ice cream, candy and soft drinks. Other buildings on Main Street
which were eating places at various times and some of the managers were Chris
Skow, Ed Pedersons, Ervin and Eileen Schell and the Orman Ice Cream Parlor.

Throughout the years, food has been available at the Brush Lake pavilion and at
the Skaley Store where Gertie Skaley served many people. At the present time,
the Brush Lake Diner in the pavilion is available for dining from Memorial Days
(sometimes Mother's Day) until Labor Day. The hours are Friday to Sunday with
longer hours for holidays.

At the present day, there is no eating place in Mercer.

CAR DEALERS

There are telegram ads that indicate the earliest car dealer in town was the
Hedahl Brothers who sold Fords. See picture on page 414. Later McFadden and then
McFadden/Freeberg advertised cars. In the late 1920's, Jake Braun sold
Chevrolets and the Heim-Just Garage probably sold Pontiacs.

The Hedahl garage was located behind the store and was in existence until the
spring of 2004 when it was burned. Ole Hedahl was the mechanic.

CITY FEED MILL

Shortly after the arrival of the Ketterling family (John, Olga, Richard, age six
and Ida, age four) in Mercer in April 1906, land was purchased for a mill and a
family home.

In his hometown of Bowdle, S.D., John had worked for the Bowdle Roller Mill
Company. With their encouragement and support, he decided to build and operate a
flour/feed mill in the young village of Mercer.

        Photo: The City Feed Mill in Mercer, Johannes Ketterling, owner.
        (Courtesy of Richard Ketterling collection)

Two buildings were quickly built, the mill in Block 5 across the street from the
Singer-Berreth Livery on Rice Street and the family home on Lots 1, 2, 3 on
Block 4. The connection with the Bowdle Mill was continued and the Mercer City
Mill sold Diamond and Kaiser (Bowdle) Flour. Farmers would bring their own wheat
and oats to the mill to be ground into flour and cereal products.

In addition to the usual activities of a mill (grinding and cleaning grain),
John also operated what was one of the first cream buying stations in the area.
John operated the mill until the middle of the 1930s. It was damaged by a
cyclone in the 1920s but was operational. In the summer of 1935, the building
was torn down and the lumber was used to build a house in Block 14 for Richard's
family.

CREAM STATIONS

The cream buyer was a vital person in the community because the farmers needed a
place to bring their cream to be sent to the market. Many of the early cream
stations were part of an existing business, e.g., the City Feed Mill. The cream
was tested by the buyer for butter fat content and this was used to determine
the amount of the "cream check."  The buyer then sent the cream in the cans by
rail to a creamery in Carrington or Jamestown. In later years, the cream was
picked up by truck and hauled to a creamery in Mandan.

Attempts to begin a creamery in Mercer failed. The farmers also brought their
eggs to the grocery stores and these were exchanged for groceries. Sometimes
during the summer months, cream was not taken in on Saturdays due to the Sunday
layover and no refrigeration.

In the August 25, 1911, edition of the Telegram, this item appeared: "Mercer is
known as the cream station of the Northern Pacific. Two years ago, the train
crew called this the 'beer station.'  At that time we had full cases of beer
shipped in and we returned the empties and were money out. Now we ship out full
cans of cream and have the empties returned to us and we are money ahead."

Some of the early cream buyers were Christoph Singer, James and Ira Washburn,
Emil Schlaht, Ross Gardiner and John Ketterling. Apologies to those omitted.

GRAIN ELEVATORS

The three elevators were on the Mercer skyline by 1910.

The one remaining elevator today (2004) was the farthest east and began as the
Great Western Elevator and was built in 1908. The first manager was James Rice
who resigned after a year. The next manager was A.B. Greenfild. In 1911, Crown
Elevators bought out the Great Western. This elevator was then sold to the
Peavey Grain Company. In the 40s a corporation was formed by farmers in the
Mercer area and called the Mercer Farmers Elevator, Inc. The present owner is
Merlyn Skaley. It was demolished in November 2004.

The middle elevator was built in 1910 by the Andrews Grain Company who owned it
until the mid 1940s. The first manager was Herbert Wiest. He continued until
Halfdon Berge became manager. One of the second helpers, Richard Ketterling
became the manager of the Andrews Grain Elevator in Dunseith, N.D. This elevator
was bought out by the Peavey Grain Company.

        Photo: The Mercer elevators with the section house and depot in the
        background. (Circa 1910)

        Photo: Christian Stradinger (right, holding pail) was manager of the
        Regan and Lyness Elevator. (Courtesy of Edna Stradinger Glad collection)

The last manager was John Miller. The elevator was burned by the Mercer Fire
Department in 2000.

The west elevator was the Regan and Lyness and a long-time manager was Christ
Stradinger. The Mercer Elevator Co-op was formed in March of 1909. As the
picture below illustrates, the entry for the grain haulers was on the south side
with the driveway along the south side. This elevator was torn down after WWII
and it became part of the annex for the eastern elevator.

        Photo: Steamer tractor pulling empty grain wagons north along Main
        Street

Sale of Petroleum in Small Town Mercer By James Gessele

Little information is available concerning the sale and distribution of gasoline
and oil in Mercer's early years. Obviously its inhabitants and surrounding
farmers needed kerosene for heating, cooking and light. They needed gasoline for
the burgeoning use of automobiles and tractors. With the inception of statehood
in 1889, North Dakota's fledgling communities already felt the presence of a
major oil company. An August 15, 1889, issue of the Larimore (North Dakota)
Pioneer printed an ad for a local dray service advertising itself as an agent
for Standard Oil products conveniently located across from the railway depot.(1)

Within few years Standard Oil Company of Indiana was playing an active but
stormy role in the state's commerce. An article in a 1908 issue of the local
newspaper, The Mercer (North Dakota) Telegram, attested to this when it revealed
that State Secretary Alfred Blaisdell leveled charges of unfair pricing against
the company.(2) Apparently Standard Oil charged higher prices for its products
in towns where it faced little or no competition. It was the era of Teddy
Roosevelt's trust busting, when large corporations faced charges of collusion
with one another in cornering markets for their products. Another common charge
made against Standard Oil was that it had forged sweetheart deals with the NP
Railroad for exclusive delivery of its oil products to the small prairie towns.

On a local level, the need for gasoline was apparent early on. The June 19,
1908, issue of the Telegram carried a headline, "The Mercer Auto Livery" and
heralded John Thurlow's purchase of an automobile that was available for rent. A
later issue announced services available at the livery, in all likelihood the
first local repair and service garage. Thurlow, section foreman and machinist
for the Northern Pacific Railroad, worked out of the section house and was
touted for his skill in bicycle, automobile, stove, gasoline and steam engine
boiler and general machine repairs.

Ads in the earliest 1908 issues of the local newspaper indicate O.S. Hedahl &
Company was Mercer's purveyor of gasoline and kerosene. Later issues from
1910-1919 carried ads by Standard Oil for Polarine motor oil, Parowax (paraffin
wax) for sealing canning jars, and company endorsed appliances such as
Perfection oil heaters and cook-stoves and Rayo oil lamps for light. Although no
local merchant's name was associated with these products, we must assume
Hedahl's carried these products as well.

Most certainly delivery of petroleum products by rail had reached a crucial
level. In 1916 the country faced a national rail workers strike, and the
Telegram reported the local impacts that would be felt from such a work stoppage
and that "the gas tractor owners around here are laying in a supply of
gasoline."(3)

In the case of gas and oil deliveries we can assume, as in the case of the 1889
Larimore Pioneer article, that an independent dray service served as a jobber or
agent. We have no solid information concerning the first rural delivery service
or who may have operated it. But personal recollections of Edna Gessele Lilja
give credence to a service in the early 1920s. She recalls vividly as a little
girl how she went into hiding whenever Ira Washburn appeared on the Henry
Gessele farm with his horse-drawn tanker to make a gasoline delivery. Her mother
had repeatedly vowed to send her away with Ira if she didn't behave. The record
shows the Washburns did conduct a dray service in that time period.

The first real documentation of a Standard Oil facility in Mercer is found in
the 1920 village tax ledger at the McLean County Treasurer's office. All
taxpayers and amounts paid are listed, and Standard Oil, along with the grain
elevators, is placed in a special "lease" category. This explains the origin of
a bulk oil facility along the rail line sandwiched between the eastern most
grain elevator and the once existent, but now dismantled, livestock pens and
chutes. The oil storage consisted of a warehouse, elevated tanks, unloading
dock, pump house and pump boom. This lease site was still in use in the 1970s
even though gasoline was no longer delivered by rail. Tanker trucks delivered
bulk fuel after the reconstruction of Highway 7 (200) in 1952. A site survey is
found in Northern Pacific Railway lease and easement maps at the McLean County
Recorder's office.

In October 1926 Red Trail Oil and Transfer Company of Mandan, ND, acquired Lots
13 and 14, Block 6, Mercer Townsite(4) (the northeast corner of Main and Regan
Streets) and opened a Standard Oil garage/filling station/bulk oil facility. The
station featured two "visible" ten-gallon pumps: elevated ten-gallon glass
containers filled from underground fuel storage tanks by hand-operated lever
pumps at street level. Fuel flowed by gravity into vehicle fuel tanks and
clearly marked gallon intervals inside the glass containers indicated the amount
dispensed. Rural bulk service was provided by means of a 3-compartment wagon
tank resting on a horse-drawn wagon. Bulk storage was located at Standard's
lease facility along the NP Railway. Dewitt Flinn of Wilton, ND, managed the
business under lease terms from 1926 to 1929. Flinn's father operated a bulk oil
facility out of Wilton at that time. In 1929, lease management of the Red Trail
oil business fell to Jacob Just, an early homesteader south of Mercer in 1902,
and his son Emil H. under the name "Mercer Motor Company." However, there is
some confusion as to the name of the business. In 1932, ownership of Red Trail
Oil and Transfer, by now a huge company doing business in several North Dakota
communities, was transferred to a trustee under terms of foreclosure on a
defaulted mortgage. A McLean County Recorder's document indicates the name of
the business was "Just and Company." However, old receipts indicate Just
continued operation of the garage and filling station under the name "Mercer
Motor Company." Bulk service was taken over by a competitor, Jacob Braun, across
the street.

        Photo: (At right) Mercer Motor Co. sales receipt to O.B. Just Threshing
        Co., September 12, 1933. Note: gasoline sold for 20.2¢ per gallon and a
        quart of oil for 25¢. Outdated receipts were still used even though the
        business name had changed to Heim & Just Garage in 1932. (Courtesy Chris
        Heim, Jr.)

        Photo: Company motto from reverse side of Mercer Motor Oil Co. sales
        receipt. (Courtesy of Chris Heim, Jr.)

A partnership between Emil Just and Christ Heim was forged after 1932 under the
name "Heim & Just Garage - General Auto Repairing" that continued until 1941.
That year the Just estate acquired Lots 1 and 2, Block 5, Mercer Townsite (the
southwest corner of Main and Wing Streets) from C.P. Christenson and moved the
building onto those lots. The original metal-clad building stands today and is
used for storage. One can still read the old company name emblazoned across the
front. In 1941 Christ Heim acquired the vacant Lots 13 and 14, Block 6, where
the building had stood and used it for equipment storage. In 1941 Heim also
turned his sights on Jacob Braun's competing business across the street that was
suddenly up for sale.

        Photo: Christ Heim and Emil H. Just in front of their business next to
        Sam's Café on Main in 1932. (Courtesy of Chris Heim Jr.)

Rural resident Jacob Braun, Sec. 6, Twp. 146-79 (Mercer), had grown disgruntled
with farming in 1924, leased the operation to brother-in-law Fred Mansky, and
with his wife Christina (Miller) and four children moved into town. He set out
to become a businessman and tried various ventures, including roller skating
concessions at the Brush Lake pavilion and the Mercer town hall on the southeast
corner of Wing and Rice Streets. In 1928 he eventually opened a garage/filling
station on Main Street (still standing today as a machine shop) on Lot 24, Block
7. The Standard Oil facility prominently displayed one Red Crown "visible"
ten-gallon pump on Main Street and one each White and Blue Crown "visible" pumps
on Regan Street. Emanuel Schlaht and Carl Rennich were employed as mechanics,
and by the 1930s Jacob's son Herbert and young Reinhart Stradinger were full-
time employees as well.

        Photo: Jacob Braun Standard Service on Main and Regan. (Courtesy Merv
        Rennich.)

Braun expanded his business on this site. In 1929 he purchased adjoining Lot 23
on Main Street and opened an International Harvester implement shop. His
brother-in-law, John Miller Jr., worked there as an assembler and mechanic. At
one point Jacob went into auto sales and became the local Chevrolet dealer, in
competition with the Just-Heim Garage across the street where, ostensibly,
Pontiacs were sold.

Braun expanded into bulk petroleum, and it is quite probable that he took over
the local bulk oil sales from the Red Trail Oil Company in 1932 when it changed
ownership. From a marginal quality snapshot dating to 1935 we can discern Braun
owned a small, early 1930s model Chevrolet tanker truck emblazoned with
"Standard Oil Company." In front of the truck stands the antiquated horse-drawn
wagon tanker that likely came with assumption of Red Trail Oil Company's assets.
He needed a bigger and better transport, so in 1939 he borrowed $400 from
daughter Laura - she had by then completed business college and was employed at
the state capitol in Bismarck - and bought the latest model Chevrolet truck. In
October 1941 Braun sold the bulk dealership to Ted Gessele and the
garage/filling station facility to Christ Heim. The Brauns moved to Stockton,
California, where Jacob was employed as a mechanic in a food processing plant
and Christina worked in a cannery until their retirement.

        Photo: Interior Braun Standard Service 1937. Jacob Braun right and son
        Herbert left. (Courtesy of Meinhardt Braun)

Christ Heim left the Just-Heim partnership across the street in 1941 and
operated the former Braun Standard Oil filling station on Main Street until the
early 1950s under the name "Heim Service Garage." Although clients could still
purchase fuel and get an oil change, Christ's priority was to use the station as
a machine shop/storage facility for his farming operations located in the NE¼,
Sec. 3, Twp. 146-79, just outside of town.

With the advent of upgrades in the state highway system in the 1920s -
especially to local Highway 7 (currently 200) - other filling stations made their
appearance. In that era the highway alignment was through town: Enter town from
north on Brush Lake Road, east on Wing Street, south on First Street East, east
along north side of railroad out of town. In November 1926 McLean County had
obtained an easement for roadway purposes and constructing a curve at the
intersection of Brush Lake Road (today County Road 33) and Wing Street
(southwest corner of Outlot A, Olesen's Addition). In 1932 Martin Peterson
signed a lease of ½ cent per gallon for rental with Standard Oil of Indiana for
the operation of a small roadside filling station at this site. The building
still stands near the curve in the road. A unique feature of this facility was
the sale of Brush Lake block ice stored in sawdust from an icehouse nestled in a
nearby mound of earth. Travelers fueled up on their way to a picnic at the lake,
bought their ice (still available in the late 1940s), and then laid up a supply
of the best tasting Nehi orange soda in town.

Farther down the road, beginning at the southeast corner of Main and Wing
Streets (Lots 23 and 24, Block 6), owner Nils Hedahl had granted McLean County
highway right-of-way in 1929. This was for the purpose of constructing a roadway
curve at that intersection extending all the way to its intersection with Regan
Street at First Street East. Hedahl sold his property and in 1930 a filling
station opened under the Sheridan Service Company represented by Herb Nathan. A
lease agreement was reached with White Eagle Oil Corporation for the
installation of two "visible" ten-gallon gasoline pumps. In 1932 Fred
Zechmeister became proprietor and signed a lease with White Eagle of ½ cent per
gallon for rental. Later in 1940, Zechmeister signed a lease with Socony-Vacuum
Oil Company (Mobil Oil) for the installation of a 20-gallon "visible" pump and
one computer pump, the first indication of an electrically operated gas pump in
town. Emil H. Just assumed ownership of the station in 1941 and operated it
until 1953. A unique feature of this site was a canopy to protect clients and
workers from the elements.

A decision by the North Dakota Highway Department to reconstruct and reroute
Highway 7 (200) in the late 1940s had a major impact on Mercer's gas stations.
By 1952, the new roadway skirted the south side of town and the Peterson, Just
and Heim businesses went into decline and soon out of business. From this
emerged a new filling station/garage facility on the southwest corner of Main
Street and the new highway. Owned by Theophil Just with a lease from Standard
Oil, operations began in 1952. Eventually a small adjoining café was added to
the business. In 1956 Archie Kline joined Just as a partner. In 1961 John
Schlafman assumed the lease. In 1973 Just sold the station to Dennis Fiedler,
who in turn sold the site to Martin Anderson in 1975. In 1982 the business was
sold to Ed Schumann. The station is still in operation but as an independent and
no longer affiliated with any major oil company.

Barely two months after Ted Gessele took control of bulk services in 1941, had
the United States entered World War II. With that conflict came rationing,
especially of fuels, and town dwellers had little gasoline to buy or spare.
Their rural cousins, however, faced no restrictions, because the nation and its
army needed to eat. Indeed, farmers were urged to increase their cultivation.
Ted went about setting up shop, which included opening an office on Main Street
in his grandfather's (Christoph Singer) former cream station/shoe repair shop on
Lot 16, Block 6. The bulk oil business flourished and really began to soar in
the postwar era and early 1950s. The business expanded to two delivery trucks
and Kermit Torgerson and later Reinhart Stradinger came on board as second
drivers. A two-way radio dispatch unit was set up in the Gessele home in 1957
and operated by wife Alvira. Although Ted was a master at anticipating a
farmer's need to refuel storage tanks, phone orders became the norm after the
arrival of West River Mutual's upgraded telephone service in the community. The
boom in gasoline sales reached its nadir in the 1960s. Farmers were too
successful and the Federal Government, in addressing the problem of surplus
grain, instituted landbank and set-aside acre programs to take farmland out of
production. Although sales diminished somewhat and Gessele reduced operations to
one truck, he set out selling and installing oil furnaces throughout the area to
sustain his customer base. The business remained successful and faced only one
pitfall: the worldwide fuel shortage in the fall of 1973. Gessele retired at the
end of that year and sold his business to Duane Johnson. Thereafter, bulk oil
business operations were located out of Turtle Lake, ND, under Johnson and
subsequently under Mick Gross. Eventually Rud Oil of Center, ND, assumed control
of this business.

(Endnotes)

3 Ibid., September 2, 1916

  subsequent land transactions cited in this report.

        Wing Streets.
