HEALTH HISTORY OF MERCER By Bev Christensen

Keeping the family healthy was a challenge for the early Mercer pioneers. Often
illness, accidents, childbirth, and death had to be handled without professional
help.

Annetta McFadden, a registered nurse, came to Mercer from Fergus Falls,
Minnesota. She was often called upon to help the sick and always responded. She
arrived by train in February of 1906 and was promptly summoned to stay with Mrs.
Helm (Juanita) Davidson for six weeks, until her baby was born. Dr. Brown
ordered strict bed rest for Mrs. Davison.

In March of 1908, the Mercer Telegram reported, "the many who have been waited
on in sickness by this sister of charity will always remember the quiet, patient
woman who watched and nursed them through long days and nights, often braving
drenching rain, storms or blizzards on her mission of mercy." Annetta married
George McFadden July 6, 1910 in St. Paul.

The midwife was also a cherished member of the community. She did not only deal
with childbirth, but all kinds of illness and trouble. She usually fell into her
trade naturally, because she was so desperately needed. Most homesteaders were
young people who were starting their families. Some early area midwives were
Abby (Mrs. Laurence) Harrum, Louisa Gessele (Mrs. Jacob) Bender, Katharina Mayer
(Mrs. Jacob) Skaley, Juliana (Mrs. Jonas) Christensen, and Christina (Mrs.
Martin) Christensen.

        Photo: Annetta McFadden. (Courtesy of Patricia Kostelnik)

The German-Russian settlers relied heavily on a ritual called "Brauchen,"
brought with them from their Russian homeland. The practitioners, usually women,
attempted to cure or help the sick when no medical help was available. The folk
remedies and rituals were faith-based on the triune God. Among these women was
Rosina Wolf (Mrs. Jacob) Weise.

Early settlers often relied on home remedies, sharing and helping each other
with the care for the sick. Only when someone was seriously ill was the doctor
called.

Dr. Barton practiced medicine in Turtle Lake before Dr. George Heinzeroth and
his bride arrived in 1907 from Chicago. By 1908, Dr. Heinzeroth had one of the
first automobiles in the area, which aided him in his country visits. Many
illnesses occurred during inclement and stormy weather, and the early roads were
so primitive that they would be a challenge for today's cars.

Dr. Heinzeroth drove northeast sixteen miles in February 1908 to deliver
Shirley Christensen on her parents' Mercer homestead. Shirley said that her
mother had complications and would not have survived without the doctor. Several
years later, Shirley had an appendicitis attack and Dr. Heinzeroth was summoned
from Turtle Lake to their farm. When his car got stuck in snow by the cemetery,
he walked.

Mercer also had a drug store in the early days. In April of 1908, the Mercer
Telegram stated, "Mr. Charlie Wise invites you to call and meet his new
pharmacist, Mr. T.L. Linn." He replaced R.S. Burchart. Insurance papers show J.
Burrows was listed as owner of Drugs and Barber Shop on Lot 11, Block 5 of
Mercer in 1908. The Mercer Telegram reported Dr. Heinzeroth purchased the Mercer
Drug Store in June 1908.

The August 8, 1913, Mercer Telegram stated, "Dr. G.E. Heinzeroth will be in
Mercer every Wednesday from two to four P.M. at E.M. Plowman's office."

Dr. Beardsley, of Chicago, a friend of Dr. Heinzeroth, began practicing medicine
at Mercer in June 1908. Patients included Jens Bille, who was seen for an
appendicitis attack, H.C. Wiest with a felon (infection on finger or toe), and
Will Schmidt, Mrs. Charlie Wise's brother. Dr. Beardsley sent Will Schmidt to
Jamestown for an appendectomy, accompanied by Ferd Schmidt. Unfortunately, Dr.
Beardsley pulled down his shingle in September of 1909 and took over the late
Dr. Barker's practice in Underwood.

A new drug store was planned to open in McFadden's Store in the fall of 1909.
C.A. Rust of Underwood was behind this venture. Roy Rust was to come to Mercer
to open the new drug store, but he died in January of 1910. His death was
thought to be caused by accidental swallowing of carbolic acid. He left a young
bride of a few days in McClusky.

Dr. Brown of McClusky also began seeing patients in the Mercer area before 1906.
He enlisted Mrs. J.B. Wasson to help nurse scarlet fever patients in February
1908. Dr. Brown and Dr. Heinzeroth collaborated to surgically repair Martin
Wassenberg's hernia in 1911. Dr. Brown delivered all of Mrs. Helm Davidson's
babies. When he came to Mercer for a professional call, he could spend the night
with them.

Dr. Paulson of Turtle Lake also made home visits in the Mercer area. He
accompanied Halfdan Berg to Fargo in April of 1912 for an appendectomy. In June
of 1912 he was called to William Conkling's home. William's twelve-year-old son,
Elmer, fell beneath the wheels of his father's steam breaking outfit and
severely fractured his right femur leg bone.

Dr. Ralph Deming and his wife Mary arrived in Mercer in April 1914 from Fergus
Falls, Minnesota. He was an assistant physician in the State hospital there for
three years.

Dr. Deming obtained his medical education at the University of Pennsylvania and
the Hahnemann Medical College of Philadelphia. After graduating he acted as
Chief Resident Physician and Surgeon in a large hospital. Later he went to
Europe where he spent eighteen months in the clinics of Berlin, Vienna and
Paris.

Juanita Davidson wrote, "He and his wife Mary were really delightful people.
Doctor (Deming) had attended Heidelberg in addition to his American education
and Mary was the great niece of William Dean Howell. Mercer was delighted to
have a doctor, and they made many friends."

Dr. Deming put in a complete line of drugs and set up practice in the former
Winnor-Torgeson lumber yard office. He apparently started using that building or
his house as an infirmary. In April of 1914, Dr. Deming made several trips out
to treat the ten-year-old daughter of Sigrud Glad (Dagny). She was very sick
with pneumonia, but recovered. Simon Szelap's young son was kicked in the face
by a colt, and because he was so badly injured, Dr. Deming took him to Bismarck.
In August of 1914, Dr. Deming operated on Miss McComb for appendicitis.

MERCER HOSPITAL

The November 13, 1914, Mercer Telegram stated, "Mrs. Godfred Wagner from south
of Mercer is an infirmary patient under the care of Dr. Deming. At this writing
she is very low." She recovered and was discharged in December of 1914. At the
same time, the doctor's wife was very sick with typhoid fever. Mary Deming also
recovered.

January 8, 1915, the Mercer Telegram stated, "Theodore Belson, sixteen-year-old
son of Tom Belson, died Saturday at the local infirmary here at Mercer. The
latter part of the fall, he was brought into the hospital suffering from a badly
injured leg, which developed into blood poison... His death has caused a gloom
all over Mercer, and the country north of town where he resided."

A few months later, Mercer was planning an up-to-date hospital. On March 12,
1915, The Mercer Telegram stated, "over half the stock has been subscribed. The
site selected for the hospital is an ideal one, being located on the corner
directly west of the (Fred) Freeberg residence. The first floor will consist of
a reception room, operating room, pharmacy, diet kitchen, and wards. Plans are
for two large wards on the second floor. The building will be heated with hot
water and a complete water works system will be installed. While the hospital
will be under the complete control of Dr. Deming, the doctors of the surrounding
towns will be able to bring their patients here for operations and medical
attention. Mrs. Krogmoe, a competent graduate nurse, will be the matron in
charge."

The Mercer Hopital Association was incorp-orated in March 1915 for $10,000. Most
of the community bought stock. Stockholders included the Andrews Grain Co. and
the Salzer Lumber Co. The temporary Board of Directors was E.N. Hedahl, E.M.
Plowman, H.C. Weist, F.J. Winkelman, August Swenson, George McFadden and F.O.
Freeberg.

        Photo: Mercer Hospital. (Photo courtesy of Ruth Christensen)

Lots 1-4, Block 7 were deeded from Nils Hedahl to the Mercer Hospital
Association April 7, 1915. The Hospital Board was elected on April 9, 1915.
Herb Weist was President, Ole Hjelle-Secretary, and Fred Freeberg-Treasurer.
Directors were Nels Fibelstad, Fred Warner, Joe Peterson, and George McFadden.

Fred Winkelman, the local contractor, erected the new Mercer Hospital that
opened July 1, 1915 under Dr. Deming, physician and surgeon.

On Sept. 10, 1915, The Mercer Telegram stated, "Miss Norton, a trained nurse
from Mandan has accepted a position at the hospital."

Dr. Deming also played baseball at Mercer. On May 29, 1914, The Mercer Telegram
reported, "Dr. Deming, who was at the receiving end, played a heady game and
showed plainly that he had been there before. Mercer defeated Turtle Lake 14 to
3 in that game."

Some of the babies born at the Mercer Hospital under Dr. Deming in 1915 were
Willis Gardiner, Merle Berge, and Paul Winkelman. Some of the babies born in
1916 were Mary Weist, Lila Sommers, Ruth Ovre, James Plowman, Brandt Hjelle, and
a son to Simon Szelaps. From 1916 to 1917 there were 288 recorded births in
McLean County, an increase from 93 in 1908 to 1909.

A local baby contest was held in April of 1916 that resulted in a baby parade on
May 5th. It started at the train depot and ended at the town hall. Mercer
businesses were closed for one hour during the parade.

        Photo: Mercer baby parade. House is the Karl Rennich's residence. (Photo
        courtesy of Evelyn Freeberg)

Sometimes situations were more serious. In September of 1916, Mrs. Halver T.
Halverson died after an illness of several months. She left a husband and
several children. Their homestead was north of Mercer on Roger Ketterling's
land. In October of 1916, Dr. Deming was called to McClusky when Chris Sperber
was accidentally shot. Unfortunately, he did not survive. Dr. Deming also
served as coroner during this time.

When the U.S. became involved in World War I, Dr. Deming joined the Army. "Many
of us learned to love them (the Demings), but when our country went to war in
1917, Doctor offered his services. They left us and we never saw them again,"
wrote Mrs. Davidson.

Although small hospitals served a purpose, they usually were not lucrative.
Without a doctor, the Mercer Hospital's future was in jeopardy. The Hospital
Association continued to hold annual meetings for the stockholders. The hospital
building became a private residence for the Stradingers who lived there in the
1930's. The Fred Gaub family lived there in the early 1940's.

On December 1, 1945, the Mercer Hospital Association by signatures of Nels
Fibelstad, President, and C.W. Freeberg, Secretary, sold the property for $1700
to Virgil Curtis, Henry Krein, and A.M. Christensen, who were Trustees of the
Church of God. It became their parsonage. The Mercer Hospital Association
dissolved in 1946, and later the hospital building was sold and moved to Fred
Bohara's farm.

Accidents were among the many health hazards that existed in the early days of
Mercer. The Mercer Telegram reported on November 26, 1908, that Dave Miller was
accidentally shot by Fred Dietrich of Hurdsfield while deer hunting with a bunch
of men near Expansion. Jake Nelson of Mercer was 100 yards away and ran to
assist him, "and it was largely due to Jake's presence of mind that Dave is
still among the living, for he was rapidly bleeding to death when Jake grabbed
handkerchiefs and tied up the wounded arm, and thereby stopping the flow of
blood. The party at once abandoned all further thoughts of hunting and returned
at once to their shack, from where Jake Delzer drove 18 miles for a doctor."

On August 4, 1916, The Mercer Telegram reported the death of Marvin,
twelve-year-old son of A.E. Nelson. He caught his leg in the fly wheel of his
father's feed mill on their farm south of Mercer, and later died at a Bismarck
Hospital.

Contagious diseases were a problem for early settlers. Safe drinking water was
not always available. Typhoid fever occurred when water was contaminated with
the Salmonelle typhi bacteria. It infected the small intestines, and spread to
the blood, producing a high fever and weakness.

In 1908, Matt Schmidt's family, north of Mercer, suffered from typhoid fever.
Dr. Heinzeroth and Mrs. Charlie Wise helped care for them. In 1910, typhoid
fever accounted for seventy-six deaths in McLean County. Ernest Christensen,
11-year-old son of Fred and Lydia, died of typhoid in 1933. By the middle of the
century, antibiotics became an effective treatment, and drinking water was
safer. That resulted in fewer cases of typhoid.

        Photo: Dr. George Heinzeroth. (Courtesy of Loren Heinzeroth)

Food poisoning was a problem in Mercer in January 1910. Many people ate oysters
at the Belmont Hotel on New Years Eve. Shirley Christensen Ingman, born in 1908,
wrote "Each summer we suffered at least one session of 'summer complaint'
(vomiting and diarrhea), which lasted about a day. Since whole families came
down with it at once, it was considered contagious. My thinking is that it was
most likely food poisoning. There was no refrigeration, and the summer heat
certainly penetrated even the coolest basement, where left over food was
stored." Those who had ice boxes were fortunate.

Tuberculosis or "Consumption" was responsible for more deaths and greater
economic loss than any other disease. A total of 316 deaths were reported by
tuberculosis during 1904-1906 in North Dakota. The state funded San Haven
Sanitarium opened in 1912 for the treatment of tuberculosis patients. Mrs.
Edwin N. Hedahl entered the TB sanitarium at Dunseith in February of 1915, and
died the following October. Esther Peterson's first husband, Bennie Bohnet, died
there also. In 1946, Darryl (Mrs. Martin) Peterson of Mercer, died of
tuberculosis.

Diphtheria, a bacterial infection that spread by the respiratory route, was the
chief infectious killer of pioneer children. Sore throat and fever were first
seen. The local effects of the toxin included the death of throat tissue with
the formation of a fibrin membrane. The membrane could obstruct the airway and
cause death by suffocation. Approximately two out of every three children under
two years who were infected with diphtheria died. About 50% of children aged two
to five also died. Public funerals for children who had died of diphtheria were
prohibited. In epidemics, schools and churches were closed.

Several area residents were infected by diphtheria. Alvin Speiber of Mercer died
of diphtheria in August of 1908. Dr. Heinzeroth was called to John Thurlow's of
Mercer in November of 1911, as John was sick with diphtheria. In 1922 there were
9 diphtheria deaths reported in McLean County. In the spring of 1936, Milo
Calheim, age 14, died of the disease. William, the teenage son of Mike Makeeff
Sr. also died from diphtheria. Treatment of diphtheria was strict quarantine,
and the early and liberal use of antitoxin, if and when available. In 1916, the
State Board of Health made the Schick test for diphtheria available to
physicians all over the state. Today children are vaccinated against this
disease.

Pertussis, or whooping cough was a serious, highly contagious, bacterial
respiratory disease. It occurred mainly among infants and young children. In
December of 1910, six-week-old Olive May Murphy and her little brother died of
whooping cough. Rev. Oral Brown delivered the funeral sermon at the home of Mrs.
Murphy's parents, the Pichards. The James Murphys lived five miles southeast of
Mercer.

In 1915, the children of Martin Christensen had whooping cough and baby Marie
died from it. Her grief stricken mother, Christina, wrote, "When little Marie
was born, the doctor said, she could not live. Oh, how I prayed and begged the
Lord for permission to keep her... but the Lord took her farther away."

In October of 1938, Alvin Jans, six-week-old son of Fred and Bertha, also died
of whooping cough. Fortunately, today infants are vaccinated against this
disease and treated with antibiotics.

Pneumonia was a serious illness that was sometimes fatal for early settlers. A
mustard plaster would often be applied to the patient's chest, prior to the
availability of penicillin after World War II. Some treated it by rubbing skunk
oil on the chest. Little Alice Nelsen, daughter of O. Pete and Kate Nelsen, died
of pneumonia in 1915, several months after inhaling smoke from a fire in their
sod house northeast of Mercer. Nine-year-old Leonard Gessele, son of Henry and
Katherine also died of pneumonia.

The most tragic, acute infectious disease epidemic to ever hit North Dakota was
the great Influenza Pandemic of 1918-1919. It was also called the Spanish flu,
or la grippe. In 1918, as World War I ground to an end, another battle gripped
the world. The great flu epidemic swept around the world, killing anywhere from
20 million to 40 million people. It struck at a time when many physicians and
nurses were out of state in military service. The entire health care system was
rapidly overwhelmed. It was especially dangerous because it could quickly lead
to pneumonia, and most who succumbed to this mutated super-flu were in the prime
of their lives, ages seventeen to thirty-five.

The first cases in the U.S. showed up in over-crowded stateside military camps
in March of 1918. Christian Sorlee of Mercer was inducted into the Army at
Washburn on July 21, 1918, and was sent to Camp Custer, Michigan. Less than 3
months later, on October 18, 1918, Chris died of pneumonia at the age of 26. In
a 48-hour period at Camp Custer, ten North Dakota recruits died. John Adolph
Singer was twenty years old when he died of the flu in September of 1918 at
Great Lakes, Illinois.

The flu traveled rapidly along the transportation routes of America, carried by
infected people. It traveled to Europe again, this time on crowded transport
ships that carried thousands of young American soldiers. Ole Hedahl of Mercer
died in England during the flu epidemic. This super flu of 1918-19 caused more
casualties and fatalities than World War I.

In December of 1918, Fred Freeberg wrote, "Not a dozen in town escaped the
Flu... and we have had many deaths from it also."  Mrs. Helm Davidson wrote,
"That fall had been a hell for everyone. I dreaded to hear the phone ring for
fear it would mean another one of our circle was gone. Whole families would be
in bed, and I carried many meals to many homes. I remember one night about 8
o'clock the phone rang and a voice said, "Mrs. Davidson, this is Dr. Heinzeroth.
I am eight miles in the country and haven't had a bite to eat since early
morning. Will you have supper ready for me when I get there because I have to
call on half the people in Mercer before I go home?"

Some other Mercer citizens that died from the Spanish flu were, Emma (Mrs. Fred)
Winkelman, age twenty-three and mother of little Paul, Mrs. John Schell, Mrs.
Philip Wanner, four-year-old Emma Schell (daughter of Christoph and Rosina), and
Mrs. Soren Peterson.

Shirley Christensen Ingman wrote, "In 1919 the flu epidemic raged through our
community, taking even the strong and sturdy, so frail little Grandmother (Maren
Miller Peterson) did not have a chance. Mama (Mrs. Jonas) was also seriously ill
with the flu and unable to attend the funeral service (of her mother). There was
no church building, so the service was held outside our house (in March), as
people avoided going into the homes of flu victims. One exception was our
neighbors, the German Lutheran pastor and his wife, the W.L. Kellers. She went
into the bedroom with Mama."

Pastor Keller was asked after the flu epidemic why he and his wife never caught
it, and he replied they prayed a lot, and ate a lot of garlic.

Dr. George Heinzeroth continued to practice medicine in the Turtle Lake-Mercer
area until 1951. He delivered around 3,000 babies during his practice. He died
November 6, 1952, at the age of 82 and is buried in Riverside Cemetery at Fargo,
North Dakota.

Dr. Harold Kuplis and family arrived in Turtle Lake in 1952, and the Turtle Lake
Hospital opened that year. He provided health care for area patients and his
wife was a registered nurse. He retired in 1985 and they moved to Florida. Mrs.
Kuplis is deceased.

One hundred years of statehood has revealed great improvements in the health
care of North Dakota's citizens. Improved refrigeration, diets, and
environmental sanitation has virtually eliminated typhoid fever and fatal
intestinal diarrheas. Immunizations have abolished epidemics and antibiotics are
available for infections. Public health offices exist in all North Dakota
communities. Our community is served by the Turtle Lake Hospital and Clinic only
ten miles west, and the McClusky Clinic thirteen miles east of Mercer. Ambulance
service and EMTs are available for emergencies. Home health and hospice care is
also available. Indeed, health care in the Mercer has come a long way in the
last century.

        Photo: The early day baby parade event on the school grounds - facing
        south. (Photo courtesy of Evelyn Freeberg)

Mercer Hotel

        Photo: Mercer Hotel, circa 1910.

The Mercer Hotel had an interesting history of owners and managers. The
location was on the north part of Main Street on the west side of the street on
lots 3 & 4 in Block 5 of the original town site.

The McLean County Townsite Co. sold the lots to Nels Olesen on September 14,
1908, for $300. On September 28, 1908, he sold the two lots to Ole S. Hedahl
for $3000. The next transaction was on March 4, 1910, to Nils Hedahl for $3500
who then sold the property to James R. Washburn on April 8, 1910, for $3500.
Washburn sold the property to Florence Mae Washburn (daughter) on December 29,
1910, for $3500. She sold the site to Nels Olesen on July 9, 1913, for $100.
Olesen sold to Nils Hedahl on July 23, 1915, for $250 who sold it to E.A.
Raymond on October 17, 1916, for $200. In 1920, a foreclosure sale deeded the
lots to the First State Bank with Ella Hjelle as the owner. In 1944, it became
the property of McLean County. (Legal data from the records of the McLean
County Recorder.)

        Document: Belmont Hotel ad, 1913.

During the time of revolving owners, the hotel was leased and operated by Christ
Sackmann, John G. Singer, Frank Pettigrew, R.S. Butchart, Seifert, Nels
Peterson and Art Shelton. The last hotel manager was John Schindler. Harry and
Jesse Kline had a boarding house during the 1940s. In the mid 1940s the
building was bought by Jake Laib who used the lumber to build a house on his
farm.

At the present time, the site is owned by the City of Mercer and is the location
of the City Garage.

The very first hotel was a small two-story frame building on the east side of
Main Street which was built in 1906/07 by Fred Sorenson for Nels Olesen who
named it Hotel Olesen. This building burned and was rebuilt in 1910 across the
street. The newer and larger two-story hotel, built on the west side of Main
Street on Lots 3 and 4, Block 5, had a large room on the first floor for a ball
room and dining room. It was the scene of many of the social events in town.
There were stories of basket socials, harvest and masquerade balls, dances and
concerts. In January 1910, a benefit supper of oysters resulted in food
poisoning with sickness but no fatalities.

Before the first hotel was built, visitors found room and board in the railroad
section house. This was built and used by the railroad building crew. After
the completion of the depot, this building became a private residence. It still
exists and is owned by the Brewer family. For many Mercerites, it is remembered
as the Emanuel Schlaht family home.

Mercer Land Office

        Photo: The land office is the little building to the left of the Mercer
        Hotel.

As noted on page 27, the sale and exchange of land was very active during the
first years of the village. Until 1908, the McLean County Register of Deeds
published all the transactions relating to homesteading in McLean County which
at that time included the four eastern townships which are now in Sheridan
County.

As described on page 18, the homesteaders had to prove up their stake, and after
that, many sold their land. The land officer most often noted was Franz
Breitzmann, who was a surveyor.

The real estate office of Edward Plowman was established before 1910, and his
building on the west side of Main Street, south of the hotel, was in existence
until it burned in the 1950s.

It is not known when the Plowman Realty closed.

Livery and the Drays

The livery was an important part of transportation in the early days. It was
the place where buggies and horses could be rented and where horses could be
stabled. Two of the town's first livery men were Clarence Rhone and Karl Degg.
Karl Degg built his livery on Lots 9-11, Block 4 on Rice Street in 1906. He sold
it to Adolph Singer and Rudolph Berreth in 1907 and their Livery-Feed Barn was a
busy place for many years. Other livery operators were Charles McLaughlin,
Chris Nelson, J.R. Washburn and Ira Washburn. Ira's livery barn was the last
remaining one and it was sold to Emanuel Hinsz in the 1960s. It was one of
the first buildings in the new city. Apologies to those omitted.

        Photo: Jake Diede's truck. (Courtesy of Carol Diede Stack)

In the beginning, the "drays" were horse and wagon operations. In later years,
the horses and wagons were replaced by truck. Those operating dray services
include Fred Marzolf, John Miller, Jr., Reinhart Stradinger, and Jake Diede.

Lumberyards and Contractors/Carpenters

The first mention of a lumberyard is in the Mercer Telegram of December 1907.
The Winner-Torgerson Lumber Co. was managed by Theodore Knutson. However, there
must have been lumber available either local or from other towns before that
because there was construction of houses, churches, the school house, the claim
shacks and commercial buildings. Business must have been brisk because houses
were built in a few days. According to an April 30, 1908, news item, Nels
Olesen's house was completed in two days.

In August 1909, the Salzer Lumberyard was built, with John Fisher as the
manager. (He later married Guilina Felland.) Later in 1909, Christ Stradinger
moved to Mercer to manage the Stradinger Lumberyard with his brother Henry. It
is not known when that yard was built. In February 1913, the Stradinger Lumber
Yard was sold to Herb Wiest, George McFadden and Ole Hjelle, who converted it
into a dance hall. Later it became American Legion headquarters, was eventually
sold to Halfdan Berge and finally it went up in flames.

Theodore Knutson became the manager of the Salzer Lumber Yard in December 1912
when the Fisher family left Mercer. In December, George Krug managed the yard
until it closed in the 1940s. The office of the Salzer Lumber Yard is still
standing in Mercer but is slated for demolition.

There were many carpenters in the town. One who is remembered from the early
years is Fred Winklemann. He and his brother Victor came to the area from New
York. They built many of the houses, farm buildings, rural schools, commercial
buildings and churches that are still in use today. Fred was the main contractor
for the 1916 school house. Fred married Emma Sackmann of the pioneer Christoph
Sackmann family. She died in 1918 during the flu epidemic and Fred left Mercer
shortly after that. Victor married Ida Ketterling, of the pioneer John
Ketterling family, and the family left Mercer in 1918.

        Photo: This is the current Salzer office building. It once was Dr.
        Demming's office. It was destroyed in 2004.

Among the later carpenters were Edward Sackman, Emil Russ, Duane Helm, Ervin
Jans and Jim Murray. Apologies to those omitted.

MERCER BUTCHERS/MEAT MARKETS

The first meat market was operated by James Washburn. The butcher who is best
remembered from pioneer days is Christoph Sackmann. He butchered and made the
sausage the German-Russian way (lots of garlic and pepper) until shortly before
his death. He taught his son, Ted, the sausage making art and Ted then
continued with the recipe when he moved to Eureka, SD, to operate a store and
butcher shop. That recipe is still being used and the sausage is available in
the area surrounding Eureka.

In 1914, Adolph Singer took over the Sackmann business located on Main Street on
Lot 6, Block 5. Singer was the town's butcher until 1919 when he went into
retirement. His sons Theofil, Dave, and Arthur managed the meat market until
1924 when it was sold to Joe Dokovna.

Another butcher who had a market in Mercer was Ed Pederson. He also started a
locker plant. There were no home freezers and the customers needed a place to
save the meat from hunting and butchering. Ed and Hattie Pederson also had a
restaurant and bar.

Jake and Rosie Rust bought the Pederson locker and meat market in March of 1951.
Jake would butcher the animal, cut it up and wrap the meat and put it into the
customer's locker. In 1963, the Rusts sold the meat market.

Operators who followed were Harley Holton and Ervin Moser. Teddy Neumiller had
the last meat market in Mercer.

Apologies to those who may have been omitted.

        Photo: (Above) Meat Market under the ownership of Adolph Singer.

        Photo: (At right) Christ Stradinger (left) and Chris Sackmann (right) in
        1909, owner of the Mercer Meat Market.

History of the Mercer Post Office By Willa Gardiner Murray

The process for the establishment of a post office for the city of Mercer
located in McLean County was begun on October 2, 1905. The office was located
three blocks north of the Northern Pacific Railroad on the east side of the
street. The estimated population of Mercer at that time was 200 including
farmers.

        Photo: Past Postmaster Reinhart Stradinger. (Courtesy of Lila
        Stradinger)

Nels Olesen became the first postmaster, followed by George McFadden one year
later. James McFadden received the position on March 8, 1911. He served less
than a year and was succeeded by Edward M. Plowman. George McFadden was
reappointed to the position on February 27, 1915, and served until June 3, 1919,
when Edward Plowman returned to the postmaster's position. He served until June
1, 1923. Bernard (Ben) C. Hjelle then became Mercer's longest serving postmaster
until his retirement on July 31, 1959. Reinhart Stradinger became acting
postmaster on July 31, 1959, but did not receive his commission as postmaster
until July 18, 1961. During Mr. Stradinger's term the Post Office Department
reorganized and became known as the United States Postal Service. Upon Mr.
Stradinger's retirement in 1981, Willa Gardiner Murray was appointed officer-in-
charge and received her commission on February 21, 1981. She is the great niece
of George McFadden, the second postmaster of Mercer and the first female to
serve in this position in Mercer.

Mercer had two rural routes at one time, one traveling north of the village and
one heading south. The first carrier service began on December 6, 1916, with
Victor Winklemann serving a short time followed by Alex Singer. Succeeding
carriers were Roy Nielsen, Ole S. Hjelle, Harold W. Johnson, Martin Peterson,
Floyd Sprout and Arnold Westerlind. Mr. Westerlind was the longest serving rural
mail carrier. He began his service on January 1, 1950, and retired in December
1980. Upon his retirement, the Mercer route was converted to a highway contract
route which was opened to the public and issued to the lowest bidder. Tony
Klein of McClusky was the lowest bidder and began serving the route in April
1981. The administration of this route was removed from the Mercer office in
1981 and is under the supervision of the McClusky Postmaster.

        Photo: Rural mail carriers in the 1930s and 1940s: Roy Nielsen, Sr.
        (left) and Floyd Sprout (right).

Some of the clerks serving the Mercer office were: Cora Hjelle, wife of Ben
Hjelle; Ella Stradinger; Reinhart Stradinger; Edna (Stradinger) Glad; Anna
(Pederson) Diede; Violet (Miller) Gessele; Willa (Gardiner) Murray; Pam
(Freeberg) Lill; Phyllis Nielsen; Margie Fiedler; Julie Natchatila; Katherine
Krush; Bruce Hjelle, Ole Hjelle; Margaret Hjelle; Harold Stradinger; Josephine
(Gardiner) Wagner; Marie Gardiner and Marlene Wardner.

The early neighboring rural post offices were:

* Ethel - Farm post office established January 15, 1898, in Wise Township on the
shore of Brush Lake. Its postmaster was rancher Dan Williams. It was named for
nearby Ethel Lake, named for the daughter of John Merry, a local rancher. It
closed on 10/15/1900 with mail to Turtle Lake.

* Byers - Farm post office established April 21, 1904, in Byersville Township,
five miles south of Butte, with Henry A Kenny its first postmaster. It was
named for its township, which was named for Jacob Byers, a pioneer settler in
the area. It closed December 15, 1913, with mail to Dogden.

* Skogmo - Rural community founded in 1903, fifteen miles north of McClusky. It
was named for its postmaster John T. Skogmo. The post office was established on
October 4, 1904, and closed March 3, 1932, with mail going to Kief.

* McComb - Farm post office authorized on July 5, 1904, in Wise Township six
miles north of Mercer. Its postmaster Ramsey R. McComb named it after pioneer
settler Melvin O. McComb. The post office was rescinded October 4, 1904.

* Maxwell - Rural post office established June 27, 1905, in Medicine Hill
Township nine miles northeast of Turtle Lake. It was named after its postmaster
Lafayette Maxwell. It was rescinded December 13, 1912, with mail to Turtle Lake.

* Eastman - Rural post office established April 23, 1903, in Park Township,
eight miles south of Mercer. Its postmaster was Ida O. Pace. It was named for
Philip Kimball Eastman, a prominent area pioneer who was the first postmaster at
Wilton. It closed May 31, 1905, with mail to McClusky.

        Photo: Current Postmaster, Willa Gardiner Murray.

THE MERCER TELEGRAM

The first edition of the Mercer Telegram was on August 20, 1907, with W.T.
Wasson as the publisher. In January 1909, Nels Olesen bought the paper, but by
the fall of that year, he had sold out to George Heinze to take up banking.
Olesen gave up on that venture and returned to the Telegram, buying half
interest in the enterprise. It is not clear how long Heinze served as editor or
what happened to his half share, but Olesen remained the sole owner until March
1913 when he sold the business to Trix Monson of McClusky. T.D. Monson was at
the helm as editor/publisher but only until July 11, 1913, when the paper
reverted back to Olesen. Olesen returned for the July 18 edition and remained in
control until the end of the year. But he left the everyday, mundane editing
work to a young R.F. Boehm, an employee in the First State Bank. In the
meantime, Olesen became a full time evangelist, but at the end of 1913 he
disposed of his venture and turned it over to Boehm. Boehm continued at the
Telegram until November 1914 when he went off to college.

The newspaper was taken over by businessmen McFadden, Hedahl and Hjelle, who
hired Ed Plowman in December 1914 to serve as editor and publisher. Plowman, a
realtor by trade, ran production of the paper editor in the Olesen building or
in the Plowman building Lot 5, Blk. 5. Publication of the Telegram continued
until June 1919, and thereafter it ceased to exist.

The first printing office was a small building on Block 6 of the original
townsite on the east side of Main Street. In September 1909, E.N. Hedahl
purchased the building. He remodeled it and used it for his telephone exchange.
It is believed that this building was the central telephone office that was used
until the 1940s.

Nels Olesen needed to build a new printing office. The location is presently the
home of Lila (Reinhart) Stradinger.

The September 17, 1909, edition had this description of the new building: "The
new building will be a 24 × 30 building with full seven foot basement which will
be used as pressroom. The floor will be cement and foundation concrete. The
upstairs will be divided in three parts: main office, composing room and stock
room. The composing room will be 12 × 14, the stock room 10 × 12 and the main
office 18 × 21. If present plans carry we will have a cylinder press, folder and
gasoline engine before snow flies. Not only with all these improvements, but The
Telegram will also be enlarged and all the pages printed at home. This will be a
great venture of a town of this size but we have unlimited faith in Mercer and
know that the people of Mercer and surrounding country will all join us in
declaring 'There's no place like Mercer.' (There were frequent notes in the
newspaper about flooding in the basement.)

Copies of the Telegram are on microfilm at the North Dakota Heritage Center in
Bismarck.

DEPOT AGENTS

(See history of the railroad and depot on pages 18-23)

The first depot agent/telegraph operator mentioned was Charles E. Williams in
1908. He was followed by Curtis Kubler in 1912; later, Mr. Mattson, Fred
Sommars, A.N. Stewart and native son Julius Sackman. Julius Sackman began his
agent career with Northern Pacific Railway as a "relief worker" as a teenager.
He became a full-time depot agent in the late 1930s and served in various
stations before returning to Mercer in 1951. He was Mercer's last agent. After
he retired in 1968, the station was closed.

The agent and his family lived in the family quarters on the second floor of the
depot.

MERCER TELEPHONE

The first mention of telephone service in Mercer was about the North Western
phone system located in the Doering Store in 1907. The first operator was Mary
Schumacher who continued until 1910. The Mercer Telephone Company was then
relocated in the Hedahl store beginning in 1909. In June 1910, Halfdan Berge
bought the Exchange. Operators there included Emma Sackmann from 1910 to 1915
when Ida Washburn took over. Other early known operators were Doris McConagley
and Anna Brown.

        Photo: Mercer Northern Pacific Depot. (Courtesy of Richard Ketterling
        collection)

The one operator that most early residents remember is Emma Schlaht, who
succeeded Anna Brown. The office - also her home - was on the northern end of
Main Street. Lydia and Emil Just bought the exchange from North Western
Telephone Company and Lydia operated the exchange in her home from 1943 to 1947.
The Justs sold the exchange in 1947 to the City and Dora Jorgenson was the
operator who had the switchboard in her home on Main Street. The dial phone
system became operable on August 5, 1957, by the West River Mutual Aid Telephone
Corporation. The present telephone system is the West River Telecommunication
with offices in Hazen, North Dakota.

        Photo: Emma Schlaht

Park and Koenig Townships south of Mercer operated a telephone company and
according to an entry in the secretary's ledger, began operating on February 10,
1916. Officers were President Oscar Totdahl, Treasurer Jacob Kurle, Secretary
Henry Gessele and Directors Fred Fischer and Philip Wahl. There were
approximately thirty subscribers and duties for the subscribers included line
maintenance which was rotated among them. Fees were assessed and delinquent
subscribers were disconnected. The last entry was in the 1940s. There was also
rural telephone service north of the village but no records have been found.

        Photo: Dora Jorgenson and her granddaughter Darlene. (Courtesy of
        Darlene Jorgenson Schilling)

STORES

McFadden General Merchandise/ Freeberg

This was one of the first stores in Mercer built in 1906/07 by George McFadden.
The First State Bank occupied part of the building. F.O. Freeberg bought the
store on April 1, 1924, and it was operated by Mrs. Minnie Freeberg and son,
Conrad. It was called the Mercer Cash Store. In the late 1920s, the store
burned and was replaced with the present brick building. After Mrs. Freeberg
retired, the store was managed by Conrad and Evelyn Freeberg until 1979.

        Photo: George McFadden in the doorway of the McFadden Store. (Courtesy
        of the McFadden family collection)

        Document: Ad from the 1908 paper.

The building was unoccupied until 1989 when it was leased to Jim and Mozel
Murray who were subsidized by the Mercer Development Corporation. Murray's
Market (a grocery store) was opened on November 15, 1989, and closed in January
1992. At the present time, the building is still owned by Evelyn Freeberg and is
used for a variety of functions: bakes sales, rummage sales, lunches and other
social gatherings.

        Photo: The front of the McFadden Store: Geo McFadden and F.O. Freeberg.

        Photo: A view of the inside of the Freeberg store.

        Photo: Another view of the outside window, showing the women's side of
        the store. (Courtesy of Evelyn Freeberg).

        Documents: Sales slips from 1930 and1910.

In the early days, the post office was located in the building.

Dakovna General Merchandise and Hardware Store called the People's Store

This store was built by Alle Dakovna in August 1915 and was on the south end of
Main Street. He had come to the area earlier as a hide buyer. The store was
operated by the family, Alle, his daughter Pauline Livingstein and son Joe
Dakovna until 1940.

It was sold to Gottlieb Fischer in 1940 and was a general store. He operated it
until the late 1940s. At various times, the buildings included a butcher
shop/locker plant and café. Finally the buildings were owned by the Jim Murray
Construction. The building was replaced in 2001.

Hedahl Hardware/Furniture

(More history with the Hedahl family history on page 248)

In April 1906, Edwin and Ole Hedahl came from Manfred, ND, in search of a
suitable site for a hardware store along the newly built Northern Pacific
Railroad. They chose Mercer. O.S. Hedahl and sons Edwin and Swen built a small
store on Main Street north of the Mercer State Bank. Business prospered and the
building was enlarged and furniture was added to the stock of merchandise. Later
they added the Ford Motor Agency including a service department. Ole Hedahl was
the chief mechanic. The father, Nels Hedahl joined the firm in 1910 and stayed
until he retired in 1920 and moved to Fargo. Ole was drafted in World War I and
died of influenza in 1918 in England.

The store was sold in 1924 when Edwin and son Erling moved to Bismarck where
they started an auto service sales store, now known as the Hedahl Auto Parts.

Hjelle /Gardiner/Schell Store

In the mid 1920s, the Hjelle Brothers, Ole and Ben built a grocery store between
the First Mercer State Bank and the Hedahl Hardware Store. In 1926, this store
and the Hedahl Hardware were purchased by Ross Gardiner, and in 1938 his son
George opened a Gamble Store in the building.

In 1952, George and Verna Gardiner bought the store and continued to operate the
general merchandise and Gamble Store until November 1977. The store was sold to
Joe and Ida Dugan who operated the store until 1979 when it was sold to Ervin
and Eileen Schell. They operated the store until 1989 when all the contents were
sold.

Presently Ervin and Diana Jans occupy the building as a shop for their
Construction Business.

        Photo: Ross Gardiner in the interior of his store in 1937. The picture
        was taken by a traveling photographer. Ross and his son George ran the
        store together for 10 years. (Courtesy of the Gardiner family)

        Photo: The building that was Schell's Hardware and Food Market still
        stands in Mercer.

        Photo: The Gardiner Store: Mary Ann Westerlind in the left aisle, and
        Ross Gardiner, Gordon and Debbie Westerlind, at right. (Courtesy of the
        Gardiner family)

Doering Brothers General Store

This store was located on the east side of Main Street on Lot 18, Block 6
(presently an empty lot). It was built in 1907/08. In May 1909, it was sold to
T. Baron and Stohler. Baron quit and Stohler sold the store to the Mercer Co-op
in April 1910.

The Mercer Co-op was governed by a board which had the Rev. Frank Peterson as
President; John Ketterling as Vice President; Nels Olesen, Secretary, John
Kurle, Treasurer and Fred Just, Director.

The Mercer Co-op Store was called the Farmer's Store and opened on May 20, 1910
with Nuenberg and Greenfield as managers. They were replaced by Calheim and
Swenson. After Andrew Calheim retired, Swenson was the sole manager. The Coop
Store burned on August 25, 1915, and was not rebuilt.

        Photo: Salzer Lumber Company with its German name.

Rice/Littke Implement and Schell/Gaub Hardware Store

James Rice was the first implement dealer in Mercer. A July 23, 1909, item in
the Telegram stated that James Rice had located here in the implement business.
Before that, he operated one of the grain elevators for a year. In August 1909
he put up a 16 × 24 repair shop for his machinery located in Block 8 on the west
side of Main Street. In June 1910, the McLean County Townsite Company deeded
this lot to James and Gertrude Rice. According to the advertisements in the
Telegram, he sold a variety of farm items such as twine (at ten cents/pound),
wagons, buggies, plows, cream separators, etc. He also was the dealer for the
John Deere Company. The John Deere Iron Club was the most complete iron wagon on
the market.

In October 1928, the John Deere Implement was sold to Karl Littke, who operated
the business until 1943 when it was sold to Christoph Schell, Jr. Mr. Schell
remodeled the building and added a basement and another room. The Schells
operated a hardware store until Christoph's death in 1961. Olga Schell sold the
building to Herbert Gaub in 1962, and Herb and Martha Gaub operated the Gaub
Hardware and Plumbing in the building. In 1971, they moved their business to the
Logue building on the east side of Block 7. In the early 1980s the Gaubs retired
and sold the hardware inventory.

The Rice building was a part of the Mercer Main Street until the 1970s when it
burned. The Mercer Post Office is now located on the site.

        Document: This ad ran in 1915 in the Mercer Telegram.

        Photo: Schell Hardware, Christoph Schell, owner. He bought the store in
        1943. (Courtesy of Luella Schell Kluck)

Entertainment and Celebrations

Throughout the years, the Mercer residents had "fun." Some of the early
activities were discussed in the Telegram.

In March 1908, the Mercer Dramatic Troupe presented a three-act Temperance Play,
"Out in the Street," in Turtle Lake, McClusky and Denhoff, in addition to
at-home performances. It had songs, drama and lasted two hours. Admission for
adults was 35 cents and for children 20 cents. The "dramatic personnel" were
O.S. Hjelle, George McFadden, H.C. Wiest, Carl Vandercook, Swen Hedahl, Harry
Paulson, Miss Natwick, Marie Hedahl, Annetta McFadden and Emma Sackmann.

In June 1909, moving pictures and illustrated songs were given at the Mercer
School House. There was a change of pictures every Monday night.

On July 17, 1909, there was a social dance given at the A.N. Davenport farm and
the proceeds were used for the Mercer Valley baseball team supplies. Ice cream
and cake was served and the ladies were invited to bring cakes.

The masquerade ball on January 14, 1910, was the event of the season. It took
the judges, Messrs. Rice, Burdick and Wiest thirty minutes to pick the winners
during the grand march. The best dressed lady was Miss Marie Schumacher (the
telephone operator), the best dressed gentleman was Walter Murphy (a carpenter),
and the most comical dressed gentleman was Ray Meyer. The music was by the
Morgan Brother's Harp Orchestra and the meal was served by hotel landlord
Peterson.

The basket social on February 4, 1910, was for the benefit of the amateur
baseball boys. The ladies contributed about twenty-five baskets which brought in
more then $50 with the bids ranging from $1.00-$5.00.

In March 1915, the Saturday night show in the auditorium put on by the Mercer
Home Talent Comedy was a success. Some of the participants were Fred Winklemann,
Art Shelton, Ole Hedahl, Claude Baramore, Ross Gardiner, Andrew Nelson, Adaline
Washburn, Antonette Morton, Marie McFadden, Ida Ketterling, Regina Singer, Helga
Nelson, Evelyn Knutson, Harry Nelson, Anton Hedahl, Roy Nelson, Carson Angele
and Bernard Hale. "It was a scream from start to finish."

In July 1915, a cabaret ice cream social was held in the town hall sponsored by
the Mercer Women's Study Club. Proceeds were given to the town well fund. A
musical program was given and the city orchestra furnished music throughout the
evening. Ice cream and cake were served during the evening. At 10:30 p.m. the
tables were cleared and the evening was spent in dancing. The businessmen in
the post office block donated a dollar each and graveled the street in front of
the business places.

The Mercer Booster Band was organized in February 1910, and after the
instruments arrived on March 4, 1910, practice began. A bandstand was built in
March 1911 by businessmen "to show their appreciation of the way the band boys
were pushing their work in perfecting their organization." It was located on the
corner lot of Regan and Main Streets and band concerts were held there and also
at Brush Lake. Herb Wiest was the president of the band; George McFadden was the
vice president; W. Christianson, librarian; C.H. Davenport, director; John
Rogge assistant director; George Stohler, secretary and Eddie Heugelen,
treasurer. It is not known when the bandstand was moved to Brush Lake where it
also served as a podium for politicians and others who wanted to speak.

Members of the original band were Will Hunt, Halfdan Berge, Ira Washburn, Ed
Plowman, Herb Wiest, Mike Crow, Jessie Klein, John Rogge, James Murphy, Carl
Degg, Alec Singer, Lawrence Benson, Ole Hedahl, Andrew Nelson, Eddie Heugelen,

        Photo: Members of the 1915 Mercer Boosters Band were 1. Geo McFadden, 2.
        Rogg, 3. Chester Howell, 4. Andrew Neilsen, 5. Ole Hedahl, 6. E.O.
        Kleve, 7. John Ketterling, 8. Nels Angele, 9. H. Berge, 10. Wm Ludwick,
        11. unknown, 12. unknown, 13. H. Wiest, 14. Ed Plowman, 15. Ted
        Knutson.(Courtesy of Richard Ketterling collection)

Nels Peterson, John Ketterling, George McFadden, Walter Murphy, Archie Williams,
Charlie Williams, Theodore Knutson, Walter Christianson, George Heinze, George
Stohler, James Rice, William Ladwig, Adolph Singer, Harry Peterson, Rudolph
Singer and Nelson Angele. It was noted that very few of the members had ever
played any kind of instrument but their willingness to practice and perform made
them "sound good anyway." The picture of the Booster Band is dated 1915.

The first band picnic was to be held in August 1910 at Brush Lake but rain
postponed the band concert. However, two fast baseball teams were able to play
six innings before an injury and rain ended the picnic.

There were dance bands which played for dances at the Brush Lake pavilion,
private homes/barns, Mercer City Hall and at the hotel. It must have been the
custom, because a dance was usually held before the opening of a business, the
Dakovna store as an example.

The Mercer orchestra presented concerts. Member were Ella Myrah (later Mrs.
O.S. Hjelle) piano; Herb Wiest, violin; Ed Heugelen, coronet; and Walt
Christianson clarinet.

In later years, the musical events continued. It is not known how long the
Booster Band continued to practice and perform. However there were various
groups which were available for dances and dancing was a social event until
after World War II. At the present time, wedding dances take place in Turtle
Lake or other cities, or even as street dances in Mercer.

On April 6, 1958, a Mercer Community Choir presented a concert to standing room
only attendance. The sixty choir members were from the four Mercer churches. The
directors were Ellen and Pastor Lautt of the Baptist church. Soloists were Edwin
Fiedler, Tillie (Mrs. Christ) Heim, Rev, Lautt, Olga (Mrs. Julius) Sackman and
Andrew Rust. Donna Fiedler and Joyce Gessele were accompanists. The free will
offering of $63.54 was added to the school improvement fund.

        Photo: The Mercer Community Choir presented a concert April 5, 1958.

Members of the chorus were: Janice Skaley, Roberta Roseno, Karen Wentz, Pat
Christensen, Arlis Wagner, Connie Freeberg, Kirsten Nielsen, Dora Jorgenson,

Pfenning, Dorothy Postel, Karen Thompson, Dorothy Makeeff, Lillian Sackman,

Wahl, Tillie Heim, Tillie Wanner, Larry Fueller, Christ Heim Jr., Jacob Rust,

The City of Mercer held a Centennial celebration in honor of North Dakota's
Bicentennial on May 27 and 28, 1989. The agenda on page 60 shows the activities
that took place.

The next celebration will be Mercer's 100th birthday on July 1, 2, 3, 2005.

Amateur Sports

In addition to the tasks of getting settled in the new village, Mercer people
also took time out to participate or watch sporting events.

The first mention of a baseball game in the Telegram was in the July 24, 1908,
issue when Washburn defeated Mercer 10 to 1 and then in August 7, 1908, Washburn
again won 19-10. There is no mention of who the players were.

In the May 21, 1909, issue, the names were Slyter, Wheeler, Klein, Hjelle,
Stephenson, Heinze, Williams and Ross Gardiner. The team wore red suits; however
the score was McClusky 16 and Mercer 6.

A headline article for the August 6, 1909, issue described the Mercer Valley and
Mercer Scrubs baseball game (at right).

The first basketball game noted in the Telegram was in November, 1912, when the
team of Greenfield, Hedahl, Sommers, Klein, Hjelle and Berge defeated Goodrich
20 to 1 - great defense! During this time, the Mercer Bloomer Girls team was
organized. They began as a baseball team but soon reorganized as a basketball
team. Members of this team were Pauline Singer, Tillie Sackmann, Emma
Sackmann, Rika Degg and Marie McFadden. The coach was Art Shelton. (See
picture) In March 1913, the girls' basketball team lost to Washburn 10 to 9,
but the men were victorious over Washburn 25 to 12.

        Photo: (At right) Members of the girls basketball team between 1912-15
        were (front, from left) Pauline Singer Weist, Art Shelton, Tillie
        Sackmann; (back) Marie McFadden Gardiner, Emma Sackmann, Rika Degg,
        unidentified. (Courtesy of Richard Ketterling collection.

        Photo: Members of the Mercer Baseball team in 1920 were (front, from
        left) Ross Gardiner, Jack Snyder, Art Shelton, Ole Hjelle, Floyd Sprout,
        Julius Sackman; (back) Grant Ovre, Roy Neilsen, Geo Krug, Ben Hjelle,
        and Ted Haas.

        Photo: Members of a 1940s Mercer Baseball Team are (front, from left)
        Emanuel Hinsz, Melvin Wagner, Jake Diede, Holdrich Mayer, Walter Sprout,
        Theophil Neumiller, Meinhardt Skaley, Emil Schlaht; (back) Martin
        Ockert, Floyd Sprout, Sidney Nielsen, Rudy Schmollinger, Reiny
        Schmollinger, David Fink Jr., Christ Schell Jr., and Melvin Dalos.
        (Courtesy of Luella Schell Kluck)

In 1915, the men's baseball team was called Berg's Cubs and the basketball team
was the War Dogs. Throughout the years, the Mercer opponents often were from
McClusky, Turtle Lake, Underwood, Goodrich, Washburn and Bowden. Travel was
often by hand car on the railroad.

In 1921, the McLean County basketball champions were from Mercer. Members of
that team were Julius Sackman (Captain), Teddy Sackmann, Floyd Sprout, Ed
Sackman, Kenneth Schmidt, Ludwig Totdahl, Herbert Schmitt and Grant Ovre. The
coach was Prof. Duncan.

Amateur sports continued at Brush Lake where a baseball diamond was built and
maintained. At the present time, there are no organized teams, only "pick up"
games.

        Photo: (At right) The 1921 McLean County Basketball Champions, from
        Mercer: (front) Capt. Julius Sackman; (middle, from left) Teddy Sackman,
        Floyd Sprout, Eddie Sackman, Kenneth Schmitt; (back) Ludwig Totdahl,
        Herbert Schmitt, Grant Ovre and Prof. Duncan. The team posted a season
        record of 25 wins and one loss. (From the Washurn Leader)

Blizzards/Fires/Winds

The title of blizzards/fires and winds summarizes the fears of the early
residents and even though modern equipment reduces the threat, the danger is
still present today.

BLIZZARDS

In the early days, blizzards were an ever occurring event during the winter
months. There were many items in the early Telegram about the cold and the snow
with a noteworthy item in a December 1916 issue. The classes were dismissed in
the first year of the new brick school house because the temperature was minus
42°. Also in 1916, Mercer and other villages along the Northern Pacific
Railroad were without a train for forty-two days because the snow kept drifting
over the railroad tracks, making the work of the snow plows useless. For the
Mercer residents, the mail, food and other needs were hauled by sled and horses
from Drake.

See the story "A Prairie Blizzard" on page 406 of the Reminiscences about the
storm on February 22, 1922.

Recalled by Mercer residents were the winters of 1948-1949 and also the
following winter. For both of those events, the National Guard was called to dig
out the hay stacks, farms, and the roads.

In 1951, Mercer was isolated for almost three weeks and faced fuel and food
shortages. There was a shortage of coal, bottled gas and all the milk and yeast
were used up. The only milk available was condensed sweetened milk and baking
bread was not an option. School attendance was limited, the "farm kids" were
not able to get to school and the town kids and teachers weren't always able to
get to school either. One man became ill and he was taken to the hospital in
Bismarck in an unconventional way. He was taken by jeep to Turtle Lake driving
over the railroad tracks. A rotary plow had opened the road to Bismarck and his
journey was continued by auto. (This item was a featured article in the Bismarck
Tribune.

        Photos: Two photos of the snowstorn in April of 1997, with a recording
        of 100 inches of snow. (Above) Eileen Schell stands by a snowbank.

        Photo: Students playing on the snow in front of the school, 1936.

        Photo: 1939: Standing in front of the frosty Christmas tree in the
        center of Main street are (from left) Ted Sackmann, Marie Sackmann,
        Minnie Freeberg and Rudy Orman. (Courtesy of Evelyn Freeberg)

Even though there are still winter storms and blocked roads at this time, it is
rare to be isolated for any length of time. Modern snow removal equipment is
available and roads are opened quickly.

FIRES

The dread of early settlers were prairie and in-town fires because fire fighting
equipment was not motor powered. In Mercer and the surrounding areas, there
were many recorded fires. A few examples:

In 1905, a prairie fire burned a path from Brush Lake to near Butte.

In April 1908, a blacksmith forge started a prairie fire that burned for two
miles.

In September 1908, a prairie fire started near Melville Lake in Medicine
Township and burned into the Prophet range.

In August 1910, a fire on the west side of Main Street destroyed the pool hall,
the town hall and the First State Bank. The pool hall and the bank were
immediately     rebuilt

The McFadden/Freeberg store was burned in the late 1920s. The brick structure
was replaced with the present front.

In October 1938, a prairie fire started by the railroad at Mercer burned all the
way to Pickardville and burned 100 tons of hay.

The city hall was destroyed by fire in 1950. This building had been used for
church services.

The Plowman building on the west side of Main Street was burned in October,
1953.

WINDS

Wind damage continues to take place in Mercer. Many of the trees that were
planted by the early home owners have become weakened by age and drought and
become victims of high winds. In 1923, a cyclone damaged the City Feed Mill and
the St. Paulus Lutheran Church located four and one-half miles northwest of
Mercer was destroyed by a cyclone. The church was never replaced.

FLOODS

There are no records of any major floods in Mercer.

Churches and Cemeteries in the Mercer area

William Lewis Keller, Pioneer Lutheran Pastor in the Central Dakotas By LaRose
Ketterling

Printed with permission from the Germans from Russia Heritage Society.

The Reverend William Lewis Keller was the pioneer German Lutheran missionary
pastor who organized six German Lutheran congregations in the Mercer-Turtle Lake
area in McLean County, North Dakota.

William Lewis Keller was born in Brooklyn, New York, on September 22, 1854, and
was baptized and confirmed in the Presbyterian Church. His father was a
carpenter and the son followed his father's occupation. A turning point in the
son's life came when he was working high up on a construction job, became faint
and fell nearly three stories. He quit the job on the spot.

        Photo: William Lewis Keller, 1854-1932 (Courtesy of Alvin Keller)

A family friend had a farm in Gottenberg, Iowa, and the young Keller went to
help him on his farm. The family was a member of the Lutheran Church and young
William attended services with the family. The pastor of the church, Reverend
Paul, became William's mentor. Because he desired to become a communicant, he
studied with Reverend Paul and became a Lutheran convert.

At the age of thirty-five, he entered the Evangelical Lutheran Theological
Seminary in Afton, Minnesota, which, after several synod and seminary mergers,
became the present Wartburg Lutheran Seminary in Dubuque, Iowa. In 1892 he
became an ordained Lutheran pastor. His first call was to a parish in West
Virginia where he served for one year before returning to Minnesota to teach at
a seminary near St. Paul.

During this time, the bachelor pastor became interested in a member of the
church choir. Ottilie Kroenke was from Germany and was visiting a sister in St.
Paul. He sought the advice of his mentor, Reverend Paul, wondering if Ottilie
might be interested in being a pastor's wife. After a four-week courtship, they
were married in 1893 and became parents of twelve children.

        Photo: William Lewis Keller and wife Ottilie Kronke - 1893. (Courtesy of
        Alvin Keller)

In the beginning of the twentieth century, immigrants from Eastern Europe,
especially Germans from South Russia, were arriving in America in large numbers.
After a brief stopover in the Yankton, South Dakota, area, they moved north, and
some homesteaded in McLean County in central North Dakota. Many of these were
Lutheran and the need for German-speaking pastors was great. In the fall of
1903, Pastor Keller answered the call and arrived with his family in Underwood,
North Dakota, where they spent the winter with the Reverend August Affeld and
family.

In the spring of 1904, Pastor Keller filed first papers for a homestead on 160
acres six miles north of Mercer in McLean County (Sec. 2, Twp. 147-79, "Wise").
The final papers were filed on September 17, 1909. Utilizing his skills as a
carpenter, and with the help of pioneer builders, Fred and Victor Winklemann, he
began the construction of his farm. The barn was built first and the family
lived there until the house was ready. The family prospered on this farm until
1926 when Pastor Keller left the area to serve two country churches in the
Elgin, North Dakota, area.

In 1930 Pastor Keller's health began to deteriorate and he and his wife moved to
Carrington, North Dakota, to live with their son Alvin who was a pastor there.
Shortly after the move the pastor had a stroke. When the family gathered at his
deathbed, he told them, "Today I'm dying and I don't want any of you to cry
because all of my life I've been looking forward to seeing my Savior." (His son
Alvin remembered this wish.) He died on November 8, 1932. Mrs. Keller died at
the age of 104 in 1977. Both are buried in Jamestown, North Dakota.

Pastor Keller wrote out his sermons in longhand and his wife edited them. He
then memorized them and would preach in German or in his Brooklyn-accented
English. Perhaps one of his most memorable funeral services was the one he and
his son Pastor Walter Keller conducted for the funeral of the seven-member Wolff
family who had been murdered. The service took place outdoors on the Wolff
farmstead north of Turtle Lake, North Dakota, in April 1920. The father
preached in German and the son conducted the English service.

Of the twelve children in the Keller family, ten grew to adulthood. All six
surviving sons, Walter, Martin, Otto, Meinhardt, Alvin and Amos, became Lutheran
pastors. The daughters were Lydia, Alice, Julia and Grace. All of the family are
deceased. The last, Alvin, died in 2000 at the age of ninety-two. Several
grandsons became leaders in the Lutheran Church. John Keller, the second son of
Walter (all three sons of Walter are Lutheran pastors) is internationally known
for his work with chemical addiction counseling. Robert, son of Martin, is a
retired Bishop of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (ELCA) in the state
of Washington.

Shortly after Pastor Keller established his home north of Mercer, he organized
the first of six "Keller" churches in the Mercer-Turtle Lake area. Located four
miles west of his farm and nine miles northeast of Turtle Lake, it was named
Frieden's (Peace) Evangelical Lutheran Church (Section 7, Twp. 147-79, "Wise").
It was organized in 1904-1905 and was known locally as the "Hofer" Church.
Founding German-Russian family names included among others Hofer, Sackmann,
Fueller, Fink and Birst. The church building was destroyed by a tornado on July
8, 1923. The majority of the membership decided not to rebuild in the country,
but established the Peace Lutheran congregation in Turtle Lake. The cemetery of
the country church is still being maintained and still receives burials. One of
the graves in the cemetery is that of Mrs. Keller's mother who had been living
with the family at the time of her death.

        Photo: Zion Evangelical Lutheran Church, rural Mercer.

Before there was a post office in Mercer (October 2, 1905), German Lutherans
were gathering in their homes south of Mercer for worship. Services were
conducted by either Reverend Keller or by lay members. Balthasar Kleingaertner
was prominent as a lay preacher, having gained some experience as a devout
follower of the Bruedergemeinschaft (a pious Bible study group) in his homeland
village of Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia in South Russia. On February 20, 1906, the
second of the "Keller" churches, Zion Evangelical Lutheran congregation, was
organized and included a list of German-Russian founders with family names like
Kleingaertner, Laib, Bossert, Wagner, Singer, Kurle, Schell, Just, Flemmer,
Bender, Fischer, Schlafmann, Berg and Wall. Two acres of land located seven
miles south and one mile west of Mercer were purchased for the church and
cemetery Sec. 10, Twp. 145-79, "Park"). The cornerstone was laid on July 8,
1906, and the dedication was in October 1906. The Zion congregation disbanded in
1976. The cemetery is maintained and still receives burials.

        Engraving: Emmanuel Evangelical Lutheran Church, rural Mercer. (Drawing
        by Patricia Schon)

        Photo: St. John's Evangelical Lutheran Church, rural Turtle Lake.

The third of the "Keller" churches was the Emmanuel Evangelical Lutheran Church
(the "Schimke" Church). It was located eighteen miles northeast of Mercer in
Sheridan County (Sec. 6, Twp. 148-78, "Holmes"). The church and cemetery were
established in 1906, and founding family names included Krause, Hensel, Stelter,
Suelzle, Klatt, Schmollinger, Jesz, Schimke, Schon, Fiedler, Dockter, Bohnet,
Pfeiffer, Sprecher and Schott. The church had a unique iron cross on the roof
instead of a steeple. The cross was created by William Herringer, a blacksmith
in Butte, North Dakota, in memory of Adolph Schott, Sr. and is found today on
the grave of William Herringer in the Butte cemetery. This church disbanded in
1952, and the cemetery is presently being maintained by family members.

The fourth "Keller" church was St. John's Evangelical Lutheran Church (the
"Presser" Church). It was located sixteen miles northeast of Turtle Lake (Sec.
33, Twp. 149-79, "Aurena"). It was organized on the afternoon of November 12,
1907, by Pastor Keller and seventeen families. The first constitution drawn up
for the congregation required each member to pay $3.00 per year for the pastor's
salary and $1.00 per year for hay for the pastor's horse. In addition, it also
required a fee of $3.00 for confirmation, $1.00 for a baptism, $3.00 for a
funeral and $5.00 for a wedding. The church building, 22 × 42 feet, was
constructed in 1909. Each member paid $25.00 into the building fund. Members and
Pastor Keller, with his sons, donated labor and hauled materials. This church
disbanded and the building was sold. The cemetery is being maintained and still
receives burials. By this time, Pastor Keller was serving five churches and was
traveling by horse and buggy. He was able to hold services here every two weeks,
and served this congregation until 1924.

From 1907 until 1916, the German Lutherans living in the town of Mercer
worshipped in St. Paulus Evangelical Lutheran Church (the "Braun" Church), the
fifth "Keller" church. It was located four and one-half miles northwest of
Mercer (Sec. 6, Twp. 146-79, "Mercer"). The first recorded event, as noted in
the Mercer Telegram was the April 9, 1909, confirmation service for sixteen
young people. Members of the first class reflect the surnames of the original
German-Russian families who settled in the community: Singer, Degg, Thurn,
Braun, Keller (the eldest son of Pastor Keller), Wahl, Hofer, Sackmann, Presser
and Berg. The church was dedicated on July 11, 1911. A cemetery was platted and
is presently fenced but minimally maintained. The church was destroyed by a
tornado and was never rebuilt.

        Photo: Hoffnung (Hope) Evangelical Lutheran Church, Mercer, North
        Dakota. (Courtesy of Richard Ketterling collection)

The January 21, 1910, headline in the Mercer Telegram read: "Why not a church in
Mercer?" At the time the Mercer area German Lutherans were members of the three
rural churches served by the Reverend Keller. The other Lutherans, mostly
Scandinavians, attended services conducted by English- or Norwegian-speaking
pastors in the Mercer schoolhouse. Reverend Keller and members of St. Paulus
began plans to build a church in the town of Mercer (Sec. 2, Twp. 146-79).
Construction of the Hoffnung (Hope) Evangelical Lutheran Church began in the
spring of 1917. The church was dedicated that fall and the members of St. Paulus
became the nucleus of the congregation. Charter German-Russian family members
were Ketterling, Singer, Rennich, Wolf, Kleingaertner, Winklemann, Wagner,
Sackmann, Wise (Weisz) and Martzolf.

In 1917, Pastor Walter Keller, oldest son of Reverend William Keller, joined his
father in the ministry of the six congregations he had organized. Pastor Walter
and family lived in the German Lutheran (Zion, Emmanuel and Hope) parish
parsonage until they moved to Jamestown in 1921. From 1921 until 1926, Reverend
William Keller served the six congregations until he left the area. (Note: The
personal information about Pastor Keller's life is from an interview of the
Reverend Alvin Keller done a year before his death on September 20, 2000. -
Author)

The following letter to the editor of the November 25, 1932, Staats-Anzeiger
newspaper was written by the Reverend August Affeld following the death of
Pastor William Keller. It is an appropriate eulogy for a truly pioneering
missionary:

  Morton County, Rosebud, North Dakota
  November 17, 1932

  Dear Honorable Editor Brandt:

  Please include this item of the death of Reverend W.L. Keller in your worthy
  newspaper because this is of great interest to many people.

  Pastor Wilhelm L. Keller served in the vineyard of his Lord for forty-two
  years, twenty-eight of which were as a missionary in North Dakota where he
  drove many long missions and survived many storms. He was laid to rest during
  a fierce snowstorm in a cemetery in Jamestown, North Dakota on November 10,
  1932. With that, a blessed life came to an end.

  Pastor Keller was the son of Ludwig Keller and Julia Bohme and was born on
  September 14, 1854, in New York City. He was baptized on January 1, 1855, and
  confirmed on March 21, 1869, by Pastor B. Krose. His childhood and younger
  years were spent in the home with his beloved parents. After the death of his
  mother, he moved to Iowa at the invitation of his uncle to find employment in
  a shoe shop.

  But our God had a higher calling for the young man. Because of Pastor Besel,
  he attended church services and the pastor found that the God-fearing young
  man, even though he was 30 years old, was willing to study theology. It came
  to pass that in the fall of 1885, Keller began his studies at the Evangelical
  Lutheran Theological Seminary in Afton, Minnesota, to prepare himself for the
  ministry.

  Upon completion of his studies in 1889 and accepting a call to Newberg, West
  Virginia, he was ordained and began to serve his first parish. During his
  two-year service he experienced all the different activities of the Lutheran
  teachings. In 1891 the congregation and seminary staff at Afton, Minnesota,
  called him to become pastor (counselor) for the students and the parish
  pastor. After the relocation of the seminary in 1893 from Afton to St. Paul,
  he remained two more years as pastor for the Afton congregation. In 1895, he
  accepted a call to the parish in Lamberton, Minnesota. There he remained for
  nine years with so much respect and trust that the synod missionary officials
  in Columbus, Ohio, repeatedly issued a call for him to become a missionary to
  Mercer, North Dakota. However his congregation was reluctant to let him leave.

  In the middle of a severe winter and heavy snow and with faith in God, he
  answered the call; on January 31, 1904, he arrived in North Dakota with his
  wife and four small children. Here he served his Lord and Savior for twenty
  years under hardship and precarious conditions and organized six
  congregations. After that he served parishes near Elgin, North Dakota, for
  two more years. In 1930 he accepted the results of his advancing years and
  retired from active ministry and went to Florida to live near his daughter to
  regain his health.

  Pastor Keller was always a faithful and likable person and was highly
  respected and loved by his colleagues. He was a distinguished master of the
  ministry. During his ministry of forty-two years, he performed 703 baptisms,
  102 weddings, 358 confirmations, 104 burials and administered the Lord's
  Supper to 1,736 persons.

  In 1893 he married Miss Ottilie Kroenke of St. Paul, with Pastor George Paul
  officiating. God blessed this union with twelve children, and six sons and
  four daughters survive their father. In his last years, Pastor and Mrs. Keller
  lived with their second youngest son, Alvin, a pastor in Carrington, North
  Dakota. It was here that he suffered a stroke, which was complicated by
  pneumonia. When the chances for survival decreased, the children who lived in
  various parts of the United States were called to be with their father, and
  all were present except the oldest daughter who lived in Florida. On the
  morning of November 8, 1932, Pastor Keller, secure in the belief of his
  Savior, departed into eternity.

  His widow, Ottilie Keller, and the following children survive him:  Pastor
  W.W.A. Keller of Jamestown, North Dakota; Mrs. F.W. Kruger of Jacksonville,
  Florida.; Pastor Martin Keller of Max, North Dakota; Pastor Otto Keller of
  American Falls, Idaho; Pastor Meinhardt Keller of Poth, Texas; Mrs. Sidney
  Murch of Arthur, North Dakota; Pastor Alvin Keller of Carrington, North
  Dakota; Mrs. Edwin Schulz of Elgin, North Dakota; Amos Keller, a student at
  the Wartburg Seminary in Dubuque, Iowa; and Miss Grace Keller, a student at
  the Lutheran Academy in Hebron, Nebraska. Also among the survivors are two
  brothers, sixteen grandchildren and many other relatives. (We express our
  sympathy. We were personally acquainted with the deceased. - Editor)

  For the church services, the writer spoke in the German language and the
  Pastor J.F.L. Bohnhoff in English. Included in the funeral service was the
  reading of a telegram from Pastor George Landgrebe, president of the Dakota
  District, and from other pastors who could not be present because of the
  snowstorm. Pastor Bohnhoff officiated at the graveside service.

  Thanks be to God, for we Christians do not stand at the grave of a loved one
  like others who have no hope. We mourn only their leaving, but rejoice and
  look forward to a reunion in eternity where there will be no parting. Yes,
  blessed are those who died in the belief of their Lord.

  August Affeld, Pastor

(Obituary translation by the author)

Zion Lutheran Church

Originally written by the Rev. Robert G. Dirks, submitted by LeRoy Laib and
updated by LaRose Ketterling

        Photo: Zion Lutheran Church at the 1919 dedication. (Courtesy of Martha
        Schell Schlafman)

Zion Lutheran Church was organized on February 20, 1906, by twelve German
Lutheran families and their first pastor, Rev. W.L. Keller, pioneer missionary.
Occasional services had been held for two years previous to this in the homes of
the members, at which time the group had gone by the name of Andrews
congregation. At the organizational meeting it was decided to purchase two acres
of land for a church site and to build as soon as money was available. With the
assistance of gifts from friends as far away as South Dakota, it was possible on
July 8, 1906, to lay the cornerstone for the first church building located seven
miles south and one mile west of Mercer, North Dakota, near the center of the
state. The church was dedicated in October of 1906. In the year 1908, the
members of Zion congregation voted to join the Ohio synod. The first church
building was very small and was replaced by another structure in 1919. The
cornerstone was laid on July 9 and the building was dedicated on November 9,
1919.

Zion congregation has always been a part of a multiple parish, which at various
times included at least five other Lutheran congregations in and around Mercer,
most of which were begun during the ministry of W.L. Keller. One of these was
Hope Lutheran church (1916-1957) located in the town of Mercer. In January of
1957, Hope Lutheran congregation merged with Our Savior's, a congregation of the
Evangelical Lutheran Church, also located in the town of Mercer. In March of
1957, the Lutheran parish was formed which consisted of Zion Lutheran and Our
Savior's. This parish was disbanded when Zion Lutheran Church closed and most of
the members became affiliated with Our Savior's in 1973.

Zion congregation numbered about 100 baptized members and served an entirely
rural community. Services were begun in the German language which was
discontinued in the 1950s and services were conducted in the English language.

One son of Zion Lutheran Church served in the ministry, the late Rev. Albert
Wagner.
