German Lutheran Church in Mercer

St. Paulus/ Hope Lutheran Churches

St. Paulus, known locally as the Braun Church, was located 4½ miles north west
of the village of Mercer. It was organized by Pastor William L. Keller in
1907/1908. A building was built and a cemetery was platted. The church was
dedicated on July 2, 1911.

In 1909, 16 young people were confirmed reflecting the names of the German
Lutheran families in the area: Paulina, Christine, and Kate Singer; Pauline
Thurn; Maggie and Rogel Degg; Christine Figela; Marie Braun; Walter Keller (the
son of the Pastor); Alexander Singer; Rudolph Wahl; William Roab; Jake Hofer;
Emmanuel Sackmann; Leon Presser and Edward Berg. In March 1910, there was
another confirmation and the final class was in April, 1915.

        Photo: Hope Lutheran Church, 1916 dedication. (Courtesy of Richard
        Ketterling collection

A headline in the Jan.21, 1910 edition of the Mercer Telegram read "Why not a
church in Mercer?" Services for the Scandinavian Lutherans and the other
denominations were held in the school house, the city hall or private homes by
visiting pastors. In 1916, the members of St. Paulus began to plan for a church
in town. On May 8, 1917, Lot 10 Block 3 of the original town site was sold to
the German Evangelical Lutheran Hope Congregation by Edwin N. Hedahl. St. Paulus
Church was closed in 1917 when the building of Hope was completed. The St Paulus
Church building was destroyed by a cyclone in 1918. The cemetery has 2
identifiable graves, Mrs. Louise (John) Braun who was buried in 1918 and Jacob
Miller. The cemetery is fenced in and is minimally maintained.

The builder of the Hope Church was Fred Winklemann at the cost of $2000.
Furnishings as recorded in the treasurer's record was:

        Bell for $64.85 + freight and delivery cost (dray) of $23.23.
        Altar and pulpit $ 178.00 + freight and delivery cost of $37.11
        Gas lamps $9.00.
        The cost of building supplies was not recorded.

Charter members were from the St. Paulus congregation.. They were the families
of Johann Ketterling, Christoph Singer, Karl Rennich, Christian Wolf, Christ
Kleingartner, Christof Sackmann, Fred Marzolf, Gottfried Wagner. Also members
were Frederick Winklemann, Mrs. Schmitt, Mrs. J.R. Washburn, Mrs. John Berreth,
and Adolf Singer. The church was dedicated in the fall of 1917.

In 1920, the house of the Ketterling family located directly south of the church
was purchased for a parsonage. This house served as the parsonage for the German
Lutheran parish until 1945 when it burned. All the records of the 4 Lutheran
churches were destroyed. The "Rice" house was purchased for the parsonage.

        Photo: St. Paulus Lutheran Cemetery. (Fence design by Karl Rennich)

Pastor W.L. Keller served the parish until 1926. He was joined by his son, Rev.
Walter Keller who was ordained and served from 1917-1921.

The 3 German Lutheran churches organized by Pastor W.L. Keller - Zion German
Lutheran Church south of Mercer, Emmanuel German Lutheran church (Schimke) 18
miles NE of Mercer and Hope German Lutheran Church in Mercer formed the Mercer
German Lutheran parish. Pastors serving the parish after the Rev. Walter Keller
moved to Jamestown were: the Reverends A. Rink1921-1922; P. Mohr 1923-1924; J.
Huetmeyer 1924-1934; O. Bruntsch 1934-1937; G. Simfendorfer 1937-1939; G. Kern
1941-1945; E. Vetter 1947-1949; F. Doyon 1949-1953 and A. Kubick 1954-1956.

The Hope congregation disbanded and joined Zion Lutheran and Our Savior's
Lutheran church to form the Mercer parish in 1957. The church building and the
furnishings were sold to the East Crooked Lake Lutheran congregation and moved
north of Turtle Lake.

Saint Ansgar Canish Lutheran Congregation

St. Ansgar Danish Lutheran Congregation was organized November 24, 1905, by the
Danish settlers north of Mercer, with the help of Pastor P.M. Petersen of
Kenmare, North Dakota. (Ansgar, under King Horik, built the first Christian
church in Denmark). First officers of St. Ansgar Congregation were: Peder
Christensen-President, Nels Olesen-secretary, and C.P. Christensen-treasurer.
Early records were written in the Danish language.

    Early members were:

        Photo: St. Ansgar congregation: (from left) Chris Walle, 1½-yr-old
        Walle boy, Soren Nelsen, Jens Bille, Fred Christensen, Chris P. (CP)
        Christensen, Ed Skow, Peter Christensen, Jonas Christensen, Carlie

        (Mrs. Tony) Christensen, Peter Nelsen, Tony Christensen, Kate (Mrs.
        Pete) Nelsen, and Hannah Walle (Mrs. C.P.'s sister). Taken at Jonas
        Christensen homestead around 1911. (Courtesy of Christensen collection)

Church services were held monthly in the member's homes and were conducted by a
pastor or lay preacher from Kenmare, North Dakota. The largest Danish settlement
in North Dakota was at Kenmare. The preacher would take the train to Balfour
where a congregational member would pick him up, and he was housed in a member's
home for the weekend. After services on Sunday, a large potluck dinner was held.

St. Ansgar congregation called Rev. Frederick Petersen from Viborg, South
Dakota, in 1907. When he and his wife Anna, and three year old daughter Clara
arrived in the spring of 1908 on an immigrant train, they took up a homestead on
Section 11 in Wise Township, one half mile east of Pastor Keller's homestead.
The 1910 census listed Fred as age thirty-six, married six years, a farmer, born
in 1891 in Denmark. His wife Anna was thirty-two years old, and they had one
child, Clara, age five.

St. Ansgar's Ladies Aid was organized in January of 1910 at the home of Pastor
Fred Petersen. Their first President was Mrs. Fred Petersen, Vice President was
Mrs. Jake (Minnie) Nelson, Secretary was Mrs. Anton (Josie) Christensen, and
Treasurer was Mrs. Jonas (Juliana) Christensen. Meetings were held in the
ladies' homes. Early members besides the officers were: Mrs. Peder Nelson, Mrs.
Julius Johnson, Mrs. Jens Bille, Mrs. Christ Walle, Mrs. Peter Matteson, Mrs.
Sam Anderson, Mrs. Peter (Johanna) Christensen, Mrs. O.P. Nelson, Mrs. Jens
Nelson, Mrs. Martin (Christina) Christensen, Mrs. C.P. (Anne) Christensen.

The Oct. 27, 1911, Mercer Telegram reported "St. Ansgar Ladies' Aid will give a
supper and have a bazaar at the Belmont Hotel on Saturday November 4, 1911.
Supper is 25 cents for adults and 15 cents for children."

The March 29, 1912, Mercer Telegram reported that Missionary Jens Dixon of
Kenmare held services at the home of Rev. Petersen, Martin Christensen, and in
the Mercer School during Easter. He stayed at Pastor Petersen's home. The St.
Ansgar cemetery records list a Baby Petersen that was born and died in 1912.
Parents were Rev. and Mrs. Petersen. In November that year, the Petersen family
moved to Moorhead, Iowa.

A lay preacher, Missionary Peterson from Kenmare, came frequently for services,
and everyone was very fond of him. Four to six times a year a Kenmare pastor
came to baptize and serve Holy Communion. Margaret Christensen, daughter of
Martin wrote "I guess we'll never forget those meetings in our homes. The
potluck dinners...stories told by the pastors and Missionary Peterson to the
children while the Mom's fixed the dinners after the morning services... how
they turned the chairs around in a circle and knelt at them for their communion
service. I think the thing that impressed me the most was all those men getting
together with the pastor while the moms cleaned up the dishes, and they sang
their hearts out from the old Sangerns, or Danish hymn books, without music...
remembering their church experiences in Hutchinson where many of them had sung
in the choirs."

After 1916, Rev. Ulvilden from Mercer held services in English in Sprout's
school for the Danes. He baptized June Sylvia Nelson, Clara Ethel Bille,
Clifford Calheim, and Henry Karl Christensen in 1917. Rev. Knutson baptized
Charlotte Johnson and Aimee Christensen in 1919, and Marion Christensen in 1920.
Rev. Hansen baptized Ernest Christensen in 1921. Rev. Lund baptized Eleanor
Christensen in 1923, and Perry Nelson in 1926. Rev. Christensen baptized Earl
Christensen and Arnold Calheim in 1925. Other baptisms with no pastor listed
were James Morris Olsen, Clifford, Raymond, Milo and Elmer Calheim, and Grace
and Mary June Christensen.

The Ladies Aid met monthly in the homes, weather permitting. Usually Mrs. C.P.
Christensen would read from the Bible, and business was conducted. The Ladies
Aid gave financial support to the Santal Mission in India. The summer of 1922,
Mrs. Keller was elected an officer, and she hosted Ladies Aid. In 1923, Mrs.
Oscar (Connie Kalland) Belsheim joined the group.

Although land was donated for a church and cemetery in the southwest corner of
Section 35-148-79 by Martin Christensen, a church was never built. In March
1928, St. Ansgar congregation voted to join Our Savior's congregation in Mercer.
St. Ansgar cemetery was deeded to Our Saviors Lutheran Church, and platted in
1931. It contains 1.75 acres. St. Ansgar's Ladies Aid purchased the baptismal
font for Our Savior's that is still in use there in 2004.

(Compiled from St. Ansgar's Church record book)

Our Savior's Lutheran Church

On Christmas Day 1907, there was a very large attendance at the Norwegian
services in the Mercer school. The ladies spent the afternoon decorating the
tree, and pleasant memories were made for the little folks, according to The
Mercer Telegram.

        Photo: Our Savior's Lutheran Church.

The September 3, 1909, Mercer Telegram reported, "Rev. N.L. Rockwell will hold
services at the school house Sunday September 5 at three o'clock PM. The Mercer
Sunday School was reorganized last Sunday with Nels Olesen as superintendent,
and Mrs. George Heinze as assistant. Everybody is invited to send their children
to these services every Sunday at 10 o'clock AM."

Even before Our Savior's Congregation began, there was a Christian women's group
at Mercer whose purpose was service to the poor and needy. It was organized in
December 1910 at Mrs. Samuel Andersen's home. The Helping Hand Society's first
President was Mrs. J. Helm (Juanita) Davidson, Vice President was Mrs. Charles
McLaughlin, and Secretary-Treasurer was Mrs. James Rice. They met every other
week to sew for the poor and needy and to raise funds for charity. They also
held Sunday School. The teachers were Mrs. J.H. Davidson, Mrs. Fred Freeberg,
Mrs. Will Murphy and Mrs. Sam Anderson. They encouraged the organization of a
Scandinavian Lutheran church at Mercer.

Minnie Freeberg, an early resident, wrote in Reminisces, "We had no church, so
every time there were Danish services north of town, we would hire a team of
mules and go there to attend services, even if we could not understand
everything. One Christmas we had our Children's Festival in the pool hall.
Traveling pastors would come through our town and would have services in the
school house. Sunday school was organized that first fall."

Our Savior's Evangelical Lutheran Congregation was organized in December 1915 by
Rev. A.M. Turmo of Turtle Lake and they voted to call a pastor.

The Norwegian Lutheran Ladies Aid was formed on March 3, 1916, at Mrs. Nels
Hedahl's home. The first officers Mrs. Nels Hedahl, President, Mrs. O.S. Hjelle,
Vice President, and Mrs. E.M. Plowman, Secretary-Treasure.

Rev. Reinhart Ulvilden was installed September 3, 1916. Charter members in 1916
were Ole S. Hjelle, Ella Hjelle, John Hjelle, Brandt Hjelle, Nels Hedahl,
Ingeborg Hedahl, Anton Hedahl, Margaret Hedahl, Edwin Hedahl, Erling Hedahl,
Nels Fibelstad, Mrs. Nels Fibelstad, Jerome Fibelstad, Nellie Fibelstad, Ole N.
Hedahl, Halfdan Berge, Merle Berge, Knute Widen, Mrs. Knute Widen, Ada Widen,
William Peterson, Ella Peterson, Peder C. Nilson and Mrs. Peder Nilson

The first services of Our Savior's Congregation were held in the old Mercer
school until early 1917, when the new school was completed. Rev. Ulvilden
preached there as well as at the Sprout School (Wise Township #1) north of
Mercer. He was a talented singer and violinist and started a large Mercer
community choir.

Minnie Freeberg wrote "It wasn't long before we had a resident pastor, Pastor
Ulvilden, and he organized a Choral Choir of forty members, which was quite an
undertaking. If we were not there for practice, we had to have a written excuse,
and that happened only once when one young man could not be there for practice."

On March 25, 1917, Rev. R. Ulvilden called a meeting and a constitution was
adopted. Elected officers were: Trustees-Nils E. Hedahl, Knute J. Widen, and
Nels A. Fibelstad; Treasurer-Ole N. Hedahl; Secretary-H. Berge; and Deacon-E.N.
Hedahl.

Rev. Ulvilden and family left Mercer in June 1918. They moved to Omaha, and
later to Minot, North Dakota. During World War I, half the proceeds taken in by
the Ladies' Aid was given to the Red Cross.

Rev. Harold Hanson served from 1920 to 1922, with services held in the
schoolhouse. From 1922 until 1928 the congregation did not have a pastor, and no
regular services were held.

The Ladies Aid called a meeting for those interested in reviving the work of Our
Savior's on July 25, 1927. District President Rev. David Stoeve of Fargo was
present. It was decided to solicit new members and money to support a pastor.
The following committee was formed: south of Mercer-John Ness and Ed Pederson;
Mercer and Vicinity-Nels Fibelstad, B.C. Hjelle, and Halftan Berge; and north of
Mercer-Krogh Ovre and Jake Nelson.

In early 1928, St. Ansgar Danish Evangelical Lutheran Congregation from north of
Mercer joined Our Savior's Congregation. St. Ansgar was organized on November
24, 1905, by the Danes with the help of Pastor P.M. Petersen of Kenmare. First
officers were Peter Christensen-President, Nels Olesen-Secretary, and C.P.
Christensen-Treasurer.

Although land was donated by Martin Christensen for a Danish church and
cemetery, a church was never built. St. Ansgar Cemetery was deeded to Our
Savior's in 1928, and they have maintained that cemetery since then. Money
donated by the Danish Ladies Aid was used to purchase the baptismal font still
used today at Our Savior's.

On February 25, 1928, a special meeting was held at the home of B.C. Hjelle to
admit new members to Our Saviors. The trustees incorporated the congregation and
recorded the deed for the lots purchased by the Ladies Aid for $158.58.

The committee to solicit funds for the erection of a church building included
Fred O. Freeberg, Chris P. Christensen, Victor Carlson, Ed Pederson, O.S.
Hjelle, and William Peterson.

In the summer of 1928, Our Savior's and St. Olaf Lutheran Church formed the
Mercer-Turtle Lake Parish. Rev. Harold W. Sorensen, of Shevlin, Minnesota,
served this parish from 1928 to 1940. He was born September 23, 1879, and lived
at the St. Olaf parsonage with his wife, two daughters, and five sons. All five
of Rev. Sorensen's sons became Lutheran pastors.

In 1928, Our Savior's congregation voted to build a church 32 feet by 60 feet.
On May 21, 1929, a bid was signed with Mr. Stuverud for $6,780.

The basement was dug by local volunteers, which included William (Bill) Peterson
and his brothers, Victor Carlson, John Ness, Ole Estenson, and Anton Nelson.
Bill said they used four horses hitched to each scraper, and John Ness's tractor
to dig the basement east and west. When Mr. Stuverud arrived, he decided he
wanted the church to run north and south, so it had to be redone.

        Photo: The Sorensons: (front, from left) Margarit, Mrs. Sorensen,
        Rueben, Rev. H.W., and Synneva Sorensen; (back) William, Ingvald,
        Arthur, and Victor.

Mr. Stuverud had finished only the basement when he was killed in a car accident
near Carrington. Bill Peterson said Mr. Stuverud's men wanted to quit, but since
the lumber and crew were here already, the council made a deal with them to
finish the outside of the main church. Mr. Stuverud's estate was paid $1,200,
and then Our Savior's put out bids for the inside work.

Guy Thompson of Elbow Lake, Minnesota, bid $4,086 for the frame part of the
upper church, which was accepted. Our Savior's encountered financial problems as
the great depression set in. On May 29, 1930, the Ladies Aid donated $760 to the
church on the condition that the congregation would also borrow $1,000 to finish
the upstairs of the church, according to plans.

The finishing work was done by J.C. Beatties for $1,760. The Ladies purchased
material for homemade benches in 1931. The basement was finished in 1932. In
1935, the Ladies Aid purchased the alter rail with upholstered kneeler, altar
base, and lectern.

Dedication services for Our Savior's Lutheran Church were held June 21, 1936.
Dr. David Stoeve of Fargo delivered the sermon and laid the cornerstone. Seven
year old Carol Ulvilden played a violin solo and other music was provided by
Mrs. O.S. Hjelle, Miss Eunice Hjelle, and Margit, William and Victor Sorensen.

During Rev. Sorensen's ministry services were held every other Sunday,
alternating morning with evening services.

Rev. H.W. Sorensen called the first Luther League to order on December 1, 1929,
and a constitution was drawn up. First officers were: President-Vivian Scarvie,
Vice President-Walter Christensen, Secretary-Edna Stradinger, Treasurer-Ancher
Tothdahl, and Choirster-Phyllis Freeberg. The Luther League met after evening
services and the entire congregation participated. In June 1940, the Max Circuit
Luther League convention was held in Mercer, with the women serving the meals.

From 1936-1940, members were asked to pledge the proceeds from one acre of wheat
to help with expenses. In 1940, the minister's salary was reduced from $500 a
year to $350, and a pension plan was adopted. In 1942 the pastor's salary was
increased to $400 and in 1945, it was raised to $500. The mortgage was burned in
1944.

In 1945, the Ladies Aid began monthly Bible Study under Rev. Sorensen. A
stewardship concern led to freewill offerings and a "fall festival" once a year.
After about thirteen years it was transformed into the yearly mission festival.

The women served lutefisk suppers to raise funds to purchase new pews. In 1949
the council voted to start a Parish Board of Education, and the pastor's salary
was increased to $700, plus the Easter and Christmas offerings.

Rev. Sorensen served Our Savior's for twenty-one years, and retired in 1949. He
moved to Monrovia, California and died in September 1952. He is buried at North
St. Olaf's Cemetery, Turtle Lake, beside his wife.

In 1951, pews were ordered to replace the homemade benches. In the spring of
1951, the Mercer-Turtle Lake Parish was formally dissolved, and Our Savior's
became a part of the McClusky Parish. From 1928 until 1952, it had been a part
of the Max Circuit of the Evangelical Lutheran Church, but now it became part of
the Harvey Circuit. A mid-week Bible Study was started in 1951 and met until
1965.

January 8, 1953, the Men's Brotherhood was organized under Rev. T.A. Rykken for
Bible study and discussions. They also awarded scholarships for youth attending
a Lutheran college.

In 1957, Hope German Lutheran Church merged with Our Savior's. Also at this
time, Zion Lutheran Church south of Mercer and Our Saviors formed the Mercer
Parish. The James Rice house was purchased for the parsonage. In 1960, Our
Savior's became part of the American Lutheran Church.

        Photo: Dedication for Our Savior's Lutheran Church was held June 21,
        1936.

        Photo: Women's Mission Federation delegates were (from left) June Berge,
        Anna Berge, Ruth Christensen, Edna Glad and Minnie Freeberg. (Photos
        from Our Savior's scrapbook)

The 50th Anniversary of Our Savior's Lutheran was held on October 2, 1966.
Pastor Korsmo gave the morning sermon. In the afternoon Emil Schlaht spoke,
Walter Christensen read a history, and Mrs. W. Hanson and June Fettig sang
solos, accompanied by Mrs. Ludwig Totdahl. Rev. Hanson and Pastor Walter Keller
spoke, and Pastor Alvin Keller gave the sermon. The congregation had a total
membership of 201, with 136 confirmed.

In April of 1974, an electronic organ was purchased from Guy Larson Music in
Bismarck. Zion Lutheran Church south of Mercer closed in 1976, and most of their
members joined Our Savior's.

Great Plains Supply of McClusky began constructing a new parsonage in November
1979, and the Rice House parsonage was sold. The new house was moved onto the
site and Pastor Lemke moved into it in January 1980.

In 1983, Our Savior's again formed a joint parish with St. Olaf of rural Turtle
Lake. Pastor Russell Rhoads and his wife Janet moved into the St. Olaf parsonage
in July 1983. Our Savior's parsonage was rented to Clara Larson from 1984 to
1989 and sold to Albert and Regina Schell in 1991.

Pastor Rhoades initiated Young Adults, a group that meet once a month for social
fellowship. It is now called Fun Adults. He also started a monthly Men's
Devotional Breakfast or Lunch, depending on the time of year. During this time,
Our Savior's became part of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of America. New
shingles were added in 1984, and carpet, central vacuum, and a handicap ramp in
1986. Pastor Rhoades accepted a call to Berthold, North Dakota, December 1987.

Pastor Craig Larson began serving his first parish in August 1988. In October,
steel siding was installed. The sidewalk was replaced in 1990 and the sanctuary
was painted in 1991.

On July 14, 1991, Our Savior's held its 75th Anniversary Celebration. The
Worship Service was conducted by Pastor Larson. Other participating pastors were
the Reverands Rhoads, Korsmo, Hanson and Rev. Andrea Degroot-Nesdahl, Assistant
to the Bishop.

In 1991, Our Savior's had 108 baptized members, of which 84 confirmed. In August
1993 Pastor Craig Larson, Rebecca and girls left for Lake Havasu City, Arizona.

Pastor David Berg and Constance came in February 1994 from Huntington Beach,
California. This was his first call. He was active in the TL-M Drug and Alcohol
Core Team. In 1997 they moved to Grand Forks, North Dakota, where he took a job
as hospital chaplain.

        Photo: A visit to Mercer: (from left) Western North Dakota Synod ELCA
        Bishop Duane Danielson; H. Rueben Anderson, Bishop National ELCA; and
        Pastor Randy P. Emgarten, Our Savior's Lutheran Church. (Photo by Bev
        Christensen)

Pastor Randy Emgarten from Watertown, South Dakota arrived at his first church
on August 2, 1998. In 1999 the basement was remodeled and pew cushions were
added upstairs.

Pastor Randy is active in the Leo's Club at the TL-M High School, is Lions
President, Camp of the Cross director and pastor for staff, a Mercer Community
Center Director, and a member of the Turtle Lake-Mercer Dollars for Scholars
Board of Directors.

In August 2000, presiding Bishop H. George Anderson, head of the Evangelical
Lutheran Church of America visited Mercer. He was in North Dakota regarding the
rural crisis. Bishop Anderson's parents taught school in Mercer from 1921-23.
While in Mercer he toured the school, and had coffee in the church basement.

        Febelstad and Edna Glad. (Photo by Alvira Gessele)

Mercer Bethel Church By James Gessele

As the Dakota Conference of the Evangelical Church began its missionary program
throughout North and South Dakota in the early 1900s, it carried its ministry
largely to German-speaking immigrants, some who had come from Germany, mostly to
others who had come from South Russia.

One by one, preaching points were established in the Dakotas, in towns and rural
areas particularly, in an effort to bring the gospel to these people. Such was
the case for the Bethel congregation, sometimes known as the Wilton
congregation, located about ten miles south of Mercer, N.D.

In the summer of 1916 a desire materialized among neighbors and friends for an
Evangelical Church in the vicinity. That same fall the Reverend Henry Sailor, a
pastor from Underwood, N.D., paid a visit and organized the group, holding
services in the homes. In the spring of 1917 he held a revival meeting. Interest
awakened and opportunity for organizing began when Karl and Christina Goessele
gifted church land. A warranty deed dated April 4, 1917, granted a parcel 16 ×
20 rods (two acres) to "Heinrich Wagner, Ludwig Wagner, Karl Goessele, Philipp
Wall and Frederich Neumiller, Trustees of the Bethel Church of the Dakota
Conference of the Evangelical Association." Soon plans were laid for a church
building and by June of that year it was completed and dedicated. It was located
nine miles south, one mile west, and one-half mile south of Mercer (Park
Township, SW¼ of the NW¼, Sec. 27, Twp. 145-79).

Ten families took the initiative to create this congregation and became charter
members: the families of Eduard Gessele, Karl Gessele, Daniel Klein, Frederich
Neumiller, Heinrich Wagner, Ludwig Wagner, Philip Wall, Friedrich Wanner, Philip
Wanner and Philip Wanner Jr. Soon other families joined this nucleus: those of
Samuel Berg, Henry Gessele, Christian Neumiller, Gustav Neumiller, John Reuer
Sr., Edward Vossler, Fred Wall, Mike Wall, Christian Wanner, Emil Wanner, John
Berg, Henry Schaeffer and John Strobel. With the passing of time the children of
these families became part of the congregation.

Rev. Sailor served the Bethel congregation for two years, 1916-1918. At the
Annual Conference session of 1918 the congregation was placed on the McClusky
charge and served by the pastor residing in McClusky, N.D., the Rev. R.R.
Bloedau. He served until 1922. At that time three McClusky area congregations
(Jehovah, Emanuel and Zion) and the Goodrich congregation were already in the
charge. That meant the pastor served two congregations a Sunday and would
alternate his appearances and preaching in a given church every other Sunday.
This arrangement prevailed a number of years, and in the pastor's absence laymen
assumed responsibility for the day's worship.

From available pastoral reports it is clear worship services and church business
in the charge were conducted exclusively in German, a practice followed until
the appointment of Rev. E.K. Heimer in 1935. His report in 1935, the first ever
in English, spoke to the problem of the church not reaching its youth because of
language issues. To the consternation of some older members in the charge to
whom Heimer referred as "a few old kickers whom the Lord could not use," the new
minister sought and won approval for evening services "in the American." Of the
Bethel congregation he wrote: "The Wilton church seems to be at peace and have
the cause at heart." Heimer, an outspoken critic of the status quo, was
forthright in what he expected of his flock. He had a family of seven children
to support at a time when pastors were paid no regular salary. He relied on the
good will of his parishioners but often took matters in his own hand. In one
incident, he one day appeared on a parishioner's farm with a trailer in tow just
as the potato harvest was being gathered. He made it quite clear what part of
the harvest was his. In another incident he prevailed upon the same farmer to
give him a cow. Heimer placed the animal under his sons' care and it was
quartered in a pasture on the outskirts of McClusky.

The congregation continued its services and ministry in the rural setting until
1945. In November 1946 the Evangelical Church merged with the United Brethren in
Christ and thereafter the official name became Evangelical United Brethren
Church. For inexplicable reasons during the years 1946-1948, no regular services
were held, except occasional observances. But with the arrival of Rev. Edwin H.
Werner in 1949, a new interest opened in the church's life and ministry. Under
his enthusiastic leadership, plans were developed for the relocation of the
church building. Issues of inadequate location, poor roads and changing times
seemed to warrant such a move. The idea was to move the edifice to Mercer, but
that was deemed inadvisable once its poor condition was established. A new
building appeared to be the only alternative and a building committee was
appointed, including Rev. Werner, Henry Gessele, Edward Vossler, Bertha Wanner
and Ella Berg. In the meantime, the roof on the dilapidated building was
shingled, the windows were re-paned and the sanctuary given a housecleaning.

        Sketch: Mercer Bethel Church. (Artist sketch of church built in 1952.)

At its October 14, 1949, meeting the Building Committee made a final decision to
relocate in Mercer and to construct a new building. On October 28 a Women's
Society of World Service was organized; its mission was to undertake fund
raising projects in support of the new building. Winter weather lay ahead and
Christmas would soon arrive. There was no adequate heating system; the floor was
so cold during housecleaning that water froze to it when scrubbing got underway.
So an oil burner was installed and vented through one of the windows. Ted
Gessele installed fans throughout the room, and the Christmas service on the
prairie came off with everyone in relative comfort.

By the fall of 1951, the Women's Society had raised $1,000 through Kuchen and
fancywork sales and through food sales at auctions. On October 21, 1951, the
Building Committee took action to purchase lots from Fred Eckman in Mercer in
Block 20 of Olesen's Addition and to sell the old church. (Eventually the old
church was purchased by the local Church of God congregation and moved into
Mercer. Both edifices still stand in town today.) Ground breaking was set for
October 26 with plans to construct a basement and a rough structure that fall.
Unusually cold weather set in and the project was halted until spring. Work
resumed in May 1952 and the new church was dedicated on August 24 at an
estimated cost of $20,000. Bishop E.W. Praetorius conducted dedication
ceremonies.

At mid-century the number of congregations in the McClusky charge had narrowed
to two: Bethel and Jehovah in McClusky. Subsequently, services were conducted on
a weekly basis. A renewed interest in the church arose and an all-out effort was
made to erase the construction debt. Final indebtedness was lifted in the fall
of 1955.

During the same decade, the need for better parsonage facilities became obvious.
The issue was discussed at a Local Conference meeting in January 1959, a joint
session between McClusky and Mercer, and a temporary building committee
appointed. The committee became permanent in November 1961. Adeline Wanner,
Aletha Vossler and David Stelter represented the Mercer congregation. Approval
for the project came in March 1962. The old parsonage in McClusky was demolished
in April 1962; in October 1962 the basement of the new home was poured.
Construction resumed late April 1963 with a carpenter and donated labor from the
congregation. The pastor and his family moved into the facility November 1,
1963. The parsonage was dedicated June 21, 1964 by Bishop H.R. Heininger. The
estimated construction cost was $16, 500.

The congregation celebrated its fiftieth anniversary in 1966. At that time the
Evangelical United Brethren Church had established fraternal relations with the
Methodist Church to study possible merger of the two fellowships. That was
indeed carried out in 1968-69. Thereafter the church was named the United
Methodist Church. Rural and small town populations in North Dakota went into
decline and Bethel's membership base was quickly eroding. The congregation
remained intact for a twenty-fifth anniversary celebration of its town church in
1977. The church closed its doors in 1981 because of membership losses and the
fact it could no longer function financially. Its remaining membership shifted
to United Methodist congregations in McClusky and Turtle Lake.

First Baptist Church of Mercer by Vernia Rust Hausauer

The first service of this church was conducted sometime during September 1902.
Ten people assembled for an afternoon meeting in the twelve-foot square home of
Mr. and Mrs. Heinrich Wagner. This home was located twelve miles north of
Mercer.

It became apparent that the growing congregation would need a larger place to
worship and it was in 1906 that the Tabor Baptist church was built on land
donated by Mr. and Mrs. Samuel Rust, Sr. There were thirty-five members at that
time.

In 1908, Mrs. Heinrich Wagner donated two acres of land for a cemetery. The
same year a barn was built by the church for the horses.

The first regular minister that served this church who was shared with the
Rosenfeld Baptist Church was Rev. Benjamin Schlipf. He served from 1905 to
1909. During 1910-1914, Rev. Adolph Guenther served the church. This was
followed by a period of five years when the church was without a pastor and the
laymen of the church conducted the services. Rev. Christian Bischof served from
1919 to 1922. Rev. S. Fuxa served from 1922 to 1926. During this time the Tabor
Mission Station became organized as a separate church. Rev. Heinrich Braun
served during 1926 to 1933 while he was minister of the McClusky church. From
1935 to 1939, the Rosenfeld Church again shared Rev. Albert Bibelheimer with us.
In 1939 to 1946, we shared Rev. August Rosner with Turtle Lake Baptist Church.
Following that, Rev. Fred Schmidt served both the Turtle Lake and Mercer
churches from 1946 to 1951.

        Photo: First Baptist Church of Mercer. (Photo taken in 1996)

Following these years the church was able to have its own pastor.

1953-1953       Rev. Emanuel Brockel
1954-1959       Rev. and Mrs. Ben Lautt
1960-1964       Rev. &  Mrs. Albert Krombein
1964-1969       Rev. & Mrs. Otto Feisel
1969            for  4 months Interim Pastor Samuel Finsky
1969-1972       Rev. & Mrs. John Silvey
1973-1977       Rev. & Mrs. Arthur Freitag
1977-1987       Rev. Perry Schnabel
1988-1992       Rev. & Mrs. Don Schmid
1997-1997       Rev. & Mrs. Dan Herringer
1998 -          Rev. & Mrs. Vernon Schneider

Due to a decline in membership the church was moved into Mercer in 1947. Under
the leadership of Pastor Schmidt, the church was placed on a full basement and
remodeled to give a roomy entrance with a tower to the front of the building.

In 1952, a parsonage was built on two lots donated by Mr. & Mrs. John Wagner.
The parsonage was sold to Mr. & Mrs. Arnie Demchuk in 1996.

The church building received some changes in 1956 as the interior of the church
was completely redecorated. These renovations served the needs, but by 1968,
the need was felt for more education facilities and a new sanctuary. Evelyn
Freeberg donated land to the church and ground breaking was held on June 13,
1971. It was in these new facilities that the church hosted the 1972 Northern
Dakota Association.

The educational aspects of our church have been making great strides for the
Lord. We continue to enjoy Sunday School, Vacation Bible School, the Baptist
Youth Fellowship and Women's Missionary Fellowship. The church offers
additional horizons and opportunities for outreach as the members participate in
programs at the Sheridan Memorial Home in McClusky, World Day of Prayer, Turtle
Lake Swing Bed and the Bismarck Baptist Home.

Many changes have taken place in the past years so that the people still have
difficulty with the name of the church. The name was officially changed in June
1969 to the First Baptist Church of Mercer.

        Photo: Rev. and Mrs. Vernon Schneider

Mercer Church of God By Rev. Herb Wanner

The Church of God had its beginning in Mercer in the early 1940s. Its founder
was Rev. Reinhold Klaudt, father of the well known Klaudt Indian Family singers.
The church started by conducting street meetings. The former city hall was
obtained as the first building to house the church. In those days street
services were common, as it would reach the farmers of the area when they
brought their cream and eggs to sell in town on Wednesday and Saturday nights.
In turn they would pick up groceries and farm equipment parts, have their
plowshares sharpened and other repair work done at the local blacksmith shop.

        Photo: Pastor and Mrs. Arlan Swanson. (Courtesy of Chris Heim Jr.)

Among the most memorable pastors and families to serve the congregation were
Rev. Ralph and Bernice Brostrom, Rev. and Mrs. M.L. Lowe and Rev. John and Hilda
Dafee. Of these, the Lowe and Daffee families continued the traditional street
meetings periodically during their ministry here. The Lowe family took deep
roots in the area with several of their children marrying and starting their
families here. Gladys married Arnie Makeeff, Clinton married Doris Jorgenson and
Juanita married Meinhardt Wagner. The Wagners raised their family on the Wagner
family home south of Mercer. Juanita passed away a few years ago.

After the former city hall burned, the congregation purchased the Evangelical
United Brethren church building, which was located south of Mercer. The church
was moved next to the old hospital building, which now had been converted to a
parsonage, located one block east of downtown Main Street.

After Rev. Dafee came to serve as pastor, he and Herb Wanner constructed a
basement next to the building and moved the church again and at that time a
complete renovation of the rest of the building followed. The dedication proved
to be a most memorable occasion, a large crowd attended so that the building was
unable to hold them. Every seat and available standing room was taken, including
the basement. People were standing outside, and some that came from a distance
left because cars were parked all over town and traffic was backed as far as to
the highway.

Families that made up the congregation were Mr. and Mrs. Virgil Curtis; Mr. and
Mrs. Otto Wahl; Mr. and Mrs. Rudolph Weidrich; Mr. and Mrs. Emil Wanner; Mr. and
Mrs. Walter Netzloff; Mr. and Mrs. August Schiller; Mr. and Mrs. Christ Heim;
Mr. and Mrs. Herb Wanner; Mr. and Mrs. Fred Bohara; Mr. and Mrs. John Makeeff;
Mr. and Mrs. Henry Krein; Anna Stute; Olga Hofer and Frances Wasson.

In later years in the 1970s and 1980s, with the decline of the small towns the
Church of God and the United Methodist in Mercer shared a minister who was
provided by the Church of God. Then for several years, students and professors
from Northwest Bible College in Minot supplied ministers to both churches. Later
the United Methodist ceased to operate and the Church of God purchased that
building. Both churches eventually closed as the declining population in the
rural areas made it impractical to continue to function. Both buildings have
since been sold to private individuals.

        Photo: The Ralph Brostrom family.

The Box T Ranch Bible and Saddle Camp

Excerpts are from an article written by Laverne Swendsen in the McClusky Gazette
on August 23, 1996.

The Box T Ranch Bible Camp, a non-denominational Bible and Saddle Camp, is
located sixteen miles from McClusky in the southwest corner of Sheridan County,
ND. It is on a ranch owned by Florence and Lewellyn Tewksbury.

When the Tewksburys moved to the ranch in 1954, their goal was to serve the Lord
so they invited two boys to spend the summer where reading the open Bible on the
dining room table three times a day is a way of life for the Tewksburys. They
continued hosting two boys each summer until 1969 when they committed themselves
to a summer Bible Camp. Sons of family and friends were invited with fifteen
boys attending the first year. The first girls' camp was held in 1985. Campers
have come from Florence's native state, Maine, to California, from Alaska to
Florida and many states in between as well as several countries.

The Tewksburys fund the camp as a labor of love for their Lord and firmly
believe that he will provide. They do not solicit funds and there is no fee for
the campers, but they receive contributions from individuals and churches.

Campers gather in a large room for Bible study and music. There are frequent
breaks for chores and recreation. The afternoons are devoted to work about the
ranch. The day closes with devotion. Meals are eaten at two long dining room
tables. The campers sleep in dormitory style rooms in the two story home of the
Tewksburys.

Work around the ranch includes refinishing furniture, painting buildings,
cleaning shelter belts, cutting fire wood and gardening and weeding. Each camper
chooses one of the ranch's horses to care for during his stay. Cowboy boots and
saddles are available and the camper must feed, bridle and saddle his horse.
There are competitive events on horseback and the final event is a trail ride.

Other recreation includes soft ball, battle ball, hide and seek, lawn pool, and
swimming in a nearby lake, or in the camp pool. For rainy days, there are
volleyball and basketball nets in the barn's haymow and checker and chess
tournaments.

Planning for camp is an on-going event for the Tewskburys. They scout auction
sales for furniture to be refinished and saddles and other ranch equipment.
Florence cans, mends and shops for sales and specials.

A recent camper summarized the summer: "The time has gone so fast. We're so
busy, we don't have time to be bored."

Mercer Hillside Cemetery

The Mercer Townsite Co. deeded the land to Nels E. Hedahl, Mercer on May 17,
1913, and on October 8, 1917, Nels and Inga sold the land to The Hillside
Cemetery for $50. Additional land was later deeded to the cemetery by William
Peterson. The cemetery was platted on September 10, 1917.

Cemetery burials were compiled by Willa Gardiner Murray. The dates are from the
grave markers or the cemetery map Included are the date of birth and date of
death when available.

There are unrecorded burials and some records were lost in a fire.

        Photo: Mercer Hillside Cemetery

Mercer Bison

Mercer School District 1907-1976

The notes included are from dated Telegram issues available from 1907-1919, and
information extracted from the Alumni Reunion booklet of 1972. The year books
from 1948-1972 were reviewed and pertinent information was included. Personal
recollections were incorporated. The school board members listed for 1907-1949
are complete, however the records from 1950-1972 are a partial list because many
of the school records are incomplete.

The information in this chronological section includes the school census when
available; members of the school boards; roster of the teachers which is from
the 1972 Alumni Reunion booklet and the graduating classes with pictures of the
graduates when available. The pictures are from the year books (1948-72);
private collections and the group class pictures which have been displayed in
the science room.

There have been graduates every year from 1922 through 1972 with the exception
of 1924. The number of graduates per year has been 2 to 16 in 1955 for an
unofficial total of about 370.

This section was compiled by LaRose Ketterling (not a Mercer graduate) with
contributions from Willa Gardiner Murray, Martha Diede Thompson, Pamela Freeberg
Lill, Frances Laib Rittenbach and Eunice Hinsz Vossler.

Please forgive the errors and ommisions. They were unintentional. We tried to
collect as many pictures as possible, but unfortunately not all could be
reproduced.

        Photo: Mercer School-1909: Students were Jim Watson, John Fandrich, Anna
        Nielson, Jennie Nielsen, Alvin Doering, Victor Olson, Roy Nielsen, Lydia
        Doering, Rudolf Singer, George Butchard, Elizabeth Singer, Katrina Lang,
        Ida Ketterling, Bertha Sackmann, Johnnie Singer; Arthur Singer; Jake
        Singer, Kate Singer. (Photo courtesy of Richard Ketterling collection)

In 1906/1907, a one room school building was built in the center of Block five
of the original Mercer townsite. The first day of school for thirty-three
students was in the fall of 1907 with Miss Olga Natwick of Ada, Minnesota as the
teacher. Most of the students were German speaking only and Miss Natwick spoke
no German. It must have been a difficult year but she did return to teach for
another year.

1907: Directors unknown E.R. Freeman was the clerk

1908: Members of the school board were G.B. Campbell, president; H. Thompson
  and E.N. Hedahl, directors; Theodore Knutson Treasurer; E.R. Freeman, clerk.

  Olga Natwick was the teacher for thirty eight students. The end of the school
  year was May 14, 1909. There was a traveling library.

1909: Members of the school board were Helmer Thompson president; Robert Lucas
  and E.N. Hedahl, directors; Theodore Knutson, treasurer; R.S. Butchart, Clerk.

  Minnie Jones was the teacher for thirty-three students. First day of school
  was September 6, 1909

1910: Members of the school board were E.N. Hedahl, president; Helmer Thompson
  and R.E. Lucas, directors; Theodore Knutson, treasurer; R.S. Butchart, clerk

  Minnie Jones was the teacher for fifty students in seven grades. E.O. Kleve
  was hired as a second teacher.

  Two new schools were built in Medicine Hill Township.

  School opened 9/6/1910. Some of the students were:

  1ST grade: Helga Nelson, Theodore Sackmann, Calvin Sorenson, John Okert

  2nd grade: Elsie Singer, Edward and Julius Sackmann, Armond and Arthur
  Murphy

  3rd grade: Regina Singer, Melvin Romsas, Richard and Ida Ketterling

  4th grade Carson Angele, Arthur Singer, Anthony Hedahl, Echo and Opal
  McLaughlin

  5th grade: Ella Hedahl, Marie McFadden, Anna Nelson, Gladys Angele, Tillie
  Sackmann

  8th grade: Clara Pickert, Laura Jones, Jennie Nelson, Florence Jones, Myrtle
  Lemming, Nelson Angele

  In December, a teacher came to Mercer, but there was no place to board so she
  left.

1911: Members of the school board were Helmer Thompson president; John
  Ketterling and J.C. Murphy, directors; J.B. Fischer treasurer; Theodore
  Knutson, clerk.

  Teachers were E.O. Kleve and Clara Whicher for forty-two students.

  There was a movement to build a new school and in August, the school was
  enlarged - it now had two rooms.   School election bond passed to build a new
  school.

        Photo: Students going to Brush Lake for a school picnic in 1911. (Photo
        courtesy of Richard Ketterling collection.)

        Photo: Mercer school house with addition. (Photo courtesy of Evelyn
        Freeberg)

1912: Members of the school board were H. Thompson, president; J.C. Rice and
  J.C. Murphy directors; J.B. Fischer, treasurer; Theodore Knutson, clerk.

  Teachers were Art Shelton, Lillian Carlson, Ellen O'Hara.

  German class was taught by Mr. Angele, the section foreman.

  E.O. Kleve was elected Sheridan County Supt. of Schools.

  Art Shelton was named school principal.

  Teacher Minnie Jones married J.B. Peterson.

  May 31, end of school year.

1913: School board members J.C. Murphy, president; M. Nielsen and James Rice
  directors; W.F. Ludwig, treasurer; Theodore Knutson, clerk

  Teachers were Ida Washburn, Lillian Carlson, Olga Sletten.

  8th grade exams for Grant Ovre, Dallas Wise, Floyd Sprout, Elmer and Wilbur
  Conklin

  Taking part in the Easter program were Arthur Singer, Anna Nelson, Gladys
  Angele, Regina Singer, Roy Nelson, Bertha Sackmann, Rose Davidson, and Ella
  Blanchard.

1914: School board members were James Rice, president; H. Thompson and M.
  Nielseon, directors; John Ketterling, treasurer; Theodore Knutson, clerk.

  Teachers were Ida Washburn, Ella Hedahl, Antonette Morton, Adeline Washburn.

  Teacher Lillian Carlson married Edward Plowman.

        Photo: School children, 1914, by the white schoolhouse. (Photo courtesy
        of Richard Keterling collection).

1915: School board members were J.C. Murphy, president; Helmer Thompson and
  Martin Nielson, directors; John Ketterling, treasurer; Theodore Knutson,
  clerk.

  Teachers were Clara Berge, Mary Flynn, Jennie Nielsen.

  Library of 150 books purchased by the Women's Study Club.

  Taking part in the Christmas program were Elsie Singer, Everett Knutson,
  Bernard Hale, Katie Wise, Evelyn Knutson, Rose Davidson, John Wise, Irene
  Hale, Loyde Henderson, Helga Nelson, Erling Hedahl, Nettie Sackmann, Margaret
  Hedahl, Fred Wise, Katie Wolff, Lena Williams, Teresa Wolf, Mary Frances
  Davidson.

1916: School board members J.C. Murphy, president; Helmer Thompson and Martin
  Nelson, directors; John Ketterling, treasurer; Theodore Knutson, clerk.

  Teachers were Clara Berge, Mary Flynn, Jennie Nielsen, F.M. Washburn.

  The school was closed on January 14, couldn't keep the rooms warm.

   School bonds for the new school-school house to cost $8,000, need $5,000.

  May 19, graduation from 3rd grade - Rose Davidson; from the 4th grade -
  Theodore Sackmann, Olga Singer, Molly Rennich, Edward Sackmann.

  June 9, school house vote passed.

  July 21, a contract was let for the new school to W.H. Carson @ $12,800 and
  $2,000 for heating.

  August 4, Mark Burns started working on the construction of the new brick
  school house.

  August 18. the foundation was laid for the school.

  September 29, the brick work complete on the school house.

        Photo: 1916: Constuction of the new Schoolhouse. (Courtesy of Richard
        Ketterling collection)

        Photo: The completed schoolhouse. (Courtesy of Richard Ketterling
        collection)

  November 21, the new school house was dedicated with former ND Gov. L.B. Hanna
  and Mr. McCurdy as speakers. Ole Hjelle presided at the dedication and George
  McFadden delivered the welcome address. Music was provided by Mrs. Ole Hjelle,
  E.N. Hedahl, Rev. Ulvilden, Adolph Singer, Bob Boehm, George McFadden and the
  school children.

  December 15, move to the new school house with George Krug as custodian.

  December 18, first day of school, temperature was forty-two.

        Photo: Mercer Class '51

With the consolidation of the rural schools in the Mercer School District, the
school was running out of space for the expanding school population. In November
1951, the School Board advertised for bids for an addition to the school.
Construction of the new gymnasium began in May 1952 with John Tuscher as the
foreman. He resided at the C.W. Freeberg residence during the construction
phase, The contractor used the tractor of local farmer, Edwin Gessele to hoist
the girders into position. Local residents, Merle Berge and Rueben Hinsz were
hired to assist with the construction. The gymnasium was completed for the
1952-53 basketball season. The original gymnasium was remodeled into two
classrooms.

        Photo: Construction phase of new gymnasium.(Courtesy of Christensen
        collection)

  Class of 1972

Organization of the Mercer and Turtle Lake School District TL/M

Meetings were held in March 1972. The organization vote was on May 12, 1972,
with elections on June 6, 1972.

Mercer High School closed in 1972, and grades 1-8 closed in 1976.

Purpose of reorganization

To bring about the formation of a new school district which will provide a more
nearly equalized educational opportunity for pupils of the elementary schools
and the high schools; a higher degree of uniformity of school tax rates between
districts; and a use of public funds for the support of the school system.
Involved were McLean, Sheridan and Burleigh county school districts. Burleigh
County withdrew.

  Members on the reorganization committee were:
  Warren Olson and Edwin Britton of Turtle Lake
  S.I. Johnson, Superintendent of Turtle Lake
  Clinton Lowe, Superintendent of Mercer
  Elmer Peterson and John Laib of Mercer
  Bennie Keller, Turtle Lake Board
  Robert O'Shea, Mercer Board

students - can't have one without the other.

Mercer School Paper

The first school paper entitled the M.H.S. Booster, began publication under the
direction of Mr. Quanbeck. Early records for 1929 list Finley Nelson as editor
in chief, Brandt Hjelle as business manager, Pearl Peterson as secretary, Sidney
Nielsen as club activities, John O. Hjelle as art and humor, and reporters Ruth
Ovre, Merle Berge, Signe Carlson and Minnie Seyfert.

The Booster was a bi-weekly newspaper published by the pupils of Mercer High
School and sold for two cents per issue or 25 cents per year.

Highlights of the Jan. 19, 1929, issue were "that the state examinations will
begin January 23 and continue for the rest of the week. On Tuesday night of this
week the choir met to practice with all the prominent members of the
organization present." In the local news section of the Booster, it was reported
the Mercer Cash Store had been made somewhat larger, having during recent months
been somewhat crowded for space. The score for the independent basketball game
between the Mercer Bison and the Hurdsfield Demons was a victory for Mercer with
a score of 27 to 11. The week before the Christmas holiday the high school girls
and boys teams played at home. The Mercer girls were defeated with the final
score being 8-5. The boys were tied at half (4-4) with a Bison victory 13-10.
Captain Sammie Rust directed the team strategy at important points of the game
as well as played a wonderful floor game.

Sometime during the early 1930s, the paper's title was changed to The Cricket.
This paper was a monthly publication with the contents also compiled by the
school paper staff under the supervision of an advisor.

The first editions of the school papers were cut from stencils and mimeographed.
Later the paper was produced on a ditto copy machine. The last Cricket was
published in May of 1972 when the Mercer High School consolidated with the
Turtle Lake school system.

        Photo: 1967 Cricket Staff: (front, from left) Janie Stute, Sheryl
        Gessele, Steve Christensen, Doris Fischer, Assistant Editor Gust Stute,
        Editor Judy Brewster; (back) Advisor Mr. Susag, JoAnn Gessele, Jerry
        Littke, Palma Gardiner, Willa Gardiner, Joyce Ketterling, Joel'l Schon,
        Linda Klatt, Darlene Fischer, Lynda Achan, Georgia Gardiner, Linda
        Neumiller, Debbie Wagner, Elaine Schumann. (Photo from yearbook)

Mercer High School Yearbook

The first yearbook was published in 1948 and carried the name of the school
mascot, Bison. Delma Fischer and Myra Schlaht were the two graduates with Delma
taking on the job as first editor of the Bison.

A yearbook was published every year with exception of 1957 when the president of
the school council ruled that the yearbook was too expensive, so there wasn't
any yearbook for that year. In 1958 a spiral bound yearbook was printed, but
this year's book was entitled "The Pioneer." This was the only softcovered book
produced. In 1958, the yearbook was once again being named "The Bison." This
final "Bison" was issued in 1972 with Norma Klatt and Laurie O'Shea as
co-editors. Their advisor was Miss Pamela Freeberg.

Mercer School Music

        Photo: Mercer Grade School band in 1937: (front, from left) VaLora Levi,
        Delma Fischer, Myra Schlaht, Ramona Wise, John Westerlind, Wilbert Laib,
        Edwin Orman, Alfred Martzolf; (middle) Donald Sackman, LeRoy Laib,
        Martha Bauer, Violet Miller, Donald Narum, Darwin Levi, Roy Nielsen Jr.,
        Gene Logue, Meinhardt Rennich, Meinhart Wagner; (back) Alice Boschee,
        Melvin Wagner, Pat Hjelle, Roger Hjelle, LaRose Ketterling, John Bauer,
        Teacher Ruth Bruntsch. (Photo courtesy of Richard Ketterling collection)

The Mercer School never had a band and instrumental music was limited to
individual performances. Perhaps the first appearance of a "band" was the rhythm
band during the school year of 1936-37 with Miss Ruth Bruntsch the director. The
instruments were sticks, bells, symbols, noisemakers such as tambourines and a
triangle. A great time was had by all the musicians.

The High School Glee Clubs of 1932-33 and 1933-34 were girls only. In 1948 Girls
Glee Club was directed by June Berge, a MHS grad.

Mercer School Basketball

Basketball was the main competitive sport at the Mercer School. The 1920s had
both boys and girls competing with the surrounding schools. Often the railroad
was the means of transportation during the basketball season.

Basketball was played in the gymnasium of the brick school house until 1952,
when the new free standing gymnasium was built with more seating for the Bison
fans. This gymnasium is now the Mercer Community Center.

It is not known when the name "Bison" was adopted as the school mascot. It is
also not known when the school colors, black and white, were chosen.

The Mercer School song was sung to the "On Wisconsin" tune. It is not known when
this song became the "official" school song.

        Onward Mercer, onward Mercer
        On to victory
        We're for Mercer, we're for Mercer
        Always we will be.
        Rah! Rah! Rah!
        We'll stand by you while you're fighting
        For this high school team
        Fight fellows fight, fight, fight
        We'll win this game.

        To the black and white forever
        Colors of our school
        To our own beloved high school
        We will e'er be true
        Rah! Rah! Rah!
        Firm our purpose, square our shoulder
        May we ever be
        Proud to bear our high school flag
        To victory.

The chronological sequence for the activities for the Mercer School teams was
compiled from school records, the school year books (1948-72) and personal
recollections. Some of the pictures received were not reproducible as were many
of the pictures in the yearbooks. Whenever possible, we attempted to name all
the people in the picture. Some of the older pictures (1920's) were fragile.
Enjoy the memories.

Mercer School Carnival

In the fall of 1944, the first school carnival was held with the crowning of
carnival queen, Violet Miller, and king, Roy Nielsen Jr. In the yearbook of 1949
the coronation is described as follows:

"Clinton Lowe and Peggy Just were crowned king and queen of the Mercer High
School Carnival of 1948-49. Miss June Berge played the "Coronation March" and
Billy White and Joy Beierle unrolled a white carpet upon which the king and
queen and their attendants marched. Dickey Wahl led the processional carrying
the crowns on a blue satin pillow. Next in the line was the carnival queen of
1947, the king and queen followed by their attendants, Donna Fibelstad, Donald
Lowe, Juanita Lowe, Wesley Vossler, Eunice Hinsz and Pat Schmitt. The queen wore
a sheer blue formal. Her attendants wore blue, pink and white formals
respectively. Delma Fischer, queen of 1947, placed the queen's crown with
fitting words and Peggy Just gave her thanks and appreciation for the honor.
Peggy Just received a single strand pearl necklace from last year's queen, Delma
Fischer. Following the coronation, the king and queen were each presented with a
gift from the school."

A program with local entertainment was held before the concessions opened for
the evening. Concession stands manned by the students included the baseball
throw, fishing pond, guessing weight contest, cake walk, dart throw, bingo,
boxing and wrestling.

Voting for the king and queen candidates was done through the purchasing of
tickets, which were deposited in the container with the name of the candidate of
your choice. The female and male with the most tickets were crowned royalty for
the current school year.

The highest profit carnival was the 1964 event with a profit of $1,199.35 for
the school. The twenty-five and final carnival was held in 1968 with the
crowning of queens, Sheryl Gessele and Sandy Rust and king, Fred Westerlind.

Hot Lunch Program

The school hot lunch program was started in the Mercer Consolidated School
January 17, 1950, with Mrs. Ted Johnson as cook. Type A meals were served with
milk at a cost of $.75 per week for each school child. Children eating there
occasionally and faculty members paid $.25 per meal. When the project started,
there were around forty-five eating, but the number increased to about sixty.

The project was sponsored by the Mercer Women's Study Club. The Homemaker's Club
put on a food sale and raised money to purchase a Kenmore electric roaster, six
dozen forks and one dozen knives for the project. Five former 4-H Club boys
donated cash. The girls 4-H contributed a substantial amount of various cooking
utensils that they had acquired for their organization. The Sportsmen's Club
sponsored a card party and turned the proceeds over to the lunch program. The
P.T.A. gave $25. The school board purchased the Perfection electric range as
well as tables and had the building rewired for power, heat and light so as to
carry the additional load with utmost safety. A basket social was sponsored by
the Study Club to raise funds toward the purchase of a nine-foot Philco
refrigerator. The stove was bought from the Schell Hardware, the refrigerator at
Freeberg's, the electric roaster at Sears Roebuck, all at actual or near cost to
us. Pederson's contributed a free locker and 500 napkins. Groceries were
purchased at Freeberg's and Gardiner's at wholesale prices with frequent
additional donations by same.

The 1950 Bison yearbook thanked all the clubs and all the people who donated
materials and cash donations to make the project possible.

The first school lunchroom was located in the lower level of the school near the
first gymnasium. In 1961 an addition was added which housed new areas for a
science room and lunchroom.

Mrs. Andrew Rust took over the cooks position in 1952 and served until 1954 when
Mrs. Christ Lockrem filled the cooks job until 1956. Mrs. Sam Beierle held the
cooks position from 1956 to 1959 when Mrs. Walter Browning became her assistant.
Mrs. Emil Rust and Mrs. Andrew Rust cooked from 1961 until 1965 when Mrs. Rust
resigned to help her husband with their business, Rust Manufacturing. Mrs. Jake
Rust was then employed and served up meals for the students until 1971. The
final cooks were Mrs. Emil Russ and Mrs. George Gardiner.

        Photo: 1971 cooks were (from left) Rosie Rust and Helen Russ. (Photo
        from yearbook)

        Photo: 1971 custodians were (from left) Ed Sackman and Emil Russ. (Photo
        from yearbook)

Forsaken Schoolhouse

  Poor forsaken country schoolhouse
  Standing there so sadly;
  Windows all are boarded up,
  Paint is peeling badly.

  Tragedies and romances
  Took place within those walls
  And many of its students
  Now walk in famous halls.

  The books and desks are dusty
  And silent is the bell,
  But such a store of memories
  Within those walls must dwell.

Permission to print from the author:
Evelyn Nienow Irwin
Douglas, ND now of Minot, ND
From the: Wild Prairie Roses,
A collection of Verse by North Dakotans.
1980.

Country Schools

Between 1907 and the 1950s, there were at least thirteen country schools
attended by children with Mercer addresses. In addition, many attended the
Holmes consolidated school, which was located in Holmes Township in Sheridan
County. The schools were often called by their location; example Wise Township
#1 was the "Spout School" since it was located across the road from the Sprout
farm. There were four schools in Wise Township, four schools in Park Township,
four schools in Medicine Hill Township and one country school plus the town
school in Mercer Township. The country schools were disbanded in 1959 when
consolidation took place and the children were bussed to the Mercer town school.

Many of the school buildings became township halls or other local meeting
places. Some of the buildings were bought by local farmers and became storage
sheds and some were dismantled and the lumber used for other buildings.

The country schools were a special place for the rural families. In addition to
learning the "3 R's," they were the social gathering place for school programs,
carnivals, pie, box or ice cream socials, a way of life for the rural families.
In the beginning, as the population increased, more schools were added in the
township.

Each country school had a school board, which hired its teachers. The teachers
set the classroom climate and were responsible to the County Superintendent of
Schools who visited each school during the school year. The length of the school
term varied from three to seven months.

The school ground was usually an unfenced patch of prairie. Often there was a
barn to house the transportation and always there was a "boy's" and a "girl's
outhouse." The flagpole was the center of interest on the grounds. The Pledge of
Allegiance was the first order of the day with the raising of the flag. Some
schools had swings, merry-go-rounds and other play equipment, but space for a
ball diamond was essential.

All of the country schools, with the exception of the Holmes consolidated, were
a one-room school building with an entryway. Most of the buildings were designed
the same way with most of the windows facing east, west or south. The front
steps led to a landing, which opened into the entryway. One side of the entryway
was usually the coal bin. The pass through hall was used to set the lunch pails.
The most important equipment in the main part of the schoolroom was the stove.
Often this was a large jacketed round stove and was in the central location. It
was also often a challenge to manage. Across the back of the room was a shelf
with coat hooks for the children's outer wraps. Girls' wraps were hung on one
side and the boys on the other.

Furniture consisted of desks of various sizes. Some of the desks were designed
for two people. There was a teacher's desk with a chair. The slate blackboard
was across the front of the room and always there were posters for the Palmer
penmanship graphics. If there was room, there was a bookcase for library books
and supplies such as chalk erasers, paper and sweeping compound. Some schools
had a piano or organ, sandbox, table or little red chairs, a globe on a cord, a
school clock, a picture of George Washington and a copy of the Ten Commandments.
There was always a "recitation bench" usually without a backrest. This was
placed in front of the teacher's desk for recitation time.

A common water pail and dipper with a basin was placed on a table or bench. The
students or the teacher supplied the water. Children and teachers usually walked
or rode horseback to and from school.

Medicine Hill Township Schools

Medicine Hill Township is located on the west border of Sheridan County 148N,
Range 79 W. Its south border is with Wise Township and its west border is with
Wiprud Township.

Families listed in the 1910 census were Frederick Presser, Fred Spies, Ole

Norman Nelson, Marcus Nelson.

Medicine Hill School #1 is located in Section 28 and was built in 1914. The
building is part of a house in Turtle Lake.

Medicine Hill School #2 is located in Section 8. The building was burned.

Medicine Hill School #3 is located in Section 11. The building was completed
around 1916. It was a one-room schoolhouse with an attached shed that held the
coal. There were two outhouses and a barn on the school grounds. The playground
consisted of a swing set and a merry-go-round. Some of the games played outdoors
were fox and geese, anti-over and drop the hanky. Most of the students walked to
and from school and their lunches were packed in metal gallon size syrup pails
with a handle and contained jelly sandwiches and cookies.

The last day of the school year, the parents brought a picnic lunch. After
everyone had eaten the students played softball against the fathers, while the
mothers packed up the food and cleaned the schoolhouse for the year.

The school's first teacher was Constance Kalland. Others were Edith Nelson, Mrs.
Joe Peterson, Martha Diede Thompson, Evelyn Tarasenko, Delores Schott Haugen,
Mary Ann Miller Westerlind, Mae Washburn, June Berg, Leona Bohnet Neumiller and
Mrs. Wilson. Evelyn Herringer Schimke taught the last seven years (1952 to 59).
The school closed in 1959 due to the Mercer School District reorganization.

        Photo: Medicine Hill Township School #3. (Photo courtesy of Joyce
        Dockter Fiedler)

The building is no longer standing. Emil and Helen Russ tore the building down
in the 1970's and used the lumber to build an attached garage to their house in
Mercer.

(This was written by Joyce Dockter Fiedler who attended School #3 for six
years.)
