Mercer Township School

The 1914 map of Mercer Township indicates that there was a rural school in
Section 28. It is a mystery. There are no available records of this school.

The October 23, 1914, "Telegram" published a notice for bids to erect a school
house in Mercer School Dist.

The December 18, 1914, "Telegram" reported: "The new school house in the Mercer
School Dist. has been completed and turned over to the directors this week."

One person who attended the school for one year in 1916 was Herbert Thompson.
After that year, the school was closed and Herbert and the other children in
that area attended the Mercer Public School. Herbert's teacher was Ida Washburn.
It is not known how long the school was open.

        Map: Township 146 N., Range 79 W., Mercer

Wise Township Schools By Pat Christensen Mohrbacher

There were various country schools in operation in Wise Township from about 1903
until 1959 when most of North Dakota school systems had been reorganized and
Wise students were then bused to Mercer. (In Hattie Ovre's story, "My Fourteen
Months on the Claim," [see page 403] she says that the township was organized
the year they came to settle on their claim, which probably was 1903. She said
that her brother-in-law, Sevald Ovre's shack was used as the first schoolhouse
in the township that same fall. His claim was located in the middle of the N½
of Section 22. Carlie Hansen and her cousin, Violet Christensen, walked to a
building near the Melvin McComb's farm for school about 1905.) This school was
apparently still in use in 1910 when The Mercer Telegram reported on June 3,
"Rev. Joseph L. Watt teaches school in the McComb district, and occasionally
holds divine services in the school house." On the 1914 Wise Township map there
is a "Town Hall" pictured on the McComb land, which is in the NW¼ of Sect. 10.
This was probably the building that was earlier used as the school. In 1909
Krogh Ovre advertised in The Mercer Telegram for a person to drive the students
of Wise Township to School #1. This is the only evidence we have of busing being
done in the early days.

It is not known for sure when the official schoolhouses were built in the
township. Schools were typically numbered in the order in which they were built.
We do know that Sprout's School No. 1 was in existence by May 12, 1911 when a
notice in The Mercer Telegram states, "An entertainment and basket supper will
be held at Wise School No. 1, six miles north of Mercer, Friday evening, May 19.
Proceeds to be used for the benefit of the school library. Everybody invited."
Not all the school buildings were completed yet, however, because another notice
in the Oct. 18, 1911 Telegram says, "Accepting sealed bids for building a school
house for Wise District 36, submitted by Pastor Fred Petersen, clerk." There
were apparently four schools operating in 1913, because four teachers were on
the payroll that spring. On April 3, a $50 teaching salary was paid to Clarence
Morton, Tessa Sprout, Mae Norton, and Mrs. Renis Andersen. Perhaps they were all
built by 1913, because the last and largest recorded expenditure for permanent
improvement and furnishings occurred in 1912-1913, which for that year was
$1,645.

Schoolhouse No. 1 in Wise Township, was known as Sprout's school because the
Walter and Floyd Sprout families lived and farmed across the road from it for
many years, and perhaps because Tessa (Mrs. Walter) Sprout taught there. It is
located on the East side of Township 33 about five miles north of Mercer. (SW¼
of Sect. 11). Schoolhouse Number 2 was located in the southwest part of the
township (NE¼ of Sect. 32) and sometimes referred to as the Mayer or Singer
school because of the families who attended there. Number 3, located at the east
end of Brush Lake (NW¼ of Sect. 26), was dubbed the Brush Lake School. Number 4,
in the northwest part of the township (SW¼ of Sect. 5), has been referred to as
the Lehn or Levi School.

        Photo: Children holding hands in front of Sprout's Schoolhouse, about
        1948. (Photo courtesy of Christensen family)

        Photos: Children on giant Strides at Brush Lake School, 1936-1937.
        Students at left are _____, Ervin Kleingartner, Irene Makeeff, Meinhart
        Boschee, Arnie Makeeff, Meinhardt Kleingartner, Laura Kleingartner,
        Lillian Boschee. (Photo courtesy of Christensen family)

There was no running water, electricity, or phones in the early days of the
schools. Water was brought by the parents and kept in a crock or pail for
drinking, and in a basin for washing hands. There were two outhouses, one for
the girls and one for the boys. There was a small barn, sometimes with a
hitching post, located on each school grounds to house the horses that the
teachers and children rode or drove to school. At least three of the schools had
"Giant Strides" for playground equipment, some had teeter-totters, and in later
years some had merry-go-rounds. On the "Giant Strides," four children could
swing around a type of maypole holding on with their hands to the metal bars
attached to long chains.

Mostly, the school children played games that needed little equipment. They
played "Pum Pum Pull Away," a race type game, "Anti-I-Over" (or
"Anti-Anti-Over") using the barn, "Hide and Seek," "Ring Around the Rosy," "Kick
The Can," or "Red Rover" in the warmer weather. When it was cold and snowy the
children played "Fox and Goose" on freshly fallen snow, or played with sleds on
nearby hills. They made forts, or "igloos" when the snow was firm. If it was
too cold or stormy, indoor games included board games such as "Tic Tac Toe,"
"Fruit Basket Upset," "Blind Man's Bluff," "Skip to My Lou," "Jacob and
Ruth,""In and Out the Window," "London Bridge," and "Last Couple Out."  In later
years, when the schools used oil burning stoves, Rose Nielsen Dietz remembers
playing in the former coal bin room on stormy days. In 1922 when Martha Ovre was
eighteen and in her first year of teaching at the Mayer School, there were some
rowdy games of basketball inside the schoolhouse before someone decided it
should not be allowed.

Sometimes the schools had pump organs to lead the singing. Ruth Ovre Christensen
remembers learning to play a few songs on the school organ with one finger in
the winter of 1926-27. There wasn't one at Sprout's School when Martha Diede
taught there in 1936-37, so the County Superintendent's office lent her a
phonograph to play records. Years later at Brush Lake School in the early 1950s
Martha and students raffled off a goose at 10 cents a ticket and made enough to
buy an organ for the school for about $7.00. (See page 145)

Shirley Christensen Ingman attended Sprout's School in the first through part of
the fifth grade, 1914 to 1918, and has many fond memories of those school days.
She remembers seats being too hot or cold in the winter, depending on how close
to the stove you sat. Recess at noon was an hour long, and there were usually
short recesses in the morning and afternoon also. The discipline was strict,
and staying after school was a personal disgrace. Shirley's brother, Walter, who
attended this school the same time as she did, in first through part of third
grade, went on to be North Dakota State Treasurer for eleven years.

Shirley remembers box lunches that had homemade bread, meats, and cheese, but
seldom any fruit. Myron "Gene" Singer attended School No. 2 for eight years from
1940-1948. He remembers that during World War II the school got some government
"commodities," and they cooked eggs and other things on the coal stove. Rose
Nielsen Dietz, who attended Brush Lake School for 8 years from 1947-1955,
remembers the mothers taking turns bringing hot dishes so the children could
have hot lunch.

In the early days of the community, teachers sometimes used a corner of the
schoolhouse as living quarters, especially in the winter months when travel was
difficult. The schools were often used for parties, basket socials, plays,
music, voting, etc. A Mercer Telegram article dated Feb 23, 1912 says, "There
will be a basket supper at Wise School No. 3 at Brush Lake Friday evening March
1. A prize will be given for the best trimmed basket, also the best speller."

The Sprout's School No. 1 was also used for worship, baptisms, Sunday School,
and Vacation Bible School. Reverend Ulvilden from the Norwegian Lutheran Church
in Mercer occasionally came out and held services there for the Danish
congregation. July 21, 1911 The Mercer Telegram reports that "Ansgar Danish
Evangelical Lutheran Congregation will hold services in the school house
tomorrow and Sunday at 10:30 A.M. Rev. Kildsig and Rev. Lund of Kenmare will be
present." St. Ansgar never built a church, so they had to use homes or schools
for their meetings until they joined with Our Savior (Norwegian) Lutheran Church
in Mercer in 1928.

In August of 1922 Rev. W. Keller held a confirmation service at Sprout's
schoolhouse. The students in the class included Ragnhild Glad, Shirley
Christensen, and Martin and Louise Trulson. Later Shirley, Clara Bille, and
Lydia Keller, daughter of Rev. Keller, held Sunday School classes there. For
quite a few years, from the 1920s until the mid 1950s, Vacation Bible School was
held for two to four weeks in the summer. Children came from the whole area to
attend. Ella Winge, who grew up south of the school, helped teach VBS two
summers. In 1946, she taught with Beatrice Norwick, and in 1947 with Janice
Holverson. Some other Bible School teachers were Rosalind Holte, Evelyn Green,
Agnes Bille, Shirley Christensen, and Lorraine Nordlund.

Rev. William Louis Keller, German Lutheran pastor and missionary, his wife,
Ottilie, and their ten children homesteaded northeast of the Sprout's
Schoolhouse, and lived there from about 1904 to 1924. The children attended this
school, and all six of their sons, Walter, Alvin, Otto, Martin, Meinhardt, and
Amos, became Lutheran pastors. Daughter Lydia taught at Sprout's for two school
terms from 1918-1920. (See page 65 for Keller family history)

Lydia Keller was apparently quite athletic, perhaps because she had so many
brothers. Memorial Day 1911 there was a "splendid dinner," flagpole drill, and
band at Brush Lake. Melvin Romsa won the boys foot race, and Lydia Keller (about
12 years old) won the girls race. The Mercer Telegram reports, "Melvin Romsa,
the best runner among the boys, was put up to race with Lydia Keller, the
champion girl runner, but he fell short about ten feet and Lydia carried off the
grand prize, glory and all."

In March 1920, one of the most severe blizzards in the history of North Dakota
struck the area when Lydia Keller was teaching at the Sprout's School. She kept
the children at school all night while the winds shook the building, ripping off
a storm window. They had plenty of coal to keep them warm, but had little to
eat. See page 146 for Lydia's story. This was probably the same blizzard
Ragnhild Glad Sondrol remembers in the Lehn School No. 4. Their teacher, Mrs.
Tessa Sprout, also kept the children overnight, and like Lydia, had no phone to
notify the parents that their children were safe. She let some of the boys go
out to get some hay for the horses, and also to a nearby bachelor's home for
food. It was a dangerous thing to do, but fortunately, they made it back to the
school safely.

        Photo: The Lehn schoolhouse today.

In 1922, Ruth and Harley Ovre attended the Mayer school, with their sister,
Martha, as their teacher. There were lots of big boys attending school there
that year. The Dan Mayer's family had six children in school.

After 1959 when most rural schools were closed, many of them continued to be
used for community and township meetings, 4-H club meetings, voting and the
like. The Lehn/Levi School No. 4 is presently located intact on Bill Field's
farmstead where it is being used as a granary. Brush Lake School No. 3 has been
remodeled into a cabin and is in use on the peninsula at Brush Lake. Wise
Township School No. 2 did not have enough students to operate, and closed as
early as 1944. It has been Snortland's cabin at Blue Lake since about 1962.
Sprout's Schoolhouse No. 1 is still standing in its original location near
Highway 33, and is being renovated and restored as a historic site.

Holmes Consolidated School By Joyce Dockter Fiedler

Many of the Mercer area settlers who lived north and east of Mercer sent their
children to the Holmes Township Consolidated School in Sheridan County. It was
organized in 1909 and was located in Section 15 of Holmes Township. First day of
classes was in 1910.

Members of the first board of directors who had Mercer addresses included E.A.
Holmes, John Pfeifer, Jacob Skaley and Martin Dalos.

It was a two-story building with a basement and had two large classrooms. In
1912-13 there were fifteen students who attended school for 64 days. The census
was nine boys and six girls. There were eleven in the first grade and two each
in the fourth and seventh grades plus one private student. It was a three-month
school year. Of the fifteen, the average attendance was six (data from the
teacher's register, courtesy of Sheridan County Supt. of Schools).

Lida Rockney was the teacher and E.O. Kleve, a former Mercer town schoolteacher
as the co-superintendent. The salary of the teacher was $55. Students enrolled
in 1912-13 were: Agnes and Roy Anderson (Ole Anderson), August Dockter (John
Dockter); Arot Jess (Manuel Jess); Andrew, Jacob, Eva Lintz (Wilhelm Lintz);
Emanuel, Mike and Jimmie Makeef (Michael Makeeff), Bertha and Christian Roloff
(Gust Roloff) and Elizabeth, Mary and Carrie Schmidt (Edward Schmidt).

The daily program schedule included opening exercises, reading, seat work,
numbers, busy work and a 15-minute recess before the hour noon break. The
afternoon included reading, writing, spelling, one fifteen-minute recess and
busy work. The starting time was nine and dismissal was at four.

Beginning with the 1926-27 school year and until 1940, there were two teachers.
The teacher when the school disbanded at the end of the 1958-59 school year was
Joy Harrum Kline.

After the school disbanded in 1959, the building was demolished. The final board
members were Prosper Pfeifer, Art Dockter, Rueben Hegel, Mantz and Albert
Skaley.

The school was the hub of many community activities in addition to school
programs, carnivals and athletic events.

Teachers from 1913 to 1960 were: Claude Slyter, John O'Conner, Pearl Haugen,
Gena Lockrem, Anna Thoen, Margaret Gude, Hilm Mickison, Anna Monson, Myrtle
Marrow, A.L. Yates, Lloyd Henson, Albert Loiland, Carl B. Olson, Burton Keifer,
Harold Folkins, Melvin Dalos, Garland Reinboldt, Dagney Frantzing, Lois
Peterson, Bertha Mayer, Sara Bingler, Adeline Meion, Ella Dalos, Hazel Johnson,
Mr. and Mrs. Art Aklend, Farida Stain, Lena and Herbert Pfeif, Mr. and Mrs. Paul
Timfac, Mr. and Mrs. V.J. Smith, Martha Krause, Mrs. Gust Taylor, Holdrich
Mayer, Linda Dockter, Martha Nathan Dockter, Emery Schmidt, Ethel Herchert,
Gloria Knodel, Ralph Strommer, Hilma Ahl, Margaret Sprout, Mrs. Clifford Himmer,
Verlajean Kummer, Darvin Engel, Joy Harrum Kline.

Reflections of Rural School Teaching By Martha Diede Thompson

The high day of high school graduation was the biggest event in this girls' life
in 1935. The economy was in shambles plus drought and depression were poor
incentives for furthering one's education.

There were not many choices for women who had motivation to enter professions.
Nursing and teaching were the most popular. It was definitely a man's society.
Money was as scarce as hen's teeth so to better one's self, girls took jobs
mostly as domestics for $1.50 a week to $3 a week.

        Photo: Martha Thompson

In the spring of 1936, there was a shortage of rural schoolteachers. As
certificates expired for experienced teachers, the state used temporary
certificates to anyone 18 years or older by giving teacher's examinations valid
for two years. The fee was $2 and a passing grade of 75 percent was required on
the subject matter of agriculture, geography, history, civics, grammar,
literature, physiology, arithmetic, pedagogy and reading. I was fortunate to
pass the examination and thus started my teaching career.

The first teaching assignment was in McLean County, Wise District, Mercer, N.D.
in a school known as the Sprout School. The year was 1935 with an enrollment of
twenty-seven pupils, grades 1-8, salary $50 a month and the length of term eight
months. I was nineteen years old and had students taller than I. Contracts
stipulated the we were to be at school from 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., do the
janitorial work which included building fires in coal burning heaters, take care
of ashes, carrying coal, chop kindling wood and scrub the floor once a month.

The children brought drinking water from home. Each family brought a towel to be
used for washing hands before eating lunch. Money was scarce so the teacher
furnished soap (Lifebuoy).

The teachers boarded and roomed with school families for an average of $15 a
month, which covered meals from Monday through Friday. I stayed with a family
one-half mile from the school the first year, the second year I slept in the
school building but had meals with the family across the road.

As was mentioned before, the economy was in shambles. Districts didn't have
finances so that white chalk was about the only supply furnished. There were no
art supplies, workbooks, copying machines and toilet tissue. Library books were
scarce so these books were supplied by the State Library Commission. The postage
was paid by the teacher.

After five years in McLean County, I transferred to Sheridan County. Many
districts didn't hire married women and when a woman became pregnant, her job
was terminated.

When I married, we lived at the foothills of Prophet Township where we had
prairie trails for roads; consequently horseback was the main transportation.
The distance to school was four miles across the hills. Duties were the same as
the other rural schools, only difference was I had to carry everything in
saddlebags such as grain for the horses, noon meal, library books for the
students and anything extra for the benefit of the students.

Times were tough but we persevered, children learned in spite of all. We didn't
have non-readers or dysfunctional students. We never heard about the mentally
retarded as they were kept at home and they were very few and far between.

In 1939, things began to improve, roads were built, fuel oil replaced coal
stoves, books and workbooks and hectograph (copying tray, one sheet at a time)
became available. Districts were able to purchase drawing paper, toilet tissue,
soap, colored chalk, paid postage and other minor items.

As time went on, many rural schools were phased out due to low enrollment and
reorganization.

Reflections of a Country School Marm By Joy H. Kline

I graduated from Mercer High School as a salutatorian at the tender age of
seventeen. That very summer I went right on to school at Minot State Teacher's
College where I earned my certificate. Therefore, I figured I was all set to
teach. Times were tough and I had to work for my room and board to get through
school. I was hired as a governess for two small children. Early in the morning
and after school and on the weekends I worked hard at that job. My first school
teaching experience, at age eighteen, was a country school. This school was also
my home. I was hired for $80 a month. My ten pupils were all ages and all grades
up through eighth. The children walked to school until it was too cold, then the
parents brought them.

        Photo: Joy Kline

My learning experiences were great that first year. I was a janitor and nurse
besides being a teacher of eight grades. As winter approached, the freezing cold
and early darkness settled in. I locked the door early because I was afraid
after dark. No TV, phone, hot bath or car. Just me! To keep busy and
entertained, I ordered boxes of books from Bismarck to read. The wild horses
kicked against the walls and fought until early dawn. So it became a habit of
reading late into the night. That's a habit that's been mine until this very day
at my age now of ninety-one years. At seven o'clock in the morning I arose and
warmed the school and put the flag up. We had a hand bell, which I would ring.
At recess I always played outside with the pupils. We played "Fox and Goose" and
"anti-over-the-barn." During blizzards we played and sang inside.

Everyone brought their lunches. We had a pail and one water dipper for all to
use. After a while, I learned how to cook on the high coal stove near the middle
of the room. The children were happy to come to school and I was happy to see
them. So was the beginning of my school teaching.

The next year I was hired for $50 a month because the depression had taken hold.
The toughest part of being paid was picking up the check, which I had to do
myself. No such thing as mailing a check. This second year of teaching was much
better because I boarded and roomed with a farm family. While the Mr. and Mrs.
went out doing chores early in the morning, I watched their baby girl. Now the
loneliness was over. The new school year brought all eight grades. Some of the
pupils were larger than I. The big boys carried in the coal for me, which made
my janitor work easier. The fall brought a new challenge. One day as we sat in
school, we spotted a prairie fire headed our way. One of the older boys ran home
to summon his father who came and was able to put out the fire. What a scare!

In the winter there were other challenges, like getting to school. One Monday
morning it was 40 degrees below zero... at least! My transportation that day
was a horse because the snow was so deep. After attempting a big snow bank the
horse and I went down in a plop. I finally got up and out. Then, pulled on my
horse who finally got out and away we went. When I arrived at school there were
no matches to light the fire. I was so cold but tightened up my saddle, put the
bit in my horses's mouth and headed for the nearest neighbors. Halfway along my
frigid journey, I spotted smoke coming from school chimney. What a blessing!
Some older pupils had arrived and started a fire. So I returned stiff with cold
and the kids took my horse to the barn for me and ushered me in beside the stove
to thaw out. Those were the days!

After several years of teaching rural schools and I turned twenty-seven years
old, I tied the knot and started raising a family. When the children were older,
I returned to Minot State Teacher's College in Minot, N.D. Then I started
teaching all over the state of North Dakota. I taught twenty-five years. With
all told, what a wonderful vocation teaching children, molding minds and
characters. I loved every second of it!

Night of the Blizzard By Lydia Keller Krueger and Mary Evans Andrews
One Teacher's Story: Wise School #1 or Sprout School

This March day began like many others - cold, cloudy and windy. I was the young
teacher of a one room school near Mercer, N.D. From our farm home to the school
was just over a mile, a nice walk in good weather. But today my father, (Rev.
W.W.L. Keller) took my ten-year-old brother Alvin (Keller) and my little sister,
Elizabeth (Keller) and me to school in the horse drawn sled. We were all
bundled up against the cold, but before we reached the school house, pellets of
wind whipped snow began stinging our cheeks.

Before noon a gale was blowing. The snow was like a thick curtain that nearly
hid the little barn behind the school building. As the hours passed, the storm
became a raging blizzard, and I told the children we might have to spend the
night at the school. Some begged to go home, especially two brothers, Leslie
(Ovre) ten, and Harley eight (Ovre), who had their own horse and small sleigh.
But I forbade them to leave.

        Photo: Harley Ovre, student.

When we finished with our lessons, I played the pedal organ and we sang our
favorite songs. We played hymns, too, and prayed for the storm to end, but it
only grew wilder. I began reading stories the children requested, including
Longfellow's story poem Hiawatha.

By this time, it was plain that we could not leave the building. But Leslie and
Harley insisted on going to the barn to feed their horse. We had a rule that
anyone who had to go outside during a snowstorm must be securely roped around
the waist. I tied a long rope to each boy and, holding hands, they set out for
the barn. I watched the thick piles of rope uncoil. If too much was let out, it
would mean they had missed the barn about fifty feet away. To my relief, the
ropes stopped snaking out under the door. The boys were safe.

After a while, an out-of-breath snowman burst into the room. It was Leslie, and
he was alone. "Oh Miss Keller, the wind knocked Harley down and I can't find
him. You can't see your hand in front of you, the snow's so thick. I'll follow
his rope from here".

"No, Leslie, don't you go out again," I ordered, "We'll get him in - everyone
help pull."

It took most of us pulling on the rope, but we dragged Harley to the door. I
carried him inside. He was nearly unconscious and couldn't answer me. We pulled
off his frozen outer clothing and rubbed his frostbitten hands and face. When he
could talk, Harley mumbled his thanks repeatedly. "I couldn't stay awake, Miss
Keller," he said with his teeth chattering. "I thought I was a goner."

After we had his circulation going strong, I sat him next to the potbellied iron
stove. The boys kept it glowing with lignite coal. We had plenty of that in a
storage closet. Already it was growing dark, so I lit our one and only kerosene
lamp and turned it as high as I dared. Everyone was hungry again. "What can we
eat for supper?" Alvin asked.

"Let's see what we have." I spread a clean paper on my desk. "All of you bring
your lunch pails and dump them here. Empty every bit- even the crumbs."

The children obeyed. There wasn't much- some chunks of homemade bread, half of a
fat German sausage, a few half-eaten apples and the carrots that Leslie forgot
to take to his horse. I divided the leftovers equally, and we tried to melt some
snow for drinking water. I placed it in a saucepan to melt on top of the stove,
but that took too long. Instead of waiting, most of the children ate the snow.
The meal was not very satisfying. Elizabeth, the youngest, began to cry for her
mother. I rocked her on my lap and put on her warm outer clothing.

"Bundle up for the night, boys and girls," I told them. "Then lay your heads on
your desks and try to sleep. Put on your overshoes, coats, caps, scarves and
mittens. I'll keep the fire going."

I never closed my eyes that night as the children slept. Wind gusts slammed into
our small wooden building, making it tremble. One storm window was wrenched off,
and I prayed the other two wouldn't go.

When morning finally came, the storm was still roaring like a freight train. Our
food was gone and we were hungry, but we were safe and warm. (Later we learned
that winds dropped the temperature to -40F that night). I kept reassuring the
children that someone would come for us as soon as the storm let up.

We began class with our usual opening song. Then I kept everyone busy with
lessons. At last, toward noon, a tall man stomped up to the door. It was my
oldest brother, Walter (Keller), who had fought his way through the storm to
reach us. Mother had tied a pack of food on his back in a double blanket. I
lifted it off and pried it open as fast as the warm indoor air could thaw the
blanket. Inside was plenty of bread, sausage, slices of smoked roast goose, and
jars of milk. The milk was frozen solid, but I soon had it thawing in a pan on
the stove. Every one of us hugged and thanked Walter. When he got out of his
frozen coat, it stood alone in a corner!

By mid afternoon the wind finally died down, making it possible for my father to
get through to the school. His team of big, strong horses pulled our sturdy
sled across and around snowdrifts packed as solid as wet sand. The children
piled on the sled, with Leslie and Harley following in their light sleigh.
Walter and I floundered behind.

Father saw everyone safely home. The children's parents said they hadn't really
worried. They knew how much "Miss Lydia" loved those boys and girls and she
would keep them safe. But everyone was relieved that the long ordeal was over.

Reprinted in part from the Instructor, March, 1989

Don Grosz's Country School Memories As told to Bev Christensen, July 2004

Don Grosz taught the Medicine Hill country school #2, or the "Sondrol School" as
it was known in 1956-57. At that time, the State offered college students a $300
incentive if they would agree to teach a rural school. He also received a salary
of $2,200 for the year.

Don said he was very overwhelmed the first day of school, and thought he had
probably made a mistake. He had around thirty lessons a day to teach, and he did
not know how he was going to do it all. It turned out to be a super year, and
the parents were very supportive.

The students were Duane and Gene Schaefer, LeVerne and Eugene Schon, Myron Lick,
Sandy Weible, Donald, Carl, and Carol Rittenback, Doug Presser, Elray Sondrol,
and Bonnie Blotter. On Fridays, younger siblings could visit school.

        Photo: Don Grosz

At Thanksgiving time, they had a feast at the school. At Christmas time, the
parents helped him make a stage platform out of old barn doors. They made stage
curtains out of bed sheets, and the school was packed for the Christmas program.

The students belonged to "Young Citizen's League," and they had officers. Each
student had a duty or two to help the teacher, such as cleaning blackboards and
erasers, cleaning the outhouses, sweeping the floor, making posters, and
decorating the windows. Don accompanied his students outside during noon recess.

One day Miss Lynne, the County Superintendent, dropped in unexpectedly. He was
so nervous that he did not eat lunch or go to outdoor noon recess with the
students. He was sickened when one little girl came into the schoolhouse with a
bloody nose. As Don attended to the girl, he thought his teaching career might
be over for lack of control of the students. He was later relieved to see that
Miss Lynne had written in the class record book that she was happy to see such a
great atmosphere at their school.

The next fall, Don returned to college, and then taught in the Mercer Public
School and other places after that. He said that his best year of teaching was
at the little country school in Medicine Hill Township north of Mercer.

Mercer School Memories By Mary Frances Davidson Faurot Class of 1922

I am having my daughter write this. I am soon to be ninety-eight years old and
with Evelyn Knutson was in the first graduating class of Mercer High School in
1922.

If my memory is correct, when I was born in 1906, there was no school in Mercer.
By the time I was old enough to go to school there was one. I'm sure you have
the date. We lived out on my parent's ranch, but they moved into Mercer the year
before I started school. My first grade teacher married a good friend of my
parent's who was also from Hannibal, Missouri. She was then Lillian Plowman, I
can't remember her maiden name when she was teaching.

My mother was elected to the school board and became president of the
schoolboard. She was influential in getting the town to put in a high school.
When I finished eighth grade, they put in a ninth grade, then tenth and so on.
Only Evelyn and I were in these classes. I've always had fun saying I graduated
valedictorian of my class of two. And then the whole graduating class went off
to Jamestown College and roomed together. Evelyn graduated from Jamestown, but
my family returned to Missouri after my freshman year and I went with them and
then to the University of Missouri.

I remember the school had four rooms and four teachers. We usually had a teacher
who lived at our house.

Evelyn and I were both quite young when we graduated. I was sixteen and I know
she was younger than I. I skipped second grade because my teacher thought I had
covered it pretty well in first grade. Then I skipped seventh too. That was
interesting.

Because the school was not accredited, the eighth grade students had to pass a
state test to graduate. They found taking the test made many of the students so
nervous they couldn't do well so began giving practice tests to sixth and
seventh graders. When Evelyn and I were in sixth grade, they gave the test to us
for practice and we both passed. The teachers didn't know what to do with us so
they decided to skip us to eighth as we were a bit young to graduate. They
decided to put in the high school for us.

Have a nice reunion. I hope your deadline is not too rigid as I'm a bit late
having spent most of January in Mexico.

I put in the Frances as I was Mary Frances when in school.

Father-John Helm Davidson; mother-Nita Davidson; sister-Rose, born 1908;
brother-Frank, born 1913 and Helm Junior, born 1920. Came to Mercer area bout
1904 and returned to Missouri in 1923.

By a Member of the Class of 1927

At recess everyone ran for the giant strides or teeter totters and if they were
lucky enough to get one they kept them all through recess.

The spelling bees were fun. Choosing up sides and the last one standing would be
the winning side, of course.

We always looked forward to the school picnic at the end of the year at Brush
Lake.

Anyone misbehaving was sent to the superintendent's office. I don't know what
the punishment was but most everyone had a fear of being sent there.

We had declamation and music concerts each year. The winners got to go to the
county contest.

We had to take state exams in high school which were sometimes difficult.

We didn't have proms in those days but we had junior-senior banquets and we
thought they were pretty special.

At basketball games all the girls cheering section were dressed in black skirts
and white blouses and a small black and white banner on the sleeve with M.H.S.
on it. We had some simple action cheering that we all took part in.

You probably have a record of all the teachers, but I'll name a few just in case
you want them.

Elva Mary Urban, first grade 1923; Edith Hedahl, 2nd grade 1924; Ella Kempf,
fourth grade 1926; Myrtle Schmid, 5th grade 1927.

Some high school teachers between 1933 and 1936: Ludwig Totdahl, Stanley Norem,
Marcus Wagle, supt., Miss Martha Manning and Ardis Rice.

By Aileen Rice Anderson Class of 1928

What a large part Mercer School played in the lives of students in the early
1900s.

Each year the arrival of new teachers was an event. The curious and the
welcomers gathered at the depot. Usually there was at least one young and pretty
lady. Sometimes she married in Mercer and there was always that possibility.

While we lacked TV, there were silent movies once in a while. Our role models
were the older students in the school. Mostly we joined in a school play or even
a community performance. Remember the very high stage in the gymnasium?
Regularly, there were programs in honor of significant dates. And there were
memorable banquets.

County contests were very important. Sometimes the judges traveled even from so
far away as Bismarck to rate the contestants, a few going on to the state
contests.

The basketball games were of first importance. I think there were highly
competitive men's teams and that sometimes Mercer won. The girls basketball team
played three-court rules, enough to ruin any enthusiasm. We were perfectly
content to revel in "good sportsmanship" recognition. And after the local games,
we had such splendid refreshments - an absolute favorite was the garlic dill
pickles.

One of the happiest social events at the school was the basket social. The
contents of each basket were the "best" of fried chicken, potato, fruit or
vegetable salad and gorgeous cake. The adornment of the outside, the choice of
colors was very important and the secrecy didn't fool anyone. The most popular
"gal," often the teacher, would be identified by ever-increasing bids, all aware
that there was no stopping until the highest price of the evening resulted in
the community's choice of romantic couples having the dinner together.

Recess was important. The Fargo Forum stories about a tragic murder in our
locale was denied reading to young students. Believe me, there was a grapevine
or network that kept all of us equally informed.

4-H clubs kept some of us involved. Sunday school was all-important, acquainting
us with Bible stories, prayers, hymns, valuable literary history and ideals.

There's so much talk today about bullies. I don't remember being unhappily
treated by schoolmates. I think we were all too close to parents and family
awareness to get by with cruelty.

The greatest testimonial to the importance of Mercer school was the impulse
given to continue education and to realize that we were prepared for the
challenges of the world ahead.

By Annetta Gardiner Just Class of 1943

I attended Mercer Consolidated School grades one through twelve.

Grades one through three were in one room. My teacher for all three grades was
Miss Dutoit - I remember the little red chairs we sat on during reading. When it
was time for me to read, I would stand beside Miss Dutoit. She would put her arm
around me and help with my reading. She was special!

Miss Thompson as my fourth, fifth, and sixth grade teacher. I remember what she
wrote in my autograph book, "By friendly deeds is friendship won. If you want a
friend you must first be one." I tried to follow that advice.

Mr. Heath and Mrs. Pettys were my seventh and eighth grade teachers. Mr. Heath
played the harmonica. He started a harmonica band. We all learned to play the
harmonica. We even played at a PTA meeting.

Starting high school was exciting and a little frightening. The year started
with freshman initiation. The junior class was in charge. We had to wear silly
looking outfits and do what the juniors asked us to do. It was all harmless. I
think the only sport was boys basketball. The team was really good during my
freshman and sophomore years. The pep club supported the team. The girls in the
pep club wore black skirts and white tops - the school colors. Play day and
music contests were fun. I still have the ribbons I won. The students and
parents would work evenings setting up and decorating booths. The mothers would
help the girls bake and make candy.

I had good teachers throughout grade and high school. We were taught to respect
the teachers, they in turn respected us.

I graduated with a class of four girls in 1943. Our class motto was "No victory
without labor."

By Leontine Schoell Class of 1944

There was nothing very exciting in my years of high school. Most of the people
that started with me moved away so I ended up in a class of two in 1944, that
was Tillie Kruger and I. The teachers I remember are Mr. and Mrs. Reddington,
Walter Braun, Mr. Syverson and Ms. Luessen. The teachers in my freshman and
sophomore years was Mr. Syverson and Walter Braun, in my senior year Ms. Luesson
was added.

Cartoon drawings are were done by Don Kern. He sat behind me and did lots of
drawing.

This is something I remember from our junior or senior year: There were few
moments of excitement in Mr. Braun's room. Leotine Schoell was cleaning her
teeth with her small knife and when it snapped shut she yelled, "Mr. Braun, Mr.
Braun!" When he inquired of her difficulties, she replied, "Can't you see?" Upon
looking he noticed a small knife caught between her lips.

Graduation night I ended up giving the valedictorian speech as Tillie Kruger was
getting her high school education in three years. Graduation evening she was
short some credits, so I was the qualified one to give the speech.

Our colors senior year were coral and light green, but I can't remember our
motto.

Name not given Mercer High School Student

I went to Mercer School for 12 years. I have many pleasant memories from Mercer
including:

Picnics at Brush Lake at the end of the school year.

Spelling contests.

Senior class plays.

The alumni reunions. I attended three.

It was nice to have brothers and sisters in another classroom nearby-not so
scary on the first days of school.

I have gone to three reunions and enjoyed them very much. Am looking forward to
centennial book. Thanks for the memories.

By Roy Nielsen Jr. Class of 1947

Curriculum involved State Board and supplemental correspondence courses

The curriculum at our school met state board specifications. I remember those
state board examinations. We could take supplemental courses from North Dakota
State. These correspondence courses made it possible to graduate in three years
from high school.

Teachers

One can recall a teacher in the lower grades by the name of Betty Dahl - who
eventually married Dr. Lowell Satre, Lutheran Theological Seminary teacher
(Greek or Hebrew). She blessed her classroom with her teaching ability and moral
substance.

Mrs. Archie Kline was very much of a disciplinarian and did not leave us short
of well-organized course work.

Mr. Delmar Petys was one of the superintendents. In my case he turned out to be
an orthopedic medical professional as well. During recess at school I broke my
wrist jumping off the bleachers to get a basketball out of the net. The
procedure, as an end to end bone set, accomplished by one person pulling on the
hand of the broken wrist, another pulling backward on the shoulder of that arm.
Tongue depressors, gauze and tape were used to hold the bones in opposition and
the arm was put in a sling. When the railroad was opened "by rotary-plow" we got
to a doctor and it was just a little crooked so I didn't care to have it
rebroken to reset.

Roscoe Redington and wife Agnes were superintendent and teacher at Mercer. Their
son Donald invited me to their home and it was the practice for all to pray
before eating. The Redingtons were of the Wilton area.

Russell Schmidt was another fine teacher, also a man of God. He would put the
boxing gloves on with you and give a gentle attitude adjustment. He taught that
Christians weren't second class citizens.

One teacher (possibly Syverson) was our scout maser. We were doing a tracking
exercise northeast of town. We got hungry and decided to eat before the
scheduled time. A small hay pile was started on fire to heat food and it wasn't
long and we were fighting a prairie fire with our jackets. One of the scouts was
Gene Logue.

The World War II years brought the reality of war to our school. The attack on
Pearl Harbor was announced in our schoolroom.

The loss of former residents soon became real. The loss of pilot Duane Rice was
just one of those traumatic events. The Rice's were family!

The return of Ben Hjelle's son from Guadalcanal, Phillipines, yellow with
malaria and shell-shocked brought more reality. The Hjelle's were family and we
praised God for his return. During the war - rationing, war bonds, and man power
adjustments. In the fall it happened that some high school students stayed out
for the threshing run if you were to have your crops threshed. Emanuel Schlaht
was one of those operators and Teddy Schlaht drove one of the bundle teams on
the threshing run. Lots of good food, but we hit places that had "alkali water"
which produced intestinal problems.

Remembrances that are not school related

The railroad brought our mail and following the train going through town we knew
when it was time to go to the post office and stand and wait for the mail to be
distributed - Ben Hjelle, postmaster.

Soren Nielsen was a friend of the family and caretaker at the Lutheran church we
went to. When one came to Soren's place his yard was full of wildflowers he had
transplanted and he would be reading the Bible through a reading glass. He would
grit his teeth when he found us in the furnace room at the church and he did a
good job shepherding. We will see him again.

On Sunday it wasn't uncommon to visit neighbor's Topper Rasmussen and Oscar
Gunderson - both bachelors. Oscar Rasmussen retired to a Minnesota lake and
fishing soon was old without old friends.

Conrad Freeberg bet me $5 I couldn't eat a jalapeno pepper - he lost, but
delayed payment. Conrad taught me the difference between "prescription" and
"subscription," dumping and washing cream cans and candling eggs.

By Delma Fischer Kost Class of 1948

When I was asked to write some memories of my twelve years at Mercer School, I
was blank. It has been fifty-five years since I graduated in the class of 1948.
I'll try to come up with some ideas that may be of interest.

To introduce myself - I am the oldest of the children of Fred and Elizabeth
Fischer. My siblings are Darvin, Wilber, Myron and Doris. We lived on a farm
about six miles southwest of Mercer and we rode a school bus every day. Emanuel
Hinsz was our bus driver for many years.

1948 must have been the smallest enrollment that Mercer High School ever had
because there were only two graduates - Myra Schlaht and I. I don't really
remember but I think that in grades 9-12, there were only eighteen students. I
suppose after that redistricting started with country schools closing and the
students going to town and my parents were very concerned about the future of
the school. Merging with a neighboring school didn't even seem to be a
possibility because of roads, transportation, etc.

When I started school, grades one through four were all together. I spoke very
little English, but I wasn't the only one so we got by and we learned from one
another. I always loved going to school and enjoyed the challenge of learning
new things. Grades five through eight were together also. In high school there
were the superintendent and one or two teachers.

I started summer school at Minot Teacher's College a week after my graduation
and got my degree with no major problems. Of course, my education was lacking in
some areas - no typing, no lab, just general science and math. We just had the
bare requirements set up by the state for graduation. We had to learn our
material well since we had to pass the state exams to earn our credits. The
outstanding advantage that we had was that our teachers really cared about us. I
was so blessed to have Pearl Kline as my teacher for many courses. I think she
taught in every field. She inspired in me a love of English and even as a
teenager. I knew that I would be an English teacher.

Our parents and teachers encouraged us to read and to take advantage of our
opportunities and to learn on our own. The school didn't have much of a library,
but my mother ordered boxes of books from the Bismarck Library Commission and we
developed a love for reading. Most of my twenty-nine years of teaching were
spent as the English teacher at Sawyer High School.

I like to tell my grandchildren to never under estimate or put down the small
school. I graduated from the smallest and look how smart and successful I have
been. The graduates of Mercer High School don't have to take a back seat to
anyone!

By Mary Presser Steckler Class of 1949

Thank you for thinking for me. I find it very difficult separating my memories
of school and growing up in Mercer. I was surrounded by grandpas and grandmas,
aunties and uncles and friends. Grandpa and Grandma Wagner, Grandma Wise,
Grandpa and Grandma Stradinger, Grandma Kline, Grandma Singer, Grandma Meyer,
Grandma Gardiner, Grandma Washburn, Grandma Degg, Grandpa Miller, Auntie Dora
and Uncle Louie Jorgensen and many others. I remember the Skow family. They were
neighbors and can remember Woodrow walking to work. Buddy was in school and a
real neat kid. The Rice farm, where the Rennich family had a repair shop across
the old highway from Grandpa's station. I remember the German Lutheran church
and parsonage, the pavilion, the old hotel (the Pfeiffer family lived there),
Bill Norris' barbershop, Sam and Doxie Norris' café. I remember Sam lighting
that stuff on the lid of the can. It smelled bad, but helped him breathe. The
Orman's had an ice cream shop. The Wednesday night free shows on Main. Farmers
came to town and cars were parked so they could watch the movie. We spread our
blanket on the ground and would be transported into the wild-wild west.

Ross Gardiner's grocery store. Can remember him coming to visit grandpa. He
would bring a couple nice apples and they would visit and then scrape the apples
because neighbor wore their teeth and each had a spittoon. Ben Hjelle in the
post office. Fred Zachmeister had a Standard Station - later owned by Emil Just.
The telephone office run by Emma Schlaht. Soren Nielsen - janitor of the
Norwegian Lutheran Church and an old Danish man who never married. He loved the
outdoors and plants. Tom Gardiner had the blacksmith shop. Mr. and Mrs. Logue
had a variety store and barbershop on main street. They had a son, Gene and a
daughter, Bonnie. F.O. Freeberg had the bank and grocery and clothing store.
Harry Kline had the saloon and Ed and Hattie Pederson had a locker plant and
restaurant. Christoph Schell had a hardware store. They lived in the house to
the west of it. Grandpa and Grandma Littke used to live there. There were three
elevators and a lumberyard. I can remember going sledding down the hill from
Haftan Berge's house in the Rice's backyard (barnyard). The depot in Mercer.
Riding in a two-wheeled cart pushed by my grandfather to deliver and pick up the
mail when the train came in. The Mattson's were living in the upstairs of the
depot and he was the depot agent.

I took piano lessons from Margaret Hjelle and then Phyllis Freeberg. I can
remember Ernest Seibold family living in a house that Conrad and Evelyn Freeberg
moved into. The Seibold's had three children, Delmar, Bobby and Dorothy (I
think). The house Ted and Marie Sackman lived in. The had two children Wesley
and Delores. They moved to Eureka, S.D. and I believe Mr. and Mrs. C.P.
Christensen bought it. Now I think that is Martha Thompson's home.

Because my granddad was on the school board, I knew some of the teachers. Mr.
and Mrs. Pettys and my mom's friend Gladys (Thompson) Ness and others. We had
Merwyn Freeberg's wedding reception in the sunken garden. I was the mock bride
and Phyllis Bonnet was the mock groom. John Braun was also on these school
board. Three of their children were Walter, Martin and Mary. Walter was the
principal when I was in the third and fourth grades. I can remember the Andrew
Sackman family, they had twin girls, Vera and Verna, and one boy about my age.
His name was Ralphie. He had some fingers missing. The Roy Nielsen house, now
being torn down. I can remember Ross and Marie living in the little house across
the street from the Nielsen house. They had a barn and there were horses in it.

I can remember going to "Study Club" with my grandmother at the O.S. Hjelle
house. So many memories and so much caring about your accomplishments.

I can remember being sent across a snow covered stubble field north of the
school to tell the boys to get back to school. They had gone to see the plane
that landed across the highway. It was a coyote hunter. It was very interesting.
I know none of us made it back when recess was over so we had to miss recesses
and stay in. All of the girls got to go out but me. I don't know how long we had
to stay in but Margaret Wicklander was the teacher. There were two sets of
stairs going up to the principal's office. You certainly did not want to go up
there or even be seen going up there.

I remember the "giant strides," the hopscotch squares on the sidewalk, the
marble rings in the grounds. I remember the programs at school and church were
very important to us. One of my favorite subjects was biology. It was taught by
Pearl Lockrem Kline. She made the subject very interesting and is one of my
favorite teachers. I remember Palmer Syverson and his beautiful penmanship. He
taught math and told spooky stories (I think). I can remember my grandparents
having all the "Mercer" bachelors for Thanksgiving dinner. Martin Rasmussen
(Topper), Anton Nelson, Nels Fibelsted, Soren Nielsen and Oscar Gunderson. He
dug the rocks on his land and built fences with them. Grandpa used to deliver
the meal to Carl Frantzen, "The Old Swede."

I can remember hauling water. We would drive south of town to the Wise farm or
go east on the old highway to Washburn's Spring. The train used to stop there to
take on water. I remember watching (from a distance) as the rotary snowplow
would go through the cut right south of the Sackman's house. I can remember
sliding down drifts on a scoop shovel with Delma and Verdel Braun and also with
Marvin Calheim. I can remember walking over the snowdrift - over the trellis at
grandpa's front gate to go to school. Seems as if we had a lot more snow then.
My memories are many. If I have not mentioned some names, it is certainly not
because they have been forgotten, but my intention was not to write a novel or
even a short story. Don't know if you can use any of this, but it is great to
say "I grew up in Mercer." Thank you for this privilege of writing a bit about
it.

There were three gas stations in Mercer. Jake Brown had the bulk station on
Main. He delivered gas to Grandpas before Ted Gessele. There were no cars parked
at the school, other than those belonging to the teachers. The country kids were
hauled in. Harvey Pederson finally got a car that had a rumble seat. Roy Nielsen
Jr. could take his parent's car and some friends and go to Brush Lake if he
would take his kid sister and I along. But that went over like a lead balloon. I
can remember having a birthday party at my house for Ramona Klaudt. She didn't
have a doll so we all chipped in and got her one for her birthday.

Speaking of cars, Charlie Butz came to town driving a convertible. They had
moved into a farm home on the old highway between Turtle Lake and Mercer. That
created a stir. I can remember going to Brush Lake with the trucks and Grandpa
and they would cut and haul ice blocks for the pop cooler in the station. I can
remember fourth of July parades, ball games, roller-skating and Memorial Day
parades. Can remember playing for June Berge or she played for me.

I remember playing "Cowboys and Indians" with the Klaudt kids. We were always
the Indians.

This was a p.s. - supposed to be short, but got to remembering and rambling
again. Hope this does not bore you silly and there will be something you can
use.

By Donna Fiebelstad Kiesacker Class of 1950

My memories of Mercer School began in the sixth grade. Prior to that I attended
a one room rural school. 1943 - World War II was in progress, the country was
emerging from the Great Depression. Rationing of many items was in effect.
Everyone's life was affected. Schools were affected. Teacher shortages, cutback
on programs, no sports, no frills. It was the basics. Most of the young men were
in the military as well as young women. Other folks had gone to work in defense
plants in other areas of the country. So town school was an adventure after the
one room school. It had electric lights, central heat, indoor toilets in winter,
a library and encyclopedias and classmates. Mrs. Edson from Bismarck was my
first teacher in Mercer. She was a short, older lady, excellent teacher and had
good discipline of the classroom of grades five through eight. I liked school
and adjusted easily.

Mercer being a Class C school meant we took state exams beginning in seventh
grade. Passing grades meant we progressed to the next grade. In the seventh
grade it was agriculture and health or geography. Eighth it was arithmetic,
history and language. We spent time reviewing for these exams and were always
apprehensive until we received the results and heard that we had passed. Then
there was much rejoicing!.. Eighth grade graduation was a big countywide
affair at Garrison. I had a ready-made dress for the occasion, my first since
the Shirley Temple dress in first grade. Also nylon hose, nylon had been
developed during the war. The war was over and many new things were available.
The economy was slowly improving.

The fall of 1946, seven freshmen entered the halls of Mercer High School. They
were Phyllis Bonnet, Donna Fibelstad, Videll Fiedler, Perry Makeeff, James
Schlaht and Ted Schlaht. Principal H.C. Knutson and Pearl Kline taught the high
school classes. There were a total of sixteen students in high school. Sophomore
students were Leona Bohnet, Marie Bossert, Eileen Laib and Meinhardt Wagner.
Junior class consisted of Delma Fischer and Myra Schlaht. Senior class consisted
of Violet Miller, Roy Nielsen Jr. and John Westerlind. After enduring a week of
freshmen orientation we were in! The upper classroom treated us to quite a party
sampling all sorts of weird things typical of an orientation.

Sophomore year we lost several classmates. Phyllis moved to McHenry and Videll
transferred to McClusky. We gained Shirley Heitzmann and Patrick Schmitt. Our
class of seven remained intact through graduation in 1950.

Being a Class C school, specific requirements in subject material were set up by
the State Department of Education and state exams were written for each subject.
There were no exceptions. Classes included general science, general math,
English I through IV, literature I through IV, biology, algebra I & II, PDP,
typing I & II, American history, health, psychology, business law, drivers ed.,
glee club and phy ed. were the classes I recall. There weren't any frills. Our
teachers were very dedicated. Mrs. Kline was an excellent teacher especially in
English and gave us a great foundation that has served me well through life. The
teachers were as interested in character development and in us becoming good
citizens. Other teachers included Jack Coyne and M.B. Schuler and Walter Braun.
Mr. Coyne coached basketball and Mercer went to District.

Each school day began with the pledge of allegiance and with students reading a
portion of scripture and reciting the Lord's Prayer. A copy of the Ten
Commandments and pictures of Presidents Washington and Lincoln hung in each
classroom. Town students all went home for lunch. Country kids brought lunches
until the hot lunch program, which began in about 1948-49. Lasting friendships
were developed through being together each noon hour. Many marble games were
played, as well as softball, not to mention the giant strides and the teeter
totters. The fall high school carnival was another fun learning experience as we
would prepare for it to raise money for the school. Setting up booths, making
fudge and divinity and popcorn balls. It culminated in the crowning of the king
and queen from the student body. This activity brought out the whole community.
We also participated in having one of the first annuals to be bound and have a
hard cover. There were class plays and talent nights put on for the community.
We had class officers. The glee club sang for school functions as well as for
funerals, etc.

Our class of seven graduated in May of 1950, the largest class post-war. We
looked forward to this day of commencement. That is what it was! In looking back
some fifty plus years, I'm grateful for the education I received at Mercer,
friendships formed and for the community as a whole to which I felt accountable.
I look forward to the reunions and especially to the one in 2005.

By Eunice Hinsz Vossler Class of 1951

My years at Mercer School started the year of 1943 as a fifth grader. I came
from a one-room country school. Mercer was a big change. WE now had hot water,
heat, drinking fountains, electric lights, indoor bathrooms (during winter
months), janitors, classrooms (combined to two grades), school pictures and a
large black bell operated with the pull of a large rope inside the hallway. This
bell rang at 8:30 a.m. first bell; second 8:45 and it was heard all over town.

Our classes started with the pledge to flag. To the rear of the room was George
Washington's picture and the Ten Commandments. Our teacher was Mrs. A.M. Edson,
a kind, little lady.

On to the sixth grade, our teacher, Mr. Art Schrenk, had an interesting
classroom. I remember him with his awards. In spelling when we got a grade of
100 he autographed a colored picture and posted it on the blackboard until the
end of the month and then we took them home.

Mercer being a Class C school required state exams. Health and agriculture in
the seventh grade. History, geography, English and math in the eighth grade.
This was a real challenge. Mrs. Pearl Kline taught most of these subjects. She
handled it with excellence. She had us review past year's tests over and over.
The tests were written twice a year.

Moving on into the ninth grade was good, easier because we didn't have any more
state tests. Our class started with eight students. We gained three country
students, Eleanor Reuer, Elton Just and Wesley Vossler joined Luella Schell,
Alma Gessele, Juanita Lowe, Eunice Hinsz and Gloria Nielsen. Our first big event
was initiation. What a party! We were ordered to wear strange clothes and hats.
Carried cans of toys, etc.

The curriculum was limited, offering only the basic subjects. It was required
that we take physical ed. and music. We had some really great teachers and
passed to basement classrooms for science and biology. Each room had a set of
encyclopedias, dictionary and other reference books. This was a great help.
Teachers I remember were H.. Knutson, John Coyne, M.B. Schuler and Walt Braun.

We had girls glee club directed by Miss June Berge. We used sheet music and some
of our numbers were: "Oh! What a Beautiful Morning," "Fairest Lord Jesus,"
patriotic hymns and our school song to the tune of "On Wisconsin."

Other events were school parties, class plays, carnivals, and junior and senior
banquets. We had a yearbook my freshman year, a school paper called the
"Cricket." Boys basketball, the Mercer Bison, black and white were the school
colors. Our gym was small but we had some powerful ball games.

Our junior year we lost five classmates. Some moved, others went to other
schools. So our 12th grade left us with three students. My memories of Mercer
are great! Many good times and good student-teacher relationships. I'm proud to
be a 1951 graduate of Mercer High School.

By Deloris Makeeff Howe Class of 1953

My years and memories of Mercer and Mercer High School days.

I went to a country school until high school days except for fifth grade when
our country school was closed and we came to Mercer School.

One thing, we lived close to town so in times of blocked roads, we often walked
to school and home. On occasion when a snow storm would come up during the day,
our dad would come walking with extra clothing and scarves so we could bundle up
for the cold, stormy walk home.

Our class began with seven total, one of the smallest during that time with six
graduating four years later. Our class was not a close-knit group even though we
were small.

One tradition in those times was the freshmen initiation by the sophomore class.
Freshmen spent the week dressing in peculiar clothing dictated by the sophomores
culminating with an initiation party Friday night. They would bring you to a
room individually blind folded and give you different things to eat (example:
grapes would be called pig eyeballs, etc.) Our class didn't like that idea, so
when our turn as sophomores came we kept the clothing tradition, but
discontinued the eating idea. We still had a party with fun but no ugly eating
ideas and a new era was born.

Changing classrooms for different classes was also new to us in high school and
freshmen and sophomores would go to a classroom downstairs. There was usually a
thundering sound coming from the stairway as we came and went from a classroom
upstairs that contained all ninth, tenth, eleventh and twelfth grade students.
During our junior and senior years we were permanently stationed in the lower
level classrooms.

The school hot lunch program started sometime during my four years in high
school.

As juniors in high school it was a tradition to give the seniors a banquet.
Juniors or seniors were only invited and dressed formal wear for a beautiful
evening. In its place now is the junior-senior prom.

High school graduation always included two special events, baccalaureate and
graduation ceremonies. Baccalaureate was a special time held in a church the
Sunday before graduation with a religious connotation. Laws have changed all
that so today mostly only graduation ceremonies were held.

Choosing a class motto and class colors was fun. Each year the senior class
would take a skip day (as it was called) in which the class took a Friday in May
and left on a trip for Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Our class went to the Black
Hills touring and sight seeing. We found two volunteer drivers (one was our
school superintendent) and an additional female chaperone to stay with girls at
night.

I remember being class president during our senior year, the town kids going
home to eat which made our lunch hour long and boring, occasional school parties
on Friday nights, volleyball for most of our phy ed. classes, and singing in the
girls glee club with June Berge as director.

I also remember filling in as a substitute teacher in the primary classroom
including grades one through three when the teacher was gone.

These are some of my memories, but there are more.

By Sylvia Schlaht Anderson Class of 1954

I received your letter yesterday here in Ariz. I tried to put the wheels in
motion, but not sure what kind of memories you are wanting. So will try and
write some of the things I remember as highlights for me.

I remember some of the names of teachers I had in the elementary grades. They
were Miss Eggi, Miss Holmes for two years, Mrs. Knudsen (fifth and sixth), June
Berge (Fettig) (seventh and eighth). High school - Mr. Knudsen, Pearl Kline, Mr.
Langemo, Mr. Marotti.

One thing I remember about Mr. Marotti, who I think taught history. We thought
he was way off when he told us that some day men would go to the moon. Well,
after if happened, I guess he knew more than we thought he did at that time.

There were four of us that started first grade and also graduated together in
1954. The four were Fritzie Kline, Janice Just, Tony Schell and Sylvia Schlaht.

I remember the Christmas programs in the grades and the fun we had at recess. We
had seesaws, giant strides, softball games, jacks, marble games during the nice
weather. In the winter we played Fox and Goose, King on the Hill and made
snowmen. The activities in high school were volleyball, pep club, glee club,
school carnival with king and queen contest.

There were twelve in our class that graduated with some going on to college. Of
the twelve that graduated, four have passed away.

We may have missed some things like band, but we have a close relationship with
the students in the school as well as the community.

By Phoebe Stute Haugeberg Class of 1956

Just as the kids do today I liked recess the best. My fond memories are actually
of the extra curricular activities, but still a part of school. We always had a
great basketball team - don't recall all the players but Charles Kline, Arlo
Singer, Arlo Eckmann - later on Bob Freeborg, Bob Sackman, Wilbur Fischer, Jim
Rust and Erv Stute.

The girls only had volleyball as their sport - far different than today. The
school class plays were a fun experience as were all the choral groups under the
direction of Mrs. Berg.

I came to Mercer school from rural so only spent four years there. Hope this is
helpful.

By Marlene M. (Fueller) Taylor Class of 1957

Marlene Fueller attended Mercer School for my four years of high school,
1953-57.

Had excellent teachers and I especially enjoyed cheerleading and attending all
the basketball games. The parties and playing volleyball were also a lot of fun.
Got valuable experience working on the school paper and annuals. Never missed a
thing being at Mercer High. A great four years.

By El Roy Hinsz Class of 1958

It was no secret that I hated going to school. Many mornings my mother gave me
the "knuckles on the head" to get me moving and get to school on time.

My memory of Mercer School is walking to school in the snow on a bitter cold
morning and being greeted by a huge selection of four and five buckle overshoes
as soon as you opened the door. Many of them still had the remains of animal
dung because most of us farm boys and girls did chores before school and
everyone only owned one pair of overshoes. Soon as the ice and snow melted off
the shoes, our school had the strong odor of barnyard. Sometimes just for
meanness I would set my stinky overshoes on top of some girls nice clean shoes.

A few of my school years my dad drove the school bus, but I never got to ride on
it since we lived in town. When I tell my grandkids here in California I walked
to school in the snow, they laugh. If only they knew!

By Eileen Just Spilman Class of 1963

As a member of the Mercer High School graduating class of 1963, I was asked to
share some memories. The first thing that came to mind was the memory of who was
in my class. While we had a few others that were part of our class for a short
period of time, we did have thirteen students in our graduating class. They
were: Karen Brewster, Mona Fiedler, Doris Fischer, John Fibelstad, Darlene
Jorgenson, Eileen Just, Arlys Laib, Bonnie Lou Schell, Ernie Schumann, Nettie
Jean Tewksbury, Sharon Rust, David Rust and Nicki Wall.

Thinking back to my school days and looking at my life since, what do I remember
most about Mercer school? I remember that I was not a leader at that time but
with thirteen students in my graduating class and approximately fifty each year
in the high school, there were plenty of opportunities for each one of us to be
a participant. I think back to the "music department." No we did not have a band
or orchestra, but we did have chorus and that brought the opportunities to sing,
not only for the Christmas program, etc.; but also involved competition and a
trip to Bismarck each year. While we were proud of our ratings, etc., we also
really enjoyed the freedom of wandering around the big city of Bismarck for a
day.

The athletic department is huge in many schools. Ours consisted of the
basketball team and cheerleaders. The Pep Club also was part of the athletic
department and included just about every student. Many of my favorite memories
consist of bus rides to ball games in Hurdsfield, Denhoff, Goodrich and other
towns. Also cheering on the "Bison" at home games. The Pep Club and other groups
sold lunches at ball games also as a fund raiser.

Our "drama department" was our junior and senior plays. Again, everyone had a
part not just a select few. We practiced many, many evenings before we presented
the play. The nights of the performances always drew a large audience from the
community.

The school carnival was another memory that came to mind. No only was the night
of the carnival lots of fun, ending with the coronation of the king and queen,
but also decorating and preparing the booths, and working our shift the night of
the carnival.

"The Cricket" was our school newspaper. It gave us the opportunity to write
articles about the happenings throughout the school, but also involved printing
and distribution. The annual had to be prepared each year as well. Here the
memories consist not only of the photo shoots, putting each page together, but
the anxious wait for the day of arrival when you filled your annual with
signatures and remembrances from all your schoolmates. Let's not forget that the
seniors were able to travel to Bismarck one day where we each had our senior
photos taken. And then there was the day the representative came to school and
we got to pick the design for our class ring.

During our high school years we had two homeroom classrooms in what originally
was the old gym in the school basement. There were two smaller classrooms, one
on the west side that when I first began school, was our cafeteria. During my
high school days it was a study hall and later was our library. The east
classroom was our lunch room for a while and then became the typing room. The
old stage was used first as a library/workroom and then as a coat room. We were
very fortunate to be students when the new addition was added to the north
(back) of the school which added a new science room (also math classes were held
here) and a new kitchen and cafeteria. The new addition also added two more
bathrooms. Music classes were held on the stage.

I believe we must have had the best school cooks in the county! Even living a
half block from the school, I ate hot lunch every day. My personal favorite was
mashed potatoes, sauerkraut and hog dogs. When I began in elementary school, I
remember that the milk came in bottles with paper caps. When I was older, I
remember the milk machine were we could fill glasses of milk - often times even
chocolate milk. When we purchased a glass of milk during milk break, we checked
our name off on a sheet of paper and at the end of the month our milk bill was
added up. At a penny a glass the bill was never too high!

Perhaps the highlight of the senior year, other the baccalaureate and graduation
day itself, was the senior class trip to the Black Hills. We piled into cars and
traveled in a caravan to see the sights in western South Dakota. Remember the
cabins that we stayed in! Definitely not the Ritz, but for many of us it was our
first out of state trip.

Looking back to elementary school days, I remember playing behind the school
(before the science and lunchroom addition was built) on the swings and teeter
totters. How much fun it was to jump off the teeter totter when you were on the
bottom, letting the other person to come down quickly! Also to see how far you
could jump off the swing. Winter time found us playing King on the Hill and Fox
and Goose on the west side of the school. Spring time it was marbles right in
the front of the school to the left as you entered the building. Hopscotch
boards were drawn on all the sidewalks. When we were in grade school, the little
kids would play ball on the field to the east of the school while the big kids
used the diamond the west side - down the hill. Everything stopped once the bell
rang, though and we all had to head back into the building. Occasionally, as a
student we were allowed to ring that bell - what a thrill to pull on that rope
calling everyone back inside.

The Christmas programs were always big productions with lots of practices. We
always felt so important to be on the stage performing - especially in the new
gym when the heavy burgundy colored curtains were pulled back to reveal us. I
remember one year I was the narrator for the program and everything had to be
memorized - no reading. I believe along with everything else I had to memorize
for that program that I had to learn the majority of Luke, chapter two.

Speaking of stage memories - the first memory I have of being on stage was
performing "I'm a Little Teapot, short and stout, here is my handle, here is my
spout..." Hopefully we were in a very early grade when we did that.

I remember that "new technology" we as a class ordered when we were in Mrs.
Kline's seventh and eighth grade classroom. It was an outline map of the United
States on which we could use a special wax crayon - write in the state names and
capitals. Then it could be wiped off and used by the next student to practice
their U.S. geography.

When tests were distributed who would not take a big whiff of the intoxicating
smell of the dittos? Somehow or other the mimeographed test did not smell quite
the same.

Pride in our school and all school property was instilled in us at a very early
age. Mr. Eddy Sackman kept our school clean and forbid the child who would have
written anything on a bathroom wall or made black shoe marks on the gym floor.
Don't forget the wooden box rack with individual slots to put your snow boots in
when you got to school in the morning so you did not track snow throughout the
building.

Mercer School may have been small, with few students and faculty. We may not
have had a band, orchestra, foreign language department, football team or many
other things. What we had were knowledgeable teachers, interested parents and
community members and it was Mercer school that helped prepare me for life.
Through the basic courses I took at MHS I gathered the knowledge I needed to
enable me to further my education at Lutheran Bible Institute and Minot State.
Even now looking back, I have always felt that Mercer School offered me what I
needed during my grade school and high school years and I am thankful for the
opportunity to attend MHS.

By Darlene Jorgenson Schilling Class of 1963

These are just a few memories!

The first thing that comes to my mind - meeting Elaine Hinsz, my friend at the
post office and walking to school every day. We both attended all twelve years
at Mercer school.

Getting to school and Eddie Sackman, our janitor, meeting us at the door to see
how clean our shoes or boots were. He took great pride in keeping the floors
clean and shiny.

Bertha Schlaht, my fourth-sixth grade teacher left a big impression on me. She
was real strict on our penmanship, I also enjoyed her art classes.

Eating in our first kitchen by the old boiler room, then moving to the east side
where Lizzie Beierle was cook and I helped in the kitchen over noon hour.

The new gym - I think I was about a third grader, being able to go there for all
our activities and going through the tunnel as we all called it.

How hard our classes worked to get the most parents there to the PTA meetings.
Who ever had the most there, their classes got new books for the library.

At recess time in the winter - our sled rides down the big hill by Our Savior's
Lutheran Church. Then hating to see Grandma's face after school as another
button was missing from my coat.

The new addition of our kitchen and science rooms in 1961. What pride we all
felt. I worked in the kitchen for an hour and a half in my junior and senior
years with Ida Rust and Helen Russ.

Mr. Kessler's typing class and those one minute speed tests. I'm glad I was able
to take this course, as I've used my skills a lot in typing.

We had wonderful teachers in our elementary and high school classes who were so
willing to work with us and give us help if we only asked. They worked hard with
us or any project we were involved in.

Mrs. Wolitarsky, our music teacher, had a terrific music program where almost
everyone was involved. We attended many concerts and festivals and brought back
good ratings for our school and community.

Representing our school with good sportsmanship as a cheerleader for four years.

Having our annual carnival - decorating, finding prizes, etc. My favorite was
the cakewalk. I was pretty lucky most of the time and came home with a cake.

Being chosen carnival queen of 1963. An honor I never expected to receive, then
being called Queenie by Floyd Sprout and Emanuel Hinsz.

Mercer High was special as we were able to have a junior and senior class play.
No prom, but our Senior class trip to the Black Hills, seeing Mt. Rushmore and
my first trip to South Dakota.

The students were all pretty close just like a family; it didn't make a big
difference if you were a freshman or a senior. Everyone talked to you.

The school paper the "Cricket" was fun to work on. It included news from the
elementary as well as the high school.

Last but not least, whenever there was an activity going on at the school and I
needed to help serve or bring something, we knew I'd be asked for some of
Grandma Jorgenson's famous doughnuts, long johns or bismarcks.
