These are just a few of my memories. I could write a book.

Oh yes, the storms and then the country kids that got to stay with us. My first
school bus ride to the country - stayed with Bonnie Schell.

By Jerald Daffe Class of 1965

Having just moved from out of state and knowing no one, a timid, scared fourth
grader entered the school system. A warm smiling teacher, Mrs. Schlaht, and a
friendly classroom of fourth, fifth and sixth graders made this the beginning of
nine wonderful years of education. Which by the way, I still treasure and see as
the foundation for later academic success.

Grade school memories include costume parties, Christmas plays and the last day
of school at Brush Lake. Those not being so adept on roller skates spent time in
squirt gun wars at the edge of the lake. Fortunately in later years a few
compassionate girls helped me get the hang of those "rolling shoes." Oh and as
it relates to Christmas plays, there was one where some of us wore crepe paper
skirts as part of being stars in heaven. Now that was an experience!

Wintertime brought special activities. When the road became snow and ice packed,
recess and noon hours were a time for sled riding down the little hill past the
Lutheran Church. A great run included going beyond the road. Some kids even
brought their sleds on the buses and left them tied at the school.

Not to be overlooked is the year we would swing as high as possible and then
"bail out" into the snowdrifts. At times we referred to it as parachuting. What
great fun except for those occasions when part of your anatomy hit more frozen
dirt than fluffy snow.

One other memory, with Mrs. Kline's help, I finally learned how to distinguish
the eight parts of speech and to diagram sentences. What a relief.

The memories of high school could easily take pages. So, I'll continue it to a
few special thoughts. Basketball and more basketball - the thrill of victory,
but the freshman and sophomore years had more agony of defeat. But that changed.
Thank goodness. Remember how nervous we were when all Class C schools became B,
and it was time to play those "big schools."

Then there were those many class plays. Week after week we spent two and three
hours practicing at least four nights a week. I really liked "Chintz Cottage."
It was so much fun except for the part when you are supposed to be unconscious
and carried by two girls who accidentally drop you on your eight cracked ribs.
(Notice I give no names.)

Other memories include preparing for weeks and then attending music and speech
contests in Bismarck. We were pushed to excel in whatever we did. Being from a
small town and small school was never allowed as an excuse for not doing our
very best. Thank you - Mr. Kessler, Mr. Grosz, Mr. Lowe, Mrs. Wolitarsky and
Mrs. Nielsen. Many times your words of encouragement came to mind while pushing
through heavy loads to receive advanced degrees.

No reflection on the past would be complete without a few more statements. My
dad drove a school bus route and took us to away ball games. No matter where we
were, if I was at the free throw line, Dad would shout loud enough for everyone
to hear, "Sink it, son."  When he had a stroke, the school and community held a
special benefit, which was a tremendous help to our family.

Another special memory is the closeness of the Class of 1965. All eight of us
worked together on school activities and "got along" with each other.

My final memory is the acceptance and encouragement to follow your spiritual
choices and beliefs. As a conservative Christian, no one ever suggested I was
odd or different. What a blessing to live your faith and lifestyle and be seen
as normal among your peers!

By Doris (Fischer) Wall 1968 graduate

The first thing I remember about coming to Mercer Grade School in 1960 was the
school bus coming into our yard. When we lived in Turtle Lake we always walked
to school. Now we're picked up along with other neighbors and taken to school
and back home. This was great until I realized we had to get up earlier to get
on the bus and also got home a lot later as we had to wait until it was our turn
to be dropped off.

Another thing I remember was that there were two grades to a room and one
teacher taught both grades. I remember thinking that was not how school was
done, but it turned out to be a good experience. It was great having a twin
sister, Darlene (Fischer) Lasher, as the teachers would get us confused -
especially in grade school years when we would occasionally switch seats to test
the teachers.

Upon reaching the eighth grade, several of the girls in my class were picked to
sing in the high school girls choir - I was really excited to do that as I did
enjoy singing and then came eighth grade graduation, our big chance to move
downstairs to high school!

High school had lots of memories: freshman initiation!! Dressed up in odd
clothes and tests to do in front of the high school assembly was embarrassing
but also fun. As sophomores we got to "initiate" the incoming freshman so that
seemed to ease the embarrassment of the previous year. Going to music
competitions was a great experience and we went every year. Of course the
carnivals were always fun to set up and be part of. Classmate Merlyn Skaley and
I ran the "ring toss" several years. Tumbling for audience entertainment during
half time at the ball games was quite a thrill as well as unnerving for fear of
making a mistake. The memory of being stranded in Mercer after a ballgame
during the Great Blizzard of 1966 was quite an experience as my father Emil,
brother Melvin (Class of 1967) and I ended up staying at Dan's Bar for several
days. When the storm let up, our neighbors Alvin Wall and his son Wade (Class of
1968 and my future husband) made it to town and took us home.

During our senior year, KBMR radio selected our school to be "On The Air." Gust
Stute, Jr. and I were selected to participate and we got the top twenty songs
from our high school to be played during our afternoon at the radio station.
Well, the high school students picked rock n'roll songs and were going to a
country music station! When we gave them the list of songs, we were told that
they had none of them so we had to scramble to pick out songs we thought our
schoolmates would like to hear. We read the news and weather as well as talked
about our school and the activities at Mercer High School.

Class plays were always fun and with so few students, many of us played parts in
both junior and senior class plays. And who can forget the memorable "Senior
Trip" to the Black Hills! We cooked most of our meals and had fun working
together. Being at Terry Peak, riding the ski lift, touring the Wonderland Cave
and seeing Mount Rushmore are several memories that stand out for me.

By Larry Gessele Class of 1969

My first memory of Mercer School was getting out of the station wagon that
served as our school bus, entering the school and seeing Eddie Sackman, at the
end of the hall, directing the new country school kids to their correct rooms.
Mine was the third and fourth grade room, which was packed with over thirty
kids. Quite a shock coming from a country school of nine kids and a class of
two.

I soon learned that the laws of the jungle applied to the playground and I
looked up at the superintendent's office with great fear and trepidation as some
fifth and sixth graders informed me that third grade boys "that misbehaved" were
taken to that office, never to emerge again.

One boy that all of the rest of the third grade boys looked on with envy and
wonder was Gerhart Just, as he could blow bubbles through his nose. In our eyes,
that talent put him at the top of the social order.

Another memory that sticks with me was the day President Kennedy was shot. I was
in the eighth grade and we were in the gym watching a class play. Word was
passed from student to student. When we got back to our room, Mrs. Hausauer
still couldn't tell us for sure what happened. We didn't find out President
Kennedy had died until we got home.

High school was great with the basketball games, the carnival, class plays and
all the hi-jinx that go along with it. Wade Wall, Bob Wardner, Gust Stute Jr.,
and I did have great fun putting on the Alvin Chipmunks skits.

One had to be ever vigilant at basketball practice especially when we were
practicing free throws, as your trunks would often end up at your ankles. Merlyn
Skaley was especially adept at this, as many of us found out.

Our class got very good at setting tacks. Our favorite target was Donnie Wall as
once the tack hit home, he would jump about six feet in the air and take off
down the aisle.

One masterful incident does come to mind as it took planning, teamwork and
daring. Bob Wardner, Wade Wall, Merlyn Skaley and I came up with a plan to take
a shoe lace and tie it from Donnie's belt loop to the back of his desk chair
without his knowledge and then set a tack. I had to keep Donnie's attention,
which was easy as we talked about what all teenage boys love to talk about -
girls! Bob had to keep Mr. Schindler busy as he was the study hall monitor and
that left Merlyn and Wade Wall to do the dirty work. Everything went according
to plan and boy - when that tack hit home, it was great! Donnie jumped about six
feet and took off down the aisle dragging his desk behind him, knocking books
and papers everywhere! Even Mr. Schindler had to hide his laughter behind his
newspaper. It was perhaps, our finest hour!

One final memory that about sums up my feeling about the experiences at Mercer
school occurred as our senior class was pulling out of Rapid City and heading
home after our senior trip. The song "It's a Beautiful Morning" by the Rascals
was blaring on the car radio and that really summed up our mood on that day and
as I think back on that stage of life (after life's experiences wear you down a
bit) and the experiences in Mercer School, "Yeah, it was a 'beautiful morning'."

By Sheryl Gessele Gabriel Class of 1969

I attended all twelve years at Mercer with many great memories including the
teachers, but especially my classmates and the many friends I made.

In grade school, I remember how excited we were when the rural kids joined us.

When we got to high school, everyone was in one big room. As freshmen, you
couldn't wait to move across the room to the senior side. Even though there were
four grades in that one room, it felt like one big class.

My fondest memories of Mercer were all the social activities - the plays, music
festivals, basketball games and, of course, the senior class trip!

Both of my kids hated school and I always told them too bad you didn't go to
Mercer, you'd have loved it.

By Willa Murray Class of 1969

My twelve years in the Mercer Public School system started with Mrs. Tewksbury,
grades one and two teacher, and the Dick and Jane series for beginning reader.
My memories of Mrs. Tewksbury are that she greeted us with a smile and never
raised her voice or scolded us. Oh, how I disliked the trips to the girls'
bathroom! Those steps to the restroom were so steep for a first grader.

Third grade was the grade every second grader looked forward to because of Mrs.
Jacobson's rhythm band. What music the third and fourth graders could make with
the wooden blocks, sticks and triangles!

Fourth grade started with Miss Zwicker, but sometime during either Thanksgiving
or Christmas she became Mrs. Helm. She too, like Mrs. Tewksbury, almost always
wore a smile, but now some of us had learned the bad habit of slightly
aggravating the teacher so she did lecture on occasion.

Mrs. Schindler was both my fifth and sixth grade teacher with fifth grade being
the year of the Greek and Roman god's studies. I know now why I had to learn
them. They come in really handy when I'm filling in a crossword puzzle. A
Mother's Day gift from her students were very important to her and each year she
helped us do a craft to present to our mothers on their special day.

Seventh and eighth teacher was Mrs. Hausauer who had the task of teaching us
about North Dakota through Our State Book. I think she was the one that got me
addicted to crossword puzzles since we had to do the one in the Weekly Reader
and if there were any proper nouns you had better use a capital letter for the
first space or she would mark it wrong!

On to high school and too many teachers to list except one. Mrs. Wolitarsky, our
English and music teacher. You really learned your notes and timing under her
and what a beautiful voice she had. Preparing for the school carnival was always
a highlight for every high school student and the surrounding communities.
Rehearsals for the junior and seniors class plays were also a fun time and
filled up our evening for several weeks before and after basketball season. The
whole community waited for the basketball season. Young and old came out to
support the team with the most enthusiastic fan being Mrs. Lowe, the coach's
wife.

Two May events the seniors looked forward to were the senior trip to the Black
Hills of South Dakota and graduation. Thirteen seniors and six chaperones spent
several days touring Wind Cave, the Reptile Gardens and Mount Rushmore the
beginning of May followed by our last time together as Mercer students - our May
1969 graduation ceremony.

By JoAnn Gessele Shaw Class of 1970

I remember the excitement when we received new students in our class - I don't
remember if it was in Mrs. Tewksbury's first or second grade class. The country
schools closed and students came in to "town schools."

Mrs. Tewksbury had a baby during the school year when we were in first or second
grade. I was totally shocked when my mom told me Mrs. Tewksbury had a baby - we
did not even notice she was pregnant! People just didn't talk about those things
back then.

When we were in the third - fourth grade classroom, we were all convinced that
Miss Zwicker's boyfriend, Don, was the Don who was a teacher downstairs in the
high school. Miss Zwicker had to put the rumors to rest - I think, we even got
to meet the real Don, Donald Helm. I also remember Miss Zwicker going around the
cafeteria and collecting our potato skins because she loved them.

We built wonderful snow forts back behind the school by the steps on the
northeast corner. Bob Wardner was usually the foreman of the project as he
seemed to have a talent for constructing them. Bob was a big friendly teddy bear
and we always had fun with him.

Remember how you began your freshman year on the west side of the home room in
high school and moved across the room until you were on the east end your senior
year? I believe that hierarchy was developed so that as a senior privilege, you
could watch the horsing around going on up in the "cloak room," and the teacher
couldn't see it! My sister, Sheryl, was usually in on the horsing around.

By Joel Christensen Class of 1970

OK, like any school assignment, I've procrastinated until the last minute.
Hopefully you'll get this Monday the second. There may not be any "usable"
material here but I'll give it a shot.

For starters, I remember taking a typing class and helping with the school
newsletter (what did we call that?). There was a high ratio of girls to boys as
I recall.

I came to Mercer as a second grader in 1958 when Medicine Hill township school
closed. I had been a class of one, so thirteen (I think) seemed huge. I was kind
of proud that someone brought the Medicine Hill merry-go-round to Mercer. It's
still there I believe.

It was traumatic for my class calling Beverly Helm "Mrs. Helm" in the fourth
grade after getting so used to "Miss Zwicker" in the third.

It was fun peppering kids with snowballs when they exited the front door, but if
a snowball ever went inside through the door, there was trouble.

Gordon Westerlind showed me how to drive down the hill behind the science room
without hitting any trees. I thought that was so cool.

Didn't Merlyn Skaley take one English class from Mrs. Wolitarsky and three by
correspondence his senior year? He also was marking the remaining school days on
the wall behind the desk.

When I was a freshman, one of the junior girls (Darlene or Doris Fischer maybe?)
duped me into signing a phony petition of some kind. I think it was a class
experiment to see if a freshman boy could think clearly while talking to a
junior girl. I believe they got 100 percent of us to sign!

Harlan Wentz taught physics class of three, Steve Wagner, Kevin Vossler and me.
I don't think Harlan was "qualified" to teach physics but he studied twice as
hard as his students and I found out in college that we'd covered as much as any
other high school physics class.

How many technical fouls did Wes Kessler get while coaching grade school
basketball? He was really intense! However, we did win the county championship
for him and Don Grosz.

Somewhere in grade school a teacher took a nationality poll. I remember thinking
"I'm sitting here with almost all Germans!" No wonder everyone, including later
teacher Tim Schindler, told Norwegian jokes!

Thank you for the work you're doing. It was kind of fun just remembering the
school days so I can imagine how much fun the centennial will be.

Organizations - then and now

The Helping Hands Society of Mercer, 1910-1912 Compiled from the minutes by
Diana Jans

Members were: Mmes. Charles McLaughlin, Nels Hedahl, Sam Anderson, Charles
Williams, John Fisher, Fred Freeberg, Theodore Knutson, Edwin Hedahl, J.H.
Davidson, James Rice, James Murphy, Martin Wassenberg, George Heinze, Will
Murphy, J.H. Nuenberg, J.R. Washburn, Nels Fibelstad, Vern Anson, Krogh Ovre,
J.F. Pettigrew, John Rogge, William Ladwig, Campbell Howell and Misses Alma
Anedahl and Marie McFadden.

A meeting was held at Mrs. Sam Anderson's for the purpose of organizing a
society. The following were elected: President, Mrs. J.H. Davidson; Vice
President, Mrs. Charles McLaughlin; Secretary-Treasurer, Mrs. James Rice.

The following motions were made and carried:

  The society to be called "The Helping Hands Society"
  The object was to raise money for the general good
  The Society to meet every two weeks on Wednesday
  The term of office to be for six months
  That lunch at each meeting be limited to four items including coffee
  That a fine of $2 be assessed to the party serving more than four items
  That the Society does plain serving for others

January 18, 1911 - Meeting at Mrs. John Fisher was spent tying two quilts for
the Farmers Store.

February 2, 1911 - Meeting at Mrs. Freeberg's was spent tying a quilt for Mrs.
Sam Anderson.

February 14, 1911 - A Valentine social was held at the Belmont

March 1, 1911 - Was at Mrs. Nels Hedahl's. The afternoon was spent doing fancy
work.

March 15, 1911 - Was at Mrs. Knutson's. The afternoon was spent sewing aprons.

April 12, 1911 - Since the Society was organized in December, twenty-three
members have joined. Money taken in from the Valentine Social and dues from
each meeting is $35.50.

April 26, 1911 - The Society met at Mrs. Vern Anson's. Each member worked on
individual fancy work. Thirty-two were present.

July 12, 1911 - The Society decided something should be done about the Mercer
Sunday School. It was decided it will be held at 3:00. Being the School was
under repair, it was held in the storeroom of the Farmers Store for two Sundays
until the school was ready for use.

August 5, 1911 - The Society gave a lawn social at 7:30, serving ice cream and
cake. It was served at Mrs. McLaughlin's home.

In October a Halloween party took place at the Belmont.

November 15, 1911 - The afternoon was spent quilting a quilt for Mrs. Murphy.

February 7, 1912 - The time was spent doing fancy work. A guessing contest was
brought in by the hostess, the winner getting the biggest piece of cake.

February 13, 1912 - A chicken pie social was done following the meeting.

March 13, 1912 - Fancy work was done at Mrs. Freeberg's.

May 22, 1912 - $2.00 was donated to have Rev. Brendly of Turtle Lake visit.

June 12, 1912 - The Society donated $10.00 toward lumber to build benches at
Brush Lake.

July 12, 1912 - The afternoon was spent at Brush Lake supervising the erection
of the benches donated by the Society.

July 31, 1912 - It was too warm to be inside so the Society decided to have a
picnic at Brush Lake.

August 21, 1912 - The afternoon was spent with a number of guessing games.

October 23, 1912 - The Society held a meeting to decide whether some changes
should be made or disband.

November 1, 1912 - The Society decided to disband and divide the money equally
in the two banks to draw interest until such time as a church should be built.
$182.95 was in the treasury to be used for a church.

Homemakers Clubs Information compiled from scrapbooks

The Dakota Homemaker's Club Creed

"I believe my home is sacred; a place where love, faith, hope and devotion have
their beginning; where each has his rights respected by others; where joys and
blessings, sorrows and disappointments are shared in common; where God is
revered and honored, fellow men respected and love is law.

"I believe it is my duty to live up to the best that is in me to attain this, to
fear things unworthy, to conquer difficulties by daring to attempt them, to be a
companion as well as counselor to my family, and to teach and live; love of
home, country, fellow men and God."

Hustling Homemakers

Throughout the history of Mercer, there have been three homemaker's clubs. The
first to be organized was the Mercer Hustling Homemakers. It was organized on
June 16, 1934 at the home of Mrs. Marie (Theo.) Sackmann. It became affiliated
with the McLean County Extension two years later.

Charter officers were Marie Sackmann, President; Mrs. Harold Johnson, Vice
president; Dagny Fibelstad, Secretary; and Bertha Schlaht and Christine Braun,
project leaders. Other charter members were Frieda Schlaht, Katie Miller, Louise
Just, Tillie Heim and Nettie Just. During the years others who joined were
Hattie Pederson, Lydia Gaub, Hazel Stuart, Ida Schell, Joy Kline, Esther Miller,
Martha Gaub, Esther Peterson, Helen Eckman, Verna Just, Olga Sackman, Emma
Hinsz, Regina Schell, Anna Diede, Bertha Ketterling, Dora Jorgenson, Tillie
Calheim and Lydia White.

The club motto was "Home Comfort," the wild rose was chosen for the flower, and
green and white were the club colors. Meeting time was the second Thursday of
each month at 2 p.m. The first major project was sheets and bedding.

The club noted its 40th anniversary on June 30, 1974, and at that time two
charter members, Katie Miller and Dagny Fibelstad were still active. One of the
club projects that is still in existence is a club quilt which was donated to
the McLean County Historical Museum in Washburn.

The club disbanded in 1984.

Brush Lake Homemakers

The Brush Lake Homemakers Club was organized on November 10, 1948, at the home
of Mrs. Jens Glad. Several members of the Mercer Hustling Homemakers Club
assisted in the organization. There were nine members and the first officers
elected were Mrs. Jens Glad, President; Mrs. Art Levi, Vice President, Mrs.
M.H. Skaley, Secretary, Mrs. David Fink, Jr. Treasurer and Mrs. Melvin Dalos,
Program Chairman.

Additional members throughout the years were Mrs. Albert Bonnet, Mrs. Reinhold
Fueller, Mrs. Fred Haux, Mrs. Alvin Lick, Mrs. Ernest Littke, Mrs. Clarence
Neff, Mrs. Leonard Schmidt, Mrs. Floyd Sprout, Mrs. Gideon Ketterling and Mrs.
Meinhardt Kleingartner. Meetings were held in homes, the Brush Lake school
house and the Sprout school house.

The motto was "Don't Dodge Difficulties," the club colors were rose and white,
and the flower was the prairie rose.

Some of the projects and activities throughout the years were: garden project at
the Albert Bonnet farm; Riverdale tour of the dam; picnics at Brush Lake;
Christmas family parties and the spring fashion style show.

Roll call for the meetings included: a picture of your choice of electric stove
or refrigerator and why; favorite Christmas recipes; exchange of flower seeds;
name a redecorating hint; how did you meet your husband; lunch box suggestion.

At each meeting there was a promptness prize and also a fine of 10 cents if
there wasn't a roll call item. Each member was required to do a "birthday
stunt" during the month of her birthday.

The club was disbanded in the 1950s.

Round the Clock Homemakers Club

The Round the Clock Homemakers Club was organized in Mercer on November 18,
1974, with help from the Hustling Homemakers Club.

Charter members and the officers were President, Joan Presser, VP Faye Neff,
Secretary Diana Jans, Treasurer Marlene Wardner, Program Chair, Betty Schatz and
Special Projects, Eileen Schell.

The colors chosen were pink and lavender, the flower the petunia, and the motto
"Love and care of our home and family."  The monthly meeting time was the second
Thursday of the month at 7:30. The majority of the meetings were held in
members' homes or in the parlors of Our Savior's Lutheran Church. Yearly dues
were $1.50 plus a lunch donation each month for the hostess prize.

Throughout the years, other members were Willa Murray, Barbara Murray, Judy
Westerlind, Lila Stradinger, Leatrice Schilling, Gertrude Laib, Millie
Gustafson, Sharon Boschee, Ida Dugan, Eunice Vossler, Eleanor Gessele, Lorraine
Schon and Dina Schumann.

Projects for the club included: Sheridan Memorial Home bingo gifts; baby quilts
for newborns of members; family picnics; Christmas dinners; Valentine teas;
mattress covers and a thirty-cup coffee pot for the 4H camp in Washburn; lunch
at auction sales; McLean County fairs; May and Easter baskets for area shut ins;
lap robes for the VA hospital in Fargo; floats for Mercer 75th anniversary;
floats for the Washburn Centennial and a float for the parade for Mercer's
celebration of the state's centennial in 1989.

Special club trips included the Dakota Zoo, International Peace Garden, Medora,
and the Pioneer Village in Rugby.

The club disbanded in the early 1990s.

Mercer Women's Study Club
Compiled from minutes and scrapbooks

The Mercer Women's Study Club was organized on November 4, 1912, at the home of
Mrs. F.O. Freeberg. The club was organized to promote friendship, to get in
touch with each other, to shed house wife cares for an afternoon of study, to
get inspiration that comes from contact of mind with mind, and to help better
the community in any way possible. It was federated on October 15, 1913.

Charter members were Mrs. F.O. Freeberg, Mrs. W.F. Ladwig, Mrs. George McFadden,
Mrs. E.N. Hedahl, Mrs. Herb Wiest, Mrs. James Rice, Mrs. J.H. Davidson, Mrs.
O.S. Hjelle, Miss Mae Washburn and Miss Lillian Carlson. Mrs. Rice was elected
president but was replaced at the second meeting by Miss Washburn.   Miss
Carlson was elected secretary. Alternate Saturdays were chosen for meeting time
and the year's program was devoted to the study of US history. The motto chosen
was "Row not Drift." Foliage green and white were chosen as colors and the sweet
pea as the flower.

During the first years, records were not consistently kept, however
contributions were made to the Dunseith Hospital (San Haven) and a box of
clothing was sent to the Florence Crittenton Home in Fargo.

Throughout the years, the monthly meetings included a current affairs test from
Time magazine. Other involvements were with the polio fund, the Foundation for
the Blind, The March of Dimes, the Red Cross, cancer drives, mental health, the
International Music Camp in the Peace Garden and a book mobile. The North
Dakota Federation of Women's Clubs donated the portrait busts of major North
Dakota Indian tribes which can be seen in the North Dakota State Historical
Society of Bismarck. The Mercer club hosted state and regional conventions
through the years.

In 1962, the Mercer Club celebrated its golden anniversary. During the fifty
years, 137 ladies had been members and twenty-one of them had died. Members in
1962 were:  Mrs. Dora Jorgenson, President; Mrs. Emma White, Vice President;
Mrs. Florence Tewksbury, Secretary-Treasurer and Mrs. Sidney Nielsen, Chaplain.
Others were Mrs. Gena Lockrem, Mrs. Pearl Kline, Mrs. Oliver Dewald, Mrs. Joy
Kline, Mrs. F.O. Freeberg (the only charter member) and Mrs. Leila Faul.

Some special achievements of the club as recorded in the 50th anniversary
booklet were:

  1913-1914 - founded the school library
  May 1916 - Club sponsored the Baby Day celebration and collaborated with Dr.
             Deming and the hospital staff with a baby parade (See page 48)
  1916-1917 - organized the cemetery association and secured a fence for the
              grounds
  1919-1920 - adopted war orphans
  1920-1921 - served hot lunches for the school children
  1922-1923 - purchased trays and dishes for community use
  1923-1924 - purchased school ground equipment
  1926-1927 - purchased a school belfry and bell
  1932-1933 - conducted an immunization campaign
  1941-1942 - each member pledged to buy at least one war bond (amount sold
              $3,300)
  1943-1944 - filled kits for overseas servicemen
  During World War II - sponsored the servicemen's page and directory published
                        in the McLean County Journal (See page 182)

It is not known when the Club disbanded.

Boy Scouts

In 1940-41, there were twelve boys preparing to be Boy Scouts. They were
sponsored by the Mercer Men's Civic Club with Roy Nielsen, Joe Dakovna, Jake
Braun and B.C. Hjelle on the troop committee. Woodrow Skow was the Assistant
Scout Master and D.E. Pettys was the Scout Master.

The boys were divided into two troops with Leverne Sackmann and LeRoy Skow as
patrol leaders. Other members of the short lived troop were Meinhardt (Red)
Braun, Albert Wagner, Marvin Livingstein, Carl Fink, Harold Stradinger, Lloyd
Westerlind, Vilas Just, Otto Wagner and Myron Sackmann. The members passed the
tenderfoot test and became national members when they received their pins
during a public ceremony. The troop disbanded after the graduation of most of
the members.

During the following years, there were troops for year or so but there wasn't a
continuous scouting program.

Brush Poppers

The Brush Popper is a club for persons who are interested in horse back riding.
It was organized and incorporated in the late 1940's after WWII. The founders
were Reinie Schock, John Rust, Ted Kurle, Bob O'Shea, Alvin Wall and Harold
Nordwall.

The club built an arena and race track south of Brush Lake on property owned by
the Mercer-Brush Lake Community Association. The arena had corrals, and a
"crow's nest".  Seating was "do-it-yourself" on the hill. They sponsored horse
races and rodeos and participated in parades. Sundays were family time with
horse back riding, games, visiting and eating.

One of the big early events was a 2 day trail ride thru the Badland in Theodore
Roosevelt National Park at Medora, ND. A group of about 75 people of all ages
and 45 horses took part in the trail ride in July, 1966.

The first day of travel (auto) ended in Medora where the members set up a
temporary tent camp site. The first experience that the riders had on the next
day (Saturday) was to cross the very muddy Little Missouri River on horse back.
Soon they reached the first plateau where a herd of about 100 buffalo greeted
them These were approached with much caution. On the second plateau, more
buffalo were waiting for them. There were also antelope. The scenery was
spectacular, quite different from the prairie at home. The camp evenings usually
started with a supper of steak and the trimmings and then singing of camp songs
with guitar music.

On Sunday after a camp breakfast and a short informal worship service, the
riders explored another part of the park. Then it was time to get ready for the
ride home and the horses got a well deserved ride in trailers. (Information
about the trail ride from Reinie and Clara Schock)

The arena was abandoned and the membership now includes people from a wider
range. There are fund raisers for various charities in addition to programs
established by the group.

        Photos: The Brush Poppers on a campout and trail ride. (Photos courtesy
        of Reiny Schock)

        Photo: The Brush Poppers Horse Club carries an American flag and a club
        banner as the final unit of the Mercer North Dakota Centennial Parade in
        May 1989.

Brush Poppers hold annual special ride

The Brush Poppers Horse Club held their annual ride on Sept. 12, 2004, with
forty-plus riders participating. An additional crowd of visitors and family and
friends joined the riders for the supper that followed the ride.

The annual event, the last ride of the season, is held for special needs adults
and children. This year's event started and ended at the Nick and Jillian Goven
ranch north of Turtle Lake, a self-described "camp" for the family and their
friends. The peaceful and rustic setting features barns and corrals, along with
other amenities for ranching adventures.

Cooks for this year's ride, grilling hotdogs and hamburgers, were Wes Neumiller
of Wilton and Shawn Schafer of Turtle Lake. The additional food items are
potluck, contributed by both riders and non-riders.

Mercer Car Show By Mozel Murray and Mary Ann Anderson

During the summer of 1997 an idea to have a car show in Mercer was born. The
idea originated when Billy Klemetson, Rich Goetzfried both of Brush
Lake/Bismarck and Jim Murray of Mercer began discussing it. The ideas discussed
that evening led up to Mercer's "First Ever Car Show" and the rest is history.

The initial car show committee consisted of Mr.& Mrs. Billy Klemetson, Mr. &
Mrs. Richard Goetzfied, Mr. & Mrs. Jim Murray and Mr. & Mrs. Mike Anderson.

The group decided their goal was a show that provided an old fashioned good time
to be had not only by the public but especially for the car show participants.
With the date of September 13, 1997, set, all that was needed was a little luck
and a beautiful day.

The day arrived with perfect car show weather and approximately twenty-five cars
rolled onto Main Street Mercer. An annual event was born. In 2003, the "7th Ever
Motor to Mercer Car and Bike Show" boasted 110 classic car/motorcycle
participants. Activities include DJ "Digger Jay" Jason Meidinger providing
"50's-60's music throughout the day, engine blow-up, burnout, games and awards
to both participants and the public.

The community comes together at this annual event and has grown to include fund
raising booths by various organizations of Mercer. The public along with the car
participants enjoy the small town atmosphere, fun and food.

Likewise the car show committee has also grown to include: Mr. & Mrs. Darren
Murray of Mercer, Mr. Jason Meidinger of Mercer, Mr. & Mrs. Virgle Murray of
Bismarck and Mr. & Mrs. Ray Eichenberger, Bismarck. Many friends and relatives
help on show day.

Both young and old agree this event is a keeper. So get you classic car or bike
out and join the fun at the next "Motor to Mercer Car Show."

        Photos: The Mercer Car Show was held again in August of 2004. Pictured
        are some of the cars that were on display. (Photos courtesy of Mozel
        Murray)

Commercial Club/Booster Club By Diana Jans

Mercer may be small in population, but the people have big hearts who take pride
in community accomplishments, and everybody is a booster. This has been true
from the town's very beginning, as evidenced by the Commercial Club, as it was
then called, and its first big project of buying trees and establishing the
town's first park near the depot in 1908. The young community took pride in
itself as we read in the poem published in the September 24, 1909, edition of
the Mercer Telegram, lauding the commercial establishments of Main Street at the
time.

The Commercial Club's most sustained activity was in promoting good roads and
maintaining them. In the beginning, road maintenance was a township or village
responsibility. The Mercer Telegram relates in several articles through the
early years how John Ketterling organized crew members from the club ranks to
grade Main Street, other village streets and nearby township roads. The
Commercial Club was active in this as well as providing roadway signs far into
the 1920s.

        Photo: Assisting with table waiting during the Mercer Booster Club's
        25th annual pancake and sausage supper held in May of 1990 were (from
        left) Lulubelle Diede, Florence Brunner, Mozel Murray and Tina Schatz.

        Photo: Helping with frying pancakes were (from left) Dusty Fandrick and
        Ron Schatz.

Through a period of the 1930s, the club sponsored the town's first outdoor free
movies for promotional purposes and utilized the exterior wall of one
establishment as the viewing screen. This and other booster activities took a
back seat to the World War II years of the 1940s.

Although there is no record of a Commercial Club at mid-century, we can credit
community booster activity for three major achievements at that time: the return
of free drive-in movies for the public, the installation of a central water
distribution system and Main Street roadway improvements.

Best recollections place the resumption of free movies beginning in 1951.
Businessmen in town felt the need to keep their farm market share. During summer
months, full-length features were played outdoors every Wednesday evening at
sunset, attracting huge crowds.

Initially in 1956, five or more town residents had decided to install their own
central water system. But more and more residents expressed interest in hooking
up, so a special meeting was called. The residents banded together, each making
a $250 deposit towards installation of water mains. The city was divided into
three districts, and the mains were installed at a cost of $12,000, one third
the cost if the village had put in the system. When the project was completed it
was sold to the village for $1 to operate.

In 1960, Mercer black-topped Main Street from ND Highway 200 (formerly TH 7) and
Wing Street, westward to its intersection with County Road 33 (Brush Lake Road).

Business owner Walter Hoff saw a need for the formal return of a booster
organization, so on November 5, 1962, he called to order twenty businessmen and
their wives for the purpose of organizing a club to promote interest in the town
of Mercer. Mercer Booster Club was the name decided upon.

Walter Hoff was the first President, George Gardiner, Vice President, and Anna
Diede, Secretary-Treasurer. Members were: Wally and Opal Hoff; Ted and Alvira
Gessele; George and Verna Gardiner; Conrad and Evelyn Freeberg; Andrew and Ida
Rust; Howard and Vivian Brewster; Herbert and Martha Gaub; Jake and Anna Diede;
John and Laura Schlafman and Ted and Alice Neumiller.

The first project was Santa Day. Andrew Rust made a sleigh for Santa and Ed
Kurle brought in his team of horses to pull it. On Santa Day, a film for the
kids was held at the Community Center, now City Hall, and stores put up bags of
candy for all the kids.

In February 1963, the first pancake supper was planned to raise prize money for
the year's remaining holiday events. Several fund raisers were done to promote
business. Fish were tagged in Brush Lake, and a jackpot drawing was held every
Saturday night. Gift certificates were given in each store. Bingo was played at
Brush Lake on the 4th of July to fund the cost of fireworks.

The first donkey ball game was held at the school gym on December 6, 1963.
There was also a basketball game of businessmen vs. farmers. $110 net was
received from the game.

On October 10, 1964, the Mercer Booster Club set a first in the state, a
manufacturing day was created. More than twenty manufacturing firms in the
state displayed their products on Mercer's Main Street. Many of Andrew Rust's
inventions were on display. Andrew invented the bale buncher, cattle chutes,
head gates and post hole diggers. Highlight of the day was the release of many
colorful balloons from the roof of a building. Some of the balloons contained
gift certificates of money. The Republican candidates were on hand to speak as
well as a number of local candidates. A rock picker demonstration was held at
the Arnold Westerlind place. The Hazen and Towner cheese factories gave out
samples of their products. Mercer Booster Club served coffee throughout the day.

One enterprise that gave Mercer some stature and name recognition throughout the
Dakotas and Montana was Andrew Rust's business. It outgrew his old shop with new
inventions. On August 10, 1966, he built a new one, 40 × 100, on Highway 200. He
had added a hay stack mover to his inventions. George Gardiner was a big
encouragement to Andrew. He told him to plunge ahead. George handled the
business end and combination sales and distribution. He set up dealers
throughout the whole state and in South Dakota and Montana. Mr. Rust was a great
asset to Mercer. Even after his death, his wife Ida kept the business going for
several years. The building is now owned by Ray and Willa Murray. (See page 40)

The Booster Club even became involved in community development. It acquired
abandoned property and constructed a park on Lots 1-10, Block 5. A volleyball
court and horseshoe court were built. Several picnic tables were set up and the
Booster Club maintained it. Eventually all of the lots were sold. The Baptist
church bought two lots next to the church for a parking lot. Four lots were sold
to Alvin Wall with the stipulation a house had to be built on them within six
months or go back to the Booster Club. Remaining Lots 1-4 were eventually
acquired by Ronald Schatz and a house was built on them.

In June 1964, the Booster Club arranged hospitality parking in Mercer for a
wagon train traveling through the region. The wagon train gave free rides and
the Booster club reciprocated by providing free roller skating at Brush Lake for
the wagon train members.

The Booster Club donated money for cement crosses and name plates at the Mercer
Hillside Cemetery and donated money for paving the road into Brush Lake. The
club donated $25 each year for snow removal on Brush Lake to keep the fish alive
over the winter. The club bought material for one of the classrooms at the
school and erected a sign near the highway promoting the town.

An appreciation supper was held for the community and cabin owners on Labor Day
for bringing business to Mercer. Many raffles were held to raise money for the
club. Pull tab jars were started at Dusty's Bar with the profits going back to
the community.

The Booster Club represented Mercer in the North Dakota Centennial parade. On
May 25, 1989, Mercer had its first tractor pull sponsored by the Booster Club.
Bleachers were donated by the Brush Poppers Rodeo Club, a scale was donated by
the highway department, a tractor was donated by John Deere of Washburn and
insurance was provided by First Wilton Insurance. The day was enjoyed by all.
The Booster Club held a parade to coincide with the all-school reunion.

The club disbanded in January 2000 due to lack of businesses in Mercer. The
Community Center (the school gym) has assumed the duties of the Booster Club,
keeping up with Santa Day, Easter egg hunt and Thanksgiving drawing.
(Information is from the Club's minutes.)

Other business operating when the club was formed included Gardiner's U-Save,
Ted Neumiller's Meat Market, the bar owned by Wally Hoff (who started the club),
and Ted Gessle, Standard Oil agent.

        Photo: The Mercer Booster Club observed its 25th annual Pancake and
        Sausage Supper in May of 1990. Special recognition was given to people
        who were members of the club 25 years ago. They included (front, from
        left) Vivian Brewster, she and her husband, Howard, operated Brewster's
        Cafe on Main Street; Herb and Martha Gaub, operated Herb's Plumbing,

The Golden 50s Senior Citizens
Compiled from club minutes

For almost forty years, the Lord's Prayer and the Pledge of Allegiance have
opened the meetings for the Mercer Senior Citizens Club, known as the Golden
50s. In the beginning, the group met in the City Hall, however soon it was too
small, and in September of 1981, arrangements were made to purchase the vacant
Mercer school building from the Turtle Lake-Mercer School District. At that
time, Emil Schlaht was the President. Even though the club owned the entire
school complex, only the newer addition was utilized. The club sold many of the
school furnishings, blackboards, bulletin boards, desks, cupboards, etc., for a
minimal fee. The gym, built in the 1950s, was rented to various organizations
also for a nominal fee. A library of school books and donated books was
maintained in the science room which had been renamed the Pool Room. These were
available to members and the public.

The kitchen and dining room were also available for use and were utilized for
birthday parties, church celebrations, family reunions and other occasions. The
kitchen was equipped with stove, refrigerator and serving needs.

The funding for the activities of the club was/is provided by donations, a
county mill levy and pull-tab gaming. The members volunteered to be the
distribution center for commodity foods, and contributed financial aid to the
Meals on Wheels program and also took turns delivering the meals.

In September1987, the club received a federal grant of $12,000 from Title 3, the
Older American Act. The money was used to renovate and repair the building,
inside and out. This included repair of the roof, painting the various rooms,
repairing and replacing doors and windows, upgrading the bathrooms, carpeting,
tuck pointing, etc. Most of the projects were done by members with some jobs
hired out.

One of the projects was removing the school bell. A cement slab was poured on
the south side of the front entry to the school for the placement of the bell.

Some of the activities of the members included quilting bees, bingo, and bingo
games with the residents of the Turtle Lake swing bed, participating in the
Mercer 75th celebration and the North Dakota Centennial in 1989. A museum of
antiques and school memorabilia was established in several classrooms and was
available for tours. Throughout the years, the County Health Nurses have been
available for blood pressure check, flu and tetanus shots and for health
education programs.

The membership has been from twelve to twenty in any given year. The Golden 50s
is a member of the McLean County Council on Aging and has had many exchange
visits with the clubs in the county. It also has had an interest in the Silver
Hair Legislation. The month of May is Older Citizen's Month and it has been
celebrated with special meals with guests.

        Photo: Present Mercer Golden 50s Senior Citizens members are (front,
        from left) Carol Zinke, Joyce Demchuk, Martha Schlafman, Bertha Jans;
        (back) Vivian Brewster, Regina Schell, Dina Schumann, Eileen Schell. Not
        pictured: Martha Thompson, Emma Hinsz, Ervin Schell. (Photo by Bev
        Christensen)

        Photo: Club officers in October of 1981 were (from left) outgoing
        president, Emil Schlaht; incoming president, Bertha Schlaht; vice
        president, Regina Schell; and secretary-treasurer, Mollie Nielsen.
        (Photo from Washburn Leader)

In 2002, the club turned the building back to the City of Mercer and the club
now meets in the Mercer City Hall. At the present time, there are eleven active
members who continue to meet once or twice a month for business and fellowship.
The current members are Regina Schell, Vivian Brewster, Ervin and Eileen Schell,
Emma Hinsz, Martha Schlafman, Dina Schumann, Martha Thompson, Bertha Jans, Carol
Zinke and Joyce Demchuck.

Some of the early members were: *Alvin and Ruth Wall, *Ted and *Alvira Gessele,
*Elmer and *Esther Peterson, *Larry and Marie Haar, *Howard and Vivian Brewster,
*Herb and Martha Thompson, *Sidney and Mollie Nielsen, Ida Rust, *Lillian
Sackman, *Martha and *Emil Wagner, *Emmanuel Schlaht, *Emil and *Bertha Schlaht,

Mercer Sportsman Club By Marlene Wardner

Very early issues of the Telegram make several references to a sportsman
organization known as the Modern Woodmen.

The Mercer-Brush Lake Sportsman Club started in the 1950s. The purpose of the
organization was to aid others who associate in the coordination of sound
policies and programs in an effort to further, by education and implementation
of programs, the conservation of natural resources and outdoor recreation.

Dues were established at $1.50 per year and they would hold at least seven
meetings per year. The dues were due in January.

The club usually sponsored a Valentine dance every year. They raffled turkeys,
hams and candy to raise money to pay for one-half the cost of a band. Usually
whoever owned the bar paid for the other half.

The Sportsman Club would purchase pheasants and various members would raise the
birds. The Game and Fish Department would release them in the fall at various
locations in the area to increase population for hunters. Older members of the
club mentioned that pheasants survived the winter better when they had the
old-fashioned straw stack to hibernate in during the winter.

Some of the events the Sportsman Club promoted were the big goose contest,
longest pheasant tail feather, largest buck contest and coyote drives.

Over the years, they had various people give demonstrations on walleye fishing,
videos of elk hunting, predator calling, deer hunting and ice fishing.

In  1981, the Game and Fish Department checked the oxygen level in Brush Lake
and the surface was 10.8 and the bottom was 10.6, so the ice conditions were
very good for the winter survival for the fish. Other years, an aerator was
placed in the lake to supply extra oxygen. In September 1981, 5,000 walleye
were released at Brush Lake.

In 1981 the dues were raised to $5.00 and in 1984 it was voted that honorary
members were not to pay dues. Honorary members at the time were Al Kline, Bob
Warner, Howard Brewster, Albert Schell and Meinhardt Skaley.

In December 2003, The Mercer-Brush Lake Sportsman Club was officially disbanded.

        Photo: Several hunters show their "birds" after a successful hunt. (From
        left) Harry Kline, unknown, unknown, and Al Kline, stand in front of the
        cafe on Mercer's Main Street. (Photo courtesy of Evelyn Freeberg)

Mercer 4-H Clubs By Marlene Wardner

A visit to the McLean County Extension Office supplied worthwhile information
about the many 4-H Clubs in the four townships in the Mercer area. Records are
available from 1930 onward and the first one identified as a Mercer Club was in
1934. It was called the Busy Bees' 4 H Clothing Club and the leader was Mae
Washburn. Some of the members were Josephine Gardiner, Anna Marie Gardiner,
Alice Braun, Emma Lu Johnson, Lila Singer and Doris Pederson. A second 1934
club was the Beaver's Clothing 4-H Club, Mae Washburn was also the leader for
this one and some of the members were Edna Braun, Helen Westerlind, Beatrice
Kline and Viola Singer.

One of the clubs in 1937 in Park Township was the Willing Workers. John and

The Go-Getters 4-H Club south of Mercer was a traveling group. In 1937, they

The Lakeside 4-H Club was organized in October, 1949 as an Agricultural Club.
The first projects included raising swine and beef cattle along with grain and
garden produce. Clarence Neff and Meinhardt Skaley were the first leaders.
Warren Tewksbury was the McLean county Agent who helped with the organization of
the club. Members participated in local and county achievement days, county 4-H
camps and competed in the Valley City Winter Shows. The club cooperated with
the Brush Lake Pals to present programs for the PTA and in Rural Life Sundays in
their respective churches.

Charter members were Alvin Bonnet, Larry Fueller, Lois Skaley, Harley Bonnet,
Ervin Neff, Marlys Skaley, Ervin Stute, Harold Zinke and Reinhold Zinke. In
1954, they received an outstanding award for rat and mice control. At the
beginning, Lakeside was considered a boys' club and the girls club was called
the Mercer-ettes.

Local Government

Mercer City Government

There are no written records available for the Mercer government before 1946.
Yearly highlights of the minutes were recorded by the auditor.

1946: A village/township meeting was held on September 6, 1946. Those present
      were Christ Schell, Jr., Archie Kline, Emil Schlaht, Emanuel Hinsz and Ted
      Gessele.
1947: In January, the village's first set of ordinances received their first
      reading. All fifteen were numbered and signed. In March there was a
      village election. A vote was taken regarding building or buying a hall and
      for putting down a well. There were twenty-nine yes votes for the hall and
      three nays; there were twenty-six yes for the well and two nays.
1948: A Mr. Stee was called to discuss a well. There was $942.52 in the
      treasury.
1949: The road to the cemetery was built and graveled for $150.
1950: Mr. Stee was present and fifteen bids were received for the well project.
1951: A special meeting was called to discuss the need to close all well and
      cellar holes.
1952: The proposed dial telephone system was discussed.
1953: A new pump house was built.
1954: Council approved a resolution to blacktop the highway through town.
1955: The liquor ordinance was changed to allow opening from 8 a.m. to midnight.
1960: Council discussed joining the Turtle Lake Fire Department.
1961: Main Street parking was discussed. It was decided to paint stripes on both
      sides of Main Street and park cars parallel on both sides.
1962: The Rust Machine Shop constructed a street sweeper for the city. Five
      ballot boxes were constructed for $10.
1963: The Teen Canteen was allowed to use the town hall once a week or every
      Wednesday for $2.00. A drinking fountain was to be installed somewhere
      along Main Street.
1965: The council decided to investigate the installation of a sewer system with
      a government grant.
1966: The City applied for an FmHA loan for the sewer system.
1967: The City purchased land from Emanuel Hinsz for the sewer lagoon system.
      The Public Service Commission was asked to keep the Mercer railroad depot
      open. A discussion was held regarding reorganization of the village to a
      city form of government.
1968: ON FEBRUARY 18, 1968, MERCER LEGALLY BECAME A CITY.
1969: Mercer entered into a year's contract with Mclean County for policing the
      City. Payment was $50.
1976: Mercer became a host agency for a Green Thumb worker.
1978: The City purchased property from Evelyn Freeberg for a new well house. The
      building of a new post office was discussed and a letter was written to
      the US Postal Service.
1980: Members of the Booster Club were present to discuss plans for the 75th
      Anniversary Celebration. The Sportsman Club was granted permission to
      proceed with anniversary plans.
1981: The school building was leased to the Senior Citizens for twenty years.
      They were to furnish 75 percent of the heat and the City would assume the
      remaining 25 percent. The City would furnish water and sewer service.
1982: It was agreed to proceed with digging the new well at a cost of $6,368.
      Cost of the wire and pump house would be sought. The well would be on the
      Westerlind property. John and Lloyd Westerlind were to grant easements for
      fire hydrants and water main access on their property, but not for meters.
      Lots 12 and 15 were purchased from Emma Hinsz. The well was dug, the pump
      installed and the water tested with excellent results. Estimated total
      cost was $22,485.00. Not all bills were paid due to shortage of funds.
1984: Evelyn Freeberg offered to sell her Main Street building to be used as a
      place for people of all ages, possibly a café or place for senior citizens
      and youth activities. The Senior Citizens group turned over the gymnasium
      to the City. Medicine Hill, Park, Wise and Mercer Townships will work with
      the City to maintain use of the gym. It was decided to use the gym for
      exercise classes, showers, anniversaries, weddings, basketball, volley
      ball and other desired events.
1985: The City government passed a resolution suggesting the community appoint a
      five-member board, one from each district, and a seven-person advisory
      board for the Community Center. The five board members were to be included
      in the bylaws. The name chosen for the center was the Mercer Recreation
      Center.
1986: The City purchased the former Ted Gessele office and garage unit on the
      east side of Main Street. The Senior Citizens purchased the school from
      the City for $1.00. There were grants available for repair.
1987: The West River Telephone Company installed telephone lines underground.
      Plans were made for state centennial celebration activities to be held in
      the City and at Brush Lake.
1988: State centennial plans called for signs to be posted showing locations of
      former businesses. All electrical poles were to be painted red, white and
      blue. Plans were finalized for the celebration: band music, special
      speaker Bruce Hagen, boat show, pony rides, Washburn Little Wheelers,
      Shriners, commemorative button sales, kiddie parade, and a main parade.
1989: A City bulletin board was approved.
1990: The Recreation Center board reported their operational costs were well
      covered by donations and tournament fees.
1991: Recycling containers were set up. Council decided to budget for one new
      fire hydrant each year - at a cost of $800 each - until adequate
      protection was achieved.
1992: All homes and businesses were assigned house numbers.
1994: Farmers Union Insurance reported that use of liquor at a Recreation Center
      wedding dance would be covered but not its sale.
1995: An aerial view photo of the City was hung at City Hall.
1998: A new roadside sign was installed to assist travelers in finding Brush
      Lake and Butte.
2002: The Mercer Centennial project was discussed. It was announced there would
      be a history book and an all-school reunion. The dates chosen were July
      1-3, 2005. The Senior Citizen Club turned over the school building and new
      addition to the City by quit claim deed. A vote by members of the
      Recreation Center announced a name change for the center to Mercer
      Community Center.
2003: A City internet website was established to include information about the
      City Centennial and all City businesses. The City announced it would
      purchase railroad property west of Main Street. Liability with the
      remaining elevator put consideration of railroad property east of Main
      Street on hold.

City Park (Depot Park)

In June 1908, Nels Olesen made a gift to the people of Mercer by donating a
block of land north of the telegraph office (depot) on the east side of Main
Street for a city park. The Commercial Club placed an order for trees and
shrubs and the land was broken up and harrowed. The Women's Study Club
maintained the park. There were benches and picnic tables and many picnics and
social events took place in the park.

The trees are tall now and the park is half of the original size. It is owned
and maintained by the City.

        Photo: The present Mercer City Park.

Sheriff's Department.

Water, Sewer and Refuse

One of the earliest problems of Mercer residents was the water supply. If the
townsite had been located one and one-half miles farther east, there would never
have been a problem. There the railroad tapped into an aquifer at that site and
erected a water tower for its locomotives. (See page 22)

The Mercer residents had to provide their own source of water. Most homes had
private deep wells dug and rainwater was collected in cisterns. If the well's
supply was inadequate or there was not enough rain to keep the cisterns full,
water was hauled in from a spring on the homestead of Mae Washburn. This spring
was from the aquifer used by the railroad water tower. Drinking water was
delivered by J.R. Washburn and his son, Ira, in ten-gallon cans for one cent per
gallon. Delivery was by wagon or sled. Delivery was also available by a tanker
wagon. The shed and its odd-shaped cupola protecting the spring still exists and
is on land owned by Ervin Neff.

        Photo: Ira Washburn's well house (watershed), taken in 1988.

        Photo: Ira Washburn was the Mercer water supplier.

For refrigeration, ice was cut on Brush Lake, stored in a pit and packed in
sawdust. It was often delivered in a wheel barrel. This became obsolete with
the advent of gas or electric powered refrigerators and freezers.

Beginning in November 1909, the need for a town well was noted in the Telegram.
For the next six years public functions were held to provide for the town well
fund. Activity began in earnest in the summer of 1915. On July 31, 1915, a
cabaret luncheon was sponsored The Womens' Study Club, which pledged $25 for
the well. The luncheon was at the town hall and was followed with a dance.

On August 10, 1915, a town hall meeting was held to discuss the location of the
well and to appoint a committee to secure the well diggers. The selected
location was on the corner lot of the hospital (Lot 24, Block 7 of the original
townsite) and was to be located seventy five feet from the street. The well
digging began on August 30, 1915, and water was found at 160 feet. In July 1916
the tank and windmill were ordered and it is assumed that with them in place,
water was available for use. It is not known when the well was closed, however
the site of the well has been identified and is on the east side of the Mercer
Machine Shop. A picture presumably taken from an elevator shows the windmill in
place. (This picture can not be reproduced)

In 1950 another city well was dug and was located next to the city hall. Town
users could get water in cans. In 1956, town residents banded together, each
making a $250 deposit, and two to three-inch water mains were installed.
Connection was made to the city well and a pressure tank installed at city hall.
This water distribution system was turned over to the village in consideration
of $1 and the municipality took over its operation. Over time, this water
source was deemed to be unsafe because of elevated amounts of dissolved natural
gas. In one noted episode, Christ Heim sought needed water for his cattle and
had filled a large storage tank at the pump house at night. Striking a match to
check the water level in the tank, a minor explosion ensued and flames shot up,
singeing his eyebrows and hair. Eventually, another water supply was found and
this well was plugged in 2000.

In 1982, an adequate water supply for the city became available in the aquifer
located on the Washburn land east of town and now owned by Lloyd and John
Westerlind. Pipes were laid connecting the new source with the existing water
mains. After considerable discussion, the Mercer City Council opted to not
participate in the Rural Water project.

Up until 1966, sanitary sewer needs were met by private septic systems. In 1966,
a municipal sanitary sewer system became reality when mains and manholes were
installed and a lagoon was constructed on the east side of the town. It was
funded by a loan from FmHA and the system was paid off in July 2000.

Refuse collection began in 1974 and is still being done by various contractors.

        Photo: Mercer city pump house.

History of the Mercer Rural Fire Protection District and the Mercer Fire
Department By Byron Fiedler

All content was taken from notes and minutes from past records. Any person not
listed is not intentional. Thanks to those who served before us, saw a need and
acted on it.

Mission Statement:

We will promote life safety and reduce human suffering and property loss through
education and prevention and recognizing that every individual is valuable and
has great potential.

Since the beginning of time, fire has been a mixed blessing for mankind. Man has
learned to control and use fire as a tool to his benefit but has also learned
that fire out of control is detrimental to life, property and the environment.

In the early years of the growing community of Mercer, the people were well
aware of the benefits of controlled fire for cooking meals, blacksmithing,
heating homes and businesses, and clearing land for farming. They also were
aware of the dreaded cry of FIRE!!, the kind that was out of control, consuming
crops, livestock, homes, barns, businesses, and sometimes lives of those who
could not get out of the wildfire's path. A wildfire, no matter how it got
started, needed to be brought under control and put out, but how?

The town of Mercer and the surrounding community were like any other in their
developing years. Fire fighting involved tools like plows, shovels, hoes, cans
or maybe a tank of water, women's dresses or other clothing to beat out flames.
Horses, and later vehicles and tractors, aided in hauling water, tools, and
people, to help stop the fire's spread. Sometimes the best efforts were
fruitless and the wildfire would burn for days, consuming everything in its path
until it was controlled by mother nature or a combination of such and the
efforts of the people making use of fire breaks with plows, back fires, roads,
ponds and lakes, and green fields.

Fire trucks or fire fighting apparatus did not become widely used until the
thirties, forties, and fifties, with the town of Mercer depending on the towns
of Turtle Lake and McClusky for help when a fire call would come. Turtle Lake
provided the coverage for Mercer and the surrounding area until October of 1966
when both of Turtle Lake's fire trucks were lost in a fire that destroyed the
large building that they were housed in on Main Street.

Mercer was without fire protection, which concerned everyone, and soon the idea
of starting Mercer's own fire department was the talk of the community. The
project was set in motion when a community meeting was called and a committee
was formed that was to make the proper contacts for the formation of a new fire
district.

On or about the 5th of December 1966, petitions were filed in the office of the
McLean County Auditor requesting the formation of a rural fire protection
district to be known as the Mercer Rural Fire Protection District.

Otto Vetter, McLean County Auditor, and Robert R. Neuharth, Sheridan County
Auditor, determined and certified that the petitions and signatures on them met
all requirements of the law. The Auditor of McLean County then set the date of
March 9, 1967, at 2:00 o'clock P.M. at the Mercer Sportsmen Club to have a
hearing on the petitions before the County Commissioners of McLean and Sheridan
Counties. The purpose of this meeting was to give all persons residing and
owning taxable property within the proposed district a chance to air any
grievance they might have. Boundaries for the new district were declared: They
were all lands within the Mercer School District. An organization meeting date
was set by the McLean County Auditor, copies of the resolutions were filed with
the County Auditors of McLean and Sheridan Counties, votes were taken by the
Boards of Commissioners that the resolutions be adopted. All voted yes.
Resolutions for the formation of the Mercer Rural Fire Protection District were
adopted on May 2, 1967, and officially signed and sealed on May 3, 1967.

        Photo: Firemen on the fire truck are (from lef) James Schumann, Derek
        Fiedler and Byron Fiedler. (Photo by LaRose Ketterling)

The organization meeting of the Mercer Rural Fire Protection District was held
at Mercer on May 26, 1967, at 2:00 P.M. at the Sportsmen Club. Present were
twenty-one electors who were owners or had interest in the land that would be
assessed for taxation in the district. The meeting was called to order by
William F. Lindell, temporary chairman, and Albert Chesworth temporary
secretary.

The election of directors was held, and Ted Gessele was elected President and
Director for a term of two years, Lloyd Westerlind as Vice-President and
Director for a term of one year, Arley Vossler as Secretary-Treasurer and
Director for a term of two years. Minhardt Fiedler and Jens Glad were elected
Directors for a term of two years. Edwin E. Wagner, Albert Skaley, and Dennis
Fibelstad were elected Directors for a term of one year.

The first meeting of the newly organized Mercer Rural Fire Protection District
board of directors was held on May 31, 1967, at Ted Gessele's office on Main
Street, Mercer. The directors were very busy in the coming months of 1967, as
they worked on a loan with the First National Bank of McClusky for operating
expenses, fire truck equipment and housing for the equipment. The directors
advertised in the Fargo Forum, looking to purchase a used fire truck. They also
solicited quotes for a new fire truck and apparatus body from several
distributors.

The old Andrew Rust blacksmith shop was purchased for housing for a sum of
$2300.00, and became the new fire hall.

On January 19, 1968, bids were opened for a new fire truck. The only bid for a
fire body apparatus was submitted by Forestner Fire Equipment, Madelia,
Minnesota, for $7097.00 and it was accepted. The bids for the truck chassis were
from Froehlich's Ford $3395.00, Knudtson Implement $3248.00, and Albrecht
Chevrolet $2990.30. The bid from Albrecht Chevrolet was accepted with the
additions of a heavy duty radiator for $18.00 and heavy duty rear springs for
$14.88, bringing the total to $3023.18. Mercer was about to get its first ever,
new fire truck for a grand total of $10,120.18.

On July 27, 1968, the Mercer Rural Fire Protection District members met for a
special business meeting. The first item of business was for the first ever
budget for 1969. A motion was made by Edwin Wagner, seconded by Jens Glad to
submit a budget of $300.00 for operating expenses and $4000.00 for the payment
and interest for fire equipment for 1969. The motion was approved. Word was
received that the new fire truck should be delivered about August 15, 1968. The
board discussed putting in fire phones in the businesses.

On August 21, 1968, the board members met to approve the installation of a fire
bar in the dial house, which would allow fire call phones to be put in some
homes and businesses. Turtle Lake was to be contacted about getting a mutual
agreement made so each town could help each other on fire calls. While the
meeting was in progress, the new bright red fire truck arrived. A demonstration
was given by Hartley Walter and Floyd Forestner to some of the board members.
After the demonstration, a motion was made by Lloyd Westerlind and seconded by
Albert Skaley to pay Forestner Fire Equipment Company the sum of $7097.00 for
the fire apparatus and equipment. The motion was approved.

The Mercer Fire Department is Organized

On October 28, 1968, a special meeting was held at the Sportsman Hall to
organize a fire department. There were 37 present. The following were elected to
posts: Ted Gessele, Chief; Arnold Westerlind Assistant Chief; Reinhart
Stradinger, Second Assistant Chief. Other members appointed for Fire Department
duties were Myron Makeeff, Ernest Littke, Richard Postel, Herbert Rauser, Albert
Bonnet, Joe Schon, Percy Fibelstad, Dennis Fibelstad, Dan Birst, Leonard
Gessele, John Laib, Ervin Schell, Emil Fisher and Edwin Wagner. Next order of
business was to decide where the fire phones would be placed. A motion was
approved to place the phones in the following places, Jacob Rust, Mike Fettig,
Ted Gessele, Herbert Gaub, Allan Roll, George Gardiner, Reinhart Stradinger and
Fred Beierle.

Over the years several highlights in the fire department's history stand out. In
1977 the fire hall got some needed repairs, the walls and ceiling were
insulated, the meeting room wall was taken out along with the small front
office, some windows were closed up and insulated, a new fourteen foot insulated
overhead door was installed, two inches of concrete was poured over the floor
and the water tank was installed on a stand.

        Photo: Tom Wagner (left) and David Presser are firemen at work.

At a special board meeting on June 28, 1984, the discussion surrounded a
situation where the Insurance Reserve Fund sent the Fire District a check for
$20,801.38 in fire insurance refund money. The secretary felt this was in error
and checked with the State Insurance Department on the figure, and was told it
was not a mistake. The question was "what to do with this money"? The money was
deposited in an interest-bearing savings account for the time being. Indeed, a
special directors meeting was held on September 24, 1985, at the fire hall to
discuss a letter from the Commissioner of Insurance requesting the return of
over $18,000.00 that was given to the fire district in error. Chairman Larry
Gessele and Secretary Byron Fiedler met with Insurance Commissioner Earl Pomeroy
to settle the overpayment issue. The Fire District would repay $8000.00 and the
State would keep the annual Insurance Refund money for the next five years and
anything owed the State after that date would be absorbed by the State. A full
refund payment would be made to the district in the year 1990.

In 1988 a mutual aid agreement drawn up by the McClusky Fire District to the
Mercer Rural Fire Protection District was reviewed and accepted. The
possibilities of a new fire hall were discussed and it was decided to check into
grants, cost sharing, and other opportunities to defray the cost of a new
building. A special meeting was called in September of 1988, to meet with Jim
Gilmore from Lewis and Clark Regional Development. The meeting was to get input
on the possibility of getting a grant for the construction of a new fire hall. A
public meeting was held at the Mercer City Hall for review of the possibility of
a grant and after a long debate on the costs for a new fire hall even with a
grant, the consensus of all people attending was that it was not feasible for
the Fire District to build. Alternatives for funding as well as building options
were discussed, and the decision was made to keep all possibilities of building
a new Fire Hall open and try to get other methods for building funds.

In 1989 problems with the pump drive on the fire truck had developed and the
board considered purchasing a used truck at $19,000. The proposal was dropped, a
school bus with a new engine and automatic transmission was located and
purchased, and an engine and transmission swap was done by Edward Schumann,
Byron Fiedler, and Raymond Murray. The project cost was $6,000.

In 1993 the Building Fund was discussed, noting that a new fire hall could
possibly be built in the next year or two depending on fund growth and if the
City would desire to join the venture. At a special directors meeting held on
April 18, 1994, the board of directors again discussed the building fund and
heard that the City of Mercer could contribute $5-$7 thousand dollars toward the
building fund. The purchase of the old house and lots on the north corner of
Main Street as a construction site for a future fire hall was discussed but was
tabled for another year to check other possibilities.

On September 18, 1994, the board of directors met in special session to install
by resolution an increase in the dollar amount levied within the Fire District
for the purpose of construction of a new fire hall. On January 10, 1995, the
board of directors met with Paul Rechlin from the Lewis and Clark Regional
Development Council for a possible grant to construct a new fire hall. At a
January 18, 1995, firemen's supper and meeting, an historic motion was approved
to encourage any woman in the community to join the fire department as a
fireman.

In April 1996 the board learned that the application for a grant to construct
the new fire hall was turned down again. The application came in just under the
pay line for accepted projects. Byron Fiedler stated that there still might be a
chance to get funded if another project failed. On December 20, 1996, the Lewis
and Clark RDC called to inform the secretary that the grant application for a
new fire hall was accepted. $77,000 was awarded at the time.

At its annual meeting in 1997, the board learned that Mclean County would
sponsor the grant for the construction of the new fire hall. The board of
directors gave the go ahead for the project, estimates would be received, and
the Lindell Law Office or an architect would be hired to help with the bid
letting if needed. Bids were opened for construction of the new fire hall. Eagle
Rigid Span, Blue Star Construction, Morton Buildings, and Heney Buildings were
reviewed. Eagle Rigid Span was the low bid at just under $100,000. The bids were
forwarded to Lewis and Clark and Eagle Rigid Span was awarded the contract. On
November 6, 1997, backhoe work started on the old fire hall site. Roger
Ketterling, Frank Wardner, Ronald Schatz, and Byron Fiedler worked on cleaning
and leveling of the lot. Roger Ketterling brought his payloader and truck, Frank
Wardner also brought his truck to haul debris away and haul in fill gravel.
Byron Fiedler used the City of Mercer's road maintainer to level the lot.

Construction went well on the new fire hall, with board members helping on some
items. The fire trucks and equipment were housed in the City of Mercer's shop
building and also at Ed's Service. In June 1998 the new fire hall was mostly
completed and trucks were moved back inside the new building.

In 1999 a tanker truck was acquired through the Forest Service and repaired and
painted with the Forest Service paying 50% of total costs. The truck itself was
free, and the Fire District agreed to maintain it for the duration of its use.

        Photo: The first fire department building, formerly the Andrew Rust
        blacksmith shop.

        Photo: The present fire department building.

In 2001 the grant to purchase a new brush fighter truck was accepted. A used
1996 Chevy 1-ton crew cab dually 4 × 4 was purchased and an all aluminum flatbed
with storage compartments ordered to hold a skid-type firefighting and foam
producing unit.

In 2003 the FEMA Fire Act grant was successful and allowed the Fire District to
purchase equipment totaling $43,722. A used 1989 Chevy crew cab dually 4 × 4
with a utility box was purchased from OMB Surplus Property to be used as a brush
truck or equipment truck. In 2004 the FEMA Fire Act Grant was accepted, allowing
the Fire District to purchase needed equipment totaling $28,359.

Living up to its purpose, the fire department has responded to emergency
situations. Fire calls of any significance in the past included the following:

On December 11, 1975, a fire call to the Fibelstad Brothers farm ended with
their garage-shop building burning to the ground.

In February 1981 fire destroyed two cabins at Brush Lake. The fire marshal was
called in to investigate because evidence was found that intruders had possibly
caused the fire.

In 1989 the fire department was called to a fire at the Tony Lill residence on
the north end of Mercer where high winds fanned the flames from a previous
controlled burn into their yard damaging some trees.

In 1991 the department was called to Brush Lake where boys playing with matches
started a fire that consumed several acres of grass and the pump house and
equipment used to aerate the lake in winter. The Turtle Lake Fire Department was
called for backup because of the close proximity of the fire to many cabins.
