Community Center

The present MCC (Mercer Community Center) has been known by several names. It
was built in the 1960s as an addition to the 1916 brick school house. It was an
auditorium/gymnasium and was the scene of concerts, graduations, school
carnivals basketball games, and other community and social events. When the
school became part of the Turtle Lake-Mercer School District in 1976, the "gym"
became city property.

In 1981, the original school building, a more recent addition and the gym were
leased to the Senior Citizen's Club, and in 1986, it was sold to the Senior
Citizens for $1.00. With the help of grants and other sources of income, the
school building, the gym and the addition were renovated and repaired. From
1981 to 1984, the gym was called the Mercer Recreation Center. In 1984, the
Senior Citizens gave the Recreation Center back to the City.

Since the late 1980s, the Center has been governed by an elected Board.
Operation expenses are provided by grants, donations and membership fees. During
this time, the Senior Citizens continued to have their meetings and activities
in the new addition (kitchen and science room) to the school building on the
north side.

The Center has been and is still used for athletic events, exercise groups,
family reunions, weddings, funerals and other related events. It also hosts
Santa Day and the Easter Egg Hunt.

Recent improvements have been made. A new heating system, improved plumbing,
insulation, updated bathroom facilities and improvements in the kitchen have
been done with funding from grants and private donations.

In 2002, by a vote of the members of the Center, the name was changed to the
Mercer Community Center.

        Photo: The Mercer Community Center

Mercer Community Development Corporation (MCDC) By Marlene Wardner

The Mercer Community Development Corporation was organized on October 26, 1989,
for the purpose of helping to establish a grocery store. Mercer had been
without a grocery since August 1989.

Two grants, $5000 from the Ottertail Power Company and $1000 from the West River
Telephone Corporation, were received and stocks were sold. The goal was to
raise $30,000. At the time the corporation dissolved, there were ninety
different shareholders holding 216 shares.

The corporation elected the following directors: Lewellyn Tewksbury was named
President; Tom Beierle, Vice President; and Marlene Wardner, Secretary-
Treasurer. Directors were Allan Laib, Ray Murray, John Westerlind and Byron
Fiedler. Succeeding presidents were John Westerlind, Allan Laib, Lloyd Brunner
and Byron Fiedler.

Mozel and Jim Murray opened the Murray Market on November 15, 1989, in the
Freeberg Store on Main Street. This building had been the site of the McFadden
Store, the first store opened in Mercer. In spite of advertising and other
promotion, the store closed in January 1992 because of lack of business.

There were several potential businesses interested in funding but the
corporation members voted to dissolve, and the November 3, 1993, meeting was the
last meeting of the corporation. Each stockholder was mailed a percentage of
the final assets.

In April 1990, the City was presented with a Community Development project award
by Gov. George Sinner.

Federal Programs

Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC)

The CCC was a federal agency created by an act of Congress in 1933 and formally
organized in 1937. The CCC was established to furnish work and training for
unemployed young men and also to set up a nationwide program to conserve and
build up the country's natural resources of timber, soil and water. Many trees
were planted, dams built and parks created.

The young men enrolled voluntarily in this program. They lived in camps which
had sleeping tents and mess tents. In some areas barracks were built for living
quarters. The work day was from 5:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. with regular meal times.
Clothing was furnished by the government and the wages were $30/month with $25
sent home to families. Many of the young men from Mercer who served in the CCC
were drafted or enlisted in the military during World War II.

The CCC was abolished by the Congress in 1942.

Works progress Administration (WPA)

In 1933, the United States was struggling in a serious economic depression.
Banks had failed, mills and mines were either closed or operating under capacity
and the Midwest was hit with a drought and many people were out of work.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt, in an effort to improve conditions, introduced
the "New Deal." This obligated the federal government to assume responsibility
for the welfare of the American people. The WPA was organized by executive order
in May 1935. In cooperation with the state and local governments, the WPA
conducted a broad program of public works and community services. The project
lasted until WWII when employment rose and federal relief was no longer needed.
The project was eliminated in June 1943.

North Dakota got more WPA funds per capita than any other state. Average monthly
pay was $40 per month, which was just barely enough to live on during the
Depression. In order to get work on the WPA, it was necessary to be almost
destitute. To qualify, income and need were taken into consideration - similar
to the guidelines used today for emergency assistance and commodity give-a-ways.

In Mercer, one of the projects was to do road work on ND Highway #7 (now #200),
Highway #41 and some of the county and township roads. Crews widened the roads
with shovels and then hauled gravel with wagons or well-worn trucks (fuel was
scarce and expensive). It was very hard manual labor but the people were
grateful to work and earn money. Base pay for unskilled labor was $35.00/month.

As recorded in the time book by foreman John Ketterling in 1937, the crew was
the following: Sam Norris, Emanuel Schlaht, Halfdan Berge, Edwin Levi, Christ
Skow, Arthur Levi, F.G. Wagner, John Ketterling, Richard Ketterling, August
Aichele, Ed Fischer, John Wise, Emil Just, Theo. Just, Christoph Schell, Emil E.
Just, Robert Westerlind, Bennie Miller, and Hogan Winge.

The Mercer crew also had a one-ton truck.

The age range was 28-66 and the average monthly check was $40.00. The total for
1937 was $1768.10.

The McClusky Canal By Vernia Rust Hausauer


In 1966, the Bureau of Reclamation created the Garrison Diversion project to
provide water for irrigation and other use for central North Dakota. The
diversion project uses Lake Audubon as the water supply for the McClusky Canal
delivery system. The construction on the first part of the McClusky Canal
started in 1970. It is about 73.6 miles long.

The project required raising of Lake Audubon thirteen feet, thus altering refuge
habitat. Restoration activities included erosion protection of shoreline and
islands, creation of new islands and wetlands and the purchasing of replacement
habitat.

Despite Garrison Diversion promises and potential, it can be called a mixed
blessing. Farms that had existed since homesteading days have been severed,
divided and disrupted by the canal construction.

The area is a summer destination for fishing, camping, hunting and vacationing.
The refuge is located for public use and has good potential for future
compatible development.

        Document: Ad circa 1960-1970

Mercer in the Military

William Henry H. Mercer (Mussar) ( the name sake of Mercer County and the city
of Mercer) and James R. Howell, early Mercer area homesteaders, were Civil War
veterans. William Musser was a Corporal in the 49th Pennsylvania Infantry with
allegience to the Union. (See gravesite page 23)

The United States entered World War I in October 1917 and sent hundreds of
thousands of "Doughboys" to Europe.

Mercer was well represented in the military during World War II and the home
front supported its sons and daughters. There was an active organized support
group, the Mercer Servicemen's Club, which maintained close contact with those
in the service. Each weekly edition of the McLean County Journal had a Mercer
Service Men's Directory with the names and addresses of the service men and
women from the Mercer area. The July 1944 issue included 75 listings and
included four Mercer "daughters." They were; WAVE Annetta Fink, WAC Eunice
Hjelle, MARINE Beemer Norris and WAVE Olga Stradinger.

The persons in charge of the correspondence were; Marian Berge Haibeck, Beatrice
Kline Halfpennig, Pearl Lockrem Kline and Marie (Mrs. Ted) Sackmann. The service
people received the Journal every week and were urged to write letters for
publication. Many did and some of the letters provided details of the war action
in different parts of the world.

        Document: Mercer Service Men's Directory

Mercer Veterans and Gold Stars

Two notable Mercer area Civil War veterans and early ranchers were William
Mercer (Mussar) and James Howell. (See history of Mercer on page 15 and of
Howell on page 17 and the family history on page 257)

A Spanish American War veteran was Laurence Harrum. He was born in 1873 in
Minnehaha County, Dakota Territory. He was a barber in Edmore, N.D., when he
joined Company I of the NDF Volunteers. He served from 1898-1900 in the
Philippines during the Spanish American War. Later he returned to Edmore and in
1903 he married Abbie Helland. In 1904 they moved to her homestead in Prophets
Township, McLean County (later Sheridan County.) He died in 1957 in the veterans
hospital in Minot and is buried in the Mercer Cemetery. (See family history on
page 247)

        Photo: Spanish American War veteran Laurence Harrum.

Mercer Gold Stars

During the early days of WWI, Blue Stars were displayed on Service Flags from
homes, churches and places of business to indicate the members of families who
were serving our country. Gold Stars were superimposed over the Blue Stars to
honor servicemen who died during service to their country. The Gold Star has
been an accepted way of honoring service persons who died in the service of
their country since President Wilson approved its use on May 28, 1918.

WWI

Christian Sorlee

Christian was born in Norway in 1891 and he was inducted into the Army in
Washburn on July 21, 1918. He was sent to Camp Custer, Michigan, and served in
the 160th Depot Brigade to August 14, 1918. He then served with the Supply
Company, 78th Infantry when he died of the Spanish influenza at Camp Custer on
October 18, 1918. He was buried in the St. Ansgar Cemetery, north of Mercer.
(See history page 350)

Ole Edward Hedahl

England, Oct. 1918.
Grade: Wagoner, Sept. 21, 1918

Ole was inducted at Washburn on June 14, 1918. He was sent to North Dakota
Agricultural College and served in Training Detachment, to Aug. 13, 1918. He
was with the Ambulance Company No. 151, 113th Sanitary Train until his death.

Ole was overseas from Oct. 6, 1918, until his death. Ole died of pneumonia at
Stockport, England on Oct. 20, 1918. He is buried at Brookwood American
Cemetery, Brookwood, England.(1)

His stepmother, Clara Berge Hedahl, was identified as a Gold Star mother and
went to England to visit his grave in the early 1930s.

        Photo: Ole Edward Hedahl. (Photo courtesy of Richard Hedahl)

John Adolph Singer

John Adolph Singer, son of Adolph and Margaretha Singer died from the Spanish
influenza on September 22, 1918. He was born on April 10, 1895, in Glen Ullin,
ND, and came to Mercer with his family in 1907 where he grew up and attended
school. He enlisted in the Navy in 1918 and died of the flu while in basic
training at the Great Lakes Naval Center, Ill. He is buried in the Mercer
Cemetery. (See family history page  345)

WWII

Raymond Calheim

The first man to die in action in WWII was Raymond Calheim who died on May 29,
1943, at Attu, Aleutians Islands.

Raymond was born on December 25,1919, to Andrew and Mathilda Calheim in rural
Mercer. He was buried in the Fort Snelling cemetery in Minneapolis, Mn.

He was a member of Our Savior's Lutheran Church in Mercer and attended Wise
Township (Sprout) School. He received a certificate of award in 1936 for
punctuality and perfect attendance for five months.

He enjoyed hunting and trapping and worked as a farm hand.

He was drafted into the US Army in September 1942 and trained at Ft. Ord, Calif.
with the 50th Combat Engineer Battalion.

        Photo: Raymond Calheim. (Photo courtesy of his sister Lila Stradinger)

(Information from his sister Lila Stradinger)

Duane Rice

Captain Duane Rice, a paratrooper, was killed in an airplane accident in
England, May 12, 1944, when two bombers collided during training for the D-Day
invasion.

John Duane Rice was born in 1919 in Reedsburg, Wisconsin, to James and Gertrude
Martinson Rice, Mercer pioneers who were living in Wisconsin for a short time.

He attended the Mercer Schools and graduated from Mercer High School in 1937. He
attended the University of North Dakota for two years and then transferred to
the University of Washington. He entered the US Army on June 15, 1941 and
trained as a paratrooper. He was sent overseas in April 1943. He served in North
Africa and Italy and was wounded during the Sicilian campaign for which he
received the Purple Heart. (Information from his family)

        Photo: Duane Rice. (Photo courtesy of his family)

Garner Webster

Garner Webster died in a non-combat jeep accident in Italy in September 1944.

He was a CPL in the Signal Corp of the US Army. His body was returned to North
Dakota in 1948 and he is buried next to his mother, Ella in the Turtle Lake
cemetery.

Garner was born on Dec. 27, 1921, to Melvin and Ella Lockrem Webster. His mother
died when he was six years old and he and his infant brother, Chester, were
raised in the home of their Uncle Christ O. Lockrem and Gina Peterson Lockrem.
There they had two older "sisters", Gertrude (Mrs. Glenn Love) and Pearl (Mrs.
Archie Kline). He grew up in the Mercer area and graduated from the Beulah High
School.

        Photo: Garner Webster. (Photo and information courtesy of Kathleen Love
        Seegar)

While in the military service, he wrote this poem for his family:

The End of the Day By CPL. Garner D. Webster

        At the end of a day, let me rest in peace,
        Let me gaze at the setting sun,
        Let me relax and be at ease
        Glad that my work is done.

        Let me go to sleep when the evening falls
        To dream sweet dreams of home
        Where faces of those I love, I'll see
        As my mind unconsciously roam.

        Let me rest, and I'll be satisfied
        With the life which I now lead.
        Sleep, to refresh my weary mind,
        Is all I ask and need.

(Information from Kathleen Love Seeger)

WWII on the home front

During World War II, America increased productivity on all fronts because
Americans at home conserved their resources in order to help the war effort.
Mercer was no exception and was very involved in helping out the troops by their
use of bald or retreaded tires, gas rationing, corresponding with service men
and women and counting ration stamps for shoes, food and other essentials.

The Office of Price Administration, a federal agency established in 1941, set up
War Price and Rationing Boards in every county. The Boards were local people
and would set the ration level for each person in the county. Some of rationed
products included gasoline, rubber, sugar, canned goods and butter. To buy one
of the rationed products the consumer needed to present a ration card or stamps.
The consumer could not buy more products than they had stamps for, however, they
might be able to trade with someone else that had stamps for an item they
needed.

        Document: War Ration Coupon Book for WWII.

The Korean Conflict

Two Mercer natives died in action during the Korean Conflict.

Marvin Pederson

PFC Marvin Pederson died in action on February 14, 1951, in Korea. He was
buried in Fort Snelling, Minneapolis on November 13, 1951.

Marvin was born on October 4, 1931, one of sixteen children, to Edward and
Hattie Pederson in Pickard Township, Sheridan County. He attended the rural
school in Pickard Township and in Mercer. After finishing the elementary grades
in Mercer, he worked for his brother on a ranch in Nevada. He was confirmed and
was a member of the Our Savior's Lutheran Church in Mercer.

        Photo: Marvin Pederson. (Photo from yearbook)

He enlisted in the US Army in 1948 and was inducted on Nov. 7, 1948. He
received his basic training at Ft. Riley, Kansas and Ft. Lewis, Washington. He
was a truck driver and then transferred to the Infantry. He was sent overseas
in July 1949. (Information from his obituary)

Meinhardt R. Rennich

PFC Meinhardt R. Rennich was born December 29, 1929, in Mercer to Carl, Jr. and
Louise (Kleingartner) Rennich. He attended elementary school in Mercer and in
1937 moved with his parents to McClusky.

He attended the McClusky School and in 1948 he began working for the local
Chevrolet dealer, the McClusky Motor Co. On August 5, 1950, he married Jane Mae
Lang of McClusky and they set up house keeping in a small unit behind the Moore
Hotel.

        Photo: Meinhard Rennich. (Photo courtesy of his brother, Mervin)

On March 26, 1951, he was drafted into the US Army and completed his basic
training at Camp Roberts, Calif. After a brief furlough home he was sent to
Korea on August 13, 1951, arriving there on August 28, 1951. He was a machine
gunner with Company G, 2nd Battalion, 7th Cavalry Regiment, 1st Cavalry
Division. In a campaign to give UN forces a favorable position should an
armistice be signed, Company G was ordered on October 3, 1951, to take hill
number 418, located about ten miles north of the small town of Yonchon. In the
process of taking the hill, Company G suffered over 90% casualties. Meinhardt
was killed in action by enemy fire. He had been on the front for thirty-two
days.

Meinhardt's body was returned to the United States and on January 24, 1952; a
military funeral was held for him in the McClusky High School Auditorium. He was
buried with military honors in the McClusky City Cemetery.

(Information from his brother, Mervin Rennich)

At every Memorial Day service held at the Mercer Cemetery, the veterans of all
wars are honored by the American Legion Post No. 133. Included is music, an
address by local clergy, a 21-gun salute, a reading of the names of deceased
veterans and the sound of "Taps." The white crosses are a permanent reminder of
the military service of the native sons and daughters.

American Legion Submitted by LeRoy Laib

The American Legion was born March 15-17, 1919, in Paris, France.

The American Legion was organized in North Dakota in 1919, with the first post
at Bismarck on May 21, called the Lloyd Spetz Post #1.

The first state convention was hosted by Bismarck on Oct. 16, 1919. Temporary
Chairman Julius Baker called the convention to order. At that time there were
seventy-six posts organized in North Dakota, with a total of 4,406 members, with
forty-two posts present at the first convention.

J.M. Hanley of Mandan was selected the temporary chairman to preside over the
first state convention. Claude L. Dawson was elected the first state commander
of the North Dakota American Legion.

Dues at that time were $2 with forty percent (80 cents) going to state
headquarters, of which 25 cents went to national headquarters. Dues at the
present time are $20.

The meaning of the emblem is as follows:

(1) The rays of the sun form the background of our proud emblem, and suggest
that the Legion's principles will dispel the darkness of violence and evil.

(2) The wreath forms the center, in loving memory of those brave comrades who
gave their lives in the service of the United States that liberty might endure.

(3) The star, victory symbol of World War I, signalizes honor, glory, and
constancy. The letters U.S. leave no doubt as to the brightest star in the
Legion's sky.

(4) Two large rings, the outer one stands for the rehabilitation of our sick and
disabled buddies. The inner one denotes the welfare of America's children.

(5) Two small rings set upon the star. The outer pledges loyalty and
Americanism. The inner is for service to our communities, our states and the
nation.

(6) The words American Legion tie the whole together for truth, remembrance,
constancy, honor, service, rehabilitation, child welfare, loyalty, and
Americanism.

Mercer did not have an American Legion Post, therefore, most of the veterans
were members of the posts in McClusky Post #124, Turtle Lake Lawrence Stephenson
Post #133, or Butte Lawrence E. Meidl Post #270.

McClusky Post #124 did not have a history in the book entitled "American Legion
in North Dakota - the first 75 years 1919-1994."

Lawrence Stephenson Post #133 of the American Legion of North Dakota was
organized at Turtle Lake. The charter was issued on Jan. 2, 1920. The post was
named in honor of Lawrence Stephenson of Turtle Lake, who died of influenza
while training in military service during World War I.

        Photo: LeRoy Laib (at right) marches in a parade representing the
        American Legion. He was the post commander of the Turtle Lake-Mercer
        Post #133.

The Lawrence Stephenson Post #133 of Turtle Lake performs the Memorial Day
services for the Mercer Community as well as the Turtle Lake community.

An American Legion was chartered at Dogden on Feb. 3, 1921. It was named Peter
Semevolos Post #204. After five years due to members moving away the post was
dissolved and the remaining members joined the Legion post at Velva. Later the
name Dogden was changed to Butte.

A renewed interest to start another post at Butte was shown after many veterans
returned from World War II. Late in May of 1946 the Butte Post #240 was
organized and named after Lawrence E. Meidl, a rural Butte soldier who died
during World War II.

        Photo: A corner at the Mercer Cemetery reserved for the military.

Agriculture's Role in the Community By Christof C. Heim, Jr.

As pioneers began to settle in the community and the surrounding areas of
Mercer, North Dakota, initially their resources of livelihood depended upon the
industry of farming. The production from farming supported the sale of goods and
services. Producers produced only enough grain and food to supply their own
needs. Very few crops were marketed during the early years. If there was a
surplus, grain was usually sold on the market for a profit. Multiple methods of
tilling the soil and reaping of crops commensurate with raising livestock became
the intrinsic way of life. The precedence of time in agriculture predominately
set the stage of what farming has become today. Thus, the way of farming began.

During the early years, farmers endured hard labor by using hand tools and
subsequently began using horse-drawn machinery to farm. Farmers needed very
little in the way of machinery other than a plow, harrow, drill, and a good team
of horses. Farming methods have changed considerably. Technology has
revolutionized farming in bringing about new improved machinery and modern
methods of farming. In retrospect, the new machines have solved much of the
manpower problems and practically eliminated the workhorse which was so
important on the farm during the early years. Horses remained the main source of
power until the early twentieth century. Today, on many farms, the horses are
generally used for recreational purposes only.

An overview of the history of farming, particularly the development of the farm
tractor in the 1850s brought a whole new mechanized dimension to the production
of farming. The advent of steam power, and later gasoline powered engines, was
more significant during the industrial revolution than what was realized. At
this time it would be most difficult for one to predict or even to anticipate
the role of what tractors have become in the farm industry as it is known today.
The early tractors were designed for the tasks such as plowing. Horses were
still needed for the careful work such as cultivating, making hay, tending herds
of livestock, and transportation.

History records that the steam engines were invented in the late 1700s in some
form or a combination thereof using steam under pressure to supply mechanical
energy. Steam engines later were applied to moving vehicles by the early 1800s.
It was not until the 1850s with the introduction of the high-pressure boilers
that the steam engines were put to farm equipment. Between 1885 and 1914, the
steam engine was the dominant source of power in farming. Steam engines were
delicate, complicated, and required a great deal of maintenance. By the second
decade of the century, farmers had the alternative to steam. The internal
combustion engine appeared in about 1905.

The earliest internal combustion engines were stationary. Subsequently, some of
them were mounted on wheels so they could be transported from field to field.
They were powered by either kerosene or gasoline and delivered more horsepower
for their weight. At first, they were bulky, expensive, and unreliable. More
machines used gas than steam by 1912.

Gas had replaced steam in most mechanized operations by the end of the First
World War. By 1920, while horses were still in evidence on many farms, the
gasoline tractor revolutionized the processes of breaking, plowing, and
threshing. It was not until 1941 that more than half the farms possessed
tractors. Gasoline tractors were first mass produced starting in 1916 by
Fordson. After 1913, the age of steam came to a rapid close, and a few steam
engines were still in use by 1920. The diminution of the steam engine and the
growth of the gasoline engine were between the transitional years of 1915 and
1923.

Mercer, founded in 1905, was at the center in the development of the surrounding
farm community. The 1908 and 1909 issues of the Mercer Telegram published
advertisements for the sale of early tractors and binders. In July 31, 1908, O.
S. Hedahl & Company promoted the sale of their "Acme Queen" binder, and in May
14, 1909, advertised the first ad for their tractor the Case Steam Breaker.
Another ad in the July 31, 1908 issue, the Turtle Lake Implement Company
advertised their "New Acme" or "Champion" binder, too.

        Document: (From the Cricket)

The first indication of gas tractors in the Mercer area came in the May 9, 1913,
issue of the Mercer Telegram when it reported, "A new J.I. Case gas tractor was
unloaded at the depot for a farmer south of town yesterday." In the May 30,
1913, edition of the same newspaper, it was disclosed that "the gas tractors,
one belonging to J.C. Murphy and one to J.H. Rogge, are tearing up the soil in
great shape. Each rig has turned several hundred acres this spring."

The earliest method of harvesting was the use of the cradle and flail that was
introduced in America about 1776 and was used until the 1840s. The cradle was
actually a broad scythe with a light frame of four wood fingers attached to it.
The cradle was an efficient tool to cut the grain so that by a turn to left the
operator could throw the grain into a swath, making it ready to be raked and
bound into sheaves. Two acres was considered a day's work for cradling grain.

The flail was used to separate the grain from the straw. It was made up of two
hinged poles that were used to pound the grain until the kernels broke free from
the heads. Eventually, the grain header box was built and was a big improvement
in harvesting grain.

Methods of harvesting became more progressive enabling the farmer to be more
productive. The header box was an implement that was similar to the swather
having a long platform, sickle bar, and reel. In contrast to the swather, the
header box had an attached elevated extension to the platform on one end that
carried the grain upward to be unloaded into a hayrack that was travelling along
side. Unlike the binder, the header box lacked the mechanism to tie the grain
stalk into bundles. The header box was usually pushed forward by teams of
horses, the driving wheel was ground driven, which powered the moving parts
inclusive to the sickle, reel, and canvas. The grain was usually cut short as
the name of the implement implies - header - and was hauled to some other site
where it was stacked for drying so that it could be threshed. When Mercer was
founded in the early 1900s, farmers were still using header boxes while binders
were making inroads. The header box was the predecessor to the McCormick reaper
and the grain binder.

The world's first reaper by built by McCormick in 1831 and was used extensively
between 1852-1865 with the various improvements being incorporated from time to
time. The first reaper needed two people for operation, one person to ride the
horse and one person to rake the cut grain from the platform. Between 1862-1864,
the McCormick automatic self-rake reaper was innovated to a one man operation.
The automatic rake sweep swept the grain off the platform depositing the grain
on the ground in neat gavels ready to be bound by hand binders, usually a crew
of four to five men. The advance reaper was a combination reaper and mower that
was sold by McCormick from 1869-1879. The reaper was the predecessor of the
binder that was put into use in 1875.

McCormick built the first practical self-binder in 1876. One man who could cut
and bind the grain in one operation. The early binders were horse-drawn being
powered by a rotating ground driven wheel. Improvements were made so that they
could be drawn with tractors equipped with power take-off shafts.

The binder was used to cut the grain and was the predecessor of the modern day
swather. The binder put the grain into bundles while in contrast the swather
made windrows. The binder cut an eight-foot wide swath of standing grain and
collectively tied the grain stalks in a bundle with a tying device using binder
twine. The bundles weighed approximately fifteen-twenty pounds and were about
twelve-fifteen inches in diameter. The binder would thrust the bundles onto a
carrier that would hold about five or six bundles depending on the size of the
cut grain. The operator of the binder would release the accumulated bundles on
the carrier to non-uniform rows in the field. Subsequently, the bundles had to
be put up in a shock.

        Photo: Horses were also used for transportation, i.e. moving this house
        from Wilton to Mercer in 1932. (Photo courtesy of Chris Heim Jr.)

The grain shock was the method used to dry the grain. The shock consisted of
about fifteen bundles of grain that stood on their butts into a tent-like shape.
At times, several bundles were placed on top of the shock to shield it from the
weather elements. It was imperative that the grain be dry so the thresher could
separate the grain kernels from the straw and chaff. The author remembers
shocking with his mother and still hasn't figured out how she could shock
barefooted in the stubble. It was very hot one day and he wanted to quit
shocking. His mother said, "Let's put up sixty more shocks and then go home."
They put up fifty-nine and quit. The field was finished.

        Photo: Shocks of wheat.

Consistent with the times, threshing rigs were the only means of threshing the
grain. The rigs consisted of a steam or a gasoline powered tractor,
threshing/separator machine, cook car, water tank and/or fuel car that supplied
the resources needed to provide the energy for the tractors. The cook car was
similar to what we know as a mobile chef car today.

From the end of World War I to 1940, the introduction of custom threshing crews
on various farms surrounding Mercer can be attributed to John Ketterling, Nels
Fibelstad, John Laib, and other families. It would be noteworthy to mention that
the author's father purchased the 1912 Aultman Taylor 30-60 that the Fibelstads
used for threshing.

Harvesting grain in the old days was very unique and is reminisced by those who
have experienced it as an integral part of their life. The author's father
apprised him of the methods used in harvesting and threshing that existed in the
early 1940s. Most farmers owned a binder and there were a few farmers that
owned a threshing machine. These farmers used their threshing machine to do
custom work to compensate for the cost of the machine. The farmers that he knew
personally that did custom threshing were his uncle Emanuel Makeeff and Emil
Wanner. They custom threshed between 1944 and 1953. Between 1955 and 1958, he
worked for them and his father when they threshed for themselves. It was a
great experience for him when he worked with the binder, too.

The threshing machine was very unique and simple. It was the prototype for the
modern combine. Bundles of grain were pitched in headfirst on one end and were
fed into the thresher by a feeder chain. At the entrance, the bundles would be
chopped up with straw tines. Then the bundles would pass between the cylinder
and the concave, blowing the straw and chaff out of the thresher through a straw
spout. The grain was separated and collected through the sieves. Then the grain
was put into a holding mechanism a half-bushel hopper. The hopper mechanically
counted the bushels and when full, it augered the grain onto a grain truck or
wagon box for delivery to the granary or market. The straw was collected in a
huge pile to be used later for feed and bedding for livestock.

        Photo: (Above) A threshing crew about 1915-21. (Photo courtesy of
        Richard Ketterling collection)

        Photo: (Below) Another threshing crew. (Photo courtesy of Evelyn
        Freeberg)

The threshing crew consisted of about six to ten farmers or others who where
willing to work for hire. Most farmers were paid for being a part of the
threshing crew. These farmers persevered until their crops were harvested. The
sequence of harvest depended mostly upon the readiness of the grain. Threshing
records depict that members of the crew were paid 90 cents an hour during the
middle 1940s. The owner of the threshing machine paid the wages. In 1946-1947,
records reveal that threshers charged 14 cents per bushel to thresh wheat, 9
cents a bushel for oats, and 31 cents for flax.

Members of the crew consisted of six to nine bundle haulers, a fielder, and a
spiker. The owner of the thresher frequently walked on a platform on top of the
threshing machine where he could see everything, like God watching over our
lives. It didn't matter if there were ten or 150 acres to thresh, all members of
the threshing crew worked equally until all the acreage was threshed. In early
times, the bundle haulers used hayracks that were drawn by a team of horses and
in later years, a tractor.

The teams of horses were very well trained. When the hayracks were being loaded
with bundles in the field, the driver would walk alongside the hayrack with the
reins tied to the hayrack, he would instruct the team to go ahead (Giddy-up) and
then to stop (Whoa). This is how he drove the team from one shock to another to
get loaded. The fielder worked in the field helping the bundle hauler load his
hayrack; he went from hayrack to hayrack. The spiker was the person who helped
the bundle hauler unload his hayrack at the threshing machine. To protect the
horses from eating grain, straw, and from becoming injured at the threshing
machine, they would wear a mesh horse muzzle around their mouth. This worked out
very well because it was not much of a nuisance to the horses.

Threshing could not have been done without the help of the farmer's wife. The
host wife would put on a hearty dinner that was prepared in the kitchen. The
ladies would work as a team much like the men did. The author remembers when his
first cousins, Irene, Doris, and Deloris Makeeff would come to their house to
help his mother prepare the meals. The dinners and the lunches that were being
served were like feasts. Roast beef, roast pork, roast duck or goose, fried
chicken, mashed potatoes and gravies, real stuffing, and fresh vegetables to no
end. The deserts: One would think you were in heaven. I would venture to say
that each host wife would want to serve nothing less but the very best!

While many improvements were made to the tractors that drove the threshing
machines, the separator itself remained unchanged until the appearance of the
combination harvester (combine) that could cut and harvest at the same time. The
combine was built in the late 1920s; however, many threshing machines remained
in use through the 1940s.

Early combines were powered by teams of thirty-forty horses rotating the large
ground driven wheels that drove the moving parts of the combine. Eventually the
tractors replaced the horses and the combine had its own engine or took the
power from the tractor. It was in the thirties when the tractor was eliminated
and the combine became self-propelled.

The story of the production of wheat is synonymous with the existence of the
farm family. Many things had to be done for human survival. The cycle of wheat
involves many operations: preparing the ground, planting the seed, helping the
crop grow, cutting the ripe plants, separating out the grain (threshing), and
finally grinding the grain into flour. This could very well be an analogy to how
we experience life on earth from conception until death.

Farming is one of man's oldest industries and the world's most important. Just
as it was in the earlier times, farmers of today grow the crops and raise
livestock to provide the necessities of life for people everywhere. Farm
families always take an active part in life in their local communities. A
typical farm community is a busy town with several churches, good schools and a
business district. In contrast, farms today are fewer, but are much larger.
Technology has contributed much in making agriculture more proficient and
profitable.

        Document: The Grain Bulletin from Minneapolis, Minn., was sent to
        elevators in the '40s.

The farm towns and families are a tenacious people that have worked diligently
in their profession as if it were a calling in ministry. In all respect, we
salute those farmers who have contributed much to our American way of life.

Modern Agriculture By Larry Gessele

To describe modern farming is really like trying to hit a moving target as it is
changing so rapidly.

The farms are much larger today then the farms of 100 years ago. One farm family
today typically farms about the same amount of land that eight to ten families
farmed early in the century and four or five families farmed in the 1950's. That
explains somewhat, the population decline in communities that rely on
agriculture as their main industry.

Today's farm is more specialized, raising a few main crops or one type of
livestock. The farm of yesteryear typically had milk cows, beef cattle, poultry,
hogs, sheep and many different types of crops.

The machinery is much larger. One airseeder today can do in less than an hour,
what it took a 3 bottom plow, packer & drill from sunrise to sunset to
accomplish before. Gone are the days of shocking, binding and combining using
horses for the power; all the operations are done by one machine, a self
propelled combine with which you can cut and combine the grain in one operation.

One farming method that has caught hold in the dryer warmer areas is a no-till
or minimum-till system that uses a one pass seeding operation with little or no
soil disturbance and the use of chemicals to control any weed problems. This
allows the farmer to save at least an inch or two of moisture that is critical
in this part of the state. No tilling also prevents precious topsoil from
blowing away from the farmer's fields.

There are new global positioning systems that can automatically adjust your
seeding and fertilizer rates on the go, according to soil types and conditions.
There are systems now that automatically steer your machinery up and down the
field or help guide your steering.

The farming industry today is much more capital intensive. A large airseeding
unit with tractor can cost well over $150,000. A hundred years ago when Mercer
was just beginning, a typical farm budgeted perhaps a few hundred dollars; now
they put hundreds of thousands of dollars on the line each spring. The farmer is
at the mercy of Mother Nature and prays every year for a good crop so they can
market grain, pay the bills and hopefully gain some profit. It makes what the
typical Las Vegas gambler spends look like a mere pittance.

Today's farmer has considerable computing skills so he or she can get much of
their information on weather, marketing, purchasing supplies, machinery
operation and to keep farm & accounting records. In order to be effective, he or
she has to have everything in the right place, at the right time and for the
right price. Farmers have to be just as good at managing labor as at managing
their equipment. You can do everything right yet Mother Nature makes the final
call.

        Photo: A modern day tractor: Case 9170.

        Photo: A 750 MF combine.

Mercer Aviation

A lone windsock stands sentinel over the gentle hills northeast of Mercer. An
orange cone-shaped bag signals the presence of an airport. Reaching out across
what was once a farm field, the cross-lane air strip is the home of Mercer
Aviation.

John Westerlind is the owner and operator of the small McLean County airstrip.
He has been a pilot since 1955 and built the airstrip in 1967. He was a flight
instructor and pilot and now still does work on airplane maintenance. John
became a pilot in Alaska while stationed there with the Air Force in 1955. He
earned his mechanics rating in 1970 in Cheyenne, Wyoming, and in 1975 he went
into the business of working on airplanes. As a flight instructor, John worked
with quite a number of men and women to complete their training program and
qualify for the private pilot's license.

The 48 × 72 foot hangar/shop is large enough to work on two planes and room for
a third one for maintenance and storage. The planes are single engine planes
which can land on the unpaved runway.

At the present time, traffic increases during the summer months when pilots use
the airstrip for pleasure or business trips.

        Photo: John Westerlind and his plane.

        Photo: Mercer Machine

Mercer Machine

Purchased from Lee Boschee in 1985. It was the original Christ Heim filling
station and mechanical repair shop.

Services include general welding and repair, aluminum welding, machining,
fabrication as well as sell parts for Rust Stack movers. Ron and Betty Schatz
are owners.

        Photo: Stradinger Apiaries

Stradinger Apiaries

Stradinger Apiaries was started in 1981 by Joel Stradinger as a part-time
business with 400 hives. In 1986 he went full time with 1000 hives and continues
to build his operation, presently he has 2500 hives.

Spring and summer is busy with honey production followed by winter pollination
of California almond orchards in the San Joaquin Valley. It has developed into a
family operation with the involvement of his wife Rhonda and two sons, Jarod and
Tyler. The honey and wax are sold to commercial packers.

Rhonda also promotes honey by working the ND Beekeepers Association booth at
various ag shows throughout the state and visiting area classrooms.
