Brush Lake

The Lake By Mollie Nielsen

I'm glad that I live by the side of a lake
Where the hours and seasons reflect:
If I could but paint all its changes, I'd take
All the rest of my life, I expect!
For sometimes it is such a radiant blue
Then again it's a baleful, slate grey:
It mirrors the sunrise and sunset's each hue
Or foams into furious, white spray -
I have a new picture any time I take
Time to gaze for a moment at our little lake.
Each one is put into memory's file
Although last week's I'll keep out to treasure a while -
Escaping their enemies - one rosy dawn
There, floating safely, were six snow white swan!

Printed with permission from the Nielsen family.

        Photo: Brush Lake (Photo by Kevin and Brenda Vossler, 2004)

        Document: Circa 1915

People in the area hold the town name of Mercer synonymous with Brush Lake. The
combination of the two goes back at least 100 years.

Brush Lake is a spring-fed, fresh water lake that covers 275 acres in Wise
Township and is two miles north of Mercer. It is now a short trip of minutes,
but in the early days, it was a trip of at least twenty-five minutes. The origin
of the name is lost in antiquity. Indians were in the area and Indian artifacts
such as arrowheads can still be found on the shore. In pioneer days, the
collection and selling of buffalo bones along its shores was a source of income.

The depth of nineteen feet in the deepest part makes it conducive to excellent
fishing and water sports. Blue Lake, which is located northwest of Brush Lake,
is larger but is too shallow and the lake is not used for fishing. In drought
years, Blue Lake has dried up while history does not show that Brush Lakes was
ever completely dry. The area between the two lakes is considered a hunters'
paradise especially for waterfowl.

The early Mercer residents enjoyed the recreational pleasures of Brush Lake as
Mercer and area residents do now. There are many items in the Telegram relating
to the activities at Brush Lake. In 1908, store merchant Mike Doering had a
boat. In June 1909, Mrs. Charles Wise platted the Peninsula Resort on the
peninsula. The description in the newspaper was "there will be a pavilion on the
north end approached by an avenue and a circle driveway giving 42 lots with
75 × 150 fronting the lake shore. There is a space reserved for a tennis court
and the plans call for both a bath and boat house." The fate of the bath and
boat house is not known. It also added: "The lots on the peninsula are very
valuable and the rich soil will make possible the growth of a profusion of
flowers and shrubs to beautify the grounds and cottages." Trees and shrubs were
planted and the present lake shore is heavily forested.

        Photo: An early day picture of the public beach.

In April 1908, Brush Lake was stocked with fish and in May 1908 Paul Jeardeau of
McClusky built the first bungalow at the lake. In March 1908, the Carl Schaeffer
home near Blue Lake was called the "Bachelor's Den."

In May 1909, an item states, "Messrs. Plowman, McFadden and Wiest have purchased
a motor boat which will be installed on Brush Lake about June 1." The new boat
was described as twenty feet long, six feet wide and had a 4-horse power engine.
It could go about sixteen miles per hour and could seat comfortably ten to
fifteen passengers. A ride was 25 cents. Throughout the years, other motor
boats, launches, pontoons and canoes have sailed the water of Brush Lake. For a
short time, there was a golf course.

        Photo: Top photo: A copy of a golf course season ticket.

        Photo: Middle photo: Boating on Brush Lake, sometime in the early 1930s
        or late '20s. (Photo courtesy of Ray Schock)

        Photo: Bottom photo: Ice harvesting on Brush Lake. (Photo courtesy of
        Evelyn Freeberg)

        Photo: A day at Brush Lake bath house.

On May 26, 1926, nine men signed the Articles of Incorporation of the
Mercer-Brush Lake Community Association. The signers, all Mercer residents, were
F.A. Sommars, George B. Lucas, W.S. Sprout, Carl Littke, John Braun, Nels A.
Fibelstad, F.O. Freeberg, O.S. Hjelle, and James Rice. In following years, the
sons and then the second and third generations have continued to direct the
activities.

The Association started as a community project with Mercer residents the only
members. In 1958, the Brush Lake Community Association was reorganized and
broadened. Membership was opened to non-Mercer residents and in recent years,
the majority of members are from all over the area.

In 1958, the wooded pavilion was replaced and cabin sites became available.
Cabin sites are now available around the entire lake and are leased from the
Association. Roller skating, bowery dances and moonlight dances were once well-
attended and often included wedding receptions and dances. In recent years,
dances have not been held and roller skating is no longer available.

In the early years, Brush Lake was a popular venue for local and state
politicians to carry on their election year campaigns. At least one notable
dignitary made an appearance in his bid for the governorship: William Langer.
Throughout the years, the two big celebrations were Decoration Day (May 30) and
the 4th of July. The 1908 July 4th celebration was well-described and was
considered a big success.

In 1910, an editorial of "Great Day at Brush Lake" described the activities of
the school picnic and entertainment.

Great Day at Brush Lake As printed in the Telegram, 1910

The school picnic and entertainment at Brush lake, on Decoration day, was a
great success and will be remembered by many the rest of their lives. It was
cloudy and raining all day Monday and Tuesday morning it was still sprinkling
and many thought there would be no picnic; but about 11 o'clock it cleared off
and it turned out to be an ideal day for outdoor sport.

The band played a few selections after which a splendid dinner was served by
Prof. Kleve assisted by a dozen or so of our pretty girls.

After dinner the sport began. A flag pole drill was splendidly performed by six
girls and six boys. Aside from being beautiful the drill was instructive. First
the boy shielded his girl companion by holding over her head a cloth bearing our
National colors: a symbol of how the young men, who upholds our beloved flag in
time of war, protects his mother, sister and sweetheart at home. Second, the
boys and girls, while keeping step with the band music, were marching in and out
and round about, braiding their colors around the pole making a beautiful symbol
of "Union and Strength."

The boys foot race was won by Melvin Romsa. The first girls race was won by
Lydia Keller; she being from the country school. The Mercer girls decided to run
again and the prize was taken by Janne Nelsen. A tug-of-war held our nerve for
several minutes as the boys were pulling back and forth. Finally one side was
tugged across the mark. It was pleasing to see the 10 winning boys sharing their
10 boxes of Cracker jacks with their opponents.

Standing broad jump: O.S. Hjelle, 1st; J.B. Fischer, 2nd; and Ad. Washburn, 3rd.

Running broad jump: O.S. Hjelle, 1s5; Geo. McFaden, 2nd; and J.B. Fischer, 3rd;

Melvin Romsa, the best runner among the boys, was put up to race with Lydia
Kellar, the champion girl runner, but he fell short about ten feet and Lydia
carried of the grand prize, glory and all.

The band played some very fine selections among which were May Day and Home
Sweet Home.

The July 4, 1976, Bicentennial was considered a whopping success with an
estimated attendance of 2,000.

Brush Lake 4th was well attended by about 2,000
Article from Washburn-Leader, 1976

Even though the Bicentennial 4th of July was celebrated in many surrounding
communities, the Brush Lake event was well attended and called a big success. It
was estimated that around 2,000 people had been there sometime during the day.

Besides a Friday night oldtimer's dance and a Saturday night teen dance, the 4th
of July itself started at 8 a.m. with a church service. These services are held
all summer and are sponsored by the McClusky-Mercer Ministerial Association.
Pastor Art Freitag of the Mercer Baptist Church was in charge.

The boat parade, foot races and tug-of-war were enjoyed by everyone. The
tug-of-war winners gave their cash prize back in the community.

A surprisingly good turnout resulted in making the parade a pleasant success. It
included a large horse contingent, 4-H members, old buggies, old cars, Senior
Citizens, candy and tops thrown from floats, square dancers and a flower garden
of Bicentennial dresses and bonnets. A beautiful car brought by Mr. Houseman, a
former Turtle Lake man, was called "best of all."

At 2 o'clock Walt Hjelle, a former Mercerite and our highway commissioner,
reminisced about past 4th of Julys at Brush Lake. Among other things he recalled
the 5¢ rides given by Nels Fibelstad, Roy Nielsen and Halfdon Berge on their big
excursion boat.

The small fry rodeo at 6 o'clock was very competently organized by Bob Schacher
of Wilton with the help of Bob Engelbretson of Regan as announcer. We saw some
good horsemanship as well as quite rough rides by such young boys and girls.
Incidentally, Mr. Engebretson graciously announced the other events of the day
also.

Not all people over 60 years of age signed up at the Senior Citizen's booth.
However, of those who did register, the following ribbons and cash prizes were
awarded: oldest lifetime resident of this community in first, second and third
places were - Jake Rust, Lilly Sackman, and Justine Just. Coming from the
farthest distance were Mrs. Norman Whitman of Port Angeles, Washington, Reed
Argent of Steele, and Glen Hogan of Mandan.

The oldest couples were Mr. and Mrs. Philip Wall of Bismarck, Mr. and Mrs.
Emmanuel Keck of Bismarck and Mr. and Mrs. Julius Sackman of Mercer.

The oldest ladies were Mrs. Philip Wall of Bismarck, Mrs. Dora Jorgensen of
Mercer and Barbara Brockel of Goodrich. In the oldest man category were Mr.
Philip Wall of Bismark, Bill Peterson of Mercer, and Mr. Elmer Peterson of
Mercer.

The day ended with a nice fireworks display furnished by the association.

For many years, there was an Old Settler's Picnic on Labor Day weekend to close
out the summer activities.

Every weekend and vacation time, activities included family picnics, baseball
games, horseshoe pitching, roller-skating, dances, horse and other races and
carnivals. Included also was bathing, swimming, water-skiing, camping and
rodeos.

        Photo: The "Guys" at a picnic: Joe Peterson, Roy Nielsen, Ted Sackmann,
        ???, ???, ???, Halfdon Berge, Emil Schlaht, Leo Schlaht.

        Photo: The old pavilion. (Photo courtesy of Richard Hedahl)

        Photo: The present pavilion.

        Document: (At right) Another ad that was in the 1909 Telegram.

Churches held baptism services and picnics. At the present time, a church
service is held on Sunday morning in the pavilion. There is a leased restaurant
in the pavilion which is operated during the summer months.

From the middle 1940s until the late 1990s, the Meinhardt Skaley family had a
store on the east side of the lake.

The Brush Lake Cabin Owners Association is the governing body that plans the
activities and the maintenance of the area. At the present time, there are at
least 100 cabins around the lake.

During the winter months, there was/is ice-skating on the lake and in recent
years, there is a new community of houses for ice fishing.

Thanks to the foresight of several citizens, the Mercer-Brush Lake Community
Association was founded. From its inception to the current day, the Association
has assured the preservation of a valuable portion of the southwest shores of
Brush Lake - itself an unprecedented valuable natural resource - for the common
good in recreation and leisure by the common man.

Mercer Family Histories

Randy & Elizabeth (Freeberg) Anderson

Elizabeth Carol Freeberg was born in December of 1956. She is the youngest of
the five children born to Evelyn (Norberg) and Conrad Freeberg. She attended
grade school in Mercer and graduated from Turtle Lake-Mercer High School in
1975. She attended North Dakota State University for one year and graduated from
Bismarck State College in 1977 with an Associates Degree in business.

In August of 1977 Elizabeth married Randal Anderson of Turtle Lake in an outdoor
ceremony at her home. They lived in Mercer for a year and then moved to Turtle
Lake, which is still their home.

Randy was a carpenter for 10 years before becoming the rural mail carrier for
the United States Postal Service in Turtle Lake. He still enjoys working with
wood in his shop, playing softball, being on the Turtle Lake Park Board and
helping as an assistant coach for the high school football team.

Elizabeth worked in the family grocery store, as a school aide, as an aide in
the Soil Conservation Office, and sold Tupperware before becoming an employee of
the United States Postal Service. She has been the postmaster in the Coleharbor,
N.D., Post Office since 1993.

Elizabeth and Randy have three children: Kate Emily-1980, Marc Randal-1981, and
Marin Lee-1985. Kate is currently attending the University of Minnesota/Fairview
Hospital in the field of Radiation Therapy. She graduated from Minot State
University in 2003 with a Bachelors of Science degree with a major in
Radiological Technology. Marc is attending Minot State with plans of majoring in
Radiological Technology. Marin is attending Minot State with an interest in
Elementary Education.

Throughout the years the family has been involved in many sports. They enjoy
golfing and spending time at the cabin at Brush Lake.

Joseph Angele

Joseph Angele was the section foreman for the Northern Pacific Railroad and
probably came to Mercer when the railroad reached Mercer. The family lived in
the section house.

He was born about 1868 in South Russia and married Emma in 1896.

The 1910 census lists four children, Nelson, age 13; Gladys, age 11; Carson, age
9; and Elmo, age 2. The family left Mercer in April 1915.

Joseph taught German in the Mercer school.

Information is from items in the Mercer Telegram and the 1910 census.

Anfin & Alice (Howell) Arneson

Anfin Arneson was born in Norway in 1883. He settled in McLean County in 1905
and he farmed the SW¼ of Section 24 in Wise Township. Anfin joined Our Savior's
Lutheran Church February 25, 1928.

Alice Howell was Anfin's housekeeper. Later they moved to Montana, where they
married.

Alice was born in Louisiana between 1878 and 1880. She was the daughter of James
R. Howell and Eleanor Smith. Alice, her father, and her sister, Golda,
homesteaded in Prophet's Township.

Anfin and Alice did not have any children.

Louis &  Borghild (Anderson) Baardson

        Photo: Borghild (Anderson) and Louis Baardson

Borghild M. Anderson was born in Oslo, Norway, Feb. 24, 1879, and came to
America in 1902 as a young girl at the age of about 23. She worked in a hospital
at Valley City, N.D., and was trained as a mid-wife, which then brought her to
Turtle Lake, N.D. She homesteaded 10 miles south of Turtle Lake, N.D. On the
corner of her homestead she gave the Lutheran church land for them to build a
church and cemetery at South St. Olaf. The cemetery is still receiving burials.

Borghild married Louis Baardson on Dec. 23, 1906, in Washburn. Louis Baardson
was born Sept. 15, 1866, in Wisconsin. He and his parents and family came to
North Dakota in 1884 and they homesteaded east of Washburn, N.D. Louis
homesteaded east of Borghild Anderson and east of land his sister, Annie, had
homesteaded. Louis Baardson had two sisters, Annie and Mary, who were also born
in Wisconsin. Louis was mostly buying and selling cattle, even though, he did
farm some which brought the threshing people to his farm. This required a lot of
cooking and trying to find room to feed the threshing crew.

Borghild and Louis Baardson had five children who were born and raised about 10
miles south and one and one-half miles east of Turtle Lake, N.D., or from
Mercer, N.D., it was five miles south and four and one-half miles west.

Their oldest child was Reider Lenhardt Baardson born July 7, 1907, and died
April 19, 1982, at Marin, Calif., and he was married to Maple Nagelmaker. Reider
was a graduate of Turtle Lake High School in the year of 1927. They had one
child, Reid Baardson, who was born June 15, 1942, and died Sept. 15, 1991.

The second child was Leif Morgan Baardson born Sept. 30, 1908. He left home at a
young age and then went into the military. He never married. He died June 12,
1959, and is buried in the Presidio military cemetery in San Francisco, Calif.

Their third child was Raymond Baardson born Oct. 10, 1910, and graduated from
Turtle Lake High School in 1929. He was in the military and never did marry. He
died Oct. 9, 1958, and is buried in the Presidio military cemetery in San
Francisco, Calif.

The fourth child was Lucille Baardson born in 1912 and graduated from Turtle
Lake High School in the year of 1929. She went to Minneapolis, Minn., for
nursing training. She went to California and she married George Jahns. They had
two children, Allen Jahns is married to Sharon who lives in Hawaii and they have
two boys. Gary Jahns was married to Cindy and they had three children, Andrew
Jahns, Brian Jahns and Amy Jahns. Gary remarried Carman and is now living in
Encintas, Calif. Lucille (Baardson) Jahns divorced and married Glen Fox. At the
present (2002) they are making their home in Carlsbad, Calif.

The fifth child was Joy Baardson, born March 26, 1915, and graduated from Turtle
Lake High School in 1933. She went to a business school in Bismarck and later
married Carl Peterson. She was divorced and went to California. Her brother,
Reider, mother (Borghild) and she opened a restaurant called "The Purple Cow."
She later married Harold Dunn who had a daughter, Liz, her mother died giving
birth to her. They lived in Des Moines, Iowa, where they operated the Dunn
Manufacturing Company. Joy and Harold had a son, Richard Dunn, who at present
lives in Texas. Joy died Feb. 4, 1997, in Iowa.

Louis Baardson died Oct. 6, 1936, of kidney complications in the Bismarck
hospital at the age of 70. He is buried with his parents in the cemetery that
Borghild gave to the church (South St. Olaf Lutheran) on her homesteaded land by
the Red Trail. Borghild Baardson, Reider and Raymond sold the farm to Otto and
Louise (Heinle) Laib. They all moved out to California and later Borghild went
to live with Joy in Iowa. She went to stay with Lucille in California where she
died on May 17, 1963, and is buried in California.

Emanuel & Lydia (Rust) Bauer

Lydia was born July 30, 1913, north of Mercer, N.D., to Samuel and Lena Rust Sr.
She went to a rural school and worked for neighbors helping cook.

She married Emanuel Bauer of Butte on Sept. 20, 1932. They began farming and
were there for 30 years, then they moved to Minot, N.D.

Lydia worked as a nurse's aide for 12 years and helped her husband as janitor at
the Presbyterian Church for 17 years. Emanuel died August of 1973. Lydia moved
into Mercer in 1978 where she still lives.

Their son, Linus, and his wife, Myrtle, live on the home place. Lydia has two
granddaughters, Melissa and Janell, and two great-granddaughters.

Jacob & Freida (Gruszie) Bauer

Jacob Bauer was born Nov. 13, 1912, to William Bauer and Magdalena (Wanner)
Bauer on their homestead at Coleharbor. At the age of four, his family moved to
a farm southwest of Mercer.

On Oct. 24, 1937, Jacob married Freida Gruszie. Freida was born on Sept. 22,
1913, the daughter of Simon and Caroline Gruszie of Medina. Jacob and Freida
lived and farmed with Jacob's parents for approximately two years. Then they
rented a farm northwest of Mercer for five years. This is where their first
daughter, Mary Ann, was born on Jan. 24, 1942, and died about six days later.
Their second daughter, Diane Irene, was born on Feb. 24, 1944, in Turtle Lake.

        Photo: Jacob and Freida Bauer and their daughter Diane, taken in 1997.

In the spring of 1945, Jacob and Freida Bauer purchased a farm three miles south
and one mile west of Mercer. A son, Myron Dale Bauer, was born on Jan. 5, 1953.
Jacob and Freida farmed until the spring of 1963 when they sold the farm to a
nephew, Fredrick Fisher.

They moved to Ashley where Jacob was a mechanic in a garage for one year. In the
summer of 1964 Jacob and Freida moved to Bismarck where Jacob worked for 17
years as a janitor at Saxvik Elementary School.

Jacob and Freida (Gruszie) Bauer had three children:

Mary Ann Bauer passed away after living approximately six days.

Diane Irene Bauer married Orland Isaak. (See family history, page 259)

Myron Dale Bauer married Shirline Just and were later divorced. (See family
history, page 200)

Johnny & JoAnne (Grueneich) Bauer

Johnny Bauer, son of William and Magdalena (Wanner) Bauer was born at the family
farm near Mercer on Oct. 12, 1926. He was one of eight children and is the
youngest son. He attended school through the third grade having to stay at home
as he was needed to help with the farm work.

        Photo: JoAnne, Clinton, Johnny and Barbara Bauer

It was at an evangelism meeting at a rural church northwest of Wilton, Rev.
William Johns was preaching, that John met his bride-to-be, Miss JoAnne
Grueneich, daughter of Benjamin and Esther (Flemmer) Grueneich of Washburn. They
lived 22 miles driving distance away by way of the Red Trail township road.

John and JoAnne were married in October 1954, at Miles City, Mont. They remember
well the friends who held a chivaree party on the farm. Delmer and Raymond
played the accordion and guitar. George accompanied them with the harmonica.
Roger played the organ that stood in the living room. How they could play!

John tells of binding, cutting with the header when the grain was too short,
shocking the sheaves, hauling bundles and threshing at eight years of age along
with his father and brother Jake. The crew included: the Fischer boys, Emil,
Fred, John, Fred Wagner, Otto Wagner with Gottlieb helping haul bundles at times
when he could be away from his store. John tells that barley and rye were
miserable to shock because of the long beards barley has and long stems on the
rye bundles making it difficult to keep them tight.

They have two children: Clinton and Barbara. Clint nicknamed Rosey and Barb
nicknamed Susy were born at Bismarck on Feb. 23, 1956, and Oct. 24, 1957. As a
little fellow, Clint was raking, cutting and baling hay. He operated the big 930
Case when only 11 years old.

Thanks to their daughter, Barb, having been employed with the FBI at Washington,
D.C., they had the opportunity to do some traveling. They made two trips to
Washington, D.C., taking a different route each time.

Neighbors living near them on the farm were Johnny Bosserts, Fred Laibs, Bill
Wanners, Miney Wagners, Fred Fischers and Jake Bauers.

Remembrances are:

Hearing the coyotes howling in the evening, listening to the bull frogs croaking
in the sloughs, the sweet smell of the newly cut hay, raking hay with Carlie and
Joe (team of horses) hitched to the dump rake in 1955-56 and 57, seeing the
fireflies "sparkle" at night in the summer, North Dakota's beautiful sunsets,
the beautiful three-day "Indian Summer" in autumn, the gorgeous "Northern
Lights" dancing in the sky at night, handmilking 26 milk cows and selling cream
and trading 12 dozen crates of eggs for groceries.

Clint graduated from Mercer Grade School on May 22, 1970.

The family moved to a farm at New Salem Township, Newfolden, Minn., on May 23,
1970.

Clint and Barb "read" for Rev. Rodney Stueland and were confirmed at Westaker
Free Lutheran Church on Oct. 15, 1972.

Myron & Shirline (Just) Bauer

Myron Dale Bauer was born on Jan. 5, 1953. He is the son of Jacob Bauer and
Freida (Gruszie) Bauer. Myron went to the Mercer school for grades 1-3, to
Ashley for grade four and to Bismarck for the remainder.

He graduated from Bismarck High School and then moved to Minneapolis, Minn.
There he married Shirline Just on Feb. 17, 1974. Shirline was originally from
Bismarck. Myron and Shirline divorced later.

Myron and Shirline are the parents of three children:

Johnnas Casey Bauer is a stepson.

Melody Bauer was born on Feb. 7, 1979. Melody is married and has a daughter,
Valerie, born on Sept. 10, 1996, and a son, Dominic, born on April 25, 1999.

Aaron Bauer was born on Feb. 12, 1981.

William & Magdalena (Wanner) Bauer

Karl and Eva Bauer migrated from Germany to Russia. Many families left for
America but Karl and Eva remained in Russia with many other families.

During the war years of the Bolsheviks, their sons, along with the sons from
other families, were drafted into the Russian army. They had no choice. Life in
the Russian army was hard. During the war years many drafted sons were sent to
Siberian war camps.

        Photo: William and Magdalena on their wedding day.

Karl and Eva Bauer were determined that not all of their sons should be drafted
into the Russian army. With sad and heavy hearts, the decision was made that
William would sail for America at the age of 19. With war clouds darkening close
to home, William and other young German men of army age bid farewell to family
and friend and the country they loved and sailed for America. The parting was
not easy for these young men. With tears in their eyes they kept focused on the
shoreline until it disappeared.

The trip across the ocean was rough and slow. After weeks of sailing the ship
finally arrived at Ellis Island where all passengers stepped off unto dry land.

All passengers were detained at Ellis Island for several days. Anyone with a
communicable disease was not allowed to step off but had to return to Russia.
After several days of inspection and customs they were allowed to step off unto
land, New York, the melting pot of the world.

Because of all the immigrants who stepped off ship at New York City, permanent
work was hard to find. William remembered his father telling him that there were
cousins living in North Dakota. William decided to work his way west, arriving
at Coleharbor.

William worked four years as a farm laborer. Wages were poor. In 1908, William
took up homestead land in McLean County. With borrowed horses and borrowed
implements, he started farming, living in a one-room shack. This was his home.
It was in this area he was introduced to Magdalena Wanner, a beautiful blond,
slim ambitious young lady. Born in the United States, Magdalena was used to hard
work. She lost her mother at the early age of nine. She went to live with an
uncle and aunt for two years. She worked hard and much was expected from her.
She became a full-fledged homemaker in those two years. She learned to cook,
bake and knit in her new home.

        Photo: The William Bauer family in 1939. (Front, from left) Emma
        Fischer, William Bauer, Magdalena Bauer, Martha Hoppe; (back) Johnny
        Bauer, Elizabeth Laib, Freida Hultin, Jacob Bauer.

William and Magdalena were married in December of 1907. After their marriage,
they lived on the homestead northeast of Coleharbor. They farmed for eight to
ten years. In the spring of 1917, they sold their homestead land and bought land
southwest of Mercer, which they farmed. Magdalena worked alongside her husband.
She worked hard doing more than her share of work. Life for William and
Magdalena was not easy. They experienced crop failures, drought, dust storms,
grasshoppers, fires and hailstorms, but they survived. Through all these
hardships their faith in God never wavered. They made their living off the land
they loved and tilled.

William drove the school bus for many years, driving the bus when the first
child entered school and drove the majority of time during those years. Some
years during winter months when snow was too deep for a vehicle, a covered
sleigh was used. Those were long days. He left home at 4 a.m. and returned home
late at night, 10 p.m.

Magdalena was working outdoors, milking, feeding cattle, and cleaning barn. Her
days were busy. William got home in the evening and he would bed the horses and
made preparation for the next day route.

William and Magdalena had eight children. Their first child, Lydia, was born in
1909 and developed whooping cough and died in her mother's arms. The second
child, Frederick, died at the age of 13 from an horse/wagon accident.

Jacob, their third child, grew up on the family farm. He married Frieda Gruzie
and they farmed near Mercer. They sold their farm later on and moved to Bismarck
where he was a school janitor for many years.

Emma Bauer met and married Emil Fischer. They farmed southwest of Mercer. Since
Emil's death, Emma has been living with her eldest son, Fredrick and Rose
Fischer.

Elizabeth married Edwin Laib who farmed for many years. They now live in
Bismarck.

Frieda married Irvin Hultin, a Methodist pastor. They now live at Minot. Frieda
continues to work as a nurse. They have one son, David, who is married and lives
in Fargo. David and Judy (Duchscher) Hultin are parents of two girls, Emily and
Tessa.

John married JoAnn and they live at Thief River Falls, Minn.

Martha married Norman Hoppe who farms near Underwood.

William and Magdalena are both deceased. Their memories live on.

Samuel & Elizabeth (Diede) Beierle

Samuel Beierle was born June 3, 1894, in the Kronental, North Caucasus (Russia)
to Daniel and Karolina (Esslinger) Beierle. He was the sixth of 10 children,
with eight being born in the Kronental and two in America.

His family immigrated to America in 1899 and homesteaded one mile south of
Goodrich. Sam attended school in Goodrich. He served in the U.S. Army in World
War I and in 1918 was sent to France, where he fought in well-known battles
including the Battle of Verdun and the Argon Drive, where his division suffered
17,000 (about one-half) killed, wounded and captured. He came through the war
without a wound and returned to Sheridan County where he worked various jobs.

        Photo: Samuel and Elizabeth Beierle

Elizabeth Diede was born Nov. 30, 1895, near Manfred, N.D., in Wells County to
Gottlieb and Pauline (Endres) Diede. She grew up helping her dad farm in the
area and attended rural school.

Samuel and Elizabeth were married April 4, 1921, at McClusky. They lived at
McClusky for a few years and then moved to Coleharbor where Sam had his own shoe
shop and Lizzie, as she was known to family and friends, bought cream.

They later moved to Garrison where Sam operated another shoe shop and Lizzie was
a cook at the Garrison school.

They then moved to a farm three miles east of Mercer where they farmed and
raised sheep. In 1944 they moved into Mercer, living on the west side of town,
where they built a new home. After a few years they moved to the east edge of
town.

They moved a second small house onto the property where Lizzie's father lived
until his death. Sam had a shoe shop on Main Street for a few years, he farmed
west of town and served as Mercer's "cop" for a time. Lizzie also cooked at the
Mercer School.

For several years in the 1960s, Sam and Lizzie moved to Washburn during the
winter months into the living quarters at the McLean County jailhouse where
Lizzie cleaned and cooked for the prisoners.

Sam died on Oct. 17, 1976, and Lizzie continued to make her home in Mercer until
1977 when she moved to a retirement home in Mandan. She died on Feb. 18, 1978.
They are buried at the McClusky Cemetery.

Sam and Lizzie had seven children (in birth order): Pearl (Joe) Onsberg, Roy,
Albert, Leota (Leo) Reiser, Lesley, Thomas and Joy (Herbert) Schneider. The only
surviving child is Joy.

Thomas W. & Alma L. (Gessele) Beierle

Thomas Wesley Beierle was born April 20, 1934, at Coleharbor, N.D., to Samuel
and Elizabeth (Diede) Beierle. He lived in Coleharbor until the age of five and
then moved to Garrison where he started school. Several years later the family
moved to a farm three miles east of Mercer, and then into Mercer in 1944. Tom
attended school in Mercer and Fairbault, Minn. He enlisted in the Army in 1954
to serve in the Korean War. After an honorable discharge two years later, Tom
came home to Mercer and worked road construction. A year later, he started
working as a welder and equipment operator for McLean County.

Alma Leona Gessele was born Dec. 1, 1933, on the family farm ten and one-half
miles southeast of Mercer to Edward and Katherine (Bender) Gessele. She is the
youngest of seven children. Alma started country school, two and one-half miles
southwest of the farm and walked to school together with the neighbor children.
She only spoke German when she started school so another child would interpret
between her and the teacher. In seventh grade Alma came to school in Mercer,
staying with the Andrew Rust family until her parents moved to town two years
later. Alma graduated from Mercer High School in 1951. She then worked in
Bismarck and Washburn until moving back home several years later.

Tom and Alma were married on Dec. 7, 1958, and made their home in a little white
house on the west side of Mercer. A daughter, Vicky Lynn, was born to them on
Nov. 13, 1960. For several years in the early 1960s, Tom became Mercer's "cop,"
and he also transported the mail between the area towns while continuing to work
for the county. Tom and Alma also bought some land, Minneapolis Moline tractors
and other pieces of old equipment to start farming. In the latter 1960s, they
purchased 16 acres of land, one-half mile east of Mercer where they built a
feedlot to raise cattle. They bought the former Ben Hjelle home on the east side
of town and after extensive remodeling, moved there in 1976.

Tom served as a councilman for the City of Mercer and was a Turtle Lake-Mercer
school board member in the 1970s.

        Photos: Alma Beierle and Tom Beierle with their daughter Vicky Lynn.

Loving a challenge, Tom entered the race for McLean County Commissioner in 1978
and won the election. He served one term (four years) and was re-elected in 1986
continuing to serve another three terms. He experienced many rewarding
accomplishments during his 16 years in office.

Tom retired form the County Commission in December 1998. He continued to keep
busy especially enjoying driving his Model A and T cars to neighboring towns.
Tom died on Dec. 21, 2002. He was laid to rest at the Mercer Hillside Cemetery.
Alma continues to make her home in Mercer.

        Photo: Tom Beierle

Adolph & Magdalena (Singer) Bender

Adolph Singer was born Nov. 6, 1886, in Kassel, Odessa, South Russia, a German
farmer colony located about 70 miles north-northwest of the nearest major city
of Odessa on the Black Sea.

He was the son of Johann Bender and Friederika Weisser. On Nov. 15, 1910, he
married Magdalena Singer in rural Mercer, N.D. She was born Aug. 9, 1892, the
daughter of Christoph Singer and Christiana Klotzbuecher in Hoffnungstal,
Bessarabia, South Russia.

Adolph and his sister Katharina immigrated to the United States in 1905, setting
sail from Rotterdam, Holland. They arrived at a Canadian port and traveled by
train to Chicago, arriving at that city on Feb. 29. Based on Katharina's
recollections, the two journeyed to Fulton, S.D., and later in April, 1908,
moved to rural Mercer, N.D. It was here that he met Magdalena Singer, who had
arrived in this country with her parents in 1903. The Singers set sail on the S.
S. Assyria from Hamburg, Germany, April 15, 1903, landed at the port of Halifax,
Nova Scotia, and traveled by rail to Winnipeg, Manitoba. They remained here for
a month to earn enough money for train fare to Harvey, N.D. They were met in
Harvey by Wilhelm Goll of Martin, N.D., who accompanied the immigrants on their
wagon journey across now Sheridan County and to their homestead claim in McLean
County, the SW¼, Sec. 32-146-79.

Rev. W.L. Keller performed the Bender/Singer nuptial the fall of 1910, with the
bride's brother, Johann Georg (John G.) Singer, and friends Karl Berg and
Christian Kleingaertner acting as witnesses.

        Photo: The Bender family: (from left) Henry and Katherine Gessele,
        Adolph and Magdelena Bender and Jacob and Louisa Bender. This photo was
        taken about 1912 or 1913.

Following the marriage, the couple pursued farming north of Regan, N.D. In 1917,
the Benders returned to the Mercer area upon purchasing about 240 acres of land
from Magdalena's brother Johann Georg Singer. The farmstead, located in the NE¼
and the E½ of the SE¼ of Sec. 6, Twp. 145-79 (Park Township) had no buildings,
so the couple set to erecting a barn. For the interim, the structure provided
shelter for the animals, and the family established living quarters upstairs in
the haymow. Eventually they constructed a bona fide home. All the while
Magdalena spent anxious hours in fear her children would fall through open
chutes from the mow to the animal stalls below.

That same year of 1917 Adolph took belated interest in U.S. citizenship. Along
with brother-in-law Henry Gessele and friend Jakob Just as witnesses, he
journeyed to district court in Washburn, N.D., and filed a Declaration of
Intention for Naturalization. Adolph became a citizen on May 26, 1921.

Over the years Adolph fell into poor health and the couple retired from farming
in 1943. They moved to Bismarck, N.D., and immediately Magdalena took up
employment as a maid at the Grand Pacific Hotel. With a starting salary of $60 a
month, she stuck with her career for 24 years and retired at age 75. For the
next 20 years Magdalena devoted all her energy to a backyard garden and orchard.
At age 94 she had become so prolific in growing fruits and vegetables and such
an expert in the art of canning and preservation, she appeared in a special
feature article in a 1986 issue of the Bismarck Tribune.

After a lingering illness, Adolph died June 15, 1952, in Bismarck, N.D.
Magdalena moved to Seminole, Okla., in August, 1989, to live in a nursing home
near her son Otto. She died there Oct. 27, 1989. The Benders are buried in
Fairview Cemetery in Bismarck, N.D.

Adolph and Magdalena were the parents of eight children. Four died in infancy.
The surviving children were:

Martha, born April 15, 1913, Regan, N.D., married John Fischer Oct. 13, 1932,
Mercer, N.D., died Feb. 18, 2002, Bismarck, N.D.

John, born May 8, 1914, Regan, N.D., died Sept. 10, 1983, New Salem, N.D.

Emma, born Jan. 6, 1918, Mercer, N.D., married Christian Schell.

Otto, born May 19, 192?, Mercer, N.D., married June 3, 1950, Bismarck, N.D.

Carl & Frances (Peterson) Bender

Frances Peterson was born on Feb. 22, 1910, in rural McLean County, the daughter
of Martin and Milly Biggs Peterson. She attended rural schools and graduated
from Mercer High School in 1929.

She married Carl Bender in 1937 in Turtle Lake. They farmed near McClusky and
Frances taught rural schools near Goodrich. After living in Topeka, Kansas, for
12 years, Frances returned to Bismarck and resumed teaching in rural Bismarck
area schools.

She died on March 29, 1992, and is buried in the Sunset Memorial Gardens in
Bismarck.

        Photo: Frances Bender

Frances had a daughter, Mary Crum, and she and Carl had five children: Chuck,
Calvin, Ray, Kathy and Diane.

Jacob & Louisa (Gessele) Bender

Jacob Bender was born in Kassel, South Russia, Aug. 18, 1879, where he grew up
living with foster parents, Mr. and Mrs. William Finck, and working as a farm
laborer.

In 1897, he immigrated to the United States with his mother, Christina Bender.
They settled in the Eureka, S.D., area.

In 1899, his mother married Carl Gessele, who had immigrated from Odessa,
Russia, in 1884.

In 1902, Jacob married his stepsister, Louisa Gessele at Venturia, N.D. Their
oldest son, John, was born there.

In the spring of 1903, they came to McLean County along with their parents and
Louisa's sisters, Johanna, Rosa, and Amelia, and her brothers, Edward and Henry
Gessele.

Louisa, her young son, and Jacob's mother came by train to Wilton, the town of
Mercer was not yet established. Jacob and the rest of the family traveled by
wagon and horses.

They settled in what is now Park Township and later homesteaded seven miles
south and one mile east of Mercer. There they built a sod house. In 1916 they
built a two-story, eight-room house, where they lived and farmed until they
retired and moved into Mercer in 1952.

When they homesteaded in McLean County, there was no Lutheran Church nearby, so
they attended a community Reformed Church. Later they helped organize a Lutheran
congregation and held services in the homes until 1906 when they built Zion
Lutheran Church with Pastor William W. Keller as their pastor.

In 1919 they helped build a new church which was dedicated in November of 1919,
seven miles south and one mile west of Mercer.

Jacob and Louisa were both life-long members of Zion Lutheran Church.

Jacob became interested in politics and was instrumental in helping elect
William Langer as governor.

In the year 1936, he was elected delegate to the county N.P.L. convention at
Garrison. His son, Henry, took Jacob and Henry Gessele to Mercer by horses and
sled. There they joined Carl Littke and Jacob Braun. These men went to Turtle
Lake by train, by stage to Underwood and by train to Garrison.

        Photo: The Jacob Bender family: (front) Henry; (middle) Jacob with
        Esther on his lap, Emma, Louisa, Hilda; (back) Justina, Lydia, John and
        Bertha. Photo taken in 1915.

Jacob was elected delegate to the State N.P.L. convention at Bismarck. The roads
were blocked and the only way out of Garrison was by train to Max, to Drake, and
then to Jamestown, where the other men took the train to Mercer. Jacob continued
on by train to Bismarck. After the convention was over in Bismarck, Jake caught
a ride as far as Wilton. Again the road to Mercer was blocked with snow so he
walked home, a distance of about 18 miles.

        Photo: Martha and Edna, 1923

        Photo: Edna in 1928

Jacob and Louisa had ten children.

John left North Dakota in 1928 and traveled for some time, then settled at
Yorkville, Ill., where he married Marjorie Irwin in 1939. They did some truck
farming and he was a carpenter. Both are now deceased. They had five sons and
three grandchildren. One son died at birth. The others are John Jr., Harold,
David, and Richard.

Lydia of Underwood, N.D., married Fred Eman in 1928. They had 10 children, 16
grandchildren, and two great-grandchildren. One daughter died at birth. Others
are sons Melvin, Donald, James, Carlyle, and Larry. The daughters are Ruby
Lounder, Irene Johannes, Marjorie Jans, and Sharon Boozer. Lydia and her husband
Fred Eman farmed at Coleharbor for several years. She is deceased.

Bertha, Fargo, N.D., married Edward Kleingartner in 1922. He is now deceased.
They had 12 children, 30 grandchildren and five great-grandchildren. Their
children are Gertrude, who died at age 23; Dorothy, who died in infancy; Olinda
McCabe, Alice Reile, Mary Lou Levin, Bella McKenzie, Herbert, Arthur, Dale,
Franklin, Edward Jr., and Alan. Bertha and her husband Ed farmed south of Mercer
for several years then moved to a farm near McClusky. When Ed died, Bertha was
left with 11 children, age three months to 20 years. She moved into McClusky and
went into the café business. Later she moved to Fargo where she worked in cafes
and managed several coffee shops. She is deceased.

Justina, Mercer, N.D., married Emanuel Just in 1923. They had 11 children, 23
grandchildren, and one great-grandchild. Three children died in infancy. Others
are sons Leo, Elton and Myron; daughters are Viola Fredrickson, Alice Neumiller,
Loretta Schiermeister, Verline Jensen, and Rosina Free. Justina and Emanuel
farmed south of Mercer, living on the same farm for 50 years. He died shortly
after they celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary in 1973. Justina died in
1976.

Henry, Underwood, N.D., worked at various jobs until he entered the Army in W.W.
II. After one year he received a medical discharge. He never married. He is
deceased.

Hilda, Turtle Lake, N.D., married Philip Flemmer in 1934. They have two sons and
four granddaughters. Their sons are Meinhardt and Garry.

Emma, Barnesville, Minn., married Harry Dallmann in 1940. They have three
children and five grandchildren. Children are Louisa Rethmeier, Thomas and
Clyde. She is deceased.

Esther, Lancaster, Penn., married John Howry in 1944. They have one son, James,
and four grandchildren. Esther and John moved first to California, then to
Oregon where he was in the meat business. Later they moved to his hometown of
Lancaster, Penn., where they were in the meat and grocery business for several
years. She died in 2003.

Martha, Bismarck, N.D., married Holdrich Mayer in 1939. They have four children,
eight grandchildren. Their sons are Holdrich Jr., Orville, and Gordon, and their
daughter is Beverly Kreitel. Martha and Holdrich have lived in various towns
where he taught school.

        Photo: Louisa and Jacob Bender on their 50th wedding anniversary in
        1952.

Edna, Mercer, N.D., married Ernest Littke in 1940. She died on Nov. 24, 2004.

Jacob and Louisa celebrated their golden wedding anniversary in 1952 on the farm
they homesteaded. Jacob Bender died in 1957 and Louisa died in 1969, both are
buried in Zion Lutheran Cemetery, seven miles south and one mile west of Mercer.

Most of this history was taken from the McLean County Book, 1978.

William & Ella (Laib) Berg

Ella Laib was born May 13, 1926, to Friedrich Laib and Karolina (Kleingartner)
Laib at Mercer, N.D. She was raised and educated five miles south and about two
and one-half miles west of Mercer, N.D.

On May 12, 1946, she married William (Bill) Berg who was born Feb. 28, 1922, to
Samuel Berg and Louisa (Hoffman) Berg north of Wilton, N.D. Bill was raised and
educated in the Wilton area. After their marriage they moved on a farm three
miles south of Sterling, N.D., for about 15 years, when they sold the farm and
moved to Billings, Mont. Bill worked on construction and then they moved north
of Kalispel, Mont.

They have one son Gary Berg who was born in Bismarck, N.D., and is living in
Miles City, Mont., working for Bureau of Land Management. They also have a
daughter, Cindy Berg, who was born in Bismarck, N.D., and is now living north of
Kalispel, Mont.

Ella (Laib) Berg died in 1996 and William (Bill) Berg died in 1998.

Peter & Gurina (Sundlie) Bergan

        Photo: Gurina Bergan

        Photo: Peter Bergan

Peter Bergan was born in Wisconsin in 1868. He married Gurina Sundlie in 1910.
She was born in Rothsay, Minnesota, in 1885. They first lived in Lincoln Valley,
north of McClusky. They then moved north of Mercer and their neighbors were the
Jacobsons and Postals, near the lakes. Then they moved about 3½ miles south of
Mercer and their neighbors were the Pedersons. Eventually they moved into Mercer
and lived there until 1946, when Peter passed away. Gurina then moved to
McClusky, North Dakota.

Peter and Gurina Bergan had six children: Terrence, Kenneth, Pearl, Alvin, May,
and Irene.

Terrence was born in 1910 and married Cora Glaser. They had five children:
Sidney, Virginia, Gloria, Terrance, and Randy. Terrence died in 1988.

Kenneth was born in 1911 and married Verna Winge in 1939. They moved to
Bismarck, Arkansas in 1950. They had seven children: Dean, Don, Duane, Darwin,
David, Dalton, and Delores. Kenneth died in 1990, and Verna lives in Arkansas.

Pearl was born in 1913 and married Walter Shol. They had four children: Audrey,
Patricia, Faye, and Eugene. Walter also had three children from a previous
marriage.

Alvin was born in 1915 and married Francis Bradford. He died in 1992.

May was born in 1917 and married Arthur "Artie" Singer. They had six children:
Norma, Cleon, Sharon, Kelly, Karen (who died as an infant), and Stanley.

Irene was born in 1922 at Mercer. (Terrence, Kenneth, and Pearl attended
Medicine Hill School #4 when they lived north of Mercer.)

Irene remembers walking 3½ miles to school in Mercer when they lived south of
town. She graduated from high school in 1940, and was the only one of her
siblings to graduate. After Pedersons moved to town, Irene stayed with them
during the winter months so she could attend school. She said that the
Schindlers had the hotel at that time. Some of her classmates were Doris
Pederson, Ella Wing, and Beemer "Bea" Norris. Bea's parents were Sam and Doxie
and they ran the café in Mercer for awhile.

After graduating from high school, Irene, and Olga Stradinger moved to Bismarck
to learn welding, as part of the war effort. They completed their training and
then went to Fargo, but could not find any welding there. Irene then moved to
Burbank, California where her brother, Alvin was living. She worked on B17 and
B29 wings as a riveter at Vega Aircraft. During that same time, Alvin worked for
Lockhead.

Irene married Duane Vennie and they had four children. Duane was born in 1946,
Dennis in 1947, Maureen in 1948, and Vaughn in 1949. They lived in several
different places before settling down in Minneapolis in 1953, where Irene still
resides.

Halfdan & Anna (Blasel) Berge

Halfdan Berge was born in Ada, Minnesota on July 27, 1986 to Norwegian
immigrants, Bjorgulv Berge and Martha Marie Undeland who homesteaded in Norman
County, Minnesota.

Halfdan's father, Bjorgulv died April 8, 1888. His mother pregnant with a third
child was left to care for three year old Clara and 1½ year old Halfdan. Bjorgo
Martin, named for both of his parents was born March 14, 1888. Halfdan's sister
Clara came to Mercer as a teacher and then married widower Edwin Hedahl.

Halfdan, while living at Mercer in 1913, decided that his sister Clara and his
mother Martha, still living in Minnesota needed some form of transportation and
suggested they buy a horse he thought gentle and a buggy from James Rice.
Clara's Uncle Martinson was visiting in Mercer and would drive the buggy the 200
miles back to Minnesota. The horse, Sadie, seemed gentle at first but soon
became frisky and hard to handle. Clara was driving to town one day when she
met a car and Sadie bolted, snapping the top off of Clara's shiny new buggy.
When Halfdan heard about the incident, he went to Minnesota with a different bit
for the horse after which Clara could control Sadie.

Halfdan wore many hats during the early days of Mercer. It is not known when he
came to Mercer, but in the 1910 census, he was identified as single, laborer and
salesman in a general store. He also owned the Mercer Telephone Company that
was located in the Hedahl Store for a few years. He was active in the sports
field and at one time his baseball team was known as Berg's Cubs. In addition,
he also played basketball with the "town" team. He was a member of the Mercer
City Band where he played the snare drum.

He is best known as the long time manager of the Andrews Grain Elevator (the
middle one). He continued to be involved in community activities until shortly
before his death on August 27, 1955. He is buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

        Photo: Anna Berge in 1962.

        Photo: Halfdan Berge in his younger years.

Halfdan married Anna Blasel on Thanksgiving Day 1914. She was born on April 5,
1889. It is unknown when she came to Mercer. She was active in Mercer community
activities and was a member of the Mercer Women's Study Club. She died on April
16, 1965, and is buried in the Mercer cemetery.

Halfdan and Anna had three children; Merle (Doxie Norris), history below, Marion
(Richard Haibeck), and June (Matthew Fettig) history on page 229,

Information from Mercer Telegram, 1910 Census, Cemetery Records and Clara Berge
Hedahl Memories.

Merle & Doxie (Schroyer) Berge

Merle was born on August 24, 1915, in the Mercer Hospital. He was the son of
Halfdan and Anna (Blaesel) Berge. He attended the Mercer School graduating from
Mercer High School in 1932. Merle served in the military in World War II. He
was a mail carrier, general handyman and mechanic.

        Photo: Merle and Doxie Berge

Merle married Doxie (Schroyer) Norris (widow of Sam Norris). Doxie was born on
July 17, 1902, in South Dakota. Doxie and Sam had one daughter, Beemer. She
operated Sam's Café also known as Doxie's Café after her husband Sam died.
Merle and Doxie operated Doxie's Café until 1957. Beemer died in 2000.

Merle and Doxie moved to Bismarck where Merle was employed with the North Dakota
State Highway Department. Doxie was a long time employee of the Drumstick Café
in Bismarck.

Doxie died on December 21, 1979, and Merle died on December 24, 1990. Both are
buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

Jens & Sarah (Christensen) Bille

Jens Christian Bille was born February 27, 1883, at Luck, Wisconsin, a Danish
community. His father, Hans Jensen Bille, was born May 18, 1846, in Denmark.
Jens' siblings were Anna (Blicher), Bodil "Christine" (Paulson), Hans "Jorgen",
and a half brother, Emil Brockmand Bille.

Jens filed for a homestead on May 20, 1905 on the W½ NE¼ and E½ NW¼ of Section
14 of Wise Township, five miles north of present day Mercer, North Dakota. He
built a little dugout shack south of what is now McLean County #10.

A July 1908 Mercer Telegram reported Jens Bille had a serious attack of
appendicitis and was seen by Dr. Beardsley. He recovered and continued to farm
his homestead. The October 30, 1908 Mercer Telegram reported, "Jens Bille has
moved his barn over onto Miss Sarah Christensen's homestead." Jens made final
commutation proof on his homestead at Washburn on November 2, 1908. His
witnesses were Nels Christensen, Martin Christensen, Chris Skow and Julius
Johnson. His patent number was 68198.

On January 7, 1909, Jens married his neighbor, Sarah Christensen. Sarah had
filed on a homestead in Section 24 of Wise Township on April 7, 1906. She was
born September 11, 1883, at Hutchinson, Minnesota, to Peter and Johanna
(Nielsen) Christensen.

        Photo: Jens and Sarah (Christensen) Bille on their wedding day in 1909.

Jens and Sarah lived on her homestead for several years, which was one mile east
of her parent's homestead. Sarah made 5-year proof on her homestead on May 10,
1912, in McClusky.

Prairie fires were always a danger in the early days. The April 30, 1909, Mercer
Telegram reported a big prairie fire north of Mercer. It started near Maxwell,
which was near Duane Schaefer's present day farm. It burned the Bailey boy's
shack, and extended southeast past Jens Bille's homestead before it was
extinguished.

Jens' brother, Jorgen, lived at Mercer for a short while. The February 10, 1911,
Mercer Telegram reported "Peter P. Christensen sold his son, Jorgen's farm to
H.J. Bille, who bought it for his son, H. Jourgen Bille. The farm lies about 8
miles north of Mercer, and has about 25 acres broke. The selling price was only
$1,600, just about what it would cost now days to prove up a claim." Jorgen
Bille also worked as a clerk and bookkeeper in the Farmer's Store in Mercer. He
resigned in December of 1911, and moved back to Luck, Wisconsin.

Sarah and Jens had five children born at Mercer; Florence, Agnes, Vernon, Clara
and Paul. All except Paul were born on Sarah's homestead.

When the children were old enough to start school, they moved onto Pastor
Petersen's homestead to be closer to Wise School #1, known as the Spout school.

Jens and Sarah milked cows, and the March 1, 1918, Mercer Telegram reported J.C.
Bille churned 3¼ pounds of butter from two day's milk from one cow.

Florence Johanna Bille, the oldest, was born February 21, 1910. The Mercer
Telegram reported that she was delivered by Dr. Paulson of Turtle Lake, and that
she was "the prettiest girl in the union."

Florence was a beautiful, sweet child with platinum blond hair, blue eyes, and a
complexion that matched a china head doll. She was most dear. In the winter of
1924 she became ill, and the doctor came several times. Her illness was referred
to as an infection of the bone behind her ear.

Florence died February 12, 1924 at the age of 14. Her funeral was held in their
living room and she was buried in St. Ansgar's Danish Cemetery north of Mercer.

        Photo: (Front, from left) Vernon and Clara Bille; (back) Florence and
        Agnes Bille.

Agnes Bille married Martin Ockert, son of Karl, in December 1933 at St. Olaf
parsonage. They lived in Mercer for a few years and Martin was a truck driver.
Then they moved to the Jake Nelson farm, where they lived for about 1½ years.
Their children attended Sprout school at that time. They moved into Mercer in
1943, and Martin ran the corner garage that later became Heim's. Ockerts lived
in the Singer house at this time.

In 1945 the Ockert family moved to Turtle Lake, where Martin operated Ockert's
Garage. Agnes ran a restaurant for awhile in a building she rented from Dr.
Heinzeroth. That building later became the Lindteigen Construction office.
Martin moved a house into Turtle Lake beside his garage, which was just south of
the Round House.

Agnes and Martin had seven children. Arliss was born in 1934 and married Julian
Shefstad. Clarice was born in 1935 and married Marvin Hofer. Carlyle was born in
1936. Marlagaye was born in 1937 and married Donald Meier. Veron was born in
1939. Sandra was born in 1940. She married Acey O'Neil, and then later William
Huber. Gary was a nephew of Martin, but Agnes and Martin raised him from birth
in 1947 when his mother died.

In November 1955 Agnes and Martin moved to Chula Vista, California, where Martin
worked as a mechanic. Agnes was a piano teacher. Martin Ockert died in 1965.
Sandra and Gary are also deceased. Agnes continues to make her home in
California.

Vernon Jens Bille was born December 1, 1915. He joined the CCC through Minot in
1934, and after doing some work in North Dakota, was sent to Arkansas until May
10, 1935. After that he did farm work at Mercer. Vernon then served five years
in the U.S. Army paratroopers, and became an instructor. On February 22, 1945,
he married Virginia Patton in North Carolina. After the war, they were dairy
farmers in Polk County, Wisconsin. Their twin sons, Baynard and Byron were born
in 1953. Vernon and his wife, Virginia, live at Luck, Wisconsin.

Clara Ethel Bille was born March 18, 1917 at Mercer. She married William "Bill"
Diede January 3, 1938. They lived with her father on the Bille homestead for
awhile, and then rented a place in the Prophet Mountains. Other places they
lived were: a farm north of Pickardville, in the Prophet's again, Uncle Tony
Christensen's farm and then the Littke (Keller) farm. Finally in 1951 they moved
to a farm at Luck, Wisconsin. Bill worked at Duncan Yo-Yo Factory and later at
Luck Lumber Yard. Clara worked as a nurse's aid at Frederic Hospital for almost
21 years before retiring.

Clara and Bill had three children, Donald, Clinton, and Midge. Donald, born
December 30, 1938, died as an infant and is buried in St. Ansgar Cemetery north
of Mercer. Clinton was born May 15, 1941 at Turtle Lake. He died August 16,
1964, at the age of 23. Their daughter, Midge, was born February 8, 1946 at
Turtle Lake and married Wallace Anderson in 1965.

Paul Alois Bille was born June 25, 1923 in their new home on Section 11. When he
was 16, he moved to Wisconsin where he graduated from high school. He served in
the U.S. Navy. Paul married Joyce Elaine Sorensen in 1950 at Luck, Wisconsin. He
worked at the Duncan Yo-Yo Factory and then started farming. He also worked for
the County Highway Department. Joyce and Paul have three children. Kevin was
born in 1954 and married Dawn Hansen. Karla was born in 1955. She married
Charles Larson and later married Jerry Donohue. Kari was born in 1963 and
married Greg Letch. Paul and Joyce live on her grandfather's farm near Luck,
Wisconsin.

Jen's father, Hans Jensen Bille, came to live with Jens and Sarah after Hans'
wife, Ane C., died in 1912. Hans died November 5, 1927 at Mercer, and was taken
back to Luck, Wisconsin for burial.

Unfortunately, Sarah developed cancer, and in March of 1932, her daughter,
Agnes, wrote the following to her second cousin, Emma, "I suppose you know Uncle
Jorgan (Christensen) from Montana was out here. Harold and Raymond were along.
They came on Friday and left the next Friday. It sure did mother good to see him
again. Oh but she is getting thin..."

Sarah died June 24,1932 at the age of 48 after a long illness. She was buried in
the Danish cemetery north of Mercer beside her daughter, Florence.

Next came the Great Depression and more years of drought in North Dakota. It was
a difficult time for the family. In 1939 Jens, Vernon, and Paul moved to Luck,
Wisconsin, Jen's hometown. Vernon and Paul rode in the box car with their cattle
and horses and it took them three days to get to Luck. Jens and Edna Glad bought
the Bille farm in 1943.

When Clara was asked how she has dealt with all the losses in her life, she said
her faith and her relationship with God is what sustains her. Bill Diede is
deceased and Clara lives at Marshfield, Wisconsin.

Jens Bille died September 1974 at the age of 91, and is buried at Luck,
Wisconsin. Sarah Christensen and Jens Bille were both courageous young
homesteaders who will forever be a part of the history of Wise Township and
Mercer, North Dakota. Their pioneer spirit lives on through their children,
grandchildren, and great-grandchildren.

Dan & Martha (Krein) Birst

In the spring of 1945, they purchased the Carl Franzen farm located 2½ miles

Dan and Martha had two children.

Gladys was born in Turtle Lake on July 10, 1941, and is presently living
Bismarck, N.D. She married Arlan Weight and they have one daughter, Lisa, who

John & Magdalena (Laib) Blatter

John Blatter was born in Romania, on Feb. 16, 1901.

He came to America as a young boy with an uncle. He lived and was raised by this
family in the Garrison area.

In January 1922, he married Magdalena Laib at Hope Lutheran Church in Mercer,
N.D.

They lived and farmed south of Pickardville, N.D., until they bought a farm by
Regan, N.D., in 1940. Their farm was about six miles north of Regan where they
farmed and raised cattle.

        Photo: John and Magdalena Blatter, 1972.

They sold their farm in 1960 and moved to Bismarck where John was employed by
Winger Cabinets.

They also had a cabin at Brush Lake where they spent many happy hours fishing.
John died in 1973 while fishing. Magdalena died in September of 1989.

They had four children: Theodore (Ted) Blatter married Esther Bender.

Dorothy Blatter (Forderer) Saylor.

Lorraine Blatter married William Graf.

Theodore & Esther (Bender) Blatter

Theodore (Ted) Blatter was born March 8, 1922, south of Pickardville, N.D., to
John and Madeline (Laib) Blatter. There he was raised and went to school.

When Ted was 21 years old, his parents moved to a farm six miles north of Regan,
N.D. There Ted helped his dad farm and worked in the Wilton Coal Mine one
winter.

In the fall of 1945 on Nov. 28 he married Esther June Bender, born June 5, 1927,
to Fred Bender Jr. and Sophie (Brenneise) Bender.

Esther was raised nine miles north of Regan and received her education in Regan.

Ted and Esther were married in the Lutheran church parish in Mercer, N.D. A
reception was held at his parent's home in the evening. The day was beautiful,
it thawed all day but by late evening it started to snow and storm.

They lived with Ted's parent's one year, then in the fall of 1946 they rented
and moved to a farm north of Regan.

In the fall of 1956, they bought a farm six and one-half miles northeast of
McClusky, N.D., where they farmed and had a dairy business and sold milk. They
lived and farmed there for 35 years until they moved to Wilton, N.D. in 1991.

Ted helped farmers with their spring work and haying. Esther was employed with
the tax department for three years in Bismarck until the time of Ted's stroke
which left him paralyzed on the left side in the spring of 1999.

Ted and Esther have a family of three daughters:

Judy Irene Blatter was born Nov. 22, 1946. She married James Lockbeam on May 19,
1966. Judy was employed at St. Alexius Hospital in Bismarck as a licensed
practical nurse. Jim was employed by the engineering department of the city of
Bismarck. They are the parents of two children: Larry Dean Lockbeam. He is

Peter & Anna (Kirschmann) Bonnet (Bohnet)

The Peter Bonnet family history based on records of information dating back to
Christian Bohnet, who was born in 1766 in Wuerttemberg, Germany. In the 1816,
census the family name recorded the spelling as Bohnet. Beginning in 1858, the
spelling is shown as Bonnet.

The Bohnet family joined the migration to south Russia in 1809. They settled in
the colony Neudorf with about 100 houses constructed of stamped earth.

The family generations since 1766 are listed as follows:

Christian Bohnet, born in 1766, Wuerttemberg, Germany, and wife Elisabeth
Bohnet, maiden name is not known, born in 1770 in Germany, immigrated to Russia
during 1809.

Johannes Bohnet, born in 1803 in Germany, immigrated to Neudorf, S. Russia,
during 1809, married Johanna, maiden name not known.

Johann Bonnet, born May 3, 1843 in Neudorf (Kherson) Russia, married Magdalene
Dockter, born Dec. 20, 1846. They migrated to America July 1901 aboard the ship
H.H. Meier, port of immigration Bremen, Germany to New York City. Magdalena died
June 19, 1918. She is buried in New Germantown Township, Sheridan County; N.D.
Johann then married Christina Wagner in 1920. She died in 1928 and is buried in
New Germantown Township, Sheridan County; N.D. Johann died Oct. 20, 1934, and is
buried in Schiller Township, Sheridan County, N.D.

Peter Bonnet I, born May 16, 1867, son of Johann and Magdalene (Dockter) Bonnet.
He was one of nine children who was born in Saratisky, South Russia. He married
Anna Maria Kirschmann, born March 30, 1869. They migrated to American Dec. 7,
1906. They came to America by way of St. John, Dominion of Canada Port of
immigration.

They settled in the Prophet Mountains area northeast of Mercer. Many other
Bonnet relatives settled in the Lincoln Valley area of Sheridan County, N.D.
Peter and Anna Marie had 10 children, many of whom married in the Mercer and
McClusky area and raised their families there.

Their children are:

Peter II, married Christina Zindler; Magdalena, married Christ Derherim;
Katherina, married August Boschee; Jacob, married Emelia Bonnet; John married
Paula; Carrie married Millard Melom; Ed married Katie Kirschmann; Emma married
Jacob Kirschmann; Christine married Christ Wanner and Gottlieb, married Daphine
Fibelstad.

Many of their descendants and extended families to the third and fourth
generation still reside in the Mercer vacinity. Among them are the Dan
Ketterlings, Bertha Jans, Albert Bonnet, Fred Schmidt families. Other children
of Peter Bonnet I settled in the McClusky area and Streeter and Mandan, N.D.,
Aberdeen, S.D., Milwaukee, Wisc. and St. Petersburg, Fla.

Peter and Anna Marie moved to McClusky in their later years. The Robert Mantz
family purchased their farm and home. Peter died March 25, 1951, in Jamestown,
N.D. Anna Marie died July 12, 1954, in Minot, N.D. Both are buried in the
McClusky City Cemetery.

Rudolf  & Magdalena (Hofer) Bossert

Rudolf Bossert, the son of Andreas and Carolina Bossert, was born Sept. 20,
1889, in Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, South Russia. He came to the United States in
1902 and homesteaded seven miles southwest of Mercer.

On Dec. 21, 1908, he married Magdalena Hofer, the daughter of Johan Hofer and
Christina Laib. She was born on Jan. 29, 1888, in Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia,
South Russia. Her family came to the United States in the early 1900s.

He built a dwelling following the design that had been used in South Russia.
There were three parts of the dwelling, a barn, granary and living quarters. It
was made out of rocks and mud and had a dirt floor. This building was replaced
with a sod house in 1908/09, which had an entry, a kitchen-dining area and a
small bed and a living room with two beds. The sod house is still standing.

The children were born and raised in this house. Rudolf lived in this house
until his death on June 23, 1951. Rudolf and Magdalena had planned to retire and
had bought a house in Bismarck. After his death, Magdalena moved to Bismarck
where she lived until her death on July 17, 1960.

John & Louise (Arlt) Braun John & Johanna (Bentz) Braun

Among the pioneers who left South Russia with its unsavory economic conditions
and crowded land areas was Jacob Braun with his family. They went first to
Cobadin, Romania, in 1891 hoping to find land for himself and his sons.

Here conditions were much the same so a son, John, who had been born in
Borodino, Bessarabia, South Russia Oct. 20, 1880, now aged 22, emigrated to the
United States in 1901.

John went first to Scotland, S.D., where he worked on a farm doing general farm
work of the day and helping to milk 17 cows and tend 12 horses for which he
received $20 per month.

In the fall of 1902, he learned his parents had arrived in America and were
located in the Turtle Lake area. He hoped to homestead near his father so he
came as far as Washburn on the Soo Line railroad, which was the end of the line
at that time. In Washburn he asked how he might get to the Turtle Lake area and
was told he could walk or find someone going in that direction with whom to
catch a ride.

Luck was with him and he met Pete Schayer who was in Washburn hauling flax. Pete
took him to his home which is the farm where Art and Emma Schauer lived. Pete
was their father. The next morning he got up early, helped Pete load more flax
and started walking to the Wanamaker Post Office. From there the trail let to
the Charlie Billis place (now owned by Jacob Hofer). From the Billis place there
was a trail over to the northwest end of Blue Lake and to the old Carl Schaefer
ranch and from there he walked three more miles to his Uncle Carl Degg's farm
(now Emanual Makeef farm) where his parents were.

Land was not plentiful as they had supposed, but John Braun staked his homestead
in the SW¼ of Sec. 9-147-N79 in Wise township.

On Feb. 29, 1903, John Braun was united in marriage to Louise Arlt at Garrison.
At the time of their marriage they moved to Mrs. Braun's homestead which was
Sec. 6-146-N79. Here they built a sod house of two rooms. The rafters were
driftwood from the Missouri River and the floor was a mixture of clay and straw
which made a type of cement.

To the marriage of John Braun and Louise Arlt five children were born. They were
John F. deceased, August deceased, Bertha deceased, Ida (Mrs. Robert Siebold,
Apache Junction, Ariz. and Louise (Mrs. Bill Eggelston, Seattle, Wash.).

Supplies for the winter were purchased in the fall from Washburn or Denhoff as
there were no roads in the winter when the snow was deep. Coal had to be hauled
by horses from the Hanson Mine or from Underwood. Pleasures were few but when a
few people came together, baseball or horseshoes were played in the summer and
dominoes was the winter game.

        Photo: John and Johanna Braun

Mr. Braun hauled his first grain in sacks to Denhoff for sale. He remembers flax
on sod averaged 8-16 bushels per acre and brought $1 per bushel.

Mrs. Louise Braun died Nov. 28, 1918. She is buried in the St. Paulus Lutheran
cemetery, 4½ miles northwest of Mercer.

Mr. Braun was a member of the Mercer School Board and the Mercer Township Board.
He was a member of the McLean County Welfare Board since its origin. He also was
a member of the Peace Lutheran Church in Turtle Lake and had been active in many
community affairs.

Mr. Braun was united in marriage to Johanna Bentz on Feb. 13, 1919, at Mercer.
Children of Johanna Bentz from a former marriage were: Rueben deceased and
Esther (Mrs. Leslie Johnson) deceased.

To John and Johanna Braun were born the following children: Viola (Mrs. Emil
Wagner) Turtle Lake, N.D.; W.L. Braun, Bismarck, N.D.; Mary (Mrs. Orville
Sundby), Bismarck, N.D. and Martin who is deceased.

Mr. and Mrs. Braun retired to Turtle Lake in 1945 and resided there until their
death. John Braun was born Oct. 20, 1880, and died June 23, 1958. Mrs. Johanna
Braun was born Dec. 27, 1891, and died April 5, 1974.

Walter & Lucille (Kraft) Braun

W.L. Braun was born to John and Johanna Braun on March 21, 1921, on the family
farm between Mercer and Turtle Lake. He attended elementary school, and
graduated from Mercer High School in 1939. He graduated from Minot State College
in 1941. He taught school at Mercer prior to entering the army. Most of his army
service was in the North Pacific having served three and one-half years. After
his discharge, he taught school at Cavalier, N.D. He served in Cavalier's
National Guard in the 231st Combat Engineer Unit as a lieutenant while teaching
there.

In 1947 Walt started the W.L. Braun Agency in Turtle Lake, which provided
insurance, real estate, mutual funds and oil and gas leasing services. He was a
member of the Independent Mutual Insurance Association and has acted as its
Legislative Chairman and also served on its board of directors a number of
years. He was a member of the North Dakota Insurance Federation an served as its
president in 1971. Mr. Braun was a member of the Minot Board of Realtors and
later the Bismarck Board of Realtors, State and National Real Estate Boards, The
Dakota Chapter of Farm Lands Institute and the National Farm and Land Institute
and the Dakota Farm Listing Exchange. Mr. Braun was a member of the Turtle Lake
Commercial Club and served as its president.

On June 2, 1950, W.L. Braun and Lucille Kraft were married in Zion Lutheran
Church at Edgeley, N.D. After their marriage, Lucille became licensed in the
insurance business and assisted in the operation of the agency. The Braun's had
two children, Renee Candice and Barbara Carmen. Renee is married to John K.
Thorp and they reside at Bozeman, Mont. They have two children, Sasha and
Rachel. Barbara married Glen Naumann and they live in Bismarck.

Lucille was and is a member of the American Legion Auxiliary Post 133, and has
served as its president. She was a senior Girl Scout leader and community
chairman. She also directed Trinity's choirs for a number of years. The Brauns
were members of Trinity Lutheran Church in Turtle Lake and served in various
positions. Walt is a member of Lawrence Stephenson American Legion Post #133
having served as commander, adjutant, historian and post service officer.

        Photo: Walter and Lucille Braun

Walt and Lucille moved to Bismarck in 1976 where they currently reside. The
Braun's are members of Good Shepherd Lutheran Church, the Harold Schafer
Founder's Society and the Medora 1000 Club. They are president's club members of
the University of Mary and Bismarck State College.

Walt is a member of the Elks, Veterans of Foreign Wars, Landman's Association of
North Dakota, the Dakota Petroleum Club. He was on the board of Missouri Slope
Lutheran Care Center for six years.

The Braun's have set up the W.L. Braun and Lucille Braun Family Charitable Gift
Fund. This fund was set up for the purpose of providing grants to needy
organizations an charities during and after the lifetimes of Walt and Lucille.
Grants from the gift fund include scholarships at University of Mary and
Bismarck State College. Walt also assisted in establishing the Turtle Lake
Trojan Scholarship Fund with an initial major contribution on a matching basis.
