Victor & Augusta (Johnson) Carlson

Victor and Augusta Carlson immigrated from Sweden. They were married in South
Dakota in 1904.

They moved to Mercer and settled five miles from Mercer. Under the Homestead Act
of 1862 they began farming, clearing the land for crops and obtained cattle and
horses.

        Photo: Victor and Augusta Carlson on their 40th wedding anniversary.

        Photo: The Carlson family: (from left) Reuben, Paul, Signe, Gust,
        Vivian, Aaron, Ellen, Joe, Minnie and Elof.

They had 10 children: Gust, Joe, Aaron, Reuben, Elof, Paul, Minnie, Vivian,
Signe and Ellen.

For several years the Carlsons operated the pavilion at Brush Lake and rented
out boats. In 1935 they quit farming and moved to McClusky, N.D., where they
operated a bar. In 1939 they moved to the Chicago area where their children were
living and working.

Augusta died in 1952 and Victor died in 1953. There are two daughters living,
Signe and Ellen.

Anton & Josephine (Ronsgaard) Christensen

Anton (Tony) M. Christensen came to the Mercer area in 1903 on an immigrant
train with his brothers, Chris W. and Jonas. He homesteaded in Wise Township on
Section 12, where Dave and Teresa Presser now live.

        Photo: Anton and Josephine Christensen, 1909.

Tony was born August 2, 1879, at Hutchinson, Minnesota, to Danish immigrant
parents, Peter Christensen and Johanna Nielsen. He had four brothers, Nels,
Christian W., Jonas, and Jergen. He also had four sisters, Christine Sorensen,
Anne Hansen, Mary Johnson and Sarah Bille.

Tony worked on his father's farm and then took a job at the creamery at Gibbon,
Minnesota. Tony and his brother, Jonas, learned the plumbing trade at Fort
Snelling in St. Paul. Later, they worked at Fort Keogh near Miles City, Montana,
installing plumbing. He was employed for a time as a coachman for a wealthy
family in St. Paul, Minnesota, before homesteading.

Tony married Josephine Ronsgaard at Sharon, North Dakota, on November 18, 1909.
Josie was born January 18, 1884, at Stoughton, Wisconsin. She came to North
Dakota with her parents, and they homesteaded at Sharon, North Dakota.

Josie's mother, Maggie Ronsgaard, homesteaded on the 40 acres of land just south
of the Sprout School in 1909. She proved it up February 17, 1914, with patent
number 385638. Maggie spoke Swedish. One night, Maggie's shack blew over in a
severe windstorm, and she ran over to Jens Bille's home for shelter. Billes
lived where Joel Stradinger lives now.

Tony and Josie lived on his homestead, and Tony and his brother, Jonas, often
worked together. They had a bore type well drilling outfit that was round and as
large as a man's body. It was pulled by one horse, and they drilled many wells
in the vicinity, including their own. They also had a threshing machine that
they used together.

Tony and Josie also milked cows and raised pigs. The January 21, 1913, Mercer
Telegram reported, "Last Monday Mr. T.M. Christensen butchered a pig that
weighed 174 pounds dressed. The pork was sold at 10 cents a pound and brought
$17.40. This pig was out of a litter of 8, and was born July 17, 1912."

Bill Peterson said Big Pete Nielson from Iowa lived with Tony Christensen for
awhile. His sons were Finley and Clifford. Clifford went on to become a preacher
at Hettinger.

Melvin Johnson, son of Tony's sister, Mary (Julius) Johnson, spent quite a bit
of time with Tony and Josie, and helped Tony with the farm work. Melvin was born
in 1906.

Tony and Josie raised Gladys Ardell Webster and she attended the Sprout country
school in Wise Township. They were active in the Church of God while at Mercer
and Tony served as treasurer for awhile. In 1952, Tony and Josie retired and
moved to Bismarck. At first they rented out their farm. Some of their renters
were Bill and Clara Diede, and Robert and Olinda Mantz. They later sold their
farm to William Presser.

Gladys married Merle Mitchell and they lived at Detroit Lakes, Minnesota. The
Mitchells had three children, Robert, Bruce and Carolyn (Fox). Both Gladys and
Merle are deceased.

Tony and Josie were members of the Evangel Temple in Bismarck. Tony Christensen
died July 5, 1972, at the age of 92. Josie died May 11, 1976, at 92 and they are
buried at Sunset Memorial Gardens at Bismarck.

Christian Peter (C.P.) & Anna (Kalland) Christensen

Christian Peter Christensen was one of the earliest residents of the Mercer
community. In 1902 he homesteaded 7 miles north of Mercer in Section 35 in
Medicine Hill Township. His brothers, Martin and Fred, also homesteaded in the
same area. His brother, Henry bought land nearby. Sister Emma's homestead joined
C.P.'s, but she died at the age of 24 from pneumonia. His sister, Trina, was
married to Nels Olesen, Mercer's first postmaster.

        Photo: C.P. Christensen and Anna Kalland on their wedding day, 1911.

C.P. was born December 6, 1875, in Hutchinson, Minnesota. His parents, Hans
Peter Christensen and Anna Fredrickson, were both born in Denmark. In his youth,
Chris worked for awhile in a sawmill at Luck, Wisconsin, and then for Chicago
Northwestern Railroad, helping to build railroad lines. In the early days,
colleges could be attended without having graduated from either elementary
school or high school. C.P. attended Business College in Minnesota and studied
agriculture in a college in Elkhorn, Iowa, before homesteading in North Dakota.
In 1902 Chris and a friend from college took jobs helping locate folks to file
on homesteads north of Bismarck. Chris had been advised by his doctor that North
Dakota would be good for his asthma condition. So Chris and his brother, Martin,
filed on claims in Medicine Hill Township, McLean County, before there was a
Mercer. Chris farmed his late sister Emma's claim in addition to his own
homestead.

C.P. was instrumental in helping start the St. Ansgar Danish Lutheran
Congregation north of Mercer in 1905, and he served as the first treasurer of
the congregation.

Chris and Holgar Peterson purchased a threshing rig and did custom threshing for
neighbors. The September 24, 1908, Mercer Telegram noted "Messers. Peterson and
Christensen have finished threshing for Ernest Watson and pulled their rig to
the Davidson farm."

On April 27, 1911, Chris married Anna Elise Kalland at Crow River Lutheran
Church in rural Belgrade, Minnesota. Anna was born July 27, 1883, at Belgrade,
one of nine children born to Norwegian immigrant parents, Henrick O. Kalland and
Oline A. Rothenes. As a young girl, Anna's mother spent her summers in the
mountains of Norway, where they lived and tended their goats, making cheese for
winter storage.

Anna grew up on a small farm near Belgrade, Minnesota, and attended school
through the eighth grade. She then went to work for others, doing housekeeping.
Anna's mother was not well, and was not able to be very active outside their
home. They were involved in their big country church, which was close to the
Kalland farm.

Anna's father and brothers, Edward (born in 1892), Alfred, Harold, and Elmo got
jobs in northeastern North Dakota where a new branch railroad, the Wheat Line on
the Soo, was being built. Anna's sisters, Christine and Amanda, went along with
them to cook. Amanda fell in love with one of the section hands, Adolph Carl
Christensen, and they married after the project closed. Anna's older sister,
Hannah, was married to Chris Walle, who homesteaded on Section 1 in Wise
Township northeast of Mercer in 1905. Anna helped them by working in their cook
car during harvest. Her sister, Christine Kalland, married C.P.'s brother,
Martin, in 1909. Another sister, Constance, married Oscar Belsheim.

Anna helped Chris with milking the cows and the farm work. In August of 1911,
C.P and Anna built a large henhouse and had 250 laying hens. That same month,
C.P. and Holgar Peterson purchased a new Reeves Separator threshing machine at
Fargo. Alvin Christensen wrote "Farming was all done with horses except the
steam threshing rig. My dad's brother, Christ, owned a steam rig, and it was
always a thrill when they came to thresh our grain every fall. They had a crew
of around 25 men, ten bundle teams, cook's car, bunkhouse, water wagons, etc.
They burned coal most of the time in the engine, so we could see the black smoke
where they were threshing miles away. I also loved to hear the whistle in the
early morning and at night. They blew the whistle in signals so they knew what
it was for, water, coal, meals or whatever else." Annie was in charge of the
cook's car. One time C.P. tried to cross the road east by Postel's Lake with the
threshing machine, and got it deeply mired in the mud. It took great effort to
finally get it pulled out.

Anna's sister, Amanda, and her husband, Adolph, had settled in Minnesota. They
had five children, a boy and then four girls. Unfortunately, her husband was
killed in an accident in 1916. He is buried at Crow River in rural Belgrade. The
first year after he died, Amanda sent her two oldest children, Adolph and
Mildred Christensen, to live with their aunt, Annie and Chris. They attended
Medicine Hill #4 under their Aunt Connie Belsheim. Martin's son, Alvin, said
Adolph was the largest boy in their country school. One day all the boys in
school decided to see if joined together, (if they could overpower Adolph). They
found out they could not, and Adolph went on to eventually play college football
in Minnesota.

Margaret Christensen wrote, "Dad's (Martin's) oldest brother Chris and Mother's
oldest sister, Anna, married, and built a home just ½ mile east of us. Chris'
homestead joined Dad's to the east. Every Sunday p.m. they would visit us and
advise our mom and dad on their upbringing of us children. God, for reasons
unknown to us, did not bless their home with children. They devoted themselves
wholly to their fields and cattle, and worked very hard."

Martin Christensen's daughter, Grace, wrote the following in 1987. "When I
stayed with Uncle Chris and Aunt Anna 1932-1933, a year and two weeks, I will
always remember how she would smile and brighten up when young children talked
to her. I learned very much from my experience away from my brothers and
sisters, and I tried to hide my lonely feelings by helping around the farm.
Mother wrote to me often and kept me informed on what was going on at home. She
also sent me a pair of beads and 2 jigsaw puzzles, which I prized highly. My
sister, Margaret, sent me a Junior Hymnal for church and home with notes in it.
When Belsheims came one Sunday with Osborne, Elwood, and Douglas, we sang out of
the hymnal, one song after another, in parts. What fun even then, they were good
singers and I recognized they had real talent for music. Douglas and especially
Elwood were artistic, and would draw comics on paper to amuse us... Chris and
Annie got the Bismarck Tribune daily and Annie always sent the old papers home
with the boys to enjoy. Aunt Connie (Belsheim), Mother's sister, had died the
year before (in 1931). Osbourne, the oldest of the boys was 2 weeks older than I
was, so we enjoyed one another's company." C.P.'s also had a Victorola
phonograph, the cylinder type with a big horn, which the kids enjoyed.

Martin's daughter, Mary June, also wrote in 1987, "I spent a year with Aunt Anna
and Uncle Chris in Mercer in 1933-34. That year spent in herding and milking
cows, running and washing the separator, feeding chickens, doing dishes, etc.
was something I never forgot. At first I was excited about living on a farm but
it soon wore off and I was so lonely I'm sure I cried every night and prayed
fervently that I would not die til I could get back home again. I'm sure Uncle
Chris thought I was a big baby, but Annie was more sympathetic. Visits from the
Belsheims quite often made it more bearable, and the boys and I would go
trapping prairie dogs (gophers) and cut off their tails. We were paid a penny
per tail, but I'm not sure by whom. They loved to sing, and so did I, so those
prairies really rang with music." (Their mother Connie was also very musical and
directed the choir at St. Olaf Lutheran Church before she died). "Also we got
together with Uncle Martin and Aunt Martina (Sorensen, Chris' sister) and the
girls. That was fun, and I thought Uncle Martin was the kindest man I knew.
Uncle Chris used to tease Alice and Elizabeth til they cried..."

C.P. served as a member of the school board in Medicine Hill Township for twenty
years. As the treasurer, he was known as frugal, especially with the school
supplies he kept at his house. He also headed the Works Project Administration
in the 1930s. He and Anna farmed north of Mercer until 1943, when they sold
their farm to Herb and Edna Rauser. They lived on the Jake Nelson farmstead
until 1948, when they moved into Mercer. Annie still milked a cow when they
lived in Mercer. They were members of Our Savior's Lutheran Church after St.
Ansgar's closed.

C.P. died September 11, 1957, and is buried in the Mercer Hillside Cemetery.
Anna then lived with her niece in Cottonwood, Minnesota, for eight years. She
died of a stroke October 21, 1965, and is buried beside her husband at Mercer.

Fred J. & Lydia (Wagner) Christensen

One would have to assume Fred J. Christensen was of great determination to have
stayed in one place nearly 76 years of his nearly 97 years of his life. Coming
here from Hutchinson, Minn., where he was born March 6, 1885. Here he was
baptized and confirmed in the Lutheran faith.

        Photo: Fred and Lydia Christensen

His parents were Hans Peter Christenson, born Dec. 15, 1839, in Nortvick,
Denmark, coming to the United States in 1869 and Anna Kristine Fredrickson, born
Aug. 21, 1848, in Jylland, Denmark. They were married May 5, 1873, in Minnesota.

At the age of 19 Fred went to work in a sawmill in Wisconsin but with adventure
in his soul at the age of 21 years he came to North Dakota in the spring of
1906. He homesteaded about eight miles north of Mercer wanting to settle close
to where other members of his family had come a few years before. He didn't have
much choice of land and only due to relinquishment of an earlier homesteader was
he able to obtain the 160 acres of free land. Much hard work was involved to get
this land with tillable acreage. The first night on his homestead he walked
across to his brother Christ's place. He could hear the coyotes howling which
made his hair stand on edge. When he returned to his shack he wedged a pole in
both the east and west doors and went to bed with a revolver under his head.
However, all went well.

In March of 1911, he took a trip to Hutchinson, and during this time, his
brother Henry was to take care of his place. He ran out of kerosene and used
gasoline in the stove causing an explosion and fire that destroyed his shack. A
small dog also lost his life. The same year he built the kitchen and bedroom of
his present home, which was enlarged in 1928.

This old house has seen many events including the births of his 11 children and
grandsons, Randolph and Carmen Anderson; death and funeral services for his son
Ernest, age 11. Some of his children were baptized in this house. Some
grandchildren were also baptized in the house: Thomas Repnow and Michael,
Gwendolyn and Ellen Anderson. The wedding of granddaughter Gwendolyn Anderson
and Allen Schmidt was held in the farmhouse.

June 18, 1918, he took as his bride Miss Lydia Wagner of McClusky who was born
at Selby, South Dakota, to Fred and Elizabeth Wagner on Feb. 16, 1898. They were
married in the home of Rev. W.L. Keller (Mrs. Keller, the former Ottilie
Kroenke, served a wedding supper for the couple. She lived to be 104 years old
and passed away the spring of 1977.)

To this union the following children came to bless this home: Jane (died at
birth); Marion (Teroy Repnow), Underwood: Ernest, deceased; Eleanor (Emil
Anderson, deceased), Mercer; Earl, deceased (Betty Bye), Marion; Marjorie
(Clarence Scholl), Monroe, Wash.; twin sons, Orville, deceased (Wilma Fiedler,
deceased), Chicago, Ill. and Oliver, deceased (Grace Erin Sackman), Silver Lake,
Kansas; Curtis, deceased, Mercer; Joyce (Dr. Norman Lloyd, deceased) Cyprus,
Calif.

Fred and Lydia had 28 grandchildren and several great- and great-great
grandchildren.

All but two of Fred and Lydia's children attended the rural school north of
Mercer. Curtis graduated from Mercer High School in 1954. Joyce attended Mercer
High School.

Lydia passed away in April of 1948. Over the years Mr. Christensen increased his
acreage to 1040 acres and in 1966 he sold his farm to his son, Curtis and
son-in-law, Emil Anderson. They farmed in partnership. Fred passed away in 1982
having stayed on the farm all the time.

Emil and Eleanor Anderson raised five children:

Randolph attended Mercer High School and married Marlys Skaley, they live in
Bismarck. Marlys has three sons.

Carmen attended Mercer High School and married Sharon Murray. They live in
Turtle Lake and have one son and two daughters.

Mike attended Mercer School and married Mary Ann Joachim. They live in Mercer
and have the homestead farm.

Gwendolyn graduated from Mercer High School in 1971 and married Allen Schmidt
(deceased), and they have two daughters and one son. She lives in Bismarck.

Ellen graduated in the last class from Mercer High School in 1972; she lives in
Bismarck.

Curtis Christensen passed away in 1984 and Emil Anderson passed away in 2001.

The homestead is still in the family as Mike Anderson purchased it from his
brothers and sisters. The farmhouse that Grandpa Fred built still stands today
and is a wonderful place to go to relax and reminisce.

James & Nancy (Nelson) Christensen

        Photo: Jim, Mike Nancy and Thad.

James Mark Christensen was born January 10, 1957, at the Turtle Lake Hospital to
Walter and Ruth (Ovre) Christensen. After high school, he attended Bismarck
Junior College and received an associate degree in agriculture. While at BSC Jim
played basketball. As a freshman, they won the state and regional tournaments
and participated in the national NJCAA tournament.

Jim then attended NDSU, Fargo, earning a degree in horticulture in 1979. After
graduation he moved to Minot, North Dakota, and worked for Dakota Boys Ranch for
four years as a Horticulturist. Then he worked at Lowe's Garden Center as
nursery manager for eight years.

Two years after Jim moved to Minot, he married Nancy Nelson Stavn at First
Lutheran Church on March 20, 1981. Nancy taught at Berthold High School and then
at Minot State University until 1995. Nancy's son, Thad Jonathon Stavn lived
with them and attended Minot public schools until his high school graduation in
1993. Thad was active in football, hockey and wrestling, in which he placed 3rd
in the state as a junior and 2nd as a senior. On January 14, 1985, Jim and
Nancy's son, Michael James was born.

In 1991, Jim entered the University of North Dakota School of Medicine at Grand
Forks. Nancy and the boys stayed in Minot while Jim commuted on weekends. During
this time, Nancy continued to teach, bearing the majority of the responsibility
of raising two boys and maintaining their home, while being supportive of Jim.

Jim graduated from UND School of Medicine in 1995. Nancy, Mike and Jim moved to
Grand Rapids, Michigan, where Jim completed a four-year residency in obstetrics
and gynecology. Mike attended school in East Grand Rapids and played football,
hockey, and soccer. Nancy taught at Aquinas College. They enjoyed their time in
Grand Rapids and made many friends there.

In July 1999, they moved to Detroit Lakes, Minnesota, where Jim currently
practices. Nancy teaches at Minnesota State Univ. Moorhead. Mike attended
Detroit Lakes High School where he played soccer and hockey. Since graduating
from high school in 1995, Mike is playing Junior Hockey and working in
Rochester, Minnesota. Thad is pursuing a biology degree from MSU Moorhead and
Portland State University, Portland, Oregon.

Joel & Colleen (Vachal) Christensen

        Photo: The Joel Christensen family: (front, from left) Carlie, Kim,
        Annie, Lauren, Colleen; (back) Aaron, Ben, Joel and Mark Christensen.

Joel Grant Christensen was born March 6, 1952, in the Bismarck Hospital to
Walter and Ruth (Ovre) Christensen. He attended the one-room Medicine Hill
School #4 with Mary and Steve one year until it closed in 1959. He then went to
Mercer, where he graduated in 1970. He followed in Steve's footsteps by playing
basketball at Williston Junior College. Joel then went to North Dakota State
University in Fargo where he earned a degree in civil engineering.

While in Fargo he met Colleen Vachal from Ross, North Dakota. Colleen and Joel
were married on December 22, 1974, in Ross, and then moved to Omaha, Nebraska.
Joel is the Vice President of Water Operations for the Omaha water utility.
Colleen is a secretary at a local high school.

Joel and Colleen have four children. Mark was born in 1977 and he is an
electrical engineer. Mark is married to Kim Marsicek and they live in
Bettendorf, Iowa. Benjamin was born in 1981, and he attends the University of
Nebraska at Omaha. Aaron was born in 1982 and attends the University of Nebraska
at Lincoln. He and Annie Shanks have a daughter, Lauren Christensen. Carlie was
born in 1985 and attends the University of Nebraska at Omaha.

Jonas & Juliana (Peterson, Hanson) Christensen

Jonas H. Christensen was born March 8, 1878, at Hutchinson, Minnesota. He was
the sixth child of Peter and Johanna (Nielsen) Christensen. He had four brothers
and four sisters. At age 17, he was sent to work for a farmer, but his father
could take his wages until he was 21, a common practice then. Next, he worked in
a Hutchinson butcher shop. He was active in church activities, including choir
and the youth group.

Around 1900, Jonas began working in the creamery in Gibbon, MN. His older
brother Chris, and younger brother Tony worked there also. Using a horse and
wagon, he would collect milk from the area farmers. Next, Jonas and Tony learned
the plumbing trade at Fort Snelling in St. Paul. Later, they helped install
plumbing at Fort Keogh near present day Miles City, Montana.

In 1902, when Jonas was 24 years old, he came by train from Hutchinson,
Minnesota, to Balfour, North Dakota. Traveling with him were his cousin, Chris
(C.P.) and Jake Nelsen. The men hired a team of horses and wagon in Balfour and
drove southwest about 40 miles to what is now Medicine Hill Township. In this
area Jonas, C.P. and Jake selected the quarter sections of land they intended to
homestead. The men then returned to Minnesota for the winter.

In the spring of 1903, Jonas, his brothers Anton (Tony) and Christ W. and family
returned to Balfour on an immigrant train. The men rode in the freight cars
along with their horses, cows, farming equipment and household goods. The women
and children rode in the passenger cars. When they arrived at Balfour, they
continued their way with horses and wagons. Jonas' homestead was located on
Sect. 34 & 35 of 148-79.

That first summer Jonas built a one room tar paper shack to live in, and broke
up his first ten acres west of the yard with a walking plow and horses. Jonas
said his intention was to acquire 160 acres of free land, and then return to
Minnesota.

The next summer of 1904, Juliana Hanson took up a homestead one-half mile to the
southeast. She was a widow with a twelve year old daughter, Carlie, from
Hutchinson, Minnesota. Juliana's parents, Soren and Maren Peterson, and brother,
Peter, also took up a homestead in the Danish Settlement area just east of Rev.
Keller's.

Juliana was born August 11, 1869, in Skjold, Vejle County, Denmark. She came to
America with her parents when she was 16. Her parents had a wind powered flour
mill in Denmark, where she walked to school in wooden shoes.

        Photo: Jonas and Juliana Christensen

Juliana said she loved North Dakota in those early years and described it as "so
quiet and peaceful. The grass was knee high as far as one could see, and the
wind blew it about like waves on the sea. Wild flowers, birds, and small
creatures were everywhere."

According to Jonas, more than one bachelor had his eye on the young widow
"Anne". Her parents and brother helped her build a three room house on her
homestead. She and Jonas were married November 22, 1906, at Rev. W.L. Keller's
homestead north of Mercer. They then moved Juliana's house up to Jonas'
homestead to replace his tar paper shack. They purchased her homestead and then
traded it for 160 acres that bordered Jonas' land on the north.

Jonas and his brothers bought a steam threshing rig, and were soon involved in
farming to the extent that the thought of leaving North Dakota was largely
forgotten. Also, the railroad came and established the little village of Mercer
in 1905, which made their shopping and marketing easier.

Jonas' parents came to this area in 1905 to file a homestead. Peter was born in
Nortvick, Denmark, and his wife, Johanna Neilsen was born in Kolding, Denmark.
They came to America in 1869 with their oldest son, Nels. Coming with them from
Hutchinson were two sons, Nels, and Jergen and two daughters, Marie (Mary), and
husband, Julius Johnson, and Sarah. They all took up homesteads nearby.

Jonas proved up his claim in 1908. He broke up ten acres a year in 1904, 1905
and 1906. By 1908 he had 50 acres under cultivation. He had a frame house 14 ×
20 feet with an addition 10 × 14 feet. He also had a frame barn, a stone
granary, a well, eight acres fenced, and some trees planted by this time.

On February 7, 1908, Juliana decided to walk one mile west to visit her sister,
Mary and three week old son, Erven. It was a mild, sunny day with no snow on the
ground. Mary's husband was Jonas' brother, Christ W. The next day Juliana gave
birth to their daughter, Shirley Pearl. Dr. G.E. Heinzroth of Turtle Lake drove
the 16 miles to their farm in his car, one of the few automobiles in the area.
Because of complications, Juliana would not have survived if the doctor had not
been there.

Two years later on April 21, 1910, their son, Walter Ward was born. His older
sister, Carlie was 17, and a great help with her younger sister and brother.

Carlie also loved being outdoors and helping with the farm work. When she was
about 20, she had a serious accident with a team of horses. As she stepped in
front of them to let the tongue down, the horses reared up and knocked her under
them. The horses then ran and Carlie was rolled in the long tined hay rake like
a bundle of grass. A long pile of stones in their path stopped the horses. The
deep gashes from the tines of the rake left lifelong scars on her arm and leg,
and she had many other bruises and cuts. After Jonas and Juliana bandaged
Carlie, Jonas drove her 16 miles in the buggy to Turtle Lake to be examined by
the doctor. She recovered, and despite the accident, Carlie continued to work
with, drive, and enjoy horses.

In 1913, Jonas and Juliana moved two miles southeast to Rev. Frederick
Peterson's homestead in Wise Township. Rev. Peterson was an ordained pastor in
the Danish Lutheran Church. He arrived at Mercer in 1908 from Viborg, South
Dakota, and conducted Danish services in the area. After Rev. Peterson proved up
his claim, he rented his homestead to Jonas. Now Shirley and Walter were closer
to a school, Wise Township #1, better known as the Sprout School. Their closest
neighbors were Rev. and Mrs. W.L. Keller and their ten children.

Pastor Keller married Carlie and Herman Olson at the Peterson farm December 29,
1915. A few years later, Carlie and Herman moved to the Jonas Christensen
homestead. During this time, on March 2, 1917, Olson's first baby, James Morris,
was born three months premature. It was a cold March night and Herman and Jonas
took Carlie to Turtle Lake through the snow in a bobsled. James lived a
half-hour, long enough to be baptized. He is buried in the Danish cemetery near
the homestead. Carlie and Herman later had two more children, LeRoy and Lyall
Olson. They lived at Kenmare, North Dakota, from 1920 to 1941.

In the summer of 1916, Jonas worked on the road crew. Every male of voting age
was required to pay a poll tax with a few days work repairing or building roads
in his township. This work was done with horses and scrapers, picks and shovels.

During that summer the Non-Partisan League was organized, and Jonas and Juliana
became increasingly involved. After Jonas bought his first car in July of 1916,
a black Model T with a brass radiator, there were trips to county rallies and
picnics. Jonas became deeply involved in organizing and supporting the NPL, and
they became acquainted with many of the political leaders of the county and
state. By 1919, three-fourths of the judicial and executive branches of the
North Dakota government were dominated by the NPL.

        Photo: Walter and Shirley Christensen.

On Nov. 11, 1918, the armistice between Germany and the United States was
signed, while Jonas and Juliana were moving back to his original homestead. His
brother, Tony, rode up to announce the news that World War I was over.

The Danish families took turns holding monthly Danish Lutheran church services
in their homes. After Rev. Petersen moved away, a lay preacher or pastor from
Kenmare would come about once a month by train to Butte. He stayed in their
homes on the weekends that he conducted their worship service. Although land was
donated for a church and cemetery by Martin Christensen, a church was never
built. In 1928, St. Ansgar Danish congregation decided to join Our Savior's in
Mercer, and a church was built in Mercer. St. Ansgar's Ladies Aid donated the
money to purchase the Baptismal Font.

The drought of the 30s was a difficult time for farmers. Walter went to Sidney,
Montana, in 1936 to do irrigation work. The next summer he took a job at the
State Hospital. He married Ruth Ovre Oct. 26, 1938, and they lived in Jamestown
that winter. The next summer they returned to Mercer and lived at the Ovre farm.
Walter also helped his dad that summer, and that fall they built a small house
for Jonas and "Anne". Walter and Ruth then moved into the bigger house on the
Christensen homestead.

The 1940s brought prosperity to North Dakota, as rainfall was abundant, and crop
prices were higher. Jonas and Walter built a new barn in 1941. They also
purchased their first tractor around 1942, a John Deere Model D. In 1943, Jonas
and Juliana sold the homestead to Walter and Ruth.

Walter and Ruth were the parents of three daughters, and four sons. Patricia was
born April 10, 1941, Eunice was born June 6, 1943, and Mary was born June 1,
1946. Steve was born February 20, 1949, Joel on March 6, 1952, James on January
8, 1957, and Thomas was born March 24, 1961.

On August 1, 1943, Jonas and Juliana's daughter, Shirley, married Edwin Ingman,
a widower, in Seattle, Washington. She was a parish worker at Our Savior's
Lutheran Church in Bremerton, Washington, where she met Ed. They had two
children, Juliana, born Oct. 8, 1944, and Paul born April 27, 1948. Ed was a
sheet metal worker, and later a progress man at Puget Sound Naval Shipyard at
Bremerton. Ed died Nov. 13, 1985. Shirley continues to live in their home in
Bremerton.

In June of 1950, Christensens and neighbors were connected to rural electricity
for the first time. Prior to that, they had a gas engine on a Kohler power plant
generator to produce electricity.

In 1963, Jonas and Walter took their first airplane ride, flying to Seattle,
Washington, to visit Shirley and Ed and family at Bremerton.

Jonas and Juliana lived in their little house on the farm for thirteen years.
Juliana died of pneumonia Nov. 21, 1952, in the Turtle Lake Hospital at the age
of 83. After her death, Jonas moved in with Walter and Ruth, where he lived for
15 years. He continued to be active for many years, helping with the farm work.
In later years he tended the garden and trees, helped baby sit and was a great
story teller. Ruth said he was indeed a blessing to their family. Jonas died
October 15, 1967, at the age of 89. Juliana and Jonas are buried in the Danish
cemetery southeast of the homestead. Walter died August 3, 1979. Ruth died
September 13, 2003. They are buried at Mercer Hillside Cemetery. Their son,
Steve, and family continue to farm the family homestead.

Martin & Christine (Kalland) Christensen

Martin C. Christensen, age 22, came with his brother, Chris, to Mercer in the
summer of 1902. Martin was born on November 29, 1879, at Hutchinson, Minnesota,
the second of ten children born to his Danish parents, Hans Peter and Anna
(Fredricksen) Christensen. Upon leaving home, he first worked in the saw mill at
Luck, Wisconsin, with other young Danish men. He soon tired of that, when he
heard through his brother, Chris P., and brother-in-law Nels Olesen, that there
was money to be made by homesteading in North Dakota. They selected land about
seven miles north of Mercer. Martin homesteaded on 160 acres in Section 34-148-
79 in Medicine Hill Township and built a 10 × 12 foot shack. Several of his
brothers and sisters as well as numerous cousins were also bitten by the
homestead bug and moved to the Mercer area. In 1905, St. Ansgar Danish Lutheran
Congregation was formed, and Martin, age 25, donated land for a cemetery and
future church site east of his home.

In 1908, Martin met Christine Kalland at Mercer while she was visiting her
sister, Anna Kalland, a local cook for threshing crews. Next oldest sister
Hannah Kalland had married Christ Walle around 1907. Born around 1870 in Norway,
Walle came to the Mercer area in 1903. He homesteaded in 1905 on Sect.1-147-79,
and ran a threshing machine and crew in the area. In 1910, Walle's had two
children, Ole, age 2, and Korbel, age 1. They moved to Canada in 1913.

The Kalland sisters were born and raised in Belgrade, Minnesota. Christine was
the fourth of nine children born to her Norwegian immigrant parents, Henrick O.
Kalland and Oline A. Rothenes, on September 14, 1888.

        Photo: Martin and Christine on their wedding day, June 24, 1909.
        (Courtesy of Duane Christensen.

In the spring of 1909, Martin built a 17 × 28 foot, two-story house with four
rooms. He married Christine on June 24, 1909, at Belgrade, and brought her to
his prairie homestead. Eleven children were born to them at Mercer: Alvin
(1910), Emma (1911), Baby Ruth (born and died in 1912), Margaret (1913), Martin
(born and died the same day in 1914), Marie (born in 1915 and died of whooping
cough), Ruth May (1916), Henry (1917), Aimee (1919), Grace (1920), and Mary June
(1922). Their three babies that died were buried in St. Ansgar Danish Cemetery,
which is now Our Savior's. Christine suffered from depression after the loss of
her three children.

Christine's youngest sister, Constance (Connie) Kalland, came to board with
Martin and Christine in 1917. She taught one mile north at the new Medicine Hill
School #4 that Martin's brother, C.P., helped to get built. C.P.'s wife, Annie,
was Christine and Connie's sister. While at Mercer, Connie met Oscar Belsheim,
whom she married in 1920. They had four sons, Osbourne, Elwood, Donald, and
Douglas. Donald died January 21, 1923, at 3 days of age and was buried in St.
Ansgar Danish Cemetery. Unfortunately, Connie died in 1931, leaving three young
sons.

During World War I, Martin's brother, Henry, who lived with his brother, Fred,
was drafted into the service. Martin's father had died in 1914, and his mother
came and lived with Fred for awhile to keep house for him.

        Photo: The Martin Christensen home, 1910. (Courtesy of Duane C.
        Christenson)

Martin experienced bad crops and drought, and the trees that he had planted with
high hopes all died. The crushing blow to the family came in August of 1923,
when a tornado came through the area, and damaged the homestead.

Son Alvin wrote "Our family was fortunate. It was Sunday and we were all at
church services south of Mercer when it hit. A month later Dad had an auction,
and being deeply in debt, he abandoned the homestead. He managed to salvage
enough lumber to build a hayrack... And so around September 1, 1923, Dad, Mother
and eight children aboard the hayrack and wagon drawn by a team of horses,
started for Gardena, ND, about 85 miles to the north. The trip took three days,
as it was hard pulling for the horses on the dirt roads. We camped at night at
farms, one night sleeping in a haymow, and one night on open prairie, where we
heard the howl of the coyote". At Gardena, Martin and Alvin found harvest work
with a local farmer. During the winter of 1923-24, the family rented a small
house in town, where their son, John, was born on November 29, Thanksgiving Day.

The next spring, they moved to Kenmare, North Dakota, where Martin established
himself in a hauling business until 1965. Three more children were born in
Kenmare: Elsie (1924), David (1928), and Duane (1931). At Kenmare, all the
children had the opportunity to get a high school education, and many went on to
further education. Emma, Margaret, Ruth, Grace and Elsie became nurses. Mary
June and Duane were educators. David became a pastor, and John an accountant.
Henry was an opal miner in Australia, and Alvin farmed in Minnesota. Aimee was a
food service worker. David and Duane built a nine hole golf course in Bemidji,
Minn., called Maple Ridge after they retired.

Christine passed away June 10, 1942, at the age of 53 from a blood clot
following surgery. Her youngest child, Duane, was 11 years old and David was 14.
Daughters Ruth, Emma, Aimee and Grace filled in as "Mom" until Margaret finished
nurses' training in St. Paul and moved back home.

In 1987, sister Grace wrote "Margaret not only supported the family, but gave of
herself sacrificially to the service of the hospital, community and church, as
well as made a home for all of us. She kept us in touch with each other by
giving us a place to sleep when we needed it, there were letters, gifts, and
help whenever we needed it, and she has been a real Christian testimony to all
of us. She shared with us all what it means to live for Jesus and in His Will
for our lives. God bless you Margaret. You are so dear to us all. How unselfish
you are".

Margaret never married, but kept house for her father, Martin, until he died
January 22, 1975, at the age of 97. After Margaret retired as an RN, she learned
to drive, and she drove to Mercer to visit her birthplace, which she left when
she was 10 years old. Margaret attended the Christensen Homestead Centennial
Reunion at Mercer in July of 2003, along with her sister, Ruth, and brothers,
Alvin, David and Duane. She died in September of 2003, and was buried next to
her parents at Trinity Danish Lutheran Cemetery north of Kenmare.

Martin and Christine's son, David, wrote "Our parents have given us a great
Christian heritage. May that continue to be the foundation that future
generations will build upon in their lives."

Nels & Sophia (Miller) & Mathilda (Gilbertson) Christensen

Nels Christensen filed on a homestead five miles northeast of Mercer April 5,
1905. He lived in an earth home on Section 12 of Wise Township. His land
bordered Sheridan County to the east and his brother Tony's land to the west.

Nels was born June 11, 1867, in Skanderborg County, Denmark, to Peter
Christensen and Johanna Nielsen. He immigrated with his parents to America in
1868. They lived on a farm south of Hutchinson, until Nels came west in 1905,
along with his brother, Jergen, sisters, Sarah and Mary Johnson and family, and
his parents. Earlier in 1903 his older brothers, Tony, Jonas, and Chris W.
homesteaded north of Mercer.

        Photo: Mr. and Mrs. Nels Christensen, 1912.

Nels' dugout faced the south and had a wooden front. After his mother, Johanna,
died in 1911, his father moved a small one room house for himself onto Nel's
homestead. Nels was a bachelor and Peter helped Nels with his farmwork.

In 1912, when Nels was 44 years old, he married Sophia Miller, a mail order
bride, according to his nephew, Walter. The February 23, 1912, Mercer Telegram
reported, "Nels P. Christensen returned from South Dakota last Saturday
accompanied by a lady friend who we understand is his wife. Mr. Christensen left
about three weeks ago without informing anyone of his destination, but we
expected what was up and warranted the boys to carry a pocket full of rice... we
extend congratulations and wish the newlyweds a long and happy life."

This was not to be. The January 28, 1916, Mercer Telegram reported Sophie's
death, "A Telegram received from Chamberlain, South Dakota, to Nels P.
Christensen Wednesday morning conveyed the news of the sudden death of his wife
at that place... Mr. Christensen and his wife left here early this winter to visit
with Mrs. Christensen's parents at Chamberlain and upon his return some weeks
ago, he left his wife to return in the spring... Mrs. Christensen has been a
resident of this community for about three years and during which time she made
many warm personal friends..."

From the February 11, 1916, Mercer Telegram, "Nels P. Christensen returned from
Chamberlain, South Dakota, where he attended the funeral of his wife. The death
of Mrs. Christensen is indeed a sad one. Both she and her mother were burnt to
death in a fire that destroyed their home..."

Nel's nephew, Walter, said Nels had two mail order brides. The summer of 1916,
he married Matilda from South Dakota. She was born in Wisconsin to Gilbert
Gilbertson and Annie Anderson. Although Nels was married twice, he never had any
children.

In 1923, Peter's little house on Nel's homestead burned down. He alternated
living with his various children, but this did not work out well.

In November of 1926, Nels had gastrointestinal surgery at Jamestown Hospital. He
died there December 28, 1926, at the age of 58. He was buried in the Danish
cemetery seven miles north of Mercer. Two weeks later his wife, Matilda, died on
January 12, 1927. She is buried beside her husband.

Peter & Johanna (Nielsen) Christensen

Peter and Johanna Christensen came to Mercer in April 1905 and filed on a claim
in Section 13 of Wise Township. Seven of their nine children also homesteaded at
Mercer.

Peter P. Christensen was born in Nortvick, Norre Snede, Skanderborg County,
Denmark, October 28, 1842, the son of Christen and Mette (Jonasen) Nielsen. He
served in the Danish army in the 1864 war between Denmark and Germany. In the
war, Denmark lost much of her fertile farm land to Germany.

Peter's trade was harness maker and shoe repairman. The family was known as the
"Skomager" or a Shoemaker family. Peter married Johanna Nielsen on March 2,
1866, at Oster Nykirke, Vejle County, Denmark. Johanna was born January 28,
1844, in Kolding, Denmark, the daughter of Niels and Ana (Christensen) Larsen.

Peter and Johanna were the parents of ten children, six boys and four girls:
Nels, Christian, Christine, Christian W., Anna, Mary, Jonas, Anton, Jorgen, and
Sarah.

        Photo: The Peter Christensen family: (front, from left) Johanna, Sarah,
        and Peter; (back) Christine, Mary, Chris W., Jergen, Jonas, Anton, Nels,
        and Annie. (Courtesy of Christensen collection)

        Photo: Christian W. and Mary Christensen homesteaded in Section
        34-148-79. (Courtesy of Christensen collection)

Their first son, Nels, was born June 11, 1867, in Denmark. They immigrated to
America in 1868, and settled on a farm three miles south of Hutchinson,
Minnesota.

The rest of the children were born at Hutchinson. Their second child, Christian,
was born and died around 1870.

Christine was born January 1, 1872, and married Soren Sorensen in Hutchinson.
In 1904, they moved to Portland, Oregon. Later, they moved to Seattle where
Soren worked in the shipyards. Their children were: Herbert, Thorvald, Claude,
Vernon, and Alma.

Christian W. was born August 5, 1873, and married Mary "Miller" Petersen in
November 1898 in Hutchinson. She was a sister to Juliana (Jonas) Christensen.
They had seven children: Violet, Carslie, Hurluf, Ervin, Roy and Ray (twins),
and Dora.

Anna (Anne) was born April 21, 1874, and married Hans Hansen May 25, 1897, at
Hutchinson. They had six living children: Harry, Elvin, Hanna, Elvina, Susan,
and LeOtis. They farmed her parent's farm south of Hutchinson.

Marie "Mary" was born July 1876 and married Julius Johnson October 23, 1901, in
Hutchinson. They had nine children: Mable, Mildred, Virgil "Melvin", Sarah,
Peter "Lawrence", Lydia, Esther, Amos, and Charlotte.

Jonas was born March 8, 1879, and married Juliana Petersen Hansen, a widow with
a daughter, Carlie Hansen. They had two children, Shirley and Walter.

Anton "Tony" was born August 2, 1879. He married Josephine "Josie" Ronsjgaard in
1909 and they had a foster child, Gladys Webster.

Lars Christian "Jergen" was born September 5, 1881. He married Elsie Christine
Nielsen at Kenmare in 1907. They had eight children: Harold, Alvina, Raymond,
Ellen, Floyd, Lulla, Arnold, and Deloris.

Sarah, the youngest, was born September 11, 1883. She married Jens Bille in
1909. They had five children: Florence, Agnes, Vernon, Clara, and Paul.

In 1903, three of Peter and Johanna's sons, Tony, Jonas, and Chris, with his
wife and two children, Violet and Carslie, took up homesteads north of Mercer.
Chris and Mary's children, Hurluf and Ervin, were born at Mercer. In 1908 they
moved to Spokane, Washington, were Roy and Ray, the twins, and Dora were born.

On April 4,1905, Peter, age 62 and Johanna, 61, filed on a claim in Section 13
of Wise Township. Also filing on nearby homesteads were their sons, Nels and
Jergen, who were both single. Jergen proved up his homestead 8 miles north of
Mercer and then moved to Kenmare. He and Elsie moved to Sidney, Mont., in 1925
and he worked most of his life as a blacksmith.

Peter and Johanna's two daughters, Sarah, and Mary and her husband, Julius
Johnson, also took up homesteads in the Danish settlement north of Mercer in
1905. The Johnsons later moved to McClusky and farmed there.

In November 1905, when St. Ansgar Danish Congregation was formed, Peter was the
first council President. This church met in the homes of the members.

In 1908, Peter was using his blacksmith forge on his homestead in Section 13 of
Wise Township when a prairie fire started. It was in a frame structure, and the
fire spread from it to a haystack and also the barn. The fire swept off across
the prairie, taking one of S.A. Johnson's haystacks in Section 2. Jake Nelson,
who lived one-half mile southeast of Jonas' homestead, plowed a firebreak,
during which his team of horses became frightened at the flames and ran away.
They were badly singed by the flames, and barely missed a barb wire fence. The
fire ran about two miles before being put out, according to The Mercer Telegram.

Jonas often spoke of his mother, Johanna's Christian faith. Some of his happiest
memories were of his parents singing together. They loved music and sang well
together the hymns of their church and the old favorites they had learned in
Denmark. Johanna died September 1, 1911, of cancer. She is buried in the St.
Ansger Cemetery north of Mercer.

After Johanna's death, Peter gave up farming, rented out his farm and moved a
small one room house for himself to his bachelor son, Nels', who lived in a dug
out with a wooden front. Nels married Sophie Miller in 1912. She died tragically
in a house fire at her parent's home in South Dakota in January 1916. Later that
year, Nels married Matilda Gilbertson. Nels never had any children.

When Peter was in his late 70s, he bought his first Model T Ford, and learned
how to drive. One day in Turtle Lake, he attempted to back up, but instead drove
forward through a store window. Later, he bought a sedan and drove his new car
alone to Hutchinson, Minn., to visit his daughter, Annie Hanson, and family.

In 1923, Peter's little house burned down, and he alternated living with his
children. This did not work out well, and he then moved to Minden, Nebraska, to
Bethany Home for the Aged, which was sponsored by the Danish Lutheran Church. He
died at the age of 92 on June 16, 1934, and is buried in the Danish cemetery
north of Mercer beside his wife, Johanna.

Stephen & Beverly (Larson) Christensen

        Photo: The Steve Christensen family: (from left) John, Brent, Bev,
        Steve, and Josh.

Stephen Ward Christensen was born February 20, 1949, at the Bismarck Hospital to
Walter and Ruth Christensen of Mercer, North Dakota. There was a lot of snow
that winter, so when the baby was almost due, Walter arranged for an airplane
with skis to fly Ruth to Bismarck to await the birth. She stayed with her
mother, Hattie Ovre, a few days until Steve was born.

Steve has three sisters: Patricia, Eunice, and Mary Lou, and three brothers:
Joel, James, and Thomas.

Steve attended Medicine Hill Township School #4 one mile north of their farm for
his first four years of education. Then in 1959, when most rural schools closed,
he went to Mercer. He enjoyed playing basketball for Mercer and graduated in
1967.

Steve attended college at UND-Williston for two years where he played
basketball. He then attended Dickinson State College, where he also played
basketball. Steve graduated with a BS in Secondary Education in Social Science
and PE in 1972. He worked as a counselor with Vocational Rehabilitation from
1972 until the spring of 1974.

Steve married Beverly Larson at Regent, North Dakota, on December 18, 1971. Bev
was born January 27, 1951, at Dickinson, North Dakota to Glenn and Clara
(Schweigert) Larson. The Larsons farmed and ranched two miles east of Regent by
Larson Lake. Bev has five siblings: James, Roger, Dorothy, Susan, and Shirley.

Bev attended country school for two years and then Regent Public. When she was a
senior in high school, her parents moved to a dairy farm at Eagle Bend,
Minnesota. She graduated in 1969, and from Dickinson State College with an
Associate Degree in Nursing in 1971. She took state boards that summer and at
age 20, became a registered nurse. She took her first job at the hospital in
Long Prairie, Minnesota. That August she attended a coronary care training
program at St. Joseph's and Ramsey Hospitals in St. Paul.

After Steve and Bev married, she worked at St. Alexius in Bismarck in the
Intensive Care Unit. She also started attending classes at the University of
Mary, where she graduated in May 1974 with a BS in Nursing.

Steve and Bev took over his parent's family farm in May of 1974, and Bev started
working at the Turtle Lake Hospital.

They were blessed with three sons: Brent, Joshua and John. Brent Stephen was
born April 26, 1975. He graduated from Turtle Lake-Mercer in 1993 and NDSU,
Fargo in 1997 with a degree in Agriculture. He worked at Kindred, North Dakota,
for RDO John Deere until 1999, when he started farming at Mercer.

        Photo: Neighbors make hay in 1999: (from left) Lyle and Eugene Schon,
        Brent Christensen, and Cliff Alexander.

Joshua Ward was born December 28, 1976. He graduated from TL-M in 1995 and from
NDSU, Fargo in 2000 with a degree in Electrical Engineering. He has worked at
Seagate Technology in Minneapolis as a design engineer since 2000.

John Jonas was born September 18, 1981. He graduated in 2000 from TL-M High
School. He is an electrical engineering student at NDSU, Fargo and a Division II
All American Hammer Thrower.

Christensens grow small grains, oilseeds, and hay, as well as raise cattle in a
cow-calf operation. Steve's grandfather, Jonas, homesteaded the family farm in
1903. They celebrated the Homestead Centennial in July 2003.

They are members of Our Savior's Lutheran Church in Mercer. Steve serves on the
church council, and the McLean-McHenry Insurance Board. He has also served on
the Equity Elevator and Farmer's Union Board. Bev has worked part time for St.
Alexius Home Health Care and Hospice since 1987. She enjoys riding bike and
horseback, and genealogy.

"We feel blessed by God to be able to live and work here on the prairie and a
gratitude to our forefathers for their pioneer spirit, sacrifice, and commitment
to homesteading this land."

Thomas & Nancy (Joersz) Christensen

Thomas Scott Christensen was born March 24, 1961, at the Turtle Lake Hospital.
He was the youngest of seven children born to Walter and Ruth Christensen. He
attended school at Mercer grades 1-6 and at Turtle Lake for grade 7. In 1974 he
moved to Mandan with his parents and older brother, Jim, and attended Mandan
Junior High for 8th grade and Mandan Senior High grades 9-12.

While at Mandan High, Tom participated in basketball, football and track and
graduated in 1979. Tom attended Dickinson State College for two years where he
also played football.

Tom and Nancy Joersz were married in August of 1981 at Spirit of Life Church in
Mandan. Nancy is the daughter of Marvin and Lucille Joersz. Tom and Nancy
lived in married student housing as NDSU, with Nancy working at a bank in
Moorhead and Tom continuing his education and graduating in 1983 with a degree
in electrical engineering.

        Photo: The Thomas Christensen family: (from left) Cameron, Brooke,
        Nancy, Tom and Eric.

In June of 1983, Tom began working for Basin Electric Power Cooperative in
Bismarck. They lived in Mandan and on February 13, 1985 Eric David was born and
on October 16, 1986 Cameron Scott was born. Tom, Nancy and sons then moved to
Ankeny, Iowa (just north of Des Moines) in July of 1987 where Tom worked for
Iowa Power & Light in downtown Des Moines.

In July of 1989 Tom, Nancy and sons moved back to North Dakota and settled in
Bismarck when Tom came back to work for Basin Electric. Brooke Ann was born on
May 26, 1992.

Currently (2004) Tom continues to work at Basin Electric, Nancy is a homemaker
and works part-time at Grimsrud Elementary School. Eric is a sophomore at St.
John's University (near St. Cloud, Minnesota), Cameron is a senior at St. Mary's
Central High School in Bismarck, and Brooke is a 7th grader at Cathedral School
in Bismarck.

Walter & Ruth (Ovre) Christensen

Walter Ward Christensen was born April 21, 1910, in Medicine Hill Township to
Jonas and Juliana (Petersen) Christensen. Walter had two older sisters, Shirley,
age 2, and Carlie Hanson, 17. Carlie's father, James Hanson, died of TB when
Carlie was 5 years old. Walter's mother, Juliana, and Carlie homesteaded in 1904
in Sect. 2 in Wise Township, 6 miles north of Mercer. Juliana's parents, Soren
and Maren "Miller" Petersen, and her brother, Peter, also took up a homestead
nearby.

        Photo: Walter and Ruth Christensen in 1938.

Walter's father, Jonas, homesteaded 7 miles north of Mercer in 1903. He married
Juliana Hanson on Nov. 22, 1906, at Pastor Keller's homestead. Juliana was born
in Denmark in 1869 and came to Hutchinson, Minnesota, at the age of 16 with her
parents.

In 1913, Walter's family moved two miles southeast to Rev. Frederick Peterson's
homestead in Wise Township, southeast of the Keller place. Now Shirley and
Walter were closer to the Sprout School. When they were old enough, they would
walk home across the pasture on nice days. Walter and Shirley enjoyed playing
with the Keller children, their closest neighbors. They also enjoyed their Bille
cousins to the south. Walter's sister, Carlie, and Herman Olson were married by
Pastor Keller on December 29, 1915.

In November 1918, Walter's family moved back to Jonas' original homestead.
Walter, in third grade, had more boys his age at the new Medicine Hill School
#4. Alvin Christensen, son of Martin Christensen, lived just to the south.
Sidney and LeRoy Nelsen, sons of Jake Nelsen, lived one-half mile to the east,
and the boys walked to school together. They enjoyed hunting rabbits and gophers
after school.

Walter and Shirley attended Sunday School at the Sprout School with Miss Lydia
Keller as their teacher. After she moved away, Minnie Nelsen, a pianist and Mrs.
Joe Peterson started a Sunday School at the Medicine Hill School.

When Walter was 13, Jonas decided he was mature enough to ride a gang plow, a
two-lay that turned two furrows at a time and was pulled by four horses. To
handle four horses took a strong arm and hand, plus some weight to stay in the
seat when a rock hit the plowshare. Before that, Walter helped shear their sheep
with a hand tool. He also helped put up hay, shock grain, garden and milk the
cows.

At 13, Walter also began hauling lignite coal, which was stored in their
basement in the early fall. The coal was hauled in lumber wagons with double or
triple high boxes and pulled by three or four horses. Jonas bought coal at that
time at the Feganskow Mine between Turtle Lake and Underwood. It was about a
forty mile round trip and Jonas and Walter each drove a wagon, which were very
heavy when loaded.

Walter started working on a threshing crew when he was 15. He and his dad each
had their own team and wagon and they worked with the Rauser threshing crew.
John Rauser (Herb's father) and Bill Rauser, brothers, owned and operated the
threshing machine. Their crew consisted of their brothers, sons and neighbor
boys from the German Baptist community. John Rauser's farm is where Clifford
Alexander lives now. Bill Rauser lived on the former Ed Skow homestead, now
owned by Marilyn Schon.

In the fall of 1932, Walter started dating Ruth Ovre occasionally. She was the
daughter of Krogh and Hattie (Akre) Ovre. Ruth graduated from Mercer H.S. in
1932 when she was 15. She attended Valley City State Teacher's College in 1933.
The summer of 1934 was one of the worst drought years in North Dakota. That fall
she took her first teaching job at the Sprout Schoolhouse. She made $50 per
month and had 28 students in first to eighth grade. It was a difficult year, but
the next year she had only 19 students, as the Lehn (Levi) School opened again.

The summer of 1936 Walter went to Sidney, Montana with Jens Glad and Sidney
Nielsen to do irrigation work. That fall Ruth taught the Brush Lake School.

In August 1937 Walter started working in Jamestown at the State Hospital as an
orderly, where he worked for two years. The crops were poor, and he was glad to
have found a job. Ruth taught a rural school near Sawyer that fall.

Walter and Ruth were married October 26, 1938, in a double wedding with her
sister, Martha, and Reed Argent, of Steele, North Dakota. It was the first
wedding held at the new Our Savior's Lutheran Church in Mercer.

Ruth taught the Sprout School again from 1939-40. They then began raising a
family of seven children. Patricia was born in 1941, Eunice in 1943, Mary Lou in
1946, Stephen in 1949, Joel in 1952, James in 1957, and Thomas in 1961.

Around 1942, when the drought was over and crop prices were significantly
higher, Walter and his dad purchased their first tractor, a John Deere Model D.
In 1943, Walter and Ruth purchased the farm from his parents.

Walter's sister, Shirley, married Edwin Ingman on August 1, 1943 in Seattle. He
was a widower with two children. Shirley and Ed had two children, Julie, born in
1944 and Paul, born in 1948.

Walter was elected to the rural school board in 1950. In 1959 when the rural
schools closed, he was elected President of the Mercer School Board. He was a
Gideon, Sunday School Superintendent, and a Luther League advisor. In 1961 and
1963, Walter served as Democratic NPL Representative from McLean County. During
his second term he was assistant minority floor leader. He also served on the
Legislative Research Committee for four years, mostly on the Secondary Education
subcommittee.

In 1964, Governor Guy drove out to the farm and asked Walter if he would run for
Lieutenant Governor at the State Democratic Convention. Walter agreed but was
nominated instead for State Treasurer. He won his first four year term in 1964.
After losing a re-election bid in 1968, he became director of Gov. Wm. Guy's
Administration. He took a six-month leave of absence in 1970 to direct the
Democratic state campaign.

        Photo: Walter Christensen

Walter regained the Treasurer's post in 1972. He served as head of the Personnel
Board, chairman of the Governor's Committee on Refugees, and head of the State
Investment Fund. While Treasurer he worked among legislators for a higher coal
severance tax. He served on the State Historical Board and was the first
chairman of the Lewis and Clark Opportunity Foundation. For nine and a half
years, he commuted 110 miles each day from Mercer to Bismarck and back.

Ruth was active in Our Savior's Lutheran Church, helping sew many quilts, and
attending Bible study. She was elected Bismarck ALCW Conference President in
1970 and served four years. In 1972 she was a delegate to the National ALCW
convention in Cincinnati.

In 1974, Walter and Ruth sold the family farm to their son, Steve and wife, Bev.
They moved to Mandan with sons, Jim and Tom, and became active members of First
Lutheran Church.

Walter died August 3, 1979, while serving his third term as State Treasurer. A
quote from the August 3, 1979, Bismarck Tribune, "A tall man of Lincolnesque
features, Christensen wore an imposing head of silver-gray hair and spoke with a
resonant baritone voice, which he used for years in pulpits throughout the state
on behalf of the Gideons International... Gov. Arthur Link said 'Walter Christensen
was our friend and Grace and I feel a deep personal loss. The state of North
Dakota has lost one of its most loyal and dedicated citizens and public
servants.'" Walter was buried in the Mercer Hillside Cemetery.

        Photo: The Christensen family picture taken in 1986: (front, from left)
        Jim, Patricia, Eunice, Tom; (back) Mary Lou, Steve, Ruth and Joel.

Ruth remained in her home north of Mandan and active in the community. That fall
she hosted a Friendship Force lady from Germany. In 1983 she went on the Martin
Luther Heritage Tour to Germany and Norway with Evelyn Freeberg and Martha
Schlafman. Ruth was voted a North Dakota Merit Mother in 1986. She was nominated
by the ladies of First Lutheran Church, Mandan. In September 1997, Ruth moved to
the Turtle Lake Manor. In 2001 she moved to The Terrace in Bismarck, and in
December 2002 she moved to the Missouri Slope Lutheran Care Center. In July 2003
she attended the Christensen Homestead Centennial where they also celebrated her
87th birthday. She died two months later on September 10, 2003, and is buried in
the Mercer Hillside Cemetery beside Walter.

Oscar & Edna (Sackman) Clemons

        Photo: The Clemons family: Wayne, Oscar, Edna and Steve.

Oscar Clemons was born on March 19, 1911, and died on Jan. 27, 1994, in Spokane,
Wash. He married Edna Sackman in 1942.

Edna Sackman was born on July 13, 1915, in Mercer, the daughter of Chrisoph and
Christina Peters Sackman. She graduated from Mercer High School in 1933 and died
in Spokane in 2002.

Ocsar and Edna had two sons:

Wayne Clemons was born on Dec. 15, 1942, and is a pharmacist. He is married to
Pamela and they have two sons: Nicolas and Jeffry Clemons.

Steven Clemons was born on May 4, 1949, and is married to Karen. They have two
sons: Jonathan and Nathan Clemons.

William & Rosa (Cooper) Conkling

The 1914 Atlas listed the following: William A. Conkling was born in 1878 in
Iowa. He settled in McLean County in 1911 on 35-147-79, Wise Township. He
married Rosa B. Cooper and they had 7 children by 1914.

In June of 1912, The Mercer Telegram reported that Dr. Paulson of Turtle Lake
was called to William Conkling's home. William's 12-year-old son Elmer fell
beneath the wheels of his father's steam breaking outfit and severely fractured
his right femur leg bone. Apparently he recovered because the January 17, 1913,
Mercer Telegram reported that Elmer and Wilbur Conkling took 8th grade exams at
the Brush Lake School. Myron Makeeff now owns the Conkling land, which is east
of the rural water lift station along Highway 33.

Alle & Rachel Dakovna

Alle Dakovna was born in Russia in 1871. His wife Rachel was also born in Russia
and they were married there before coming to America in 1904. They came to the
Mercer area after 1910.

Alle built a dry goods store in 1915 and also was a hide dealer. The Dakovna
Store was purchased by Gottlieb Fischer in 1940. The family home is still in
Mercer and is owned by Angie and Stan Misek.

The Dakovna daughter, Pauline, was born in Russia in 1900/01 and was a clerk in
the Dakovna Store. She married ??? Livingstein and her son Marvin was born in
Mercer and attended school.

The Dakovna son, Joseph, was born in 1903 and attended Mercer School and
graduated in 1923. He operated the Dakovna Store after the death of his father.
He left Mercer in 1940 and lived in Bismarck until 1943 when he moved to
California where he was a realtor. He was married in 1941 and had two sons,
Allen and Aron. Joe died in California.

Information is from items in the Mercer Telegram, the 1920 census and the Mercer
Alumni book.

Karl & Margaretha (Sackmann, Mayer) Degg

        Photo: The Degg family: (front) Karl and Margaretha with granddaughter
        Regine; (back) John, Frederika, Carl and Margaret.

(Further explanation of the previous picture) Frederika Degg, born about 1896,
married Art Shelton. Carl Degg, born August 12, 1888, married Dora Barbara
Hepper. Margaret Degg, born October 10, 1890, married Theobald Hofer. John Degg,
born June 30, 1898, married Dora Wallenhaust. Regine Mayer, granddaughter,
married Andrew Sackman. Not pictured: Johannes Degg, born August 22, 1874, died
in Beresina, Bessarabia. Eva Degg, born December 21, 1877, married Christ
Stregger, also Gotlieb Bippus. Christina Degg, born May 2, 1880, married Daniel
Mayer.)

Karl Degg was born on Oct. 12, 1852, in Beresina, Bessarabia in South Russia. On
Nov. 28, 1873, he married Dorothea Harter in Borodino, Bessarabia. They had
eight children, namely Johannes, Eva, Christina, Elisabeth, Jacob, Carl,
Margaretha and Magdelena. Karl's first wife died in 1894 in Borodino. He later
married Margaretha Mayer nee Sackmann, the daughter of Andreas and Eva Sackmann
nee Beutel of Borodino.

Margaretha was previously married to Johann Mayer and had four children by this
marriage, namely Karolina, Daniel, Catherine and Pauline. Her husband Johannes
died in 1890. Karl and Margaretha were married in 1894 in Kloestitz, Bessarabia.
Two children were born to this marriage in Borodino, namely Frederika in 1896
and Johannes in 1898.

Karl and Margaretha immigrated to North America in May 13, 1902, on board the
S.S. Arcadia, along with other family members. They went first to North Dakota
and acquired a homestead near Mercer. Here the family farmed for many years.
Other family members had immigrated to Medicine Hat and Glen Bain, Sask.,
Canada, and Karl spent his later years there.

He died in Glen Bain, Sask., Canada, on April 6, 1923, at the home of his son
Jacob. Margaretha moved to Mercer where she lived for many years among family
and friends. She died in Sawyer at the home of her daughter on Feb. 20, 1947.

"Grandma" Degg was survived by 233 heirs. She had eight daughters, three sons,
100 grandchildren, 119 great-grandchildren and three great-great-grandchildren.

Walter & Minnie (Jans-Hegney-Max) Derheim

        Photo: Walter and Minnie Derheim.

Minnie Jans was born in 1914 in Canada to Heindrich and Rosina Jans. She married
Otis Hegney in 1929 and had two sons.

She married Peter Max in 1935 and they had four sons, Peter Jr., Melvin, Floyd
and Leonard. Peter died in a car accident in 1940.

In 1941 she married Walter Derheim at the Washburn Court House. They had two

Gottlieb & Pauline (Enders) Diede

Gottlieb Diede was born in 1863 in Karlsruhe, South Russia. He married Pauline
Enders in 1892 and they came to the United States in 1904, settling near
McClusky.

Gottlieb and Pauline moved to Mercer in 1937. Pauline died in 1941 and Gottlieb
moved back to McClusky for a number of years. He moved to Mercer and lived near
his daughter and son-in-law, Sam and Lizzie Beierle, until he died in 1957.

        Photo: Gottlieb Diede

Derheim); Elizabeth (Sam Beierle); Esther (Jake Wiebe); Clara (Palmer Pederson);
Martha (Herbert Thompson); and sons William, Ben, Otto, Jake and Joe.

Jake & Anna (Pederson) Diede

Jake Diede, son of Gottleib and Pauline Diede, was born June 2, 1908. He was one
of a family of 5 boys and 6 girls.

On February 9, 1935, Jake married Anna Pederson, daughter of Edward and Hattie
Pederson.

Anna and Jake lived east of Mercer, N.D, until they moved into town in 1944.
Jake was a cattle buyer and also did trucking. Anna taught in rural country
schools. In 1947 she went to work part time in the post office for Ben Hjelle.
She also worked for Reinhart Stradinger when he was postmaster. Anna and Jake
both retired in 1976 and Anna passed away in January 1983. She is buried in the
Mercer Cemetery.

Jake remarried to Eva Boozeny on June 22, 1987, died July 2, 1990, and is buried
in the Mercer Cemetery.

Six children were born to Jake and Anna. They all attended Mercer school. They
were:

Dale was killed in a car accident in 1974.

Doran died as an infant.

children, Andrew and Alexandra; Daniel (Kathy) and Jason.

Barbara married Norm Steinle and had three sons: Darren Murray (Kelly) with

Gene & Eunice (Kirking) Dockter

Gene Johnny Dockter was born to Johnny and Elsie Dockter on Jan. 18, 1943, in
Turtle Lake. He lived on a farm near Lincoln Valley until 1946 when the Dockters
moved to the family farm north of Mercer.

Gene attended Medicine Hill Country School for eight years and graduated from
Turtle Lake High School in 1961. He graduated from Valley City State College in
1965 with majors in English and history. He taught English at St. Thomas High
School, St. Thomas, N.D. for three years.

Gene and Eunice Kirking, daughter of Oliver and Eleonora Nissen Kirking, were
married on Aug. 3, 1968, in Drayton, N.D. Euni graduated from St. Thomas High
School, St. Thomas, and the Institute of Medical Technology in Minneapolis,
Minn. She was employed as a lab technician at a medical clinic in Grand Forks.
They moved to Sauk Centre, Minn., where Gene taught junior high English and
history classes as well as coached.

Gene and Euni returned to the family farm in 1977 upon his father's retirement.
They have two children: Jonathan Kirk who was born on Oct. 19, 1975, and
Kimberly Ann born Jan. 21, 1980. Jonathan graduated from UND and lives in Grand
Forks where he's a store manager. Kimberly graduated from the University of Mary
with a degree in elementary education. She and Ben Luger were married on Aug. 2,
2002. Ben is a graduate of UND and is employed as a youth minister at Good
Shepherd Lutheran Church, Bismarck.

Johnny & Elsie (Schimke) Dockter

Johnny Dockter and Elsie Schimke were united in marriage on Oct. 13, 1940, at
Emanuel Lutheran Church, a rural church located about 12 miles south of Butte,
N.D. After they were married, they rented a farm north of McClusky and lived
there for six years.

In 1946, they purchased the former Littke farm, which was located 11 miles north
of Mercer and moved there in October of 1946.

Elsie and Johnny spent over 35 years working together in partnership on their
farm. Along with hard work, they found time to raise a family and participate in
community and church activities. They were members of St. John's Lutheran Church
(a rural church located about 14 miles north of Turtle Lake) and later Trinity
Lutheran Church in Turtle Lake.

        Photo: Johnny Dockter (center, back) and his children, (front, from
        left) JoAnn Johnson, Gene Dockter; (back) Janice Geigle and Joyce
        Fiedler.

Johnny and Elsie had four children: Joann and Gene who are twins born on Jan.
18, 1943; Janice born on Sept. 10, 1946; and Joyce born on Dec. 3, 1947 along
with seven grandchildren.

JoAnn married Glenn Freborg in 1962 and he died in 1998. She married Erv Johnson
in 2003 and they live in Minot. (See separate history page 262)

Janice married Edwin K. Geigle and they live in Bismarck. (See separate history
page 240)

Joyce married Dennis Fiedler and they live on the Fiedler farm north of Mercer.
(See separate family history page 230)

After farming for over 35 years, Elsie and Johnny retired from farming in 1976
and moved to their house at 404 Kundert St. in Turtle Lake. They enjoyed many
activities together in their retirement years, some of which included time spent
with family and friends, fishing, bowling and more.

Their son and daughter-in-law, Gene and Euni (Kirking) Dockter moved to the
family farm in 1977 and reside there today. (See separate history page 226)

Elsie and Johnny were married for 60 years. Elsie died on July 20, 2001, and
Johnny continues to live in their house in Turtle Lake.

Johnny Dockter was born in Anamoose, N.D., on Sept. 1, 1915. He was the son of
John M. Dockter, born in South Russia in 1890 and immigrated to the U.S. in
1907, and Marie Spear born in Romania in 1896 and immigrated to the U.S. in
1903. Johnny grew up on his family's homesteaded farm in Holmes Township
northwest of McClusky. He attended the Consolidated School about a half-mile
south of where the family lived. His family consisted of two brothers, Walter
and Art; and two sisters, Helen (Albert Bonnet) and Eleanor (Fred Wittman).
Walter lives in Bismarck, Helen lives in Turtle Lake and both Art and Eleanor
are deceased.

Elsie Mary Schimke was born on May 11, 1917, in Butte, N.D. Her parents were
John Schmike, born in 1879 in South Russia, and Magdalena Kleingartner, born in
1885 in South Russia. Elsie was raised on the family's homesteaded farm about
eight miles south of Butte, N.D. She attended a rural school in Byersville
Township in McLean County. Her family consisted of three brothers, Otto, Hilbert
and Edward and one sister, Ida (Henry Krause). All are deceased.

Arlo  & Janice (Pfeifle) Eckmann

Arlo Eckmann was born in February 1937 at Mercer, the son of Fred and Helen

High School in 1955. He attended the North Dakota State School of Science in
Wahpeton and received a degree in electronics. He worked for the Bismarck Police
Department for nine years and retired from OHMEDA Medical Products in 1986.

        Photo: Arlo Eckmann

member of the Bismarck Eagles and Moose Clubs.

He married Janice Pfeifle on Nov. 17, 1962, in Bismarck. They had two children,
Renee (Mike) DeWall and Kevin (Laura).

Arlo died on July 13, 1995, in Bismarck and the funeral services were on July
17, 1995, in Faith Lutheran Church with burial in the North Dakota Veterans
cemetery in rural Mandan.

Fred & Helen (Singer) Eckmann

Fred Eckmann a Wishek, N.D., native was working in the Turtle Lake area where he
met Helen Singer. They were married in 1935 and after seven years of different
occupations settled on the Williams farm 4.5 miles southwest of Mercer. The
Eckmanns farmed most of their lives, retiring to Bismarck in 1961. They still
kept an interest in farming west of Mercer. They raised two sons.

        Photo: (Front, from left) Helen and Fred Singer; (back) Arlo and Janice,

Arlo, born in 1937, graduated from Mercer High School in 1955, attended Wahpeton
science school with a degree in electronics. He served in the U.S. Army from
1958-1960. In 1961 he joined the Bismarck Police Department for nine years and
retired from OHMEDA Medical Products in 1986. Arlo passed away in 1995 and is

and five grandsons.

Michael & Matilda (Schtung) Eichelt

Michael Eichelt was born April 7, 1864, in Wamulka, Russia. He married Matilda
Martin Schtung in Berlin, Germany in 1896. She was born on August 2, 1877, in
Bawnarik, Russia.

Michael emigrated from the port of Hamburg, Germany on the vessel Augusta
Victoria and entered the U.S. at New York on June 15, 1901. He came to North
Dakota in August 1902, and petitioned to become a citizen. He homesteaded on the
NE¼ of Section 35 in Medicine Hill Township, about seven miles north of Mercer.
After living here for five consecutive years, he was granted U.S. Citizenship on
December 4, 1907, and proved up his claim. He then returned to Germany
(Berkawitz, Prussia) to his family and stayed there for two years.

Michael and Matilda and their first three children, Emil, Gottlieb, and
Hildegard, who were born in Germany, returned to his claim at Mercer. Two more
children were born in North Dakota, August and Edward. The September 23, 1910,
Mercer Telegram reported that Matilda had a baby, that she was a paralytic, and
that "she is now somewhat improved." Michael was a farmer, and also a Christian
man who read his Bible through four times. He was a big man with large hands and
he had a beard.

        Photo: Emil and Alice Ikel (eichelt)

Emil was born October 6, 1897. He changed his last name from Eichelt to Ikel. He
had three children with Anna Heltwein: Alfred, Jack and Robert. Anna died four
days after Robert was born. Emil later married Alice, and they had four
children: Irene, Vivian, Arnold and Lorelei. Emil was killed in an accident at
the Armours Meat Packing Plant in West Fargo. He is buried in Glyndon,
Minnesota.

Gottlief was born October 9, 1899. It is believed that he was accidentally
gassed to death at a copper mine in Butte, Montana, in 1943.

Hildegard "Hilda" was born in 1908. She never married and died in Spokane,
Washington in 1964.

Edward was born in 1913. He was last heard from around 1953.

        Photo: The August Eichelt family

August was born October 15, 1910. He married Amy and they had five children:
Donald, August Jr., Daniel, Herb, Jule, Elaine (Haberl). He died February 1984.

Times were difficult, and Michael and Matilda lost their homestead in 1912 in a
foreclosure sale. He then moved his family to a farm south of Mercer. Matilda
died of a stroke November 15, 1915, in Wells County at the age of 38. She is
buried in Germantown Township east of Fessenden, North Dakota.

Michael lived with his son, August, before he died on February 11, 1938. He is
buried in the Mercer Hillside Cemetery.
