Jerome & Dagny (Glad) Fibelstad

Jerome Fibelstad was born June 11, 1899, at Wells, Minn., the son of Nels A. and
Petrina (Pederson) Fibelstad.

On June 6, 1929, He and Dagny Glad, who was born August 20, 1903, in Sortland,
Norway, were married at the St. Olaf parsonage rural Turtle Lake.

Dagny was the daughter of Sigurd and Amalia (Nilsen) Glad. They, too, were
Norwegian immigrants and homesteaders in McLean County, Medicine Hill Township,
rural Turtle Lake.

        Photo: Dagney and Jerome Fibelstad

Jerome and Dagny made their home on the Fibelstad homestead northeast of Mercer
where Jerome had lived since age seven. They were members of Our Saviors
Lutheran Church. Jerome was a charter member. Jerome farmed until the mid-60s
when he retired due to poor health. Dagny was a rural school teacher in McLean
and Sheridan Counties 10-15 years.

Jerome and Dagny were the parents of Donna, Dennis, Percy and John. Their first
son Jerome died in infancy. Donna, Dennis and John all graduated from Mercer
High School. Percy graduated from McClusky High School.

Jerome and Dagny were involved in township, church and community activities.
Dagny was a charter member of the Hustling Homemakers Club.

In 1966 they moved to Mercer. Jerome died in 1975. Dagny moved to Bismarck in
1980 and lived there until her death in 1992. Both are buried in the Mercer
Cemetery. Their children all live in North Dakota. Dennis at McClusky, Percy in
Bismarck. John and Family in Minot. Donna and husband Cecil Keisacker at Lakota,
N.D.

Nels A. & Petrina (Pederson) Fibelstad

Nels Andrew Fibelstad was born Dec. 25, 1870, near Mor Og Romsdal, Norway.
Petrina Olava Pederson was born near Hemnes, Norway about 1870.

Nels was five years old when he, his parents and two siblings immigrated to
America in 1875.

        Photo: Nels Fibelstad

They settled in Fairbault County near Bricelyn in southern Minnesota. At age 19
Nels became the head of the household due to the untimely death of his father
and two younger sisters due to typhoid fever. Nels was also a mail carrier
besides farming.

In 1897 Nels and Trina, also an immigrant from Norway, were married in Bricelyn.
A son, Jerome was born June 11, 1899. A daughter, Pernille (Nellie) was born
Oct. 22, 1900.

In 1905 the lure for "homesteading" became a passion for Nels. They migrated to
North Dakota and homesteaded in Prophets Township, Sheridan County 4½ miles
northeast of Mercer. Nels was a community promoter.

The Fibelstad family were charter members of Our Saviors Lutheran Church. Nels
helped organize the Mercer Shipping Association and the Brush Lake Association.
He was active in township affairs as well.

Trina was known in the community for her culinary abilities. Her bread and
butter making skills were appreciated by the bachelors in the community for whom
she made and sold these items.

Trina died in 1920 from complications caused by the 1918 influenza epidemic.
Nels never remarried and continued to live on the homestead until the mid-50s.
He made his home with Jerome and Dagny and family.

In 1955, Nels moved to his daughter Nellie's home in Minneapolis. He died in
April 1960 at the age of 89. He is buried beside Trina in the Mercer cemetery.

Arnold & Erdina (Rust) Fiedler

Erdina Rust was born Dec. 25, 1923, the daughter of Samuel and Lena Rust Sr.

On March 5, 1946, she married Arnold Fielder. He was the son of Christ and
Justina Fielder, Butte, N.D.

They made their home in Mercer where Erdina taught at the Mercer Public School

They moved to Minot where Erdina continued to teach in the public schools.
Arnold worked at a bank in Minot, N.D. Later they moved to Sun City West, Ariz.
Arnold continues to work with banking and real estate. Erdina is directing music
for a Baptist church.

They have one son, Bernard and his wife Margaret, who live in Wisconsin. The
Fiedlers have three grandchildren.

Edwin & Mary (Rust) Fiedler

Edwin and Mary (Rust) Fiedler were married Nov. 20, 1936. They lived five miles
north of Mercer most of their married life.

Edwin was the son of Christian and Justina (Hensel) Fiedler who lived near
Butte, N.D., in Holmes Township. They had eight children: Dan, Otto, Herbert,
Edwin, Arnold, Meinhardt, Marie and Ida (Fiedler) Rust. Edwin was born March 17,
1914.

        Photo: Mary and Edwin Fiedler

Mary was the daughter of Sam and Lena (Mehrer) Rust of Mercer. They, family
lived in Medicine Hill Township of McLean County, approximately 13 miles
northwest of Mercer. Mary was born April 20, 1916. She was one of 13 children,
and one was lost on the ship to America, due to a near full-term miscarriage.
Brothers and sisters were Vernon, Jacob, Andrew, Sam, John (died in a accident
at 13 years of age), a second John, Esther (Rust) Peterson, Helen (Rust) Russ,
Lydia (Rust) Bauer, Mary, Erdina (Rust) Fiedler, Elvina (Rust) Fiedler and
Katherine (Rust) Miller.

Edwin and Mary were active in community events. They were charter members of the
Brush Poppers Horse Club which developed an arena in the Brush Lake area and
hosted many rodeos.

Edwin enjoyed softball, golfing, fishing, hunting, farming, singing and his
harmonica.

Mary enjoyed reading, singing and playing her piano and guitar. She was a
gracious hostess and many guests were treated to her home cooked meals. Sunday
guests were a common occurrence.

The greatest satisfaction came from fellowship and work they did through the
Mercer Baptist Church. They were faithful members, and both taught Sunday
school. Edwin was a deacon for many years and was always there to help when any
repair needed to be done. Mary was also active in the Women's Mission Fellowship
and sewed many articles for the White Cross Missions Projects. She also sewed
most of her girls' clothes.

The older two children attended the Wise School #1 until it closed in 1953. The
balance of years the three children attended the Mercer Public School.

Their children were:

Donna Marie, born May 19, 1940, married Arvid A. Wagner.

Mona Faye, born August 29, 1945, married Harold Schmeets.

Edwin Byron, born September 29, 1955, married Marjorie Swanson.

Edwin died Sept. 3, 1992, and Mary died Sept. 15, 2001.

Minehardt & Elvina (Rust) Fiedler

Elvina Rust was born March 20, 1919, near Mercer to Samuel and Lena Rust Sr. She
grew up north of Mercer on a farm and attended school there.

        Photo: Minehardt and Elvina Fiedler

Minehardt Fiedler was born March 5, 1916, in rural Butte to Christ and Justina
Fiedler. He grew up on his parents' farm 15 miles south of Butte. As a young man
he farmed with his mother.

Elvina and Minehardt were married on Dec. 12, 1940, in rural Mercer. They lived
in Holmes Township one-half mile southwest of the family farm for six years

They have one son Dennis and his wife Joyce (Dockter) Fiedler, and two

David & Margaret (Dietterle) & Rosina (Helfenstein) Fink

David Fink was born Feb. 5, 1882, in Arciz, Bessarabia, and died Nov. 8, 1975,
in Garrison, and is buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

He married Margaret Dietterle on Jan. 19, 1906, in Kloestitz, Bessarabia. She
was born March 16, 1884, in Arciz and died Feb. 9, 1918, at her home in rural
Mercer.

David and Margaret Fink came to America from South Russia in April of 1908. They
brought their one child, Olga, with them and lived with Margaret's mother Rekia,
south of Butte. After losing two husbands, Rekia came to America with her two
sons, Henry and John Smollinger.

David worked as a farm laborer for a year and moved to a farm five miles north
and two miles west of Mercer. He still worked as a farm laborer until he could
get horses and whatever implements he needed to start on his own. In 1910 he
bought some land about three quarters of a mile east of where they lived. He
built a small two-room house, a small barn and dug a well.

Margaret was remembered for her good bread. She did all the sewing, raised a
garden, canned and preserved the meat they raised, like pork, geese and
chickens.

David was a grain and cattle farmer. He was also a butcher and sausage maker and
was the neighborhood butcher and sausage maker.

They attended the country Lutheran Church.

When Margaret died in 1918 from the flu, David was left with six children, the
oldest only 12 years old.

In 1921 David married a widow, Rosina (Kost) Helfenstein, from Hazelton. She had
five children. Rosina died in August of 1935, due to a stroke in 1933.

After a while, David moved to Mercer and was the janitor at the Mercer School.
When he retired as janitor he became an excellent gardener. In 1959 he entered
the Lutheran Retirement Home in Minot, and in 1970 his health failed and he
moved to the Underwood Nursing Home. He was 92 years of age when he died.

The Fink children were:

1. Olga, born Oct. 26, 1906, in Arciz, Bessarabia. She married Julius Sackmann
on Jan. 18, 1927. Julius was born Aug. 12, 1901, in Java, S.D., and died June

John Finkelmeyer

John Finkelmeyer was born around 1846. He filed on a homestead in 1903 in
Section 3 of Wise Township. He filed a five year proof on his claim August 28,
1908.

In December 1907, The Mercer Telegram reported that John Finkelmeyer was sick
with asthma and that he was alone on his claim north of town. His neighbors were
looking after him, and A.J. Buell hauled a load of coal for him.

The 1910 census listed John as 64 years old, divorced and a farmer.

A July 1, 1910, Mercer Telegram quote, "On account of sickness, I am obliged to
sell my farm, which lies 6 miles north of Mercer, 66 acres are broken of which
23 are in crop. The balance of 94 acres can be broken. It has a fine 20-foot
well with stone curbing and a 24 × 24 house. With this farm go 5 lots in Mercer,
3 middle, and 2 corner lots. Give me a fair price and the land is yours- John
Finkelmeyer."

        Photo: The John Finkelmeyer stone home.

John again listed his farm for sale in March 1915, this time cheap. According to
the McLean County Courthouse land records, the property was sold to E.C. Hess
and Emil A. Frey on March 13, 1916, for $2,400. It is thought John then moved to
Florida.

Jacob Rust lived on the Finkelmeyer farm before he married Rosina Strobel in
1933. Their daughter, Vernia was born in the stone house in 1933 and they lived
there until around 1942.

The next owner was August Schiller. He put a coal stoker into the cellar of the
stone house. In 1957 Schillers moved into a new house that he built on the
farmstead. Today the Finkelmeyer homestead is owned by Russell and Deloris
Makeeff.

Edward & Lydia (Weisenburger) Fischer

Edward Fischer (second child) was born Nov. 26, 1906, to Fredrick and Katharina
(Wagner) Fischer.

He married Lydia Weisenburger, daughter of Jacob (John) and Margaret
Weisenburger on Oct. 17, 1929, at Halliday, N.D. They lived with his parents
until 1932, when they moved to a farm three miles south of Mercer. In 1935, they
moved into Mercer and in 1940 to Max, N.D.

Edward worked on road construction on Hwy. 83, was a janitor at the Max School
and did carpentry in the Max area. In 1951, they moved to Riverdale, N.D. where
he worked for the Corps of Engineers and Lydia cooked at the hot lunch program
at the school. In 1958 they moved to Bismarck.

        Photo: Edward and Lydia Fischer

Lydia died Oct. 24, 1966, at the age of 56, of a stroke. Edward lived there
until 1971 when he developed diabetes. He lived in Max in an apartment until
suffering a heart attack and complications from diabetes, then lived at the ICF
in Garrison Hospital from 1982 to 1984. He then went to the Garrison Nursing
Home where he died Dec. 11, 1987. Both are buried at Sunset Gardens in Bismarck.

Edward and Lydia have two children:

Chalmer, born Jan. 4, 1937, lives in Littleton, Colo., with his wife Janice
(Berger). They have one son Bradley.

Dellora, born Nov. 16, 1933, lives in Max with her husband, Edwin Schmidt.
Dellora attended grade one in Mercer Public School and has many memories of
Mercer and visiting the Fischer cousins, uncles and aunts there. They have three
children, Mark, Bonnie and Bruce, six grandchildren and two great-grandchildren.

Friedrich & Katharina (Wagner) Fischer

(Taken from the McLean County History Book, 1978.)

On Feb. 16, 1901, Friedrich and Katherina Fischer were married in Borodino,
Bessarabia, Russia.

Friedrich was serving in the Japanese-Russian War when their oldest child Fred
was born. John and Edward were also born there. They lived in a village and
farmed adjoining land. Their village was close to Odessa because they remember
hauling wheat there by wagon.

John Wagner, Mrs. Fischer's brother, had immigrated to the United States some
years before and as they exchanged news they heard about the United States being
the land of opportunity with its cheap land and homesteading. They were unable
to make a good living in Russia because there were too many people and not
enough land. When they made the decision to sail, they sold what they could and
left everything - hand plow, wagon, four horses. They packed only their clothes
and bedding.

        Photo: The Fischer family: (front, from left) Katie, Katharina,
        Fredrich, Fred; (back) Edward, Gottleib, Emil, and John.

Fred recalls the ocean trip over to the United States. They were on the
steamship for about three weeks. Conditions were bad and sickness took its toll;
many people didn't survive the trip. He wasn't sick but he can still remember
the sights and smells.

They left Russia in the fall of 1910 and spent their first Christmas in Bismarck
in a hotel because they missed the train that ran north to Washburn.

When the 25 immigrants reached Washburn, their destination, they were met by
their uncle and his neighbors who came with wagons to take them home. They
stayed with various relatives, and the Fredrick Fischers stayed with John
Wagners in their sod house until spring. Then they got their own land about 13
miles southwest of Mercer where they lived from 1911-1913. They built a house
out of bricks carved from mud. Gottlieb, now deceased was born there.

In 1913 they purchased the home place which is now the Emil Fischer farm. There
was a nice five-bedroom double-story house on that farm.

Friedrich died in 1937 and Katharina in 1965.

All of their children attended school in Koenig Township and attended Zion
Lutheran Church, rural Mercer.

A short history of their children follows:

Fred Fischer (separate story page 234).

Edward Fischer (separate story page 332).

John Fischer (separate story page 235).

Gottlieb Fischer was born in 1910 and died in 1968. He married Matilda (Tillie)
Schafer. They farmed before going into the grocery store business in Mercer and
in Bismarck. In 1967 they moved to Seattle, Washington. Their children are
Delbert, Arlene, and Norma. They have four grandchildren and three step-
grandchildren.

Emil Fischer (separate story page 233).

Katie Fischer Lelm was born in 1914. She married Eddie Lelm, now deceased, and
has resided in Peoria, Illinois, for many years. She has a stepson Donald;
daughter Eileen who died in her childhood years; Gary and Nancy. Katie has five
grandchildren, three step-grandchildren and one step-great-grandchild Audra.

immigrated to America in 1910 with his parents, Frederick and Katherine (Wagner)

John & Martha (Bender) Fischer

John and Martha Fischer grew up as neighbors in the area some 10 miles southwest
of Mercer. Martha was from the Adolph Bender family, John from the Fredrick
Fischer family, about 2½ miles to the south.

John's family came from South Russia in the area not far from the Black Sea City
of Odessa. His dad, Fredrick, had married Katharina Wagner. John was about one
year old when his parents, along with his older brothers, Fred and Edward,
immigrated to this country.

Martha's parents had met and married in the United States. Her father had
immigrated to this country as a young man and her mother, Magdalena, had come
with her parents, the Christoph Singers. All were from the South Russia area.

John and Martha were married Oct. 13, 1932, near the start of the depression
that spanned most of the 1930s. They lived with John's folks at the beginning,
but soon made their home on land bought from the Federal Land Bank.

On this land was an old farmstead about ¾ mile northwest (Sec. 12-145-80) of his
folks' place. They managed to acquire little by little the equipment and animals
required to make the land a farm. Some of what they needed was provided by their
parents. Their son, Marvin, was born on Nov. 12, 1935.

In the 30s and 40s there were a lot of neighbors; farms were small and numerous.
A mile to the north was the Otto Laib farm, about the same distance to the west,
the August Keck place, 1½ miles to the south, the Christ Wagner place. The John
and Theophil Reuer families were located on farms a couple of miles to the east.
The Totdahl and Baardson farms were also within a mile of their place, but they
were residents only during the very early years. Marvin went to the country
school about ¾ mile to the southwest. Also attending that school were children
of the Keck, Schlickenmayer, Laib, Hepper, Emil Wagner, and Emil Fischer
families.

John and Martha, and later Marvin, farmed the surrounding land, raising cattle,
hogs, chickens, etc. They acquired additional land over the years to enlarge the
farm as finances permitted.

In 1957, Marvin went off to college, graduating in 1961 with a BA in journalism.
He worked for a time in Bismarck at KFYR and later at the Capitol as a State
Reporter. But the lure of the land brought him back to the farm in the spring of
1963. He farmed with his dad and took over the operation in 1972 when John and
Martha retired to Turtle Lake.

About the same time, plans for construction of the McClusky canal were beginning
to take shape and land for right-of-way was being purchased or taken by eminent
domain from area farmers. John had to give up a good portion of his land,
including the farmstead. To replace it he bought a parcel about 15 miles
southeast, near New Johns Lake. Marvin started another farmstead on the
remaining land about one mile northeast of the former location. Marvin married
Charlotte Knapp in 1977. They and their four children, Thomas, Mark, Jennifer
and Phillip Knapp, resided in Bismarck and Marvin continued farming over the
years. John made the 12-mile trip out to the farm on most days following his
retirement to help with the farm work.

        Photo: Martha, Marvin and John Fischer, taken in the late 30s.

John died September 23, 1989. In October 1997, Martha moved to Primrose
Apartments in Bismarck. Martha died Feb. 18, 2002. Marvin retired from farming
in 2003. Subsequently, he and Charlotte moved to Centennial, Colorado, to be
near their children and grandchildren. The land is leased to a neighbor and the
US government. The US Fish and Wildlife Service burned the original house that
was home to the family for many years and also bulldozed all vestiges of human
activity on the original farm site. So the site today (2003) remains in its
primal state except for a few rows of planted trees and some earth scars left by
the demolition.

Martin J. Folstad

Martin Folstad filed for his homestead Oct. 18, 1902, on the W½  NW¼  lot 4 in
Section 22 of Wise Township, and the NE¼ NE¼ in Sec. 21. This land extends from
the northwest corner of Brush Lake to Blue Lake.

Martin filed a five-year proof on Jan. 16, 1908. His witnesses were Sevald Ovre,
Melvin O. McComb, Harry Wicher, and Charles Wise, all of Mercer (and all
neighbors).

On the 1937 Atlas, Sevald Ovre owned the Folstad homestead. Today it is owned by
Stutes and Warren Lee.

Conrad & Evelyn (Norberg) Freeberg

Conrad Wilson Freeberg was born Dec. 29, 1912. His parents, both of Swedish
descent, were Minnie and Fred Freeberg. He had an older brother, Merwyn and a
younger sister Phyllis.

He was baptized by a Danish pastor, L. Fadamark when he was 22 days of age. The
Pastor at that time only came to their area once in a while. On February 20,
1927 he was confirmed in the Hope Lutheran Church in Mercer by Pastor Huetmeyer.

Conrad attended the Mercer Public School and graduated in 1929. He then attended
college at Jamestown as did his brother and sister. He later helped his mom and
dad in the Mercer Cash Store and First State Bank. In 1939 he attended college
at the University of Minnesota.

He met Evelyn Norberg at Brush Lake. They were introduced by a mutual friend. It
was Aug. 8, 1939, and in those days big name bands used to come to Brush Lake.
Lawrence Welk even came to play for dances in this area. They both knew that
"this is it!" and they were married Nov. 15, 1939, at the Washburn Courthouse by
Judge Hill. His wife and daughter were witnesses. There were very few big
weddings in 1939, so they eloped. John Hjelle was with them later and announced
it in the Tribune the next day.

        Photo: The Freeberg family in younger days: (from left) Bob, Conrad,
        Evelyn, Connie, Lynn, Pam and Beth.

They had five children, Robert Gene married Eva Kloehn. They had one daughter,
Dawn. Constance Jeanne married Gary Gonser. They had two daughters, Ginger and
Jennifer; Lynn Dianne married Marvin Van Vleet and they had two sons, Scott and
Mitch. Marv died in 1994. Pamela Candace who married Tony Lill, and they had two
daughters, Stephanie and Tonia. Tony died in 2001. Conrad and Evelyn both wanted
five children and wanted to adopt their fifth child.

Senator Langer was helping them in this, but after 10 years along came Elizabeth
Carol and there was no longer a need to adopt. They let Mr. Langer know and he
wrote a letter congratulating them and said he also had four daughers and it was
great. Beth married Randy Anderson and they have three children, Kate, Marc and
Marin.

Conrad and Evelyn lived in three different homes in Mercer and in 1950 they
built their present home and named it Freeberg's Folly.

They both worked in the Freeberg family store and during the war Conrad lived
with an uncle and aunt in Seattle and worked at Boeing Air Craft. He then worked
as a mail clerk on different trains in N.D. and later worked with Earl Cypert
buying oil leases.

They took over the store and were with Fairway Foods and a branch bank of the
Washburn Bank.

Conrad died February 3, 1967.

Evelyn Norberg, was born in Dogden, N.D., later called Butte on Dec. 23, 1917,
the oldest of four sisters to Knute and Lydia Norberg. She was baptized in Zion
German Lutheran Church by Pastor Walter Keller, who also married her parents.
She went to country school and later went to Butte High School and graduated in
1939. There were seven students in her class and at this date they are still
living. Evelyn was second to the youngest.

        Photo: The Freebergs in recent years: (from left) Beth, Pam, Lynn,
        Connie, Evelyn and Bob.

Evelyn was confirmed in St. Paul's Norweigan Lutheran Church in Butte by Pastor
Hjellm Hansen. She worked at the local post office and telephone office for
three years. She also worked at Woolworth's in Minot for a while.

Following Conrad's death Evelyn continued at Mercer Cash Store until Fairway
Foods quit coming to small towns.

She married a long time friend in 1984, Lloyd Nelson from Minot. He was retired,
but played an accordion in the Blue Jays band. He died in September of 2003 and
Evelyn continues to live in Mercer. She loves to feed birds, garden, attend
church, seeing family and friends and calling Mercer her home.

Frederick & Minnie (Swenson) Freeberg

Frederick O. Freeberg, one of the early settlers in McLean County, came to
Mercer in early 1910 to open the Mercer State Bank. His parents were Swedish
immigrants who settled on a farm in Goodhue County, near Cannon Falls, Minn., in
the mid-1800s. After graduating from high school, Fred spent two years as a
teacher in a country school near Cannon falls. He then took a Commercial course
at Minneapolis Business College and graduated in 1907. His banking experience
began as bookkeeper and stenographer at the Farmer's and Merchants Bank in
Cannon Falls, Minn.

Mr. Freeberg came to North Dakota in the fall of 1909, when he went to Kenmare,
North Dakota, to a similar position in the First National Bank there. In
February 1910, he worked in the Mercer State Bank in Mercer as cashier. This
bank had been organized in the fall of 1909 with a capital stock of $10,000.
Other officers were President - T.L. Belseker, vice president - Ole S. Hedahl,
asst. cashier - Robert F. Boehm.

Fred Freeberg and Minnie Swenson were married in the Spring Garden Lutheran
Church near Goodhue, Minn., in June 1910 and came to Mercer to live. Although
there was very little money for deposits in this new country, the Mercer State
Bank grew and prospered. During the Depression it was one of the few banks that
remained open. In 1924, Mr. Freeberg purchased the Mercer Cash Store from the
former owner, George McFadden. He was also one of the charter members of the
Brush Lake Association. Minnie Freeberg took an active part in the store
business in addition to her many community activities. She was a charter member
of the Mercer Women's Club, organized in November 1912. She also was a member of
the Choral Union Society, started by Rev. Ulvilden in the early days. Fred
Freeberg was also a community leader and was interested in the development of
agriculture in this new state.

        Photo: The Freebergs: (from left) Conrad, Frederick O., Minnie, and
        Merwyn. Not pictured: Phyllis.

Mr. Freeberg continued in both the store and bank businesses until his
retirement, when his son Conrad and his wife, Evelyn, took over the management
of the store. Conrad was also an assistant in the Mercer State Bank until it
closed. After Conrad's death in 1967, Evelyn Freeberg continued to run the store
for many years.

Fred and Minnie Freeberg had three children: Merwyn, Conrad and Phyllis, all of
whom attended Jamestown College. Merwyn married Martha Manning of Antler, N.D.,
and they had four children, Mary Jane, Sharon, Jim and Richard. They lived in
San Mateo, Calif. Merwyn and Martha have died. Phyllis married Bob Thompson from
Michigan and they had three children, Alan, Steve and Susan. Bob was in the Army
and they were stationed in various places until they retired in Florida where
they still reside.

Robert & Eva (Kloehn) Freeberg

Robert Gene Freeberg was born May 20, 1940, in Bismarck, Burleigh County, N.D.,
to Conrad W. and Evelyn E. Freeberg. Robert was baptized on June 16, 1940, in
Our Savior's Lutheran Church in Mercer. He was confirmed in the same church on
April 6, 1956.

Robert "Bobbie" was raised in Mercer, McLean County, N.D. where he attended
Mercer School grades one through 12. He graduated with a class of 12 from Mercer
High School in May of 1958. While in high school Bob worked for the Lloyd
Westerlind farms and the family's hobby farms.

Bob attended Jamestown College for two years from 1958 to 1960. The following
year he attended Bismarck Junior College during 1961-1962 and graduated with an
associated arts degree from that school.

The "Berlin Crisis" brought a draft notice to be issued and Bob joined the
United States Air Force. After training in communications, Bob was assigned to
Ramstein Air Force Base Ramstein, Germany from February 1963 to February 1965.
During this assignment, Bob was decorated with the "Air Force Commendation
Medal" for bravery.

While in Germany, Bob attended the University of Maryland European Division and
completed a record 28 Air University courses as well as traveling to most of the
European counties.

While on a Christmas excursion to Brussels, Bob met Eva (Eva E. Kloehn) from
Seymour, Wisc. Eva was teaching in an American School in Kaiserslautern,
Germany.

Bob and Eva were married Aug. 7, 1965, in Seymour, Wisc. They resided in
Jamestown, N.D., where Eva taught school and Bob was involved with retail sales
and foreign auto repair work. Bob attended Valley City State College during this
time and graduated with a bachelor of education degree in May of 1969.

At the invitation from the distributive education department at the University
of N.D., Bob enrolled at the university and received a Masters of Education
degree in December of 1971. While attending the university, Bob worked for
"Bob's Cat House" as an Arctic Cat sales person and participated in
cross-country snowmobile racing.

Bob joined Belmont Builders and Realtors in June of 1972. He then became a
partner with Belmont Realtors in January of 1975 and was manager-broker and
sales person with the firm until it was sold in December 2001 to an expanding
Coldwell Banker Firm from Fargo, N.D. He is still associated with that firm.

During Bob's career as a realtor he has awarded many awards and accolades. He
was chosen the 1975 North Dakota State "Realtor of the Year." He served as the
North Dakota State Realtors Assn. President in 1980. He holds several
designations including CMB (Certified Manger Broker) and CRS (Certified
Residential Sales) and GRI (Graduate Realtors Institute). In 2001 Bob was Chosen
North Dakota/South Dakota "CRS Realtor of the year." He is a member of the Delta
Tau Epsilon and OmegaTao Rho Fraternities.

Basketball, hunting and the outdoors were Bob's passion while in school in
Mercer. He also enjoyed playing basketball at Jamestown College, and while in
the Air Force and also with several independent teams after returning to North
Dakota. Hunting is still a top priority along with lake home projects and
birding with an avid birder (Eva), snowmobiling, and camper traveling in North
America. Mountains and geology are the most interest to Bob. A most memorable
moment while hunting was harvesting a pronghorn just a few miles west of Mercer
that was entered into the Pope & Young (archery) record book for North Dakota.

Bob and Eva have one daughter, Dawn and two grandchildren, Kayla and Andre. Dawn
and her husband, David Espindola reside in Eden Prairie, Minn.

Reinhold & Frieda (Orman, Nantt) Fueller

Reinhold Fueller was born Sept. 25, 1908, on a farm northeast of Turtle Lake. He

George & Verna (Hinsz) Gardiner

John & Sarah Ann (Love) Gardiner

The history of the Gardiner family in Mercer began with the John R. Gardiner
family. John was born in Durham, England, to Mr. and Mrs. Peter Gardiner. He
came to the United States in 1879 and settled in Streeter, Ill. The following
year he met and married Sarah Ann Love, a native of Staffordshire, England.
Sarah was born on June 17, 1862, and immigrated to Streeter in 1878. They had 10
children of which five died in infancy.

In 1908, John and his family homesteaded 12 miles northeast of Mercer. They
moved to Wilton where John worked as a blacksmith in the coal mines. The
Gardiners returned to Mercer in 1924 where John and his son, Thomas, started
their own blacksmith shop which was located where the present Mercer Fire
District building now stands.

John died on April 30, 1938. Andrew Rust purchased the business in 1945 and at
that time Thomas moved back to Bismarck and settled in Moffit, N.D. where he
operated a blacksmith shop.

The children of John and Sarah were: Thomas (he moved to Bismarck in 1945, then
settled in Moffit, where he operated a blacksmith shop until his death in 1952);
Ross of Mercer (separate story); Earl, who moved to Minneapolis as a young man,
(he is deceased); Walter was a military career man; and Ethel married William
Williams and resided in Stockton, Calif. until her death.

        Photo: John and Sarah Gardiner

Ross & Marie (McFadden) Gardiner

Ross, son of John and Sarah Gardiner, farmed with his father John until 1915 and
at that time he found employment in Mercer at a store owned by George McFadden.
This business was located on the site presently occupied by Freeberg's Store.

Ross married Marie McFadden, sister of George, on Dec. 26, 1915, at Mercer. They
purchased the Ole Hjelle store, which he operated until his retirement in 1952.

The Gardiner Store is now the property of Ervin and Diane Jans and houses their
carpentry business.

        Photo: Marie and Ross Gardiner

Ross also owned a grocery store in Turtle Lake, which was managed by his
daughter, Annetta and son-in-law Vilas Just. This building is now occupied by
West Lite.

Ross and Marie had six children:

Elenor Nelson of Rapid City; Willis who died in infancy; George of Mercer; Anna
Marie Finstad of North Hollywood, Calif.; Josephine Wagner who died in August of
1999 - she and her husband Albert operated a SuperValu store until Albert's
death in 1975; Annetta Just of Bismarck.

Fred & Lydia (Kleingartner) Gaub

This is the family of Lydia Kleingartner, daughter of Balthasar Kleingartner and
Louisa Walz and Frederick Gaub, son of Frederick Gaub and Elizabeth Hottmann.

Lydia was born in South Russia. She came to America with her parents through the
Port of Halifax. Accompanying her parents were Lydia, two sisters and three
brothers. Two married sisters had come to America previously. They came to
McLean County through Winnipeg, Man., Canada, as the two sisters had already
settled there.

Frederick was born in South Russia. The mother, Fred and sister Christine
immigrated to South Dakota as mother Elizabeth had relatives in the Eureka and
Java, S.D. area. His father came later as he was in the Russian Army. He was not
well and died after arriving here.

After their father's death, Elizabeth married Fred Wanner Sr. who had several
grown children. To this union was born four sons. Fred Gaub had one sister and
four half brothers.

Christine married a man named Heim. To this marriage were born two sons. Heim
died leaving her with two small sons. During the 1930s Fred and Elizabeth
Wanner, Christine and her sons, along with three of the half-brothers moved to
Elk Grove, Calif. The fourth half-brother, Christ Wanner, remained in North
Dakota.

Fred Gaub and Lydia Kleingartner were married in September of 1909. Six
daughters and one son were born to this union.

Ida married John Schell Jr., children were Ervin, Lenora, Anna, Alvin, Richard,
Eugene and Donald. She is deceased.

Lydia married William White Sr. and their child was William White Jr. She is
deceased.

Emma married Floyd White.

Herbert married Martha Bossert. He is deceased.

Olga married Edwin Bossert and their child was Dale. She is deceased.

Edna married Eugene Hinsz and their children were Gerald, Wayne, Dean and Lori.
She is deceased.

Lorraine married Joseph Schon and their children were Patricia, Joel'l and
Kathy.

Fred and Lydia settled on a farm six miles south of Mercer. They were members of
Zion Lutheran Church. Fred enjoyed tractors and machinery. Farmers would often
come to him for help repairing their engines. He would leave to work on
someone's equipment and not return for two or three days. Another love of his
was threshing machines and the engines that powered them. He was a machine
operator for the Fiblestad threshing machine and later for the John Schell
threshing machine.

In the 1940s they moved to the south side of Mercer. There they farmed and
milked cows. While living at Mercer they were members of Hope Lutheran Church.

Lydia was an excellent cook. She raised a large garden, milked cows, and raised
poultry, along with hogs. Butchering day was a big day, as all the family would
gather to help.

Fred died in 1953 and Lydia continued to live in Mercer until health required
her to move to a nursing home. Lydia died in December of 1979.

Edward J. & Katherina (Bender) Gessele

Edward J. Gessele, son of Carl and Margaret Wiest Gessele, was born in McIntosh
County, N.D., on Feb. 4, 1887. He was the third child. He had two brothers,
Henry and Carl; and four sisters, Louise Johanna, Rosina and Emilie.

Edward's father, Carl, lived in Hutchinson County, S.D., the winter of 1884 and
in the fall of 1885, moved to Venturia, N.D. Here is where Edd received his
early education up to the fourth grade, only attending class for one month his
first year. Edward told of the times his father drove to Ispwich, S.D. with two
oxen to grind wheat into flour. This trip took five days to make the 95 miles.

In 1903 the family moved to McLean County to a farm eight miles south and one
mile east of Mercer, N.D. Here they roughed up a barn and lived in it until the
sod house was finished. Edd was now 16 years old and plowed sod barefooted with
his hand plow and four horses. Edd grew to manhood and on March 1, 1910, he
married Katherina Bender.

Katherine, the daughter of John and Friederika Weisser Bender, was born in
Kassel, South Russia, on May 16, 1889. She was the eighth child. She had two
brothers, Fred and Adolph; and six sisters, Christina, Caroline, Regina,
Philipina, Eva and Justina. She lived on a small farm outside of Kassel where
her father was a butcher. Katherina started school at age seven and her
education was very limited. She was confirmed in the Lutheran Church in Kassel
at the age of 15.

At age 16, Katherina and her brother, Adolph, set sail for the United States
from Rotterdam Holland. They arrived in Canada and traveled to Chicago by train
arriving there Feb. 28, 1905. Katherina related how she found the journey
pleasant with music and dancing on board the ship. After she and Adolph reached
Fulton, S.D., they received harsh treatment from body lice. In Fulton she worked
as a maid and laborer to pay off her passage.

She came to Mercer and worked in the hotel for one and one-half years. During
this time she met Edward Gessele and they were married in the McClusky
courthouse. They moved to a farm one and one-half miles east of Edward's home
place in McLean County. Here they were blessed with seven children, three sons
and four daughters. The first child, Emma, was born March 15, 1911; Henry
followed in 1913; John in 1915; Martha in 1917; Hilda in 1919, Herbert in 1921
and Alma in 1933.

Emma married Emanuel Hinsz, Henry married Adeline Werner, John married Emma
Ruck, Martha married Emil Wagner, Herbert married Bernice Schlaht, Hilda died in
infancy, Alma married Thomas Beierle. All are deceased except Emma Hinsz and
Alma Beierle.

Edd and Katherina had 11 grandchildren and 21 great-grandchildren. They moved to
Mercer in November 1946. Edd died in 1979 and Katherina in 1982. They were laid
to rest at the Mercer Hillside Cemetery.

        Photo: The Edward Gessele family: (front, from left) Edward, Herbert,
        Alma and Katharina; (back) John, Martha, Henry and Emma.

Henry & Katharina (Singer) Gessele

Henry Gessele, the son of Karl and Margaretha (Wiest) Goessele, was born April
25, 1890, in Blumenthal Township, McIntosh County, ND. On November 26, 1912, he
and Katharina Singer were joined in marriage by Rev. W.L. Keller in Mercer, ND.
Katharina, the daughter of Christoph and Christiana (Klotzbuecher) Singer, was
born September 21, 1894, in Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, South Russia. Henry's
parents had immigrated to Dakota Territory in 1884 from the German colony of
Buchayevka, Odessa, S. Russia. Katharina's parents had immigrated in April 1903.

Henry and Katharina resided on the Karl Goessele farmstead 8½ miles south, one
mile east of Mercer, ND. Within a year of their marriage they built their own
frame house. Here they were the parents of fourteen children. By 1934 Henry had
been deeded the farm by his father Karl. A new stucco home was erected in 1935
and completed in 1942. One son, Edwin, and two daughters, Martha and Frieda,
died in infancy. Their eldest son, Lenhardt, died at the age of eight. Five sons
and five daughters grew up on this farm:

        Photo: Henry and Katharina (Singer) Gessele, 1967.

Theodore, born December 19, 1915, Mercer, ND, married Alvira Berg July 20, 1940,
Wibaux, MT, died January 18, 1997, Minneapolis, MN; two children, James and
Joyce; two grandchildren.

Helen, born September 4, 1917, Mercer, ND, married John Knoll and Mike Fawcett,
died May 6, 1998, Lake Havasu City, AZ; one daughter Margaret; one grandchild.

Edna, born April 3, 1919, Mercer, ND, married Vernon Lilja September 2, 1939,
Moorhead, MN; two children, Lyle and Donna; five grandchildren.

Ella, born September 21, 1923, Mercer, ND, married Rudolph Berg November 14,
1942, Wibaux, MT; three children, Sandra, Donald and Terry; eleven
grandchildren.

Edwin, born September 21, 1923, Mercer, ND, married Eleanor Reuer February 22,
1950, McClusky, ND, died December 24, 1990, Bismarck, ND; three sons, Larry,
Vernon and Mark; three foster nephews; three grandchildren.

Arthur, born November 9, 1925, Mercer, ND, married Beverly Liebelt and Barbara
Jungheit, died May 3, 1993, Fallbrook, CA; five children, Tracy, Kelly, Barry,
Penny and Jodi; five grandchildren.

Lyla, born May 26, 1927, Mercer, ND, married Morton Bly and Stanley Nicolson,
1965; one daughter, Gayle; two grandchildren.

Leonard, born June 7, 1929, Mercer, ND, married Violet Miller November 30, 1947,
Turtle Lake, ND, died April 4, 1994, Apache Junction, AZ; two daughters, Sheryl
and JoAnn; four grandchildren.

Aletha, born February 21, 1931, Mercer, ND, married Arley Vossler October 22,
1950, McClusky, ND; five children, Shelton, Kevin, Tamara, Bryan and Lori; eight
grandchildren.

Mervyn, born September 21, 1933, Mercer, ND, married Marilyn Schell April 12,
1958, Bismarck, ND; two daughters, Karen and Lois; three grandchildren.

The farm economy of the 1920s and the Great Depression and Dust Bowl years of
the 1930s were arbitrary and sometimes harsh and unforgiving on the family in
the early years. The couple quickly learned survival hinged on resourcefulness.
Henry followed a whim and became a popular auctioneer in the area from 1916
through 1952. He served as a maintenance man for the State Highway Department
during the 1930s. He purchased a threshing machine and organized threshing crews
- including his five sons - from 1928 to 1944, when combine harvesters made
their debut. Katherina learned to sew clothing from flour sacks, took up fine
needlework, and took charge of milking cows and tending the flock of chickens.
Every Saturday cream and eggs were hauled to Mercer in the trusty Plymouth and
the proceeds paid for food supplies. The Gesseles resorted to boarding rural
school teachers, including Pauline Krusch of Wilton and Anna Pederson of Mercer,
at $20 per month and never mind that a single drawn curtain afforded privacy for
the teacher and the family.

Henry and Katharina were nevertheless active in community and church affairs.
Henry served on the board of supervisors for the South McLean Co. Department of
Agriculture Soil Conservation Service for over ten years; he also served a stint
as Park Township school clerk. Katharina devoted time to her church WSWS ladies
group, serving as secretary for several years. Her minutes, written in fractured
German, can still be read in "Frauensmission der Bethel Gemeinde" documents.
They took to raising a foster child, Nancy Marie Miller. Before retiring from
the farm in the fall of 1952 and moving to Bismarck, they lent support in
planning and building the Bethel Evangelical United Brethren church edifice in
Mercer.

Son Edwin assumed operations of the farm, and by 1967 was granted title by
warranty deed. The Gessele's retirement in Bismarck was anything but benign.
Henry founded and operated a lawn and garden service, and Katharina took up
domestic service and childcare. Katharina survived a bout with cancer but
succumbed to heart failure on May 24, 1968 in Bismarck. Henry died February 27,
1969, Bismarck. Both are buried at Sunset Memorial Cemetery in Bismarck.

Jakob & Christiane (Albrecht), Elisabetha (Jooss), Katharina (Steinbach)
Goessele (Gessele)

Jakob Goessele was born August 31, 1827, in the German colony of Grossliebental,
Odessa, South Russia. He was the second son of seven of record born to Johannes
and Eva Katharina (Auch) Goessele.

On December 21, 1850, he married Christiane Albrecht in Grossliebental. She was
born June 2, 1829, the daughter of Johann and Katharina (Schmidt) Albrecht in
Lustdorf, Odessa, S. Russia. Jakob's parents were among the founding colonists
in the new settlement of Neu-Freudental, Odessa, S. Russia, in 1828. Jakob, a
colonist farmer, took up residence in Lustdorf with his wife, and a daughter
Charlotte was born June 23, 1852. By autumn 1853 both mother and daughter had
contracted smallpox and died.

Jakob remarried on February 10, 1854, in Lustdorf to Elisabetha Rosina Jooss,
born January 14, 1832, and daughter of Gottlieb and Margaretha (Aldinger) Jooss
of Lustdorf. Jakob and Rosina were the parents of seven children:

Elisabeth, born May 6, 1855, in Lustdorf.

Rosina Katharina, born September 5, 1857, in Lustdorf.

Karl, born June 21, 1859, in Lustdorf, married Margaretha Wiest February 23,
1882, in Neu-Freudental, married Christina Bender June 27, 1896, Ashley, ND,
died July 11, 1949, Bismarck, ND.

Louise, born August 30, 1860, in Lustdorf, married Jakob Albrecht July 3, 1883,
Neu-Freudental.

Jakob, born November 28, 1862, Neu-Freudental, died February 9, 1867,
Buchayevka, Odessa, S. Russia.

Katharina, born February 5, 1865, in Buchayevka, died February 20, 1867,
Buchayevka.

Katharina, born April 15, 1869, in Buchayevka.

In 1864 the Goessele family had moved to Buchayevka, a newly established
settlement of German colonists near Neu-Freudental. Son Jakob and daughter
Katharina succumbed to diphtheria in February 1867. Wife Rosina died here on
January 3, 1882, from tuberculosis.

Jakob married a third time, a Katharina Steinbach, on June 28, 1883, in Neu-
Freudental. Jakob's son Karl and family emigrated to America in November 1884.
Jakob remained in S. Russia until after his wife's death in the fall of 1902
when he traveled by rail to the Russian port of Libeau and sailed to Liverpool,
England. From there he sailed on the S.S. Lake Erie on October 7, 1902, and
arrived in Quebec, Canada, on October 18. He traveled by rail to Ashley, ND,
where he rejoined his son Karl in Blumenthal Township, McIntosh County. He was
part of the spring 1903 Goessele trek that made its way to Park Township, McLean
Co., ND. In 1903, he applied for naturalization and made homestead entry for the
E½ of the SW¼ and Lots 3 and 4 of Section 18 in Edgemont Township (today in
Sheridan County) one mile east of the Karl Goessele farm. His homestead file
indicates a frame dwelling on his claim, but he likely resided with his son
Karl. In 1911, he joined his grandson Eduard and family on their farm one mile
west in the NW¼ Sec. 24-145-79. In 1913 he deeded his homestead claim to
Eduard. He died on the Eduard Gessele farm in 1919 and is buried in Zion
Lutheran Cemetery seven miles south and one mile west of Mercer, ND.

Jakob's father, Johannes, was born April 11, 1775, in Kirchberg/Murr, Marbach,
Wuerttemberg, a quiet Swabian town 15 miles northeast of Stuttgart, Germany. His
mother, Eva Katharina Auch was born January 6, 1801, in Bonlanden, Esslingen,
Wuerttemberg. Johannes had emigrated to South Russia in 1817 and, as a miller by
trade, he moved about extensively from village to village. The Goessele
(Gessele) ancestry is traced to the state of Wuerttemberg (Germany) through
Johannes, where his father, Georg Christoph of Beihingen, Wuerttemberg, was also
a miller by trade. The ancestry continues back another four generations through
several villages, and then all traces end in the early 1600s with indentured
Goessele servants on an aristocratic Ludwigsburg estate north of Stuttgart.

Karl and Margaretha (Wiest) Goessele (Gessele)

Karl Goessele was born June 21, 1859, in the village of Lustdorf, Odessa, South
Russia, directly on the Black Sea. He was the son of Jakob Goessele, a colonist
farmer, and Rosina Jooss. On February 23, 1882, he married Margaretha Wiest in
Neu-Freudental, Odessa, S. Russia. She was born June 18, 1860, the daughter of
Heinrich and Johanna (Hofmann) Wiest in Rohrbach, Odessa, S. Russia. Karl and
Margaretha resided in Buchayevka, Odessa, S. Russia until November 1884 when
they set sail for America on the S.S. Silesia with their one-year-old daughter
Louise in tow. Margaretha was by then carrying the couple's second child.
Accompanying them were Margaretha's parents and her eight younger siblings.

They arrived in New York, November 21, 1884, and set out by train for Yankton,
Dakota Territory. They wintered in neighboring Hutchinson Co. (SD), and Karl
made application for naturalization on April 1, 1885, in Bon Homme Co. By
September 1885 the family had moved to Blumenthal Twp., McIntosh Co. (ND) where
Karl filed for homestead. In May 1886 Karl filed for pre-emption proof of
settlement at a cost of $200 for the quarter section of land (SW¼, Sec. 4). In
Karl's "Pre-Emption Proof - Testimony of Witness" file his two neighbors,
Christian Albright and Jakob Wilhauer, testified that he had settled on the land
by September 24, 1885, that he had built a 16 X 24 foot sod house, sunk a
12-foot well and broken eleven acres of land. In the published filing for
pre-emption, the McIntosh County Herald misspelled the surname as "Gessele," and
Karl filed an affidavit attesting to the error. This is the first documentation
of a name spelling change that remains to this day.

Karl and his family resided here until 1903, however county records indicate the
homestead was sold to one John Feiok of Hutchinson Co., SD, in March 1889 for
$600. Why the land was sold and Karl opted for a life as tenant farmer remains a
mystery. Margaretha fell ill and died September 1, 1895.

Karl and Margaretha were the parents of seven children:

Louise, born July 15, 1883, Buchayevka, Odessa, S. Russia, married Jakob Bender
May 17, 1902, Berlin Twp., McIntosh Co., ND, died September 22, 1969, Bismarck,
ND.

Johanna, born January 24, 1885, Hutchinson Co. (SD), Dakota Territory, married
David Sauer December 24, 1905, Park Twp., McLean Co., ND, died February 28,
1909, Dogden (Butte), ND.

Eduard (Ed), born February 4, 1887, Blumenthal Twp., McIntosh Co. (ND), Dakota
Territory, married Katharina Bender March 1, 1910, McClusky, ND, died February
7, 1979, Mercer, ND.

Karl, born August 1888, Blumenthal Twp., McIntosh Co. (ND), Dakota Territory,
died 1903, Park Twp., McLean Co., ND.

Heinrich (Henry), born April 25, 1890, Blumenthal Twp., McIntosh Co., ND,
married Katharina Singer November 26, 1912, Mercer, ND, died February 27, 1969,
Bismarck, ND.

Rosina, born February 25, 1892, Blumenthal Twp., McIntosh Co., ND, married David
Sauer May 1, 1909, McClusky, ND, died August 17, 1966, Portland Ore.

Amelia, born April 30, 1894, Blumenthal Twp., McIntosh Co., ND, married Johannes
Braunberger February 22, 1914, Lincoln Valley, ND, married Christian Dokter
October 3, 1934, McClusky, ND, died April 18, 1981, Portland, OR.

Karl took a second wife, Christina Bender, in Ashley, ND, June 27, 1896.
Christina brought one child, son Jakob Bender, to this marriage. Christina was
born June 9, 1853, in the village of Kassel, Odessa, S. Russia, the daughter of
Johann and Katharina (Reuther) Bender.

        Photo: Karl Goessele and second wife Christina Bender

Karl's widower father, Jakob, had immigrated to the United States from South
Russia in the fall of 1902. In the spring of 1903 the Goessele family moved to
Park Twp., McLean Co., ND. Stepdaughter Louise and stepmother Christina
journeyed by Soo Line train from Wishek to Wilton, ND. The remainder of the
family traveled by wagon, possibly north along the Steele Trail and the Fisk
Trail through Logan and Kidder Counties until they reached the Denhoff-Washburn
Trail and thence westward to their new home. The Goesseles established residence
on the E½ of Section 23, land granted originally by the U.S. Government to the
Northern Pacific Railroad Company for the purpose of aiding in construction of
the railway. The townsite of Mercer had not yet been established and the
Goessele's mail address was Eastman, ND, a rural post office located in the
Frank Pace farm home in the NW¼ Sec. 24-145-79, directly east of the Goessele
farmstead. According to North Dakota Place Names, by Douglas A. Wick, Ida O.
Pace was appointed postmistress of the facility April 23, 1903. On October 13,
1904, Karl Goessele was appointed postmaster, but the order was rescinded. The
facility remained at the Pace home until May 1905.

That year of 1903, Karl's sons Karl and Henry fell seriously ill with
meningitis. Karl died and was placed in a temporary grave on the Frederick Just
homestead until such time the rural Zion Lutheran Cemetery was established in
1906 and where his grave is now located.

Karl was a tenant farmer on this railroad land located 8½ miles south, one mile
east of Mercer, ND, until June 12, 1905, when he officially acquired title to
the E½ of Sec. 23 and the SE¼ of Sec. 26 for $1,920 from investors in Iowa,
California and Illinois. These land barons had purchased the acreage on February
9, 1905, for $1,430.67 from the Hackney-Boynton Land Company in St. Paul, MN.
Boynton in turn had received title to the same land two days earlier from the
Northern Pacific Railroad for the sum of $188.28. Oddly enough, Karl was able to
obtain a mortgage from the Bankers Loan Company of Wishek, ND, for $1,200 in
October 1904, a full seven months before he legally owned the land.

Karl and Christina spent their remaining years on this site, raising their
children to adulthood and marriage. Son Ed was married in March 1910 and moved
to the former Frank Pace farm (NW¼ Sec. 24-145-79), then owned by O.A. Knutson
ofMinnesota. Karl eventually purchased this farm from Knutson in 1918. Son Henry
remained on the home site to run the farm and was eventually given title in
January 1934.

Karl was a relatively heavy smoker, and even Christina was once caught by one of
her step grandchildren hiding a roll-your-own cigarette under her apron. In
later years the couple ascribed to their own home remedies and cures and their
home constantly reeked of Alpenkraeuter, a popular patent medicine among
Russia-Germans. They garnered a reputation for visiting nearby Heckers Lake,
wading into the water and collecting leeches that had attached to their legs.
These they plucked off and took home to raise in the cool basement for later use
in blood letting. Christina died December 26, 1938, Mercer, ND. Karl departed
for Oregon to live with his daughter Amelia until after World War II when he
returned to North Dakota. He died July 11, 1949, Bismarck, ND. Karl and
Christina are buried in Bethel Cemetery 9½ miles south and one mile west of
Mercer, ND. Karl's legacy is that in June 2005 his farm will have remained in
the Gessele name for 100 years through three successive generations.

Theodore & Alvira (Berg) Gessele

Theodore Gessele, son of Henry and Katharina (Singer) Gessele, was born December
19, 1915, in rural Mercer, ND, on the Karl Gessele homestead in Park Township
(Sec. 23, Twp. 145-79). On July 20, 1940 he married Alvira Berg in Wibaux, MT.
Alvira, the daughter of John and Lydia Wagner Berg, was born July 12, 1919, in
Wilton, ND, on the Samuel Berg homestead in Wilson Township (Burleigh County,
Sec. 18, Twp. 144-79). Ted's father was a first generation American born to
German-Russian immigrants who arrived in this country in 1884. His mother was
born in Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, South Russia and immigrated to the U.S. with
her parents in 1903. Alvira's parents were immigrant German-Russians who arrived
in the U.S. with their families in 1901. The Bergs hailed from Rosenfeld,
Odessa, South Russia; the Wagners came from Berlin, Odessa, South Russia.

        Photo: Theodore and Alvira (Berg) Gessele

The couple began married life in Mandan, ND, where Ted was employed in a local
creamery. In the fall of 1941 they returned to Mercer where Ted had purchased
the Jacob Braun Standard Oil Bulk Agency. The sale hinged on also purchasing -
at $500 - the Braun residence, still standing, at the northwest corner of Regan
Street and 1st Street East. Ted established an office in his great-grandfather's
former cream station on Main Street and set out delivering Standard Oil products
to farmers. The business flourished, especially after a radio dispatch unit was
added and new telephone service came to Mercer. Alvira manned both of these out
of the home to facilitate orders. Ted retired from the business in the fall of
1973 after thirty-two years of service.

Ted and Alvira were the parents of two children:

James, born February 16, 1941, Bismarck, ND, married Barbara Curry, June 7,
1975, Minneapolis, MN; divorced.

Joyce, born September 3, 1942, Mercer, ND, married Donald Gulseth June 13, 1965,
Grand Forks, ND; two children, Matthew and Leah (Leonard) Traxter.

A quiet and unassuming man, Ted was nevertheless a trailblazer. He will always
carry the distinction as McLean County's first television owner in 1952, even
before any television signals were transmitted or available in the state. In
1966 he became even more daring when, after only two flight instruction lessons,
he purchased a four-seat Cessna airplane. It was a challenge, but he prevailed,
and his flight log reveals over 800 hours of flight time and over 200 guest
passengers.

Alvira maintained the household, assisted with the bulk oil business orders,
worked part-time as a waitress for Doxie Norris at Sam's Café, and became
heavily committed to seamstress work. The latter was a talent she acquired as a
thirteen-year-old on a pedal Singer sewing machine. She became adept at
refashioning and reassembling hand-me-down clothing and went on to fashion
wedding and formal wear. She garnered a community-wide clientele that included
most of the young women in town.

Both Ted and Alvira were committed to the community's welfare and were active
participants and leaders in its various organizations. They were members of Our
Savior's Lutheran Church and there, too, served in various leadership posts.
After retirement the couple spent winters in Arizona. In 1988 they sold their
Mercer property and became full-time Sunbelt residents. They lived in Arizona
until December 1996 when Ted became seriously ill and they returned to
Minneapolis to live near their children. Ted died there in January 1997. Alvira
lived in an assisted-living care facility until her death on April 23, 2004.

Jens & Edna (Stradinger) Glad
From the McLean County Heritage Book

Jens Arnold Nickoli Glad was the oldest son of Sigurd and Amelia Nelson Glad. He
was born on a farm in the Medicine Hill Township, north of Turtle Lake on Dec.
25, 1909. He attended rural schools, then high school at Turtle Lake. He also
attend Wahpeton Science School at Wahpeton, N.D. During summer he helped his
father on his farm. Then in the 30s when there was a drought and no crops, he
went to Sidney, Mont. in the fall and helped with the beet harvest. In 1937 he
got a job in McLean County to measure land for the Triple A.

Jens had two sisters, Mrs. Jerome (Dagny) Fibelstad of Mercer and Mrs. Melvin
(Ragnhild) Sondrol of Turtle Lake. He had one brother, Arne, of Bellingham,
Wash.

        Photo: Jens and Edna Glad

Edna Stradinger Glad was the second child of Christ and Elizabeth Stein
Stradinger. She was born Feb. 27, 1912, at Mercer, N.D., and started school at
Manfred, N.D. She also attended school at Turtle Lake, Tuttle and Mercer,
graduating from Mercer High School in 1930. She attended Minot Teachers College
and taught in rural schools in the Mercer area for 10 years. Salaries weren't
too high. She started out with $50 a month and a seven-month term and you did
your own janitor work which included building the fire. Some of the stoves were
hard to get going some mornings. The buildings weren't insulated the best - so
you would roast on one side and freeze on the other while sitting around the
stove. The lunch boxes were set on the floor near the stove. Many times the
sandwiches were frozen.

As time went on, things improved. Salaries went up to $74 a month and an
eight-month term and hot lunches were introduced. Most of the time the teacher
prepared the hot meal. The number of pupils varied. Sometimes 18 to 23
youngsters and all grades. Then some schools had only eight or ten.

In the summer, in order to earn a little money, she helped clerk in the Mercer
Cash and Hjelle Stores. She also worked in the Post Office. One summer she spent
at Oswego, N.Y., where she worked at the Endicott-Johnson shoe factory.

Jens and Edna were married at the St. Olaf Lutheran Parsonage on June 6, 1938,
with Rev. Sorensen performing the ceremony. Her sister Olga and Milan Peterson
were their attendants.

After they were married, they went out west to Washington State. On the way out,
they spent their honeymoon at the Badlands at Medora, and Yellowstone Park.

Jens got a job at Yakima, Wash., thinning apples in the orchards. Top wages were
27¢ an hour. He also helped shock grain. In July they returned to North Dakota.
Edna came back to teaching and Jens measuring land. They lived in the "Bunk
House" on his parent's farm the first two years. In April 1940, they bought what
was known as the "Jens Bille" farm north of Mercer. They were members of Our
Saviors Lutheran Church in Mercer.

Jens had served on the Our Savior's Lutheran Church board, Wise Township Board
and the Brush Lake Association Board. He also served the Soil Conservation and
A.S.C. Boards.

They both were 4-H leaders. Edna was the first leader of the Brush Lake Pals and
Jens was leader of the Lakeside Club.

In 1972 their farm received the South McLean County Soil Conservation Award.

Back in high school days, there was great rivalry between Turtle Lake and
Mercer's basketball teams. One winter evening was the "big game." Turtle Lake
chartered the N.P. train to take a load of fans to Mercer to the game. When
coming into Mercer, they let the people know they were coming by blowing the
whistle a few miles out of town and all the way to Mercer. One of the fans on
the train was Jens. The walls on the Mercer Hall almost burst with fans that
came to see the game. Well, Edna was there too, but she was a Mercer fan. Mercer
won a very exciting game. It seemed no one remembers hearing the Turtle Lake
train leave Mercer.

They sold their farm to Edna's nephew, Joel Stradinger. They wintered in Arizona
and spent the summer in Bismarck. Jens died on May 21, 1998, and Edna lived in
Bismarck until she moved to the swingbed unit in Turtle Lake hospital where she
died on July 24, 2002. Both are buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

Sigurd & Amalie (Nelson) Glad

From the "land of the Midnight Sun" to the "Land of Opportunity" was a big step
to take.

The "land of the Midnight Sun" mentioned here is Norway. More specifically, the
Lofoten Islands north of the Arctic Circle. Jens Adolph (Sigurd Glad) was born
Mary 28, 1870, in Sortland, Vesteraalen, Norway, and Amalie Kaspara Nelson was
born Sept. 14, 1878, in Sortland, Vesteraalen, Norway.

Jens lived and grew up on Long Island (Lang) and Amalie on Duck Island (Aand) of
the Lofoten group. They married on Dec. 1, 1902. He was a fisherman, mostly for
codfish in and around the Lofoten Islands and the North Sea. He also helped on
the small family farm.

Being a fisherman in those days was a cause of fatherless families and great
worry for loved ones on shore. It was a rugged and dangerous occupation. Many
such fishermen were drowned, shipwrecked or lost at sea, since during this time
there were no modern communication systems to keep track of them. Jens had a
reputation of helping these men who were shipwrecked to safety.

Another thing about Norway was the tradition of the oldest son taking over and
eventually inheriting the family farm. Along with this also came the
responsibility of caring for their parents until they died. Jens was the oldest
son and therefore in line for this privilege.

        Photo: Sigurd Glad homestead, Medicine Hill, 1907. The team was called
        Buck, Dick, Dime and Jerry.

The custom of the oldest son inheriting everything was not fair in Jens' eyes.
He eventually gave this responsibility to the next oldest son upon coming to
America.

All these reasons, along with the hope that America was a land where his
children could grow up in a democracy, where all were equal, led Jens Adolph
Sigurd Glad to immigrate. At the age of 35 leaving a new wife and small
daughter, Dagny (Fibelstad) behind, he first came to Cripple Creek, Colo. to
work in the silver mines. A year later in 1906 he sent for them to join him in
America within the area of North Dakota where there was free land to homestead
on. He would never see any of his immediate family again as he was the only one
to immigrate.

Having no money, knowing very little or no English, they started out. Their farm
consisted of 160 acres of land and a 10' × 20' claim shack for a house. They
left behind the beautiful fjords and green countryside of Norway for the flat
prairie.

After seeing what she had come to, Amalie was ready to go back to the old
country. Her trip over to America consisted of a long sea voyage, seasickness,
being detained at customs for not having a husband, a long train ride, and
finally a ride on a lumber wagon to the homestead. She also brought with her a
bad cold as she faced the miserable, wet spring weather of May, 1906.

Eventually a frame house was completed. Three more children were born: Ragnhild
(Sondrol), Jens Glad and Anne Glad. Their farm prospered and they learned the
new occupation of farming. They also learned English and became a first
generation American family.

Sigurd died on the farm in 1945. Amalie died at her home in Mercer in 1954.

In 2004 only Ragnhild Sondrol of Turtle Lake and Anne Glad of Bellingham, Wash.
are still living.

Laurence & Abbie (Helland) Harrum

By Joy Harrum Kline, in the McLean County Book, printed in  1978 and update.

Laurence Harrum was born in 1873 at Minnehaha County, South Dakota, near Sioux
Falls, on his parents' homestead. (His teacher changed the spelling of his name
from Harum to Harrum.)

He was a barber in Edmore, North Dakota, when he joined Company I of the North
Dakota Volunteers. He spent from 1898 to 1900 in the Philippines during the
Spanish American War. Later, he returned to Edmore.

Abbie Helland was born in Egersund, Norway, in 1880 and came to America alone at
the age of 16 to join her brother, Lars, on a Bonanza Farm at Park River, North
Dakota. At 18, she took a short course in nursing and Midwifery in Minneapolis,
Minn. (This came in handy all her life.) Afterwards, she and a girlfriend filed
on adjoining claims in McLean County.

Laurence and Abbie were married in 1903 in Lakota, North Dakota, and came to
live on her homestead. Times were hard and they decided to spend six months on
the claim and six months in Mercer where he had the first barber shop.

        Photo: Abigail Helland Harum, 1917, (nurse) on her homestead in North
        Dakota.

In the summer of 1904 at the end of the railroad at Denhoff, North Dakota, a
young couple and their worldly goods had arrived. They hired the mailman with
his buckboard to take them to Abbie's homestead in McLean County, nine and a
half miles northeast of Mercer. Later, it became known as Prophets Township,
Sheridan County. Elmer Harrum, Laurence's brother, had built them a homestead
shack so they had shelter, and even though it was a small one, Abbie said it was
fun. Elmer had a claim not far away.

According to the Mercer Telegram dated November, 1908, "Mr. Harrum went by train
to Turtle Lake to help Martin Evju in the barber shop for two days and then to
McClusky for two days to harvest the Mercer crop of whiskers on Friday and
Saturday."

Another excerpt from the Mercer Telegram, dated January, 1908, states "the first
New Year's Ball held in Mercer was given by Mr. and Mrs. Laurence Harrum at the
Mercer Hotel - the banquet and dance were well attended, perfect harmony
prevailed and the floor was crowded with dancers from start to finish. Mr. and
Mrs. Harrum deserve praise for their preparation for the dance and banquet and
for their ability as entertainers."

Mr. and Mrs. Harrum sold the farm in 1918 and moved to Mercer where he had built
a new barbershop. They were active in civic and church affairs and were early
members of Our Savior's Lutheran Church.

Their children were:

Lauretta Harrum Kotoski, a registered nurse who died in childbirth in 1928. She
had one daughter, Trianna Alvarada, who teaches in Hollywood, Calif.

One son, Lawton C. Harrum, served in the army and is an air force veteran of
World War II. He lives on the 104-year-old Harum place at Valley Springs, South
Dakota. He has one daughter. He is deceased.

A daughter, Gladys Moritz Finsaas, graduated from Mercer in 1928 and attended
from Valley City State College, and is an elementary teacher and housewife. She
lives in Montana and has three children: a son and two daughters. She died in
2002.

Another daughter, Joy Kline, graduated from Mercer High School in 1930, and
attended Minot State College, is a housewife and has been an elementary teacher
for 25 years. She has four children: one son and three daughters. She is retired
in Mercer.

A daughter, Virginia Aichele Ford, was an air force wife. She died of leukemia
in 1974, leaving a son and a daughter.

Laurence Harrum died in 1957 at age 83 at the Veterans Hospital in Minot, N.D.
Abbie died in 1968 at age 88 at her daughter's home in Texas. Both are buried in
Mercer Hillside Cemetery.
