Edwin N. & Clara (Berge) Hedahl

Edwin Hedahl was born on a farm near Twin Valley, Minnesota, October 6, 1885, to
Nils Erickson Hedahl and Marit Svensdatter Dale. Edwin was the oldest child
born to Nils and Marit. He was followed by Marie, Ole, Selmer and Ella. Edwin's
mother, Marit died when he was 12 or 13.

Edwin's uncle, Ole Dale, had settled in Manfred, North Dakota. A trip to visit
his uncle Ole and cousins was an easy way for Edwin to begin to explore the
newly developing regions of North Dakota. Edwin attended Aaker's Business
College in Fargo, North Dakota, when he was in his late teens. He learned enough
bookkeeping so he was able to build on it as he managed his various business
ventures. It was while he was in the Fargo area he met and became interested in
Minnie Martineson who lived near Ada, Minnesota. Edwin N. Hedahl had two first
cousins, one named Eddie and another named Edwin. It was about this time that he
decided to add the N. to his name to help keep his identity straight.

        Photos: Edwin and Clara's wedding photos.

The Northern Pacific Railroad was opening a branch line west from Carrington and
establishing a number of town sites. Ole Hedahl's oldest son Sven was about
Edwin's age and the two of them set out by bicycle to explore the prospects.
Their object was to look over the town sites along the newly built railroad
connecting Carrington and Turtle Lake and to choose a suitable location for a
hardware store. They went from Hurdsfield to Turtle Lake and on to Garrison but
decided that the most promising town along the route was Mercer. That winter
Edwin got a job at the Quarve Hardware Store in Fessenden to learn as much as he
could about the hardware business. The next spring he and Sven set out for
Mercer with a loan from Ole to help them get started. That was about 1906.

Edwin filed on a homestead (the southwest corner of the present junction of
highways 41 and 7) and built a two-story house (tall and narrow) and located a
hardware store on the main street. He then went back to Ada, Minn., to marry
Minnie Martineson, daughter of Ole Martineson, in 1907.

As the business prospered, the building was enlarged and they added furniture to
their stock of merchandise. Later on they enlarged again to accommodate the
addition of the Ford Agency and equipment to service cars. Sven stayed only a
year or two before he moved on to other interests. Edwin was joined by his
younger brother Ole, who became chief mechanic.

Edwin and Minnie lost their first child, a girl, a few days after her birth.
Erling was born in 1909. By the time Erling was born, Edwin and Minnie had given
up the homestead and moved to a cozier house nearer the center of town.

In 1910 Edwin's father was ready to give up farming. He and Inga, Ella, Tony
(Anton) and Margaret moved to Mercer. Edwin and his father, Nils Erickson
Hedahl, became business partners. Ella met William Peterson, who was farming
near Pickardville, east of Mercer and soon they were married. Tony was 10 when
his folks moved to Mercer, but he was soon old enough to begin work at the store
part time. He learned to be a good mechanic. Nils retired in 1920 and moved to
Fargo.

The town and the surrounding farming area began to settle quickly. A lumberyard
was opened by Ted Knutson. Minnie and Mrs. Theodore Knutson were the first
English speaking women to move to the Mercer community and soon became good
friends. The Knutsons lived on the east edge of the townsite; the Hedahls just
outside of town on the southwest. When both women became pregnant, the husbands
became concerned about their isolation during the day. Edwin and Theodore
managed to string a telephone line between the houses and the stores so that
each party could be reached in an emergency and the two women could visit with
each other and relieve their loneliness.

Soon other businesses opened up. Jim Rice opened a farm machinery store and met
Gertie Martineson when she came to visit her sister Minnie. Ole and Ben Hjelle
opened a bank. Ella Hjelle was a talented musician and soon there was a choir of
which Edwin was a member. There were music lessons for any child whose parents
could buy a piano. Another bank opened. There was a mercantile store, a hotel
and even a hospital. The Davidsons and the Plowmans from well established
families in Hannibal, Missouri, came to try their hand at ranching. There were
settlers from Norway, Sweden, Denmark and most of all there were the Germans who
had chosen to leave Russia which was no longer hospitable to them as it had been
to their parents and grandparents.

Living in Mercer during the early days required some adaptation. Take water for
example. If the town site had been located half a mile farther east, water would
have been no problem. As it was, well water was not easily accessible, and the
residents had to depend on rain or on water hauled in. A well on the homestead
of May Washburn provided the source for most of the drinking water that was used
in the town. May's father and later her brother, Ira, delivered it around town
in ten-gallon cans. The price was one cent per gallon. Naturally the water was
used sparingly even after the rain barrel under the eves was displaced by a
cistern. Often the rainfall was not enough to keep the cisterns full. In the
winter, ice was brought in from Brush Lake and melted for wash water or extra
water was brought from the Washburns. Brush Lake ice was also used for
refrigeration. The Washburns added ice to their service, storing it in a pit and
packing it with sawdust, and delivering it to their customers in a wheelbarrow.

Electric power was not available until 1920, and for a long time it was
furnished only from 6 a.m. until 12 midnight. A momentary blackout twenty
minutes before the current was to go off served as a warning ending any social
events and sent guests scrambling to get home.

Brush Lake provided a major source of recreation for early residents of the
Mercer Community. Unfortunately there were no fish and Ed, who enjoyed fishing,
regretted this. In spite of the general opinion that fish would not live in the
water, he made several trips to get small fish to plant in the lake, and
eventually his efforts met with success. He also believed that the community
should own the lake waterfront, and he helped organize an association that
purchased the land for community recreation.

Minnie's sister, Gertie, had married Jim Rice, and they were getting well
established in the community.

Clara Berge's brother Halfdan moved to Mercer and found a job as a grain buyer
at a local elevator. He married pretty Anna Blaisdell, who was working in a
local restaurant.

When Erling Hedahl was about three, he was already fascinated by mechanics and
vehicles. Edwin was driving a Model T Ford. He had the habit when he came home
for noon dinner of parking the Ford on a little rise in front of the house so
that he could eliminate cranking it by releasing the brake and letting it coast
until it started. Erling had, of course, observed this carefully. One day after
Edwin had gone into the house, Erling climbed into the car, released the brake,
and took off. He steered carefully down one block, turned the corner, went
another block, turned and was almost home. Several neighbors saw what was
happening. Edwin was washing his hands when he realized that Erling wasn't in
the house. He saw Erling manuvering the car toward home and squeezed the soap so
hard it came through his fingers. When Erling spotted his Dad he became a little
excited and accidentally turned the car into a telephone pole guy wire and
brought it to a stop. Erling wasn't hurt and only minor damage to the car.

        Photo: (From left) Neilon, Beulah and Erling Hedahl.

Underlying the excitement of a growing town and a prospering business, there was
a thread of tragedy. Tuberculosis had hit the Martineson family. Minnie's
sister, Clara, in Kalispell, Montana was the first. Then it was Minnie Hedahl.
She was diagnosed when Erling was quite small. She spent at least a year in San
Haven at Dunseith, North Dakota. One of Erling's few memories of his mother was
from a brief visit home. He was excited and wanted to run to her, and she had to
hold her hand up to indicate he should not come near. Minnie Berge Hedahl died
in 1915. Edwin asked Minnie's aunt, Mrs. Martha Berge of Ada, Minnesota, to come
to Mercer to care for Erling, who was then six years old, and to keep house.

Minnie's sister Gertie had not been well and was fearful that she too might
develop TB. She persuaded Mrs. Martha Berge's daughter, Clara Berge, daughter of
Bjorgulv and Martha Berge to apply for a teaching job in Mercer and offered her
free board and room if she would help her care for the two girls. Clara's
brother Halfdan was already living there and her mother was making plans to go
there to care for Edwin's child Erling, so she felt she could also go there.
Clara came to Mercer in 1915 and taught first in a two-room school in town and
later the Brush Lake School. Clara and Edwin were married on June 2, 1918. They
had two children, a daughter, Beulah, born in 1920 and a son Neilon, born in
1923.

It was during the early 1920s that Erling, then about twelve years old, began
following instructions in a newspaper and built a crystal radio, the first radio
in Mercer. There was great excitement when he picked up voices and music (and
static) on the little set. Edwin was very proud and people came from all over
town to listen to the radio.

World War I took its toll on the firm, when Ole was drafted and left in July of
1918. He contracted influenza on the way to England and died shortly after
landing there. His stepmother was identified as a gold star mother and went to
England to visit his grave in the early 1930s.

With the end of WWI, the hardware business was in deep trouble. Without a
government guarantee, the price of wheat dropped to rock bottom. The immigrant
farmers were unable to pay for the hardware and other supplies that the Hedahl
company had furnished. It soon became apparent that the business could not
support everyone. Nils Hedahl, with his wife Inga and daughter Margaret, moved
to Fargo. They secured a rooming house and took in boarders. Margaret finished
high school in Fargo and got a job at Black's.

Tony stayed in Mercer to work for Edwin. In a struggle for survival Edwin added
groceries to his business and had also secured the Ford dealership. Tony had a
knack for mechanics and was soon in charge of service. Edwin also tied to open a
branch in McClusky. In the spring of 1923, a tornado went through Mercer and
McClusky. Edwin was standing in the backdoor of the store watching the storm
approach, but otherwise damage to the Mercer store was minimal. In McClusky,
however, the building was flattened and there was little to salvage. There was
no insurance on the building so that ended the venture in McClusky and was the
beginning of the end in Mercer as well.

Edwin filed for bankruptcy, the Mercer store was closed, the Mercer home was
sold, and somehow, Edwin managed to salvage enough to move the family to a
section of land east of Mercer with the intent of establishing a dairy farm in
1924.

Farming was not Edwin's choice of occupation. In 1928 he secured the Bismarck
agency for the Durant car, and the family moved to Bismarck. It was an
unfortunate time to start a new business. The crash of 1929 proved to be the end
of the Durant car and necessitated a slow rebuilding of a business, this time in
wholesale automotive supplies serving the southwest corner of North Dakota. A
sideline during those years of rebuilding was wholesaling of binder twine during
the summer months. He loved to travel from town to town looking at the crops.
His pioneer hope and enthusiasm seemed to be renewed each spring. He died in
November of 1942.

The business for which he laid the foundation was continued first by Beulah
during World War II and then by Erling and Neilon who returned to Bismarck to
manage it after their military service was complete. Beulah made a career in
education and was on the faculty of the University of North Dakota. The business
continues to be a viable part of Bismarck today.

        Photo: Clara and Edwin after they moved to Bismarck.

Christof & Otillia (Makeeff) Heim

Christof Heim was born July 17, 1904, the son of Daniel and Sophie Somerfield
Heim in Butte (formerly known as Dogden), North Dakota, in Medicine Hill
Township approximately 12 miles north of Mercer. This is where he lived and was
educated with is two brothers and five sisters.

Christof attended Lincoln Auto and Tractor School in Lincoln, Neb., and
graduated with honors March 5, 1924. After graduation, he returned to Mercer
where he pursued his career in auto mechanics and farming.

He married Otillia (Tillie) Makeeff Feb. 13, 1932. Rev. Harry Brown performed
the ceremony in the parsonage at McClusky, N.D. They took their honeymoon
driving their new 1928 Chevrolet Coup to California and returned via the Black
Hills in South Dakota.

        Photo: Christof and Otillia were married in 1932.

        Photo: Otillia and Christof

Otillia Makeeff was born Dec. 1, 1909, the daughter of Mike and Sophie Pfeifer
Makeeff in Butte. Her parents moved to a farm northwest of Turtle Lake, N.D.,
where she grew up. She graduated from the eighth grade in a country school in
1923. Otillia had two sisters and five brothers.

Christof and Otillia's married life began by purchasing a two-story house in
Wilton, N.D. Teams of horses moved the house to a lot they purchased in Mercer
adjacent to old Highway 7 where they lived until 1956. The house was then moved
to the farm where it still exists today.

Christof worked with Emil Just in partnership to open a repair shop. The
partnership was established sometime after 1932 that continued until 1941. Most
interesting is that their advertisement "Heim Just Garage, General Auto
Repairing," is still visible today on the building that is located on the
southeast corner of Wing and Main Streets. The partnership disbanded under a
mutual agreement and each respectfully pursued their own careers.

On Sept. 25, 1941, Christof purchased the Jacob Braun Standard Oil filling
station. This move greatly enhanced Christ's career in the auto and tractor
mechanic repair business. Thus, he became the sole proprietor known as "Heim
Service Garage." See history of Mercer petroleum and garage services on page 44.
He provided station services selling Standard Oil products and Good Year tires
until the middle of the 1950s. In the late years, the station was used as a
machine shop for his farm operation until it was sold to Leland Boschee in 1978.

In retrospect, the Heim home provided shelter and hospitality for stranded
travelers. One incident was when Christof and Ted Gessele rescued a bread truck
driver that was stuck in a snowdrift on old Highway 7 just east of Mercer. He
almost died because he was inhaling gas fumes from a portable gas heater and,
suffice to say they saved his life. This could not have been done without the
support of others. Service is the pathway to real significance. It is through
ministry that we discover the meaning of our lives.

Christof's hobby was restoring antique tractors, most specifically the big Avery
and the Aultman Taylor. On several occasions, he would hook up these big
tractors to pull the hayrack or the flatbed trailer giving rides through the
gravel streets of Mercer. The community loved the sounds and to see these
tractors in motion.

Christof loved farming and raising Hereford cattle. In 1945, he bought a
farmstead and it still remains in the family.

The Heim family were members of the Mercer Church of God and served in ministry
in many capacities and contributed much to community activities. The proudest
moment was when Otillia was one of the concert soloists for the Mercer Community
Choir. Christof and Otillia were most influential in mentoring the Christian and
traditional values of life. They were very veracious and tenacious in their
faith to give their family a heritage that was based upon Biblical truths.

Christof passed away at the age of 71 on Dec. 25, 1975, from an accident while
working on his car in his repair shop. Otillia was 83 years when she passed away
at the Trinity Nursing Home, Minot, N.D, on Aug. 27, 1993. They are both buried
in the cemetery at Turtle Lake.

There are four boys and two girls in the Heim family. The first born were twin
boys (Ervin and Milton). They were educated at the Mercer Public School each
receiving their diplomas and were taught auto mechanics while working with their
father in the garage.

        Photo: Ervin and Eleanor Heim and five of their children on their 40th
        wedding anniversary.

Ervin Elwood went to Billings, Mont., where Frontier Chevrolet employed him as a
mechanic and car body repairman. He married Eleanor Mettler on May 28, 1955.
Subsequently, they moved to Lake Port, Calif., to continue his career. They
returned to Billings, Mont., in 1978 where he became employed with the Sanitary
Department for the city. He retired on May 31, 1993.

Ervin is a professional mouth organ player. Ervin and Eleanor have six children,
three daughters and three sons. They have 10 grandchildren and three great-
grandchildren.

        Photo: Milton and Carol Heim with their two daughters and one son.

Milton Dale attended the International Bible College, Saskatchewan, Canada, for
two years where he earned a diploma in Bible. He went to Billings, Mont., to
work as a mechanic at East Parkway truck stop.

His first marriage to Mardella Mettler on Dec. 26, 1954, from Billings had two
daughters and one son. This marriage had six grandchildren and two great-
grandchildren.

Milton went to Seattle, Wash., where he worked for Pacific Coca Cola Bottling
Company for 35 years and retired in September of 1997. He earned a certificate
in welding from Edison Technical School. The second marriage to Carol Furlong on
Sept. 18, 1964, from Tacoma, Wash., had two daughters and one son. This marriage
has six grandchildren. Milton is an accomplished musician and plays a variety of
instruments.

        Photo: Christof, Jr. and Agnes (Mitzi) Heim and their two sons and
        spouses, one daughter and three grandchildren.

Christof Charles Jr. graduated from Mercer High School in 1958 and attended Gale
Institute in Minneapolis, Minn., where he earned a diploma in railroad
transportation. He began his railroad career on June 4, 1959, with the Northern
Pacific Railroad, which became the Burlington Northern Santa Fe, and retired
Dec. 31, 2001. During those years a leave of absence was granted to work for
Amtrak for eight years.

Christof Jr. volunteered for the draft and served in the Army as military
policeman from 1963 to 1965. In Korea he took academic courses at the Far East
Division of the University of Maryland and studied martial arts earning a black
belt in Tong Su Do, the Korean version of Japanese Karate. He was honorably
discharged at Fort Collins, Colo.

Christof Jr. attended Dickinson State College in 1966 where he met Agnes M.
(Mitzi) Oster, dental assistant, whom he married on Labor Day, Sept. 4, 1967.
Upon the birth of their first born, Mitzi's career then became an excellent
homemaker for the family, which she has enjoyed with love and compassion.
Christof graduated from Minot State College in 1974 with a Bachelor of Science
Degree in Business Administration. They have two sons, one daughter and three
grandchildren.

Chris and Mitzi were proprietors of the Great Plains Distributing Company from
1974 through 1984. As a joint venture to this business, Chris also was a tax
practitioner. During the years 2000 and 2001, he worked for Coach USA as a
dispatcher in transporting railroad crews. He rented the family farm and began
farming in 1972, purchased it in December of 1991, and farmed until 1999. The
farm was rented out in 2000.

        Photo: Douglas and Gayle Heim

Douglas Dwight graduated from Mercer High School in 1962. He worked in Bismarck
for Quality Builders for 25 years. In 1986, he moved to Denver, Colo., to work
for Viking Freight Lines (now FedEx) as a truck driver. His hobby is a
collection of Ford cars and toys. Douglas enjoyed playing basketball in high
school. He was voted the most valuable player in 1961 to 1962, receiving a
trophy for this accomplishment. Douglas married Gayle Eckenrode from Hazen, N.D.
in 1963. Gayle is currently working for Claires Boutique as district manager.
They have one son and two grandchildren.

        Photo: Gloria and Jessie Newton and their two sons.

Gloria Ann graduated from Mercer High School in 1968 and attended Northwest
Bible College in Minot, N.D., while earning an Associate Degree in 1970.

Her former employment was working as a file clerk for a law firm and she is
currently employed with Electronic Manufacturing for National Cash Register. Her
mother gave Gloria her first piano lesson and she has become an accomplished
pianist. Her interests are music, piano and singing. She married Jesse Newton
from Prosser, Wash., on Dec. 22, 1970, at the Evangelical Brethren Church. Jesse
is an electronic technician for research and development for Glenayre
Electronic, Atlanta, Georgia. This marriage has two sons.

        Photo: Gene and Ruby Rau

Ruby Jean graduated from Mercer High School in 1971. She attended Northwest

Her hobbies are parachute jumping from airplanes, snowmobiling and terrain
four-wheeling. She married Gene Rau from Minot on June 30, 1979. He is
self-employed owner manager of Geno's Construction Company and Rau Rentals. They

Ben (Bernard) and Cora (Smirl) Hjelle

John O. & Alice (Driver) Hjelle

John O. Hjelle was born in Mercer, ND on November 15, 1913 to O.S. (Ole) Hjelle
and Ella Myrah. He was the oldest of five children, sister Eunice, and brothers,
Brandt, Patrick and David. He attended the Mercer Public School and graduated in
1932. He attended Luther College in Decorah, Iowa, and graduated in 1936.

After graduation, he joined the editorial staff of the Bismarck Tribune as a
reporter in 1936. During that time he served as managing editor, sports editor
and telegraph editor. At that time, the newspaper had a circulation of 6500 and
a newsroom staff of four.

        Photo: John Hjelle. Photo courtesy of Bismarck Tribune

He married Alice Marie Driver, daughter of Dr. and Mrs. Fred C. Driver of St.
Paul, on December 19, 1943, and they had two daughters, Ann Marie and Kathryn
Lynn.

In May 1945 he resigned from the Tribune staff to accept a position of secretary
to the former U.S. Senator Milton R. Young He became the senator's
administrative assistant in January 1947. During this time, the family lived in
Arlington, Virginia.

He was named Editor of the Bismarck Tribune in August, 1948 by Mrs. Stella I.
Mann, publisher. He continued in that position until he retired in December 1979
after a forty-year association with the Tribune.

During John's editorship, beginning with Mrs. Mann as publisher and ending when
A. Glenn Sorlee was the publisher, the Tribune experienced its greatest growth..
Mr. Sorlee stated "Mr. Hjelle earned and held the highest respect of his peers
not only in this area but in newspaper editorial departments through out the
country."

He possessed an exceptionally wide range of interests- from athletics, to
government and politics, to water resource development, to conservation and
environmental concerns. He was honored by a number of local, state and national
organizations, including the State Bar Association of North Dakota and the Soil
Conservation Society of America.

During his lifetime he was a member of the Masonic Lodge and the Bismarck Elks
Lodge. He was a charter member of the Missouri Slope Isaak Walter League
chapter.

He died of cancer on April 16, 1982, in Bismarck. His funeral was at the Trinity
Lutheran Church on Monday, April 19, and he is buried in the Bismarck Fairview
Cemetery. He was survived by his wife, two daughters, sister and two brothers.

Information compiled from newspaper articles.

O.S. & Ella (Myrah) Hjelle

Ole Hjelle was the first born of 11 children on March 7, 1983, in a 12 foot by
14 foot homestead house near Volga, South Dakota to Norwegian immigrants, John
and Anne (Stumley) Hjelle. The family moved to Decorah, Iowa, in 1890. O.S.
Hjelle graduated from Luther College in 1905, excelled in all sports and later
contracted with major league baseball for a career in baseball, but thought that
the profession was not good for anyone who would some day marry.

He moved to Mercer, North Dakota, in 1907 after teaching in Gardner and Hixon,
North Dakota, for two years. While teaching he became reacquainted with Ella
Myrah one of several daughters of a Spring Grove, Minn., (located about 35 miles
from Decorah) family, whose father in the year of 1884 bought a section of land
near Gardner, North Dakota.

The Myrah family commuted from Spring Grove, Minn., to Gardner, North Dakota
seasonally until 1910. In 1908 Ella came to Mercer to teach north of town in the
"McComb" school. Ole and Ella were married in 1912. They had five children,
John, Brandt, Eunice, Pat and David. The family attended Our Savior's Lutheran
Church where Ella was involved in playing the piano and other church activities.
She was also very active in Mercer community organizations and later in
Bismarck,

        Photo: The O.S. Hjelle family: (seated) Ole, Ella and Eunice; (back,
        from left) Brandt, David, Pat and John.

Ole became cashier and manager at a branch bank of Ted and Will Lierbo's Turtle
Lake bank (First State Bank). The bank was closed during the depression. He also
operated a grocery and general store, owned farmland near the Prophet Mountains
and also south of Mercer (Anton Ness land). Mrs. Hjelle owned and operated a 10-
room hotel for a short period of time. They recalled the town was locked up when
the Gypsies were in the area.

When the family was living in Mercer, Ella would annually invite the area
bachelors to come to her home for a Christmas dinner and would have a momento to
give them, along with bags of Christmas nuts and candy to take home.

In the early 1940s they moved to Bismarck, North Dakota, where sons Pat and
David completed high school and Ole worked with the bank of North Dakota Land
Department. The farms were rented out with the Ness farm receiving almost weekly
attention from Ole as he really loved that operation, as well as Mercer and
their friends in and around that area.

Ella was born Feb. 22, 1889, passed away on Jan. 24, 1967, with Ole following
three years later on June 14, 1970. Son Brandt was born on Oct. 2, 1915, and
died at age 59, son John born Nov. 15, 1913, died on April 6, 1982 at age 68.
Eunice died in February of 2004 at the age of 85. The brothers Pat, age 74 and
David, age 72, live in Minneapolis, Minn. There are 10 grandchildren and six
great-grandchildren.

Walter & Viona (Anstrom) & Norma (Berg) Hjelle

Walter Hjelle was born on Aug. 8, 1918, in Roundup, Mont., the son of Bernard
(Ben) and Cora Smirl Hjelle. The family came to Mercer in January of 1919. He
attended the Mercer school and graduated in 1936. He attended Valley City State
Teacher's College and then worked at the North Dakota Motor Vehicle Department.
He served the U.S. Border Patrol in Texas and North Dakota from 1941-44. He was
in the U.S. Army security intelligence corporation. In 1945 he was assigned a
tour of duty with the United Nations Assembly while it was being organized. He
married Viona Anstrom and went into partnership with his father-in-law at the
Coast-to-Coast store in Garrison and in 1952 he purchased the business. He moved
to Bismarck in 1960.

        Photo: Walter Hjelle. Photo courtesy of Bismarck Tribune.

He served in the North Dakota Legislature as the state representative from
McLean County from 1959-61. He was appointed North Dakota State Highway
Commissioner by Gov. William Guy in December 1960 and served in that position
for 21 years from January 1961 to December 1981. For the 1983-85 legislative
session, he served as state representative from District 49 in Bismarck. He was
reappointed State Highway Commissioner and served from 1985 until his retirement
on Dec. 31, 1988.

He was an active member in many organizations and received many awards. He was
active in Kiwanis, the American Legion and the Masonic and Elk Lodges. He was a
member of Good Shepherd Lutheran Church in Bismarck.

Walter and Viona had two children, Larry and Barbara. He married Norma Berg on
Oct. 12, 1967. He had a stepdaughter, Sharon Berg. Walter died on July 4, 1996
and was buried in Sunset Memorial Gardens in Bismarck on July 9, 1996.

James & Eleanor (Smith) Howell

One of Mercer's earliest settlers was a Civil War veteran from Indiana. He
settled on the southwest side of the Prophet Mountains in the early 1900s.

James Robinson Howell was born in Goshen, Indiana, in 1844. His parents, George
and Phoebe Howell, were born in New York. At the age of sixteen, the Major (as
he was called in the Mercer Telegram) became interested in politics and joined
the Junior Rail Splitters Club. In 1860, James R. and his parents were living at
Goshen, Indiana. The following spring, April 1861, James R. enlisted in the U.S.
Volunteer 21st Indiana Infantry Regiment. He started serving as a drummer boy,
and ended up in heavy artillery for the Union during the Civil War. During his
four years of active service, he was promoted several times. According to his
military records, he had blue eyes, dark hair and was 5 feet 8¾ inches tall. He
was promoted to a Corporal in 1863. He was hospitalized in a U.S. Hospital in
Baton Rouge, Louisiana, in August 1965 and then did clerk duty for two months
while he recuperated. He was discharged in 1866 after the end of the Civil War.

Mr. Howell caught the immigration fever, and crossed the Missouri at Omaha. He
helped construct one of the trans-continental telegraph lines to the Rocky
Mountains.

James R. Howell married Eleanor Smith around 1869 or 1870. Eleanor was born in
Massachusetts in 1845. Her father was born in New York and her mother was born
in Massachusetts.

In the spring of 1879, James R. returned to New Orleans and was appointed Chief
Clerk of the U.S. Engineer office at that place. He held that position until
1880.They lived with Phoebe Smith in Massachusetts according to the 1880 census,
and James was a purchasing agent.

In the summer of 1883, James R. Howell came to Dakota Territory and farmed until
1897. His early political career started in 1889 as Enrolling and Engrossing
clerk in the House of Representatives at Bismarck. In 1890, he was Bill Clerk of
the House in South Dakota. In 1891, he became Chief Assistant Secretary of the
Senate; in 1895, the Major, as he was nicknamed, represented his district in the
State Senate.

According to the May 7, 1908, Mercer Telegram, Major Howell purchased his ranch
near present day Mercer, ND, in 1900 and moved his family here. It was in the
SE¼ of Prophets Township on the SW side of the hills. He named it "Coteau
Ranch." The ranch was a favorite stopping place for travelers in early days. He
entertained friends with camp fires and reminisced about the Civil War and the
campaign stories of 1856. Before the railroad came in 1905, freighters from
Denhoff to Turtle Lake made Major Howell's ranch a stopping place on their
journey.

According to the 1914 Sheridan Atlas, Mr. Howell settled in Sheridan County in
1902, in Prophet's Township and his post office address was Mercer.

The Howell's had ten children, eight living: Eleanor, Lucy, Charles, Alice,
Anna, James "Chester", Golda, and George McCoy.

In 1909 the Howells participated in organizing the Eastern Star of McClusky. In
early 1910, Eleanor underwent several critical operations in Aberdeen, South
Dakota. In November 1910, she had surgery at St. John's Hospital in Fargo. She
died June 9, 1911, at Fargo at the age of sixty-four, and is buried in the
McClusky city cemetery.

        Photo: James Howell

Eleanor S. Howell was born around 1871. She married Charles Wilkins and they
lived at Henniker, New Hampshire.

Lucy A. was born around 1874. She married William Nesbitt and lived at Lemon,
South Dakota, in 1911.

Charles W. was born around 1876. He lived in the Prophet Mountains in the early
1900s and then lived at Newton, Montana, in 1911.

Alice Howell was born around 1878 in Louisiana. She filed on a homestead on
Section 6-146-78 on September 18, 1902, and proved it up five years later. After
her mother died in 1911, she continued to keep house and care for her father
until he died in 1917. She then worked for Anfin Arnison, a homesteader north of
Mercer. Later they moved to Montana where they married.

Golda Howell was born around 1879. She filed on a homestead on Section 6-146-78
on September 18, 1902. She was unable to prove it up, maybe to illness or death,
so her father, James R., as legal heir, filed the final five year proof in 1909.

Anna S. Howell was born around 1883. She married Mark H. Burns, a cowboy with a
lot of charm, and they farmed and ranched near Hurdsfield, North Dakota. After
her mother died, they moved to Mercer, where Mark operated a dray business,
making deliveries with horse and wagon. He was also a constable or Sheriff in
Mercer and told his grandchildren he had arrested Black Bart, a California
criminal.

The December 10, 1915, Mercer Telegram reported Anna S. Burns died suddenly of
heart failure, after being sick only a few days. "Her death was a great shock
not only to her immediate family but to her many friends in this locality.
Pallbearers were Krogh and Sevald Ovre, Anfin and Eric Arneson, W.S. Sprout, and
Adam Schmitt." She left a husband, four small children, her father and several
siblings. Burial was at the McClusky City Cemetery.

Mark Burns worked on digging the basement of the new Mercer school in the summer
of 1916. Daughter, Golda Burns, graduated from that school in 1926. She married
Louis Frederick and lived at Odessa, Washington. They had two children: Jacque
and Dean. Betty Burns graduated from Mercer in 1931 and married John Gasser Jr.,
who taught school at Mercer from 1929 to 1931. His father, John Gasser Sr.,
lived at Mercer and was struck and killed by lightening in the summer of 1914.
Betty and John lived at Port Angelus, Washington, and had three sons: Jack,
Larry and Dale.

James "Chester" was born around 1889. A July 1908 Mercer Telegram reported
"Chester Howell drove to Underwood, accompanied by the Major, and took the Soo
Line to Montana to work on the Government reclamation project above Williston.
The Major attended the convention and looked after his west end constituency."
In early 1911, Chester was living at Dodson, Montana. He returned to Mercer that
summer. In 1915 he is pictured in the Mercer Band. He died in 1920 around the
age of thirty-one and is buried in the McClusky City Cemetery.

George McCoy Howell was born around 1890 in South Dakota. He helped his father
farm and ranch. An interesting article from a July 1908 Mercer Telegram reads "A
DARING RESCUE - On the glorious Fourth, while celebrating the national holiday
on the beach at Brush Lake, Miss Minnie Jones lost control of her stead, and but
for the alertness and presence of mind, born of long work in the saddle beneath
a broad sombrero, a sad accident would have resulted. George Howell was the
chivalrous youth who overtook the runaway steed, and rescued its fair rider from
danger."

The Major continued to live on his homestead after his wife died. In February
1916, he was admitted to the Mercer Hospital. He had been quite sick for several
weeks, and he improved. That summer an auction sale was held at the Howell
ranch. James Robinson Howell, a Civil War veteran who never received any
pension, died in 1917 and is buried in the McClusky City Cemetery beside his
wife Eleanor.

Irwin & Frieda (Bauer) Hultin

Frieda Bauer was born June 17, 1924, to William and Magdalena Bauer at their
home southwest of Mercer, N.D. She grew up at this home and attended the Mercer
Public School. One of her teachers at the school told Frieda "When you were
born, you were tiny. You fit into a shoe box and I could hold you in the palm of
my hand."

Although the farmstead was only six and one-half miles from Mercer, the school
bus route was 14 miles one way. Frieda, her two brothers and three sisters were
bussed to the Mercer school. Their dad was the bus driver during their school
years. They were the first ones on the bus and the last ones off the bus.

Being bussed to school when the snow was too deep for the school bus or any
vehicle to get through was an experience in itself. The transportation then was
a covered sleigh. It was a long ride, up at three a.m. and home between nine and
ten p.m.

At the age of 17 years, she left the farm to become employed at the Turtle Lake
Café. The proprietor of the café drove out to the Bauer farm and asked William
and Magdalena if they would allow Frieda to work as a waitress at his café. The
next day with clothes and suitcase in hand, Frieda was at her place of
employment, the Turtle Lake Hotel and Café. She enjoyed her "waitress" work and
the people she met. After several years she left waitress work to become a sales
clerk at the General Mercantile Store.

In the fall of 1947 she resigned her sales clerk job and enrolled at the
Lutheran Brethren Bible College. After graduating from Bible College she
enrolled in the nursing program at the Swedish Hospital in Minneapolis. After
graduating from the nursing program, she returned to North Dakota and joined the
nursing staff at St. Alexius Hospital in Bismarck, N.D. From Bismarck she left
for Rugby, then to Fergus Falls, Minn. Later on she became school nurse and Dean
of Women at the Lutheran Brethren Hillcrest Academy.

Due to her father's ill health, she came back to Turtle Lake and was employed at
the Community Hospital. While at Turtle Lake, she met Irwin Hultin, pastor at
the United Methodist Church. They were married Aug. 3, 1964. During her
husband's ministry she was a partner with him in his work. Frieda was also a
certified lay speaker.

        Photo: Irwin and Frieda Hultin

They have one son, David, who lives in Fargo, N.D. He and Judy have blessed them
with three grandchildren.

In 1986 Irwin retired from the ministry and moved to Minot where they live at
the present time.

Frieda retired from nursing from the Trinity Nursing Home in 2003. Her life and
career has been exciting and fulfilling.

Ervin Jans was born to Fred and Bertha Jans March 31, 1941 at home 12 miles

The knees are better now and the building is as strong as ever. He has built two

Heinrich & Rosina (Schott) Jans

Louie & Dora (Davenport) Jorgenson

Louie Jorgenson was born on Sept. 21, 1885, in Lonsrup, Denmark. He was the son
of Peter Jorgenson and Laurice Andersen. He married Dora Ellen Davenport on Dec.
4, 1913. She was born on July 17, 1894, in Caledonia, Minn. She was the daughter
of Alfred Nelson Davenport and Sarah Elivira Taylor.

        Photo: The Alfred and Sarah Davenport family: (front, from left) Claris,
        Walter; (middle) Alfred, Ruth, Sarah, Hazel, Sylvester Newton (Knute);
        (back) Lloyd, Leonard, Bill, Harry, Dora, Rachel.

Louie came to America in 1904 and made his home with an aunt, Mrs. Marie
Peterson in Illinois until 1911 when he came to North Dakota.

He settled in Sheridan County where he homesteaded. After Louie and Dora were
married, they lived on the farm until 1940 when they moved to Mercer where they
lived until their deaths. Louie died on Oct. 31, 1948, and Dora died on Jan. 20,
1980.

They were engaged in farming before moving to Mercer. He was then employed by
the State Highway Department. Dora was very much involved with their children
being in women's church organizations, leading bible studies, sewing and helping
with many quilts for missions. She also helped with the hot lunch program, PTA,
Study Club and Homemakers.

        Photo: Dora and Louie Jorgenson on their wedding day.

She baked her famous doughnuts, Bismarcks and Long Johns for Doxie's Café.

She also managed the Mercer Switchboard. Dora had Doris (Jorgenson) Lowe,
Darlene (Jorgenson) Schilling, Lois (Skaley) Krous and Violet (Miller) Gessele
to help her out when she needed a break.

Louie and Dora were the parents of seven children, two of whom died as infants:

Dorothy Ella born Dec. 3, 1921, and died Dec. 15, 1921.

Hazel Mae born Sept. 24, 1927, and died Nov. 24, 1934.

        Photos: Dora and Louie Jorgenson

Lewis Alfred, known as "Boofus" born Feb. 5, 1915, in Pickardville, North
Dakota. He married Ann Doreshanick on Nov. 19, 1938. He died May 12, 1957.

Sarah Laurie, known as "Sis" born April 6, 1917, in Sheridan County. She married
Norman Pederson Aug. 16, 1947. She died Jan. 14, 1984.

Elizabeth Ellen, known as "Jack" born Dec. 30, 1919. She married Alec Wardner on
Jan. 26, 1940.

Franklin Marvin, known as "Sonny" born Jan. 13, 1926, at Regan. He died Nov. 10,
1983. Sonny made a career in service to his country. He was in the U.S. Marines
during World War II from 1944 to 1946. He joined the army and served during the
Korean War and Vietnam War. He served as a military policeman in his later years
of service.

Doris Marie born Sept. 9, 1934, at Wilton. She married Alfred Clinton Lowe on
Oct. 23, 1952.

Emil H. & Lydia (Mayer) Just

Emil H. Just was born October 13, 1910, to Jacob and Katharina Vossler Just, and
died September 30, 1976. He is buried in the Garrison Cemetery.

Emil married Lydia Mayer, daughter of Gustave and Pauline Mayer of rural Turtle
Lake. Lydia was born June 11, 1912, and died in August, 2004.

        Photo: Emil and Lydia Just

Children of Emil and Lydia are:

1. Peggy (Just) Schmitt, husband Patrick Schmitt live in Minot. They have four
children, Lori, Linda, Mike and Mark and six grandchildren.

2. Janice (Just) Grabinger, husband Russell Grabinger live in Mandan. They have
three children, Scott, Beth, and Cory, and four grandchildren.

3. Clyde Just, wife Clarice (Mautz) Just live in Omaha, Neb. They have five
children, Michele (deceased), Bruce, Paul, David, Michael and two grandchildren.

4. Dwayne Just, wife Donna (Beckedahl) Just live in Minot.

As a young man Emil H. Just, along with Chris Heim, established a gas station
and garage in 1933 on Main Street in Mercer. In 1936 Emil left the gas station
to farm his father's land near Mercer. In 1940 he purchased the Mobil service
station located on the north end of Main Street on old Highway 7. Here Emil also
operated a repair garage with Lawrence "Shorty" Wahl.

        Photo: Dwayne and Clyde Just.

        Photo: Emil with his daughter, Peggy and Janice.

Emil and Lydia also purchased the telephone exchange from NW Bell in 1943, which
they operated until selling it to the town of Mercer in 1947. During this period
Emil also had a short term business interest at the Brush Lake pavilion,
operateda sub-dealership for Ford Motor Company, and was involved in retail gas
distribution.

He served several years on the Mercer School Board and various community
committees. Emil was also a constant sponsor and fundraiser for the local
amateur baseball and basketball teams. He remained in business in the Mobil
station until 1953, when Highway 7 was re-routed to the south side of Mercer.

In 1953 he purchased a Standard gas station in Garrison where he then moved his
family. In 1965, Emil sold this business and became the first manager of McLean
Manor Retirement Home in Garrison, in partnership with his wife Lydia, until his
death in 1976. Lydia was a resident of Garrison when she died August 27, 2004.

Emil & Louise (Wagner) Just

Emil and Louise Just were both lifelong residents of Mercer. They loved the area
and had no desire to ever leave. They thoroughly enjoyed the people in the
community, having many relatives close by, the land and their home.

Emil's father, Frederick Just, came to the United States in April 1894. After
arriving he stayed with two of his brothers in McIntosh County, N.D. On Dec. 2,
1899, Frederick married Rosina Foederer at Ashley, N.D.

In 1902, Frederick and his brother Jacob bicycled to McLean County. They found
land south of Mercer, N.D. and filed their homestead claims next to each other.

Frederick went back to McIntosh County to get his wife and son Emanuel and moved
them to Mercer by wagon and a team of horses. The livestock walked the 120 miles
to the new homestead. Emil was born on this homestead on Jan. 27, 1914, the
fourth living child of seven, also the 11 child of 15 born to his parents, eight
of the children died as infants.

        Photo: Emil and Louise on their 25th

Louise's father, Frederick G. Wagner left Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, South
Russia, and arrived in America in December 1909 and shortly thereafter came to
McLean County, south of Mercer where he made his home for the rest of his life.

On Nov. 6, 1910, he married Mathilda Naeher, who also arrived in McLean County
from Hoffnungstal, South Russia. Louise Wagner Just was the third of 15 children
born to Fred and Mathilda at their homestead five miles south and one mile west
of Mercer on September 23, 1914.

        Photo: Louise and Emil Just, taken in 1979.

As both Emil and Louise's parents were charter and active members in Zion
Lutheran church, and both attended school in Mercer for their elementary
education, they grew up knowing each other as well as each other's families.

They were married at the Lutheran Parsonage in Mercer, on Dec. 17, 1935. For
many years they farmed, the last farm was located one mile south of Mercer.

He also hauled cream to the Mandan creamery, stopping at farms on the way south
to pick up their full cans of cream, and delivering the empties on his way home.

They moved into Mercer in 1956. At that time Emil was in partnership with his
brother Theophil in the Standard Service Station. Later Emil ran the gas station
along with the cream station in downtown Mercer.

Following that he worked for Ben Dockter on construction. He also sold bottled
gas tanks out of his home in Mercer.

As her children became older, Louise was often seen in Mercer working at the
Hardware Store for Herbert Gaub, as well as the meat market and locker plant.

Louise could also be found working in her flower garden many hours during the
summer months. Especially in later years, her hobby was sending cards,
Christmas, birthday and anniversary remembrances, to her many friends and
relatives. Over the years she was a member of the Homemaker's Club, 4-H leader,
a member of a group of Mercer women who gathered to celebrate their birthdays
and also an active member of the Mercer Friday Morning Coffee Club. Many of you
might remember Louise for writing up the Mercer News as found in the county
newspapers.

They leave behind as their legacy their children, grandchildren and
great-grandchildren. While both Emil and Louise were only able to attend and
graduate from eight years of education at the Mercer School, they were very
proud of the fact that all five children attended and graduated form Mercer High
School.

They attended many functions at the Mercer School over the years including PTA
meetings, school carnivals, class plays, music and Christmas programs. Living
only a half block away form the school, they also provided a home away from home
for many farm students who stayed in town for school activities until their
parents could come get them after evening chores.

Their children include:

Milton (Berneice Wageman) who presently lives in Kallispell, Mont. Milt has four
children and nine grandchildren. He died in November of 2004.

Melvin (Janet Nagy-Hinkle) lives in Aurora, MN. They haveone daughter.

        Photo: The children of Emil and Louise Just: (from left) Milton,
        Lynette, Eileen, Mavis and Melvin.

Eileen (Robert Spilman) lives in Bemidji, MN, and has two daughters and five
grandchildren.

Mavis (Allen Campbell) lives in Zurich, Mont., along with her two sons.

Lynette (Roger McLean) lives in Grand Rapids, MN, with their two daughters.

Emil and Louise were long time Lutherans in the community. Their parents were
charter members of Zion Lutheran Church south of Mercer, where both Emil and
Louise were confirmed, after studying about their faith in the German language.
When they lived one mile south of Mercer, they attended church at Hope Lutheran
Church in Mercer until that congregation disbanded.

Louise was organist for the services at Hope Lutheran as well as Sunday school
teacher.

At that time, they joined Our Savior's Lutheran Church where Louise was a long
time Sunday school teacher, active in the Ladies' Aid, quilter and treasurer of
the congregation for many years.

Throughout her years, she was actively involved in the Sunday School Christmas
Programs as well as Bible school. For years Emil arrived at church early on
Sunday mornings and made sure the chimes invited the congregation to the
services.

They both received their wish of having Mercer as their home community until the
time of their passing. Their final place of interment is the Mercer Cemetery a
part of the community that they cherished all their lives. Emil died in 1984 and
Louise in 2002.

Frederick & Rosina (Foerderer) Just

Frederick Just, fifth child of Christof and Barbara (Frey) Just was born Feb.
25, 1877, in Kassel, South Russia, and was baptized two days later on Feb. 27,
1877.

He came to the United States in April of 1894 with his brothers, Philipp and his
family and Jacob, and his sister Katharina. They made their way to McIntosh
County in the new state of North Dakota and stayed with brothers Christof and
George who had arrived 10 years earlier and were established there. Their
parents arrived one full year later in April of 1895.

On Dec. 2, 1899, Frederick was united in marriage with Rosina Foerderer at
Ashley, North Dakota. Rosina was born in Glueckstal, South Russia, on February
17, 1881, daughter of Johann and Magdalena (Diegel) Foerderer. She came to this
country in May of 1889 with her parents and three brothers.

In 1902, Frederick and his brother Jacob bicycled approximately 170 miles north
from Ipswich, South Dakota, where they had been looking for work, to McLean
County, North Dakota, and filed their homestead claims next to each other six
miles south of present Mercer, North Dakota. Frederick made claim to the NW¼ of
Section 11, Twp. 145-79 (Park). Frederick went back to McIntosh County to get
his wife and his son, Emanuel, and they proceeded to make the move to their new
home. One descendent recalls hearing how they moved everything by wagon and a
team of horses; even the livestock walked the 120-mile trek to the new
homestead.

After building a sod house and breaking the ground, Frederick and his neighbors
set about the task of establishing a church home. In 1906 they built Zion
Lutheran Church, located seven miles south and one mile west of Mercer, North
Dakota. Before 1906, Frederick had provided burial plots on his land for
deceased members of the German-Russian community south of Mercer. Frederick was
very active in the church, often serving as teacher and lay reader.

Two years later, they built a frame house, which son Theophil in later years
moved into Mercer.

Some 15 years before her death on Sept. 23, 1934, Rosina suffered a paralyzing
stroke and remained bedridden the rest of her life. Frederick and his children
cared for her during her remaining years. Their only daughter, Hilda, was
delegated to keeping house and caring for the children. Rosina Foerderer Just is
buried at the rural Zion Lutheran Cemetery.

Frederick held an auction in 1940, selling all his machinery and livestock. He
decided to join friends of his who were taking a trip to the West Coast and
visiting friends in Washington State. His intentions were to rent or buy a small
house in Mercer when he returned from the trip. Unfortunately, on October 10,
1940, while en route to Washington, he was killed in an automobile accident near
Big Timber, Mont. Frederick is also buried in Zion Lutheran Cemetery rural
Mercer.

The original homestead is still in the Just family, and the land is farmed by
sons of Emanuel Just.

Seven children were raised on this farm:

Emanuel, born Jan. 29, 1901, McIntosh County, ND, married Justina Bender Feb. 7,
1923, Washburn, ND, died February 16, 1973, Bismarck, ND; eight children, Leo,
Viola, Alice, Lorretta, Elton, Verline, Rosina, and Myron.

Reinhold (Roy), born Feb. 14, 1904, Mercer, ND, married Mathilde (Tillie) Metz
July 29, 1927, Washburn, ND; three children, Adeline, Lorraine, and Roy Allan.

Hilda Helen, born Oct. 1, 1907, Mercer, ND, married Jacob Buchholz Oct. 30,
1930, Mercer, ND; five children, Rodger, Ella, Betty Lou, Verna, and Joyce.

Emil E., born Jan. 27, 1914, Mercer, ND, married Louise Wagner Dec. 27, 1935;
five children, Milton, Melvin, Eileen, Mavis, Lynette.

Leonard, born June 3, 1915, Mercer, ND, married Betty Jane Kamin Oct. 18, 1944,
Peoria IL, died Feb. 7, 1973, Bismarck, ND; two children, Mary Kay and Larry.

Theophil, born Nov. 15, 1916, Mercer, ND, married Verna Renfrow Feb. 17, 1940,
Turtle Lake, ND; five children, Raylene, Martin, Lloyd, Gerhart, and Frederic.

Andrew, born Oct. 18, 1921, Mercer, ND, married Velma Pfeifer Feb. 12, 1944,
Mercer, ND; four children, Carol, Dennis, Keane, and Shirley.

Jacob & Katherina (Vossler) Just

        Photo: (From left) Otto, Jacob, Emil, Katherina holding Ted, Olga and
        Ella.

Jacob Just: Born Feb. 22, 1880, in Kassel, Southern Russia, the seventh child of
Christoph Just and Barbara (Frey) Just. Parents homesteaded in the Wishek,
North Dakota, area. Jacob came to America with a sister and an uncle in March,
1894, age 14. Jacob received his education in the old country. Jacob came to
McIntosh County North Dakota. Jacob became a United States citizen on May 22,
1901, at the age of 21. He traveled by bicycle with his brother Fredrick to
McLean County North Dakota and filed his homestead claim south of Mercer in
1902. He met the love of his life, Katherina Vossler, on March 22, 1903, and
married her in Wilton.

Katherina (Vossler) Just: Born Sept. 20, 1881, in Kassel, South Russia. Her
parents were Fredrick and Fredricka (Adam) Vossler. She came to the USA in 1894
arriving in New York Harbor. She lived in Wishek, North Dakota, with her parents
and brothers. She later came to the Mercer area to help a sister. Both
grandparents worked very hard in those early days as did all early settlers on
the land. Jacob worked in the coal mine in Wilton. He married Katherina and he
raised grain and cattle south of Mercer. He also had a livery stable in Turtle
Lake for a couple of years.

        Photo: Katherina and Jacob Just

They had to face many things such as weather, storms, fires and crop failures.
They didn't have the fancy machines then to help with the threshing, all the
children had to help. And they had to rely on the threshing crews to come from
the south with their big machines. Neighbors pitched together to help out.
Clearing the land was a chore. Wives had to cook big meals to feed the workers.

Jacob Just was a strict parent. He died at age 72 of a stroke. He was
instrumental in starting churches with other neighbors. Religion was a very
important part of their lives. Katherina was very musical, she played her mouth
organ and sang beautifully, she also made many beautiful quilts. She was a
fantastic cook. In later years she had to leave Mercer and resided in the Eureka
Nursing Home where her son Otto and daughter Martha lived and worked. She
cheered many people with her tunes on the mouth organ. Jacob and Katherina Just
raised nine children, six boys and three girls.

Otto (O.B.) Just (Separate Story)

        Photo: Ella Logue and children Bonnie and Gene.

The second child of Jacob and Katherina is Ella Just Logue. Her Christian name
was Helena Katherina Just. Some teachers early on decided to shorten her name
and it seemed to stay that way so all her legal records were Ella K. She grew up
in the Mercer area. Grade school was in a farm school and she attended high
school through her sophomore year and then quit. Ella managed a restaurant for
her father for a few years. She left for the Minot area some time in the late
1900s where she met her husband, Clarence Logue. They were married on July 30,
1928. They lived in Helena, Mont. where he opened a barbershop. Their son, Gene,
was born there on Aug. 16, 1929, in a hospital in Havre, Mont.

        Photo: Clarence Logue

A little history of Clarence Logue. He was born in Little Falls, Minn., to
William D. Logue and Carrie Mabel (Myers) Logue. William came from the Cresco,
Iowa, area. He was Irish on his father's side. Carrie Mabel was from the Bowlus,
Minn., area. Clarence's parents moved to Devils Lake and then later to York,
North Dakota. Clarence's dad was a barber. Clarence went to college in Missoula,
Mont., and graduated from the school of journalism and had been injured twice in
WWI overseas.

He lost both his parents in 1919, so that was a tragedy in the family.
Clarence, Ella and Gene moved to Mercer in the early 1930s and opened a
barbershop and mercantile store in Mercer. Memories of that time were the dirt
roads, the heavy rains, the lizards claiming priority for the right of way on
the roads in town. There was no running water and every family member laid down
claim to be first in the bathtub due to the shortage of water. Clarence was
active in getting a legion club organized. He helped participate in the Memorial
Day ceremonies at the cemetery to honor all the deceased.

The family remained in the Mercer area until 1945 at which time they moved to
Moorhead, Minn. Clarence was having health problems and couldn't keep barbering.
Alvin Just purchased the business and stayed there for several years after he
returned from the service.

Clarence Gene Logue graduated from high school in Mercer. He moved to Moorhead
also in 1945 and worked in filling stations and attended Moorhead State
University. He met and married Edith Lorraine Christiansen. Gene was in the
guard and was in the service during the Korean Conflict. Gene was stationed in
Camp Rucker, Alabama. At that time, soldiers could have theirfamily with them.
They had two sons at that time, Donald and Robert. Both boys graduated from
Moorhead High School.

Robert joined the Navy and made a career in the service. He also was an employee
of United Airlines. Now he is semi-retired. He is married to Dixie Olson. They
recently retired to the Shidbey Island, Washington state. Bob has two children,
Scott and Leah.

Don Logue started his career with the post office young and has risen through
the ranks and is now postmaster in the Fargo Postal System. He is quoted often
in the Fargo Forum and has been a speaker promoting the breast cancer stamp,
monies, which are given to the cancer fund. Don as four children, Chad, Kim,
Lori and Annpell who are all married. Chad is a career military man in the
Marines. Cheryl Faye, daughter was born after the family was back in Moorhead.

Edith and Gene have been blessed with three children, eight grandchildren and at
last count, 15 great grandchildren. They were fortunate to be able to celebrate
their 50th wedding anniversary in 1998. Unfortunately Gene became very ill with
cancer. He was unable to fight it. Gene passed away May 15, 2000. He is missed.
Cheryl married James Welle who owns a construction company in Hawley, Minn.
Cheryl is assistant manager for the Grain Dealers Association. She is also a
licensed paralegal. They have two children, Chuck and Tiffany.

The next child of Clarence and Ella Logue is Bonnie M. Logue Haugen. She
finished grade school in Mercer, attended high school in Moorhead and attended
Concorida College for two years in pre-nursing and then went on to the U of
Minnesota to complete her nursing education. She graduated in 1955 with a B.S.
in nursing. She continues to work as a nurse at the Fargo VA hospital. It has
been a challenge to keep up with the times and changes in medicine. Lots of
continued education is needed and lots of on the job training with the new
equipment. She has four children, Arthur, Catherine, Brenda and Sandra. They are
all busy and active.

Art referees sports in the Fargo-Moorhead area. Catherine lives in New Market,
Minn. and worked for Herrigan Distributors in St. Paul. They have carpeting
tiles and other floor materials. She handles all the rebates that the company
has. Brenda lives in Papillion, Neb. and is in real estate. Sandy is a
beautician and owns a salon in Fargo called E-Clips Salon.

Ella has 13 grandchildren, from 26 years on down to two. The oldest
granddaughter is getting married Feb. 14, 2004.

Emil Just - Separate Story

        Photo: Edna and Ted Just

Theodore Just: (Teddy) was born April 10, 1913 in Mercer. He lived on a farm
east of Mercer and farmed. He married Edna Kleingartner who was born on Oct. 23,
1917. They have two children, Gerald Just and Donna Just. They moved into town
and lived in a home south of the grain elevators. Teddy and Edna lived in
McClusky and Wishek. They later moved out west to live where their daughter,
Donna, moved to after getting married to Ervin Grosz.

Gerald Just married Dolly Miller. Jerry attended school in Mercer, McClusky and
Wishek where he and his sister graduated from high school. Jerry attended
college and had a career in banking for many years. Later he was in sales at a
car dealership and is now retired and enjoying golfing, relaxing and keeping his
blood pressure down.

Both he and Dolly enjoy life and are kept busy attending their two grandson's
activities in football and wrestling. They have one daughter, LeeAnn, who is
teacher in the Fargo school systems where she is working with problem children.
LeeAnn is married to Bryan Thoreson. Bryan is in the plumbing business with his
dad. Dolly continues to be employed by Bethany Homes in Fargo. She is originally
from Goodrich, North Dakota.

        Photo: Martha Just

Martha Just was born on Oct. 25, 1915, in Mercer. Her beauty shines from within
and without. She was designated the family caregiver of the Just family. Martha
attended farm school, Mercer High School. She is an outdoors type of girl. She
enjoyed horseback riding, hunting and fishing.

Martha was a hairdresser for a while but then changed direction and started a
career in caring for elderly people, first in a nursing home in Jamestown. She
was there from 1938 to 1940. In 1940 she moved to the Eureka, South Dakota area,
where her brother, Otto, was administrator of the Lutheran Home for the aged.
Martha has always been a hard worker and worked up to a management position. She
remained in the nursing care field and retired in 1980. She treated everyone
with loving care. She is respected in the Eureka community and in her family and
has set a good example to all. Her retirement years are being spent helping to
make quilts in her home church that are sent overseas to needy families. For a
lady that didn't do much cooking for so many years, she surprises her relatives
and friends with her cooking and pickle making. Her table is always ready for
company and shows them an enjoyable time. She is the glue that holds the Just
family together at present. Martha's health is fairly stable and she is aging
gracefully. She is great and admired and loved by all. Eureka's gain is Mercer's
loss.

        Photo: Alvin and Lorraine Just

Alvin Just was born in Mercer on Dec. 1, 1918. Alvin grew up in the Mercer area
and was a graduate of Mercer High School Alvin is known by the nickname of
Sparky. He indeed did sparkle. He was spunky, the life of the party. Alvin grew
up on the farm and worked hard as did all the other siblings in the Just family.
Alvin joined the Army and served in the North Africa area during the war against
Germany and Italy. He had the rank of Sgt. when he was discharged.

Alvin married Lorraine Boulter in Jamestown on May 11, 1943. They made their
home in Mercer after Alvin was discharged from the service. They purchased the
business of Clarence Logue. Alvin had taken barber training at Fargo and was
barbering in Mercer for a short time. He took up electrical training and moved
to the Chicago, Ill., area where he and Lorraine remained until retirement.
Alvin and Lorraine had two sons, Dale and Darrell. Both boys attended most of
their school years in Chicago, graduating there. Alvin and Lorraine moved to
Davis, Ill., to a man-made lake and built a beautiful home. All were welcome
there. Alvin and Lorraine are both deceased.

Dale lives in Colorado and is a teacher, coach and part-time bartender. He is
married to Peggy and has a stepson.

        Photo: Jacob Just with his sons: (from left) Vilas, Arthur, Alvin,
        Theodore, Emil and Otto.

Darrel remains in the Mesa, Ariz., area. He has been a teacher and music
director in the Mesa area. Alvin and Lorraine also lived in Mesa for some years
after moving from Davis, Ill. Lorraine moved into her son Darrell's home when
her health was failing.

        Photo: Arthur and Francis Just

Arthur Just was born Feb. 8, 1921, in Mercer and spent his early years there and
attended school through high school in Mercer. He joined the military and was
stationed in the Sioux Falls area where he met Francis Croisent. They were
married in Mercer on Dec. 14, 1942. Artie was a medic in the service. He
enlisted in the service at Fort Snelling, Minn. No children were born to this
union. They were divorced in 1952. Artie came to the Moorhead, Minn., area and
worked at different jobs mostly mechanic related. He met Arlene Bojo and married
her on June 16, 1953. They had one son, Larry. Artie and Arlene later moved to
Eureka where Artie started a job at the Lutheran Home. Larry graduated from the
Eureka school system. This marriage also ended in divorce.

Art had health problems and was treated at the Fargo VA Hospital. Later he
returned to the Sioux Falls area where he was reunited with his first love and
remarried. They spent some good years together and enjoyed some good times. Both
liked to travel and camp. Larry had entered the military, serving in the Marine
Corp. Art and Frenchy were waiting for his son, Larry and his friend, to come
home for Christmas, Dec. 24, 1985, when the door bell rang and they found a
highway patrolman standing who gave them the bad news that their son and his
friend had been killed in a car accident in Rapid City, South Dakota. They hit a
patch of ice and rolled over an embankment. What a sad Christmas. Art and
Frenchy lived in Madison, South Dakota following their remarriage. They are both
now deceased.

Otto & Annette (Sackman) Just

Otto Just (O.B) was born in Mercer on Jan. 18, 1905. He grew to manhood in
Mercer, attended grade school in Park Township, high school in Mercer and left
for college in Valley City, then went to Indianapolis, Ind.

In pursuit of a business career, he returned to Mercer and taught school. He
later moved to Eureka, South Dakota, in 1938. He became an administrator of the
Lutheran Home for 43 years. He also was part owner in partnership of a grocery
store with his brother-in-law, Ted Sackman.

In addition to this, he also had a political career. He was a state
representative for two years in South Dakota, served in the State Senate for two
years and then State Representative again for two years. He was Register of
Deeds for McPherson County and then county auditor as well. His education
definitely paid off. His political career was from 1944 to 1961.

He died on June 9, 1985, in Eureka and is buried in the Zion Lutheran Cemetery
in Eureka.

O.B. met Annette Sackman, whose parents are Christoph and Christine (Peter)
Sackman who immigrated from South Russia. They moved to the Mercer area in 1906
from Bowdle, South Dakota.

Otto and Annette (Nettie) were married Sept. 30, 1928, in Mercer. She was a
homemaker, also ready to pitch in at the Lutheran Home when needed. She was
active in the church, prior to moving to Eureka. Annette also taught school in
the Mercer area. She graduated from Mercer High School and from college in
Valley City. She was born July 29, 1909, in Mercer. She lived in Eureka, S.D.,
and died March 3, 2005.

        Photo: Otto and Annetta (Sackman) Just and their daughter, Kathryn.

Otto and Nettie had one daughter, Kathryn (Kay) Christine Just. Kay married Dean
Krein in Eureka on Aug. 4, 1957. She was born Dec. 21, 1937, in Jamestown. Kay
graduated from Eureka High School, went to college and returned to Eureka. Dean
was born on Feb. 2, 1936, in Eureka.

Dean bought the grocery store and managed that for many years until his
retirement. He and Kay are very active in the Eureka community.

They raised three daughters.

Mary Kathryn Krein was born on March 27, 1961, lives in Hettinger and is a lab
tech at the hospital there.

Ann Krein was born May 15, 1953, and married Jeff Frazier. They are both in
physical therapy. They have one son David Jeffrry who was born Jan. 25, 1989.

Sarah Krein was born on April 19, 1967, graduated with a nursing degree and is
living in Ann Arbor, Mich.

Vilas R. & Annetta (Gardiner) Just

Vilas R. Just, son of Jacob and Katharina (Vossler) Just, was born July 30,
1923, at Mercer, N.D. He graduated from Mercer High School in 1941.

He moved to Portland, Ore., where he worked in the shipyards until enlisting in
the U.S. Army. Vilas served in the South Pacific during World War II. He was
discharged from the Army in 1946.

Vilas returned to Mercer and married Annetta Gardiner, daughter of Ross and
Marie McFadden Gardiner. Following their marriage, they located in Turtle Lake,
N.D., where they managed the Gardiner U-Save Grocery Store. In 1961 Vilas went
to work for Lutheran Hospital and Homes Society. He worked as administrator at
Central Dakota Nursing Home, Jamestown, N.D., Hazen Memorial Hospital, Hazen,
N.D. and The Lutheran Home, Eureka, S.D. Vilas retired in 1989 and currently
lives in Denver, Colo. Annetta resides in Bismarck, N.D.

Children of Vilas and Annetta are: Deanna (Just) Vollmer married Gary Vollmer.
They are living in Rapid City, S.D., and have three children, Darren, Anne and
Gregary.

Michael Just is married to Noel (Schumaker). They are living in Hazen, N.D., and
have three children: Shannon, Shane and Shantel.

David Just lives in Glendale, Calif.

Dennis A. & Vicky L. (Beierle) Keller

Dennis Adam Keller, the eldest of five children, was born at Rugby, N.D., to
Adam and Katherine (Marquart) Keller. Dennis lived in Esmond until the age of
three, when the family moved to rural Washburn.

In 1972 the Kellers moved into Washburn. Dennis graduated from Washburn High
School in 1975, and then attended college in Wahpeton, graduating with a
business degree. He worked for Kinney Shoes for three years.

        Photo: Dennis and Vicky Keller and their children Joshua and Kassondra.

Vicky Lynn Beierle was born at Turtle Lake to Thomas and Alma (Gessele) Beierle.
Being an only child, she spent many hours with her dad, feeding the cattle and
helping with the haying and farming. She grew up in Mercer, attending Mercer
Public School through sixth grade and then Turtle Lake-Mercer School graduating
in 1979. Vicky worked in Bismarck at a department store for about a year.

Dennis and Vicky were married Jan. 16, 1981. They made their home in Bismarck
for a few months before purchasing a home in Mercer. Dennis was hired at the
Falkirk Mine near Underwood and has worked there for the past 22 years while

They built a home one mile west of Mercer and have lived there since the fall of
1990. In 1997, with the advice and help of Vicky's dad, Tom, they began farming.
The Keller family are members of the First Baptist Church in Mercer.

Walter & Bertha (Sackmann) Keller

Walter Keller, the oldest son of Rev. William Keller and Ottilie Koenke was born
in 1895 and came with his family to Mercer in 1903. The family homesteaded six
miles north of Mercer. He was confirmed in April of 1909 in St. Paulus Lutheran
Church (Braun), rural Mercer by his father.

Walter attended the Wise Township #1 (Sprout) School. He attended high school
and the Lutheran seminary in St. Paul and was ordained and preached his first
sermon on Christmas, 1914, at St. Paulus. He served St. Paulus and then Hope
Lutheran Church from 1915 to 1921. He served St. John's Lutheran Church in
Jamestown until he retired. He died in 1982 and is buried in Jamestown.

Bertha Sackmann was born on Oct. 26, 1899, in Walworth County near Java, South
Dakota. She was the daughter of Christoph and Christina Peters Sackmann. She
came to Mercer with her family in March of 1906 and was a member of the first
class of Mercer school in 1907. She married the Rev. Walter Keller on May 16,
1920. She died on June 30, 1990, in Jamestown and is buried there.

Walter and Bertha had five children:

William Keller was born and died in 1921. He is buried in the Mercer cemetery.

        Photo: The Walter Keller family: (from left) Paul, James, John, Walter,
        Mary and Bertha.

Paul Keller was born on May 22, 1922, in Jamestown. He married Florence Diamer.
He is a Lutheran pastor.

John Keller was born on April 23, 1924, and married Doris Kumpf on Sept. 5,
1946. He is a Lutheran pastor. He served a parish in Medina before becoming a
hospital chaplain. He is internationally known for his work with the chemically
dependent. He founded the chemical treatment center at the Lutheran General
Hospital in Park Ridge, Ill.

John and Doris have three children:

David Keller was born in 1947. He is married to Susan Kasowski. He is an
ordained Lutheran pastor.

Philipp Keller was born in 1950 and married Bonnie Coyle and his second wife is
Linda Siels.
