George & Annetta (McFadden) McFadden

The first Irish family in Mercer Village was the McFadden family. They came to
the USA from County Cavan, Ireland, beginning in 1900. They landed in
Philadelphia and then began working their way west to Minnesota before setting
down their roots in McLean County, N.D.

George McFadden and his sister, Catherine 'Josephine' McFadden were the first to
arrive in the U.S.A.; followed soon after by their brother, James Henry, who was
known to his friends as 'Harry.' The last to arrive in the area was their
younger sister, Maria.

George McFadden was born on the family farm in the townland of Drumartin, County
Cavan, Ireland on April 20, 1881. He was the second of 20 children born into
this McFadden family. Being the first-born son, George's education was of prime
importance to his father. He did well in the local schools and eventually
obtained a scholarship to attend Mountjoy College, a private boarding school
(high school) in Dublin, Ireland. Upon graduation, he returned home to his
family in Drumartin and made plans to immigrate to America. By this time, his
mother had died and his father had remarried. It was the custom in Ireland, at
that time, for the children of the first marriage to emigrate or to marry and
establish their own farm making way for the children of the latest marriage. In
June of 1900, his passage being paid for by his Uncle Joseph McFadden in
Philadelphia, George sailed from Liverpool, England, on the "SS Belgenland." He
was 19 years of age and listed as a student. His younger sister, Catherine
Josephine, accompanied him. Upon arrival at the Port of Philadelphia, they were
met at the docks by their Uncle Joseph and brought to his house. They remained
there for a short visit and then, carrying a lunch packed by their uncle for the
trip, they traveled by train to Minnesota. In Fergus Falls they were to live
under the wing of another uncle, William McFadden, who had his own brood of
eight children. William was the head farmer on the grounds of the Fergus Falls
Insane Asylum in Minnesota. William's daughters also worked in that facility. Of
special interest to this story is the eldest daughter, Annetta Zillahe McFadden,
who was the supervisor of nurses at the asylum.

Catherine Josephine, who was always called "Josephine", was said to have been a
quiet girl and not very talkative. She earned her living working as a
seamstress. She married Edwin "Fred" Ramsey, a friend of George's, and they
lived in California. She had no children. Josephine died May 27, 1945 in Los
Angeles.

George lived in Fergus Falls for a while and eventually decided to establish
himself in Mercer Village, N.D. about 1905. George was appointed to be the
postmaster in Mercer on Nov. 2, 1906. He opened a general merchandise store
there and, while a new building was being completed, he lived as a lodger in
Nels Olesen's Hotel. George made many return visits to his uncle's home in
Fergus Falls and eventually convinced his cousin, Annetta, to come to Mercer and
work in his store. Her abilities as a nurse would come in handy in the little
town because, at that time, there was no doctor in residence.

In the meantime, George McFadden, kept expanding his business ventures. There
were plans made in 1909 by C.A. Rust of Underwood to open a new drug store to be
headquartered in McFadden's General Store, which was still in the building
stage. The basement was completed Sept. 16, 1909, and the carpenters and
bricklayers arrived in October and the building rapidly rose into the air. Just
before the drug store was added, Mr. Rust suddenly passed away and that part of
the venture was abandoned. In June of 1910, George purchased a house in
Washburn. In early July of the same year, he "left on Monday to take a 10 day
visit at different points in North Dakota and Minnesota." A few days later the
reason for the 'visit' was revealed.

From the Telegram: "July 15, 1910. Married at St. Paul on Wednesday, July 6,
1910, Mr. George McFadden of Mercer and Miss Annetta McFadden of Fergus Falls,
Minn. Both of the contracting parties are so well known to our residents that
they need no introduction. The Telegram joins in wishing them all the joys of
married life." George and Netta settled down to married life in a new house in
town. This house is still standing.

The next McFadden to arrive was George's younger brother, James Henry (Harry).
He was 16 years of age when he completed his apprenticeship as a surveyor in Co.
Monaghan and set sail from Londonderry, Ireland, on the ship "Anchora" which
arrived at Ellis Island on April 10, 1903. He traveled west and worked as a
surveyor for the railroad being built in Montana. Around March of 1910, Harry
came to Mercer to visit his brother. After several weeks, he left to return to
work in Montana and by July he was back again in Mercer to permanently settle
down. He worked as a clerk in the McFadden General Store. Harry, who was slight
in stature, apparently made up for his size with his jovial personality. He
joined in the social life of Mercer, as did the other McFaddens. In the spring
of 1911, he was appointed postmaster for Mercer Village. In the early part of
September, 1911, Harry came down the typhoid fever. Despite the loving care of
his brother and sisters, he died on September 30 at 24 years of age. He is
buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

        Photo: George and Annetta McFadden with their daughter Blanche.

Maria McFadden, a younger sister, left Ireland and landed at Ellis Island aboard
the ship "Furnessia" on July 13, 1909. Maria, born in Co. Cavan on Nov. 28,
1890, was 18 years of age when she arrived in America. Her presence would
eventually be a lasting one in Mercer Village. In later years, six other
brothers and sisters would come to America, but they settled elsewhere in the
east or West Coast of the country. Maria (whose name was pronounced as Mariah,
but who later changed her name to Marie) also came to her Uncle William
McFadden's home in Fergus Falls. In April of 1910, Marie arrived in Mercer to
work in Miss Amdahl's Millinery shop.

In October of 1910, Annetta "Nettie" McFadden, George's wife, had a serious
illness that threatened her life and she became paralyzed. She was confined to
her home for three months and was often visited there by her mother who came
over from Fergus Falls to tend to her needs. To the relief of all concerned,
Annetta made a slow, but steady, recovery and was soon seen riding about the
countryside in a carriage driven by her husband. This illness, however, left her
in a frail condition for the rest of her life. Nevertheless, on April 10, 1912,
George and Annetta McFadden welcomed the birth of their daughter, Blanche Leary
McFadden. Blanche recalled being told that she was born during a snowstorm and
that her father delivered her.

George continued in his various business ventures in the area. In October of
1912, he obtained 160 acres of land in McLean County through the Homestead Act.
Annetta had already purchased 160 acres in Montana in 1908. In 1915, Mercer
Hospital was incorporated with the board of directors listed as: E.N. Hedahl,
E.M. Plowman, H.C. Weist, F.J. Winkelman, August Swenson, George McFadden and
F.O. Freeberg. George was reappointed postmaster of the Mercer post office on
Feb. 27, 1915.

Another McFadden to come to Mercer was Cyrus McFadden, who was known as 'Ed.' He
was born in St. Peter, Nicollette, Minn. He was a younger brother of Annetta
McFadden. He and his wife Mildred and their two sons, Maurice and Seth, came
from Great Falls, Mont. in August of 1916. Ed had signed on to work with his
brother-in-law, George, in the McFadden General Store. Around this same time,
George McFadden and Fred Freeberg started a business called "McFadden and
Freeberg, Overland and Willys-Knight Dealers."

Maria McFadden also assisted in the general store for a time. She soon crossed
paths with another newcomer, Ross Gardiner, who was from Streeter, Ill. In March
of 1915, both Maria and Ross participated in the local talent show in the
auditorium before a full house. In April of that year, Mrs. Gardiner, Ross's
mother, gave him a surprise party and "Miss Morton and Miss McFadden were among
those from town there." A few days later Ross left for Larimore, N.D., where he
would spend the summer working for C.F. Williams. When he returned, the
courtship resumed. At this time, Ross was employed by Crown Elevator as a
'second man.' Ross and Marie were married in a Lutheran ceremony on Sunday, Dec.
26. Soon after, both Ross and Marie were working in McFadden's General Store
and continued doing so even after it was sold to Mr. Neiman and then later to
Mr. Freeberg. Ross worked in that store until 1936 when he bought the Ole Hjelle
Store and went into business for himself. When Ross retired, the store was taken
over by his son, George. Ross Gardiner also built and opened a grocery store in
Turtle Lake. This store was run by Ross' daughter, Annetta, and her husband,
Vilas 'Curly' Just.

Marie and Ross Gardiner contributed to the growing population of Mercer with the
addition of several children to their family. Starting with Elener in 1916,
followed by Willis in 1918, George in 1920, Anna Marie in 1921, Josephine in
1922 and Annetta in 1925; this family left a lasting mark in Mercer. Descendents
of Maria and Ross still live and work in Mercer. Their granddaughter, Willa
Murray, whose father was George Gardiner, is the current postmistress for
Mercer. Ross passed away in Mercer in 1956 and Marie died in a cancer research
hospital in Arkansas in 1952. They are buried in Mercer Cemetery.

All the McFaddens were brought up as staunch Presbyterians in Ireland, but since
there was no Presbyterian Church in the Mercer area, they attended the Lutheran
Church. The family called upon Maria's cousin, Rev. George West, an itinerant
Presbyterian minister, to come to Mercer for a visit in September of 1918 and
baptize their first two children.

Eventually, George McFadden found the winters in North Dakota too cold for his
liking and decided they would move to a warmer climate. He took several trips to
California and made plans to move his family there once he could establish
himself in Los Angeles. It is said that the basement of McFadden's General
Store, and/or the basement of the local pub, was the site of production of some
'high spirits', which were to be used as income to fund this move to California.
The transportation of these spirits proved unsuccessful in at least one case and
the operation was discontinued at the urging of the authorities in California.
Around 1922, George moved his little family out to Los Angeles. He had started
up a small construction business in the Los Angeles area with another Mercer
resident, Fred J. Winkelman. This business, called McFadden & Winkelman (or
Winkelman and McFadden) built a small hospital and a school and other small
public buildings. Fred Winkelman was the actual builder and George McFadden ran
the business. George, ever the entrepreneur, became involved in other things
outside of the construction company. He was a partner in the Inglewood Golf
Course in Los Angeles and his occupation in 1930 was as a merchant of wholesale
golf supplies. As luck would have it (the luck of the Irish?) oil was discovered
on the golf course property and George became a wealthy man. He never changed
from his simple, friendly and down-to-earth ways, however, and he continued to
place primary importance on his family. George and Nettie were happy to be near
the many members of their family that also lived in Los Angeles. He and his wife
and young daughter sailed to Ireland in 1925 to visit with his old friends and
family for several months. He also enjoyed trips back to Mercer to be with his
sister and her family. Nettie McFadden passed away in Los Angeles on Dec. 2,
1955. George died in Tarzana, Calif. on Dec. 4, 1971, at the age of 90. His
daughter, Blanche and her husband George Bartunek, live in Long Island, New
York.

George McFadden once told his grandson that he was not a very hard worker, but
instead, was always a very lucky man.

This story written and compiled by a niece of George, Josephine and Maria
McFadden, Patricia Lee McCabe Kostelnik.

Dan & Maggie (Neuharth) Miller

Aug. 27, 1898, Jacob and Lydia Miller's eighth child, Dan, was born on the farm
in Neu Kassel, South Russia. Dan was the last child of Jacob and Lydia to be
born in Russia. He immigrated along with his family to the United States in
1902.

Dan married Maggie Neuharth on Dec. 1, 1920. Maggie was born Dec. 13, 1896, and
she moved to the United States with her sister and brother-in-law. For the first
year of their marriage, Dan and Maggie lived with Jacob and Lydia on their farm
located south of Mercer, North Dakota. In 1921, Dan and Maggie moved to their
own farm located about one mile from Jacob and Lydia.

Dan and Maggie had 10 children:

Adeline born Nov. 19, 1921.

Richard A. born Dec. 24, 1923.

Walter Lester born Sept. 6, 1925.

Vern Ruth born July 8, 1927, and died at three months of age.

Herbert Ramond born June 25, 1928, married to Arlene Johnson Nov. 26, 1955.

Lester Vern born Nov. 17, 1929 and died at four months of age.

Chester L. born Aug. 1, 1931.

Harley Vern born May 11, 1933.

Milo Alvin.

Robert Dale.

Dan and Maggie continued to live on their farm until 1958, when they moved to
Bismarck, North Dakota.

Dan passed away on March 16, 1959, and Maggie passed away in July of 1962.

Jacob & Lydia (Martin) Miller

Jacob was the youngest child of Frederick Mueller Jr. and Barbara Utt. Jacob was
born at home on the farm on July 28, 1870, at Neu Kassel, South Russia. Jacob,
like his father, served in the Russian Army sometime between the last part of
1888 and 1889. Jacob was converted and baptized in 1895.

Jacob married Lydia Martin on Oct. 28, 1889, by Rev. Hangbe at Neuberg, South
Russia. Lydia was born on Feb. 10, 1870, at Bohansky, South Russia. Lydia was
converted in 1891. She was baptized on May 18, 1894, by Rev. Carl Filbrant.
Jacob and Lydia established their home in Odessa, South Russia, where they lived
immigrating to the United States during the later part of 1901.

Jacob and Lydia conceived 21 children during their lifetime. Lydia had four
miscarriages, three children that died within their first year of life and one
that lived about 18 months and 13 that survived.

Jacob and Lydia's children:

Rose (the first child born in Odessa, Russia); Lydia died at one year of age;
John died sometime prior to the birth of the next child; John, probably named
after the deceased John; Kathern or Barbara, premature and died at birth; Fred
born Feb. 19, 1895 and named after Jacob's father; Edward lived less than one
year; Dan, the last child to be born in Russia; Edward born Jan. 7, 1902 on the
trip over. He became the first U.S. citizen because he was born on a U.S.
registered ship; Otto born Nov. 7, 1903, the first of Jacob and Lydia's children
born in the U.S.; Mollie born April 29, 1905; Ida born Jan. 8, 1907; Edna born
Feb. 4, 1908; Sarah born Nov. 4, 1910; Bennie born Dec. 19, 1911 and Ernest
Joseph born Oct. 9, 1920.

Jacob and Lydia had heard so many promising stories about the United States from
family and friends that had moved there, that they decided to go. In 1901, Jacob
and Lydia, their four kids and Jacob's father Frederick Jr. started on their
trip to the United States. Jacob's father was blind by this time and had to be
cared for by Lydia. Along with their family, Jacob and Lydia brought a 15-year
old boy across with them. His real name isn't known, however, he was called
John. Lydia was expecting when they started their trip in late 1901. They
traveled by wagon and train from Russia to Western Europe, where they boarded a
ship bound for the United States.

They arrived in New York in the later part of 1902. The United States customs
official changed the family name from Mueller to Miller. Once the family cleared
customs, they took a train to South Dakota where they were met by Jacob's
brother, Fred. They spent a short time in Yankton, South Dakota, before
traveling to Kulm, North Dakota. In March of 1902, Jacob, W.W. Wolitarsky and
Mike Schlaht went to Washburn, North Dakota, to file a homestead claim for
Jacob's family. Jacob's homestead was in the SW¼ of Section 24-145-80. While in
Washburn, the men got caught in a snowstorm. They spent the next two weeks
sleeping in the office of the grain elevator. After two weeks the men followed
the railroad tracks to Wilton. They took the train from Wilton to Kulm.

In May of 1902, Jacob moved his family first to Kulm and then to their new home.
The move as accomplished by covered wagon and accompanied by two other
families - the Schlaht and Wolitarsky families. The families had stopped in Kulm
to acquire some cattle and horses, which they moved to their new home.

Jacob bought more land for $3 per acre. They had hauled enough shiplap lumber to
build a 12' × 16' shack. They lived in this until summer when they built a sod
house. The children slept in the covered wagon until the sod house was
completed. Upon arriving at their new home, the Millers set about building a
house of sod with homemade bricks. The lower part was built of sod walls two
feet thick and to form up the window sills they used their homemade bricks. The
bricks they made and used were six inches wide and 11 inches long and consisted
of clay, straw and water mixed together. They lived in the sod house until 1914
when a six bedroom house was constructed and they lived in this house until they
retired in 1925. After setting up the homestead, Jacob borrowed farm machinery
to work approximately 25 acres of flax.

In the early years, the three families that migrated together had each purchased
three horses and set about helping one another break land. The men went east to
Harvey for threshing to earn extra money for their families.

Jacob's father, Frederick Jr., set up a homestead near Jacob and Lydia.
Frederick was blind so Lydia would make at least one trip a day to his homestead
to help him. Frederick Jr. died in 1910. Jacob inherited his father's farm,
which he and his sons had been working all along.

Jacob bought his first tractor in 1914. Until this purchase he had to trade for
the use of a tractor.

In 1918, Jacob and Lydia's son Fred joined the United States Army Truck Corps
and went to France.

In 1925, Jacob built a six-bedroom house in Turtle Lake, N.D. In 1926, Jacob
moved Lydia and most of the family into the new house. Their daughter, Rose, who
was married continued to live on the farm until 1929.

In town, Jacob and Lydia were very active in the Baptist Church. He served as
Sunday school superintendent, teacher, deacon and trustee. He attended to his
own affairs and let others attend to theirs, but he was always willing to give
any assistance wherever needed.

He served on the school board even before he had his second citizenship papers
due to the shortage of people to serve in that capacity.

Lydia was very active in the church and was "Grandma" to many of the young folks
of this community.

Jacob passed away July 2, 1939, and Lydia passed away on March 13, 1947.

At the height of his farming days, Jacob owned 11 quarters of land with three
complete farmhouses. He was a pioneer in the use of custom threshers, from
horsepower, steam and gas. After he moved to town, the land was farmed by
Jacob's sons and sons-in-law.

Johann & Caroline (Braun) Miller

Johann Miller was born March 25, 1870, in Borodino, Bessarabia, South Russia, to
Christina and John Miller. At the age of 23, he married Caroline Braun in
Romania. Caroline Braun's father died when she was two years old so she and her
sister, Julia Braun, were raised by a family named Giesler.

        Photo: Johann Miller

Johann Miller, together with his wife and seven children, came to this country
in 1911. Before coming to this country, Johann Miller was a farmer and
bricklayer and worked at a courthouse in the town of Borodino. Because their
father worked at the courthouse, Johanna and John had to deliver the newspaper
in the village.

Upon arriving on the vessel Maine at the Port of Baltimore, they took a train to
the end of the line, Turtle Lake, N.D.

The Johann Millers lived in a two-room sod house on the John Braun farm until
spring. Johann and the older children all worked as laborers for other farmers
in the area.

In the spring, Johann rented a farm until the year 1915, when he purchased a
farm two miles west of Mercer, which he operated until 1937. At this time, they
retired and moved into Mercer. In 1942, Mrs. Miller passed away. Johann then
sold that home and moved into a small house next to his son, John, where he
lived until his death. Johann died at the age of 93. Both Mr. and Mrs. Miller
are buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

To Johann Miller and Caroline Braun were born 10 children. Two, Caroline and
Maggie, died as infants and are buried in South Russia.

Christine born in Borodino, married Jacob Braun.

Johanna born in Borodino, married Ferdinand Manske.

John born in Borodino, married Katherine Rust.

Jake born in Borodino, died at the age of 16 and is buried in a country cemetery
(St. Paulus) west of Mercer.

Lydia born in Borodino, married Rudolph Wall, both deceased.

Julia born in Borodino, married Peter Zevik.

Elsie born in Borodino, the youngest of the children born in Bessarabia, married
Edwin Braun, and then she married Theophil Neumiller.

Benny born at Mercer, North Dakota and married Esther Jesz.

Martha born at Mercer and married Matt Peptowski, and then married George
Williams.

Walter born at Mercer and married Naomi Bonnet.

Johann (John Jr.) & Katherine (Rust) Miller

John, son of Johann Miller Sr. and Caroline (Hein) Braun was born Aug. 20, 1898,
in Borodino, Bessarabia, South Russia.

Katherine (Katie) Miller, daughter of Samuel Rust and Lina (Mehrer) Rust, was
born Oct. 29, 1905, rural Turtle Lake, McLean County, N.D.

        Photo: Johann and Katherine Miller, last photo taken together, 1974

The couple was married on Oct. 16, 1925. They lived in Mercer all their married
life with the exception of one year when they lived in the state of Washington.

John was a self-employed truck driver and later managed area grain elevators.
Katherine was a full-time homemaker and mother. John Miller Jr. died on Sept.
23, 1974. Katherine Miller died on Jan. 27, 1976. Both are buried in the Mercer
Hillside Cemetery. The couple had two daughters, Mary Ann (Arnold Westerlind)
and Violet (Leonard Gessele) and seven grandchildren: Debbie (Westerlind)
Sparrow, Gordon Westerlind, Frederick (Fred) Westerlind, Roy (Skip) Westerlind,
Steven Westerlind, Sheryl (Gessele) Gabriel, Joann (Gessele) Shae.

Robert & Patricia (Christensen) Mohrbacher

"Patty" attended the Sprout's one-room school in Wise Township for first and
second grade (1947-49). She remembers trips to school in a covered sled pulled
by horses, when the roads were bad in the winter. In third through eighth grade
she went to the Medicine Hill school 1 mile north of the farm.

In 4th through 8th grades she was the only one in her class. Pat attended Dakota
Lutheran Academy high school in Minot for 3 years, going to Mercer High School
for her junior year. She graduated from Dakota Lutheran in 1959, and then
graduated from the Lutheran Bible Institute in Minneapolis in 1961.

After one year at Augsburg College she married Robert Duane Mohrbacher on August
11, 1962, and they moved to Lakewood, Colorado, a suburb of Denver.

Bob worked for the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation as a mechanical engineer designing
gates, valves and other mechanical equipment for modifications to Hoover and
Grand Coulee Dams, and equipment for many other dams and irrigation projects.
He also worked in the Bureau's technical publications department for 9 years.
He retired in 1994.

Pat finished her BA in English and Secondary Education at the University of
Denver in 1967. She worked at various jobs, mostly volunteer, for the church,
schools, community, and 4-H clubs. Besides her hobbies of camping, hiking,
traveling, cooking, and family history, her main interest has been in her family
and in Christian Education at Holy Shepherd Lutheran Church where Bob and Pat
have been members since 1963. Pat worked for 10 years as an Educational
Assistant at Dennison Fundamental Elementary School, retiring in 2003.

        Photo: (From left) Pamela, Robert, Julie, Patricia and Danial
        Mohrbacher.

Pat and Bob have three children.

Pamela graduated from Augsburg College in Minneapolis in 1989 with a degree in
business and finance, and she married Dean Klenz the same year. Dean, who
served with the Marine Corps in the Persian Gulf War, is a veterinarian. Pam
has worked at various school, church, and bookkeeping jobs. They have two
children, Kendra and Drake, and they live in Roseville, Minnesota.

Julie graduated from St. Olaf College in 1991 with a degree in psychology. She
went on to Luther Seminary in St. Paul and is now a pastor of the Evangelical
Lutheran Church in America. In 1991 she married Dan Brooks who is an elementary
school teacher and Library Media Specialist with Jefferson County Schools in
Colorado. They have three children, Rachel, Isaac, and Anna, and they live in
Arvada, Colorado.

Dan is an electrical engineer who graduated from the University of Colorado in
1995. He works for Evergreen Research, an engineering consulting firm, mostly
on medical equipment such as dialysis machines and a blood sterilizer. He and
Margaret Chamberlin were married on June 13, 2004. Margaret works in the health
care field, and they live in Lakewood, Colorado.

Raymond & Willa (Gardiner) Murray

Employment on the McClusky branch of the Garrison Diversion brought newlyweds
Raymond and Willa Murray to Mercer in May of 1973.

Ray was employed by William Clarimont Construction as a dragline oiler until
June of 1975 when he began his apprenticeship with Murray Construction learning
the carpentry trade under the Veteran's On-the-Job training program. He went
back to heavy construction in 1978 working with Ray Herr Construction. In
October of 1980 he began working for Holen Construction and is presently
employed at Holen's.

Willa helped her mother, Verna Gardiner, run the Brush Lake Pavillion Café the
summers of 1973 and 74 along with helping in the Gardiner's U-Save Store and
Herb's Hardware. Willa also held the position of city auditor for several years.

In October of 1975 she became employed with the United States Postal Service at
Mercer upon the retirement of Anna Diede. Under Postmaster Reinhart Stradinger'
mentoring, Willa was encouraged to work part-time at the Bismarck facility along
with the Mercer position. Mr. Stradinger retired in December of 1980 and she was
appointed postmaster on Feb. 21, 1981. She continues to assist the Bismarck Post
Office when asked to serve on special details.

They have two children: Levi born July 17, 1980, and Tess born June 12, 1983.
Levi resides in Bismarck and is employed with Holen Construction. Tess is a
student at Minnesota State University at Moorhead working toward a degree in the
para-legal field.

Ray enjoys maintaining and driving the classic cars he has restored while both,
Willa and Raymond, enjoy riding Harley Davidson motorcycles, weather permitting,
often accompanied by their son, a second generation Harley rider.

They are members of Our Savior's Lutheran Church where Willa helps with the
Sunday School and Vacation Bible School programs. Ray takes great pride in
keeping the church parking lot cleared of snow in the winter.

Neff, Clarence & Adelina (Hegel) Neff

Clarence Neff, the son of Henry and Emma Herr Neff, was born on Jan. 20, 1912,
on the family farm northwest of McClusky. Clarence met and courted Adelina
Hegel, the daughter of Philip and Rosena Voegele Hegel who lived 16 miles
northwest of McClusky in Holmes Township. Both Clarence and Adelina attended the
Homes Consolidated School.

They were married on Oct. 8, 1934, and made their home in the same area on a
rented farm. While on this farm, their son, Ervin was born on Oct. 2, 1935. They
lived there for several years until they bought their first farm a few miles
further to the northwest. In 1945, Clarence and Adelina bought a farm (the
Hedahl Dairy farm) which is located a mile east of Mercer in McLean County where
they have lived since. With the help of son Ervin, Clarence and Adelina raised
grain crops, milked cows and cultivated large gardens.

        Photo: Clarence and Adelina Neff, taken at their 50th wedding
        anniversary in 1984

Clarence and Adelina were active members of the Mercer Methodist Church and they
took part in the activities by teaching Sunday school, Circle and piano
accompanist. In 1985, when the Mercer church closed they transferred their
membership to the McClusky Methodist Church where they are still members.

Clarence was 4-H leader for five years and served on township and Mercer school
boards. Adeline was a member of the Brush Lake Homemakers. In later years they
retired from milking cows which allowed time for the joys and busy activities of
three grandchildren. Adelina took up sewing, needlework, quilting and
babysitting the grandchildren. Clarence stayed busy repairing appliances and
electric motors, plus helping others in farming needs.

Their son Ervin married Fay Rixen on Oct. 14, 1962, and they have three
children, Brenda Lee, Byron Allen and David John. They also have a great-
granddaughter, Ione Fay.

Adelina and Clarence will celebrated their 70th wedding anniversary in October
of 2004.

Anton (Nielsen) Nelson

Anton was born in 1877 and came to the United States in 1892. He joined the
Danish community in Medicine Hill Township, north of Mercer. He had a farm one
mile south of Mercer and had many tenant farmers to help him with the farm work.
He was a kind man who was every child's uncle.

        Photo: LaRose Ketterling "helping" feed the chicks on Anton's farm.

        Photo: Anton and his team, taken in 1934.

Two current Mercer residents have memories of living on Anton's farm. One is
Mary Ann Miller Westerlind who was born on the farm but moved when she was less
than a year old. Her memories are not too sharp. However, LaRose Ketterling and
her family lived on the farm from 1930 to 1935 and she developed her love of
animals and nature by "helping" him.

Jacob & Minnie (Christensen) Nelson

Jacob Christian Nielson, the 10-year old son of Christian and Ane Margrette
Nielson, left his family home in Denmark in 1893 for America. Jacob's father had
died in 1888 and the son was sent to stay with relatives in Hutchinson, Minn.
All his mother could afford was passage for Jacob alone in steerage on a
passenger ship to New York. Steerage was a section occupied by passengers paying
the least fare and receiving the worst accommodations. Fortunately for Jacob,
the name Nielsen was well known in Denmark seafaring circles, and the ship's
Captain invited the lonesome traveler to eat with him in his cabin.

When Jacob went through immigration in New York, the name Nielsen was
Americanized and Anglicized in the Protestant religion, then under the English
influence and for the rest of his life he was known as Jacob Nelson, the name
spelling most familiar to the old-timers around Mercer. His friends also
shortened his first name to just "Jake" and in McLean County he was remembered
as Jake Nelson.

Upon his arrival in Minneapolis he was met by his Uncle Soren Mikkelson and
taken to Hutchinson where he met all his relatives and his future bride whom he
would marry 16 years later, after homesteading in McLean County, North Dakota.

The North Dakota prairie was often looked upon as a wasteland by many people
from Minnesota, and when they saw it, they either fled back to Minnesota or went
all the way across to the tree country in the mountains and the west coast.
However, Jake had no inclination to be a lumberjack and when he came of age, he
decided to leave Minnesota and homestead on the North Dakota prairie. Maybe it
reminded him of the sea so familiar to some of his ancestors before him? In
1903, he began to prove up on a homestead located in McLean County, Medicine
Hill Township, about seven miles north of the present town of Mercer.

While the people are supposed to shape the land, it seems that the land did a
little shaping of its own in the homestead years. During the first winters on
the prairie, Jake worked on railroad construction between the present towns of
Underwood and Wilton, and in the Dogden coal mines near Butte to help pay for
seed money, farm equipment - mainly a walking plow, and his own grubstake.
During the summer after spring breaking and planting, the first priority
construction was building a tarpaper shack on the homestead and furnishing it
with a stove, table and a bed, plus a few cooking utensils.

Jake and some of his closest neighbors, Christ Christensen (or just CP), Martin
Christensen, and Jonas Christensen built their tarpaper shacks on the homestead
corner closest to one another. Being neighborly and visiting other homesteaders
was one type of recreation that cost little money and provided considerable
entertainment and comfort for the homesteaders during those first winters on the
prairie.

Breaking ground, planting and harvest occupied just about the entire first
summers. New ground was plowed with a walking plow, grain was seeded by hand,
cut with a scythe and threshed by hand. The first trips were made on foot, and a
sack of grain was carried on a strong shoulder with frequent rest stops. It was
more fun when there was a little competition with the neighbors and each tried
to carry his sack of grain farther than the other.

As the homesteaders prospered, horses and wagon took the load off the
homesteader's shoulder. The grain was hauled to market and food and coal was
brought back to the homestead. However, the homesteader wives often said the
horses got more rest than they did. Unless there was a real need to have the
wagon, either walking or bicycling was the popular way to town. After all, the
workhorses had to have their rest and could not be used for frivolous trips to
town. Jake and his neighbors had a community owned bicycle for such trips. The
only problem was when everyone wanted to go to town, each had to take a turn on
one bicycle.

By 1909, Jake had built a house on his homestead and on Jan. 5, 1910, he married
Minnie Marie Christensen, the lady he had met when he first arrived in
Hutchinson. Minnie was a first generation citizen born Nov. 9, 1884. Her parents
came from Denmark to Hutchinson where her father and oldest brother farmed and
established the Hutchinson Nursery.

During the early years on the homestead, Minnie wrote to her parents often.
Those cards and letters showed she was unimpressed with the severity of the
North Dakota winters. To help slow down the winter winds, Jake started one of
the first tree groves (later called shelterbelts) in McLean County. The trees,
mainly plains cottonwoods, boxelder, willow and ash, came from the Hutchinson
Nursery. Many of those trees still stand today on the old homestead site north
of Mercer.

One of the first fields of alfalfa was planted on the Nelson Homestead. Jake was
one of the first farmers to import seed and raise alfalfa. He won several blue
ribbons for prize seed at the County Fairs, and regularly attended the county
alfalfa picnics sponsored by the Alfalfa Growers and the county agent Norling.
Over the years Jake was noted as the "Alfalfa King of McLean County," but to his
closest friends he was just plain "Alfalfa Jake."

        Photo: (From left) Perry, LeRoy and Sidney Nelson, taken in 1927

Between 1911 and 1926, six children were born to Minnie and Jake: a boy born
June 29, 1911, died the same day; a boy born Nov. 15, 1912, stillborn; Sidney
born Oct. 30, 1913; LeRoy born June 19, 1915, died June 1, 1935; June born in
March of 1917 and died March 10, 1917; and Perry born March 6, 1926. Jake and
Minnie continued farming on the homestead until Jake died on Jan. 27, 1937, and
Minnie on Oct. 19, 1938.

Of the three surviving brothers, Sidney Webster Nielsen continued farming in the
Mercer area. On Dec. 24, 1938, he married Amalia Genevieve Evans (Mollie) from
Underwood. They have five children: Joan (known by her second name, Rosemarie)
born May 31, 1941; Diana (Kathleen) born Jan. 20, 1943; Kirsten born Jan. 17,
1944; LeRoy born June 27, 1947, and Lyndon born Oct. 5, 1949.

Brother Perry Helm Nelson, after a tour of duty in the Navy during World War II,
married Eunice Margaret Kline from Mercer. They have two children: Valerie born
July 31, 1952, and Vickie born Sept. 25, 1953. The family lives in Bozeman,
Mont. where Perry is a retired Fish and Wildlife Biologist and Eunice works at a
laboratory at Montana State University.

Perry & Eunice (Kline) Nelson

Perry Helm Nelson was only 12 years old when his last parent died. He lived for
a time with his aunt and uncle in Minnesota. He returned to Mercer where he
attended Mercer High School. He enlisted in the Navy before he finished high
school.

He had a tour of duty in the Navy during World War II, aboard the USS Yorktown.
Upon his discharge, he and Eunice Margaret Kline from Mercer were married Dec.
21, 1946. Perry then went to college earning a master's degree from Montana
State College in Bozeman. Perry worked as a biologist for the Montana Game &
Fish.

        Photo: Perry Nelson

Eunice and Perry have two children: Valerie Jean born on July 31, 1952, and
Vickie Leigh born on Sept. 25, 1953. Both the girls were born in Bozeman, Mont.

Perry passed away on April 16, 1999. Eunice is still living in Belgrade, Mont.

Valerie married Thomas Fusco, who is an investigative lawyer, and they have one
adopted son, Jacob, born in 1995 in Korea. They live in Maryland.

Vickie married Steven Glancy who is a chemist and they live in Ohio.

Roy & Elva (Urban) Nielsen Sr.

Roy Nielsen, Sr., was born on Nov. 2, 1901, in Erwin, S.D. He was the son of
Martin and Karen Nielsen, who homesteaded in Sec. 10, Mercer Township, McLean
County.

On Aug. 7, 1929, he married Elva M. (Seebach) Urban who was born on March 9,
1901, in Hebron, N.D. Elva received her formal education in Hebron, Dickinson
Teacher's College and the University of North Dakota. She taught for five years
including her years in Mercer.

        Photo: Roy and Elva Nielsen, Sr., wedding picture, 1928.

The couple lived in the town of Mercer where Roy was a rural mail carrier for 30
years, often carrying mail in the winter by horse and sleigh. Roy owned and
farmed the family homestead. The couple moved to Wahpeton in 1948 where he
purchased and operated Nielsen Electric until retiring in 1968. They lived in
Wahpeton until their deaths, Roy on April 2, 1969, and Elva on July 15, 1989.

While living at Mercer they were members of Our Savior's Lutheran Church where
Elva was active in Sunday school and confirmation teaching. Elva was delegate to
the Max Circuit - Women's Missionary Federation.

        Photo: The Roy Nielson family in 1946: (from left) Gloria, Roy Sr., Roy
        Jr., Elva and Urban.

        Photo: Roy and Elva in 1957 on a boat ride around Manhatten.

Their oldest son Roy Jr. was born Oct. 4, 1930, in Bismarck. He married Louise
(L'Huillier) in Manhattan, Kansas, where he received his doctor of veterinary
medicine from Kansas State University in 1959. They have six children and six
grandchildren: Roy III (son) and Roy IV (grandson) are owners of Revival Animal
Health, Inc. which Dr. Roy founded after retiring from veterinary medicine. This business moved into a new million-dollar facility in 2003.

Gloria (Rev. Dwight) Ellefson was born Aug. 4, 1933, at Bismarck. Gloria
graduated from Lesley College in Massachusetts with a MA in mathematics. She
taught accellerated math for 23 years. Gloria's husband, Pastor Dwight, served
parishes in South Dakota and Colorado. They have three children and four
grandchildren.

Urban was born Feb. 24, 1940, in Bismarck. He married Doris (Heidinger) in
Wahpeton. They have two children and three grandchildren. Urban died on July 23,
1995. Prior to his death he had as many as six novelty stores in Las Vegas, Nev.

All glory goes to our God for our years in Mercer.

Sidney & Mollie (Evans) Nielsen

Sidney Webster Nielsen and  (Amalia 'Mollie' Genevieve Evans) were married on
Christmas Eve in 1938 at the St. Olaf parsonage north of Turtle Lake. Merle
Berge and Echo Peterson were the attendants. Pastor Sorenson was the pastor; he
also served the church in Mercer.

It was still in the Depression years and so they decided to just continue on at
the family farm about seven miles north of Mercer. Both of the parents had died
within that same year. Besides the farm, Sidney had a small income as a part
time mail driver. In those years the roads were so bad that the route had to be
divided in the wintertime. He had two teams of horses, with one stationed at a
neighbor's farther north. A boxlike structure on sled runners was his means of
travel. It was equipped with a small stove and was a fairly comfortable, if
slow, way to go.

        Photo: Mollie and Sidney Nielsen, 1938

Farming had never been easy and those years meant a lot of hard physical work.
They milked around 20 Holsteins by hand and separated all of that milk - also by
hand. The separator parts were also done 'by hand' twice a day and was the 'yuk'
job of the day! Sidney had four horses to do his fieldwork. He really did not
care for them and especially for the one that decided it was time to quit any
old time and would just lie down in her harness. When he got a lumbering old
tractor with iron wheels he thought he was indeed fortunate!

About that time he also decided that his wife would never make the best milkmaid
in the world, so he bought a milking machine. That was such a novelty that they
had more visitors to see it than they had to see their new baby daughter, who
was born on May 31, 1941. They named her Joan Rosemarie, sort of for all of the
grandparents. That year they lost some of their pastureland and had to move.
They went to the Krogh and Hattie Ovre farm about three miles north of Mercer.
They were just north of Brush Lake and always appreciated the view of the
Prophet Mountains to the east. They were also in a better position to become
dairy farmers as the trucks could more easily get to them. The farm had a large
barn but had been run down over the years. It was not fenced and often hunters
would shoot at game right by the house. With little girls about, this was
frightening. They also missed the beautiful trees which Sidney's dad had planted
on the home place.

Sidney was a good farmer and soon had put into practice many good farming ideas
such as strip cropping, tree row plantings, alfalfa and corn plantings. He built
two silos and the cutting of silage was one of the big jobs of the year. Also
over the years he fixed up the barn, built a milk house, dug a new well, built
miles of fences and put up many new buildings including a house. Later with the
diligent hoeing of the girls he planned a beautiful windbreak of tree plantings.
Much of the labor was done with the help of good neighbors and many hired men
until the children were big enough to help. By the time they quit milking, they
were putting around 60 cows through the milk house stalls. Even on Sundays,
therefore, he had to put in close to eight hours of work.

When they moved to the new farm, they soon became the parents of two more girls.
They were Diane Kathleen, born Jan. 20, 1943, and Kirsten Genevieve, born Jan.
17, 1944. Since something crippled Mollie during the fourth year of her life,
she was left physically not too strong, these three babies were quite a chore.
She had many wonderful girls and women who helped her through those years. Mrs.
Gurina Bergan, Mrs. Jorgensen, Ella Winge and Lila Calheim were some of the
mainstays.

Then when the girls were a little bit grown up, they had two sons. They were
LeRoy Evans, who was born on June 27, 1947, and Lyndon Sidney, born on Oct. 5,
1949. Over the years the children became a source of great happiness and
blessings. They had their share of heartaches and problems too. They were a
great help to their father. Mollie was never much of a farmer's wife as far as
farm work was concerned, but did try to conserve money by doing all her own
sewing, baking and gardening. Also she tried very hard to feed the family with
good, healthful meals and saw that they had plenty of rest. More important their
spiritual life was nurtured with daily devotions and daily good reading and
faithful Sunday school and church attendance.

Today Rosemarie is married to Pastor Mel Deitz and they have four living
children: Shawn Evan, Kristin Melynne, Timothy Niel and Stephen Matthew. Three
children died because of a genetic heart problem. They are Village Missionaries
and pastor at churches that can't afford or get a pastor. They are now in
Newell, S.D.

Kathleen is married to Pastor Jim Kasemen, and they pastored a Word of Faith
Church in Redwood Falls, Minn. They also have four children: Desiree Sue,
Annette Roseanne, Tisha Marie and Jonathan James. They also have a foster baby,
Daniel. They now live in Branson, Mo.

Kirsten married Norman Skarstad. They lived at Montevideo, Minn., where he was a
part-time worker with the youth of their Lutheran church and is an Amway
distributor. Kirsten taught home economics in that high school. They were Peace
Corps workers in Micronesia when they were first married. Their children are
Ingrid Beth and Paul Anthony. Kirsten is now married to Bryne Limpert and they
live in Branson, Mo.

LeRoy and his wife, Phyllis (Schneider) were on the home farm until 2001 when
they moved to Wyoming He graduated from LeTourneau College in Longview, Texas,
and was a Lieutenant in the naval air force. They have three children: Trent
Webster, Kimberly Jean and Tammy Joy.

Lyndon married Janet James of Hot Springs, Mont. He completed two and one-half
years in an aeronautics course at LeTourneau College and then transferred to the
State University at Bozeman, Mont. He worked on his master's degree in wildlife
management. They have two children: Maria Chantel and Jeremy James. They now
live in Stevenson, Mont.

Rosemarie and Kirsten are graduates of Concordia College and both of them have
home economics majors. Kathleen went to the Bismarck School of Nursing for one
year and then went to Devils Lake where she obtained her license as a practical
nurse.

Their parents helped them all as much as they could and some years were not
easy. Mollie taught school for 11 years to help send them through school.
Usually that meant teaching in fields in which she was not too well prepared and
so perhaps did not always do a skilled job. However, she tried to be a good
example to the young people and always worked with them in much love. As a
result, she did very little civic work. Sidney, however, was on every imaginable
board. He served on the school board, the church board, the township board, FHA
board and McLean Dairy Board. He as served as Sunday school superintendent and
has always been in faithful attendance at brotherhood meetings. Between the two
of them, they have given 30 years of service to the Lakeside and Brush Lake 4-H
Clubs. She taught Sunday school for close to 30 years and has always worked with
the Ladies Mission Society. Currently she is the treasurer of the North Dakota
Mother's Association and is serving on the board of Special Education.

They are members of the First Baptist Church of Mercer and are grateful to God
for His leading and for His infinite goodness to them,

Sidney died in 1982 and is buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

Soren (Nelson)  Nielson

Soren Nielson was born on Aug. 8, 1870, in Denmark where he received training in
landscape gardening and as a male hospital attendant. He came to the United
States in 1903 and lived in Spencer, Iowa for a year. He attended Angsar College
in Hutchinson, Minn. In 1905 he came to North Dakota where he joined the Danish
community northeast of Mercer and took up a homestead.

        Photo: Soren Nielson in his garden.

        Photo: (From left) Christ Stradinger, Anton Nelson and Soren Neilson.

In 1922 he purchased a home in Mercer where he lived until his death on Jan. 8,
1951, in the Bismarck Hospital. He is buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

He was known as a hardy pioneer and nature lover. He was a familiar figure in
the Mercer community where he was always busy in the summer beautifying some
lawn or garden.

Soren was a devout member of Our Savior's Lutheran Church, the Sunday school and
Bible Class and a generous giver toward the young people's summer Bible camp and
parochial school. His love of mankind made Soren a cheerful contributor to all
worthy undertakings, local and otherwise.

Richard was born April 4, 1925, on a farm south of Mercer. He was the son of

Susan Kay was born Oct. 27, 1956, and graduated from Wilton High School in 1975.

have one son, Steve Christopher, born Oct. 30, 1979, and who currently works

Dale Duane was born April 27, 1960, and graduated from Wilton High School in

Besides farming the home place, Dale works for the McLean County Highway Dept.

Richard passed away on Dec. 12, 2000, and is buried in the Sunset Gardens in

Robert & Florence (Narum) O'Shea

Robert O'Shea, son of the late Joseph and Alvera O'Shea of Blackwater Township
and Florence Narum, daughter of the late Nels and Hilda Narum of Rosemont
Township, all of McLean County, were married May 15, 1947, at Garrison.

Robert served in the Navy during World War II and Florence attended Minot State
College and taught school five years before and after their marriage. Robert
worked for the Walt Hjelle's Coast to Coast store in Garrison. In 1952, they
moved to the Ray Peterchick farm southwest of Douglas in Douglas Township and
farmed for two years before buying the John Braun farm located between Turtle
Lake and Mercer in Mercer Township, where they have lived since.

In the years of 1950 to 1952, there was so much snow, people were unable to get
to town for necessities. At times some groceries had to be dropped out of
airplanes for the farmers as well as feed for the animals. Some folks had to be
flown out of medical attention. During one storm, Bob was caring for their two
and one-half year old son along with milking about 20 cows, while Florence was
stranded at the Henry Kerzman farm near the school she was teaching.

Bob and Florence have been active in many organizations. Bob served on various
boards and is currently State Representative from District 8, as did his
grandfather, Jerry O'Shea, 67 years ago.

Bob and Florence built a new home in 1975, having one of the first wooden
basements in the area.

Their children include:

Darrel graduated from the Wahpeton School of Science, is an iron worker and
welder and is employed at Coal Creek near Underwood. His wife, the former Zona
Stengel of Underwood, attended NDSU for three years. They have two girls, Dawn
and Dusty, and one son, Brian.

Jerry served four years in the Navy as an OR technician, stationed at San Diego,
Alaska, and in the Pacific. He was on the ship, which moved refugees from
Vietnam.

Laurie married Joy Schock of Kulm, N.D., and has earned a degree in music and a
minor in business from Valley City State College. He taught at the Valley City
High School and is now teaching in Sidney, Mont. Joy also has a degree in
business education.

Kim, the youngest and only daughter, attended Bismarck Junior College, was
employed by the First Security Bank of Underwood, and is married to Dennis Kurle
of Mercer. Dennis also attended BJC and is a foreman for Twin City Testing at
Coal Creek near Underwood. They have one daughter, Anne, and one son, Casey.

By Robert and Florence O'Shea, taken from the McLean County Historical Book,
1978

Krogh & Hattie (Akre) Ovre

Ovres came here from Iowa in 1902 before Mercer was a town. Krogh and his
brother, Sevald, filed on claims just north of Brush Lake in Sections 22 and 23
of Wise Township that fall.

Krogh Ovre was born September 14, 1865, at the Oksas farm in Leksvik Parish at
Rosvold, Norway, near Trondheim. His father, Nels Ovre Nelsen, was born at the
Myhr farm in Norway on March 12, 1835. Nels married Christiana Guneriusdatter
Nov. 7, 1862, at Leksvik, Norway. Krogh, the oldest son, had two sisters, Anna
and Ida, and three brothers, Julius, Nels, and Sevald.

In 1868, when Krogh was three years old, his family immigrated to the US. They
settled at Eau Claire or Chippewa Falls, Wisconsin, and then in 1874 they moved
to Highlandville, Iowa. Krogh's father was a carpenter. Some of the furniture he
built is on display at the Vesterheim Norwegian American Museum at Decorah,
Iowa.

Krogh married Henrietta (Hattie) Akre on Oct. 26, 1893, at Big Canoe Stone
Lutheran Church, Highlandville, Iowa. Hattie was born in Winneshiek County, near
Highland-ville, Iowa, March 23, 1875. Her parents were Martha Saervold and Johan
Johaneson Akre. Her father was born on Akre, near Bergen, Norway. Her sisters
were: Inga, Anna and Ingebor "Belle" (Wassenberg). Belle homesteaded near Mercer
in 1909. Hattie's brothers were: Martin J., Rev. Ole, John, and Jonas J. Akre.

        Photo: Krogh and Henrietta Ovre

Four children were born to Krogh and Hattie in Iowa: Carl "Norman" (1894), Mabel
(1896 and died in 1897), John Morris (1898 and died in 1899), and Grant (1900).

In the summer of 1902, Krogh and his brother, Sevald Ovre, who was born March
26, 1879, built a large hotel in Harvey, North Dakota. That fall they filed on
homesteads north of Brush Lake. Krogh and Hattie returned to Iowa for the
winter.

Hattie and Krogh and two small sons, Norman and Grant left Iowa in March 1903
and came to Balfour, North Dakota, by rail in an emigrant car. The car was
packed with homesteaders hoping to file a claim and get rich quick. Ovres drove
a team from Balfour and stopped at a big ranch house by Brush Lake, where the
bath houses were later built. They stayed there until their 12 × 12 shack was
built.

More homesteaders moved in. The Ovres' nearest neighbor to the north was the
Elmer McRoberts family. Most of the others were bachelors and Hattie started to
bake bread and sell it to them.

In May, Krogh and Sevald went back to Harvey to finish the inside of the hotel
they built the year before. Hattie and young sons were left to hold down the
claim. It went all right until the middle of June when a tremendous downpour
began followed by the worst electrical storm she had ever seen. About 1 A.M. the
door flew open, the house shook, and Hattie thought the shack was going. She
managed to close the door and wrapped the boys in quilts. She put them down on
the cellar floor and sat on the steps until morning. It rained all the next day
too.

        Photo: Sevald Ovre home-steaded in 1902.

The Fourth of July came and Hattie and Mrs. McRoberts fixed a picnic lunch. Mr.
McRoberts hitched his team up to the lumber wagon and drove them down to Blue
Lake where they spent a pleasant day.

There was a store and post office at Turtle Lake, four miles further west than
it is now, where Hattie and Mrs. McRoberts would go to pick up their mail.

The latter part of July, Krogh came home from Harvey. They traveled to Washburn
and bought a milk cow from a man by the name of Sunstrum. They also bought
provisions for another month.

At that time, County Supt. Lofts from Washburn came to visit them. They
organized the township and opened the first school in Wise Township in Sevald
Ovre's shack the fall of 1903. Sevald lived with his brother Krogh and family
and they worked together.

The first blizzard struck the 12th of September. Hattie moved her cow and calf
up to their hay stack, so she saved them. Hattie remembered there were lots of
people that lost cattle in that storm and one man lost his life looking for his
cattle. Krogh came home the day after the storm. They built a bedroom and a coal
shed onto their house and prepared for the winter. It turned out to be a long
hard winter with lots of snow. The first warm day was Easter Sunday, April 11,
1904. Ovres were invited to Charlie and Elizabeth Wise's home on the peninsula
at Brush Lake for Easter dinner.

Ovre's daughter, Martha was born May 3rd. At the same time, Hattie's brother and
sister in Iowa kept writing that their father was dying from cancer. He was
requesting to see Hattie, but she could not leave the homestead until June 2nd.
A 14-month residency was required from the date of actual residency, plus $1.25
per acre, to waive the five-year residency requirement.

June came and Ovres sent for a livery man from Balfour. They traeled by train
and arrived back home in Iowa on June 8, 1904, the day after Hattie's father
died. They moved into the home they had left, but it did not seem the same. She
said there was something about the Great Plains out here that was unforgettable.

On September 12, 1904, Krogh filed commutated homestead proof at Bismarck. His
witnesses where Ramsey R. McComb, age 54, Elmer McRoberts, age 31, Matt Schmitt,
and Charles Wise, all neighbors.

Three years after Ovres filed for their claim, the railroad was extended from
Denhoff to Turtle Lake. In 1905 Krogh and Hattie and family moved back to their
homestead by Brush Lake to stay. Hattie said that she never regretted that
decision. See Hattie's "My Fourteen Months on the Claim" in Reminiscences of
Mercer on page 403.

In 1908 Krogh and his brother, Sevald, built A.N. Steward's land office in
Mercer. That year Sevald filed five year proof on his homestead. In 1916 they
built Medicine Hill School #4 in Section 26 south of Ed Skows. They built a
large barn on Krogh's homestead in 1917, which is still standing north of Brush
Lake today.

Two more sons were born at Mercer, Leslie Orlando, born June 17, 1908 and Harley
Kenneth, born May 12, 1910. Their youngest child, Anna "Ruth" was born July 14,
1916, in the Mercer Hospital. Ruth said she was told that she weighed 12 pounds
at birth and was fed barley water in the hospital for stomach problems.

        Photo: Norman Ovre

Carl "Norman" Ovre attended country school in Wise Township, and started high
school in Velva in 1908 when he was 13 yrs. old. Norman was inducted into the
Army at Washburn on July 21, 1918. He was sent to Camp Custer, Michigan and
served in the 160th Depot Brigade to August 14, 1918. He then served with the
Battery D 40th Field Artillery division until his discharge in February 1919.
His sister Ruth remembered it was a great day when he returned home from World
War I. Krogh and Hattie held a big barn dance in their hay loft to celebrate
with friends and neighbors. Norman helped on the farm, and also worked for the
CCC during the 1930s. He never married. He died February 4, 1946, at age 51 at
the V.A. Hospital in St. Cloud, Minnesota, and is buried at Mercer Hillside
Cemetery.

        Photo: Grant Ovre

Grant Ovre graduated from eighth grade at the Brush Lake country school in 1913.
He was a member of the Mercer Men's Basketball team that won the McLean County
Tournament in 1921. He worked in the oil fields of Wyoming, Texas and Canada
from 1923 to 1928. From 1929 to 1935, he worked on the home farm at Mercer. In
1935, Grant moved to Berwyn, Illinois. He married Dorothy Peter on March 5,
1941, but that marriage ended in divorce. In September 1954, he married Edna
Bauman, a lady with two children, Carl and Robert Hass. Grant worked for
International Harvester and General Motors. He died December 5, 1967, and is
buried in Concordia Cemetery, at Forest Park, Illinois, near Chicago.

Martha Ovre attended Mercer High and then Concordia Academy for two years. In
1922, she taught at the Mayer's country school in Wise Township. She was 18
years old and it was her first year of teaching. Her brother, Harley, an eighth
grader, drove her and Ruth, a first grader, to school with a horse and buggy in
the spring and fall and a sled in the winter. There were lots of big boys that
year among the 14 children attending. There were some rowdy games of basketball
in the schoolhouse before someone decided it should not be allowed. In 1925,
Martha taught grades 3- 5 in town at the Mercer School. Martha, Ruth, and Harley
lived together in Bill Norris' upstairs.

        Photo: (From left) Reed and Martha Argent and Walter and Ruth
        Christensen at their double wedding in 1938.

From 1928-32, Martha worked at Hjelle's First State Bank and Hjelle's store in
Mercer. She attended summer schools at Valley City State, obtaining a Standard
Teaching Certificate the summer of 1933. Martha taught at the Sprout School in
Wise Township during 1932 -33 and 1933-34. Martha and her sister Ruth, a
student, walked to school in good weather and lived in a curtained off corner of
the schoolhouse in the winter.

Mr. Ludvig Totdahl, Superintendent at Steele, North Dakota, called Martha in
1934 and said they needed a good disciplinarian to teach seventh and eighth
grade there. So Martha moved to Steele and taught there until 1938. On October
26, 1938, she married Reed Argent of Steele in double wedding with her sister,
Ruth.

Martha and Reed had three children, ReMar (Voxland), Marthyn (Buzz), and John
Argent. Martha died Aug. 28, 1963, from cancer at age 59 and Reed Argent died
December 5, 1982. They are buried at Steele.

        Photo: Leslie Ovre

Leslie Ovre graduated from Mercer High in 1925. He attended Luther College at
Decorah, Iowa. In 1926, Leslie took a year off from college and taught the Lehn
school in Wise Township. He returned to Luther College, graduating in 1931 with
a B.A. degree. Les began his career in social welfare as a caseworker in Emmons
County in 1933. He was County Administrator of Welfare in Logan County where he
met Paula Hildegarde Hahn. They were married June 4, 1939, and Les worked with
the Ransom County Welfare.

Les entered the Army at Sort Snelling, Minnesota, June 6, 1942. He served in the
Asiatic Pacific Theater and was discharged at Fort Warren, Wyoming, on August
28, 1942, as a private. He then attended officer's candidate school in Fort
Warren, and entered the US Coast Guard at Ketchikan, Alaska, January 1, 1944. He
separated from the service October 16, 1945, at Seattle, Washington. Les and
Paula returned to North Dakota and Les completed graduate school at the
University of Minnesota. They moved to Fort Totten and then to Grafton where Les
worked for Public Welfare Programs. In 1950, he took a job at the State office
in Bismarck. In 1962, Les was named Executive Director of Public Welfare. He
retired in 1972 after 10 years as Director of Human Services for ND. They had no
children but took in Paula's two nieces after their mother died. Les died Sept.
29, 1989.

        Photo: Harley Ovre

Harley Kenneth Ovre graduated from Mercer High in 1927. He farmed on the family
farm until the 1930s. He then took a job with the Civilian Conservation Corps.
Harley entered the Army at Fort Snelling, Minnesota, March 13, 1942. He served
in the European African Middle Eastern Theater during WW II. He was discharged
as a private at Camp McCoy, Wisconsin, Nov. 9, 1945. He reentered the Army at
Camp McCoy, Feb. 15, 1947, and served in Korea. He was discharged at San
Francisco on Oct. 14, 1953. Following his discharge, Harley lived in the San
Francisco area for several years. He was married briefly to Muriel, and had no
children. He entered the Veteran's Home at White City, Oregon, and later moved
to the Nursing Home at Underwood, North Dakota. Harley died August 24, 1981, and
is buried at Mercer.

        Photo: Martha and Ruth Ovre

Ruth Ovre graduated from Mercer in 1932 at the age of 15. When she was 16, her
father, Krogh, died of a heart attack on December 15, 1932. Ruth attended Valley
City State one year and Minot State one summer. The summer of 1934 was one of
the worst drought years in North Dakota. Ruth taught the Sprout School that
fall, her first year of teaching. She made $50 a month and had 28 students with
no helper and she said it was a difficult year. It was a nice winter and she
walked over 2 miles each way almost daily. Sometimes Walter Christensen would
come by and give her a ride. The next year Ruth taught at the Sprout School
again with only 19 students, as the Lehn School in Wise Township opened again
that fall. The winter of 1935-36 was very cold, and there was a six week period
when the temperature never rose above zero. During that time, Harley gave Ruth a
sleigh ride to school. A few times when the weather was stormy, Katie (Mrs.
Floyd) Sprout had her spend the night with them.

The fall of 1936, Ruth taught at the Brush Lake School. On August 14, 1937, her
Uncle Sevald died of heat stroke while herding cattle north of Brush Lake. He
was generous with his nieces and nephews and helped them with college expenses.
He had also worked for the railroad and traveled extensively. He was buried in
the Mercer Hillside Cemetery.

In the fall of 1937, Ruth took a teaching position near Sawyer and stayed with
Theobald and Margaret Hofer and family. They were family friends from Mercer who
moved there after his eyesight no longer allowed him to farm.

On October 26, 1938, Ruth married Walter Christensen at Our Savior's Lutheran
Church at Mercer. They had a double wedding with her sister, Martha, and Reed
Argent. This was the first wedding held at Our Savior's newly completed church.

Ruth and Walter lived in Jamestown that first winter, and then moved onto the
Ovre farm the spring of 1939. That fall they moved to the Christensen farm. Ruth
taught at the Sprout School one more year and then began raising a family of
seven children: Patricia, Eunice, Mary, Stephen, Joel, James, and Thomas.

Hattie sold the Ovre farm to Sidney and Molly Nielsen in 1941 and moved to
Bismarck. She died October 15, 1952, and is buried in the Mercer Hillside
Cemetery beside Krogh. In 1974, Ruth, Walter, Jim and Tom moved to Mandan.
Walter died August 3, 1979 and Ruth died September 10, 2003. They are buried in
Mercer Hillside Cemetery.

        Photo: Ovre barn, Joe Peterson's Avery threshing rig, 1920s.

Edward & Hattie (Hove) Pederson

Edward Pederson was born Feb. 3, 1884, to Peder and Berith Pederson, Bricelyn,
MN. Hattie Hove was born Nov. 19, 1886, to Andrew J. and Anna Rolands Hove.
Edward and Hattie were married May 1, 1907. They lived in Max and Pettibone
before moving to Mercer in 1918.

        Photo: Edward and Hattie Pederson

Ed and Hattie were members of Our Saviour's Lutheran Church. They ran the café
and bar, later dropping the bar and adding a meat market and locker plant. In
1951 they sold out and retired. Ed passed away in 1970 and Hattie in 1979. They
were the parents of 16 children, two died as infants.
