Michael & Katherine (Miller) Schlaht

Michael Schlaht was born Feb. 16, 1862, in Neu Gluecksthal, South Russia. In
1885, he married Katherine Miller who was born on Jan. 6, 1865.

Michael and Katherine made their home in South Russia until 1906 [1901,
according to Petition for Citizenship] when they left for America. They settled
in McLean County 13 miles southwest of Mercer where they homesteaded. They built
their home and barns out of mud and rocks. Michael died in 1918 leaving his wife
and children to manage their large farmstead and home. Four years later,
Katherine married Mr. Hager and moved to Canada. They later moved to Portland,
Ore., where they lived until his death. Katherine died Dec. 31, 1932.

Michael and Katherine were the parents of 12 children: eight who were born
before they came to America. Fredrick, 1886, Jacob 1888, Christina 1890,
Gottlieb 1892, Frederick 1893, John 1895, Emanuel 1897 (died in infancy) and
Emanuel 1899. The first five died at a young age in the flu epidemic. Emma was
also born in South Russia. Emil, Henry and Martha were born in America. Henry
died in infancy.

Emil & Bertha (Marzolf) Schlaht

Emil was born on Sept. 2, 1903, and married Bertha Marzolf on Nov. 28, 1931.

rural schools. She taught at Mercer and various other towns. She died June 25,

Emil and Bertha had two sons, James and Leo.

Emma Schlaht Hall

Emma was born Dec. 1, 1900, in South Russia. She was one year old when she came
to America with her family. She operated the Mercer Central Telephone office for
many years. Emma was born with short arms and legs with other normal body parts.
She loved to crochet and sewed her own clothes. She met her husband, Raymond
Hall, by joining a pen pal club. They were married in 1942 and lived to Memphis,
Tenn. He died in 1948. In her later years, she returned to North Dakota and
lived at the Baptist Home in Bismarck until her death on Dec. 1, 1984.

Ferdinand (Ferd) Schmitt

Ferd Schmitt was born in 1880 in Tipton County, Ind. As a young man he moved to
Mercer where his older brothers, Joseph and Matt were living. Ferd filed a
homestead claim four miles northeast of Mercer about 1902. Ferd lived on this
claim, and the additional land he purchased, until his death in 1965. Ferd was a
bachelor and seemed to like it that way.

As a young man, he had flame red curly hair which he hated. It is told he would
use soap to plaster his hair down, but it never worked. Ferd never owned or
drove a car and always farmed with horses until renters leased his land. He
loved wildlife and animals of all kinds, especially his horses. His
transportation was a team and buggy, wagon or sled. He managed a trip to Mercer
about every two weeks during the summer, but only once a month in the winter. If
he happened to consume a bit too much spirits - no problem, for his faithful
team always knew the way home.

        Photo: Matt and Ferdinand Schmitt at Ferd's farm in 1956.

He enjoyed company and always had cold, leftover pancakes to serve and perhaps a
spot of blackberry brandy.

Ferd's land and surrounding properties in the Prophet Mountains provided great
hunting for many of his friends from the Mercer area. These hunts and fellowship
were very special to him. He was a marksman with a rifle and stories were told
about Ferd bringing down upland game on the fly with his 22-caliber rifle. Ferd
died in 1965 and is buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

Mathias & Mary (Hobbs) Schmitt

Mathias "Matt" and Mary "Molly" Schmitt married and filed a homestead claim
seven miles north of Mercer in 1889.

Matt was born in 1877 in Tipton County, Ind. And Mary (Hobbs) Schmitt was born
in 1879 in Hobbs Station, Ind. In 1923 they sold their homestead and moved to
Atlantic, Iowa, where Matt became employed with the U.S. Post Office. They had
five children, all born in Mercer. Their children are:

Glen Schmitt who moved to Iowa.

Gertrude Schmitt who moved to Iowa.

Herbert Schmitt who moved from Mercer in the late 1920s and returned in 1948 to
work the Ferd Schmitt farm northeast of Mercer. Herbert's son, Patrick Schmitt,
also lived in Mercer from 1948 through 1952.

Kenneth Schmitt who moved to Nebraska.

Viola Schmitt who moved to Iowa with her parents.

All of the children except Viola attended rural school north of Mercer and
eventually attended high school in Mercer. Both Herbert and Kenneth played on
the Mercer High School basketball team when they took the county championship in
1921. Two of Matt's brothers also moved to Mercer in the early 1900s. They were
Joseph, who died at the age of 22 and is buried in the Mercer Cemetery and Ferd,
who homesteaded four miles northeast of Mercer.

Fred & Magdalena (Laib) Schoell

Magdalena Laib was born Dec. 19, 1890 at Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, Russia to

Adolph & Margaretha (Berreth) Singer

Adolph Singer was born February 19, 1863, in Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, south
Russia (today Ukraine). He was the son of Jakob Christoph Singer and Margaretha
Hofer. On January 31, 1892, he married Margaretha Berreth in Kloestitz,
Bessarabia, S. Russia. She was born April 24, 1866, in Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia,
S. Russia, and the daughter of Leonhard Berreth and Elisabetha Aickele.

The Singers resided in Hoffnungstal until 1894 when they immigrated with two
small children to this country and settled in Ashley, ND. In 1897 they took up
homesteading in Morton County near Glen Ullin, ND, where Adolph made first
application for naturalization in November. In 1905 the Singers sold the
homestead and moved to Beck's Ranch in Sheridan County. In 1907 the family moved
to Mercer where Adolph and his brother-in-law, Rudolph Berreth, went into
business after acquiring a livery stable and dray line from Karl Degg. Their
home was one of the first constructed in the fledgling village and still stands
today on the northeast corner of Rice and Regan Streets. In 1914 he purchased
the local meat market from neighbor and close friend Christ Sackmann and
operated the business until his retirement in 1919.

Adolph and Margaretha were the parents of fourteen children (three sons died in
infancy):

Alexander, born September 10, 1892, Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, S. Russia, married
Dora Schindler February 17, 1914, McClusky, ND, died in auto accident January 6,
1924, Mercer, ND.

Paulina, born October 15, 1893, Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, S. Russia, married
Herbert Wiest August 15, 1912, Washburn, ND, died November 24, 1968, Spokane,
WA.

Christina, born 1895, Ashley, ND, married John Schindler 1913.

Rudolph, born 1897, Glen Ullin, ND, married (spouse unknown), died 1952, Salt
Lake City, UT.

John Adolph, born April 10, 1898, Glen Ullin, ND, died from Spanish influenza
September 22, 1918, Great Lakes Naval Center, IL.

Theofil (Dave), born 1900, Glen Ullin, ND, married (spouse unknown).

Arthur Immanuel, born October 8, 1900, Hebron, ND, married (spouse unknown),
died 1958, Oregon City, OR.

Regina, born 1902, Glen Ullin, ND, married Ray Stubbs.

Elsie Ella, born June 3, 1904, Glen Ullin, ND, died in auto accident June 22,
1925, Mercer, ND.

Olga, born 1906, Mercer, ND, married Arthur Carlson, died June 1962, Bismarck,
ND.

Walter, born 1909, Mercer, ND, married (spouse unknown), died 1951, Fresno, CA.

Back in Hoffnungstal, at age 21, Adolph was inducted into the Russian military,
namely the Navy. His military duty spanned seven years and in that time he
became an excellent musician playing the clarinet in the czar's royal band. He
once had the honor of participating in the wedding of the czar's sister Princess
Sofia to King Constantine of Greece as a delegated musician. Adolph's passion
for music continued in this country to the point where, disinterested in
farming, he left the Glen Ullin homestead for long periods, touring with a
contingent of John Philip Sousa's band. It was a major factor leading to the
sale of the homestead in 1905. During Mercer's early years he joined Herbert
Wiest, Ole Hedahl and Ella Myhra Hjelle (O.S.) in providing music for dances and
special events.

The Singer livery stable, located near the intersection of Rice and Regan
Streets in Lots 9-11, Block 5, Original Town Site, was a thriving and busy
enterprise at the outset. Adolph and his sons tended a barn full of horses and
mules. Horses and buggies were rented to anyone who couldn't reach a destination
by rail - Minot, Washburn, Dogden, Wilton. Heavy horses were used in the dray line
service. The mules were used for long hauls, but they ran away at the least
provocation and did so much property damage Adolph had to sell them. Two
stallions were kept for breeding. The livery rented stalls to farmers who, while
shopping in town during inclement weather, needed to shelter their teams. The
Singer men labored hard unloading boxcars of coal and lumber and hauling
freight. In addition to running a business, Adolph served as the first duly
elected constable in Mercer Township.

The automobile came into use more and more - Adolph had acquired his in 1910, an
International - and the livery business dwindled. Adolph's brother-in-law, Rudolph
Berreth, had moved to Canada, so in 1914 Adolph went into the meat market
business. The younger generation of children joined in waiting on customers and
cutting meat. The meat business in that day required the extra work of cutting
ice at Brush Lake in the winter and hauling it into town to be packed in sawdust
in an icehouse for summer use in the large cooler.

Upon the nation's entry into World War I, son Alexander was married, the father
of two children and a rural mail carrier. Sons Rudolph and John enlisted in the
Navy. Spanish influenza began sweeping the nation, and shortly upon entry into
the military, John fell victim to the disease. Adolph went into retirement in
1919 and sons Theofil (Dave) and Arthur managed the meat market until 1924 when
it was sold to Joe Dokovna. Alexander was killed in a tragic auto accident in
1924 and daughter Elsie was victim of the same fate in 1925. Adolph died July
28, 1928, in Mercer after a long illness. This began with influenza, was
complicated later by pneumonia and followed by a stroke. Margaretha died
November 27, 1935, in Mercer as a result of head injuries sustained in a fall
down basement steps at her home. The Singers were charter members of the Hope
Lutheran Church in Mercer and are buried in the local cemetery.

Adolph's lineage traces back to the village of Korb, Wuerttemberg in Germany
(nine miles east of Stuttgart). The Singer name appears in church and civil
records of the fifteenth century. Margaretha's ancestors hail from
Spirkelbach/Bergzabern, Pfalz in Germany.

Arlo & Marlyn (Wiedrich) Singer

Arlo "Blackie" Singer was born on July 10, 1937, in Mercer, the son of Jacob and
Anna Schott Singer. He attended Mercer schools and graduated in 1955. He
graduated from Hanson's Body Shop in Fargo in 1965. He worked for Bismarck's
Public Works Department from 1970 until his death on Feb. 25, 2000. He was known
as an authority on the Bismarck sewer system.

        Photo: Arlo Singer

He was noted for his orange jumpsuit, his hat and toothpick. He was a restorer
of vintage 1950 Ford automobiles. For his funeral at Faith Lutheran Church in
Bismarck, a row of parked 1950s Fords which had been taken out of winter storage
paid tribute to him.

He married Marlyn Wiedrich on Feb. 13, 1965. They had one daughter, Denice
(Bryan Haag) and one grandson, Matthew Jacob Haag born on Aug. 18, 1992.

Compiled from obituary and newspaper articles.

Christoph & Christiana (Klotzbuecher) Singer

Christoph Singer was born October 24, 1866, in Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, South
Russia (today Ukraine). He was the son of Johann Georg Singer and Maria
Katharina Freuer. On November 30, 1887, he married Christiana Klotzbuecher in

and the daughter of Johann Klotzbuecher and Magdalena Justina Reule.

        Photo: Christoph Singer - Christiana Klotzbuecher

The Singers resided in Hoffnungstal until 1903, when Russian military
conscription and the family's meager landholdings compelled the Singers to
emigrate. By 1895 Christoph's younger brother Georg returned from duty in the
Russian army with horror stories about military service. Christoph's own son,
Johann Georg, was facing the same fate. This, coupled with the family's
impoverishment, (their landholdings of less than three acres barely sustained
them) convinced Christiana foremost that they had to leave. Andreas Bossert's
letters from America with glowing accounts of homestead life on the Dakota
prairie clenched the decision. In late March they sold their few possessions,
and, along with families of Balthasar Kleingaertner and Immanuel Hofer, they
boarded a train in Kauschani, Bessarabia, bound for Hamburg, Germany. By April
15 the entourage set sail for North America on the S.S. Assyria. Christoph had
a mere $15.00 in his pocket.

They arrived at Halifax, Nova Scotia, on April 25, 1903. They were detained on
board ship under quarantine for several days because cases of trachoma were
discovered among some steerage passengers. Eventually they set out for Winnipeg,
Manitoba, by train. They sustained themselves with potatoes and onions Christoph
had received in payment for his part-time work in the ship's galley. Reaching
their destination and utterly destitute, Christoph and son Johann Georg both
worked at a sawmill for one month's duration, each earning $1.00 per day. At the
end of June the family's room and board came to $30.00, and the remaining $30
was used for train fare to Harvey, ND.

At Harvey they were greeted by Wilhelm Goll, a fellow Hoffnungstaler who had
immigrated to McIntosh County, ND, in 1893 and resettled in the Martin, ND, area
in 1898. Goll accompanied the Singers and Kleingaertners in their wagon journey
southwestward to their homestead claim in McLean County, the SW¼, Sec. 32-146-79
- after 1905 designated as five miles south and three miles west of Mercer, ND.
Their wagon route was most likely along the Rancher's Washburn Trail, a major
road to the county seat at Washburn from northeastern and central sections of
what is today Sheridan County.

With help from former Hoffnungstalers and his new Dakota neighbors Friedrich
Schlepp, Friedrich Laib, Andreas Bossert and Balthasar Kleingaertner, Christoph
immediately set up a claim residence by constructing a 14 × 34-foot sod house
and sinking an 11-foot well. The season was too late for a first crop planting
so Christoph sought temporary employment as a cowhand at the nearby Baardson
Ranch. For his services he attained a cow, a pig and a few chickens, and he
undertook building a 14 × 34-foot sod barn for the animals. With winter
approaching he set out on foot to Washburn and sought out the town dump ground.
Mindful of shoemaker skills he had learned in Russia, he scavenged for any
discarded shoes and, upon his return home dismantled the footwear and recobbled
shoes for the entire family.

Over winter Christoph continued working for the Baardsons, and in spring 1904 he
purchased a horse, broke twenty acres of sod and seeded flax. In succeeding
years he increased his tillage, until in 1908 we find in his homestead proof he
had 100 acres under cultivation, thirty acres fenced and had built a 14 × 16-
foot granary. Christiana went about setting up household. The first chore was to
apply wet lime to the dirt floor and walls of the sod house. Then the walls were
papered over with past issues of the German language newspaper, Der Staats-
Anzeiger, and a final coat of lime applied.

Unlike the homeland colony of Hoffnungstal where farmers resided in the village,
life on the Dakota prairie was an isolated, lonely experience. A major weekly
social event for the Singers and several other Russia-German families was to
gather on Sundays at the Balthasar Kleingaertner homestead for worship services.
This seemed to mirror the frequent religious gatherings at the Kleingaertner
household back in Hoffnungstal. The Kleingaertners were especially devoted
followers of the Bruedergemeinschaft, a pious scripture study organization found
throughout South Russia. The Rev. William Keller, a pioneer missionary pastor
living north of Mercer, conducted services, but not every Sunday. Often
Balthasar himself took charge. He was known less for eloquence in sermonizing
and more for his singing voice. The Singers were among the 12 charter families
of the rural Zion Evangelical Lutheran Church when Keller established it in
1906.

The Singers retired from farming in 1914, sold their holdings to son Johann
Georg and moved to the town of Mercer. They purchased Lots 13-24, Block 2,
Original Town Site, from Halfdan Berge. They then constructed a house on the
site at the southeast corner of Max and Rice Streets. In 1923 Christoph came out
of retirement when he purchased Lots 15 and 16, Block 7 on Main Street and
opened a shoe repair/creamery business. This site later became an office for
Christoph's grandson, Ted Gessele, and his Standard Oil Bulk operation. With the
stock market crash of 1929 there followed many bank failures, including that of
First State Bank in Mercer where the Singers lost their entire savings. They
then had to rely on the meager returns from shoe repairs and handling of cream.
A customer once handed the quiet and unassuming Christoph $1.00 for shoe repairs
and he declined, saying it was too much. He ambled across Main Street to the
pool hall to break the bill and returned to give the customer 90 cents in
change.

        Document: Christoph Singer shoe repair ad. (From an original glass slide
        commercial advertisement shown before feature film screenings in
        Mercer's first movie theater.)

Christoph's roots reach back to Germany in the village of Korb, Wuerttemberg
(nine miles east of Stuttgart). The Singer name appears in church and civil
documents of the fifteenth century. Christiana's ancestors hail from
Guendelbach, Wuerttemberg (fifteen miles northwest of Stuttgart). The
Klotzbuecher name can be traced from there to Aalen, Wuerttemberg, back to 1426.
Christoph died September 7, 1940, Bismarck, ND, and Christiana died March 10,
1947, Mercer, ND. They were charter members of Hope Lutheran Church in Mercer
when it was founded in 1917. Both are buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

Christoph and Christiana were the parents of four children:

Johann Georg, born September 1, 1888, Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, S. Russia,
married Pauline Thurn June 26, 1911, Eureka, SD, died January 22, 1966, Salem,
Ore.

Jakob, born July 31, 1890, Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, S. Russia, died in
accidental well drowning April 25, 1894, Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, S. Russia.

Magdalena, born August 9, 1892, Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, S. Russia, married
Adolph Bender November 15, 1910, Mercer, ND, died October 27, 1989, Seminole,
OK. (See separate history.)

Katharina, born September 21, 1894, Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, S. Russia, married
Heinrich (Henry) Gessele November 26, 1912, Mercer, ND, died May 24, 1968,
Bismarck, ND. (See separate history.)

George & Barbara  (Schaible) Singer

George Singer came to the United States from Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia, Russia in
1903 and became a citizen in 1904. Arriving with him was his wife Barbara and
son Jake and daughter Katharine. Three additional children were born to this
family in the United States; Elizabeth (Mrs. Fred Fischer), Fredrich who died in
a farm accident before he was 13 and Helen (Mrs. Fred Eckmann) who was the
youngest in the family.

        Photo: (At right) George and Barbara Singer and their five children.

(See separate histories for Elizabeth and Helen.)

Their farm was located three miles west and four miles north of Mercer. It later
became known as the Jake Singer farm where he raised his family.

Jakob & Katherina (Mayer) Skaley

Jakob Skaley was born in 1877, the son of Friedrich Skaley and Karolina Montal.
On May 20, 1885, Jakob and his family came to McIntosh County near Ashley from
Beresina, South Russia. They came as far as Ellendale, N.D., by train, then
finished the trip by team. They brought their clothing, bedding, cow, hand plow
and rake and with these meager implements they started to farm. Their house was
built of sod; lumber was hauled from Ellendale for the window frames and doors.
The stove or oven was made of clay and stone; hay, weeds and chips were used for
fuel. It was stoked in the morning and evening and kept the home very
comfortable.

Jakob Skaley married Katherina Mayer in 1898. She was born in January of 1877,
the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Christ Mayer in Ashley. Jakob and Katherina lived
east of Ellendale until 1903, when along with their daughter Ida and son Albert,
they came to homestead north of Mercer. At that time, it was McLean County but
later became Sheridan County. Jakob consummated his homestead claim on April 28,
1910. Other children of this marriage were Lillian and (M.H.) Minehardt. In
1916, Jakob built a new home on the homestead which still stands today. Jakob
died in 1924 and Katherina in 1957.

        Photo: (Above) Meinhardt Skaley

        Photo: The Skaley family: (from left) Albert, Jacob, Kathryn, Lillian
        and Ida.

They had four children:

Ida was born in 1900 and married William Norris who passed away in 1943. She
later married Fern Lowell who died in 1966. Ida died in 1968. There were no
children born of either marriage.

Albert Skaley was born in 1902 and with his brother Meinhardt bought the
homestead and farmed together until 1988. Albert, who never married, died in
1997.

Lillian Skaley was born in 1906 and married Edward Sackman in 1926. (See
separate history.)

Meinhardt (M.H.) was born in 1912 and married Gertrude Dalos in 1933.  (See
separate history.)

Meinhardt & Gertrude (Dalos) Skaley

Meinhardt (M.H.) was born in 1912 and married Gertrude Dalos in 1933. They lived
and farmed in the Mercer area.

        Photo: Gertrude and Meinhardt Skaley

In 1945, they bought 81 acres on the peninsula of Brush Lake. They built and ran
a store for 20 years. They retired in 1988. Meinhardt died in 1999 and Gertrude
in 2003. There were four daughters and one son:

Lois was born in 1935 and graduated from Mercer High School in 1954. She married
Raymond Korus. They lived and farmed near Denhoff, N.D. Lois died in 1991. They
have two sons and two daughters.

Marlys was born in 1937 and graduated from Mercer High School in 1956. She
married Randolph Anderson. He also attended Mercer High School. They live in
Bismarck. Marlys has three sons.

Janice was born in 1944 and graduated from Mercer High School in 1962. She
married Lloyd Seilinger and lived in Bismarck until 1992 when they moved to
Brush Lake where they made their home. Janice died in 1999. She had one daughter
and four sons:

Merlyn was born in 1949 and graduated from Mercer High School in 1968. He
married Kathy Helm. They live in Beulah and have two sons.

Mavis was born in 1955. She went to Mercer High School and graduated from Turtle
Lake-Mercer High School in 1973. She married Mike Orvin and lives in Nashua,
Mont. They have two sons.

William & Verna (Sackman) Skorick

William Skorick was born Nov. 25, 1920, in Butte, N.D. He graduated from Butte
High School in 1941 and spent one year at the University of North Dakota.

On Jan. 4, 1942, he married Verna Sackman, daughter of Andrew Sackman and Regine
Sackman nee Mayer. Verna was born on April 27, 1922, and graduated from Mercer
High School in 1940. They were married in Mercer at Our Savior's Lutheran Church

        Photo: Verna and William Skorick and their children (back, from left)

Verna devoted her time to raising her children, working with ceramics and

Chris & Olga (Peterson) Skow

Chris Skow was born at Bowbells in October of 1895. Olga Peterson was born at
Aalesund, Norway, in April of 1893.

They were married in 1917 and moved to a small farm north of Mercer. It was here
their first son, Woodrow, was born. Approximately in 1921 they moved to the Roy
Nielsen farm, one mile west of Mercer. It was here that LeRoy was born in 1923.

The next move was into Mercer in 1929. For a few years they operated a
lunchroom, pool hall and card room in the same building where Chester's Tavern
is now (the little white schoolhouse). Mr. Skow also worked some time for the
Bank of North Dakota and Highway Department in Bismarck. In 1942, the family
left Mercer and moved to Seattle, Wash. Chris worked in the shipyard and for
Boeing until his retirement.

        Photo: (From left) Olga, LeRoy, Chris and Woodrow Skow, taken in 1937.

Woodrow and LeRoy served in the Army Air Corp and after their service, they
worked with the U.S. Postal Service.

Olga passed away in 1976, Chris in 1968, and Woodrow in 1982. Woodrow's
daughter, Pam Hagen, lives in West Seattle. LeRoy and Maureen live six months in
Apache Junction, Ariz., and six months in Tokeland, Wash. LeRoy's daughter,
Delores, lives in Granite Bay, Calif. and Deanna is in West Seattle.

Edward & Ellen (Christensen) Skow

Edward Rasmussen Skow was born August 3, 1887, in Northfield, Minnesota. His
brother, Chris, filed on a homestead northeast of Mercer on May 5, 1906, in
Section 18 and 19 in Prophet's Township. Two years later, on November 13, 1908,
Ed filed on his homestead in Section 23 and 26 in Medicine Hill Township. Ed
proved it up three years later on October 24, 1912, with patent number was
312739.

Ed did not spend all his time farming. The July 14, 1911 Mercer Telegram
reported "Mrs. And Mrs. C.P Christensen, Ed Skow, Harold Kollum and Fred
Christensen drove to Strawberry Lake to fish. They returned the next day with 15
fish."

In June of 1915 Ed Skow completed a pretty bungalow on his farm north of Mercer.

He married Ellen Martina Christensen on June 5, 1917 at Hutchinson, Minnesota.
Ellen was born on April 8, 1896 in Hutchinson to Peter H. Christensen, born Dec.
10, 1852 in Denmark, and Kristine Bertelson, born April 5, 1854 in Holstup,
Denmark.

        Photo: Edward and Ellen Skow, 1917.

Peter came to America in 1872 at age twenty and worked for awhile in the general
mercantile business. Kristine came to America before Peter and, first, lived in
Minneapolis. She married Peter Christensen June 19, 1881, and they had a total
of eleven children. Those surviving infancy besides Ellen were: Bertel Peter
(born in Minneapolis), Jensine, Minnie, George William, and Julie Verta. Peter
was the janitor at the public schools in Hutchinson for several years.

In July of 1896, Peter and Kristine settled on forty-six acres of land on the
west outskirts of Hutchinson, where he established the first nursery. He tried
many varieties of fruit trees to see which were best suited for the area, and he
was a member of the State Horticulture Society.

Ellen's sister, Minnie Marie Christensen, married Jacob Nelson on January 5,
1910. Jake was born in Copenhagen in 1883, and his father, Christian Nielsen,
died in 1888. His mother sent him to Hutchinson in 1893 to live with relatives
and in 1903 he homesteaded in Section 35 of Medicine Hill Township. The girls'
father gave them young trees from his nursery in Hutchinson to plant on their
homesteads north of Mercer.

Ellen and Edward Skow had one child, Orion Georgia. Skows moved back to
Hutchinson, Minnesota around 1927, and Ed farmed on the outskirts of town on a
small forty acre farm. He did truck gardening and nursery work. Later, Ed worked
at a game farm for about twenty years in Forest City, Minnesota. Ed and Ellen
were known as very sociable people.

Orion married Elmer Nelson. Their two sons were born at Hutchinson, Steven in
1943, and Dale in 1946. In 1965, Ed and Ellen moved to Florida to be nearer to
their daughter, Orion. Ellen died December 16, 1971 and Edward died April 2,
1972. They are buried in Dunedin, Florida. Orion is also deceased. Today,
Marilyn Schon owns and lives on the Ed Skow homestead.

Anton Sorlee

Anton Sorlee (Sorlie) was born in Norway in 1879. He immigrated to the U.S. in
1899, and in 1903 he filed on a homestead in Holmes Township, S½ NE¼ and Lot 2
in Section 31, northeast of Mercer, North Dakota.

His homestead bordered Pelican Lake, just north of Jacob Skaley's farm. He
proved it up five years later with patent number 56586.

He never married. He had a large barn where many dances were held. When Anton
became ill, he lived with Meinhardt Skaley's until he died.

Christian Sorlee

Christian Olausen Sorlee was born in Norway on December 9, 1891.

His occupation was listed as a laborer at Mercer, North Dakota, when he was
inducted into the Army at Washburn on July 21, 1918. He was sent to Camp Custer,
Michigan, and served in the 160th Depot Brigade to August 14, 1918. He then
served with the Supply Company, 78th Infantry until he died of flu related
pneumonia at Camp Custer on Oct. 18, 1918. He was 26 years old.

Christ was buried 7 miles north of Mercer in the former St. Ansgar Cemetery, now
owned by Our Saviors. He was survived by his father Olausen Sorli, brother Lars
O. Sorli and sister Anne Thorud, Skotselven, Norway, and sister Marie Sorli,
Galleberg, Sande, Norway. Anton Sorlee, rural Mercer was his cousin.

Floyd & Catherine (Honan) Sprout

Floyd Sprout was born Dec. 20, 1900, to Walter Scott Sprout and Tessa Cantwell
Sprout at Emmetsburg, Iowa.

His grandparents came from Ireland and Scotland. Floyd was an only child. His
family moved to North Dakota when he was a young boy and settled on a farm north
of Mercer. He graduated from Mercer High School and taught school for a short
time.

He met Catherine Honan, who was born May 14, 1910, in Brookings, S.D. When
Catherine was nine years old her parents passed away and she moved to Turtle
Lake, N.D., and lived with foster parents, Mr. and Mrs. William Crumb. She
graduated from Turtle Lake High School.

        Photo: Catherine and Floyd Sprout

Floyd and Catherine were married on Sept. 5, 1928, at Wilton. They lived on the
family farm for 60 years and then moved into Mercer to live in their pink house,
so fondly remembered by their grandchildren.

Floyd and Catherine had five children.

Gail is a retired beautician and Ray DeBoer live in Bismarck. Both their
children, Ray Jr., who works for the state and Deb who works for Centennial
School, live in Bismarck.

Walter is a retired construction worker and Connie live in Kennewick, Wash.
Their children are Scott who lives in Billings, Mont., and works for the city;
and Laura, who lives in Plattsmouth, Neb., is a loan officer and Mike, who lives
in Sioux City, S.D., is a bondsman.

Peggy is a retired teacher and deputy treasurer and Art (deceased) Dockter live
in McClusky. They had four children. Ken lives in Apple Valley, Minn., and is a
registered pharmacist. Ron lives in Tioga, N.D., and is a high school principal.

Judy is a retired housewife and Harry Basaraba live in Washburn and have three
daughters. Bonnie resides in Bismarck and works for 911. Karla lives in
Gillette, Wyo. and works at a clinic and Mary Kaye lives in Beulah and is a
medical technologist.

Donald works for the state department and Patsy live in Bismarck and have two
sons: Jeff attending college at UND and Aaron, a senior at Bismarck High School.

Floyd and Catherine had 14 grandchildren, 22 great-grandchildren and two great-
great grandchildren.

Floyd was a substitute rural mail carrier for 50 years while Catherine was a
housewife. Floyd loved to be involved in sports as a player and coach while his
wife loved to watch him. Both were very active in sports and community
activities. They were rich in memories, not only of the time Floyd played
baseball and basketball, but of the thrill of seeing their children and
grandchildren successful in competitive sports, something they both regarded as
one of the greatest activities in which people can become involved.

Catherine passed away on Aug. 21, 1977, and Floyd on June 7, 1984.

Walter & Tessa (Cantwell) Sprout

Walter S. Sprout was born in Iowa in 1872 to Irish immigrants, Cummings and Jane
(Smith) Sprout. He left Emmetsville, Iowa in the spring of 1908 and arrived at
Mercer on an immigration car with horses, household goods and machinery. He
filed on a homestead in Section 10 of Wise Township and finalized his three year
proof November 19, 1912, at McClusky. His witnesses were Matt Schmitt, Melvin
McComb, Ramsey R. McComb and Krogh Ovre of Mercer.

Walter married Tessa Iniz Cantwell. She was born March 4, 1878, in Illinois to
Edward and Tassie (Fordan) Cantwall from Ireland.

        Photo: Walter Sprout

Tessa and Walter Sprout had one child, Floyd, born December 20, 1900. Walter
served as Wise Township Treasurer, School Director and Constable. In 1916, he
purchased Jane Owen's homestead in Section 10.

Tessa taught country school in Wise Township for many years. She died July 8,
1932, at the age of 54 and is buried in the Mercer Cemetery. Walter died in
September of 1938 and is also buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

Arnold (Joel) & Rhonda (Novotny) Stradinger

Christian & Elizabeth (Stein) Stradinger

Christian Stradinger was born to Karl and Katherine Stradinger on Jan. 31, 1879,
in Freudenthal Cherson (Odessa), South Russia now the Ukraine. He came to
America in 1902 and settled near Anamoose, N.D. He then filed on a homestead in
Medicine Hill Township in Maxwell, N.D. He died on Feb. 1, 1944, in Bismarck and
is buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

Elizabeth Stein was born to Christian and Margaretha Schmidt Stein on Jan. 21,
1883, in Bergdorf, Cherson (Odessa). In 1905 her brother-in-law John Stein, who
had come to America a few years earlier, sent for his mother and three sisters
to come here. The sisters were Elizabeth, Caroline and Margaret.

Elizabeth and her mother each filed on homesteads in Medicine Hill Township,
Maxwell, N.D. Besides living on your claim, another requirement was to dig a
well. Elizabeth's was dug in a low place and so wasn't hard to get to water.
While living on her claim, she and her sister Margaret helped during threshing
by hauling bundles. Her sister, Caroline, married K.B. Presser. Later Margaret
went to seek other work at Anamoose. After the required time was spent on the
claim. Elizabeth also went out to do hired work. This was mostly housework.

        Photo: Elizabeth and Christian Stradinger. (Courtesy of Lila Stradinger)

Living on the prairie wasn't too easy in those days. Their mail was delivered to
the Kinney Store, which was located about four miles south of her place. Another
store in the area was the Shiprud Store to the west and in another township. As
time went on and more settlers came, the Hetzlers had a store on their farm.
This was closer to their homesteads.

Most of their means of transportation was "on foot." Elizabeth told of how she
would keep her feet warm in winter, when she would walk to her brother's or
mother's place. Her "leggings" were gunnysacks wrapped around her feet. Then she
would go to the pump and pump some water which froze instantly. She said she
kept her feet nice and warm.

She also told of a blizzard, which almost covered her shack, and of course a
snow bank piled against the door which opened outward. It was nice and warm
inside, in fact, it got too warm and the stovepipes got red-hot which almost set
the shack on fire. To get the pipes cooled down, she wet paper and placed them
at the opening of the pipes. After getting that under control, she tried getting
the door open which was a slow process. By forcing the door open a few inches at
a time, then digging the snow into the house and getting it melted, she finally
dug herself out.

It so happened that Christ and Elizabeth's homesteads were side by side. There
were many eligible bachelors around. She chose Christ to be her life partner.
They were married on Jan. 15, 1909, at Washburn, making the trip by horse and
sleigh. They were both members of the Lutheran faith, having been baptized and
confirmed while still in the old country.

After they were married, they moved to McClusky where Christ and his brother
Henry started a lumberyard. They lived there only a short time and then moved to
Mercer and started the Stradinger Lumber Yard at that town. In 1914, they moved
to Turtle Lake where he was employed by the Regan and Lyness Elevator Co. He
continued in elevator work until 1930. During this time he also managed
elevators at Manfred, Tuttle and Mercer. Later the Regan and Lyness elevator was
sold to the Riebe Grain Co. He continued in this work for a few more years, then
worked a short time with the Triple A in McLean County before moving to
Bismarck. He worked for the Blue Ribbon Hatchery only four days when he suffered
a heart attack and died on Feb. 1, 1944, at the age of 65. He is buried in the
Mercer Cemetery.

Elizabeth moved back to Mercer and lived there until 1962. She made her home
with her daughter, Edna (Mrs. Jens Glad), until 1973 when she moved to the
Prairieview Nursing Home in Underwood. She was 94 years old when she died on
June 15, 1977. She is buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

Six children were born to this union:

Ella graduated from Mercer High School and was employed at the Mercer Cash Store
and post office. She died Oct. 18, 1929, from injuries in a car accident. She is
buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

Edna graduated from Mercer High School and attended Minot State Teacher's
College. She taught in rural schools. Besides teaching, she helped at the Mercer
Cash Store, Hjelle's Store and the post office. She married Jens Glad and lived
on a farm north of Mercer. She died on July 24, 2002, and is buried in the
Mercer Cemetery. (See separate history).

        Photo: Reinhart Stradinger

Reinhart graduated from the Mercer High School and was employed on farms and
with the CCC. He served in the infantry during World War II in Italy and Africa.
After his discharge, he worked for John Miller trucking business, the Ted
Gessele Standard Oil and the Lindteigen Construction. He was appointed Mercer
Postmaster. He married Lila Calheim and they had one son, Joel. Rienhardt died
on March 9, 2003, and is buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

        Photos: Holdrich, Olga and Harold Stradinger

Holdrich attended Mercer School and was employed as a farm laborer before going
to the CCC. He entered the army and served overseas in England during WWII.
After his discharge, he started working for the Great Northern Railroad in Minot
and continued there until his death on Feb. 12, 1956. He is buried in the Mercer
Cemetery.

Olga graduated from Mercer High School and attended the Valley City State
Teacher's College. She taught school for a few years before going to Endicott,
New York where she was employed by IBM. She joined the WAVES and was stationed
in San Francisco. After her discharge she married Eugene Schwartz of San
Francisco. They had two daughters, Carol and Elizabeth. Olga died on Nov. 30,
2000 and is buried in California.

Harold graduated from Mercer High School and attended Minot Business College. He
served in the Army in the Pacific Theater during WWII. After his discharge, he
attended Bismarck Junior College and completed his business course in
Minneapolis. He lived in San Francisco. He once was married to Helen Edith
Salloum and they had two children, Debra and Jeffry. Harold died on Oct. 24,
1984, in San Mateo, Calif., and is buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

This is updated from an original written by Edna Stradinger Glad for the McLean
County Heritage book.

Dan & Mary (Werre) Strobel

Daniel Strobel and Mary Werre were born Jan. 24, 1902, and April 26, 1902,
respectively. The couple was united in marriage June 12, 1923, at Tappen, N.D.,
and lived with Dan's parents for a short time until they had the opportunity to
move a house onto another farm site on their land and drill a well. A barn of
rock and sod already existed at that site.

The couple who had 12 children, farmed and had dairy cattle. They started their
farming operation with horses and eventually purchased a tractor. During the
1930s when hay was not very plentiful they found it necessary to travel long
distances to put up enough hay to be able to keep their cattle.

        Photo: Dan and Mary Strobel and their children (middle, from left)
        Norma, Frieda, Mavis, Marian, Betty; (back) Elmer, Darwin, Melvin, Jack
        and Milbert. Not pictured: Leona.

The family attended Zion Lutheran, a country church not too far from where they
lived, where Dan served on the church board and Mary was active with the Ladies'
Aid. Dan also served on the school and election boards.

Dan and Mary sold their farm operation in 1957 and moved to Bismarck, where they
both continued to work for a number of years, Dan as a custodian for the
Bismarck school system, and Mary as a housekeeper at Bismarck Hospital. Dan
passed away Aug. 11, 1964, and Mary died Aug. 30, 1968. The couple was buried at
Sunset Memorial Gardens in Bismarck. The history of each of their children
follows:

Leona V. Strobel was born to Daniel and Mary (Werre) Strobel on April 27, 1924,
near Mercer. Joseph Ramsey was born to Alonzo and Susie Ramsey on Feb. 27, 1914,
near Pettibone. Leona and Joseph were married June 12, 1947, in Bismarck and
farmed near Pettibone until moving in 1958 to Walla Walla, Wash., where they
worked and raised their family. Joseph retired from Pacific Northwest Bell
Telephone and Leona from a Whitman College fraternity where she was employed as
the kitchen manager. Joseph and Leona moved to East Wenatchee, Wash., in 1992.
Leona died on Jan. 12, 1996, and Joseph on Feb. 3, 1998. They were laid to rest
in Evergreen Memorial Park in East Wenatchee. They had three daughters:

Carol M. Ramsey was born May 27, 1948, in Bismarck. She is married to James
Quigley and they reside in Lacey, Wash. Carol has two sons: Richard, age 34 of
Redmond, Wash. and Daniel, age 31 of Taylor, S.C. Bonnie L. Ramsey was born
April 10, 1959, in Walla Walla. She is married to Joseph Crone and they live in
East Wenatchee with their three sons: Kristopher, age eight, and Jacob and
Matthew, age six.

Frieda Strobel married Robert Addison Hammack on April 3, 1948, in Bismarck. Bob
worked for Pringle's Power-Vac in Walla Walla, Wash. They moved to Columbus,
Ohio, to open a new branch business for Pringles and later relocated to
Lewiston, Idaho, where they started their own furnace cleaning business, B & F
Power-Vac. Frieda and Bob enjoyed camping and traveling to visit family and
friends. Bob died Oct. 7, 1994. Frieda still resides in Lewiston and remains
active in the American Legion Auxiliary and Good Shepherd Lutheran Church. Bob
and Frieda had two sons: Orla Daniel (1949) and Robert Howard (1951) and one
daughter, Mary Fern (1956). Orla was killed in action in the Vietnam War on June
7, 1970.

Robert Howard Hammack has worked in all aspects of heating and air conditioning
for 30 years. He married Debbie Willett in 2001 and they reside in Lewiston,
Idaho. Debbie teachers in Clarkston, Wash. Robert Howard has three sons: Keith
Daniel (1970), Kevin Addison (1974), Kenneth Darrel (1978) and one daughter,
Shari Lynn (1980). Keith and Dorothy have one daughter, Alysha Denise (1991).
Keith is in the Air Force and they are stationed in Germany. Shari and Mike have
two sons: Chad Mike (1999) and Terry Robert (2000) and they live in Lewiston,
Idaho. Ken also lives in Lewiston and Kevin and Debby reside in Columbia City,
Ore.

Mary Hammack married David Browne in 1977. They reside in Asotin, Wash., where
David is owner/operator of the family farm and ranch. Mary works as a financial
technician in Lewiston, Idaho. They have one son, Dustin Wayne (1980) and one
daughter, Megan Renee (1982). Dustin married Cami Hammrich in 2002. Dustin farms
for Browne Ranch, Cami teaches Ag. Ed. in Clarkston, Wash. and Megan works for
the county conservation district and attends Washington State University.

Elmer Strobel was born on the Dan Strobel farm south of Mercer on Sept. 27,
1926, to Dan and Mary (Werre) Strobel. He attended Park District school and was
confirmed at Zion Lutheran Church, south of Mercer.

Elmer was inducted into the U.S. Army on Oct. 25, 1945. Following basic training
at Aberdeen Proving Grounds in Maryland, he spent some time in Camp Stoneman,
Calif. before shipping out to Hawaii. He served as camp cook at Scofield
Barracks, Oahu, and later as acting mess sergeant. He was discharged from the
U.S. Army in December of 1946.

Elmer returned home to farm with his father until 1950 when he rented the Emil
Fischer farm south of Mercer until 1957. When his parents retired and moved to
Bismarck, Elmer purchased the family farm. He farmed and had dairy cattle until
1972 when the Bureau of Reclamation purchased some of his land, including the
farm site and buildings for the McClusky Canal. That land is now a part of West
Park Lake. Elmer sold his cattle and purchased a new home in Turtle Lake and
continued to farm from town until he retired in 1986. He had built a new home in
Turtle Lake in 1976. In 1988 he married Irene (Anderson) Jones and they continue
to reside in Turtle Lake.

Melvin Strobel was born May 12, 1929, to Daniel and Mary Strobel, south of
Mercer in Park District, Section 12-145-79. He attended country school through
eighth grade. He bought his first 160 acres of land in 1952, purchased a farm of
480 acres in 1956 and added another 160 acres to his operation in 1966. In 1972,
the Bureau of Reclamation acquired 240 acres of his land so he replaced 160
acres from an estate sale.

In 1984, Melvin married Irma Skagen at Turtle Lake. He sold his livestock and
farmed from town until 1990 when he retired for health reasons. Melvin and Irma
enjoyed traveling (including a trip to Irma's native country, Germany and
entertaining family and friends at their cabin at Brush Lake. Irma died on May
17, 2001. Melvin, who continues to live in Turtle Lake, has two stepsons,
Theodore Anderson of Billings, Mont. and Gary Anderson of Kealakekua, Hawaii,
and six step-grandchildren.

Betty Strobel married Donald Rohweder and the couple moved to Pine City, Minn.,
where they raised three daughters. Betty worked at General Fab for many years
where she soldered circuit boards for large corporations which had contracts
with General Fab. Donald worked with a trucking firm out of Pine City. Donald
died on July 5, 1980, and Betty on Aug. 31, 1982.

Betty and Donald's oldest daughter, Pamela (Hoff) Cummings, is a home health
aide and Emergency Medical Technician (EMT) in Pine City and has three children.
Dawn is a surgical technician and EMT in Pine City, Heather is employed in the
field of occupational speech/language pathology in Minneapolis, Minn., and
Gareth works in retail sales in Pine City. LaVonne Rohweder, Betty and Donald's
second daughter, died in a car accident in 1973 at the age of 15. Their youngest
daughter, Candice (Candy), has been married to Dennis Reiser for 20 years and
the couple has two college age children: Lindsey, 19 and Jessa, 18. Dennis is a
plumber and Candy is a hairdresser and each operates a business in Pine City.

Marian Strobel married Albert Uhlich at St. Paul Lutheran Church in Garrison,
N.D., on June 18, 1950. They were active members at St. Paul until 1999 and
their children were baptized and confirmed there also. Albert and Marian lived
on the Uhlich family farm until the time of his death. The couple has two
children: Angela and Gaylen. Angela lives in Bismarck where she is coordinator
of clinical laboratory science programs at Bismarck State College and Medcenter
One Health Systems. Gaylen is married to former Julie Sinclair and the couple
lives in Willow Grove, Penn. Gaylen is a veterinary research scientist and Julie
is a veterinarian and attends graduate school.

The Uhlich family enjoyed the outdoors and animals. Albert and his children
loved riding horses and participating in wagon trains and rodeo parades. The
family also enjoyed traveling as much as time would allow them to be off the
farm. The Strobel family holds a reunion every two years and the Uhlichs have
attended most of them. Albert died in 1999 and was laid to rest at Fairview
Cemetery in Bismarck. Marian retired after his death and now lives in Bismarck
where she is a member of Good Shepherd Lutheran Church and enjoys Bible studies
and the senior activities.

Milbert Strobel graduated from Mercer High School in 1952 and served in the
military for two years. He moved to Walla Walla, Wash. in 1955 and later
graduated from Walla Walla Business College. Milbert married Delma Grosz,
formerly of Hazen, in 1957 and the couple had two children. Their daughter,
Terri Ferrin, has three children, two of whom are twins. Terri's husband, Tim,
works for Boeing Airplane in the financial planning department. The Ferrins live
in Federal Way, Wash. Milbert's and Delma's son Keith, who lives in Seattle, is
single and works for Boeing as an accountant.

Milbert retired from Crowley Maritime in 1993 with 34 years of service in
accounting. Delma retired in 1996 from Safeway Food and Drug, after 33 years of
retail service. They live in Kent, Wash., where they enjoy golfing and bowling,
sharing sports with their children and grandchildren, and watching them play
soccer and baseball.

Roy Strobel was stillborn to Mary and Daniel on Nov. 7, 1934.

Darwin Strobel was in the U.S. Army during the years from 1955 to 1957,
stationed at Ft. Know, Kent. and in Kirchgons, Germany. He was in the N.D.
National Guard for two years and the California Air Force Reserve for another
two years. Darwin married Janice Fried at Bismarck and the couple eventually
moved to California, where they raised their three children and Darwin worked
with the U.S. Air Force at Sacramento in accounting. He is now retired and has a
hobby ranch at Orangevale. Janice is a hairdresser. Darwin and Janice are
members of the Lutheran Church of the Ascension, where both sing in the mixed
choir and Darwin sings in the men's choir. He is also a member of the VFW.

Darwin and Janice's daughter, Janell, is married to Barry Koeppel. They live in
Clermont, Fla., and have two children. Janell works as office manager of a
construction company and Barry is a construction foreman. Darwin and Janice's
oldest son, Randall, lives in St. Peters, Mo., and works as a service man for
magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) instruments. He has one son. The third child of
Darwin and Janice, Daniel, lives in Dayton, Ohio, where he is employed as an
installer of MRI instruments.

Whereas all of Darwin and Jan's children live out of state, their three
grandchildren and four great-grandchildren all live within minutes of their
home. They all see each other regularly and Darwin enjoys babysitting for the
great-grandchildren.

Norma Strobel is married to Earl Ray Bird. They made their home in Canon City,
Colo., for many years and raised three children there. Daughter Michelle is a
registered nurse and she and her husband, Paul Wheeler, a physician's assistant,
live in Ekalaka, Mont. Michelle has three children from a former marriage: Amy,

In 1987 Norma and Earl moved back to Bismarck. Earl is employed with Monarch
Products and Norma with HJL Management. The couple plans to retire in 2003.

Mavis Strobel graduated from Bismarck High School in 1960. She was a
cosmetologist for 20 years, owning her own beauty shop in Colorado. Mavis
married Bill Wagner in 1971 and the couple moved to California in 1982. Mavis
later graduated from American College with a degree in Food Service Management
and she is currently employed as a dietary service manager. Bill is employed as

Jack Strobel graduated from Bismarck High School in 1962. He then became a
registered nurse and served in the Air Force. Jack has been a nurse anesthetist
since 1970 and works in Sacramento, Calif. In 1975, he married Gayle Reading
from Maxwell, Calif. They live in Rocklin, Calif., and have two children, Erika
and Trent., both of whom are college students. Jack enjoys camping, hiking in
the mountains, visiting the ocean and attending car shows.

Johannes Sr. & Louise (Reuer) Strobel

Johannes Strobel Sr. was born Jan. 27, 1869, at Neu Glueckstal, South Russia,
where he grew up and in 1893 married Louise Reuer. Louise was born at New
Freudental, South Russia, on Aug. 21, 1869. Johannes and Louise lived in South
Russia for six years and during that time, one daughter Christine, was born to
them.

In 1899, the couple came to the United States and homesteaded land near Bowdle,
S.D., where they would remain for 20 years. Four children were born to the
Strobels while they lived in South Dakota. They were Daniel, John, Betty and
Rose.

        Photo: Johannes and Louise Strobel and their children: (back, from left)
        Christine, Daniel, Betty, John and Rosina.

In 1919 the couple sold their land in South Dakota and purchased land in McLean
County in North Dakota, south of the town of Mercer. They loaded their
livestock, machinery and household goods on the train and shipped them to
Wilton, N.D. From there they drove their livestock by horseback to their new
home near Mercer. The machinery and household goods were loaded in wagons for
the journey to the new farm site. Johannes and Louise farmed there with their
children until they retired and moved into Mercer. They couple observed their
Golden Wedding Anniversary in 1943.

Johannes died March 16, 1947. Louise died May 25, 1948.

Second Generation

Christine (Strobel) Neumiller was born on Nov. 14, 1899. She married Gust
Neumiller at Mercer and the couple had four children: Richard (deceased), Ellan
(Schon), Lenhart (deceased), and Violet (Just). Christine died on Oct. 22, 1965.

John Strobel was born Feb. 9, 1904. He farmed the family farm until 1944 when he
moved to another farm south of Mercer. He died Sept. 29, 1948.

Betty (Strobel) Bielou was born May 15, 1907, and married John Bielou at
Startup, Wash. After her husband passed away, she returned to the Mercer area.
Several years later she moved to Bismarck into the Cresent Manor. Betty passed
away Feb. 9, 1988. John and Betty had two daughters.

        Photo: Betty Bielou and her daughters Lucille (left) and Sally.

Mrs. Lyle Cordon (Lucille) live in Bismarck and they are retired. The couple has
two children: Ken and Camie Cordon both live in Bismarck.

A second daughter Mrs. Bill (Sally) Morefield lives in Sunnyvale, Calif. Bill is
a private painter and Sally works at Stanford University as a research
associate. They have two children: Angie and Tony.

Rosina (Strobel) Rust was born Aug. 10, 1908. On July 25, 1933, she married
Jacob Rust. They farmed north of Mercer for several years and then moved to
Mercer. Both spent several years in the Prairieview Nursing Home. The couple had
two children: Mrs. Donald Hausauer (Vernia) and Rodney and his wife Lois Rust.
They have four grandchildren. Rosina passed away Jan. 29, 1994. Jacob passed
away Feb. 11, 1998.

Alma Stute

Alma was born Nov. 15, 1899, in LaMoure, N.D., to Johann (Henry) and Johanna
Stute. In 1906 she moved with her parents to a farm northwest of Mercer.

She died of influenza on Oct. 28, 1909, and was buried in Peace Lutheran
Cemetery (Friedens Gemeinde) northwest of Blue Lake.

Anna Stute

Anna Augusta Cornelia Stute was born to Henry and Johanna Hoffman Stute on Sept.
18, 1898, in LaMoure, N.D. In 1906 the family moved to Mercer by train and
settled on a farm on the south side of Blue Lake. She attended country school
south of the alkali lakes at what was called the Levi School.

To earn money, Anna raised and sold turkeys every fall. She continued to live on
the home place and cared for her aunt, Mary Hoffman. In 1967 she moved to Mercer
sharing home with her brother Walter.

She was a longtime member of the Mercer Church of God. A list of charities and
organizations that she contributed to financially would be a long one.
Supporting these groups was something she had done all her adult life. She
couldn't imagine not helping others who needed her aid.

Anna passed away at the Underwood nursing home on July 16, 1996, and is buried
in the Mercer Hillside Cemetery.

Carl Stute

Carl Stute was born Dec. 12, 1904, in LaMoure, N.D., to Johann and Johanna
Stute. They moved to Mercer by train in 1906 and settled on a farm just south of
Blue Lake. He attended the Levi school south of the alkali lakes, until the
winter weather got too rough.

To find employment, he traveled to Iowa and Illinois to pick corn. Carl worked
in the logging camps of Minnesota for a while and got caught making moonshine.
Legend has it that there are still jugs of buried moonshine somewhere in those
forests. Back in North Dakota again, he worked on threshing crews and worked for
construction companies improving roads in the area.

Carl purchased his parent's farm and lived there until his death on Oct. 12,
1970.

He loved playing his guitar and singing old songs. Children could always find
some candy hidden somewhere in his car when he came to visit.

Gustave & Charlotte (Butz) Stute

Gustave Ewald Stute was born Nov. 17, 1906, at rural Mercer to Johann Henry and
Johanna (Hoffman) Stute.

Gust was the first Stute child born after the family moved to Mercer. He grew up
on his parent's homestead six miles northwest of Mercer near Blue Lake, where he
attended rural school. As a young man he worked as a farm laborer for area
farmers. He served in the US Army during World War II from December of 1942 to
June of 1945. He served in North Africa and in Italy with Hq Co 1st Bn 362nd inf
91 div., the Powder River division. He was proud that he had qualified as a
sharpshooter in the service.

After his discharge he returned to North Dakota and purchased a farm five miles
northwest of Mercer. He served on the Wise Township board for several years.

He married Charlotte Butz on Dec. 30, 1948 in Bismarck. Charlotte Lucille Butz
was born Feb. 8, 1932, near Falkirk, N.D. to her parents, Andrew and Dixie
(Friend) Butz. Her grandparents were John and Katharina Lillie (Schmidt) Butz of
Underwood and Dennis L. and Lizzie Jane Friend of Mountain Home, Ark.

        Photo: Gustave and Charlotte Stute, 1947.

The Friend family can be traced back to the New Sweden colony in Delaware, where
Nils France (Friend) was a warden for Gov. Rising in 1645. Nils arrived from
Gothenburg, Sweden, on the ship Swan in 1648. Both the Butz and Schmidt families
seem to have come from Odessa, Russia by way of Nebraska, and settled in the
Underwood area arriving there by wagon train.

Growing up in The Depression taught her how to be self-reliant, tough and now to
make do. From an early age she and her brothers: Charles, Dennis, Joe, Dempsey
and Virgil learned the values of hard work. Her family moved back to Arkansas
for a couple years to be with her Grandmother Friend who was ill and passed away
in 1936.

After coming back to North Dakota, the family lived in various locations in the
Underwood to Mercer area while working for local farmers. One farm was the Henry
Stute farm south of Blue Lake. There she met Gust Stute and married on Dec. 31,
1948 in Bismarck. They started a farm on the north side of Brush Lake, raising
cattle and small grain. Charlotte moved to Reno, Nev., after separating from
Gust, but returns to Bismarck every few years to visit friends and attend events
with her children's families.

Gustave and Charlotte had three children: Evelyn Jan (Janie), born July 14,
1949, Gust Jr., born Oct. 17, 1950 and Larry, born Dec. 27, 1951.

        Photo: (Back, from left) Charlotte Smith, Melissa; (middle) Janie,
        Donovan; (front) Jeanine Miller

Janie graduated from Wahpeton and Mary College as a registered nurse working for
the Bismarck and Burleigh County Public Health as a school nurse and is also a
legal nurse consultant. She has two children, Donovan, born April 10, 1981, and
Melissa born March 21, 1991. Donovan is an insurance agent and has a daughter,
Jeanine Emilie Miller, born June 5, 2003.

        Photo: Larry, Margie, Aasta, and Taylor Stute.

Gust Jr. married Barbara Tweeten Feb. 14, 1986. She is the daughter of Clinton
and Sharyll (Zingg) Tweeten. Gust and Barbara have three sons: Cayce, born in
1986; Shaun, born in 1999; and Zachary, born February, 2004. Gust is employed at
Polar Ware in McClusky as a press operator. (See separate history.)

Larry married Margie Kleppe in August of 1984. Margie is the daughter of Russell
and Jean (McAllister) Kleppe. They have two daughters: Aasta Marie, born May 1,
1988, is a high school senior and Taylor Jean, born April 28, 1994, is a sixth
grader. Larry is a shift supervisor at the MDU Heskitt Power Plant north of
Mandan. Margie helps create phone books at Design Wizards in Bismarck.

Gust started developing rental lots on both Blue Lake and Brush Lake in the late
1950s. Over the years, lot numbers increased until today almost all of Brush
Lake is encircled by them. He farmed until 1993 when he retired. Gust died on
April 23, 1996, at the Redwood Village in Wilton and is buried in Mercer
Hillside Cemetery beside his parents.

Gust Jr. & Barbara (Tweeten) Stute

Gust Stute Jr. was born in 1950 in Bismarck, N.D. His father was Gustave Stute
Sr. and his mother is Charlotte Butz, daughter of Andrew and Dixie (Friend)
Butz. He graduated from Mercer High School in 1968 and from UND in 1972 with a
Bachelor's Degree in mathematics.

After farming with his father, Gust Sr., he worked at the Falkirk Mine, then
Sykes Enterprises as a software support technician and now operates presses at
Polar Ware's factory in McClusky, N.D.

        Photo: (Clockwise) Barbara, Gust, Cayce, Shaun and Zachary Stute.

On Feb. 14, 1986, he married Barbara Tweeten, daughter of Clinton and Sharyll
(Zingg) Tweeten. Barbara was born in 1960 in Turtle Lake and raised on a farm
southwest of Turtle Lake. She graduated from Turtle Lake-Mercer High School in
1979. After graduation, Barb worked as a security guard at Falkirk Mine and the
Coal Creek power plant, at Ken's Jack & Jill in Turtle Lake and later in the
bakery at Emineth's SuperValu in Washburn.

Barb and Gust have three sons: Cayce, born in 1986 and Shaun in 1999. Cayce is a
senior at Turtle Lake-Mercer High School and Shaun will be a first grader.
Zachary was born Feb. 11, 2004. They are now the only Stute family living in the
Mercer area.

Johann "Henry" & Johanna (Hoffman) Stute

Henry Stute was born Sept. 5, 1850, in Kleefeld, Hannover, Germany to Heinrich
and Anna Elizabeth Stute. The family farm was located in Wibbese, near Hamburg,
in northern Germany.

He served in the German Army Medical Corp prior to 1880, and vowed no sons of
his would fight in any wars for the Kaiser. His brother, Christoph, had taken
over the family farm in Wibbese, so he thought he could get a better job as a
bookkeeper in America, so he sailed on the German liner Kaiser Wilhelm II and
arrived in New York on June 27, 1891. Then he traveled to Ironwood, Mich., to
find work in the iron mines as a bookkeeper.

Finding he couldn't get a bookkeeping job with any mine because he spoke so
little English, he accepted a friend's invitation to go to LaMoure. There he met
and married Johanna Maria Hoffman in 1895.

Johanna Stute was the daughter of George Hoffman and Anna Marie Schmitz. She was
born in the small iron-mining town of Gosenbach, Germany, on Jan. 21, 1872. She
arrived in America in May of 1886 with her parents and her sisters, Lina, Bertha
and Mary. They made their way to Ironwood, Mich. where they had relatives
living. When her father had no luck getting a job in the iron mines, they moved
to LaMoure, N.D.

They farmed for several years in the LaMoure area. Then in 1906, the family
which now included William, Anna, Alma and Carl, packed up all their
possessions, machinery and livestock and traveled by railroad boxcar to Mercer.
They unloaded the livestock and machinery on a ramp just east of the grain
elevator.

        Photo: The Henry Stute family in 1920: (front, from left) Henry, Walter,
        Johanna; (back) William, Carl, Anna, John, and Gustave.

All the homestead land was gone in this area, but he was able to buy land south
of Blue Lake and start a farm. There Gustave, John and Walter were later born.
The land was poor cropland near the alkali lakes, but they were able to survive
even the lean years, sometimes by stretching the cattle feed supply by using
flax straw and thistles. Bad winters meant traveling cross-country to Mercer by
bobsled to get the monthly groceries and pick up the mail.

Johanna was an active member of the Congregational Church of Turtle Lake and
financially supported many charities and church missions, especially the
Crippled Children Society.

When she passed away on Sept. 26, 1941, she left one daughter, Anna, and five
sons, William, Carl, Gustave, John and Walter.

Henry died Nov. 4, 1929, and is buried in the Mercer Hillside Cemetery. He never
found that bookkeeping job or learned English well, but he did put down roots
for his family that still tie them to the Mercer area.

John & Clara (Boschee) Stute

John Henry Stute was born Jan. 21, 1910, in Mercer. He attended country school
with his brothers and sister. He later taught at country schools in Sheridan
County.

One of his pupils was his future wife, Clara Boschee. They were married June 3,
1931, and settled on a farm northeast of Mercer.

John and Clara had three children: Ella born March 26, 1932, Phoebe born July
30, 1938, and Ervin born Feb. 19, 1940. They farmed until the early 1960s then
moved to Bismarck. John became a Watkins dealer and sold Watkins products for
many years until moving to Minot.

Clara passed away on Aug. 25, 1990, in Minot. John was a resident of the Trinity
Nursing Center in Minot until his death on June 16, 1991. Both are buried at the
Sunset Memorial Gardens north of Minot. Before his death, John gathered family
histories for both the Stute and Boschee families and shared them with his and
Clara's siblings.

        Photo: John and Clara Stute family: (front, from left) Phoebe, Ervin and
        Ella.

Their daughter Ella married Gerald Moore on Aug. 9, 1954. Their children and
birth dates are: Marilyn, Feb. 3, 1969; Karen, March 12, 1971; Daryl, March 1,
1957; Michael, Sept. 21, 1960; and Donald, Aug. 26, 1964. Marilyn is married to
Bobby Lee Amos, they have one child, Mikayla Jane. Karen married James Eisner,
they have a daughter, Emily Rose. Daryl is married to Jill Annette Carlton. Ella
and Gerald reside in Rapid City, S.D. where he is a retired electrical
contractor and city inspector.

Phoebe married LeRoy Haugeberg on June 5, 1960. They live in Minot. Their
children are:

Kristi, born Dec. 6, 1966, and Kathy, born Aug. 2, 1969. Kristi is married to
Wade Christianson and has two children: Casey, born March 25, 1992, and

Kathy married Terry Hovde on Oct. 19, 1991. They have two boys: Calvin, born
Aug. 16, 1995, and Russel, born Dec. 20, 1998. Both the Christiansons and Hovdes
farm in the Minot area. LeRoy is retired from John Deere where he worked as a
parts man. Phoebe works in the office at K-Mart in Minot.

Ervin married Diane Esterby and they have three children: Rebecca, born October
12, 1966, Mitchell, June 9, 1961, and Todd, July 26, 1964. Rebecca is married to
Henry Putnam and has three children: Nicole, Jonathon and Matthew. Todd married
Kelly Jean Botko, they have one child, Sarah Rose. All of Ervin and Diane's
family live in the Minneapolis area.

Walter Edmund Stute

Walter was the youngest child of Johann and Johanna Stute. He was born Feb. 1,
1913, at Mercer. He grew up on the family farm northwest of Mercer and attended
country school with his brothers and sister.

He worked for area farmers for many years and also did general repair work. He
was an avid bird hunter and fisherman for many years.

Walter moved from the family farm in 1968 and lived with his sister Anna in
Mercer. Walter passed away on Jan. 4, 1998, at Turtle Lake. He is buried in the
Mercer Hillside Cemetery.

William & Amelia (Rennich) Stute

William Henry (Bill) Stute was born Aug. 28, 1897, in Oakes, N.D. In 1906, his
parents, Henry and Johanna (Hoffman) Stute moved their family to a farm just
south of Blue Lake. On Oct. 27, 1926, Bill married Amelia (Mollie) Rennich.
Mollie's parents were Karl and Christine (Engel) Rennich. Bill and Mollie farmed
northwest of Blue Lake until 1946, then bought a café in McHenry, N.D., that
they operated for many years.

        Photo: William and Amelia Stute, Oct. 3. 1926.

After Mollie's death in 1969, Bill continued to live in McHenry until his own
passing on March 5, 1974. Although his obituary only lists farmer and café owner
as his occupations, he had also been a grain thresher operator and also dug
wells by hand for farmers in the area.

They had one daughter, Lenora Adella Stute, born on July 21, 1927, at Mercer.
She was reared and educated in Mercer. She received her teaching certificate and
at the age of 17, began teaching in rural school including Wilton, Washburn,
Underwood and McHenry.

She married Reuben W. Syverson on Aug. 4, 1946, at Our Savior's Lutheran Church
at Mercer. They established their home on a farm in Colvin Township, rural
McHenry, where they farmed for 16 years. They lived in several places while
Reuben worked for area farmers including New Rockford, where Lenora worked in
the bakery. They eventually moved to Warwick where they made their home through
the years and Lenora was a piano teacher. In 1989 they moved to Devils Lake.
Reuben died on Dec. 19, 1991.

In 1999 Lenora moved to Fargo where she died on Sept. 21, 2003. Lenora was a
member of the Warwick Lutheran Church where she served as the church organist
for a number of years. She served as president of the Senior Citizens of
Warwick. She also wrote the Warwick News for the Benson County Press and the New
Rockford Transcript.

Lenora and Reuben had seven children: their names and dates of birth are Dwight
(Ike), Nov. 8, 1950; Lyndon, March 9, 1954; Kevin, Oct. 24, 1957; LaVon, Sept.
17, 1956; Cindy, Nov. 30, 1960; Lynette (died at birth), March 9, 19545 and
Diane, Nov. 14, 1967.

Dwight married Deanna Lunack Adams on May 17, 1974. They have two daughters:
Wendee born Sept. 25, 1971, and Aleesha born Jan. 2, 1979. They live in Minot
where he drives semi from Minot to Grand Forks for a bakery.

Lyndon is married to Peggy Abrahmson; they have two children: Christoffer born
Nov. 15, 1974, and Brittaney born Aug. 10, 1979. They live in Fargo.

Kevin is married to Jean Tuckner and also lives in Fargo where he is supervisor
for the BNSF Railway. He has two boys: Cory born July 18, 1986, and Brady born
June 28, 1994.

LaVon married Gerald L. Olson in Warwick on Aug. 13, 1977. They live in Gary,
Minn., where they work for the school system. They have two sons: Kyle, born
Sept. 28, 1979 and Tyler, born Jan. 21, 1983.

Cindy is married to Verne Lee on March 31, 1984. Their children are April Dean,
born Oct. 4, 1984; and Carrie, born Nov. 14, 1987.

Diane is single and lives in Fargo.

Orville & Mary (Braun) Sundby

Mary is the daughter of John and Johanna Braun. She was born Nov. 13, 1923. She
attended grade school in Mercer and graduated from high school there in 1942.
After graduation she worked in Chicago doing bookkeeping for a firm there. A
year later she returned to Turtle Lake where her parents, then retired, lived.
She took a clerking job at the SuperValu Store, which was owned by Vilas and
Annetta Just and was located in the building, which is now Bev's Café.

After working there for several years, she went to Stockton, Calif., where she
clerked in a department store for about six months, but got homesick and came
back to good old North Dakota. She began working in the catalog department of
Montgomery Ward in Bismarck and then later for the Morrey Alan Co. until the
time of her marriage to Orville Sundby. They were the first couple to be married
in the new Peace Lutheran Church in Turtle Lake, which is now the Goetz Funeral
Home. They were married on Nov. 25, 1948, Thanksgiving Day.

        Photo: Orville and Mary Sundby and their children Douglas, David, Mary
        Beth and Dwight.

After their marriage, they purchased a small home in Turtle Lake and Orville
went to work at the Garrison Dam. In 1950, he began working for the McLean
County Highway Dept. Mary also worked for them for about two months, cooking
meals for the men. Then in 1951, Orville started working for the Farmers Union
Co. and Mary went to work at the Red Owl Store which was owned by Arnold Franke
and located where the Laundromat is now.

On Feb. 27, 1951, their first son Douglas was born. He is married to Mary Martha
Dies. They have two sons, Jonathan and James. Douglas is a CPA and works for
Samsonite. They live in Littleton, Colo.

On June 4, 1952, their second son David was born. He lives in Ft. Collins, Colo.
where he has a bicycle shop.

The Sundby's third son, Dwight, was born Oct. 1, 1953. He is a contractor and
builds homes that are accessible for the disabled.

Their daughter, Mary Beth, was born Aug. 14, 1958. In 1987, she was diagnosed
with M.S. She worked for the Bank of North Dakota until 1995 when she retired.

In March of 1973, Orville accepted the position as manager of the Farmers Union
Oil Co. which he held until his retirement in 1987.

In 1990, they decided to build a house in Bismarck that would be accessible for
Mary Beth. Dwight started building that spring and they moved into it in the
fall.

Orville had a heart attack and stroke in March of 2002. He is feeling good but
needs a walker to get around.

Mary suffers with diabetes and arthritis and needs a cane to help her walk.

They are still members of the Trinity Lutheran Church in Turtle Lake. They
don't get to attend services there but are blessed to have Pastor Karen Nelson
visit them quite regularly which they appreciate.

They are thankful for their home which is close to doctors, hospitals and
clinics, but they do miss their family and friends in Turtle Lake.

Simon & Elizabeth (Babnick) Szelop

Simon was born June 15, 1875, in Austria and came to American in 1901. He
homesteaded southwest of Mercer where he farmed and lived until 1920. In that
year he moved to a farm north of Garrison. In 1930, he again moved and this time
to a farm 30 miles west of Garrison where he farmed until his death on Oct. 9,
1953.

He was married to Elizabeth Babnick of Wilton who passed away before Simon. They
had one daughter, Mrs. John Slobojan, and five sons - Andrew, Edmond, Harold,
