Jacob & Rosina (Wolf) Weisz (Wise)

Jacob Weisz (Wise) was born Oct. 12, 1874, and Rosina (Wolf) Weisz (Wise) was
born Nov. 4, 1876. They were among the young Germans from Russia who came to the
United States from southern Russia to make better lives for themselves.

Jacob Weisz (Wise) came to the Eureka area. He worked there for seven years to
pay his passage. In 1902, he homesteaded on a farm northwest of McClusky. He
married Rosina Wolf in 1903. They moved to the farm one and one-half miles south
of Mercer in 1909. Their children went to school in Mercer, N.D. A teacher asked
what their last name was and understood Weisz as Wise, which they learned to
spell and have used their entire lives. They had five children:

Fredrick (Fred) born Jan. 20, 1904, and died March 25, 1979. (see separate
history.)

Kathryn (Kate) born Nov. 29, 1905, and died Dec. 23, 1929.

Johann (John) born June 14, 1907, and died April 21, 1977. (See separate
history.)

Ruben born Dec. 9, 1912, and died Aug. 29, 1984. (See separate history.)

Edna died shortly after birth.

For several years in the early 1930s, Jacob and Rosina lived in a small house
they owned on the northwest corner of Mercer. They moved back to the farm during
the depression. The four room house was home to Jacob and Rosina, Ruben, John,
Magdalena and their four children and granddaughters, Viola and Alice Boschee.

The Weisz (Wise) farm was one and one-half miles south of Mercer on Highway 41.
It was a busy place with chores that always needed attention. Prices were low
and money was scarce. Nearly everything needed was raised. Coffee, tea, sugar
and hand soap was bought at the store. Lye soap for washing clothes was made.
People from Mercer hauled water from the well at the farm. Often several
vehicles were lined up. Everyone brought cream cans and other containers to
fill.

        Photo: The Jacob Weisz family: (front, from left) Jacob Weisz, his wife
        Rosina holding Ruben (age 2), Jacob's mother; (back) Fred (age 10, John
        (age 7), Kate (age 9). Taken in 1914.

        Photo: Rosina Weisz, picture taken in 1945.

Jacob was always concerned about the welfare of his livestock, Carlos, the
Border collie dog, was always at his side and shared bits of food from the
table. The first chore in the morning was to lead the horses to water. It was
also the last task at night. The horses got the choicest hay and oats. They were
brushed and curried. On rainy days, Jacob was repairing and oiling harnesses.
When the mosquitoes and flies were bad, he would light a smudge for the cattle.
The smoke seemed to keep the bugs away. The barn was kept clean. Straw was put
down for the bedding. Hay was lifted into the haymow with slings and ropes.

Jacob and Rosina always raised a garden. The cabbage was shredded and packed
into 20-30 gallon crocks. Cucumbers and small watermelons were pickled. They
raised delicious muskmelons and watermelons. In late fall when the weather
turned cold, it was butchering time. The hogs were scalded and scraped. Some of
the meat was ground to make sausage, liver sausage and head cheese. Jacob had a
knack for seasoning the sausage and smoking it just right. Lard was rendered and
used as shortening for cooking and baking. Rosina made noodles. The egg dough
was rolled thin and dried on pillows covered with white dish towels. When nearly
dry, the dough sheets were rolled and sliced and shook apart to finish drying.
They missed the grape vineyards that they had in Russia. There was always a
small wooden basket of grapes when in season.

There was deep sadness in April of 1920. Rosina's brother, Jacob Wolf, and all
of his family, except a baby girl, were murdered on the Wolf farm north of
Turtle Lake.

Kathryn (Kate) had married John Boschee and they lived in Garrison. They had two
daughters, Viola, born April 2, 1925, and Alice, born March 2, 1928. They had
two infant sons that were stillborn or died shortly after birth. Kathryn died
with childbirth at the age of 24. Early spring would find Jacob (Kathryn's
father) working up a small piece of ground which he called Kate's garden. Kate
planted irises and asters and in the corner was "old man shrub and mint called
sweet Mary." Kathryn and John Boschee and infant sons are buried in the Mercer
Cemetery.

Viola and Alice went to live with their grandparents, Jacob and Rosina, in 1932.
They both went to grade school in Mercer. John Boschee was a patient at San
Haven for many years and was unable to care for the girls. Viola graduated from
Mercer High School in 1943. She was a teacher and married James Vranna. They
have three sons: Gregory and wife Margo; Lee and wife Julie have four children,
Sydney, Luke, Camille and Maxwell and son James. Alice graduated from Mandan
High School in 1946 and married Ted Mayer. They have two daughters, Joyce and
Gladys. Ted is deceased. Alice is married to Darrel Carr and they live in
Alabama and California.

Jacob died on Nov. 27, 1941 and Rosina married Fred Grabau in 1948 and moved to
Bismarck, N.D. Rosina died in July of 1956. Jacob and Rosina Weisz (Wise) are
buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

Anders Victor & Albena (Boschee) Westerlind

Anders Victor Westerlind was known as Victor Westerlind. In Sweden they use
their middle name as the first name.

Victor Westerlind was born Sept. 15, 1880, at Goteborg, Sweden. Anders Victor
Westerlind was the son of Johan and Josephine Westerlind.

Victor came to the United States in the year of 1897, settling in Minnesota.

Victor became a United States Citizen on Sept. 30, 1926. Victor came to McLean
County in the year of 1904. He was a grain and cattle farmer. He homesteaded six
miles north of Mercer. He passed away on Sept. 6, 1958, at 77 years of age.

Victor Westerlind married Albena Boschee, the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Mathais
Boschee on Dec. 31, 1924. She was born on Nov. 22, 1907, at Kassel, Russia.

Albena (Boschee) Westerlind came to the United States in the year of 1909
settling in Grand Forks, N.D. She moved to McClusky on May 24, 1909. She then
moved to Mercer in the year of 1914. Albena became a United States Citizen on
March 21, 1917. Albena moved to Bismarck after Victor passed away in 1958.
Albena Westerlind passed away on Dec. 9, 1998, at 91 years of age.

Victor and Albena Westerlind had five daughters and three sons:

Esther Schock of Manteca, Calif.

Linnea Milligan of Manteca, Calif.

Gena Long of Forest Grove, Ore.

Helga Semmel of Bismarck, N.D.

Palmer Westerlind of Grand Marais, Minn.

Franklin Westerlind of Markham, Ill.

They have 23 grandchildren and 21 great grandchildren and one great-great

Arnold & Mary Ann (Miller) Westerlind

Arnold R. Westerlind, son of Robert Westerlind and Caroline (Kravic) Westerlind,
was born Oct. 13, 1921, Mercer.

Mary Ann (Miller) Westerlind, daughter of John Miller Jr. and Katherine (Rust)
Miller was born April 1, 1926. They were married on Jan. 1, 1947.

        Photo: Mary Ann and Arnold Westerlind

After graduating from Mercer High School in 1939, Arnold lived in Seattle,
Wash., until he enlisted in the U.S. Army in 1943. He served in the Pacific
Theater during World War II and was honorably discharged in 1946. Arnold was
appointed to a United States Postal rural mail carrier position, working out of
Mercer in 1950. He continued this position for 31 years, retiring in 1981. His
hobby was restoring antique cars.

Mary Ann graduated from Mercer High School in 1943 and attended Minot State
Teacher's College. She taught in area rural schools until becoming a full-time
housewife and mother.

Arnold and Mary Ann lived in Mercer and spent winters in Arizona after
retirement. Arnold died Dec. 2, 2002 and is buried in the Mercer Hillside
Cemetery.

The couple had one daughter and four sons:

Deborah Ann, born Sept. 6, 1947 and married Terence Sparrow. They live on a farm
west of McClusky. Deborah serves three area schools as a speech and language
pathologist. Terry is self-employed, manages a farm and ranch operation with
their son. Terence and Deborah have three children: Keeya married to Chad Hager,
Kipp married to Megan (Fiechtner) and Katherine (Kassie) married to Brad Bender.
They also have five grandchildren: Hunter and Karsyn Hager, Sophie Sparrow and
Olyvia and Ethan Bender.

Gordon D., was born Nov. 17, 1948 and married Judith Brewster. They live in
Monticelle, Minn. Gordon is vice president of Great River Energy. Judy works as
a school nurse. They have two children: Tera, married to Steve Brooks and Joe.

Frederick L., born Feb. 4, 1951, and married Sandra Gilchrist. They live in

Gustov Robert & Caroline (Kravik) Westerlind

Gustov Robert Westerlind was born in Goteborg, Sweden, on March 22, 1882. Gustov
attended school in Goteborg. At age 15, he started working in the city delivery
business that his father owned.

He came to the United States in 1902 at the age of 20. He worked as a farmhand
for two years at Lake Benton, Minn. He then entered the lumbering trade in
Wisconsin and Minnesota before coming to North Dakota. Here he homesteaded at
Mercer and began farming. He built a new home and other farm buildings in 1915.
Some of those buildings remain to this day. He married Caroline Kravik, daughter
of Ansten and Live Kravik, on Feb. 7, 1916. Caroline was born on Nov. 13, 1896,
at Fairmont, N.D.

        Photo: Gustov Robert and Caroline Westerlind on their 25th wedding
        anniversary.

Robert farmed until his death on May 12, 1956. Caroline lived on the homestead
until she passed away on Dec. 22, 1974. They are both buried in the Mercer
Cemetery.

Robert and Caroline had five children: (See separate histories.)

Theodore Westerlind lived in Edmonds, Wash. He and his wife Delores had two
children: Susan and Theresa. Ted is deceased.

Helen (Westerlind) Schlafmann married William Schlafmann and they had four
children: Ronald, Carol, Wayne and Lorrie. William is deceased.

Arnold Westerlind married MaryAnn Miller and they had five children: Gordon,
Deborah, Steve, Fred and Roy. Arnold is deceased.

Lloyd Westerlind operated a grain and livestock farm at Mercer and is
semi-retired.

John Westerlind was active in farming, also operated Mercer Aviation and is
semi-retired.

        Photo: The Robert and Caroline Westerlind family: (back, from left) Ted,
        Lloyd, Helen, Arnold and John.

Lloyd and John have their homes on Robert's original homestead. Robert's
homestead dwelling was built in 1904 and is still standing today. See page 408.

Robert and Caroline had 11 grandchildren and numerous great-grandchildren.

John Westerlind

John Westerlind was born Sept. 8, 1930, in Mercer, N.D., to Robert and Caroline
(Kravik) Westerlind. He went to school in Mercer and graduated from high school
in 1947. John helped his parents on the farm for a few years and then enlisted
in the Air Force during the Korean conflict. He served two years in Alaska and
about 18 months in California. While in Alaska, he learned to fly at Anchorage
and received a private pilot license.

After being discharged from the Air Force, John farmed with his brother Lloyd
for several years. He then attended a training center in Cheyenne, Wyo., and
earned an aircraft mechanics license. Then John went to a flight school in
Phoenix and received a flight instructor certificate. He started the Mercer
Aviation business in 1970 and still does some aircraft maintenance. See page
192.

        Photo: John Westerlind in 1950.

        Photo: John Westerlind of Mercer stands with a 50-year-old spinning
        wheel he refurbished and a new spining wheel he finished building. This
        was in December of 1999.

When his legs forced an early retirement in 1992, he transferred his mechanical
knowledge from plane repair to repairing magneto ignition systems on tractors.
He also enjoys repairing and building spinning wheels. Each wheel that he builds
is not a decoration; it is a working one. John also dabbles in a few other areas
working with wood. He produces wooden bowls and baskets. He buys most of his
wood from the Roughrider Industries in Bismarck.

John has four stepchildren and six step grandchildren;

Dennis and Lory Presser in Madison, Wisc., Hunter and Allegra.

Debra Presser, Bismarck.

David and Teresa Presser, Mercer, Lucas, Nicholas, Katelynn.

Douglas and Pam Presser, Minneapolis, Minn., Mikala.

Lloyd Westerlind

Lloyd Westerlind was born Sept. 13, 1927, to Robert and Caroline (Kravik)
Westerlind in Mercer. He attended school in Mercer. He worked at the Garrison
Dam during its early construction; he also spent some time working in Edmonds,
Wash.

He farmed for 50 years; some of the land he farmed included the ground that his
dad homesteaded. He also lived on the original homestead farm all his life.

He earned his pilot license in 1966 and still maintains his license. His hobby
has been collecting antique tractors; he has been doing this for 25 years.

        Photo: Lloyd Westerlind

        Photo: Lloyd Westerlind with his 1949 170 Cessna.

Theodor & Delores (Samuelson) Westerlind

Theodor Westerlind was born Dec. 12, 1917, to Robert and Caroline (Kravik)
Westerlind at Mercer, N.D. He attended school at Mercer and graduated form high
school in 1935.

Ted served one year in the CCC in the Priest Lake area in Idaho. He moved to
Edmonds, Wash., in 1938, and lived with an uncle while working there. Ted
enlisted in the Navy in 1942 and served in the South Pacific.

After being discharged from the Navy, he returned to Edmond where he and Delores
Samuelson were married on Dec. 14, 1946. Ted retired in Edmonds after 30 plus
years working for the Union Oil Company. He enjoyed gardening and woodworking
and also liked spending winters in California.

        Photo: Delores and Theodor Westerling in 1948.

Ted passed away on April 21, 2000, at the age of 82. He and Delores had two
children: Susan Williams and Teresa Wilson and five grandchildren. Delores lives
in Edmonds, Susan and Teresa live in Snohomish, Wash.

White Family History
William & Lydia (Gaub) White, Floyd & Emma (Gaub) White, William, Jr. & Sharon
White

William and Floyd White were born first and second sons to Charles Miles and
Emma (Wicks) White at Clarkston, Wash. They were joined to the family with three
more sons: Homer, Dale and Glenn, along with two daughters, Charlotte Marie and
Rae. Charles sold the harness business in Clarkston and bought a farm east of
Clarkston about 40 miles in the state of Idaho. Here the children were raised
and educated at Myrtle school.

        Photo: (From left) Floyd and Emma White and Lydia and William White Sr.

At the age of 16, William and a friend went to California to seek work. He
worked in the orchards, driving truck and hauling fruit. He moved to the Tracey,
Calif., area as some of his grandmother's sisters had settled there. While at
Tracey, he had the privilege to meet Will Rogers. He worked there for a large
farm driving caterpillar tractor.

At Tracey, he met Lydia Gaub who had moved from North Dakota with her
grandparents. William and Lydia were married at Tracey. He was a deliveryman for
Montgomery Ward and picked up the mail at the depot and transported it to the
post office. During their early marriage, several family members came to visit.
Emma Gaub, Floyd White and Glenn White came to visit and found employment.

Floyd and Emma were married in Reno, Nev., on their way to North Dakota. William
and Glenn were eligible for the draft into the Army. William and Lydia decided
to move the family in which William Jr. was a toddler back to North Dakota.
Everything was loaded on a pickup and trailer. Glenn accompanied them so there
were four in the cab of the pickup. On their trip to North Dakota, it was a big
job collecting enough gas coupons as gas was rationed. During the trip, draft
laws were changed and William was no longer eligible for the draft. Upon
arriving in September they were greeted with a snowstorm.

All three of the brothers purchased land in the Mercer area. Glenn was soon to
be drafted into the army and sent to Germany. William purchased land northwest
of Mercer and Floyd purchased land east of Mercer in Sheridan County.

        Photo: William and Lydia White, Sr.

The land that William and Lydia purchased was a new farmstead that had no
buildings or well. Due to the war, lumber was not available, so the house
started as a government granary. Other buildings were added slowly, but water
was always a problem. Several shallow wells were dug, but there was always a
limited supply. They purchased a store building in Mercer and ran a restaurant
for three years, then they returned to the farm. Some buildings were moved from
the adjoining homestead. The house could not be moved, as it was a sod house.

William was good at building. Everything had to be square with the world and
nails were used plentifully. Lydia raised a garden, chickens, geese and ducks
and milked cows. She also canned vegetables and fruit. William purchased a jet
well machine. He drilled wells for about five years until the rotary machines
came in and replaced manual labor and also wells were much deeper. They raised
cattle and farmed with William Jr. joining the operation. They found the winters
cold and hard to bear for Lydia's arthritis, so they spent many winters in
Arizona. William had to keep busy in Arizona so they purchased mobile homes and
set them up in a new park that they lived in.

        Photo: The William White Jr. family: (front, from left) William White
        Jr., Katie Kummet, Sharon White; (back) Gary and Caleb Kummet, William
        (Skip) White III, Colleen Kummet, Annie White.

Floyd and Emma White ranched, raising cattle and sheep. Emma helped with the
ranching and raised poultry. Children would spend nights or weekends at Emma and
Floyd's farm, and that was a treat. Floyd would laugh the whole time. They were
active in 4-H and homemakers, playing cards and just visiting the neighbors.
They sold the ranch and started spending winters in Arizona. Come spring they
purchased livestock and planted a garden on a small farm near Wilton. Come fall
everything was sold except the hen chickens, they were given to the nephew in
his chicken coop. They sold the farm and built a house in Wilton. Floyd passed
away and Emma continued to winter in Arizona for many years. She now lives in
Wilton, does handy work, raises strawberries and enjoys spending time with
friends.

William and Lydia built a home in Wilton and continued to winter in Arizona.
William died on March 4, 1999, and Lydia died on July 4, 2002.

William Jr. married Sharon Schaible and continues to farm the land. To this
marriage was born Annette, Colleen and William III (Skip). Sharon returned to
teaching when all the children started school and still enjoys it. William Jr.
is semi-retired and turned to woodworking especially woodturning.

Knut & Josephine (Kravik) Widen

Knut Widen came to the United States from Gotheborg, Sweden in 1902. In 1906, he
moved to Mercer where he filed for a homestead two miles west of Mercer. In 1914
he married Josephine Kravik. They lived on the homestead for 13 years. They had
six daughters, one of which died in infancy: Ada, Edna, Pearl, Edith and
Mildred.

Ada, Edna and Pearl attended school in Mercer. Knut and Josephine were members
of Our Savior's Lutheran Church in Mercer. In 1927, due to crop failures, Knut
and his family gave up farming and moved to Leeds, N.D. Knut died in 1941 at the
age of 61. Josephine died in 1985 at the age of 89.

Three daughters lived to adult age.

Ada Donavan, Leeds, four children: Vennis, Larry, Kathy and Joann.

Edna Market, Port Orchard, Wash., three children: Judy, Keith and Jackie.

Mildred McDaniel, Long Beach, Calif., two children: James and Thomas.

        Photo: The Widen family in 1932: (front, from left) Knut, Mildred and
        Josephine; (back) Edith, Edna, and Ada.

Herbert C. & Pauline (Singer) Wiest

Herbert C. Wiest was born Jan. 28, 1878, and was one of the first residents in
Mercer. In 1907, he filed a claim for a homestead and it was issued in January
of 1909 in Medicine Hill Township. The name of the farm was Woodlawn.

He was a leader in the musical events in Mercer. He was the president of the
city band, which was organized in March of 1910, and he played a slide trombone
in the band. He played for numerous dances and balls and had an orchestra in
1915.

He was the first manager of the "middle elevator" (Andrews Grain) beginning the
1908. He was also an active member of community organizations. He was the only
president of the hospital board in 1915 and was also elected to the Mercer
Township Board in 1913.

He married Pauline Singer on Aug. 15, 1912. He died at the age of 39 on June 25,
1917, and is buried in the Mercer Hillside Cemetery. (This information is from
the Mercer Telegram.)

Pauline Singer was the second oldest of the 14 children of Adolph and Margaretha
Berreth Singer. She was born on Oct. 15, 1893, in Hoffnungstal, Bessarabia,
and came to American in 1894. The family settled briefly near Ashley, N.D., and
then homesteaded in the Heart River area near Glen Ullin, N.D. In 1905, the
family moved to Beck ranch between Mercer and McClusky and in 1907 they moved to
Mercer.

In 1909, she was a member of the "Bloomer Girls," a basketball team which had
started out to be a baseball team. She was also active in the musical events of
Mercer.

She died on Nov. 24, 1968, at the age of 75 and is buried in Mercer Hillside
Cemetery.

Herbert and Pauline had one daughter, Mary Margaret (Mrs. Raymond ) Schultz.
Pauline lived with her family in Spokane in her later years.

Information compiled from the Telegram and Census

Haugen & Lillian (McComb) Winge

Haugen Winge was born in Norway in 1893. He came to Mercer from Trondheim,
Norway at the age of 17, around 1910. He homesteaded four miles north of Mercer
on Section 14 of Wise Township. His brother, Gust Winge, home-steaded on the SE
¼ of Section 15 in Wise Township.

Lillian McComb was born in 1891 in Iowa and moved to Mercer at the age of 12,
around 1903. Her father, Ramsey R. McComb, home-steaded in Section 10 of Wise
Township. He was born March 29, 1850 in Pennsylvania to David McComb and Jane
Richards. Her mother, Ella, was born in 1856 and died in 1931. Ramsey died April
6, 1932 of pneumonia at the age of 82. Lillian's siblings were Clara, Melvin,
and Arthur.

        Photo: Haugen and Lillian Winge

Clara married Harry Whitcher and they had three children: Mary, Harvey and
Florence. Clara taught school in various places and her children lived with
McCombs west of the Sprout schoolhouse.

Lillian's brother, Melvin McComb, owned land in Section 14 and 15 in Wise
Township in 1914. Melvin McComb and Knecht opened a new pool hall and restaurant
in Mercer in 1909. In 1912, Melvin McComb purchased the soda fountain from Dr.
Heinzeroth for the Pool Hall. The Telegram reported "They plan to make an ice
cream parlor and ladies room in the front end of the Pool Hall." Melvin never
married and died in 1956. He is buried in the Mercer Cemetery.

Haugen and Lillian Winge's two children were born at their farm north of Mercer.
Verna Winge was born December 1918. She attended the Sprout schoolhouse and
graduated from Mercer High School in 1936. She married Kenneth Bergan in 1939.
They moved to Bismarck, Arkansas, in 1950. They had seven children: Dean, Don,
Duane, Darwin, David, Dalton, and Delores. Kenneth passed away in 1990, and
Verna lives in Arkansas.

Ella Winge was born in 1921. Winges' neighbors were Theobald Hofers, Jens
Billes, Calheims, and Carlbergs. Ella attended the Sprout school and remembers
it being a very warm and cozy schoolhouse. She graduated from Mercer High School
in 1940. She remembers enjoying Our Savior's Church in Mercer. They sent her to
Bible camp and she was so grateful for that experience. She also remembers
watching the cowboy movies outside in Mercer. They would bring blankets and sit
on the ground on Wednesday nights and watch the show. After high school she
attended Lutheran Bible Institute in Minneapolis for 2½ years. She then worked
at Augustana Nursing Home for 35 years. She resides in Minneapolis.

Lillian Winge died in 1945 and is buried in the Mercer Hillside Cemetery.

Frederick & Emma (Sackmann) Winklemann

Emma Sackmann was born on May 2, 1895, in Walworth County near Java, South
Dakota. She was the daughter of Christoph and Christina Peters Sackmann.

She came to Mercer with her family in the fall of 1905 and was a member of the
first school class in Mercer in the fall of 1907. She was a member of the St.
Paulus Lutheran Church in rural Mercer where she was confirmed. She worked in
various places in Mercer and was one of the first telephone operators.

She married Frederick Winklemann on Jan. 24, 1915, in Mercer. She died on Oct.
29, 1918, during the flu epidemic.

Fred Winklemann came to Mercer with his brother, Victor, in 1913 and was the
builder of many of the buildings - houses, barns, hospital, Hope Lutheran Church
and the new school.

After the death of Emma in 1918, he left the area.

Emma and Fred had one son, Paul Winklemann, born Oct. 29, 1915. After the death
of his mother in 1918, he lived with his grandparents, the Christoph Sackmann
family. He attended school in Mercer and in 1933 he joined the CCC. He was a
career military man who enlisted in the Army in the mid 1930s. He served in
Europe during World War II. He died on Oct. 10, 1983.

        Photo: Pvt. Paul Winklemann

Victor & Ida (Ketterling) Winklemann

Victor Winklemann was born in Buffalo, New York on Feb. 12, 1889, and came to
Mercer with his brother Frederick in 1913. The brothers were building
contractors and built many of the original buildings in Mercer: houses, barns,
the Mercer hospital, the Hope Lutheran Church and the new school. He died in
1961 in Oregon.

Ida Ketterling was the daughter of Johan and Olga Fehlau Jacob Ketterling. She
was born on the Ketterling homestead in Bowdle Township, S.D., on Oct. 1, 1901.
She married Victor on April 6, 1916, in the family home in Mercer. They were
divorced in the 1930s. They lived in Bowdle, S.D., for several years and in 1920
they moved to Los Angeles. Ida died on May 1, 1986, in San Bernadino, Calif.

Victor and Ida had three daughters:

Lyvian Winklemann born on Aug. 25, 1916, in Mercer. She married Richard
Wisehaupt on April 15, 1939, in Los Angeles. They had a daughter Joan who was
born on March 6, 1944, and died on Dec. 15, 1999. Lyvian and Richard were
divorced and she married Clarence Vernand. Lyvian lives in Santa Ana, Calif.

Victoria Winkleman was born on July 12, 1919, in Bowdle, S.D. She married Joseph
Lee in Los Angeles and they were divorced. She married Willard Paul and they
live in Las Vegas. They had three children: Robert, William and Cynthia.

Florence Winkelman was born on Feb. 16, 1922, in Los Angeles and died on July
27, 2000, in San Diego. She married Frank Cesar in 1944 and they had a daughter
Robin. They were divorced and she married Dayton Lovelady and they had a
daughter Dee Dee.

Charles & Elizabeth (Schmitt) Wise

Wise Township was most likely named for early ranchers, Charles and Elizabeth
Wise. The 1900 census listed Charles Wise, age twenty-seven, married two years,
Lizy (sic) Wise, twenty-nine, Raymond, and Baby. They lived on the Brush Lake
Peninsula.

Charles G. Wise was born August 30, 1871, in Perkinsville, Madison County,
Indiana. His father was born in Indiana, and his mother in Ohio.

Elizabeth "Lizzie" Schmitt was born June 16, 1870 in Brookville, Tipton County,
Indiana. The census stated that her father (John) was born in Germany. His
father, also named John Schmitt, came to America from Heidelheim in Germany,
with his wife, Clara, and family. It is believed that they traveled on a 60 foot
sailboat from Bingen on the Rhine, the home of the fabled Lorelei. Lizzie's
mother, Gertrude, was also born in Germany.

Several of Lizzie's brothers came to the Mercer area from Indiana to ranch on
the open range. John "Adam" Schmitt was born March 9, 1875 (census record) or
1876 (tombstone), and came to this area in 1900 as a twenty-five-year-old
bachelor. He purchased the NE¼ of Section 26 of Wise Township in 1913. He
married Kate Banik and they had a son, James. He died February (church record)
or March (courthouse record) 2, 1918, at the age of forty-two at a Jamestown
hospital. He was survived by his wife, Kathryn, age thirty-seven, and was buried
in the Mercer Hillside Cemetery.

Lizzie's brother, Matt, was born in 1877. Other brothers in the Mercer area were
Joseph, Ferdinand, and Will Schmitt. William was born May 1883. Ferd, born in
1880, settled in Section 30 of Prophet's Township in 1900. He died in 1965 and
is buried beside Adam in the Mercer Cemetery.

Lizzie and her son, Raymond, born May 3, 1894, lived with her father on his farm
in Tipton County, Indiana. When her father died in 1898, she inherited a large
number of horses from him.

        Photo: Charles and Elizabeth Wise

Around 1898 or 1899 Lizzie married Charles Wise. In 1900, after their son,
Dallas, was born in Indiana, the family of four started working their way west
to North Dakota, bringing along Lizzie's horses.

Charles and Elizabeth established their ranch headquarters on the Peninsula of
Brush Lake in Section 27 of Wise Township. In 1904, their son, Theodore Perry,
was born.

The winter of 1903-1904 was a long, hard winter, according to Hattie Ovre, who
lived on the north side of Brush Lake. Hattie wrote in "My Fourteen Months on
the Claim," see page 419, in the Reminisences section.

County records show that on September 14, 1905, Elizabeth Wise purchased the
peninsula and northeast edge of Brush Lake in Section 27 from the Northern
Pacific Railway for $184.05. It contained 81.8 acres.

        Photo: Elizabeth Wise and her son Theadore.

Charles became the owner of an early drug store, The Mercer Drug Company. The
April 9, 1908, Mercer Telegram reported, "Mr. Wise invites you to call and meet
his new pharmacist, Mr. Linn." He also advertised school supplies, candy, and
magazines.

In July of 1908, Elizabeth accompanied her twenty-three-year-old brother, Will
Schmitt, to the Jamestown Hospital, where he underwent an appendectomy. Their
bachelor brother, Ferd Schmitt, then spent a week at Will's bedside, so Lizzie
could return home by train to her family.

That same year, the Matt Schmitt family suffered from typhoid fever. Dr.
Heinzeroth and Lizzie Wise cared for them during their illness.

Lizzie decided to develop their area at Brush Lake. The April 30, 1909, Mercer
Telegram reported that Mrs. Charles Wise had platted "The Peninsula, and there
will be a Pavillion, 42 lots, a tennis court, bath house and a boat house."

Meanwhile, Ray, Dallas, and Theodore (Ted) Wise attended country school in Wise
Township. Records show that Dallas graduated from the eighth grade at Brush Lake
School in 1913. Ray told his son, Rex, that he attended school "sometimes, until
about the sixth grade."

It was during their years around Brush Lake that the boys came to know young
Malvin Romsa like a brother. He was Norwegian, French, and Blackfoot Indian.
However, the boys' friendship was interrupted around 1910 when Malvin's father
moved up to the Peach River Country of British Columbia, Canada, taking Malvin
along. It continued elsewhere for decades, and Ray, Dallas, and Malvin
eventually married three Jordan sisters: Kathleen, Emma and Eleanor (Nelle) from
Oak Lake, Manitoba.

        Photo: Kitty and Ray Adkins

Raymond and his step-father, Charley, did not get along, and so at age sixteen,
Ray went to Canada with his uncle, Ferd Schmitt, and others to trap and hunt. A
May 12, 1911, Mercer Telegram reported: "Ferd Schmitt returned last week
Thursday from Canada where he went last fall accompanied by Karl Schafer and
Raymond Wise. The party arrived at Regina, Saskatchewan, November 15, 1910.
After taking in the sites [sights] for 7 days, they went to Lake Comb [Lacombe],
Alberta, from there to Wittenberg. After getting their supplies they started out
through the wilds to [Medicine] Lake. They had a team hauling their provisions.
The timber and brush was so thick that they had to cut their way through and it
took 3 days to travel 30 miles. After arriving at [Medicine] Lake they put up
their winter camp. Here the party spent 3 months hunting, fishing and trapping.
March 14th they moved to Burnt Lake 75 miles South East of their winter camp and
15 miles from [Red Deer], the county seat of [Red Deer] District. At this lake
the party got about $100,000 worth of skins (could they mean $10,000?), but
arrived too late to get many Rats (muskrats). Burnt Lake is 17 miles in
circumference and Sylvan Lake, which almost joins, is 25 miles around."

"Ferd said their last camping ground is an ideal place for Sportsmen. Fish are
so plentiful that farmers come for miles and hauled them home to feed to hogs."

When Ray went to Canada, he changed his name to Raymond Furl Adkins, taking his
father's last name. After nearly two years of running trap lines, eating "high
on the fish", and playing cards between three weekly trap line checks, Ray was
ready for his next step in life. At eighteen, Ray homesteaded north of
Ravenscrag, not far across the provincial border of Saskatchewan. It was a
portion of flat land that sat beside a fairly wide ravine that became known as
the Wise Coulee. His good friend, Malvin Romsa, joined him there.

On April 24, 1913, Elizabeth and Charley G. Wise sold their land at Brush Lake
to Samuel J. Kounts for $1000.00, and taking Dallas and Theodore, they moved to
Ray's log cabin on his Canadian homestead in the Coulee.

In 1918, during World War I, Ray Adkins was drafted into the Canadian army and
became a drill sergeant. He developed a serious inflammation of the mastoid,
which required surgery. Because of the November 11, 1918, Armistice, Ray never
saw the deadly trenches of Europe.

Around 1920, Ray began courting the local schoolmarm, Kathleen "Kitty" Jordan.
They married in Moosejaw on December 23, 1922. Their children were Rex, Blair,
and Colleen. Beginning in 1927, Ray and Kitty provided a needed home for her
sister's daughter, Kathleen, until she was fourteen. Kitty's sister, Emma,
married Dallas Wise in 1924.

        Photo: Emma and Dallas Wise

In 1926, the senior Wises and their son, Ted, moved from the coulee to Hoquiam,
Washington, a lumber town. In 1929, Dallas and Emma also moved to Hoquiam, where
Dallas worked as a swing shift fireman in a veneer plant.

In 1927, Ray sold his homestead and 300 head of horses in Canada, and with a
Model T Ford, moved his family to Harlem, Montana. Kitty's sister, Nelle,
eventually joined the Adkins in Harlem, and, by 1930, she married Malvin Romsa,
Ray's partner in the outdoor life. In 1931, the Adkins moved to the state of
Washington

In 1932, the mayor of Harlem, Montana wrote, "Mr. Adkins brought in lots of fur
from this vicinity and his stuff was always very nicely handled. I would
recommend him very highly as a trapper as from my experience with him I know
that he understands the business thoroughly."

Unfortunately, Kathleen Jordan Adkins died at age thirty-three on March 31,
1935, when their daughter, Colleen, was only eleven months old. Dallas and Emma
Wise then took Colleen into their home and raised her, along with their two
children, Ken and Gilbert (Bud).

After Kathleen died, Ray served as father, mother, cook and bottle washer for
Rex, Blair and Kathleen during all their years in Tacoma, Washington. He always
took them to the Methodist Church, even though he did not attend.

Ted Wise was an artist and a fiddle player at country dances. He had a
pick-and-shovel job with the Great Northern Railway during the Depression. He
lived in Zurich, Montana, and married Ruby Emily Mord. They had four children:
Perry, Kathy, Theodora, and Jon. Ted died in 1986 and is buried in Chinook,
Montana.

Around 1930, Charley and Lizzie moved to Montana. Charley Wise died March 20,
1934, in Havre, Hill County, Montana, and is buried in Chinook, Blaine County,
Montana. Elizabeth Wise spent her final years in a rest home in Harlem, Montana.
She died June 27, 1964, and is also buried in Chinook, Montana.

The Peninsula at Brush Lake that Elizabeth Wise platted in 1909 was purchased by
Meinhardt and Gertrude Skaley in 1946, and is still in the Skaley family today.
It continues to be a recreational area near Mercer that is enjoyed by many
people every year.

Mercer Reminiscences

The Centennial Book Committee presents here a special section of reminiscences
on prairie life in small town North Dakota. The first part of this section is
composed of a collection of four articles written by local women of the past for
what is believed to have been a Women's Study Club project and later compiled by
Beulah Hedahl in 1970. Other articles by various authors follow.

Introduction By Beulah Hedahl

The early history of Mercer, North Dakota, is not unlike that of many of the
pioneer towns. Mercer is located in central North Dakota, an area which became
accessible for settlement after the Northern Pacific Railroad extended a branch
line from Carrington to Turtle Lake. The railroad established the town sites
based on a reasonable distance between towns, when farmers depended on horse and
buggy to make the trip to town for provisions, and on experience in farming
regions elsewhere. Once the towns were located, the settlers began to arrive.
Some were like my father, American-born sons of immigrant stock, Norwegian in
his case, Swedish, German, and Danish in others, still speaking their parents'
language more fluently than the English they had learned in school. Others, from
families longer rooted in America, came from Missouri, Iowa, and Wisconsin, to
mention a few. And many others were immigrants, sometimes coming directly to
Mercer, sometimes having located in other sections of the country first but
moving at the word of new land.

The patterns had not been set before. Hope and enthusiasm could accomplish
anything. This new town should have all of the assets of any other town almost
immediately: one, then two hardware stores, two banks, a hotel, two blacksmith
shops, a hospital, two Lutheran churches, a newspaper, two lumberyards, a livery
stable and dray line, a telephone system, a general store, community-owned
recreation at Brush Lake, a pool hall, three grain elevators, a grade school and
then a high school, implement dealers, and a butcher shop. The reminiscences
which follow mention them all. But hope and enthusiasm do not quite make up for
experience: the experience of farming in a country where often there was not
enough rain and where a homestead was really not large enough for the kind of
farming needed; the experience of inflationary credit with almost unlimited
faith in the ability of every one to pay in the future encouraged by the
Government in World War I; poor crops with high prices; good crops with low
prices when wheat was no longer needed for the war.

By the early 1920s, another pattern became evident. People began moving out -
back to homes in Minnesota or Missouri, west to Washington or California,
sometimes to other North Dakota towns that seemed more promising: McClusky,
Valley City, Bismarck. And Mercer was beginning to share the fate of many other
prairie towns, settling into modest growth and an acceptance of its role as
small town.

My personal recollections come late. I was born about the time the regrouping
had started. That was the year my grandfather, Nels Hedahl, moved to Fargo to
retire. I can remember our move from Mercer to the farm east of town in 1924 and
our move to Bismarck in 1928. More vividly, I can remember that Mercer and Brush
Lake were our favorite places to spend holidays. How could one celebrate the 4th
of July if it rained so that we couldn't go to Brush Lake? How else could we
enjoy the reunion with family and friends that was always a part of it?

This leads to another aspect of the pioneer town that is also typical of Mercer.
Families were important, and often times several members of the same family
would locate in the same town. In our family my father (Edwin) was followed by
his brother Ole and then by his father and two sisters and a brother. Aunt Ella
married Will Peterson and lived on the farm near Pickardville where their
daughter, Marjorie Peterson Burck, and her family now live. Uncle Tony married
Edith Smirl, Mrs. Ben Hjelle's sister, and they, too, moved to Bismarck. Halfdan
Berge, my mother's brother, had already settled in Mercer by the time my
grandmother and mother came. Mrs. James Rice was drawn to Mercer by her sister,
Minnie Martineson Hedahl, and married and raised her family there.

For me then, visits to Mercer centered on visiting my cousins, the Berges, the
Rices, and the Petersons. I can remember listening for the afternoon train,
perhaps waiting at the depot to see whether there were any passengers, and
following the dray to the post office and waiting to see what mail was there.

Mother started this project several years ago. Her first response came from
Regina Singer Stubbs in 1964. Others have been gathered over the years - some
from people who can no longer tell us how it used to be. Others have found it
difficult to go back into the past. Yet when I reread what Mrs. Freeberg and
Mrs. Hjelle had written, the delightful anecdotes of the Singer family, it
seemed worthwhile to put them all into a form which could be shared with their
families. Perhaps someone else will write the history of Mercer more completely
in the future.

(1970)

Adolph & Margaretha Berreth Singer By Regina Singer Stubbs
Edited by Centennial Book Committee

My father and mother were among the early residents to locate in what is now
Mercer, North Dakota. They immigrated to the United States (as Germans) from the
southern part of (Russia) in 1894 with two small children: Alexander and
Pauline. Father served seven years in the (Russian) Navy. They came via steerage
and Mother was very ill all during the voyage. He spoke many times of wanting to
return for a visit but Mother never overcame [the] horror of seasickness.

My maternal great-grandparents were [Germans] from Alsace Lorraine and the name
was spelled "de Berreth." Through the years the name (simply) became "Berreth."

My parents settled briefly in South Dakota, then on to Glen Ullin, North Dakota,
where they homesteaded land in the Heart River area. During the time they
resided on the homestead, Christine, Rudolph, John, Dave, Arthur, Regina and
Elsie were born to them.

During my father's Navy career, he became quite a musician (clarinet). He would
tell us of his many experiences, one of which was being chosen as a musician in
the royal band that played at the royal wedding (of the Czar's sister Princess
Sofia to King Constantine of Greece.) The band traveled with the royal entourage
and the city of Constantinople was turned over to them. The celebration lasted
two weeks.

Never really a farmer at heart, (Adolph became bored with the homestead), so he
would leave Mother with the children and tour with a contingent of John Philipp
Sousa's band.

Finally in 1905, they left the old homestead and moved to a large ranch known as
Beck's Ranch located between Mercer and McClusky. While there, Father helped out
Mr. Beck, an attorney and sheriff, as a law enforcement officer. Olga was born
there in 1906. In 1907, our family moved to Mercer. Father and Rudolph Berreth,
Mother's youngest brother, bought the Livery Stable and Dray Line from Karl
Degg. Walter, the youngest child, was born in 1909. In all, my parents had
fourteen children, nine sons and five daughters. Three sons died in infancy,
eleven grew to maturity. For many years Father was constable of the Mercer
vicinity.

In my childhood, I recall that my parents always worked hard. There was always a
barn full of horses - all my brothers were horse lovers - and buggies. These
were rented to anyone desiring to go any place that couldn't be reached by rail:
Minot, Washburn, Dogden [Butte], and Wilton. We had heavy horses for the dray
line, many ponies for the buggies, plus a pair of endurance mules for long trips
and two stallions for breeding purposes. The mules ran away at the least
provocation and they smashed so many vehicles that my father had to sell them or
go broke. Stalls also were rented to farmers to shelter their teams while
shopping in inclement weather. My father, uncle and older brothers would labor
all day unloading boxcars of coal and lumber and hauling freight. One day a
camera fan saw Father walking with a wide board, took a picture and dubbed it
"The Flying Dutchman."

There were hard times but we always had plenty to eat and wear. I don't think we
were ever alone at a meal just as an immediate family. My uncle, grandmother and
numerous cousins lived with us. The cousins came to visit but the visit
stretched into months and years.

In 1910, Father acquired our first automobile, an International. It had high
wheels like a buggy and solid rubber tires. And what a novelty in town it was!
Mother vowed she would never ride in it, but a few days later she sat proudly
beside Father enjoying the ride. With the advent of the automobile, Dad had few
horses. What fun it was in the summertime to motor to Brush Lake for a swim
after supper. The car was always loaded with youngsters, and I guess one time no
one noticed Brother Arthur hanging on the side. He fell off; result: a broken
arm and our introduction to kindly Dr. Heinzeroth of Turtle Lake who just
happened to be in town. With eleven active children, someone was always getting
injured and I wonder how my parents stood the strain. What a godsend Mrs. George
McFadden was, the town's trained nurse from Fergus Falls, Minnesota. It seemed
she was always being called to patch up one of us. I think Arthur was the more
daring, for he was injured more than the rest of us. I say he was more daring
from the time he was quite small as I shall relate later in his history. We were
a happy lot, (yet fought) among ourselves. But let an outsider pick on one of
us, and he had to deal with the whole clan.

Cars were becoming more plentiful and the livery business dwindled, so in 1914,
Father purchased the meat market from our neighbor and close friend, Christ
Sackman. Our uncle moved to Canada; Alexander, Pauline and Christine were
married and in homes of their own. So the younger generation helped with the
meat market. We all waited on customers and cut meat. Along with the meat market
came the extra work of cutting ice at Brush Lake in the wintertime and hauling
it to town to be packed in sawdust in an ice house for summer use in the large
meat cooler.

(Upon moving into Mercer), Father and Mother had built a new home right in the
middle of town. What a lovely place it was. We were so proud of it. We spent
many joyful holiday get-togethers there. Returning to the early horse and buggy
and run-away (times), I recall Mother, Elsie, Olga, Wally (he was a baby then)
and me as we drove to visit some relatives, (the Christ Singers), south of
Mercer. When we arrived there and before Mother had a chance to take us from the
buggy, the horses shied at a flutter of paper and proceeded to run away. Mother
would not release the reins and was being dragged under the buggy until the
buggy tongue broke and the horses were free. I was on the seat and in the
commotion was thrown out. I landed about two feet from an open well. The other
children were asleep during the whole excitement.

I was too young to remember this: It happened when we lived on the homestead
south of Glen Ullin. When Arthur was about three and one-half and I was two and
one-half years old, we followed my father and brothers into the hay field. They
did not know we had followed and neither did my mother. Night came and we
weren't to be found. A search party was formed: riders on horseback, buggies,
and farmers on foot. They searched all night and found us at noon the next day.
We were barefoot, our feet were swollen from sharp thistles and brambles, and
our tongues were swollen from thirst. Years later when friends from Glen Ullin
came to visit us at Mercer, they always asked, "Which two are the ones who got
lost?"

World War I came along. Alexander was married, the father of two children, and a
U.S. mail carrier, so he was exempt from service. But Rudolph and John enlisted
in the Navy. Spanish influenza swept the nation, and John fell victim to the
dreaded disease - our first sorrow. After the war, Father retired. Dave and
Arthur managed the meat market for several years and later sold it to Joe
Dakovna. Dave left for the West Coast and Duff, then married, joined him in Salt
Lake City in 1924. Both boys were very successful in the automobile business and
Dave pioneered the mobile home business there. Many changes have taken place
since that time. There is no one of the immediate family now living in Mercer.
My grandmother, father, mother, brothers Alexander and John, Alexander's son
Harold, brother-in-law Herbert Wiest, and an aunt and uncle (Mr. and Mrs. John
Berreth) are all buried in the Mercer cemetery.

In closing, I (must mention) that Herbert Wiest, Ole Hedahl, Mrs. O.S. Hjelle,
and our father provided music for many dances and special programs in Mercer's
earlier years.

(1964)

The Edwin N. Hedahl Family By Clara Berge Hedahl
Edited by Centennial Book Committee

On an April morning in 1906, E.N. Hedahl and his uncle, O.S. Hedahl, mounted
their bicycles and left Manfred, North Dakota, to ride west. Their object was to
look over the town sites along the newly built railroad connecting Carrington
and Turtle Lake and to choose a suitable location for a hardware store. They
went from Hurdsfield to Turtle Lake and on to Garrison and decided that the most
promising town along the route was Mercer. Here they procured lots, built a
small building, and stocked it with hardware. E.H. Hedahl and O.S. Hedahl's son,
Swen, were established in business. As the business prospered, the building was
enlarged. They added furniture to their stock of merchandise. Later they
enlarged again to accommodate the addition of the Ford Agency and Equipment to
service cars.

Swen stayed only a year or two before he moved on to other interests. Edwin was
joined by his younger brother Ole, who became chief (auto) mechanic. Their
father, Nels, joined them in 1910 and stayed until he retired in 1920 and moved
to Fargo. World War I took its toll of the firm before that, however, when Ole
was drafted and left in July 1918. He contracted influenza on the way to England
and died shortly after landing there.

Establishing a business was not the only thing which occupied Edwin's attention.
Soon after coming to Mercer, he bought the relinquishment on a homestead joining
Mercer on the southwest and built a four-room house on it for (his wife) Minnie
Martineson of near Ada, Minnesota. She and Mrs. Theodore Knutson were the first
English-speaking women to move to the Mercer vicinity. The Knutson homestead
joined Mercer on the east.

When the time came that both the Hedahl and the Knutson couples were expecting
their first babies, the husbands became concerned about their wives being alone
all day. To remedy this, they established Mercer's first telephone system. They
connected the two homes with their places of business by stringing wires,
sometimes attaching the wire to anything along the way, sometimes putting in
posts where nothing else was available. At this time there were no cars in
Mercer. It can easily be imagined what a joy it was for the wives to be able to
telephone their husbands and to be able to visit with each other without walking
the miles that separated them.

Living in Mercer during the early days required some [adapting]. Take water, for
example. If the townsite had been located one and one-half miles farther east,
water would have been no problem. As it was, well water was not easily
accessible, and the residents had to depend on rain or on water hauled in. A
well on the homestead of May Washburn provided the source for most of the
drinking water that was used in town. Her father - and later her brother, Ira -
delivered it around town in ten-gallon cans. The price was one cent per gallon.
Naturally, the water was used sparingly, even after the rain barrel under the
eaves was displaced by a cistern. Often the rainfall was not great enough to
keep cisterns full. In the winter, ice was brought in from Brush Lake and melted
for wash water or extra water was bought from the Washburns.

Brush Lake ice was also used for refrigeration. The Washburns added ice to their
service, storing it in a pit and packing it with sawdust, (then) delivering it
to their customers in a wheelbarrow.

Electric power was not available until 1920, and for a long time it was
furnished only from 6 a.m. until midnight. A momentary blackout twenty minutes
before the current was to go off served as a warning, which ended any social
events and sent guests scrambling to get home.

Brush Lake provided a major source of recreation for the early residents of the
Mercer community. Swimming, skating, and picnicking were among the attractions.
Unfortunately there were no fish, and Ed, who enjoyed fishing, regretted this.
In spite of the general opinion that fish [did] not live in the water, he made
several trips to get small fish to plant in this lake, and eventually his
efforts met with success. He also believed that the community should own the
lake waterfront, and he helped organize an association that purchased the land
for community recreation.

The Hedahl's first child, born in 1907, was a girl who lived only a short time
and was buried in the newly established cemetery. Their second child, Erling,
was born in August 1909.

In 1915, (Edwin's wife) Minnie died after a lingering illness. Edwin asked
(Minnie's) aunt, Mrs. Martha Berge of Ada, Minnesota, to come to Mercer to care
for Erling, then six years old, and to keep house.

Mrs. Berge's daughter, Clara Berge, came to Mercer in 1915 to teach school. She
taught first in a two-room school in town and later at the Brush Lake School. In
1918, she and Edwin were married. They had two children, a daughter Beulah, born
in 1920, and a son Neilon, born in 1923.

The family lived in Mercer until 1924, when they moved to a farm a mile east of
town. It was during the early 1920s that Erling, then about twelve years old,
began following instructions in a newspaper and built a crystal radio - the
first radio in Mercer. There was great excitement when he picked up voices and
music - and static - on the little set. Edwin was very proud, and people came
from all over town to listen to the radio. Farming was not Edwin's choice of
occupation. In 1928, he secured the Bismarck agency for the Durant car, and the
family moved to Bismarck. It was an unfortunate time to start a new business.
The [Wall Street] crash of 1929 proved to be the end of the Durant car and
necessitated a slow rebuilding of a business, this time in wholesale automotive
supplies serving the southwest corner of North Dakota. A sideline during those
years of rebuilding was wholesaling of binder twine during the summer months. He
loved to travel from town to town, looking at the crops. His pioneer hope and
enthusiasm seemed to be renewed each spring. He died in 1942. The business for
which he laid the foundation was continued first by Beulah during World War II
and then by Erling and Neilon, who returned to Bismarck to manage it after their
military service was complete. Both of them are still active in the firm. Beulah
has made a career in education and is on the faculty of the University of North
Dakota.

(1970)

O.S. Hjelle Excerpted from biographical notes
Edited by Centennial Book Committee

(O. (Ole) S. Hjelle was a graduate from Luther College, Decorah, Iowa, in 1905,
and that summer joined three other Luther College students to play baseball at
Velva: H. Sorlien; George Rodsater, later an attorney in North Dakota; Alfred
Sevareid, father of newscaster Eric Sevareid. He then taught school in the Red
River Valley. On September 15, 1907, he came to Mercer.)

Mercer was then really a part of the Wild West. Most of the people - farmers and
businessmen - were about the same age as I and anxious to make good. With them
were mixed some big-city wrecks and gamblers. The majority of the farmers was
German-Russians and had immigrated from South Russia. Some came from Romania,
and I remember that they spoke better German than those from South Russia. (It
is more appropriate to say the Germans from South Russia simply spoke a
different German dialect. - Editor) Many could not and would not try to speak
English, and so the German I had learned at Luther College was a great help to
me.

When I first arrived at Mercer, George McFadden, with the help of his cousin a
trained nurse, ran a general store. Annetta would bring the week's store
receipts for deposit in the First National Bank in Turtle Lake, driving the ten
miles with a single horse. Mercer had no doctor and Nettie was called upon to
help the sick and always responded. Later, she and George were married and had a
red-headed daughter (whom) they named Blanche. George had to extend credit to
his customers and carried his accounts in an old McCaskey register. He had no
safe to store it in and I suppose the accounts at times added up to $10,000 or
more. So at night, he brought the case over to the bank to be stored in the bank
vault. Many a time I had to get up and let him in with his "Dull Care," as he
called it.

Christ Sackman was the village butcher. Christ was a simple, honest man with
many children. The boys were all fine athletes and three of them were on the
Mercer High School (basketball) team with Floyd Sprout and grant Ovre. They
never lost a game, and I am sure they could have beat teams from Bismarck and
Fargo.

The first hotel in Mercer was a rather small two-story frame building on the
east side of Main Street and run by Fred Sorenson. That burned down and later
Nels Olesen built a large frame two-story hotel on Lots 3 and 4, Block 5,
Original Townsite. After a few years (Olesen) started to conduct revival
meetings in our school house. He moved back to Minnesota and later to
California.

In early days, Mercer had three barber shops where charge for a shave was
fifteen cents and that for a haircut fifty cents. On Wednesday and Saturday
nights they would be crowded until late at night. We also had two lumber yards:
The Winnor Torgerson and the Stradinger yards. Another company, the Gull River
Lumber Company, bought lots but never built on them. Herb Wiest, George McFadden
and I bought the Stradinger lumber shed and converted it into a dance hall.
After some years, we turned it over to the local American Legion and they sold
it to Halfdan Berge, who owned it until it burned.

Among the early blacksmiths were Karl Rennick, a 303 pound veteran of the
Russo-Japanese War, and John Gardiner and his son Thomas. The Gardiners had been
coal miners in Illinois and came west and settled at Wilton where they were
employed at the lignite mines there. Later they filed on homesteads north of
Mercer and moved there. When I came to Mercer there were three elevators
operating: the Regan and Lyness, the Great Western and the Andrews Grain
Company. Their agents were Greenfield, James Rice and Herb Wiest. James Rice
later handled the sale of International machinery and was also in the beef
cattle business.

A Miss Amdahl and another young lady from Minneapolis had a dress-making shop
for a short while.

W.T. Wasson was the publisher and printer of the Mercer Telegram, our local
newspaper. He lived on a homestead in the Prophet Mountains and barely made a
living in the publishing business. I believe he sold out to Nels Olesen, who
later quit and left the plant. In some way then, George McFadden, E.N. Hedahl
and I obtained possession as we did not want Mercer to be without a newspaper.
We hired Ed Plowman as editor and publisher and he continued to put it out for a
few years. I think at the beginning, the main income was publishing notices of
proof of claim for homestead entries. When that business came to an end, the
paper could not pay expenses and was discontinued.

The farm land around Mercer was school, railway or homestead land. When the main
line of the Northern Pacific was built, the government gave the railway company
every other section of land for fifty miles out from the main line. Much of this
was sold to eastern land speculators and investors for often up to $20 an acre.
Some of these people hung on to their investment for thirty to forty years,
receiving a little income from hay land but paying more out for taxes, and at
last decided to sell for anything they could get. The school land was held off
the market for years waiting for better prices. Now it often sells at
unreasonably high prices.

Practically all farmers around Mercer were homesteaders and many of these were
serious characters. One of them, Blinky Fowler, a big man of middle age, came
out and filed on a homestead with the intention of making proof, obtaining a
first mortgage loan and then abandoning it and leaving. He suffered from palsy
and his hands shook so that it appeared he could hardly hold or deal playing
cards, even though he had the reputation of being a professional poker player.
One winter he ran a poker game in a room in the building next to our bank and
fleeced considerable money out of farmers. Knut Widen was an especially heavy
loser, and in the end I was, too, as Knut went broke owing us money. Why did I
not try to put a stop to Blinky's work!

Another character was Peder August Fransin, alias Gust Fransin, alias the
Terrible Swede. He was a small man but a mighty drinker and bluffer and never
took a back seat. He attended all baseball games and always bet on Mercer. Still
another was Jesse or "Shorty" Kline, a stocky-built, dark complexioned man who
later operated a pool hall in Mercer and sold some liquor on the side. The pool
hall was one door north of our bank building and usually Shorty had a poker game
going just a little inside the front door in plain sight of passersby. In a
drinking brawl near the Great Western Elevator, Charles Beahl, a farmer, bit off
one of Jesse's ears. Beahl had his team tied uptown, and it was claimed that he
made fast time to reach the team, untie and put the whip to his horses. In later
years, Jesse was married to a fine girl and moved to St. Paul, where he did well
as a builder. Mother and I often visited them on our trips to Decorah.

Among the early settlers in Prophets Township were Ethan Allen Vandercook and
his brother Carl B. Vandercook. They had friends file on quarters so situated
that they (the Vandercook parcels) could not be included in a homestead. The
Vandercooks then had use of these isolated tracts for many years. Ethan spent
most of his time traveling as a salesman. I (came to own) the land the
Vandercooks once controlled. When they sold their belongings, I bought their
grand piano.

Another interesting and ambitious St. Paul citizen, Fred Winkelmann, arrived
unknown to anyone in Mercer in the early days. He was a carpenter by trade and
built the first German Lutheran Church in Mercer, the hospital (east of our
bank) and many dwellings, among them Ben's (Hjelle) home. He did very well and
married a Sackman girl (Emma). She died very young and left him a little boy,
Paul. The grandparents, Mr. and Mrs. Christ Sackman, cared for the boy and he
grew up to be a fine young man. He moved to California and formed a partnership
with George McFadden where the two in those boom days went into the building
business and made a fortune. Winkelmann was the builder and McFadden ran the
business end.

Before the railroad was extended from Denhoff to Mercer and Turtle Lake, the
Davidsons, John Helm and Juanita Kabler Davidson, moved onto a ranch seven miles
southeast of Mercer. Their families were prominent and wealthy citizens of
Hannibal, Missouri. Grain farming was strange to them and not very profitable.
They gradually went into stock-raising and soon had a very fine herd of
white-faced cattle. Later the Davidsons moved back to Hannibal.

Ole's parents were John O. Hjelle and Ann Stumley, both born in Norway. John O.
came to the United States as a young man, attracted here by a brother who came
to this country earlier and an uncle, the Rev. Nils O. Brandt, first Norwegian
Lutheran pastor to penetrate west of the Mississippi River. Ann came to this
country as a young girl with her parents who settled in southern Dakota
Territory near what is now Brookings, South Dakota.

Ole's wife, Ella Myrah, was born at Spring Grove, Minnesota, to which her
grandparents had come some time in 1849. Her father was a farmer and
builder-carpenter, and during the early 1900s farmed during the summers in the
Arthur, North Dakota area, returning to Spring Grove during the winter.

When O.S. Hjelle graduated from Luther College in 1905, he taught school for one
year in Hunter, North Dakota, and while there met Ella Myrah. On November 23,
1912, they were married. Meanwhile Ole had joined R.T. and Will Lierboe of
Turtle Lake in the First National Bank in Mercer, so upon marriage they settled
there.

(Ella passed away January 1967. Ole S. passed away June 1970. Both are buried at
Fairview Cemetery in Bismarck, North Dakota.)

F.O. Freeberg Family By Minnie Swanson Freeberg
Edited by Centennial Book Committee

It was 1910 that Fred and I came to Mercer to establish a home. Fred had been
asked by Mr. Beiseker to be a cashier of a new bank, just organized, the Mercer
State Bank. He came here from Kenmare, where he was working in a bank, in
February 1910. In June 1910 he went to his hometown of Cannon Falls, Minnesota,
to be married to me, Minnie Swanson. We were married June 15 and came to Mercer
two weeks later.

It was quite a change to come from an old settled place like Goodhue County,
Minnesota, to a new place, a frontier. As we rode on the Soo Line train to
Carrington and from there to Mercer, I would ask at every small town, "Is Mercer
like this?" It was very windy when we came to Carrington where we changed
trains. I can remember how I wondered how anybody could keep a hat on. I was
wearing a wide-brimmed hat, A "Merry Widow Hat," as they were called.

When we arrived in Mercer, we found that the house that Mr. Wiest built for us
to rent was not ready for occupancy so we had a room at the hotel which was in
the charge of Nels (Olesen), and the Muechler girls from Goodrich were working
there. After a few days, we moved to the McFadden home where we had two rooms
and the Neuenbergs had the other two rooms. Each family was waiting for the
other to move so they could get settled in their own homes. While we were still
there, George McFadden brought his bride from Minnesota. They took the upstairs
rooms until we could move out. The days were long as we are six miles east of
Mandan where the time changes. It gave us an hour more of daylight. One evening
we were invited to a party at the Davidsons who lived about seven miles south of
town. We were to ride with another couple, and I can still remember how we
waited for them to come. Time didn't make any difference; it must have been
about ten (p.m.) before we started out for the seven miles with a team. It was
still light though. There was a large crowd, several newly married couples among
them. We enjoyed it all! Our first party in Mercer.

As soon as our home was ready, we moved in, and how nice it seemed to live in a
house again and not have to eat sitting at grocery boxes. That first day I felt
like I wanted to bake everything in our new coal range. In those days we
couldn't buy bread and other things like we can now. It was really fun to keep
house. We were never alone. My husband had promised the assistant cashier he
could board with us, and we had teachers come on weekends. Teachers had come
from Minnesota and were glad to come in and stay a few days.

We had no church, so every time there were Danish services north of town, we
would hire a team of mules and go there to attend services, even if we could not
understand everything. One Christmas we had our Children's Festival in the pool
hall. Traveling pastors would come through our town and would have services in
the school house. Sunday school was organized that first fall. We were all young
and willing to work and we were all as one.

It wasn't long before we had a resident pastor - Pastor Ulvilden. He organized a
choral choir of forty members, which was quite an undertaking. If we were not
there for practice we had to have a written excuse and that happened only once
when one young man could not be there for practice. Later on Pastor Hanson came.
It doesn't seem long since those days; although it is fifty-four years ago and
many things have happened since then. Now we have four churches in town, a nice
school with a big gym. We have water works; at that time we had wells and
cisterns or melted ice and snow for washing. We have good paved roads instead of
trails and cow paths. We have electric lights and electrical appliances instead
of lanterns and lamps; all articles of convenience connected with electricity;
dial systems instead of telephone operators.

Those were the good old days, as we call them. But there has been much progress,
and we are thankful for all the blessings God has bestowed upon us.

My husband passed away very suddenly of a heart attack in October 1945. I found
(the following) reminiscences that he gave at a class reunion in June 1930. He
told about what happened since his graduation in 1905, and I will just mention
what he said from the time he came to North Dakota:

"I had been working at the First National Bank in Kenmare only a few months when
Mr. Beiseker wrote me and offered me the position as cashier of the Mercer State
Bank at Mercer, North Dakota. I arrived at Mercer on the evening of the 10th of
February 1910. Sunday being the 11th and Monday the 12th, Lincoln's birthday, we
did not open up the bank until Tuesday the 13th. I still remember the windy and
cold day of the 10th as I walked out a short distance from town to get the key
for the bank. However, that evening there was a dance in town and my assistant
cashier, Ed Heugelen who had arrived on the same train, and I took it in and had
a good time, I presume. Things were rather different from what we both had been
used to.

"We stayed at the hotel together that winter and had the coldest room in the
hotel, the northwest corner upstairs, and in the morning, we would get up and
try to run our fist through the ice in the water pitcher, so that we could get
enough water to wash and managed to get along very well.

"Our little bank commenced to grow from the first day, although this being a new
country, there was very little money for deposits.

"We started in to write fire and life insurance, made some first mortgages,
loans, etc. At any rate we got our salary every month, which was charged up to
expenses and which exceeded the profits for the first two or three years without
a question. My salary for the first year was $75, which increased from year to
year as long as Mr. Beiseker had control of the bank. Ed Heugelen stayed with us
about two years.

"In the fall of 1918, Mr. George McFadden and I bought the bank, taking in with
us at that time M.N. Gergen, my former friend and associate at the bank in
Cannon Falls, (Minnesota). Mr. Gergen retired later on. George McFadden is still
with us. Today we have a thriving little institution.

"We are, as you know, still in the banking business, although during these last
years, a good many banks had to go down, and, personally, I feel that our bank
is in better condition today than it has ever been in the history of our banking
career.

"(Let us go) back to the summer of 1910, again being just a few months after I
arrived in Mercer. I was called to Cannon Falls on account of the death of my
father in April. In the summer I went back again, and this time I went on what
would possibly be termed the happiest event of my life, when I came back to get
married. I think you all know my wife, formerly Minnie Swanson. We got  married
June 15, 1910 in the presence of a large congregation of friends and relatives.

"This event was saddened by the death of my mother shortly afterwards, and after
the funeral, we left for our future home in Mercer, North Dakota, where we have
lived ever since, enjoying a most happy life together with no dark spots
whatever to sadden our lives.

"I brought my wife to a rather barren country, especially so it would have
seemed to you people present here today, being used to parks and trees. But we
learned to like our surroundings. The people living in the country and village
were all poor - most of the farm homes consisted of sod houses. Some had proved
up their homesteads and others were ready to prove up, and most of the country
was prairie. We had no trees at that time and do not have what would seem to you
folks very many at this time, but nevertheless there is something fascinating
about the prairie also, after you get used to it.

"On the 1st of April 1924, we bought McFadden's store and started in the store
game, my wife taking charge of same, which, with my assistance, has worked out
to be a profitable business institution to date, our business having continued
to grow from year to year.

"As you probably know we have three children: two boys and a girl, Merwyn and
Conrad both attending Jamestown College and Phyllis graduated this      year
from our local high school."

(1964)

Juanita (Mrs. Helm) Davison's Memories By Juanita Davidson
Edited by Bev Christensen

Juanita and John "Helm" Davidson moved onto a ranch seven miles south of Mercer
in the summer of 1905, before the railroad was extended from Denhoff to Mercer
and Turtle Lake. Later, Alvin and Martha Schlafman owned and operated this
ranch.

Juanita Davidson was born March 28, 1883 at Troy, Missouri to Dr. and Mrs. Parks
Kaebler. Her father was a medical doctor, and her mother died when she was
young. Her father later remarried, and the family had a black cook. After
Juanita graduated from high school, she spent six months in San Francisco with
her father's sister. She spent the next two years back in Hannibal, Missouri
where she attended the St. Louis World's Fair, card parties, dances, a country
club, a Shakespeare Club and church activities.

        Photo: The Davidson family: Juanita and John Davidson and their children
        Mary Frances and Rose, circa 1911.

Juanita and Helm were high school sweethearts. He was born November 7, 1882. She
wrote in her memories "He had always been a lover of horses and drove the
best-looking horse... A big land company from St. Paul had been to Hannibal a
year earlier and interested Father Davison in buying land in North Dakota.
Because Helm had always wanted a ranch the two of them (Helm and his father)
decided it was a good place to raise cattle and bought five sections or 3,200
acres... After he and his father (James) went to North Dakota and bought land,
we made plans for an immediate marriage... I remember my father picking me up
with his buggy and taking me to the dressmakers... and the sweet heart to heart
talk we had. I felt the sadness he was feeling in letting me go so far away from
him. I remember him saying 'Now you must come home every year, and we will go to
you once a year, and in that way we won't be separated for too long.'"

The wedding took place June 27, 1905 in Juanita's home. "Seven bridesmaids
preceded us down that beautiful old stairway and we made our vows in front of
the fireplace. A little before midnight a closed carriage with the driver
outside on top picked us up and took us to the old Union Depot, where a large
noisy crowd of old friends were waiting with rice, good wishes, and many tears.
And thus we started for North Dakota.

It was an overnight trip to St. Paul and we made it more of a honeymoon by
spending a couple days at the best hotel... It was about eleven o'clock at night
when we boarded the Northern Pacific for North Dakota, and in the morning we
awoke in the state that was to become our home. I peeked out of my berth to see
what I could see, and a treeless rolling prairie seemed to stretch for miles and
miles with only an occasional house and barn. At eleven in the morning we
reached Jamestown, there we left luxury and the easy life. Being young and very
much in love, things had a rosy glow. The chair car and the smoky branch line
train took us to Carrington, where we again changed trains... Now we were ready
for the last leg of our journey. The ride (was) in a one-passenger coach to
Denhoff - journey's end - and 25 miles from the Ranch. To our surprise the coach
was filled and we were barely able to find seats. The occupants were different.
They were not speaking English. The women wore shawls over their heads in spite
of the heat... I was told later they were 'German Russians' who had been
somewhere attending a Seventh Day Advent Convention.

The day was hot, the car was crowded... I was still wearing my going away
costume, a blue and white checked taffeta shirtwaist type dress and my straw
colored Milan turban, which my father and I had gone to St. Louis to buy... At
last we reached the end of our railroad trip, which was the end of the road
also, and were ready for the last leg - a stage to the ranch. Denhoff only had a
few hundred citizens and many had come down to meet the train... The hotel
across the street was void of any conveniences, running water or electricity. At
six o'clock in June in North Dakota the sun has not started to set and I could
see the treeless, barren, mostly unpainted little town. I had no misgivings - I
was on my way to my new home.

Out of the crowd, who had come to see the train come in, stepped a nice looking
young man, who spoke to my new husband. It seemed they had met when Helm had
been up earlier in the spring. He was a young lawyer with an Irish name and
smile. He invited us to go home with him and spend the night, saying he was
afraid we couldn't be comfortable at the hotel on account of bedbugs. We went
home with him, a small home but a hospitable one. He and his wife didn't know we
were coming and they barely knew us but they made us welcome. That was my first
experience with hospitality in a new country. It was always a happy experience.
There were no telephones, the distances so great we had no way of communication,
so we went everywhere uninvited and greeted all comers with a cordiality we
really felt. Our larders were never as bare as old Mother Hubbard's, we had no
ice or refrigerators but somehow in some way we were always able to provide
enough food for the unexpected guests.

Morning came and we were ready for our twenty-five mile trip to the ranch. I
found the stage, as it was called, was not the picturesque enclosed carriage I
had read of, but just a three-seated spring wagon without cover or comfort. It
made the trip in one day from Denhoff to Washburn, the next day from Washburn to
Denhoff, a distance of fifty miles. Horses were changed enroute. The ranch had
been called the half-way house - and I learned to look forward to the coming of
the stage, although there were times when it never even stopped. The days it
came from Washburn the driver brought us our mail, an unheard of luxury before
Rural Free Delivery. Among the passengers that day on the stage was Jim Rice, a
genial Irish bachelor who in time became one of our closest friends...

As we drove along, about ten miles from Denhoff, we could see in the distance a
