building being moved. Our driver told us it was being taken to the site of
McClusky, probably the first building in what soon became a growing town. Now we
were rolling along over a rolling prairie - not a tree in sight - only low
places filled with water which to a Missourian looked like ponds, but where the
grasses grew taller and were called sloughs. After several hours we came to a
house and barn where the Pickard family lived and where we stopped to change
horses. The Pickards were to become our neighbors, only seven miles from the
ranch - so now the ride took on a new interest, watching for the first glimpse
of our new home. Up hill and down hill - low hills - not like the bluffs along
the Mississippi, but still high enough to hide anything on the other side.

Then all of a sudden we were upon it, there it stood, the house I had been
dreaming about for months. Oh no! It wasn't much to look at - but I had been
told that many times. It had only been painted to me in drab colors but it was
what I wanted. The house itself meant little to me. We were going to make a
home. I can see it now, a two-room, story and a half house, with a lean-to shed.
It was painted red. The trail through the grass which was called a road ran in
front of the house a few feet from the two front doors, one in the shed and one
in the house proper. The ground in front sloped all the way down to where a
large low unpainted barn and the corral stood.

The buildings had been built by a squatter which meant by a man who had never
owned the land but had settled down with his family, built the house, and grazed
his cattle for miles around. When my father-in-law had bought the land, he had
bought the house also, he paid what everyone considered a very high price. I
think it was $1,500. The man was 'old' Jim Avery. The Averys had gone when we
arrived but a neighboring homesteader, Jim Estep, came out of the house. If I
remember correctly he was looking after a few cattle Jim (Avery) had left and
some stock we had sent up from home. Only youths and a couple very much in love
could have walked undismayed into that house, but undismayed we were. An old
cook stove and a table were in the shed. In the house there was a mattress on
the floor. By the stove there was a box of cow chips - our only fuel.

Although I spent eighteen years in North Dakota I don't remember ever seeing
bakers' bread in the stores. I must have tried my luck at biscuits - or maybe
Jim did. I have to confess, I had never cooked. When Helm had been there in the
Spring he had bought a big farm wagon and while he was at home he had shipped up
some horses and mules - so we were expecting to take the long trek to Denhoff
the next day to bring out the little furniture we would need until the hand-me
downs arrived by freight, which had been sent from Missouri.

In my trunk were bed linens so I proceeded to make up the mattress on the floor.
All my life I have been unfortunate in going thro life with my eyes half shut -
maybe this time it was not unfortunate - I didn't see that the mattress was
alive with bed bugs. The next morning we carried it out and burned it. We went
back the 25 miles to Denhoff next day, on the high seat of that big farm wagon,
and came back with bed, mattress, table and chairs and probably food of a sort.
I remember we could not bring meat. There was no ice, but bacon and ham we could
have and of course there were potatoes. North Dakota raised splendid potatoes.
One of the real thrills I had was when I learned one could make milk gravy with
bacon grease. I'm sure a loaf of bread had never been baked in my Missouri home,
we Missourians lived on hot biscuits, so I presume. I baked biscuits three times
a day and they must have been pretty poor as I can't remember ever having made
them at home. I had a cookbook but little talent.

A week from the day we married was the 4th of July and we decided to celebrate
in Washburn. Washburn was 25 miles from the ranch, the other end of the stage
line. It was older than Denhoff, with a fairly good small hotel, a bank,
lumberyard and people we afterwards learned to know and enjoy. We got a room at
the hotel, I dressed in my taffeta going-away dress and in the evening, before
the big day, we went out to see the town and the sights. We met up with a
nursery salesman and his wife who were staying at the hotel and formed a
pleasant threesome."

There were many Indians in Washburn and she thought about the tales of the
pioneers who had been scalped, but remembered that day was long past. She wrote,
"These people had come in from a nearby reservation to aid in the celebration
and sell their wares. In fact, the dances they put on from time to time were the
highlights of the show. A large platform had been built for a public dance to be
given in the evening and by the time we arrived it was crowded. With our new
acquaintances we found seats to watch and of course we danced... Among the
people we met on that trip were Mr. and Mrs. Funk. He was the banker and Helm
opened our little account and became acquainted. He invited us to his home where
we met his wife and we all became congenial friends. On future trips we always
went there for a visit. Years later, after we had towns close to the ranch and
we didn't have to go into Washburn anymore, Mr. Funk was mysteriously shot and
killed. It was all hush-hush and no one ever paid for the crime.

Another trip I recall that summer was the long ride to the Missouri River to get
fence posts. Mr. and Mrs. Avery had come back to the ranch to get something they
had left and we decided to go back with them to the new home they had just made
on the river, 25 or 30 miles away. By that time we had bought a western pony,
which I was riding around the country. We decided I would ride that until I
became tired and then Mrs. Avery would take over and I would get in the wagon
with old Jim. Helm was riding on the frame of the wagon so he would be able to
bring back more poles. Off we went, an all day trip. I loved riding. After a
while I decided to rest in the wagon and Mrs. Avery took the pony. Away she
went, she must have been sixty at the time and as I remember her, I think she
must have been a pretty woman with her curly hair but by the time I knew her the
hard life she had led showed in her face.

We finally arrived, it was good to see trees again... We stayed several days
while Helm cut fence poles and I enjoyed having food someone else cooked and a
woman to visit with. Then came the long trek home. This time I rode the pony,
all the way, 30 miles...

I think it was about the middle of July when the Davenport family arrived and
life changed for me. Up until that time my only other feminine contact had been
a white haired old lady, a Mrs. Estep, who was proving up a homestead a little
over a half mile from the ranch. She used to drop in every other day to get her
mail which the stage had brought and we would have a cup of tea and talk about
Missouri...

Then I looked out one day and saw children playing. A little nine year old boy
who told me his name was Willie came up to visit me. I learned there were nine
children and their parents. They had come to Gus Morgan's homestead about
three-fourth mile away where Mr. Davenport would do carpentry work and they were
living in a tent. In conversing with Willie and asking him about the family he
said, 'Ruthie is our baby and mamma says she is our sunshine on a cloudy day.' I
thought then Mrs. Davenport must be a mighty nice person. I soon met her and all
the family. There were three boys in their teens and Helm hired them to help
with haying and they moved into our hayloft to sleep. Dora (Jorgenson) was the
oldest girl and although she was only fourteen she knew much more about the
culinary art than I did. So I hired her to help. I'm sure the men on the place
were thankful for the Davenports because now our meals were vastly improved.
Mrs. Davenport baked our bread, made doughnuts, and taught me to cook many
things I had not tried before... I remember looking out of the window in a
storm and here came Mrs. Davenport and all the children drenched to the skin.
The wind had almost blown their tent over and they had run a long ways for
shelter.

The only work that could be done that year was putting up hay... After the big
loft was filled, haystacks were made here and there on the prairie. The days
were hot, but there was usually a breeze and if one could find shade the weather
was pleasant. So, afternoons would find us sitting in the shade made by the
house, waiting for the stage to go by. The Davenport boys and Helm would take
wagons and drive the thirty miles to Wilton to get lignite coal, which we used
for cooking the year around and for heating in the winter...

Toward the end of the summer Father Davidson came to visit us. He was there at
the time of the big prairie fire... One morning when I walked into the yard to
throw out my dishwater and saw smoke in the distance I immediately ran to the
barn to tell the men. Helm got on this pony to ride toward it to talk with men
in the neighborhood. He come back to start work protecting the buildings and the
haystacks. Two deep furrows were plowed around each building and each haystack
about 12 or 15 feet apart then the grass between the furrows was burned. The
wind was high and bringing the fire straight toward us. It was afternoon before
it reached us, leaving the whole earth black and ugly. The men fought all day
and into the night, even following it to help others on the second day. They
fought it with wet blankets carried between two horses. Sometimes the trails
(there were no roads) would stop it. Other places where the grass was high it
would jump the trails and go merrily on. I saw many prairie fires during the
years I lived in North Dakota, but the first was the worst. It had come from the
north probably 50 or 60 miles north of the ranch and it burned at least 30 miles
south before it was finally put out... Now with no grass to hide the rocks it
was indeed a discouraging looking sight... Helm had been disillusioned even
before the fire... That year many young men had come to North Dakota to file on
homesteads... Now Helm had filed on a homestead which joined the ranch on the
north and he and his father had been discussing plans for a house to be built
there and were we would live for fourteen months. The country was settling so
fast (Helm) realized that any place where one had cattle would have to be fenced
to keep them out of the homesteader's crops... So they decided to keep only one
section (Section 5) and the homestead.

I think the thing I missed most in those early days was not having a church. I
didn't like awaking on Sunday morning to find it was just another day, a day
like all the rest, except after chores were done, the men were not busy...

One of the neighboring homesteaders was an old Swede named Charlie Larson. He
lived in a sod shack about three miles away and he was the earliest settler we
knew. In his early years he had been a cowboy, ridden the range, and was as
bowlegged as you expected a cowboy to be...

Hospitality was as much a part of North Dakota as prairie grass. I remember our
many visits to the Jeardeaus. They lived on top of a hill... Helm had met the
Jeardeaus when he had spent a little time in Dakota before we were married...
One Sunday he had suggested we drive over to see (them)... It was just a seven
mile drive and I wore a simply-made yellow dimity that was one of the few new
dresses I had in my trousseau. Mr. and Mrs. Jeardeau were educated, had been
connected with a college in Wisconsin and had decided after their marriage to
try farming in Dakota... They had gone on a bicycle trip on their honeymoon.
They had built a better house than others in our part of the world and I was so
impressed with their shelves of books, which I afterwards enjoyed... We were so
heartily welcomed we stayed for two or three days. They had three big-eyed
little girls who... immediately called me the bride with the beautiful yellow
satin dress. There had been four little girls but the youngest had died and been
buried there on the hillside. There had been no minister so with a few neighbors
gathered around, Mr. Jeardeau had read the Episcopal burial service himself.

Ten miles across the prairie to the East... was Mr. and Mrs. Clodfelter and
their food (was) just the best ever. They were a gay household and I like to
remember the fun they had whether there was company or not... So our first
summer passed and autumn came. The homestead house must be built before the
cold, cold winter we had heard so much about.

Father and my step-mother came for a visit - their only one. I can't recall much
about it but I'm sure they must have felt the ranch was a rather desolate place.
I feel sure also they must have sensed how truly contented and happy I was. I do
remember that when they went home, Father wrote an article about his trip for
the Morning Journal and wrote glowingly of our fine livestock especially Beauty,
our driving horse. Later he sent me a red wheeled rubber tired buggy, which
created quite a sensation on the prairie. I remember, too, he said he would buy
the paint if we would paint the new homestead house white and trim it in real. I
feel sure that was because our house in Troy was painted that way and that was
where, no doubt, he had spent his happiest years...

When cold weather approached, the Davenports left their tent home and moved into
Mr. Hunt's homestead shack and built a bunk house for the male members of the
family. As crowded as they were, they could always take care of me when Helm and
the Davenport boys made the long trip to the Wilton coal mines for our fuel.

The homestead house was much better built than the ranch house, but was the same
plan. (There were) two rooms on the first floor and the half story above, one
large room. A range in the kitchen and a coal burner in the bedroom-living room
kept us very comfortable in spite of the 50 below zero weather which was
reported at one time. We had no well and brought all the water from the ranch
until the big snow arrived about Thanksgiving time and after that we melted snow
to help out.

We both walked to the ranch every day, three-fourth of a mile away. I sat with
Mrs. Gunderson, a dear old Danish lady, while Helm and Oscar did the chores.
They had moved into the ranch house while we were proving up our homestead, but
(they) had not built his shack. My, what lonely lives those young men who were
proving up land led. The country was by this time full of them. Young men who
had drifted west and who had found they could have 160 acres of land for almost
nothing and stayed. The country was dotted with the many shacks and tiny barns
which the Government required. I doubt as I look back if any one of them ever
made enough out of that 160 acres to pay them for the lonely winter days and
nights they experienced at that time. Their only reading was Sears Roebuck and
Montgomery Ward catalogues which they joked about and called their 'wish books.'

I think our first blizzard... came about Thanksgiving and it was as ferocious as
we had been told. For three days the winds howled, the snow blew, and we were
unable to see objects more than a few feet away. Green as we were, Helm
announced he had to go to the ranch to see that the stock was properly cared for
and I refused to be left alone. Buffeted by the wind, the snow freeing our eyes
shut, I walked behind Helm, clinging to him but letting his body protect me in a
way. Oscar was aghast when we arrived at the ranch. In fact, all the neighbors
were when they heard of our foolish expedition. Too many lives had been lost in
blizzards for old timers to take such chances. We learned later the Davenports
had not even gone to the barn, right there on the place, to feed their stock and
others had used string to guide them home after reaching their barns. I will say
we only made the one trip. The other two days we were content to sit by the fire
and let the winds roar.

The white world which came to Dakota in those days and lasted until April was a
beautiful clean world in spite of the inconveniences it caused. We practically
lived on the canned goods which we had ordered by the cases from Sears Roebuck.
Our evenings were happy. We took many magazines and I read aloud every night -
or we played double solitaire, or perhaps I played alone...

We had another neighbor, Harry Andrews, who was proving up a homestead a mile
away. He was our only frequent guest. I might look out the window and see him
plodding through the snow - he would stay several days and then one day I would
see him going over the hill toward his home. He always came and left without
formalities but we would enjoy having someone else to talk to and visit with.

When the snow came, transportations changed from buggies and wagons to bob
sleds. They were homemade affairs, a wooden box with two seats and a very high
back to protect you from wind and cold. This was placed on runners and was a lot
more comfortable than it sounds. The bottom of the sled was covered with hay to
make it warmer and most everyone had fur robes of some kind to cover up with. We
bought a compact charcoal burner also to put at our feet so when we did venture
out we did not suffer from the cold. The men wore sheep lined coats and fur caps
and sometimes I would borrow Helm's clothes to put over my own.

In late February the unexpected happened. The baby we were expecting the last of
March began to show signs of wanting to make an earlier appearance. We were two
frightened children, I say children because we were both so ignorant of anything
pertaining to childbirth. We made our way to the ranch house so I could be near
Mrs. Gunderson and Oscar could go for the doctor in McClusky, 14 miles over the
snow covered prairie. Poor Mrs. Gunderson was more frightened than we were and
the timid soul refused to have anything to do with us so I sent for Mr.
Davenport. Why Mr. you ask? Because Mrs. Davenport was expecting a baby any day,
and I had been told it was not good for an expectant mother to be with another
in labor. After nine children Mrs. Davenport did not hold with such tales and
here she came. Was I glad to see her! The doctor, dear Dr. Brown, a young man
not long out of college arrived in the wee hours and laughed at me for sending
for Mr. Davenport. Why did I do it, because I felt the father of nine children
knew more than we did, especially when Mrs. Gunderson wouldn't come in the room.

The Doctor decided the baby would probably not arrive until the expected time
but said I must stay in bed for the last month... I refused to let Dr. Brown
leave. He said, 'Didn't I think he had any other patients?' and I said 'yes, but
I've got you and they haven't,' so he did stay for a day and a night. He
remembered having heard that a registered nurse had gone through McClusky last
evening on the train enroute to the new town of Mercer, which was only seven
miles from the ranch so Helm went for her.

Dear Annetta McFadden, who became my very, very close friend of years standing,
came into my life and was with us six weeks. After her coming we moved back to
the homestead and there Mary Frances was born on March 23 (1906)...

While all this was happening, my father and Mrs. Kaebler (stepmother) decided to
take a trip to New Orleans, because he was feeling so badly. While there he
became worse and the New Orleans doctor told him he would have to have an
appendectomy. Father wrote me he wanted to go to Mayos at Rochester and when the
baby was old enough we would meet there. When he got to St. Louis and saw
another doctor, he was told he... had tuberculosis... something he had suspected
all along. He went home and when Mary Frances was five weeks old we started for
Missouri. Helm was so lonely that as soon as he put in his crop he joined me.

During the next year things began to change. Now Mercer became 'our town' -
trips to McClusky were rare and Denhoff and Washburn were towns of the past as
far as we were concerned. In no time at all Mercer had three lumberyards, two
banks and two general stores. Things were booming. It also had a 'Blind Pig', a
place where one could buy liquor in a prohibition state.

George McFadden, a cousin of Annetta's, owned one of the general stores and he
talked to Helm about taking a partner. Helm wrote to his close friend back home,
Ed Plowman, and Ed came up to clerk in the store and look things over. Nothing
came of it, so at Christmas Ed came out to spend the Yule time with us and
stayed for a year and a half. Harry Andrews joined us much of the time and I
usually was able to get a young girl to help with the work and with the baby.

The following summer Father Davidson came for a visit and later my sister, who
was married and living in Oklahoma. About that time the new depot was finished
in Mercer and that caused for a celebration which meant a dance. Ed and sister
decided to go. Days were long in North Dakota and it was almost ten o'clock
before darkness came. That meant people worked later and the few social events
started late. So they danced the night through, drove a team of ponies back and
arrived home while we were eating breakfast, thoroughly shocking Father
Davidson.

Later, dancing the nights through was not unusual. We held square dances at the
different houses, small as they were. Mike was good on the fiddle and someone
else 'called'. I learned to say 'Hey' with the best of them but not your
grandfather. I guess he had too much dignity... We spent many evenings, later,
dancing in the dining room to the phonograph. I particularly remember dancing
with Ama Biggs to Alexander's Ragtime Band - a new hit.

Two dances in Mercer I particularly remember, not because of the dances
themselves, but our accommodations afterwards. We wouldn't drive back to the
ranch in the later hours so one night my baby and I made a bed of new comforters
to be sold and slept very comfortably on the counter of McFadden's store.
Another night we, with Mrs. McFadden, spent the night in Mr. Rice's grain
elevator. That wasn't so pleasant, I feared all night I'd drop into a deep bin
of some kind which seemed bottomless. McFadden's store was next door to the pool
hall and one night Mrs. McFadden had slept little because some drunk was making
everyone dance by shooting at their feet.

In December 1907 Mary Frances and I moved into Mercer to be near Miss McFadden
when our second child was expected. She had not felt she could come back to the
ranch to be with me, so we had taken a little furniture and fixed up some rooms
in the second floor of the Section House - a two storied house the railroad had
built for its section foremen. Here Nettie (McFadden), baby, and I lived and
George (McFadden) took his meals with us. Helm came in often and spent the night
and always on Sundays. Now this baby was slow as our first was fast and we
waited a whole month for her arrival. When she did come it was with a bang and
the Doctor arrived when Rose was four hours old. Nettie had known her job and
all was well. Helm was not with us and things were happening so fast, in the
middle of the night, I didn't send for him. He never forgave me. When Rose was
two weeks old my father died (December 27, 1908) and I was unable to go to him.
In fact, in his last days he was more upset by fear that I would try to come,
than by death, which he knew was approaching.

The following spring we did over the ranch house and few material things ever
gave me more pleasure. We added two rooms on the back and made the shed lean-to
into a bedroom. We covered the living room and dining room floors with linoleum
that looked like hardwood, the kitchen with a blue linoleum and used matting in
the bedrooms. The walls were papered, a wide door cut between living room and
the bedroom. To me it looked very spacious and grand. Outside we built a front
porch and painted it all yellow."

On June 5, 1908, The Mercer Telegram reported, "J.H. Davidson is having a
hundred acre field broken by a steam plow." Juanita wrote, "I loved watching the
men going into the fields in the spring mornings, four men each with a team of
four fine horses. It was that spring too that we dug the deep well. The well
drillers were there many weeks, in fact, for a while ten men sat at our table
three times a day. Of course, I had a hired girl, who was always one of our
family. It was then in the early morning that I learned to drink coffee. 1910
was a big year. The country was growing up. We had many neighbors and the young
men in Mercer had gone back to their hometowns and brought out brides, four of
them, so we began to visit one another for coffee in the afternoons.

        Photo: (From left) Mr. and Mrs. Jesse Kline, Mrs. Pauline Weist, Ed
        Plowman, and Mary Frances Davidson.

In the country, we started a Sunday School in the school house, had young
peoples meetings in the homes on Sunday evening, so Sunday at last became a day
of worship and was not like every other day in the week. It was later Rev. Ira
Sapp from Washington, D.C. was sent out to contact members of the Christian
Church to try to establish an organization. He was a well educated man, very
genial, a very good preacher, but not the pious type I looked for in a minister.

It was in February we had the big baptizing. In his work among the families of
people who had formerly belonged to the Christian Church, Rev. Sapp had
contacted eight young people who wanted to be baptized. Of course there was no
baptistery, - there was not even a church, there were no streams in our part of
Dakota. So our large watering trough seemed the only place available. All winter
long it had been frozen solid. Each morning a place in the ice was chopped out
and filled with water for the stock. It was about 25 below zero when the big day
arrived. Rev. Sapp was leaving soon for Washington and these young people wanted
to be immersed. Helm put the men to chopping out the ice, expecting to fill it
with fresh water and put in a tank heater to warm it up a bit. The work was
slower then he anticipated and by the time the ice was out and the tank filled
no one could wait for the heater. Rev. Sapp stood in the water while he baptized
all eight. As each one would come up out of the water he was wrapped in a
blanket and hurried into a bobsled and driven the short distance to the house. I
met each one at the door, handed the blanket back to the driver for the next
one, and rushed this one beside a stove - boys in one room, girls in another -
and do you know the Lord looked after everyone but me, not a one of the young
people or Rev. Sapp took cold and I had one of the few bad colds I ever had in
my life."

Another religious ceremony took place in the Davidson home, when Helm performed
a wedding. "Helm had been made a squire and was eligible to perform marriages.
What started out in a joking way finally became a serious affair. Helm married
Bertha Ness and Vern Anson, using the Episcopal wedding service and prayers. We
had invited a large crowd. I well remember the turkeys, the oysters, and cakes;
and they stayed until it was almost time to do chores.

It was in 1910 that Ella Deal, an old friend from my boarding school days came
to visit us... Five brides came to Mercer that summer and afternoon coffees were
plenteous. Mercer had been settled mostly by Scandinavians, who I found most
congenial. They were most hospitable and no one ever left without coffee.
Usually there was a cake or cookies, but if not we had bread and jelly with our
coffee...

We lived in North Dakota until 1923 and even that late I don't remember anyone
trying to use an automobile in our part of the state in winter. Wagons, buggies
and cars were put away and only vehicles on runners were used.

Our Christmases were always gay. We had made great preparations for them. As I
look back now I don't see how I was ever able to do all I did. Mother Davidson
sent us huge boxes of gifts, fruit that she had put up for us during the summer,
as well as toys, clothes, etc. that we opened on Christmas Eve. Then the next
morning we had the stockings and our gifts to each other. Our first Christmas,
the Davenports, twelve in all, and our bachelor neighbors came for turkey at
noon and we had gifts for all. In a few years we had other friends with whom we
had become intimate and from then until we left Dakota, the Jeardeaus, McFaddens
and the Plowmans always spent Christmas Day with us. We had both a turkey and a
goose and... we always had supper too before we left for the Sunday School
program which I was always in charge of... After we moved into Mercer, I found
all the stray bachelors who had no family and they came in on Christmas Eve for
baked hen and cranberries. Our Scandinavian friends were dining at the same time
on ludefish and leftsa.

In 1911 a small school had been built about a mile from the ranch house and the
new teacher boarded with us. She and our little Mary Frances trudged through the
snow or Helm would take them on the bobsled. That only lasted a year and next
year we moved into Mercer for the winter months, so our daughter could have a
proper education. Our four room house was tiny, the only one in town for rent,
but I found it quite a treat to be close to people again. I had heard that Mrs.
Lierboe, the wife of the banker at Turtle Lake... had organized a Study Club
there, so I went up to see her and asked just how they had worked it out - with
no library and very few books. I came home and called about a dozen ladies to
come to my house and talk about forming an organization. The Mercer Study Club
prospered from the first and is still in the community. We attended state and
district meetings and in that way enjoyed the friendship of people throughout
the state.

In 1913 in the little house in Mercer, Franklin was born... he was a buster,
weighing eleven pounds...

When we moved back to the ranch for the summer I had an excellent girl from
Norway live with us. She took so much care of Franklin that I was able to go and
come as much as I cared to. Helm had taken Pete Peterson into partnership with
him in the hog business as a sideline. They both prospered. I remember how proud
we all were when our hogs topped the market.

Pete and Josephine were married and I lost my excellent help, and Pete decided
to farm for himself. Sometime, along the way, we had bought another half
section, so now we owned the ranch, 640 acres, the homestead which we had proved
up and lived on for 14 months and paid Uncle Sam $1.25 an acres. Then the new
320 acres which we called the North Farm. Helm had 21 miles of fence and
Hereford cattle. We built a much nicer house on the north farm than the old
ranch house. After spending many winters in Mercer we bought the (Dr.) Deming
house.

Dr. Deming had located in Mercer about 1914. He and his wife, Mary, were really
delightful people... While Doctor lived in Mercer he had made a frame house
into a hospital. He had one registered nurse. I was there with typhoid fever,
when at one time I had a fever of 106. My recovery was rapid, however, later
Helm had typhoid and was sick for three months. An abcess formed just below his
lung and Doctor said an operation was necessary. Dr. Deming had tried to lance
the abcess but Helm had had a sinking spell. Doctor and Helm were such close
friends that Doctor said he wanted to send for a doctor from Jamestown. He
arrived on the evening train. We had been successful in getting a nurse and the
operation was performed on the kitchen table. I had sent for my good friend,
Auntie Jeardeau, to be with me. I remember Ed Plowman stood by also. Friends
took care of my children and for weeks Milla, who lived with us, the nurse, and
I were alone. The only people we saw were Dr. Deming and Mill's beau, George
Krug, who she afterwards married, and who came every night.

Finally, the nurse had to leave as she had promised her services in a
confinement case and I took over as nurse. The abcess had to drain every day, by
pulling out the bandages and letting the pus flow. I noticed if that were not
done, Helm's mind would become confused and he was not himself. So when Doctor
was delivering a baby one night and couldn't come, I decided to dress the wound
myself. I sterilized the prober as I had seen Doctor do and pulled gently at the
packed bandages and the pus began to flow. When the old bandage was all out I
began packing a fresh one in. I'm sure the probe went in ten inches, but I
packed it tight and my husband was himself again. Dr. Deming said I had done so
well there was no use in his coming to do it, so until the last of May (he had
gone to bed February 22) I put the dressings in. When it had healed until we
could only go in about an inch, Doctor said it was healed and we were through.
How my friends stood by that long period of watchful waiting. I will never know.
Father Davidson had come when we were all so uneasy and he stayed until Helm was
almost well.

In 1917 Dr. Deming joined the Army. Mary left, and we bought their house. It was
a modern bungalow... but had no plumbing... The only house with a bathroom in
town was a two story white frame house Jim Rice had built for his bride... A
little later Ole Hjelle built a modern bungalow with all modern conveniences and
was the pride of Mercer. We installed some sort of chemical toilet in our attic
so we wouldn't have to go out in the cold.

It was in 1917 that Helm came riding a black Shetland pony into the kitchen one
evening. He had bought him from some gypsies going through the country and we
immediately named him Gypsy. He was about Franklin's age then and he lived long
enough for Franklin's children to ride him... I remember so well in the early
years of driving (my team) the seven miles into Mercer when it was 25 below
zero. I had gone in to buy food for a party we were going to have and when I
reached Mercer the town was deserted. I spent the afternoon playing whist in Ed
Plowman's real estate office with George McFadden and Mr. Jeardeau. Then Mr.
Jeardeau rode back to the ranch with me and spent the night.

In 1920 while living in the Deming house Helm Jr. was born. The Deming house was
in the same yard as the Plowmans, and we always felt the Plowmans were almost
part of our family. Auntie Plowman had been Mary Frances first school teacher, a
most attractive girl from Minnesota and I learned to love her dearly. Her older
boy was four years old when Helm Jr. was born.

Our years spent in the Deming house were happy years, perhaps the happiest of
our lives. We were so close to so many dear friends, the Plowmans, the Hedahls,
the Ole Hjelles, the Rices, the McFaddens, the Washburns, and so many others. We
danced at the town hall and attended some horrifying picture shows. One night we
paid 75 cents apiece to hear a radio that didn't work very well. We attended the
Norwegian Lutheran Church which was held in the school house.

Before we had a preacher in Mercer, one would come from Turtle Lake and often he
was late. The Lutherans sat patiently and said not a word until he arrived...
Even in a school house we had learned to be reverent and when the minister
arrived he found a deep quiet that made one realize we were there to worship.
Our Ladies Aid was a very active organization that met once a month. That was
really a gala occasion. Each lady brought a covered dish, and after a business
meeting in the afternoon held in a home, we prepared a supper and all the
husbands and children arrived and ate heartily and paid for their suppers.

The men too found time for their own fun, which was usually a poker game that
lasted well into the night. I remember one night when I couldn't sleep, I
decided I'd go get my husband. So I put on a dressing gown and started out. Just
before I reached Jim Rice's office where the game was in progress the game broke
up and I scampered like a scared rabbit to get home before my husband. Those
poker games were the bane of my existence and I always blamed the other fellow
for enticing my husband into them - most unjustly. Helm loved to play.

Soon after the Study Club was organized we decided we wanted a woman on the
school board. All of us went to work very vigorously to elect Mrs. Rice. The men
of the community objected to having a woman on the board and every man in town
turned out to vote against it. I don't remember now whether that was just before
or after we were given sufferage. Our candidate was defeated. Next year without
telling anyone, not even me, all the women in town went to the polls, but the
men, not realizing a woman was running didn't go and I was elected to the school
board. I felt some pride in my job. I had more time than the men and I went
thoroughly into the records of our candidates for the teachers jobs and we did
have some very good teachers. Another thing, my Mary Frances and Evelyn Knutson
had finished the 8th grade and the town voted to put in one grade higher. We did
that for the next four years of high school and I worked seriously on the
curriculum for each following year. When the girls graduated they were able to
enter Jamestown College without losing any credits. My weakness was finances,
and I left that to the men while they left the hiring of the teachers to me...

A teacher usually boarded at our house and I wouldn't want to write my story
without telling about Mary Flynn, a delightful Irish girl who lived with us
several years. The second year she came back I wrote her that Mr. Davidson
thought our house was too small and it would be better if she found another
place to board. When she came she could stay with us until she found a home for
the winter. Her sister came with her and after a few days I asked her if she had
found a place and she said, 'Yes ma'am - and I asked where and she said 'here. I
couldn't go any where else.' It was during the war and her sweetheart knew he
would be leaving soon. Many evenings Mary played and everybody gathered around
the piano and we sang, 'It's a Long Way to Tipperarry - Ka-Ka-Katie - and all
the popular war songs.

Then Ole left for Europe and died in England during the flu epidemic. Mary
didn't want to come back to Mercer the next year with Ole gone and I was
surprised later to have a letter from her saying she would like to come back for
Christmas. Over what happened next I am still puzzled. The town gave her a royal
welcome and she seemed happy enough. I soon realized that she had never realized
Ole was gone until she had dinner with his family and was told his telephone
business had been sold. I slept with her that night and we talked until almost
morning. When she got up she said she had decided she wanted to go home so we
put her on the train and that was the last time we saw Mary. When she got to
Jamestown where she had to change cars she went straight to the hospital, sent
for a priest, asked for the last rites of her church and lay down and died. The
good sisters were as puzzled as we were, although the terrible flu epidemic was
raging everywhere, she had seemed well when she came into the hospital...

I would often go down to McClusky to spend the day with the (Dr.) Browns. Our
two daily trains were one going down to Carrington in the morning and returning
about six in the evenings. I think it was the winter of 1917 when we had the
terrible blizzard and we were without a train for six weeks. The snow plow would
open the track for miles then it would snow again and fill up the tunnel it had
made the night before. We had no mail, no papers, and all the news were could
get of the outside world was what our station agent could pick up over the
telegraph wires. That was when our country broke diplomatic relations with
Germany. It was all a horrible experience. Our good friend from Turtle Lake had
been operated on and died in Minneapolis and his poor wife waited six weeks
before the body could be brought home. Soon after the road was open I went down
to spend the day with the Browns and for many miles the snow was piled so high
it was like riding through a tunnel, it was very dark. The first time the rotor
plow tried to go through it had thrown dead cattle and sheep in all directions."

Mrs. Davidson told about a seven year drought, and eventually the ranch was
sold. The Davidsons moved back to Hannibal, Missouri in 1923 to a dairy farm.
Looking back, Mrs. Davidson wrote, "Since he (Helm) had been a young boy he had
talked of owning a ranch and branding his cattle with his initials, J-D, and I
am glad he was able to fulfill that dream." Today Lyle Brewster owns the
Davidson Ranch and only one building remains. John Helm Davidson died from
cancer in 1935, and Juanita died June 21, 1975. They are buried at Hannibal,
Missouri.

My Fourteen Months on the Claim By Mrs. Hattie Ovre, who homesteaded by Brush
Lake with her husband Krogh.

We left Iowa the latter part of March, came to Balfour, N.D., by rail in an
Emigrant car. The car was packed with homesteaders, going out to file on land
and get rich quick. Just so one got a title to 160 acres of land, we would all
be rich. That was the idea of the homesteaders sot here was quite a rush for a
homestead.

We drove from Balfour on a cold windy day, the latter part of March (1902),
stopped at a big ranch house where the bath houses are now, till we got our
shack built. (We) moved into a 12 × 12 shack, as we called it, with my husband
and two little sons. Had three miles to my nearest neighbors and them I had
never seen. The grade west of the school house was all lake then, we could
hardly cross with a lumber wagon. Some more homesteaders moved in, some had
horses along, there were four neighbors that had each a team. There were horse
thieves around. So the boys took turns to watch their horses during the night.
They kept it up a week and nothing happened. One night when they were all
sleeping, the horses disappeared. They had a ranchman we stayed with, and they
had to pay him $25 to get them back. He brought them the next day, as they did
not know where to find them.

The homesteaders were moving fast now, and they were all nice people. We were
all there to made good and help each other. My nearest neighbor was a family by
the name of Roberts. Most of the others were bachelors and we started to bake
bread for them. The other provisions they had, would keep, but bread wouldn't. I
had a little laundry stove, with a drum in the pipe, where I could bake 3 loaves
at a time. I baked 6 to 9 loaves a day and sold them. I was glad to have it to
do as there was nothing else to do. My husband and his brother (Sevald) had
built a big hotel at Harvey the fall before, and had to go back to finish it so
they left for Harvey the latter part of May and I was holding the claim down, as
the saying was. It went alright till the middle of June, a big rain started
about 1 o'clock. I was glad it started so early it would be over by night, but
no, it got worse. The worst electric storm I had seen. About 1 o'clock the door
flew open, and the house just shook. I was sure the shack was going, I got the
door closed again, and I wrapped the boys in quilts, and put them down on the
cellar floor. I sat on the steps until morning. It rained all the next day too.

Fourth of July came and we tried to celebrate. I baked a white frosted cake.
Mrs. Mc had buns, and we fixed up a picnic lunch. Mr. Mc hitched his team up to
the lumber wagon, and we drove down to Blue Lake, and had a picnic. Came home at
10 o'clock in a nice moonlight eve, and really enjoyed the day.

There was a store and post office at Turtle Lake, 4 miles further west then it
is now. We used to get our mail there. Mrs. Mc and I used to go and get the
mail.

Latter part of July my husband came home, and we went down to Washburn to buy a
cow, from a man by the name of Sunstrum. Mrs. S couldn't speak English, so she
talked Swede, and I talked Norwegian, and we had a nice visit. They invited us
to stay over night, and we did. We went to Washburn the next morning and got
provisions for another month, and got our cow home.

At that time County Supt. Lofts, from Washburn, came up to visit us. We got the
people together, organized the township, and had school in Sevald's shack later
in the fall. Sevald's shack was the first school house in the Township (Wise).

We had our first blizzard the 12th of September. I got my cow and calf up to our
hay stack so I saved them. But here were lots of them that lost cattle in that
storm. One man lost his life going out to look for his cattle. He walked 30
miles before he gave up. They found him the next summer.

My husband came home the day after the storm. We built a bedroom and a coal shed
onto our house, and fixed up for the winter. We had a long hard winter, started
to snow November 1st, and 2 to 4 feet of snow on the level. There was so much
tall prairie grass then the snow stayed. It kept on snowing and blizzarding all
winter. We had 5 steps in the snow from our door step up to the level of the
snow, and it stayed till the 11th of April, Easter Sunday. That was the first
warm day. We were invited over to Charley Wises for Easter dinner. He lived on
the peninsula. We walked down on the ice in the morning. It was so nice by
evening, it was all water, so we had to stay till the next day.

I was expecting an increase (baby) soon. I did intend to go to Harvey to the
hospital, but as the winter stayed on so long, and when the weather was settled,
I didn't dare make the trip. We got a lady Dr. From up northwest before anything
happened. So on the evening of the 3rd of May, Martha was born. I had provided
for a layette, amongst that, the all necessary safety pins, but the lady didn't
have any use for them. When the time came for her to dress the baby, she had
found some common pins and commenced to put them in the band and diapers and all
over. How I begged her to use the safety pins. She told me the others were fine,
when one knew how to put them in, and she must have known, because I never found
any marks from them. But they disappeared when I got my hands on them. On top of
that, my brother and sister back home kept writing my father was dying from
cancer, and he was begging for me to come back. I couldn't leave the homestead
till June 2nd.

One morning a man stopped with 3 of the nicest and biggest horses I have ever
seen. He wanted breakfast. I gave it to him, but we knew he was a horse thief.
He had stolen the horses up by Anamoose and traveled all night. The next day the
man he had stolen the horse from came trailing. He told us he had paid $700 for
the horses that spring. We heard later he caught him and the thief paid the
penalty. He was hung. He had stolen too many.

We sent for a livery man from Balfour to come and get us. We drove halfway to
Balfour the first day, stopped at Mrs. McCousin and got to Balfour the next day.
Got home the day after my father died. I moved into the home I had left, but it
didn't seem the same. It seemed to be something about these Great Plains out
here that one couldn't forget. The country did look nice in those days. There
seemed to be a future in it, something to accomplish, something to live for.
Three years later when the railroad was extended from Denhoff to Turtle Lake, I
was perfectly willing to come back, and it was never regretted by me.

Ruth Christensen's Reminiscences By Pat Christensen Mohrbacher

"I was born in the hospital in Mercer on July 14, 1916. I was told I weighed 12
pounds at birth. I was baptized September 10, 1916 in my mother and father's
home, which was Krogh and Hattie Ovre's. My mother's brother Rev. O.J. Akre was
the minister. His wife Mathilda, Aunt Belle and Martin Wassenberg, and Papa's
brother Sevald Ovre, were my sponsors. Aunt Belle was my mother's sister. There
wasn't a Lutheran Church in or near Mercer, so we went to a church north of
Turtle Lake, Saint Olaf.

"We lived 3½ miles north of Mercer and our home was about ½ mile north of Brush
Lake. I could see the cow pasture and a big hill from my window, where I liked
to go coasting. I remember once I was coasting with my brother Harley who was
six years older than I, and Leslie, who was eight years older. Leslie put me on
the little sled and gave me a push to get started. Harley was to hold up the
bottom wires of the fence so I could coast through. Well, he almost forgot, and
when I came close he hurried to do that, but not quite high enough. The result
was I got under but the wire caught my stocking cap and took it off!! How lucky
I lost only my cap, not my head. I thank God for that.

"My mother, Hattie, enjoyed participating in Our Savior's Ladies Aid and the
Mercer Study Club. She was a cheerful person who was generous and helpful to
others. She taught me to kneel by my bed and pray a Norwegian prayer and 'Now I
Lay Me Down to Sleep. My prayers were always sincere.

"My father, Krogh, was active in civic affairs. He was the clerk of Wise
Township School District in 1914. His main occupation was working as a
carpenter. He built our house, also the barn that is still on the farm. He and
Uncle Sevald built many buildings, including a number of rural schoolhouses. As
much as I remember my brothers did the farm work.

"The big red barn on the Ovre farm was built in 1917 when I was one year old. A
favorite place to play was the haymow of our big red barn when my girl friends
came to visit me. They had dances in the haymow when it was new. I remember my
mother baking and getting ready for a celebration in 1919 when my brother,
Norman, came home after serving in the Army in World War I. I was not quite 3
years old, and I remember sitting on the steps when the young people came to go
up. Mama served lunch to the guests at the proper time. In later years one lady
reminisced to me that she met her husband at one of those times, so she was
happy about that.

"My oldest brother Norman was a quiet person and almost bald. Grant was next,
and was always good to his little sister. When I visited him in Chicago in later
years, he took me on a Ferris-wheel ride, and to a Cubs baseball game at Wrigley
Field, which I enjoyed very much. My sister Martha, 12 years older, was always
good to me. She was my teacher in country and town grade schools. She was a very
strict disciplinarian. My brother Leslie was also good to me. He was very good
in music, even played in a dance orchestra some. Harley was full of fun and had
a good sense of humor."

"My grandparents had passed away before I was born. I did have a good older
friend, whom I loved very much, Alice Howell. She lived with Anfin Arneson one
mile east of us. They didn't have drinking water on their farm so Alice would
come to the Ovre place in a buggy driven by one horse for that. She gave me a
sewing box and also the book "Pinocchio." Other neighbors were Dan Mayers, Henry
Stutes, Chris and Balzar Kleingartners, Theobald Hofers, Jens Billes, and Melvin
Carlbergs.

"I was very eager to go to school when my older brothers and sister went. I, or
my mother, would pack me a lunch, and I would go and sit in our bay window seat
with a first grade reader pretending to be in school. I learned to read before I
started school.

"I went to first grade 3½ miles southwest of home at the Mayer school with my
brother Harley and sister Martha in a Model T Ford. In the winter months we had
a bobsled pulled with 2 horses. They were put in the barn during the day and fed
hay, which we had provided. I made the first and second grades in one year. My
sister, Martha, was the teacher, that's no doubt why. My third and fourth grades
I went to school in Mercer. Amy Fahlgren was my teacher. I enjoyed Miss
Fahlgren very much because she taught me things about life other than book
learning. I had my sister as my teacher again after Amy for the 5th grade in
Mercer. The next two years Martha taught me at rural Sprout's School where I
passed the 6th, 7th, and 8th grade in two years. My favorite subject was always
mathematics. I was only 12 years old when I graduated from 8th grade with
Pauline Hofer."

"I helped Mama plant and weed in the garden. When I was 8 years old I began
milking cows, by hand, of course. I was always afraid of those who tended to
kick. If I recall correctly we milked 15 cows. Papa milked 5, Harley 5, and I
milked 5. We had the cream separator in the milk room in the barn in the summer
months, but in cold weather had it in the house.

"I always counted it as a blessing that I had a good appetite. I suppose my
favorite meal when I was a child was Lutefisk and Lefsa. We had it only around
holidays and special times with my cousins, the Martin Wassenbergs.

"My favorite pets were my innumerable cats. My young friend Mary Margaret Wiest
gave me her cat when she moved away, and that mother cat had many, many kittens.
I learned to swim in Brush Lake and enjoyed that. I never mastered riding a
bike, but I tried. "I did snow ski as a teenager. When I taught the Sprout
School in 1934-1936, I would ski 2 miles up to it and home again sometimes. When
I was 12, my sister Martha gave me a pair of ice skates for Christmas. Brush
Lake was very smooth that winter and I often walked down to the lake by myself
and taught myself how to skate. A lifelong favorite activity of mine has been
playing board games, especially Scrabble and Upwords.  (Her brothers'
competition spurred her on to be a fierce table tennis competitor, also.)

"I was never in any singing activities because I never have been able to carry a
tune. My mother, I think, was the same, but Papa was an excellent singer. I sure
would sing though when I was out riding horseback after the cattle where no one
heard me. The cattle didn't complain. In 1926 my sister Martha bought a
phonograph and I liked to play records, especially sad songs."

"We saw silent movies in the Town Hall in Mercer. When I was 13 I saw the first
"Talkie" in McClusky in 1929. We got our first radio in the early 30's."

"On Sunday afternoon we would go down to Brush Lake. There was usually a
baseball game on the diamond that we enjoyed. The Mercer team played another
town's team. My brother Grant was a good player and as a family, we enjoyed that
very much. My first ride in an airplane was at Brush Lake on the 4th of July (as
a kid). I've always liked to ride in an airplane and I used to think I'd like to
pilot one.

"I always liked sports such as basketball, volleyball, and track. I was a sub on
the Mercer Girl's Basketball team my freshman year. As I really liked
basketball, my heart was almost broken when Girls basketball was outlawed in
1929. The next three years we were allowed to play only McClusky. I was center
on the team and we played two games each year. My brother, Harley, teased me and
said I played center because the ceiling was higher in the middle. Harley was 6
years older, and shorter than I, and he teased me a great deal about height and
other things.

        Photo: Ruth Christensen in her upper teens.

"When I was a senior, Minnie Seyfert, my good friend, was Editor and I was
Assistant Editor of The Cricket, the school newspaper. We both loved poetry, and
sometimes when we worked on The Cricket at night we would read poetry or waste
time in other ways. One night I didn't come home until 2:00 A.M. and my sister
Martha, who I was rooming with in Mercer, was worried sick. L.J. Totdahl was the
teacher that influenced me the most in high school. He was strict, a Christian,
and I respected him very much. He told my mother I could have done much better
in school if I had studied more. I cared about my grades, but I enjoyed my
social life too much. I was ranked fourth in my class of 11, and just missed
getting a college scholarship which would have been very welcome.

"I went to Valley City Teacher's College for one year to earn a teaching
certificate. It was a very enjoyable year rooming with Issy Johnson (Fike),
Gertrude Lockrem (Love), and Lionne Wright who all became good friends. I
started to teach when I was 18 when I was given a contract to teach the Sprout
School. Two schools in the district were combined so I had 28 pupils in all 8
grades."

"Walter and I started dating more seriously in 1932. I never cared much about
dancing, but Walter and I sure liked to roller skate. The next summer we helped
other Luther Leaguers varnish the pews for Our Savior's Lutheran Church in
Mercer. Walt was the Luther League President then, and I went with him visiting
members to ask their advice on choosing a piano for the church. On one date
Walter and I climbed up in the steeple and he carved our initials there.

"I always wanted a ruby ring, my birthstone, and I told Walter that. So in 1937
for my birthday he gave me a ring with a ruby in it. As he was always full of
stories, he said, "Yes, I gave Ruth a ruby ring and she said we were engaged",
so he said he was stuck and was obliged to marry me.

"My sister Martha and Reed Argent, and Walter and I, were married the same day,
a double wedding. Our dresses were identical, blue taffeta knee length. Walter
and my attendants were Leslie, my brother, Conrad Freeberg, Walter's best
friend, Shirley Christensen, Walter's sister, and Pearl Peterson, my best
friend. Our uncle, Rev. Ole Akre, was the minister. Walter and I honeymooned to
Minot for one night, then back to Mercer, and on to Jamestown, where Walter had
a job as an attendant at the State Hospital. As was the custom for the groom to
carry his new bride across the threshold, he did just that at our apartment.

"I suppose I could say God called me to be a Mother, and so, of course, a
Grandmother and Great Grandmother. I wanted to get married, so when I was 22,
after dating Walter for 6 years, we married. And I did want eight children,
though I only had seven. I was the baby of the Ovre family and not unhappy, but
somewhat lonely as a child." Ruth loved having people around her, and always
maintained that a positive attitude was so very important. When asked what
legacy she would like to leave for others, she wrote, "Read your Bible daily and
attend a Christian church regularly. It is important to me because I have found
it a real blessing, inspiration and guidance always!" In answer to the question,
"What word best describes your life?" Ruth replied, "Happiness."

(Most of this article is taken from memories Ruth wrote in 1997-1998, and a
biographical booklet I wrote of Mom's memories in 1985.)

The Wedding Chapel

        Photo: The Keller Homestead.

Between 1904-1924, the Keller family home was a "Wedding Chapel."

Pastor William L. Keller was a German Lutheran Missionary who pastored six
German Lutheran churches in the area. They were Zion Lutheran south of Mercer,
Emmanuel Lutheran (Schimke) northeast of Mercer, St. Paulus Lutheran (Braun) 4½
miles northwest of Mercer, Hope Lutheran in Mercer which replaced St. Paulus,
Peace (Friedens) Lutheran (Hofer directly east of the Keller homestead), and St.
John's Lutheran (Presser) northeast of Turtle Lake.

Because Pastor Keller was the only Lutheran Pastor who resided in the area, many
couples, German and non German, were married in his house during the first
twenty years of settlement. There are many stories about traveling to the Keller
farm in buggies and other methods of transportation in the family histories.

The Keller family came to the area in 1903 and in 1904. Pastor Keller filed
first papers for a homestead on 160 acres on Section 2 in Wise Township #147-
79. The barn in the picture was built first and the family lived in it until
the house was completed. The house has been remodeled but it is still in the
original location.

For more history about the Keller family, see pages 65-67.

Remembering a Prairie Blizzard By Emma Christensen Lien

February 21, 1922, had dawned with no apparent threat of the oncoming blizzard
that would blanket its white fury over the great Midwestern plains and continue
to rage on for three days. The blizzard deposited some six inches of snow from
the Rocky Mountains eastward through Michigan. Duluth received 30 inches of
snow with drifts up to 30 feet deep. During this storm Minot, ND registered a
temperature of -30. The storm claimed a number of victims. A 12-year-old boy,
Roy Holms at Dillworth, Minn. was frozen to death, and on February 23, five
trainmen were killed when the Winnipeg Flier and a railroad snowplow collided in
the storm.

It was on this morning that my father, Martin Christensen, decided to take a
trip to Mercer for supplies. Because Father, back in 1902 had taken homestead
rights to his farm seven miles north of Mercer, he knew well each hill, ravine
and landmark on the vast plains that stretched endlessly around him. He also
learned to have great respect for the severe snowstorms that could ravage the
barren plains in winter bringing with them severe hardships for the settlers and
their livestock. Many were the stories told of "The Terrible Blizzard of 1888"
just 35 years earlier, in which nearly forty persons had lost their lives.

        Photo: Martin Christensen

While Father was busy making preparations for the trip to Mercer, three of us
children, Alvin, 11 years, my sister Margaret 8 years and myself 10 years walked
to the one room country school house one mile north of our home. Meanwhile,
Father hitching up his horse, Sport, to an enclosed single cutter (a single
seated sled with cabin built over it to protect from weather) was soon on his
way, taking mother and the younger children with him as far as his brother's
place. They were going to celebrate a birthday while father was in town. His
brother. Uncle Fred, had a farm just 1½ miles Southeast of our place.

About noon the snow had begun to sift down, leisurely at first, but by
mid-afternoon it had become much heavier. An ever increasing wind had begun to
whip up the snow threateningly. Our teacher, anxiously taking note, decided to
dismiss school early and to send us all home before the storm should become too
severe.

Walking with us were Shirley and Walter Christensen, the two children of
Father's cousin, Jonas, who lived just across a small slough from our home.
(Walter is now a member of the North Dakota State legislature). As we neared
their home, Jonas, who had been watching for us, came out and tried to persuade
us to remain with them until we our parents return home. However, Alvin
informed him that we had orders to begin the evening chores when we got home
from school and so we hurried on home.

Arriving home we found the lignite banked fires of early morning nearly burned
out and the house quite chilly. Alvin set about to rekindle the fires as I
fixed a lunch and readied the milk pails and kerosene for the evening chores.
Lignite coal was then and still is in many homes, the only winter fuel used. It
produces excellent long lasting heat under the hands of an experienced user, but
to children prodding it, it refused to cooperate. It only smoldered away with
little heat.

In time we started out for the stable to begin the evening chores, unwisely
leaving behind our reluctant and scared sister, Margaret, whom we thought we
were protecting from the storm. We soon discovered that the storm had greatly
increased while we had been indoors. Now darkness was closing in. We could no
longer see the stable which was about 200 feet west of the house, yet it did not
occur to us to turn back. We continued on as the snow stung our faces. A little
to our left, midway to the stable, towered our tall steel windmill, which now
groaned and strained under the pressure of the strong wing. This helped to guide
us in the right direction, but when we reached the stable the entry was
completely blocked with a huge snow drift. Alvin was not to be outwitted as we
together scaled the drift unto the straw roof of the stable and then the lean-to
roof of the hay shed, letting ourselves down through the trap door in its roof
onto the hay, then into the stable. Relighting the lantern, which the wind had
blown out, we were soon very busy feeding and milking the cattle.

We had nearly finished chores when I was sure I heard Margaret crying and
calling to us above the noise of the howling storm and the feeding cattle. Alvin
heard nothing but consented to go out and look, for I insisted I had her call.
As he disappeared over the roof into the thick darkness, calling for Margaret as
he went, I held open the trap door and shielded the flickering lantern from the
wind while anxiously awaiting his return. In time he returned leading Margaret
who he said he had found stuck in a snow drift on the opposite side of the
stable. Her fears for our safety, when she thought it had taken us too long,
had brought her out to look for us, only to have her fears made more sure when
she found the door blocked with a snow drift. How she had reached the stable in
the deep darkness and storm after repeated falls in the deep snow, and that I
should hear her, can only be attributed to divine protection. She wept with pain
as we rubbed her blue, frost bitten fingers with snow to thaw them out slowly.
We shook the snow from her open coat and brought her into the warm stable. She
was soon none the worse for her experience. We finished the chores and all
returned to the house. We found that the fires had not improved any and the
house was colder.

As night wore on we became more and more anxious for our patent's safety. Early
in life Father and Mother had taught us to pray, so it was natural that we now
ask God to bring them home to us safely. We had lost all desire to eat supper
and we were cold. When repeated proddings of the fires brought no better
results we crawled into bed to try and keep warm. We took mother's sad-irons (an
iron used for smoothing and pressing clothes) which always stood ready for use
on the stove, with us to bed to warm our feet.

About this time it occurred to me to place the kerosene lamp directly in the
east window so that its rays would shine out toward the road. I thought it
might help them to find where the house was if they should be out in the storm.

Time seemed endless now as we waited, ever listening. But it was not until after
10:30 p.m. that we heard the first sounds of footsteps. Moments later Father
stumbled in through the door and sank into a near chair in an exhausted state.
Now our brave front gave way to our emotions as we gathered around Father. He
was covered with snow and frost and we busied ourselves brushing his off. But it
was not until much later that night, as we sat by a warm fire, and Father had
cared for Sport, that he related to us his struggle in the storm.

His trip back from Mercer had progressed well. It was about 4:40PM when he had
come with 1¼ miles of our home. Taking note of the weather, he had decided he
could still make it to go by Uncle Fred's place and bring mother home before
night set in. To save time he cut directly across the open field, making
straight for a fence that lay half way between his and Fred's buildings,
intending to follow this fence right up to the place. Progress became slower in
the deep snow he began to encounter, and shortly the rapidly increased wind
diminished his visability to near zero, causing him to miss the fence that he
had intended to follow. Pausing to rest Sport a while, and to take account of
his situation, he felt it would be unwise to go on any further in case he should
also miss Fred's place. Beyond his place lay endless hills with only scattered
dwelling which were miles apart. Instead he decided to try and return back to
the road and home, for we children would be alone.

He thought it best to return to the road by way of the "old river bottom", a
landmark (still so called by natives of that area) that lay just to his left,
and which at this point, ran east and west for a considerable distance. This he
felt would help to guide him back to the road for it could be recognized and
followed in the storm and oncoming night. The basin was level, being about ¼
mile across, flanked in by fairly steep banks on both sides. Turning north into
the shifting wind, he made slow progress in the deep snow. The cutter, often
sinking into the snow made Sport's load heavy to pull. Darkness of night had
begun to close in when he reached the river bottom with a winded horse.

Getting out of the cutter and checking on Sport, it was apparent to him that it
would not be good to expect Sport to pull his load much longer. Unhitching him
from the sled, he decided to leave the cutter there and walk, leading Sport.

The sting of the bitter wind as it lashed his face with snow gave him a strong
urge to crawl back into the cutter out of the wind, but he resisted the impulse,
realizing that the temptation to rest might induce sleep. Instead they began to
walk, hoping to maintain a westward course against a cold twisting gusty wind.

Father, through much practice on the prairie and because of the early farming
methods in North Dakota of walking behind the plow and other farm implements,
had developed an unusual endurance when it came to walking great distances. He
did not hurry but set up an even, slow, persistent pace. Progress became very
slow and laborious as they walked through the snow that continually gave way,
sending them to their knees. Sport seemed to sense the gravity of their
situation as he kept an even pace beside my Father, helping to shield him from
the biting cold wind. Time and again my Father was seized with an almost
overpowering desire to sit down in the snow to rest, but he knew this was
dangerous to yield to as it is the most enticing temptation that comes to those
struggling in a snow storm, for in resting sleep often overtakes them and death
claims its victim through freezing. This served to spur him on. He knew that his
course was not straight for he often came against the banks of the basin. He
found it impossible to keep a true sense of direction in the shifting gusts of
wind and he realized that he must have at times walked in circles, as often
happens to those lost in a blizzard. He prayed for strength to go on.

At long last his struggling efforts were rewarded by the sound of a humming
telephone line above the howl of the storm. We were fortunate to live very close
to the main road of that day, which ran north from Mercer, continuing on past
our school. Parallel to this road was a rural telephone line which the farmers,
who had a phone, in closer fellowship. Though the humming of the wires in the
storm made communications highly impossible but to a man lost in a blizzard
desperately struggling against the elements of nature on a rampage, it was a
God-send. This gave him fresh hope and renewed his strength.

Now that he was again back to the road, he left the river bottom. There was a
small fenced in cemetery on our farm, just ¼ mile south of our driveway. As he
left this fence he tried to judge the distance he should walk to arrive at our
driveway. But as he approached the area he could find no sign or path to follow
in the darkness and heavy snow covering it. Neither was Sport able to pick it
out as he gave him the lead, for his head by now was so incased with ice and
snow that he could not sense the nearness of home. Not daring to chance losing
contact with the road and telephone line and possibly missing the buildings, he
retraced their weary steps three times to the cemetery fence and back again
trying to make more sure just where he should turn off to reach our house. The
last time he decided to come farther north. Then suddenly through the night he
caught the faint glimmer of the light I had placed in the window.

The following morning arrived with little abatement of the storm, but about noon
visability improved a little and with it came Jonas to see how we children had
fared and to see if Father had made it home to us. Assured of our safety and
Father's return he again walked home, but it was not until the next afternoon
that Father was able to get over to Uncle Fred's and relieve mother of the awful
anxiety she had lived through as she waited and prayed for the safety of her
family through the blizzard.

Prophet Mountain Springtime By Florence Renfrow

  There they lay, against the skyline,
        lifting gently from the plain.
  Sunshine shifting in the shadows,
        showing through a misty rain.
  Blending with the clouds above them,
        reaching for the winds that blow,
  They are loveliest in the springtime
        when the draws are full of snow.

  Clothed in green and in their distances,
        they are just a range of hills,
  Etched against the far horizon
        where the summer shower spills.
  Rounded bosoms soft in contour,
        no edges do they show,
  Yet the depths are all accented
        when the draws are full of snow.

  Then the purple ridges muster
        in primeval grand design,
  Showing heights and depths in contrast
        to the valley's soft incline
  Then you know why Indian legend
        named them "mountains" long ago
  For they saw them in the springtime
        when the draws were full of snow.

Printed with permission from the Renfrow family.

        Photo: The original Robert Westerlind homestead shack. (Photo courtesy
        of Lloyd and John Westerlind).

Homestead House By Florence Renfrow

  The farms grew up around them,
        One by one, the barns were built,
  And the tool sheds and the granaries,
        Like some neatly patterned quilt.
  Soon cast their shadows o'er it,
        And the trees grew straight and tall,
  And, finally, the great farmhouse
        Stood watching over all.

  And the little homestead shanty,
        So essential in its time,
  Became a little satellite
        On which the bushes climb.
  They're slowly disappearing,
        Each year a few more fall,
  And this heritage of the pioneers
        Will soon be past recall.

  Chop down the weeds and mend the roof,
        Repair the broken door
  And make of it the pleasant place
        That it was once before.
  The years of struggle, they are gone,
        We would not bring them back
  But, we can hold the memories
        In a little homestead shack.

  Printed with permission from the Renfrow family.

The Depot - Our Home By Mrs. Julius (Olga) Sackman

Living in the depot was an experience of it own. Jobs were scarce. Julius was
down on the extra list on the railroad and they had to work their way up. To
hold a job any amount of time, you had to move. Many times it was after a short
time at one place and often our little girl and I had to stay behind until it
was worth moving.

We always had a lot of cleaning and it also depended on who moved out or if some
one lived in the depot. It had it's good points and bad ones, but after getting
settled in, we were happy again.

I also had a chance to work for the railroad as a caretaker. That meant meeting
the evening train because the agent was off after so many working hours. The
train could be late and it was up to me to meet the evening train.

        Photo: Olga Sackman at age 98.

Living in the depot also made it nice for the farmers because it made no
difference if they came during working hours. The agent was always happy to let
them have their freight if we were home. This changed in years when the young
guys would relieve the agent after it was after the working hours. You had to
come back the next day for your freight.

After all the moving in our time, our last job was 20 years in Mercer when we
moved upstairs in the depot for the first time. After a few years, we bought a
home in Mercer and lived there until 1968 when Julius retired. After that we
started to spend our winters in Arizona. We sold out in Mercer and Arizona
became our permanent home. We moved back to Hettinger, ND in 1889 to be near
our daughter. Julius' health had failed the last 5 years and he died in 1990.
I am still living in Hettinger.

        Photo: The Mercer Depot

Mercer's First Television Set by James Gessele

Conservative to the core, spare of words, and short in limb and stature, my
father, Ted, could be a trailblazer nevertheless. A feat that gained him
notoriety came in early 1952, when he became McLean County's first owner of a
new gadget called television. This was before television transmission was even
available in the state.

Already in 1951, the idea of "adding pictures to sound" fascinated residents of
the state, at a time when the Federal Communications Commission anticipated
granting hundreds of broadcasting licenses to qualified applicants. By then,
Twin Cities, Minnesota, broadcasters were well on their way with this innovative
means of communication. But North Dakota stations would have to wait their turn
well into 1952 before their applications would even be considered. Under such a
timetable, applicants realized that local television stations at best couldn't
become fully operational until 1953, and station owners (usually owners of radio
stations) set out to hype interest with air-time slogans. Who can forget radio
station KFYR in Bismarck with its on-the-hour buzz of "TV in '53?"

A few people were so caught up in the fever they couldn't wait. In late 1951,
some nut - I can't recall his name - in Bismarck's south-side warehouse district
had a complete set-up aimed at capturing elusive Twin Cities' signals: a
television receiver and an antenna that reached to the clouds, yet escaped
nearby Bismarck Airport FAA height regulations. My father made the mistake of
visiting this warehouse and immediately falling under the spell of the TV
zealot - never mind that picture reception was nil. Each subsequent business trip
to Bismarck was accompanied with a side visit to "The Nut." In the meantime, the
KFYR sloganeering had its intended effect, and in the winter of 1952 my father
could no longer hold out.

Through Schell's Hardware, he secretly ordered an Admiral console model
television with radio and phonograph - in limed oak cabinetry in keeping with my
mother's scheme of décor. Gleefully he anticipated delivery, until one morning
at the usual 9 a.m. men's coffee klatsch at Sam's Café, Julius Sackman, local
Northern Pacific rail agent, stormed in and with loud disdain bellowed that
"some damn fool has taken shipment of a TV, and a big one to boot." There was no
room to hide behind a coffee cup; Dad had been "outed!"

His exposure at Sam's Café that morning paled next to what he had to bear once
he began erecting a rooftop antenna. It began with an ordinary twenty-five-foot
mast that quickly expanded to fifty feet once it was determined there was no
hope for a signal with the puny version. With still no signal, the height was
extended to a full seventy-five feet with a rotor apparatus, and there it had to
stop - TV reception or not. The antenna was anchored to the Gessele residence
rooftop with guy wires, and the roof was groaning during spells of stiff prairie
winds.

The community looked on in amusement and amazement. Without even a hint of a
picture signal as a sign of success, surely they felt my father had turned the
corner as a rational being. But then they, too, got caught up in the magic, and
soon school classmates made pilgrimages to our living room to gawk at a snowy
screen just so they could attest they had seen Gessele's TV. "Fireside"
gatherings of this nature around the glowing, snowy, blank tube continued,
reaching a zenith when the Archie Kline family was invited in for
after-Sunday-service lunch the fall of 1952. The meal was winding down, and the
Kline's three-year-old Murray excused himself to "watch TV." Suddenly from the
living room we heard the set blare forth with audio of a male voice. A stampede
to the next room ensued, but all in vain. Somehow our set had captured a
five-second snippet of a Minneapolis transmission that had strayed over Mercer
