territory, and we had all missed it - except Murray. The poor little fellow was
hounded for an in-depth description of what he had witnessed. His truncated
account of "a man with a black tie" left a lot to be desired. Even so, the event
garnered a couple column-inches in the Bismarck Tribune.

Thanksgiving 1952, our family did get its first taste of television when we
packed up and headed for Uncle Art's home in Minneapolis for the holiday. It was
a novel time but such a huge let-down to return home, forced to wait almost
another whole year before we had our own broadcasts. When they did arrive, it
was a Minot station that beat KFYR to the punch. At first, low wattage
transmissions guaranteed extremely poor reception. But things improved over
time, although viewing fare was limited an awful lot to old westerns and to
kinescopes of east coast live productions that we viewed a week later. That
became old hat quickly, and soon KFYR was screaming another slogan: "Live in
'55."

The remaining course of early television broadcast is history, but my father was
propelled on one last fling. Not leaving well enough alone, he enrolled in a
mail correspondence television repair course. Once enrolled, he learned to his
consternation he needed knowledge of algebra, something his eighth grade
education had not provided. So he turned to Arlo Eckmann, a high school student
at the time, to tutor him over the rough parts. He passed the course, and the
countless hours he spent in repairing almost every set in the community are also
history.

Vandercook Memories

Among the early ranchers in Prophets Township were Ethan Allan Vandercook, and
his brother, Carl B. Vandercook. Not a lot of information is available about
them.

Carl Vandercook participated in the Mercer Literary and Debating Society in
1908. He also participated in the Mercer Dramatic Troupe's temperance play, "Out
in the Street" in March of 1908. The Mercer Telegram reported that after he
retired from theatrical life, he was again busy busting broncos at the Spring
Valley Ranch. It is reported that they had many horses.

The marriage of Carl Vandercook and Myrtal Perrigo was reported in the December
18, 1908, Mercer Telegram. Five years earlier, Myrtal Perrigo had filed on a
claim in 1903.

Ethan Allen Vandercook's wife finalized her claim by commutation on April 2,
1908, before Judge August E. Johnson in Washburn. In October 1909, E.A.
Vandercook and Ernest Watson held a joint auction at the Watson farm, one mile
north of Mercer and quit farming. Ethan then spent most of his time traveling as
a salesman.

Zora Vandercook owned land in Sections 19, 20, and 30 of Prophet's Township
according to the 1914 Sheridan County Atlas.

O.S. Hjelle remembered that the Vandercooks had friends file on land in the area
so situated that future homesteaders could not easily file on 160 acres close
together. The Vandercooks then had use of these isolated tracts of land for many
years. When they sold their land, O.S. Hjelle purchased it, along with their
grand piano.

Today, Pallmar Schmidt knows where Henry Vandercook's name is carved in a rock
in the Prophets. It reminds us of an earlier time when Vandercooks lived and
ranched in that area.

Joseph & Iva (Lambert) Mann
Early Brush Lake Residents

Reprinted and edited from the McLean County Heritage Book and Pioneer Women of
McLean County-1952.

Joseph Mann, a Virginian by birth, came from a family that lost its slaves and
property during the Civil War. The Mann family in Virginia was distantly
related to Captain Merriweather Lewis of the Lewis and Clark Expedition.

Joseph Jr. arrived in Dakota Territory in 1882 and set out, first, as a laborer
at Fort Stevenson, and then he worked on the Great Northern railroad line
running through Minot.

He then homesteaded on land near Brush Lake, two miles north of Mercer, where he
started cattle ranching and joined a small lake community that began to
establish itself at that time. It was here that Mann joined hundreds of Dakota
Territory ranchers who faced devastating ruin the winter of 1896. A blizzard
came up that struck the Dakota plains on November 5, 1886, and, unfortunately,
his herd of cattle sought shelter at the lake side. There the cattle became
mired in the mud. As the temperature dropped, the animals were virtually frozen
in their tracks, and snow swept about and over them. Joseph, never having
experienced a blizzard, discovered their plight too late and was able to rescue
just two of them. So when spring came, the small, huddled herd was still on its
feet as the melting snow uncovered their bodies. He began again and continued
ranching until 1895.

In 1893, Mann married Iva Lambert, of French-Canadian parentage and a young
school teacher in the Turtle Lake area. Ivy, as she was called, lived with her
parents on the east shore of Brush Lake in the northern part of McLean County in
the late 1870s. She told of a terrible prairie fire that swept over their lake
side cabin home while she was alone. She saved their cabin by running to the
spring house and getting buckets of water and throwing it up on the sides of the
cabin. The milk house that stood over the spring was burned to the ground, and
the five pound crock of butter, which she has recently churned, was quite a
loss.

Ivy told of the scares they had from Indians, begging and threatening; also how
terrified the whole white population was of them during the rampage of Sitting
Bull. She remembered that one night as they were gathered about the room, they
heard the thud of horses' hooves, a wild war whoop, and gun shots. It sounded to
them as though a horde of Indians had come to massacre them. Her stepfather blew
out the lamp, and they all scurried through a trap door to the little cellar
under the floor. As they huddled there, they expected the house to be burned
down over their heads, or that they would be found and killed in cold blood. In
his haste, her stepfather forgot his gun that hung over the doorway. After a few
minutes, and not daring to go up after the gun, he sent Ivy, a mere child then,
after it. She said this did not place her stepfather on a hero's pedestal, but
she came up from the cellar, and looking out the window, she saw a lone horseman
leaving the yard in a gallop. He proved to be a neighbor lad, who thought he
would have some fun at their expense.

Ivy keep house for her half-brothers, the Merrys, who were farming/ranching in
the Turtle Lake-Mercer area. One day she prepared a special treat for her
brothers, a squirrel pie, made with gophers.

In 1894 Joseph Mann was elected the first Treasurer of McLean County, and soon
thereafter they moved to Washburn.

The Little White School House By LaRose Ketterling

The "little white school house building" still has a prominent place on Main
Street. It originally was located on the center of block five in the original
town site. It was the site of learning for Mercer School children beginning in
September 1907 until December, 1916. The land was purchased from J.A. Regan on
November 22, 1912 as a tax sale.

The building was built in 1907 with one room. In 1911, a second room and entry
way were added. See pictures on page 86.

In addition to providing a classroom for the school children, it was the place
of gathering for a variety functions. It served as an auditorium for worship
services and funerals for the Scandinavian Lutherans, Methodist, Presbyterians
and other denominations served by supply pastors. It was also the place for
basket socials, box socials, dances, concerts, plays, debates and movies.

The brick school house was built in 1916 and the first classes convened there in
December, 1916. After that the function of the little white school house is
unknown until Christof Singer bought it in September, 1923. (information from
the County Recorder.) It is not known when the building was moved to its present
location on the east side of Main Street on lot fifteen, block six. In January,
1930 it was deeded to Christof and Christiana Singer and in May, 1937. to
Pauline Singer Weist. Christof had a cream station in a small building north of
the main building. This was purchased by grandson Ted Gessele. It was later
sold to Tom Beierle and is now owned by Gerald Schlafman.

One of the best remembered occupant of the building is Sam's Café which was
owned and operated by Sam and Doxie Norris. At various times it also had a pool
table and space for card players. After Sam died, Doxie married Merle Berge who
continued to run Sam's Café until November, 1957 when it was sold to Herbert and
Melvie Wanner.

The Wanners sold to Howard and Vivian Brewster who operated a café and bar until
it was sold to Arnold and Nanna Schlafman. The Schlafmans, who operated a bar
built the present addition.

In 1976 it was sold to Jack and Davela Jenson. After that various owners had a
bar and some had a convenience store after the grocery stores in Mercer closed.
Some of the names recalled were Harry Kline, Alvin Brackett, Otto Hulsebus, Dean
Diede, Gary and Betty Flemmer, Dusty and Esther Fandrich, Gordon Schell and the
John Wippert Corp. The present owners of the bar known as Chester's Tavern are
Al Toman and Les Petrryszyn.

At the present time, it is believed to be the only original non residential
building in Mercer.

Saturday Night by Charles Weisser

First published in Heritage Review, Vol. 23, No. 1 (March 1993), (Bismarck:
Germans from Russia Heritage Society, 1993), and reprinted here by permission
from the author. Charles Weisser grew up in Ashley, North Dakota, and now
resides in Wisconsin.

It's a beautiful, hot summer Saturday morning on the farms in the central part
of the Dakotas. There's great anticipation for the day ahead. You see, today is
the day when the entire family can go to town.

Dad will tell the family that they are going to gave to work a little faster and
harder today to get everything done a little earlier in preparation for going to
town. The whole family has been looking forward to this day since the beginning
of the week. This is the day they can again meet all their friends that they
haven't seen since either last Saturday night or Sunday.

Mother will bake bread and possibly make some Kuchen for the Sunday meals. She
and the girls will wash their hair and put it up in pin curls. It will have to
dry before Saturday evening when it is combed out to make it "curly." Some of
the ladies will leave their hair in pin curls and place a shawl around their
heads. After all, it is most important that you look your very best for church
on Sunday.

The chores of feeding the chickens, calves, and pigs, and the milking will take
place a little earlier than usual. A light evening meal will be eaten (the big
meal of the day is always eaten at noontime).

Hot water will be heated on the stove (range) for the Saturday night bath. A big
metal tub will be placed in the middle of the kitchen or some other room
depending on the time of the year and the arrangement of the houses. As the days
become colder, usually a room such as the kitchen is used because the range will
provide the warmth to make the bath most comfortable. Each member of the family
will take their turns taking a bath. If the water isn't too dirty, a little
extra will be added to the tub after each person gets done. There is no running
water in the homes, so all the water is brought in from the outside by carrying
it in with a pail. Many times, the well is almost a city block away from the
house. Needless to say, water is used conservatively. Since there isn't a drain
in the house, the water is carried outside and poured among the flowers or the
garden if it is near the house. It is too precious not to serve another purpose.

Meanwhile, the merchants in town are preparing for their busiest time of the
week. During the supper hour, the appearance of the downtown area is almost like
that of a deserted town. In a few hours, that will change. The merchants will
have all their employees on duty, and some extra people will be hired for those
few busy hours that will be upon them shortly.

The sun is almost ready to sink below the horizon as everyone piles into the
car. The trunk of the car is usually loaded with a cream can or two and possibly
a case of eggs. If there isn't enough room in the trunk, the eggs go into the
back seat. Everyone slides a little closer together, with some of the younger
children sitting on someone's lap.

The farmers are starting to complain about the new cars that are being marketed.
The cars are built much lower to the ground. The trucks are wider, but not as
high. Some are saying, "Who's gonna buy these new cars? Why, you can't even get
a ten-gallon can of cream into them. They are so low to the ground that you
can't drive them to the field to get the cows anymore!"

The egg cases are quite durable. Most of the earlier ones are made of wood with
a partition in the middle. These hold thirty dozen eggs. Some wooden cases are
only half that large and are much easier to handle. They can be placed in a
crowded car much more easily. Some newer egg cases are being made of cardboard
that are lighter, but not quite as durable.

It is nearly dark as the cars begin approaching town. The gravel roads leading
to town are becoming very dusty. The dusty air just seems to hang over the
highways unless there is a breeze to carry it away. It's too hot in the car to
drive with the windows completely closed, so you have to put up with the dusty
air. To make matters worse, an occasional chuck-hole or a washboard road causes
all the dirt in the car to rise throughout the car. There is an occasional cough
as someone's lungs are trying to get rid of the dust that has settled there.
But, this is just a momentary inconvenience that you put up with. You always
expect this. The dust is usually there unless it has just rained. In a few
minutes, you'll forget all about the discomfort of the trip, and you'll be in
town with your friends.

The first stop is the cream station or the creamery to drop off the cream and
the eggs. The grocery stores also buy eggs. These, in turn, are traded in for
groceries. All of the eggs are taken out of the cases, and when the wife pays
for the groceries, the amount of eggs sold to the store will be subtracted from
the price of the groceries. In some cases, the store will owe money to the
customer. Then the groceries purchased are placed in the egg cases and put back
into the farmer's car. Sometimes this car is parked two or three blocks from the
store, and the poor carry-out person has to follow the farmer's wife to the
location of the car.

The money from the eggs and cream provide for the weekly needs of the farm
family. In addition to the groceries, some clothes, repairs for farm machinery,
and spending money for candy, popcorn, ice cream, theatre tickets, etc., are
taken from the cream and egg check. Major purchases are made after the crops are
harvested and farmers have received money from the sale of their grain.

The ladies go the grocery and dry goods stores, while the men do their business
at the garages, hardware stores, or wherever else they have things they need to
purchase. Some of the men are wearing a white shirt (no tie), striped bib
overalls and a hat.

The town is alive. People are scurrying here and there. The activity reminds one
of an anthill. In those two to three hours, all the business for those farm
families has to be taken care of for the week. Only if it rains or there is a
serious breakdown in machinery will they stop working to come to town during any
other time of the week.

The sidewalks are crowded with people going in both directions. As one walks the
streets, one can hear both the German and English languages spoken. Many times
it will be a mixture of German and English words being said in the same
sentences. Everybody you know is in town. The population of the community
triples and quadruples for that short period of time.

Beginning in late April or early may, the popcorn man from neighboring town will
set up his stand on Saturday night, making everyone aware that summer is truly
here. The aroma of freshly popped popcorn permeates the air and people all over
Main Street are enticed to dig into their pockets to find a nickel so that they
can buy a bag of that wonderful "stuff." In later years, the price is raised to
a dime. The man will continue selling popcorn until about the last week in
September. If it is unusually warm, he might still be selling popcorn through
the second Saturday in October.

While the parents are busy with their shopping, the girls and boys will parade
up and down Main Street, visiting with their friends. Some of the older girls
will try to catch the attention of the boys who are cruising around town in
their cars. The cars will occasionally stop, and the boys will invite the girls
for a ride. Some of the girls will accept the invitations, while others keep
walking in disgust at the idea of being "picked up" in this way.

There is bumper-to-bumper traffic as the cars continue to parade up and down
Main Street. U-turns at the intersections are quite common, especially at either
end of the business section. People in town are starting to complain about this
practice. "Something has gotta be done about this. We're going to have some
serious accidents at those intersections." So signs are posted making U-turns
illegal. It takes several months before the law is strictly enforced and people
learn to fully comply.

Some have decided to go to the movies. There are two showings. The first showing
begins with only a sparse crowd. About halfway through the showing, however, the
theatre is filled to the point that people will have to sit near the front if
they want to see the film; or wait until the second showing begins.

The bowling alley is a popular place to go. The alleys, pool tables and the pin-
ball machine are seeing quite a bit of action. Even though bowling is considered
a winter sport, people will bowl because it is something to do with their
friends. This is a popular hangout for young people, especially for those who
aren't old enough to go into the bars.

Much socializing also is taking place with the older people. These people are
standing in the narrow aisles of the stores [and] visiting with other customers.
Sometimes it is hard for people interested in a certain product to find the item
because of the visiting people standing in the aisles.

Many people who have grown up on a farm and have moved to town recently still
come "uptown" to do some shopping and visit with friends and relatives who have
come to town. Some "town people" will park their car on Main Street and sit in
them just to be "people watchers."

At 11 p.m. the siren sounds, telling people that the stores are about to close.
The last minute items are dealt with and finally the merchants can prepare to
close their shops. Some sweeping compound is spread on the oiled wood floors
that helps gather up the dirt that has been placed there by the heavy stream of
traffic. This and the sunflower seed shells that have been left by the customers
are all swept up before the businessman will lock the doors for the night.

In the late forties, the merchants decide that they will close their stores at
10 o'clock. These changes do not affect the bars and cafés. Many of the farmers
are angry and tell the businessmen that they will do their business in another
community. Most of the other communities, however, are thinking about making the
same changes; and so the farmers grudgingly adjust to the change.

As people finish their business, they move to the cafés (hardly anyone refers to
a café as a restaurant during the forties) to buy lunch and visit there. Many of
the men will go to the pool halls and taverns. Generally, the older [women] will
not go there (unless it is to get their husbands) because this is just not a
respectable place for ladies to be seen. The younger [women] don't have that
same "mind-set" and so will be socializing there with their husbands and other
friends. Both the cafés and the taverns are quite packed at this time. Some
[women] will wait in the grocery or the dry goods stores for their husbands
until the stores close or until their husbands come to pick them up. Other wives
will wait in the car for their family. Still others (both husbands and wives)
will go to the homes of relatives or friends in the community to further
socialize and have "lunch."

As the colder months approach, the excitement of Saturday night seems to
disappear. The farmers now have more time to do their shopping during the
daytime hours. Saturdays will still be busy, but much of the activity will take
place earlier.

In the early fifties, the businessmen decide to close their businesses at 6
o'clock during the months of January and February since there really is not that
much business during the evening hours.

In the sixties, the businesses start closing their stores at 9 p.m. This is just
the beginning of the end of the Saturday Night Affair.

As the rural population keeps shrinking due to larger and more specialized
farming, the milking of cows and raising of chickens as part of the family
income disappear. This makes the small-town merchant change his way of doing
business. There is no longer a need for the Saturday Night "Rendezvous." The
social aspect of Saturday night in the community will be met through other
activities. Saturday Night will only be a memory for those who experienced it.

The History of Mercer By Anna Blasel Berge

[This account was written in 1935 at the request of Mr. Borlaug, publisher of
the Washburn Leader at the time, and was rewritten in 1947. Mrs. Berge was an
early news correspondent for the Washburn Leader. According to the letter
written by Mrs. Berge on July 10, 1947, she asked where it was to be published.
It is not known if it was ever printed. With some appropriate editorial changes,
it is published here as it was written by Anna in a blue composition book found
by the Washburn Leader staff in their offices in the fall of 2004. This lost
"gem," found at the last minute before the centennial book went to press, is a
wonderful legacy left by Mrs. Berge and an appropriate close to this book. - The
Mercer Centennial Book Committee.]

The town was platted in [1905]. The Northern Pacific Railroad from Denhoff,
through Mercer to Turtle Lake, was completed in December, 1905. There was a crew
of about one hundred men working on the track. They cooked and slept in tents.
The railroad had not been turned over to the railroad company at this time, but
contractors were running work trains, carrying freight and passengers coming and
going as the spirit moved.

The spring and summer of 1906 was a very interesting time. Nearly every other
belated train would bring an emigrant car or two. Many of the passengers were
young fellows, coming out to make a stake, file on land, prove up and move out
again. They did not make much of "a stake" but many proved up and many more
than had intended to, stayed and are still here.

A plot of grounds was presented to William Doering by the community. The
presentation was made because he was the first child born in Mercer.

        Photo: Mercer Main Street looking north. circa 1910.

Mr. A.B. Calheim was one of the young fellows to file on a claim. He came to
Mercer in 1902 and his views of the future were not very optimistic. When he
arrived, the largest prairie fire ever known here, had blackened the prairies
for many miles.

About this time, Mr. and Mrs. Charlie Wise were living near Brush Lake. They
were gardeners and now in the summertime Mercerites go out to pick the asparagus
that was planted forty-five years before.

The section house was built in 1906 and the railroad station was constructed the
following year. Charles Williams (brother-in-law of Mr. Ross Gardiner) was the
first agent.

For the first two years after the Northern Pacific railroad was built, Mercer's
mail was brought over the Soo Line to Underwood. From there it was transferred
to Turtle Lake by horses. Mr. Soren Nielsen then brought the mail to Mercer
with a team he rented from Mr. C.P. Christensen.

King's store, the first store in Mercer was really a board shanty. It was built
in what is now the road on Main Street between Chris Heim's garage and
Freeberg's store. The lot where Heim's garage now stands was formerly a "blind
pig".

Mr. Nels Olesen had a board and tarpaper shanty, on the lots where Alvin Just's
barber shop is now standing. This was Mercer's first Post Office. Mr. Olesen
then built a hotel into which the Post Office was installed. It was across the
street from the Sorensen Hotel. The first hotel was owned by Fred Sorenson. It
was built on the lots where Norris's have their restaurant. The hotel was burned
down in 1908.

The first and only drug store was owned by Charles Rust of Underwood. It was
built in 1906 and burned down in 1912. Mr. Bouchard was the pharmacist and Bruce
Wade was clerk. It was built on the lot where Gardiners store now stands.

Workmen were busy the summer of 1906 building George McFadden's store. When
completed there was a line of dry goods and groceries. The Post Office was also
transferred to this store. A few years later the store was sold to Mr. F.O.
Freeberg. It burned down in 1929. Mr. Freeberg had a brick store built in its
place.

Mr. "Bob" Lucas and his brother George came to Mercer in 1902. They participated
in the hardships of the early settler.

They built a shack in which they lived several years before the town was
started. One winter's day the Lucas brothers drove seven miles north to visit at
Major Howell's ranch reaching there about six o'clock in the evening. The
Howells were awaiting the return of the hired man with coal, so they could cook
supper. The hired man returned at 10:30, at 11:30 supper was ready. But it was
not to be served in a hurry much to the discomfort of the Lucas brothers who
were very hungry. Major Howell, who came from the south, was accustomed to
servants and doing things at ease. Each one was served individually. And the
Howell's were a large family.

By the time supper was over they were ready to retire. They were led into a
hovel where there was frost on all sides. They were forced to smoke to keep
warm.

The next morning they were anxious to start back to their own shack. But much to
their dismay, when the team started up the whipple tree broke. As the proper
tools were not available to make a hole to mend it, they used a rifle and a
shell to pierce the holes. On their way back they passed their neighbors house.
They noticed there was no smoke coming from the chimney.

As they entered the house the lady explained that her husband had been away
several days to get coal at the mine. The children had to stay in bed to keep
warm. Mr. Lucas went home and brought some coal for his neighbor. This he did
several times before the women's husband returned.

        Photo: Ford arrival for Hedahl's Garage, Mercer. The building at the
        right is the pool hall with a barber chair and cafe.

Finally one night there was a knock on Mr. Lucas door. The man had returned. He
said his load was stalled and his horses were worn out. He asked Mr. Lucas to
help him who went with him the next morning. When they had the sleigh shoveled
out there was only a few pounds of coal left.

About this time there was an epidemic of black diphtheria. Dr. Paulson the
nearest doctor lived at Turtle Lake, ten miles away. As there was no way of
communication except by mail twice a week, no telephones and no roads between
towns at that time for traveling, some of the children died. There was no
cemetery in the vicinity so they buried their dead on the prairie.

When the Regan and Lyness Elevator was built in 1906, Mr. Freeman was the
manager. The following year the Great Western Elevator was built. This elevator
was sold to I.L. Berge. All three elevators are now owned by the Peavey
Elevator Co.

Mr. and Mrs. Chris Sackman and five children migrated to Mercer from Eureka,
S.D., in Feb. 1906. They have the distinction of being the first family to
settle in Mercer. It took them nine days to reach here. It should have taken
only one and one half days, had the weather been favorable. Due to the severe
blizzard they obliged to stay six days at Denhoff.

The already crowded hotel could not accommodate them satisfactorily, so they
were huddled into the laundry room to sleep during their stay there. The
railroad Co. paid their expenses while at the hotel. They then started for
Mercer which was not a pleasant trip. Due to the jarring of the train, all but
one lamp was broken. This was a small kerosene lamp. They arrived in Mercer at
three o'clock A.M. There was no railroad station. High snow drifts were heaped
up on either side of the track. Mr. Degg (a brother-in-law of Mr. Sackman) met
them and took them to his home one and one half mile north west of town. The
Sackman residence was started immediately after their arrival. Hot dinners were
brought in daily for the workmen from the Degg farm.

Their house was completed in March into which the family moved. Mrs. Sackman
washed clothes and baked bread for the bachelors, as a means of livelihood. The
first livery stable owned by Degg and Sackman, was built after the family was
settled. Mr. Adolph Singer built his home (an unusual long building) across
from the livery barn. Mr. Singer became manager of the livery stable. He owned
the first car in Mercer. His son Alex was the first mail carrier for the
routes.

Mr. Theodore Knutson came to Mercer Jan 13, 1906. The Winner-Torgerson Lumber Co
office was partly furnished when he arrived as agent for the co. It was to this
building that he brought his pretty young bride to live in several months. In
the fall of the same year he built his house on his homestead, on the eastern
side of town. This house burned down in 1936. This house was the second house to
be built in Mercer. The lumber yard office was bought by Joe Dakovna. It was
remodeled for a dwelling where the Dakovna family lived several years. It is now
the home of L. Jorgenson family.

The Hedahl hardware store was built in 1906. It was owned by O.S. Hedahl of
Fessenden. Mr. Ed Hedahl and Mrs. Nels Hedahl were mangers. It burned down in
1927.

A man named Wagner built the first implement shop in 1907.

The first threshing machine that was unloaded from the train, was owned by Mr.
C.P. Christensen.

A one room schoolhouse was built in 1907. The children sat on chairs around a
long table. The first teacher was Miss Olga Natwick from Ada, Minn. The school
house was moved to Main St. and is now the restaurant owned by Mr. and Mrs. Sam
Norris.

It was in this school house that Rev. Keller conducted his services. He also
held services in the town hall that was built in 1912.

The four room consolidated school house was built in 1916. Mary Frances Davidson
and Evelyn Knutson were the first pupils to graduate from High School. They were
the only two pupils of the graduating class.

The German Lutheran church was built in 1916 with Rev. W.L. Keller as first
pastor.

Our Saviors Lutheran church was completed in 1931. The first pastor was Rev.
W.H. Sorenson.

The First State bank owned by Wm. and T. Lierbow of Turtle Lake was built in
1907. It burned down in 1912 but was rebuilt the same year.

The first printing office known as "The Mercer Telegram" was managed by Frantz
[Breitzmann]. He lived with his family on the farm now owned by Jake Laib. Mr.
[Breitzmann] disappeared very mysteriously. After his disappearance, Nels Olesen
took charge, then Wm. Wasson, advertising, proving up on claim notices kept the
Mercer Telegram going. Finally the last editor of the paper was E.N. Plowman
from Hannibal, Mo. There has been no paper here since Mr. Plowman sold that part
of the building for a dwelling house. The telephone exchange was built in 1908
and joined the Mercer Telegram building. Mr. H. Berge and Mr. Moskwald were the
first switchboard operators. Marie Shoemaker, now Mrs. Marion Chapman of Turtle
Lake was the first lady to tend the switchboard. Before the telephone exchange
was built several people including Mr. T. Knutson and Mr. Ed Hedahl strung wires
on fence posts from their offices to their homes so they could communicate by
telephone.

Mr. H.L. Harrum was the first barber in Mercer.

The hospital was built in 1914. Dr. Demming was the first Dr. in Mercer so had
charge of patients at the hospital. Mrs. Krogmoe was nurse. Major Howell was the
first patient at the hospital. Merle Berge was the first child born in the
hospital.

The "Booster Band" was organized in 1910. Herman Davenport was the leader.

In 1910 the town was out of salt. Trains were blocked for several weeks. But
luckily, Mr. J.R. Washburn who lived four miles S.E. of town had a surplus
amount on hand for his cattle. He willingly gave as much as was needed.

The first two winters of the early days were unusually severe. Food and fuel
shortage were threatened at time on account of trains being blocked.

These first years were rather primitive and very trying. But the country was
young and most of the people young and optimistic so thought no more of it.
After that the population increased rapidly. People came to make their homes and
business establishments. There have been many fires here the origin usually
unknown. One man confessed to the priest before his death, that he set fire to
the Sorensen hotel that burned to the ground. He asked the priest to write to
O.S. Hjelle his confession.

Mercer has grown into a thriving little town, slowly but steadily heading toward
prominence and distinction.

(signed) Mrs. [Halfdan] Berge
